## PREFACE

To THE READER.---What this book lacks is not a simple Preface but an apology, and a very brilliant and convincing one at that. Recognizing this fully, and feeling quite incompetent to write such a masterpiece, I have asked several literary friends to write one for me, but they have kindly but firmly declined. They stated that it is impossible to satisfactorily apologize for my liberties with Lindley Murray <term>Lindley Murray (1745–1826) was a famous grammarian whose textbooks were the standard for English grammar for decades.</term> and the Queen's English <term>A term referring to standard, "correct" British English.</term>. I am therefore left to make a feeble apology for this book myself. All I can personally say is that it would have been much worse than it is had it not been for Dr. Henry Guillemard <note>original: "Dr. Henry Guillemard"—likely Henry John Guillemard (1852–1933), a prominent English traveler, physician, and zoologist.</note>, who has not edited it—for if he had, the whole work would certainly be better—but who has most kindly gone through the proof sheets. He has lassoed prepositions which were straying outside their sentence stockade and taken my

<summary>The author opens the preface with a self-deprecating apology for the book's grammatical shortcomings, noting that his literary friends refused to help and that Dr. Henry Guillemard provided some assistance with the proofs.</summary>
<keywords>preface, Lindley Murray, grammar, Henry Guillemard, English language, writing style</keywords>

# PREFACE

<margin><unclear>Init</unclear></margin>...taking my eye off the water cask and fixing it on the scenery where I meant it to be, saying firmly in pencil on the margins, "No, you don't," when I was committing some more than usually heinous literary crime, and so on. In cases where his efforts in these matters may seem to the reader to have been lacking, I must state that they really were not. It is I who have refused to rise to a higher level of clarity and correct writing style than I am suited for. 

I cannot help but mention my gratitude to Mr. George Macmillan <note>George Macmillan (1855–1936) was a partner in the publishing firm Macmillan & Co. and a supporter of Kingsley’s work.</note> for his patience and kindness toward me—a mere jungle of information on West Africa. Whether you, my reader, will share my gratitude is, I fear, doubtful; for if it had not been for him, I would never have attempted to write a book at all. To justify his having persuaded me to try, I must state that I have written only about things I know from personal experience and very careful observation. 

I have never accepted an explanation of a local custom <note>original: "native custom"</note> from a single person, nor have I recorded things as being common customs after seeing only a single instance. I have endeavored to give you an honest account of the general condition and way of life in Lower Guinea <term>Lower Guinea: A historical geographical term for the West African coast stretching from the Bight of Benin southward to northern Angola.</term> and some description of the various types of landscapes there. In reading this section, you

# TRAVELS IN WEST AFRICA

## INTRODUCTION

->Describes the various causes that compelled the author to begin the voyage.<-

It was in 1893 that, for the first time in my life, I found myself with five or six months that were not already spoken for. Feeling like a boy with a brand-new coin, I "lay about in my mind"—as Mr. Bunyan <note>John Bunyan (1628–1688), author of *The Pilgrim's Progress*.</note> would say—considering what to do with them. "Go and learn about the tropics," said Science. I wondered where on earth I should go, for the tropics are the tropics wherever they are found; so I took down an atlas and saw that either South America or West Africa must be my destination, as the Malayan region was too far away and too expensive. Then I obtained Wallace’s *Geographical Distribution* <note>Alfred Russel Wallace's *The Geographical Distribution of Animals* (1876), a foundational work in biogeography.</note> and, after reading that master’s article on the Ethiopian region <note>A historical biogeographical term for the area of Africa south of the Sahara Desert.</note>, I steeled my resolve and settled on West Africa. 

I did this all the more readily because, while I knew nothing of the actual conditions there, I knew a great deal by both tradition and report about Southeast America. I remembered that <term>Yellow Jack</term> <note>A common historical nickname for yellow fever, referring to the yellow flag flown by quarantined ships.</note> was endemic there, and that a certain naturalist—my superior both physically and mentally—had come very close to starving to death in the depressing company of an expedition slowly perishing from want and various fevers up the Paraná River.

My ignorance regarding West Africa was soon corrected. And although the vast void in my mind that it occupied—

<summary>The author describes how, in 1893, she decided to spend six months of free time exploring West Africa, choosing it over other tropical regions based on scientific interest and the reported dangers of South America.</summary>
<keywords>Mary Kingsley, West Africa, Alfred Russel Wallace, tropics, exploration, yellow fever, Ethiopian region, Paraná River</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues the Introduction, where the author describes her initial research into West Africa and the warnings she received from friends and medical professionals before her journey.</meta>

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

is not even yet half-filled, a great deal of very curious information has taken its place. I use the word "curious" intentionally, because I think many people interpreted my request for practical tips and advice as an advertisement saying, "Trash may be dumped here." This information is still in a state of great confusion, despite my heroic efforts to organize it. I find, however, that almost all of it can be categorized under the following headings, specifically:

The dangers of West Africa.
The unpleasantries of West Africa.
The diseases of West Africa.
The things you must take to West Africa.
The things you find most useful in West Africa.
The worst possible things you can do in West Africa.

To begin, I asked all my friends what they knew about West Africa. The majority knew nothing. A certain percentage said, "Oh, you can't possibly go there; that's where Sierra Leone is—the white man's grave, you know." If I pressed them further, I occasionally found that they had relatives who had gone there after being "difficult cases" <note>Euphemism for people who were family embarrassments or failures.</note> in the family; however, since they had left not only West Africa but this world, they were now forgiven and forgotten. One lady, however, kindly remembered the case of a gentleman who had lived for a few years at Fernando Po <note>Now known as Bioko, an island in Equatorial Guinea.</note>. But when he returned as an elderly wreck at forty, he shook so violently with ague <term>ague</term> <note>A fever (often malaria) marked by regular fits of shivering and sweating.</note> that he dislodged a chandelier, thereby destroying a valuable tea service and flattening the silver teapot in the middle of it.

No, there was no doubt about it: the place was not healthy. And although I had not been a "difficult case," neither had the chandelier-shaking gentleman from Fernando Po. So, I next turned my attention to questioning the doctors. "The deadliest spot on earth," they said cheerfully, and showed me maps detailing the geographical distribution of diseases. Now, I am not saying that a country looks inviting when it is colored in Scheele's green <note>A vibrant but highly toxic arsenic-based pigment used in the 19th century.</note> or a bilious yellow, but

<header>MISSIONARIES AND TRADERS</header>
<sig>B 2</sig>

These colors may result from the cartographer's lack of artistic talent. However, there is no mistaking what he means by the color black; you will find that mapmakers color West Africa black from north of Sierra Leone to south of the Congo. "I wouldn't go there if I were you," my doctor friends said. "You will catch some disease. But if you must go, and if you are as stubborn as a mule, just bring me—" and then followed a long list of requests from here to New York, any one of which—but I only discovered the trouble they would cause later.

Everyone I spoke to pointed me toward the missionaries. "There are many of them down there," they said casually, "and they have been there for years." So, I turned to missionary literature with great enthusiasm, only to find that these well-meaning people did not write their reports to describe the country as it actually was. Instead, they wrote about how the country was progressing toward what they thought it should be, emphasizing the need for readers to donate more generously and not worry about getting an insufficient "return on their investment" in terms of saved souls. I also found terrifying confirmation of my medical friends' warnings about the region's unhealthiness, along with various details about the distribution of cotton shirts that I did not spend much time reading.

However, it was from the missionaries that I gained my first impression of the social conditions in West Africa. I gathered that the population consisted, first, of the native people—the "raw material," so to speak—and that they were influenced for good or evil by the missionaries and the traders, respectively. There were also government officials, whose primary job was to support and solidify the missionaries' work—a task they performed quite poorly. But as for those traders! Well, I immediately categorized them as one of the dangers of West Africa. Later, I encountered a classic coastal legend: when a trader from that region died and went—well, it is obvious where—the Devil <note>original: "Fallen Angel"</note> immediately stepped down from his hellish throne (referencing Milton <note>A reference to John Milton’s *Paradise Lost*, where the "Fallen Angel" refers to Lucifer/Satan.</note>) to let the trader take his place. I should note that this is the version of the story told by sailors. In the land-based version of the story, the trader is replaced by a first mate from Liverpool. Of course, one does not have to believe either version—it is certainly not a story told by missionaries.

<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

Naturally, while my intellect was occupied with considering these warnings, I became determined to go, and I felt I must. Fortunately, I could count among my acquaintances one individual who had lived on the West African Coast for seven years. It is true he had not lived in the specific part I was headed for. Still, his advice was especially worth considering because, despite his long residence in the most lethal spot of the region, he was still in reasonably good health. I told him I intended to go to West Africa, and he said, "Once you have made up your mind to go to West Africa, the very best thing you can do is change your mind and go to Scotland instead; but if you aren't sensible enough to do so, avoid exposing yourself to direct sunlight, take 4 grains of quinine <term>a medication used to prevent and treat malaria</term> every day for two weeks before you reach the Oil Rivers <note>A region in the Niger Delta, then a British protectorate</note>, and get some introductions to the Wesleyans <note>Members of the Methodist Church</note>; they are the only people on the Coast who have a hearse with feathers <note>A humorous, dark reference to the high mortality rate and the formal funeral equipment of the missionaries</note>."

My attention next turned to preparing the things I needed to take with me. Having invited a flood of advice, I quickly became overwhelmed. My friends and their friends alike seemed to suffer from the delusion that I intended to hire a whole steamship and was a person of wealth beyond the dreams of greed. The only thing to do in this situation was to listen gratefully and let things take their course. They showered me with various preparations of quinine and other so-called medical comforts, mustard plasters <term>a medicinal dressing of mustard seed paste applied to the skin</term>, a patented water filter, a hot-water bottle, and last but not least, a large square bottle supposedly containing malt and cod-liver oil. This last item, reacting poorly to the African heat, burst in a rage, spat out its cork, and proved itself to be an effective but very unpleasant-smelling glue.

It is not only the things you have to take, but the containers you have to take them in, that present a complex series of problems to the young traveler. A crowd of witnesses testified to the types of bags and trunks they had found essential, and these, it is unnecessary to say, were all different in shape and material.

With all this overwhelming variety of choices <note>original: "embarras de choix"</note>, I was too distracted to buy anything new in the way of luggage, except for a long waterproof sack neatly closed at the top with a metal bar and—

It was the beginning of August 1893 when I first left England for “the Coast” <note>A common term for the West African coastline</note>. Packages of quinine with some postage still due arrived up until the last moment. A friend hastily sent two newspaper clippings. One was titled “A Week in a Palm-oil Tub” <note>A slang term for the slow cargo steamers used by palm oil traders, which offered basic accommodations for passengers</note>, which was supposed to describe the type of accommodations, companions, and wildlife likely to be encountered on a steamer going to West Africa. I was destined to spend seven weeks on such a ship, compared to *The Graphic* <note>A British weekly illustrated newspaper (1869–1932)</note> contributor’s single week. 

The other clipping was from *The Daily Telegraph*, reviewing a French book of “Commonly used phrases” in Dahomey <note>A historical West African kingdom, now part of modern-day Benin</note>. The opening sentence in the latter was, “Help, I am drowning.” Then came the inquiry, “Is this man not a thief?” and then another cry, “The boat has capsized.” “Get up, you lazy rascals!” was the next exclamation, followed almost immediately by the question, “Why hasn’t this man been buried?” The cheerful answer provided was, “It is fetish <term>a term used by Europeans at the time to describe West African traditional religions, charms, or spiritual objects</term> that has killed him, and he must lie here exposed with nothing on him until only the bones remain.” 

This sounded discouraging to a person whose work would require traveling extensively in boats and whose fixed desire was to study fetish. So, with a feeling of looming dread, I left London for Liverpool. I was not made any more cheerful by the matter-of-fact way the steamship agents informed me that they did not issue return tickets for the West African lines <note>A grim reference to the high mortality rate for Europeans in the region; many were not expected to survive to make a return trip</note>.

I will not go into the details of that voyage here, much as I am prone to wandering off-topic. They are more amusing than educational, for on my first trip out, I did not know the Coast, and the Coast did not know me—we terrified each other. I fully expected to be killed by the local royalty and upper class; meanwhile, they thought I was associated with the World’s Women’s Temperance Association and was collecting scandalous details for future magic-lantern <term>an early type of image projector using transparent plates</term> lectures on the liquor trade. These fearful misunderstandings...

All I had to teach them was that I was merely a "beetle and fetish hunter" <term>a collector of insects and religious artifacts</term> and so forth, while they had to introduce me to a new world; I found it a very fascinating course of study. Whatever the people on the Coast might say against me—regarding my constant need for hair-pins and other pins, my annoying habit of wading into water, the ant-infested abominations I brought into their houses, or objects that suddenly emitted vivid and terrible stenches—they must admit that I was a diligent pupil. I sincerely tried to learn the lessons they so kindly taught me, even though some of those lessons were difficult for someone who had never previously been even in a "tame" part of the tropics, and whose life for many years had been entirely domestic in a university town.

One by one, I took my old ideas—drawn from books and based on imperfect knowledge—and compared them against the real life around me; I found them either worthless or inadequate. The most significant admission of error I had to make—which I did humbly before I had been on the Coast for three months in 1893—concerned my perception of the traders. They were very different from what I had expected to find. I can never speak highly enough of their kindness to me. On that voyage, I was completely out of touch with government circles and entirely dependent on the traders. The most useful lesson of all the lessons I learned on the West Coast in 1893 was that I could trust them. Had I not learned this so thoroughly, I could never have returned to carry out the journey I describe in this book.

Thanks to "the Agent," <term>the resident manager of a trading station</term> I have visited places I could never otherwise have seen. Because of the respect and affection the local people have for him, I was able to travel in safety. Whether I arrived at his factory <term>a merchant's trading post and warehouse</term> by steamer or canoe—unexpected and without introduction—or emerged unannounced from the wilderness in a bedraggled state, he always received me with a gracious hospitality. I owe my ability to have benefited from the kindness of these gentlemen on land to a man of the sea—Captain Murray. Therefore, he corrected those errors and replaced them with sound knowledge from his own experiences, collected during an acquaintance with the West Coast of over thirty years. The education he has given me has been of the greatest value to me, and I sincerely hope to make many more voyages under his command, for I well know he still has much to teach and I have much to learn.

When I was in the Canary Islands in 1892, I must regretfully admit that I used to smile at the conversation of a gentleman from the Gold Coast <note>modern-day Ghana</note> who was there recuperating after a severe fever. Many of my friends mentioned even in this very recent account of the Coast "are dead now." # CHAPTER I

## LIVERPOOL TO SIERRA LEONE

->Describing how the traveler departs from England in a sturdy ship and in good company, reaching the Island of Gran Canaria in due course, and then the Port of Sierra Leone: to which is added some account of this latter place and the beauty of its women.<-

The West Coast of Africa is like the Arctic regions in one particular way: once you have visited it, you want to go back there again. Now that I think of it, there is another way it is similar: the chances of you returning from it at all are small, for the Coast is a *Beautiful Lady without mercy* <note>original: "Belle Dame sans merci"; a reference to the 1819 poem by John Keats, personifying the Coast as a dangerous, irresistible woman who ensnares her lovers.</note>.

I know that many who are familiar with the Coast will loudly disagree with the first part of my sentence, though they will loudly agree with the second. But if you were to take many of the men who most forcefully claim they wish they were home in England—swearing to "see if they would ever come to that [so-and-so] place again" <note>Kingsley uses "etc., etc., place" as a polite substitute for the various expletives or derogatory terms used by sailors and traders to describe the hardships of the Coast.</note>—and actually brought them home and let them stay there a little while, I am quite certain of the result. In the absence of attractions other than simply being home in England—despite its "glorious joys" of buses, underground railways, and evening newspapers—these same men, though their reasons would vary, would eventually be found sneaking back to the Coast with an apologetic air.

I fell under the spell of the Coast as soon as I left Sierra Leone on my first voyage out. I saw more than enough during that trip to realize there was an immense amount of work for me worth doing down there. So, I warned the Coast I was coming back again, but the Coast did not believe me. Yet, upon my return a second time

# LIVERPOOL TO SIERRA LEONE: CHAPTER I (continued)

The public displayed genuine surprise and formed an even higher opinion of my foolishness than they had during our first acquaintance—which is saying quite a bit.

During my voyage in 1893, I visited Old Calabar <note>Old Calabar: A port city in modern-day southeastern Nigeria, which served as the headquarters for the British Niger Coast Protectorate.</note>. Its Governor, Sir Claude MacDonald, had heard me speaking at length about my absorbing interest in the Antarctic drift and the importance of collecting fresh-water fish, among other things. So, when Lady MacDonald heroically decided to go out to join him in Calabar, they very kindly asked if I would join her and coordinate my departure for my second journey with hers. 

I did this most willingly. However, I fear that very sweet and gracious lady felt a great deal of anxiety at the prospect of spending a month on a ship with a person so devoted to science that they would travel down the West Coast in pursuit of it. During the early days of our voyage, she would try to amuse me by pointing out all sorts of marine objects overboard. I used to look at them and think it would be the death of me if I had to work that hard. Meanwhile, I explained aloud that "they were very interesting, but Haeckel <note>Ernst Haeckel (1834–1919): A prominent German biologist and naturalist famous for his detailed illustrations of marine life.</note> had already studied them, and this time I was looking for fresh-water fish from a river north of the Congo." All the while, I feared she thought I was unenthusiastic because I didn't go flying into the ocean to secure the specimens.

However, my scientific qualities—whatever they may amount to—did not blind this lady for long to the fact that I was, after all, a very ordinary individual. She told me as much—not in those blunt words, of course, but nicely and kindly. In a burst of gratitude toward her for understanding me, I immediately appointed myself her honorary aide-de-camp <note>aide-de-camp: A personal assistant or secretary to a person of high rank.</note>. I shall remain her sincere admirer forever, fully recognizing that her courage in going to the Coast was far greater than my own. She had more to lose if the fever had claimed her, and in those days, she was by no means under the spell of Africa. But I am getting ahead of myself.

It was on December 23, 1894, that we left Liverpool on the *Batanga*, commanded by my old friend Captain Murray, under whose care I had made my first voyage. We were supposed to leave on the 22nd, but we could not do so because the wind began to blow a bit—quite a considerable bit, in fact.

# TENERIFFE AND GRAND CANARY
->I<-

...indeed, that even the mighty Cunard liner *Lucania* could not leave the Mersey. Furthermore, the *Batanga* could not have left even if she had wanted to, because the dock gates that held her in could not be opened, so fierce was the gale. So, as I have said, it was Sunday the 23rd when we finally got away, with no further mishaps except that, because of the weather, the *Batanga* could not take her gunpowder on board. This loss nearly broke the carpenter's heart, as it deprived him of the pleasure of making that terrific bang with which a West Coaster <note>A steamship traveling the West African trade routes.</note> salutes her ports of call.

On the 30th, we sighted the Peak of Tenerife early in the afternoon. It appeared, as usual, as an entirely celestial phenomenon. A great many people miss seeing it. Laboring under the delusion that *El Pico* <note>Spanish: "The Peak"</note> is a terrestrial affair, they look in vain somewhere at the level of their own eyes, striving to penetrate the dense masses of mist that usually shroud its slopes by day. Then a friend comes along and cheerfully points out the glittering white triangle to the newcomer, somewhere near the zenith. On some days, the Peak stands out clearly from the ocean to the summit, looking every inch (and more) of its 12,080 feet; and the Canary fishermen say this is a certain sign of rain, or fine weather, or a gale. But whenever and however it may be seen—soft and dreamlike in the sunshine, or dramatic and bizarre in the moonlight—it is one of the most beautiful things the human eye may see.

Soon after sighting Tenerife, Lanzarote appeared, and then Grand Canary. Tenerife is perhaps the most beautiful, but it is hard to judge between it and Grand Canary when seen from the sea. This afternoon, the superb cone stood out a deep purple against a serpent-green sky, separated from the brilliant blue ocean by a girdle of pink and gold cumulus clouds, while Grand Canary and Lanzarote looked as if they were formed from fantastically shaped sunset cloud-banks that had been solidified by some spell. The general color of the mountains of Grand Canary, which rise peak after peak until they culminate in the Pico de las Nieves <note>Spanish: "Peak of the Snows"</note>, some 6,000 feet high, is a yellowish-red. The air which lies among their rocky crevices and wraps around their softer sides is a lovely, lustrous...

blue. I used to imagine that if I could have only collected some of it in a bottle and taken it home to show my friends, it would have appeared as a beautiful blue-violet cloud in the gray air of Cambridge.

Just before the sudden darkness fell, and when the sun was dipping below the sea's horizon, all the clouds gathered around the three islands, leaving the sky a pure amethyst pink. As a "good-night" to them, the sun outlined the islands with edges of shining gold and made the snow-clad Peak of Tenerife blaze with star-white light. Within a few minutes, dusk arrived. As we neared Grand Canary, the red flash of the lighthouse on the Isleta gleamed out of its cloud bank; a few minutes later, along the sea level, the five miles of scattered lights from Puerto de la Luz and the city of Las Palmas began to sparkle.

I will not go into the subject of the Canary Islands here, because I foresee a tendency to become long-winded. I have visited them five times now—four times merely stopping there on my way to or from the West African Coast, but on another occasion spending many weeks there. If I once start on the subject of their beauty, their trade, and their industries, who knows how large this volume might grow?

We reached Sierra Leone at 9:00 a.m. on the 7th of January. Since the place is not as well-known to the general public as the Canaries are <gloss>1</gloss>, I may perhaps venture to go into more detail regarding it. The harbor is formed by the long, low strip of land to the north called the Bullom shore, and to the south by the peninsula ending at Cape Sierra Leone—a sandy promontory where a lighthouse with unreliable habits <note>The author implies the lighthouse light was frequently out or poorly maintained.</note> is situated. Low hills covered with tropical forest growth rise from the sandy shores of the Cape, and along its coast are three creeks or bays, showing deep inlets...

# I FREE TOWN

Through their narrow entrances, smooth beaches of yellow sand are visible, bordered inland by forests of cottonwoods and palms, with the occasional massive baobab tree <note>The baobab is known for its thick, "elephant-like" trunk.</note>.

The first of these bays is called Pirate Bay, the next is English Bay, and the third is Kru Bay. The wooded hills of the Cape rise after passing Kru Bay and become spurs of the mountain—2,500 feet in height—which is Sierra Leone itself. There are, however, several mountains here besides Sierra Leone, the most prominent of them being the peak known as Sugar Loaf. When seen from the sea, they are very lovely, for their forms are noble and they are covered in a wealth of tropical vegetation. This greenery, unbroken in its sprawl but endless in its variety, seems to sweep over their sides down to the shore like a sea, breaking here and there into a surf of flowers.

Indeed, it is the general opinion of those who should know that Sierra Leone looks its best when seen from the sea, particularly when you are leaving the harbor for home, and that its artistic, moral, and residential charms end there. However, based on my own experience, I do not hesitate to say that it is one of the best places for getting lunch that I have ever come across. Furthermore, it would be hard to find a more pleasant and varied way of spending an afternoon than walking through its capital, Free Town, with a certain Irish purser—who is as well-known as he is respected among the formidable <note>original: "leviathan"</note> elderly Black ladies. Still, it must be admitted that *it is rather hot*.

Free Town is situated on the northern base of the mountain and extends along the sea-front with very professional wharves, quays, and warehouses. Viewed from the harbor, "The Liverpool of West Africa,"<margin>Lagos also likes to claim this flattering title and nowadays has more right to it.</margin> as it is called, looks as if it were built of gray stone, which it is not. When you get ashore, you will find that most of the stores and houses—the majority of which, it should be noted, are in a state of extreme disrepair—are made of painted wood with corrugated iron roofs. Here and there, though, you will see a thatched house, its thatch...

covered with creeping plants, and inhabited by colonies of creeping insects.

Some of the stores and churches are, it is true, built of stone, but from a distance, they do not look like stone because they are red in color—made of unhewn blocks of the local red stone. In the crevices of these buildings, trailing plants covered with pretty mauve or yellow flowers take root; everywhere—along the tops of the walls and in the cracks of the houses—there are ferns and flowering plants. They must get a great deal of their nourishment from the rich, thick air, which seems to be composed of 85 percent warm water, with the remainder consisting of the scents of Frangipani, orange flowers, magnolias, oleanders, and roses, combined with other odors that prove the inhabitants do not regard sanitary matters with the slightest bit of interest.

There is one central street, and the others are neatly laid out at right angles to it. None of them are paved or graveled <term>metalled: resurfaced with crushed stone or gravel</term> in any way. Instead, they are covered in a much prettier fashion, and in a way more suitable for bare feet, by green Bahama grass—except for those streets that are so nearly vertical that the heavy rains of the wet season have washed away every bit of earth and grass down to the red bedrock.

The shops, which line these streets in an uneven row, are like rooms with one side removed, for shop windows <note>original: "shop-fronts"</note> are unknown here. Their floors are generally raised on a stone base a little above street level, but unless they have been newly laid, these stones do not show because the grass grows over them, turning them into green banks. Inside, the shops are lined with shelves holding bundles of brightly colored Manchester cottons and shawls, Swiss clocks, and simple but vividly colored china; or—making an impressive display <term>brave show: a fine or striking appearance</term>—brass, copper, and iron cooking pots. Here and there you come across a bakery with trays of tempting-smelling banana fritters, and there is no shortage of barbers and pharmacies <term>chemists: druggists or pharmacists</term>. Inside all the shops, one can usually see the owner and his family with a few friends, all extremely healthy-looking <note>original: "plump"</note> and happy, having a loud social gathering together—I cannot call it a mere chat.

# THE NATIVES

There is usually a counter across the middle, over which customers and casual callers alike love to lean. Some harsh <note>original: "brutal"</note> tradesmen, notably chemists—who presumably regard this as unprofessional—attach huge nails with the points facing outward to the fronts of their counter tops in order to keep their visitors at a respectful distance.

In every direction, the local inhabitants are walking at a brisk pace, their bare feet making no sound on the springy turf of the streets. They carry huge burdens on their heads, which are usually topped by the bearer’s hat—a large, limpet-shaped object made of palm leaves. While some carry these enormous bundles, others carry logs or planks of wood, blocks of building stone, vessels containing palm oil, baskets of vegetables, or tin tea trays on which shawls are folded. Since the great majority of the native inhabitants of Sierra Leone pay no attention whatsoever to where they are going—either in this world or the next—the confusion and noise are out of all proportion to the size of the town. When, as frequently happens, a group of people walking quickly with their burdens charges recklessly into a stationary group—who have set down their loads and squatted beside them right in the middle of the thoroughfare <term>fair way: a main path or passage</term> to have a friendly shout with some acquaintances—the noise becomes terrifying.

Among these crowds of country people walk stately Muslims <note>original: "Mohammedans"</note>—Mandingoes, Akers <note>likely the Aku people, descendants of liberated Yoruba</note>, and Fulahs of the Arabized tribes of the Western Sudan. These are lithe, well-built men who walk with a peculiarly fine, elastic posture. Their graceful clothing consists of a long, white, loose-sleeved shirt, over which they wear either a long black mohair or silk gown, or a deep, bright blue garment. This gown is not entirely unlike a university academic gown, only with more fabric and more folds. They are undoubtedly the gentlemen of the Sierra Leone native population, and they are becoming an increasingly influential group in the town, which is not at all to the liking of the Christians. For, although Bishop Ingram <note>John Walmsley, an Anglican Bishop of Sierra Leone</note> admits that they are always ready to side with the missionaries against the alcohol trade <note>original: "drink traffic"</note>, their cooperation ends there, and he complains that they exercise a great influence over the local...

Christian flock. He says:

> “We are inclined to believe that the words of their Quran <note>original: "Koran"</note> are only a fetish and a charm to the common members of their group, and that great superstition prevails among them and is spread by them,” ¹

But it is difficult to understand how the Bishop can see a difference in this matter between the use of the Quran and the Bible by the Black inhabitants of Sierra Leone. Judged by the standard of everyday conduct, the Muslim <note>original: "Mohammedan"</note> is, nine times out of ten, the best man in West Africa. However, I am sorry to say, he is not entirely orthodox. The Quran I have seen many of them using consists merely of extracts and prayers written in Maghribi <note>a North African style of Arabic script</note> characters; and I have grave doubts whether they could read this any better than I could without a dictionary. 

I have also frequently seen them playing *warry* <term>warry: also known as Oware, a strategy board game in the mancala family</term> and another game, the name of which I do not know. This other game is played with little wooden sticks stuck in the ground and “something on the line” <note>original: "on the rub"; referring to a wager or a winning stake</note>. They play although they must be aware that by indulging in the pleasures of gambling, they will undoubtedly incur the penalty of having donkeys graze upon their graves—and even upon the graves of their parents. They should think of this, because *warry*, when all is said and done, is a desperately dull game.

Furthermore, they are by no means strict abstainers from alcohol. Some individuals from Accra, whom I once met, shocked me deeply by saying Muslims were divided into two classes: Marabuts <note>Marabouts; traditionally holy men or scholars who abstain from alcohol</note> who do not drink, and Sonniki <note>traditionally a term for those who drink alcohol or maintain traditional beliefs</note> who do. I do not know where they could have picked up this idea, but I observed that my acquaintances were “hard-shelled” Sonniki. 

Additionally, the Sierra Leone and Lagos Muslims regard working in leather and iron as quite respectable occupations, which is not in accordance with the views held in high Islamic circles <note>referring to a social hierarchy in some parts of the Muslim world where manual trades were looked down upon</note>. They certainly produce very good leatherwork—bags, sheaths for daggers, and similar items—not to mention the strange hats made of the most brilliant yellow, blue, and red leather strips braided together. These are very heavy and very ugly, but useful. They are actually quite “sensible” hats, for their broad brims hang down and shade the neck; they also shelter the eyes to such an extent that—

<header># I TALISMANS</header>
<sig>C 2</sig>

The wearer cannot see without frequently bending up the front brim; however, I notice there is always something impractical about a "rational" article of clothing. But then, the bulbous, dome-shaped top protects the head from the sun, rain runs off the entire thing easily, and it does not get caught in the brush. If I had enough mental strength, I would wear one myself. Yet, even if I decorated it with cat-tails or antelope hair, as is usually done, I do not feel I could face Piccadilly <note>a major street in London, then the center of high fashion and social life</note> wearing one. Besides, you have no right to travel through Africa in clothes you would be ashamed to be seen in back home.

The leather-work that receives the harshest criticism from the Christian community is the talisman or *gri-gri* bags <term>gri-gri: an African amulet or charm used for protection or good luck</term>, and it must be admitted that a massive number of them are sold. I have, however, randomly opened about eighty-seven of these and always found something that can do no man harm—whether he is black, white, or yellow—to wear over his heart. Specifically, they contain the beautiful 113th Sura of the Quran <note>original: "Koran"</note>, the "Sura of the Daybreak," which says: "I seek refuge with the Lord of the Daybreak, that He may deliver me from the evil of the things He has created; from the evil of the night when it falls; from the evil of those who blow on knots <note>a reference to sorcerers or practitioners of black magic</note>; and from the evil of the envious when he envies." This is written on a piece of paper, rolled or folded up tightly, and enclosed in a leather case that is hung around the neck. 

However, the talismans made by Muslims <note>original: "Mohammedans"</note> do not account for even a tenth of those worn; the total number of amulets is enormous. I have never seen a West African man in traditional dress without some, both around his neck and around his leg, just below the knee. I suspect that if the subject were investigated and the clothes were removed from the more fully-clothed gentlemen, you would hardly find one without an amulet of some kind. The vast majority of these other charms are supplied by *juju* <term>juju: a spiritual belief system involving amulets and spells, common in West Africa</term> priests or some enterprising traditionalist who has a *Suhman* <term>Suhman: a minor deity or personal spirit in Akan religion</term>, or private devil of his own.

But to the casual visitor in Sierra Leone, the Muslim is just a passing curiosity. You neither feel a burning desire to laugh with or at him, as you do with the locals, nor do you want to punch his head and rip his coat—

—actions you long to take toward that "perfect flower" of Sierra Leone culture. This is the type of person who yells your name across the street at you without any title of respect, and condescendingly informs you that you can go and get letters that are waiting for you while he smokes his cigar and lounges in the shade. In some similar way, he displays his second-hand, rubbishy imitation of white culture—a culture far lower and less dignified than that of either the stately Mandingo or the bush chief. I do not think that the Sierra Leone dandy <note>a man devoted to style and neatness, often used here with a tone of mockery</note> really means to be half as insolent as he appears; but the truth is he feels too insecure in his own real position, despite all the arrogance he projects. Because of this, he does not dare to be courteous like the Mandingo or the bush Fan <term>Fan: the Fang people of West Central Africa, whom the author encountered in her travels</term>.

It is the clothing of the people in Freetown and its harbor that will first attract the attention of a newcomer, despite the fact that the noise, the smell, and the heat are all simultaneously making desperate bids for attention. The average man in the street wears anything he has been able to acquire, however he can, and he does not fasten it securely. I imagine it must be capillary attraction, or some other only partially understood force, that plays a part in the matter. It is certainly neither suspenders nor buttons. 

There are, of course, some articles which, by their very structure, are fairly secure—such as a shirt or even an umbrella with the stick and ribs removed. This last-mentioned treasure usually becomes the man's property because a female relative or admirer takes in the laundry of white men. It is always worn flowing free, and it has such a charm in itself that the happy owner cares little what he wears with it—trousers, a loincloth, a red flannel petticoat, or drawers made from a rice bag are, as he would put it, "all the same" to him.

I remember one day, while in the outskirts of the town, seeing some country people coming in to market. It was during the rainy season, and when they first came into view, they were, so to speak, "under bare poles," having nothing on worth mentioning. However, each person carried a bundle wrapped in waterproof fabric <term>American cloth: a heavy, waterproofed cotton fabric, often with a glazed or leather-like finish</term>, with a closed umbrella tucked into it. They stopped as soon as they thought it was dangerous to proceed any further for fear of meeting some of their town friends. There, they solemnly dressed themselves, holding umbrellas over each other all the while. Then, with dignity...

<header>->I THE LADIES<-</header>

...and decorated, and each sporting his gingham <note>a plain-woven cotton fabric, typically striped or checked</note>, they marched into the town. Here and there in the street, you come across a black man dressed in a tweed suit, or in a black coat and top hat; and here and there a soldier of the West India Regiment <note>a British Army infantry regiment composed of black soldiers from the Caribbean and West Africa</note>, looking sharp and tidy in his Zouave costume <note>a colorful uniform modeled after North African troops, characterized by short open jackets and baggy trousers</note>. These soldiers are said to be the reason for the many barbershops scattered throughout the town, as they are not allowed to own their own razors due to their tendency to use them too frequently during arguments.

The ladies are divided into three classes: the young girl you address as "tee-tee"; the young woman as "seester"; and the more mature woman as "mammy." However, I do not advise you to use these terms during your first visit, because you might be misunderstood. For you see, by addressing a "mammy" as "seester," she might think either that you were unaware of her status as a married lady—a matter she would soon correct you on—or that you were flirting, which of course was completely contrary to your intention and would make you uncomfortable. My advice is that you strictly stick to "missus" or "mammy." I have seen this done most successfully.

The ladies are almost as varied in their clothing as the gentlemen, but always neater and cleaner; they are very picturesque and occasionally very pretty. A market woman—with her cheerful brown face and laughing brown eyes, eyes made all the softer by a touch of antimony <term>antimony: a metallic element used as a cosmetic kohl to darken eyelids</term>; her full figure dressed in a bright print dress made with a yoke at the shoulders and a long, full flounce gathered under the arms that falls all the way to her feet; with her head wrapped in a yellow or red handkerchief and her snowy white teeth gleaming through her wide smiles—is a very pleasant thing to see and to talk to. But, heavens! The sheer size of them!

The stone-built, whitewashed market buildings of Freetown <note>the capital city of Sierra Leone</note> have a remarkably clean and tidy appearance, considering the climate and the quantity and variety of items displayed for sale—things that would require the skill of a Rabelais <note>François Rabelais, a 16th-century French author known for his exuberant and exhaustive lists</note> to catalog. Here are all kinds of fruits: some which are familiar to you in England, and others that you will soon become acquainted with...

in Africa. You take them for granted if you are headed away from home, but on your return trip (if you survive to make it), you will view them as a blessing and a wonder. Further down the coast, especially in “the Rivers” <note>The Oil Rivers, a region in the Niger Delta known for palm oil trade</note>, these things are rarely available and never as perfect as they are here. Seeing lettuces, yellow oranges, and tomatoes larger than marbles is a thrilling joy once again. There are also onions, and if you are wise, you will buy them when you are outward bound. If you are looking to make a profit on the deal, you should take as many as you can get; here you can buy them for four to five shillings a box, and you can sell them further down the coast for anywhere between twelve shillings and a sovereign <note>a gold coin worth one pound sterling</note>.

Here, too, are beads, though most are of dull colors and cheap quality. Beans, however, are more than well represented. There are "horse-eye" beans, used for playing *warry* <note>a traditional West African strategy board game similar to mancala</note>; vast, pantomime-sized beans which, when hollowed out and filled with a few lead shots, make a pleasant rattle to wear on the wrist; and the harmful Calabar beans <note>highly toxic seeds used locally as an ordeal poison to determine guilt</note>, which serve no good purpose at all here. It seems bold to sell them in the open market in a town where poisoning is said to be so common that its own Bishop declares, “Small social gatherings are almost unknown because of the fear of it.” ¹

The piles of capsicums and chilies, the little heaps of Reckitt’s Blue <note>a brand of laundry whitening agent</note>, vivid-colored Berlin wools <note>fine, dyed wool used for embroidery</note>, pumpkins, pineapples, and avocados give rich and brilliant touches of color. These relieve the more somber tones of kola nuts, old iron, antelope horns, monkey skins, porcupine quills, and snails. These snails are a prominent, though quiet, feature of the market. They are beaten up and used to help make the sauce for palm oil chop <note>a traditional West African stew made with palm oil, meat, and vegetables</note>. They are dumped alive on the floor in heaps and are quite active and nomadic; as a result, people who buy other things like vegetables, wool, or meat are likely to find one of these massive snails mixed up in their purchases. For a nervous person, stepping on one of them is as alarming as the disaster of stepping on one of the native black babies that crowd the market floor. There are fifty other indescribable things <note>original Latin: "indescribabilia"</note>, and over everything hangs the peculiar Sierra Leone smell and the peculiar Sierra Leone noise.

<header>JACK CROWS</header>
<sig>I</sig>

One of the main features of Freetown are the jack crows <note>These are likely Hooded Vultures (*Necrosyrtes monachus*), which are common scavengers in West African cities</note>. Some writers say they are unique to Sierra Leone, while others say they are not, but both agree on calling them *Picathartes gymnocephalus* <note>original: "*Picathartes gymnocephalus*"; actually the White-necked Rockfowl, though the author's description clearly refers to vultures</note>. To the white people who live in daily contact with them, they are turkey-buzzards; to the natives, they are Yubu. In any case, they are evil-looking birds and no ornament to the roof ridges they choose to sit on. The local Christians ought to put a row of spikes along the top of their cathedral to keep them off; the beauty of that building is not very great, and it cannot overcome the dismal effect produced by the row of these foul birds as they sit along its summit. They sit with their wings arranged at all sorts of strange angles in a "dilapidated" fashion. One bird might have one wing stretched straight out in front and the other casually placed at a right angle; another might have both straight out in front, and others again with both hanging hopelessly down, but none have them neatly and tidily folded up, as a decent bird's wings should be. They all give the impression of having been extremely drunk the previous evening and of having subsequently fallen into some sticky mess—preferably blood. However, because they are the scavengers of Freetown, they are respected and protected by the local authorities. The natives tell me you never see either a young one or a dead one. The latter is something you would not expect, for half of them look as if they could not survive the afternoon. They also told me that when you get close to them, they have a "strong, strong smell; they smell too much." I did not try to verify this, but I am quite willing to believe it.

The other animals most visible in the streets are, first and foremost, goats and sheep. I have to group them together because it is exceedingly difficult to tell one from the other. All along the coast, the rule of thumb is that sheep carry their tails down and goats carry their tails up. Fortunately, you do not need to worry much anyway, for they both "taste rather like the nothingness from which the world was made," as Frau Buchholtz <note>A character from a popular series of 19th-century German humorous novels by Julius Stinde</note> says; they also possess a fibrous texture and a certain sharp tang. Small, cinnamon-colored cattle can be obtained here, but there are practically no horses. Every now and again, someone who does not see why a horse should not live here as well as in Accra or Lagos imports one, but it always

Some say it is because the natives who earn their living as hammock-carriers poison them; others say the *tsetse fly* kills them off; and still others—and I believe these are right—say that <term>entozoa</term> <note>original: "entozoa"; internal parasites, such as worms</note> are the cause. Small, lean, scrawny yellow dogs with very upright ears lead a miserable existence. They are afflicted by many things, but most of all by the goats, who raise their families in the grassy streets and choose to believe the dogs intend to attack them. Last, but not least, there is the pig—a frequent source of work for the local lawyers.

The lawyer in Sierra Leone flourishes like a green bay tree. All the West Coast natives, once they are no longer afraid of the dangers of their own <term>country-fashion law</term> <note>Traditional or customary local law</note> and are under European institutions—I almost said "control," but that would have been going too far—become extremely litigious. They are naturally more litigious in Sierra Leone because there are more European institutions there, including trial by jury. Any legal case, whether he wins it or not, is a pleasure to the African, because it gives him an opportunity to show off his undeniable talent for public speaking and generally to put himself on display. But no legal case gives a Sierra Leonean as much joy as summoning a white man. This is because he can bring the white man before a jury of his fellow Sierra Leoneans—what they choose to call in that miserable place a "jury of his peers"—and then bully and insult him.

There is usually at least one summons waiting for a West Coast ship, and many a proud vessel has dropped anchor in Freetown harbor with one of her officers hiding in a ventilator and another in a coal bunker. On one ship where I was a passenger, the second officer was the one "wanted." Returning to the ship after some time on shore, we found the deck in an uproar. The center of the commotion was an enormous Black lady who bore a name famous in English literature. She was a laundress by profession and was demanding that the second mate be handed over—in any condition—to the hands of the law (represented by four Hausa policemen). She held a warrant against him for failing to pay his laundry bill the last time the steamer was in Sierra Leone. Now this worthy...

# I "MY BROTHER, SIR"

<meta>There is a small v-shaped mark in the right margin next to the first paragraph.</meta>

A man, exhausted by his morning labor of loading cargo in the sweltering heat and sustained by the virtue of an unblemished life there, had gone to sleep in his cabin. He was suddenly roused from it and confronted with his female accuser <term>accusatrix</term> <note>original: "accusatrix"; a female accuser</note> and the small, frightened man she had brought with her, whom she kept introducing as "my brother, sir." Unfortunately for the lady, this was not the same brave officer who held the post of second mate, but another. Our "injured innocent," joining in the chorus of voices, expressed his thanks for being disturbed in language of remarkable fluency. He is the only man I have ever met whose powers of expression matched his feelings; it is a merciful providence for him that this is so, for I think what that man feels would sometimes burst a rock.

The lady and her brother went ashore discouraged, but the policemen stayed on board until we departed, getting exceedingly drunk in the meantime. Looking over the side, I saw one of them slump over the gunwale <term>gunwale</term> <note>The upper edge of the side of a boat or ship</note> of the boat in which they were going ashore, with his head dangling close to the water. His companions paid no attention, so I insisted that my friend the quartermaster rescue the sufferer and arrange him in the bottom of the boat. Not only was he in danger of drowning, but he risked acting as a tempting live bait for the sharks that swarm in the harbor. The quartermaster evidently thought this was a foolish weakness on my part, for he argued that it "was only a policeman, and what are policemen but a sort of customs officer, and what are customs officers but the very devil?"

This, however, did not happen on the *Batanga*, but in the days before I was an honorary aide-de-camp <term>aide-de-camp</term> <note>A personal assistant or secretary to a person of high rank</note>, remember. During this voyage out on the *Batanga*, not even Sierra Leone could find any reason to summon us to court.

## CHAPTER II

### THE GOLD COAST

->In which a description of Cape Coast and Accra is given, along with<-
->various observations on the supplies that can be obtained there.<-

Cape Coast Castle and then Accra were the next places of general interest where we stopped. The former looks impressive from the anchorage <term>roadstead</term> <note>A sheltered area of water where ships may anchor near a shore.</note>, appearing as if it had been very recently whitewashed. It is surrounded by low, heavily forested hills that rise almost directly from the seashore, and the grand scale of its old castle does not reveal its decay from a distance. Furthermore, the three stone forts of Victoria, William, and Macarthy—situated on separate hills overlooking the town—add to the general impression of permanent stability, which is quite different from the usual dilapidated state of West Coast settlements. Even after you go ashore and have regained your senses (which are often rattled by the experience of landing through the surf), you find that this solidity is genuine. It is not a visual illusion created by painted wood, as the deceptive appearance of Sierra Leone turns out to be when you view it from close quarters. It takes some mental effort to grasp the fact that Cape Coast has been in European hands for centuries; however, it requires an almost unbelievable leap of faith to realize this of any other settlement along the entire western seaboard—at least until you have the pleasure of seeing the beautiful city of Sao Paulo de Loanda <note>Original: "San Paul de Loanda"; the capital of modern-day Angola.</note>, far to the south beyond the Congo River.

My experience of Cape Coast on this occasion was one of the hottest, yet most pleasant, I have ever had on the Gold Coast. The extreme heat was due...

# CH. II VIEW FROM FORT WILLIAM

...the extreme heat was due to the climate, while the pleasure was due to my kind friends, Mr. Batty and Mr. and Mrs. Dennis Kemp. I was taken to see the grand stone houses with their high stone-walled yards and gateways decorated with sculptures; these were built by the merchants of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. I also toured the sprawling stone castle, which has water tanks carved into the solid rock beneath it. It contains spacious quarters for enslaved people awaiting transport—a purpose now almost as outdated as the cannons the castle mounts—though not entirely so, as these cool and roomy chambers now serve as housing for the local police force and their large families.

After this, I was taken up a relentless hill, on whose summit stands Fort William, a structure shaped like a pepper shaker that is now used as a lighthouse. Since our travels <note>Original: "peregrinations"</note> had been conducted in extreme heat, I was inclined to admire the beauty of this building from its base. I was looking for a shady spot to sit down when my companions ruthlessly discouraged me; they would settle for nothing less than reaching the top, where I eventually found myself. The view was exceptionally lovely and vast. Below us, between our vantage point and the sea, the town lay baking in the blazing sun. Among the solid stone buildings, patches of local mud huts were huddled together, as if they had been shaken out of a sack into the town to serve as filler <term>dunnage</term> <note>In shipping, dunnage refers to loose material used to fill spaces and protect cargo in a ship's hold.</note>. Beyond them was the wall of snow-white surf, and across it the blue sea, where our steamer rolled back and forth on the long, steady waves. The ship waited impatiently for Sunday to end so she could begin unloading cargo. On all other sides, we were surrounded by wooded hills and valleys. In the distance to the west, I could see the white town and castle of Elmina and the nine-mile road leading there. The road skirts the surf-beaten shore and is only interrupted by the mouth of the Sweet River. Over everything hung the brooding silence of the midday heat, broken only by the muffled thunder of the surf.

It is a building in the dreadful "Africo-Gothic" style <note>A term coined by the author to describe the architectural fusion of Victorian Gothic Revival adapted for West African contexts.</note>, but it compares very favorably with the cathedral at Sierra Leone; internally, in fact, it far surpasses that building. 

Afterward, we returned to the Mission House and spent a very pleasant evening, except for the realization—which felt like genuine remorse—that if it hadn’t been for my own education <note>Original: "edification"</note>, none of my friends would have spent the day trudging through a town they already know all too well. Mr. Dennis Kemp was the chairman and superintendent of the Wesleyan Mission on the Gold Coast when I was last there, and he had held this important position for some time. This is the largest and most influential Protestant mission on the West Coast of Africa, and I am glad to say it is now adding a technical department to its educational and religious branches. 

The Basel Mission <note>A German Protestant missionary society active in West Africa, known for its emphasis on industrial and agricultural training.</note> has done a great deal of good work by providing technical training to the locals, and they essentially pioneered this vital branch of their education. There is still a nearly infinite amount of this work to be done, as the African people are strangely lacking in mechanical skills <term>mechanical culture</term>; they are more deficient in this area, in fact, than in any other. All the other Protestant missions are following the Basel Mission's lead. Recognizing that much of their past failure comes from a lack of practical instruction, they are now starting technical schools: the Church of England in Sierra Leone, the Wesleyans on the Gold Coast, and the Presbyterians in Calabar.

In some of these technical schools, the kind of instruction provided is, in my opinion, poorly chosen. They teach trades that are of no immediate or great use in the current state of West African development—such as printing, bookbinding, and tailoring. However, this is not the case with the Wesleyans, who also teach blacksmithing, carpentry, bricklaying, and wagon-building...

The Wesleyan Mission has only four white ministers here. There are seventeen native ministers, and the rest of the staff is entirely native, consisting of 70 catechists <term>Lay assistants who provide basic religious instruction</term>, 144 day-school teachers, 386 Sunday-school teachers, and 405 local preachers. The total number of fully accredited members of this sect in 1893 was stated in the *Gold Coast Annual* to be 7,066.

The total amount of money raised by this mission on the Gold Coast in 1893 was £5,338 14s. 9d. This is a very remarkable sum and is most creditable to the native members of the sect, for almost all the other native Christian bodies are content to exist in a state of impoverished dependency on British subscriptions. Until last year, the headquarters of the Wesleyan Mission were at Cape Coast, but they have now been moved to Aburi in the hills, about twenty-six miles behind Accra. Cape Coast is no longer the headquarters for any governmental or religious affairs. The Government moved from Cape Coast to Accra several years ago because of the extreme unhealthiness of the former place, hoping that Accra would prove less fatal. Unfortunately, this hope has not been realized; moreover, the landing at Accra is worse than at Cape Coast, and the supply of fresh water is very poor.

Accra is one of the five West Coast towns that look good from the sea. The others do not look good from anywhere. First in order of beauty comes Luanda <note>original: "San Paul de Loanda"</note>; then Cape Coast with its satellite town, Elmina; then Libreville <note>original: "Gaboon"</note>; then Accra with its satellite, Christiansborg; and lastly, Sierra Leone <note>Likely referring to the capital, Freetown</note>.

What beauty there is in Accra is Oriental in style. Seen from the sea, Fort St. James on the left and Christiansborg Castle on the right—both sitting almost at sea level—give the town a certain air of balance and strength, along with an outcrop of low, sandy cliffs. The rest of it is a mass of dilapidated mud and palm-leaf huts, along with corrugated iron dwellings for the Europeans.

I detest corrugated iron. I fully understand it has its advantages, and I am not attacking it from an aesthetic standpoint. It actually looks decent enough when it is painted white. Near Christiansborg Castle <note>A 17th-century Danish, later British, fort and government house in Accra</note>, there is a cluster of bungalows and offices for government officials and their wives that, from a distance in the harsh, bright sunshine, looks like an encampment of snow-white tents among the coconut palms, and it is quite pretty at the same time. I also recognize that a corrugated iron roof is an advantage because it allows you to collect and store rainwater, which is the safest water you can get on the Coast—provided you have not painted the aforementioned roof with red oxide an hour or two before collecting the water, as a friend of mine once did. However, the heat inside those iron houses is much greater than inside those with mud, brick, or wooden walls, and the temperature fluctuations are more sudden: in the mornings and evenings they are cold and clammy; they are always drafty, which gives you a chill that leads to fever—and fever in West Africa is a much more serious matter than it is in most other places.

Going ashore at Accra with Lady MacDonald gave me opportunities and advantages I would not have otherwise enjoyed, such as the hospitality of the Governor, luxurious transportation from the landing place to Christiansborg Castle, a thorough inspection of the cathedral currently under construction, and the strange and highly interesting experience of attending a tea party at a police station to meet a king—a real reigning king—who kindly attended with his entourage and displayed an intelligent interest in photographs. Tackie <note>King Tackie Tawiah I (reigned 1867–1902), a famous Ga ruler of Accra</note> is an elderly, thin man with a subdued manner. His sovereign rights are acknowledged by the Government only so far as to hold him more or less responsible for any crimes committed by his people; and since the Government does not allow him to execute or flog those people, earthly power is a rather hollow thing for Tackie.

Upon landing, I was taken in charge by an Assistant Inspector of Police. After a scramble for my chief’s baggage and my own, which reminded me of a landing long ago on the distant island of Guernsey, the inspector and—

## II. ACCRA

I got into a rickshaw, locally called a "go-cart." It was pulled in front by two government laborers <note>original: "negroes"</note> and pushed from behind by another pair, all neatly dressed in white jackets, knee breeches, and crimson sashes <term>cummerbunds</term> yards long, wrapped around their waists. Now, it is an ingrained characteristic of the uneducated local that he cannot keep on a neat and complete garment of any kind. It does not matter what that garment may be; as long as it is whole, off it comes. But as soon as that garment becomes a series of holes, held together by threads of rag, he keeps it on him in a manner that is marvelous, and you need have no further anxiety on its behalf. Therefore, it was only natural that the government-issued sashes, being new, should come off their wearers several times during our two-mile trip. As they unwound dangerously around the legs of the running wearers, we had to make halts while one end of the sash was tied to a tree trunk and the other end to the man, who rapidly wound himself up in it again with a skill that spoke of constant practice.

The road to Christiansborg from Accra, which runs parallel to the sea and is broad and well-kept, is in places pleasantly shaded with pepper trees, eucalyptus, and palms. The first part of it, which forms the main street of Accra, is remarkable. The untidy, poverty-stricken native houses or huts are no credit to their owners and a constant source of anxiety to a conscientious sanitary inspector. Almost every one of them is a shop, but this does not give rise to the animated commercial life one might imagine. This is, I presume, due to the fact that every native inhabitant of Accra who has any money to spend is able to recklessly spend it in his own store <term>emporium</term>. For these shops are general stores, each of its own kind, and they seem uniformly stocked with tin pans, loud-patterned basins, iron pots, a few rolls of cloth, and bottles of American rum. After passing these, there are the Hausa quarters <term>Haussa lines</term>, a few European houses, and the cathedral; and when nearly into Christiansborg, there is a cemetery on either side of the road. The one to the right is the old cemetery, now closed, and when I was there, it was in a disgracefully neglected state: a mere jungle of grass infested with snakes. Opposite to it is the

...the cemetery now in use. I remember well my first visit to it under the guidance of a gloomy government official. He said he walked there every afternoon "so as to get used to the place before staying permanently in it"—a complete waste of time and energy, by the way, as subsequent events proved, for he is now safely away from the Gold Coast for good.

He took me across the well-kept grass to two newly dug graves, each covered with wooden hoods in a very business-like way. Evidently, those hoods were standard parts of the cemetery's equipment. He said nothing but waved his hand in a "take-your-choice, they-are-both-quite-ready" style. 

"Why?" I asked briefly. 

"Oh, we always keep two graves ready-dug for Europeans. We have to bury people very quickly here, you know," he answered. 

I finally pushed back. I had already heard a heavy dose of these kinds of details that afternoon and was unwilling to believe another thing. So I said, "It is exceedingly wrong to do a thing like that; you only frighten people to death. You cannot possibly need new-dug graves every day. There are not enough white men in the whole place to maintain such a practice." 

"We do," he replied, "at least during this season. Why, the other day we had two white men to bury before twelve o'clock, and at four, another arrived dead on a steamer." <note>The phrase "dropped in on a steamer" implies a body was brought ashore for immediate burial.</note>

"At 4:30," said a companion, a very accurate member of the staff. "How you fellows do exaggerate!" 

My subsequent knowledge of the Gold Coast has fully convinced me that moving an extra funeral just half an hour earlier than it actually occurred is the usual level of exaggeration you will find in stories relating to the local death rate <term>mortality</term>. After I left Accra, and all along the Gold Coast, there was one of those dreadful epidemic outbreaks that swept away more than half the white population in a few weeks. It is customary for the government authorities to downplay <note>original: "pooh-pooh"</note> the death rate, or to claim that it is due to the bad habits of the white men. However, this latter statement is far more untrue than any fever story an "old coaster" <term>a veteran European resident of the West African coast</term> will tell you. The authorities at home, including both merchant firms and missionary societies, follow suit and make the same claims. The true statistics—

# CHRISTIANSBORG

...statistics are difficult to obtain in British colonies because government reports are, as a general rule, very poorly prepared. They avoid giving important details like these with an almost diabolical ingenuity. Additionally, they are published so long after the incidents they describe have taken place that they are only suitable for the historical archives of the British Museum.

But to return to our official journey along the Christiansborg road. We soon reached the castle, an exceptionally spacious and solid building constructed by the Danes. It is far better suited for the climate than our modern houses, despite our supposed progress in tropical hygiene. We entered through the main gate, which was guarded by a sentry, into the courtyard. On the right were the rest of the guards; most were asleep on their mats, but a few were busy saying their prayers <note>original: "Dhikr"; these are Islamic devotional acts involving the rhythmic repetition of prayers or the names of God.</note> toward Mecca, as the devout Muslim <term>Hausas</term> <note>The Hausas are an ethnic group from West Africa; many served in the British colonial police and military forces.</note> they are, while others were winding themselves into their <term>cummerbunds</term> <note>A long sash worn around the waist.</note>. On the left was Sir Brandford Griffith's <note>Sir William Brandford Griffith (1824–1897) was the Governor of the Gold Coast at the time.</note> hobby—a select little garden of lovely eucharis lilies, mostly in tubs, and rare, beautiful flowers he brought from his home in Barbados. Shading the garden and the courtyard was a fine example of that superb beauty—a flamboyant tree—glorious with its delicate green, acacia-like leaves and vermilion and yellow flowers, and striking for its enormous bean pods. A flight of stone stairs leads from the courtyard to the upper part of the castle where the living rooms are located. These sit above an extensive series of cool, tunnel-like slave <term>barracoons</term> <note>Enclosures or barracks once used to temporarily confine enslaved people before they were transported across the Atlantic.</note>, which are now used as storage chambers. The upper rooms are high and large, filled with a soft, pleasant light and the thunder of the eternal surf breaking on the rocky point on which the castle is built.

From the day the castle was built, more than a hundred years ago, the sea spray has been swept by the evening shore breeze into every crack and crevice of the entire building. Consequently, the place is mouldy—mouldy to a degree that I, despite all my experience in West Africa, that paradise of mould, have never seen elsewhere. The matting on the floors would take the impression of your foot just as a light snowfall would. One must never judge a fellow human being unkindly—especially on the Gold Coast.

Along the front of the sea-facing living rooms is a single, massive <term>verandah</term> <note>A roofed, open-air gallery or porch.</note>. This is the area for social gatherings; after dinner, the women sit in a stiff, unchanging row on chairs while the men stand around and talk. Conversation is difficult because of the constant roar of the crashing surf. In mid-January, I found that conversation with any newcomer consisted of: "You should have been here last week." "What?" When he rejoined us, we noticed beautiful, cool green leaves sticking out from under his hat in a wreath. The Governor had not done what many an "old hand" on the coast would have done—namely, saying, "There! That fellow will certainly drop dead wearing that foolish hat," and remaining masterfully inactive. No, he had gathered suitable herbs from his own garden with his own hands and filled the inadequate hat with them.

While we were waiting for the surf-boat, we had a practical lesson in the troubles caused by the surf. Several stalwart Black men strolled back and forth along the sand in front of us, poking iron bars into it every now and then. Every so often, they left these sticking in the sand and strolled off—not, as one might hastily think, because they had grown tired of the job, but to go and fetch a spade. They were sounding the sand for the iron rails which had been capsized while being brought ashore; these belonged to a tramway currently under construction for moving goods from the beach to the storage sheds. The sweet potato should be boiled, and then buttered and browned in an oven, or fried. When cooked in either way, I am very fond of them; but in the way I most frequently encounter them, I detest them, for they risk my life both in this world and the next. It happens like this: you are coming home from a long and dangerous beetle-hunt in the forest; you have battled with massive beetles the size of pie dishes—they have flown at your head, gotten into your hair, and then nipped you sharply. You have also been considerably stung and bitten by flies, ants, and other insects, and you are most likely soaking wet with rain or from wading through streams. You are tired and you drag your feet along the ground, and it is getting—or has already become—dark with that deceptive tropical speed. Then, as a punishment for your sins, you wander into a patch of ground which last year was a local farm; by placing one foot under the tough vine of a surviving sweet potato (hidden by thick weeds), you step with your other foot onto another part of the same vine. You then promptly land headfirst in some prickly ground crop or against a tree stump, and then, if you have any human feeling in you, you say damn!

Then there are also <term>alligator-pears</term> <note>alligator-pears: avocados</note>, limes, and oranges.
