<header>THE PAW-PAW</header>
<sig>11</sig>

There is something about those oranges I should like to have explained. They are usually green and somewhat sweet in taste, and they do not have much white pith. However, every now and then, you get a large, bright yellow one from the trees that have been imported. These are very pithy and possess the full, sour flavor of <term>verjuice</term> <note>Verjuice: the sharply acidic juice of unripened fruit, historically used in cooking and medicine.</note>.

They also have the paw-paw on the Coast, known to botanists as the *Carica papaya*. It is a bland, tasteless fruit. To a newcomer, it is a dreadful nuisance. No sooner does an <term>old coaster</term> <note>Old coaster: a term for a veteran European trader or resident who had lived on the West African coast for many years.</note> set eyes on it than he immediately says, "Paw-paws are excellent for the digestion! Even if you just hang a tough old chicken or a bit of goat meat in the tree among the leaves, it becomes tender in no time, because there is such a lot of <term>pepsin</term> in a paw-paw." In reality, there is no pepsin; <term>papain</term> is actually its active enzyme. After hearing this hymn of praise to the paw-paw some hundreds of times, it becomes tiresome. You usually reach this state of exhaustion with the subject by the time you reach the Gold Coast, as it is a very common topic. The same man will say the same thing about it a dozen times a day if he gets the chance.

I became thoroughly sick of it on my first voyage out. I rashly determined to stop the "old coaster" in this habit of his, as a first step toward stamping the practice out entirely. It was one of my many failures. I soon encountered an old coaster with a paw-paw fruit in sight. Before he had time to start his speech, I boldly cut him off by saying, "The paw-paw is excellent for the digestion." I hoped that this display of knowledge would impress him and exempt me from hearing the rest of his formula.

But it did not. "You are right," he said solemnly. "The paw-paw is a powerful thing. Why, just the other day we had a sad case around here. You know what a nuisance young assistants can be—complaining about their <term>chop</term> <note>Chop: West African English slang for food or a meal.</note>, or scorpions in their beds and boots, and every other little thing. And then, once you have pulled them through those troubles, they often die of fever or start acting recklessly in the local town. Did you know poor B—? Well, he is dead now. He caught a fever and died like a baby in eight hours, even though he had been out here for fourteen years working for A— and D—. They sent him a new bookkeeper—a sensitive young thing with a <term>dairymaid complexion</term> <note>Dairymaid complexion: a fresh, healthy, or pale skin tone common in people newly arrived from Europe.</note> and the notion that he suffered from indigestion. He was incredibly anxious about it. One—"

“One night there was a large papaya on the table for the evening <term>chop</term> <note>Chop: a common West African pidgin term for food or a meal.</note>, and so B—, who was a really decent fellow, told him about how good it was for the digestion. So he thought the bookkeeper must have gone for a walk, being, as it were, a bit too unwell to have gone <term>on the fly</term> <note>On the fly: likely meaning out on a drinking spree or a social excursion.</note> just yet. “Well! Fortunately, the steward boy put that papaya on the table again for the twelve o’clock meal. If it hadn’t been for that, not a living soul would have known what happened to the bookkeeper. For when B— cut it open, there, right inside it, were nine steel trouser buttons, a <term>Waterbury watch</term> <note>Waterbury watch: a popular, mass-produced American pocket watch of the late 19th century.</note>, and the poor young fellow’s keys. For you see, instead of him digesting his dinner with that papaya, the papaya took charge and digested him, dinner and all; and when B— interrupted it, it was just getting a grip on the steel items. There’s an awful lot of pepsin in a papaya, and if you hang meat in it, etc., etc.”

I collapsed, feebly murmuring that it was very interesting, but sad for the poor young fellow’s friends.

“Not necessarily,” said the old coaster. So he had the last word, and never again will I attempt to alter the ways of a genuine <term>old coaster</term> <note>Old coaster: a veteran European resident or trader on the West African coast.</note>. What you must do with such a man is be very thankful you have had the honor of knowing him.

Still, I think we do overestimate the value of the papaya, although I certainly did once hang the leg of a goat—which no mortal man could have gotten a tooth into—onto a papaya tree with a bit of string for the night. In the morning it was completely gone, string and all; but whether it was the pepsin, the <term>papain</term> <note>Papain: a protein-digesting enzyme present in papayas.</note>, or a <term>purloining</term> <note>Purloining: stealing.</note> local resident that was the cause of its disappearance, I cannot say.

## CHAPTER III

### FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS

->Providing an account of the white occupation of this island, along with the unique manners and customs of the Black inhabitants.<-

Our outward voyage really ended at Calabar. It concluded magnificently with fireworks and other festivities in honor of Lady MacDonald’s arrival. The entire settlement, both white and Black, turned out to honor her as best they could. Their ability to do so was far greater than I could have imagined possible, based on my previous knowledge of conditions along the coast.

Before Sir Claude MacDonald <note>Sir Claude Maxwell MacDonald (1852–1915) was a British soldier and diplomat, best known for his service in West Africa and China.</note> returned to his local work, he and Lady MacDonald crossed over to Fernando Po <note>Now known as Bioko, an island in Equatorial Guinea.</note> aboard the *Batanga*. I accompanied them, which gave me the chance to observe Spanish official circles. I have always been fascinated by this island because of its intense beauty and the significant <term>ethnological</term> <note>Ethnological: relating to the study of the characteristics of various peoples and the differences and relationships between them.</note> interest of its native inhabitants. During my previous voyage and while staying in Cameroon, I had exceptional opportunities to study both of these subjects. Therefore, I will sketch the results of my observations here. I do so quite readily, as this book makes no claim to being a perfectly connected work—a fact you have likely already noticed.

I had heard several grand legends about Fernando Po and had seen the coast and much of the island before. However, although I had heard a great deal about the Governor, I had never met him until I went to his residence with Lady MacDonald and the Consul-General. He was a delightful person,

# FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS: CHAPTER III

He still remained optimistic, but when he arrived on the island, he discovered that his predecessor had died of fever. The day after landing, the Governor himself succumbed to a severe attack and was put to bed—the very same bed, he was gloomily informed, in which the previous Governor had died. At that moment, he suddenly believed every terrifying story he had been told in one awful realization, adding to those horrors his own concepts of death and purgatory, along with the hallucinations of his delirium. Fortunately, both the dire predictions and his own fears proved wrong, and the Governor recovered from the jaws of death. Without a moment's delay, he left the Port of Clarence <note>Modern-day Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea</note> and moved up the mountain to Basile, which is near the highest native village. There he built a house for himself and established a small village for the most miserable group of human beings I have ever seen. They are the survivors of a group of Spanish colonists who had been stationed in Spanish Morocco. Finding that place unable to support life, they had petitioned the government to move them and let them try colonizing elsewhere.

The Spanish government happened to be experiencing one of its sporadic bursts of interest in Fernando Po <note>The island now known as Bioko</note>, and so they sent them here. The Governor—a very kind and generous man who would be an honor to any nation—settled them and their families around him at Basile to share the benefits of the higher altitude. He firmly believed in these benefits and always offered his home to any sick white man on the island, regardless of nationality or religion. Undoubtedly, the fever is not as severe at Basile as it is in the lowlands, but it has the usual disadvantages of West African highlands: namely, an excessive amount of rain and equally soaking mists, not to mention sudden and extreme temperature changes. Consequently, the colonists continue to die off, and their children die constantly from the various <term>entozoa</term> <note>Internal parasitic worms</note> that are common on the island.

When the Governor first settled on the mountain, he was very hard to reach for business purposes. Therefore, a telephone line was run up to him from Clarence through the forest,

# I TELEPHONE UNDER DIFFICULTIES 45

Spain as a whole felt proud of this bold venture into modern technology. Alas! The ancient forests of Fernando Po <note>The island now known as Bioko</note> were also fascinated by the new toy; their leaves and branches "talked" to each other on the line so much that a human being could not get a word in edgewise. Consequently, the Governor had to order the construction of a road along the path of the wire to keep the trees cleared away. Unfortunately, the telephone remains an unreliable means of communication because another problem still plagues its usefulness: the local inhabitants' habit of stealing pieces of the wire. They are fully convinced that their thefts will not be discovered as long as they are careful not to be caught in the act. The Governor is therefore liable to be cut off at any moment in the middle of a conversation with Clarence <note>Modern-day Malabo</note>. The amount of "Hellos," "Are you there?" and "Please speak louder" in Spanish <note>original: "¡Hola!," "¿Está allí?," "Hable más fuerte, por favor"</note> that must be shouted and wasted in the lonely forests at such times—before the break is noticed and a poor messenger is sent out—is terrible to imagine.

But nothing would persuade the Governor to travel even a mile down toward Clarence until the day he was scheduled to board the vessel that would take him home. I must admit his strategy seemed effective, for he was an exceptionally healthy and cheerful-looking man. Perhaps his avoidance of Fernando Po water—a dangerous beverage—and his adherence to a type of light sherry contributed to his immunity from fever. His neighbors—the colonists and priests stationed near him—are by no means good advertisements for Basile as a health resort.

Fernando Po is said to be a relatively young island that was connected to the mainland not so long ago; the strait between them is only nineteen miles wide and lacks deep waters.<sup>1</sup> I do not see the basis for these ideas; although Fernando Po's volcanoes are not yet extinct, but merely have their fires—

# FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS CHAPTER <note>The chapter number is not specified on this page</note>

...banked. Yet, on the other hand, the island has existed long enough to develop several unique species of animals and plants, a process that takes a significant amount of time. I personally do not believe that this island was ever connected to the continent; rather, it rose from the ocean as the result of a massive upheaval in the chain of volcanic activity that runs across the Atlantic from the Cameroon Mountains in a south-southwest direction to Annobón <note>Originally: Anno Bom</note> Island, and possibly even to the Tristan da Cunha group midway between the Cape of Good Hope and South America.

These volcanic islands are all exceptionally beautiful and fertile. They consist of Fernando Po <note>Modern-day Bioko</note> (10,190 ft.); Principe (3,000 ft.); São Tomé <note>Originally: San Thomé</note> (6,913 ft.); and Annobón (1,350 ft.). São Tomé and Principe are Portuguese possessions, while Fernando Po and Annobón are Spanish, and all of them are exceedingly unhealthy. São Tomé is still called "The Dutchman's Graveyard" on account of the devastation its climate inflicted upon the Dutch when they once occupied it. Indeed, the Dutch seem to have occupied all Portuguese possessions in this area at one time or another during the long war these two powers waged against each other for supremacy in the Bights <note>The Bight of Benin and the Bight of Biafra</note>—a supremacy that neither of them ever truly attained. Principe is said to be the most unhealthy of all. The reason for the difference in health in this particular area between Principe and Annobón is said to arise from the fact that the former sits on the Guinea Current—a hot current—while Annobón sits on the Equatorial Current, which averages ten degrees cooler than its neighbor.

The shores of São Tomé are washed by both currents, and the currents around Fernando Po are in a mixed and unpredictable state. Unless you have spent significant time in these seas, it is difficult to realize the interest we take in currents down there, particularly when you are navigating small sailing boats—an activity I am forced to engage in because of my fishing. Their effect on the climate is also very pronounced. If we could only arrange for some massive event to take place in the bed of the Atlantic that would send that notorious Guinea Current back to wherever it comes from, and bring the cool Equatorial Current alongside the mainland shore, West Africa would be a completely different place.

# FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS CHAP.

From the mainland, it looks like a massive, solitary mountain that has drifted out to sea. It is visible in clear weather from a hundred miles away at sea—and is especially sharp in the remarkable clarity that follows a storm. I cannot imagine anything more perfect than the sight of Fernando Po <note>Now known as the island of Bioko, Equatorial Guinea</note> when you glimpse it at sunset, perhaps from the distant Bonny Bar <note>A coastal region in the Niger Delta</note>, floating like a mythical island made of gold or amethyst. 

It is nearly as beautiful up close, specifically when viewed from the mainland at Victoria <note>Now Limbe, Cameroon</note>, nineteen miles away. Its expressions of beauty are endless; it is usually gentle and magnificent, but I have seen it silhouetted sharply against storm clouds and looking imposing and somber from the higher reaches of its "great brother," Mount Mungo <note>Mount Cameroon</note>. And as for Fernando Po in the full moonlight—well, you really should go and see it for yourself!

The entire island is—or perhaps I should say *was*—densely forested almost to its peak with a magnificent and diverse woods, rich in oil palms and tree ferns, with an undergrowth of countless varieties of ferns and mosses. Sugar cane also grows wild here, which is rare in West Africa. The last significant botanical collection from these forests was compiled by Herr Mann <note>Gustav Mann, a German botanist</note>; his research revealed that Abyssinian <note>Ethiopian</note> plant types predominated, alongside many species similar to those found in the mountains of Mauritius, the Isle de Bourbon <note>Now Réunion</note>, and Madagascar. 

The number of European plants (comprising forty-three genera and twenty-seven species) is surprisingly high, with most British types found mainly at the higher altitudes. More surprising still was the extreme rarity of South African plant life, and the fact that not one of the types characteristic of St. Helena was present. 

Cocoa, coffee, and cinchona <note>A tree whose bark is used to produce quinine for treating malaria</note> unfortunately thrive on Fernando Po. Because the coffee here is largely free from the disease that plagues it on the mainland at Victoria, it has led to the current massive destruction of the natural forests. A few years ago, the neighboring islands were surprised to find that São Tomé was accumulating great wealth through coffee farming; consequently, Fernando Po and Príncipe immediately set out to do the same. They are now working intensely with labor crews of various indigenous people brought in from all parts of the coast, except for the...

### III THE KRUBOY AND THE PORTUGUESE

To the Kruboy, "Panier"—as he calls a "Spaniard"—is a name of horror even worse than "Portuguese," although he maintains that "God made the white man and God made the black man, but the devil made the Portuguese." <note>original: "dem debil make Portuguee"</note> He also remembers an unfortunate incident that occurred some years ago in connection with coffee-growing.

A number of Krumen <note>An ethnic group from the Kru Coast of Liberia and Ivory Coast, known for their skill as sailors and laborers</note> signed up for a two-year labor contract on the island of São Tomé, and when they arrived, the Portuguese set them to work on coffee plantations. Now, agricultural work is "women's business," <note>original: "woman's palaver"</note> but the Krumen nevertheless managed to get through it. They likely vowed to themselves, as they hopefully notched the passing months <note>original: "moons"</note> onto their tally-sticks, that they would never let the girls back home know they had been using a hoe. 

However, when their months were complete, instead of being sent home with their pay to "our country," <note>original: "we country"</note> they were repeatedly delayed. Month after month passed, and they were still on São Tomé, still hoeing. At last, the homesick men, despairing of ever being freed, set off secretly in groups of one or two. They tried to reach "our country" by crossing hundreds of miles of the storm-prone Atlantic in small canoes with almost no provisions. 

The result was a tragedy, though it could have been worse; a few—a very few—were picked up alive by English vessels and taken back to their beloved "our country" to tell the story. But many a canoe was found with a dead Kruboy or two inside, and many others, floating upside down, vividly told the story of madness brought on by hunger, thirst, and despair, which had driven the occupants overboard to the sharks.

<margin>✓</margin> My Portuguese friends assure me that they never had any thought of permanently detaining the men, and that they were only keeping them until other laborers arrived to take their place on the plantations. I quite believe them, for I have seen too much of the Portuguese in Africa to believe they would be systematically cruel to the natives. But I am not in the least surprised that the poor Krumen mistook the Portuguese *soon* <note>original: "logo"</note> and *tomorrow* <note>original: "amanhã"</note> for eternity itself, for I have frequently done so myself.

The greatest length of the island lies Northeast and Southwest, and

# FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS CHAP.

The island’s length measures thirty-three miles, and its average breadth is seventeen miles. The port, Clarence Cove—now called Santa Isabel by the Spaniards, who have been giving Spanish names to all the English-named places without anyone paying much attention—is a very remarkable place. Except perhaps for the Gaboon, it is the finest harbor on the West Coast. The factor that makes the Gaboon anchorage comparable to Clarence Cove is its superior healthiness; for Clarence is a segment of a circle, and its shores are steep rocky cliffs from 100 to 200 feet high. The place, to put it very mildly, is exceedingly hot and stuffy. 

The cove is evidently a partially submerged crater. The submerged rim of the crater forms almost a perfect semi-circle toward the sea, having depths of 4, 5, 7, 8, and 10 fathoms <term>A unit of length equal to six feet, used to measure the depth of water</term> along it, except almost in the center of the arc where there is a passage with 12 to 14 fathoms. Inside the crater, the water is deeper, reaching 30 to 45 fathoms in some places; outside the submerged rim, the water is deep again, though rocky shoals are numerous. 

On top of the coastal cliffs stands the dilapidated little town of Clarence, situated on a plateau that slopes slightly toward the mountain for about a mile before the ground begins to rise into the slopes of the Cordillera <term>A system or group of parallel mountain ranges</term>. On the narrow beach, tucked close against the cliffs, are a few merchants' stores where goods are placed upon landing. There is a small pier as well, but because it is usually undergoing repairs to its pierhead, or else is closed by the authorities because they intend to do something to it eventually, the chances are it will not be available for use. 

Consequently, it usually happens that you have to land on the beach; once you have done this, you make your way up a very steep path cut into the cliffside to reach the town. When you arrive there, you find yourself in the most boring town I know on the Coast. I remember when I first landed in Clarence, I found its society abuzz with anticipation and alarm, tinged even with horror. Clarence—indeed, the whole of Fernando Po—was about to become so rowdy and immoral as to put Paris and Monte Carlo to shame. Clarence was going to have a café; and I hesitate to describe the sorts of things people feared would go on in that café. 

<margin>)</margin>

I have little hesitation now in saying this alarm was a false one. When I next arrived in Clarence, it was just as sound...

### III “GO AND SEE THE COALS”

The town is always asleep and its streets are as overgrown with weeds as ever, although the café was open. My impression is that the sleepiness of the place infected the café and drained it of all its energy. Then again, it may be that the inhabitants were too well-protected against any bad influences, for there are fifty-two white laymen on the island and fifty-four priests to look after them<note>I am told that the financial allowance given to these priests exceeds the revenue Spain earns from the island by several pounds. Only in Spanish territories is such a supporting allowance provided to missionaries, though they receive government grants in all other colonies.</note>—the extra two being, I assume, to watch over the Governor’s behavior. However, this honorable man protested quite vigorously against that suggestion when I mentioned it to him. In addition to the priests, there are several missionaries from the Methodist mission, as well as a white gentleman who has invented a new religion. In any case, the café just fizzles out like a damp firework.

When you spend the day on shore and have exhausted the charms of the town—a process that usually takes between ten and fifteen minutes—you might ask a resident for advice on how to spend the rest of your leave. They will invariably tell you to “go and see the coals.” You might reply that you didn't come to a tropical island just to look at a coal heap, and if you ask someone else for advice, you will likely get the same answer. So, because you were told to “go and see the coals” when you left your ship, you eventually do as you are told. 

These coals are the remains of the supply kept here for the English <term>men-of-war</term><gloss>Large warships armed with cannons</gloss>. They were left behind when the naval station was moved. At first, the Spaniards thought about using them and even built a tramway from Clarence to the coal pile. But by the time the tramway was finished, their motivation had evaporated as well, and the coals remain there to this day. Every now and then, someone gets the idea that the coal is still high quality and could be used for a steamer. Some people who have tried it say it works fine, while others say it is completely useless. The end result will likely be that, a few thousand years from now, there will be a serious argument among geologists about this strange deposit of coal on <note>Fernando Po is the former name of the island of Bioko.</note> Fernando Po. They will probably invent entire continents and raise or lower the levels of the oceans to explain how it got there, and they will undoubtedly get...

I mention this experience as a warning to others about the dangers of being restless; for although I did discover something far more impressive and thrilling high up among the beautiful, flowering shrubs that form a narrow border between the sea and the forest—namely, a large <term>man-of-war's pinnace</term><note>A light boat used by a warship for transporting people or goods.</note>—I could not figure out how it got there or why it remained. 

Emboldened by this discovery, I felt compelled to continue along the southern shore. Great, densely forested mountains rose on my left while the lovely Atlantic stretched out to my right. Occasionally, I climbed over rocks and then waded across the mouth of a tiny river, the Munguba, which crept out from among the trees. It smelled quite unpleasant, but it was beautiful to look at.

Then I came upon a farm where they were preparing cocoa, and the friendly locals spoke with me about the process for a short time.

Continuing further, I reached another farm and had more conversation, receiving a great deal of information about Liberia from a native of that country. I then crossed other small rivers—the Burapulopu and the Bulabopi—until I reached a swampy forest, at which point I finally turned back, quite satisfied with my afternoon. 

As I passed the first farm again, I realized that what I had thought was a strip of dry-land shrubs was nothing of the sort. The tide had come in and completely flooded it, reaching all the way to the edge of the forest. Because the forest was much too dense to walk through, I had no choice but to wade through the water, which reached up to my waist. I stepped into the water, remembering that I had been told about the dangerous crocodiles on the island. I knew I had to cross the mouth of the largest river—a place that looked exactly like where a crocodile would hide, if one were inclined to hunt them. However, I saw none, so I assume there are none there; it is the habit of these animals, when they are near the sea, to lounge down and meet the incoming tide. ### III ENGLISH OCCUPATION

...rocky cliff where the sea was breaking; not violently, or I would not be writing this now.

The history of the English occupation of Fernando Po <note>The island is now known as Bioko, part of Equatorial Guinea.</note> is often misunderstood, and occasionally one hears our government criticized for handing it over to the Spaniards. However, this was unavoidable, as we held it only as a loan from Spain beginning in 1827. It served as a naval station for our ships, which were at that time energetically working to suppress the slave trade in the Bights <term>Bights</term><note>Refers to the Bight of Benin and the Bight of Biafra, large bays along the West African coast notorious for the Atlantic slave trade.</note>. The intention was that this island would provide a healthier and more convenient location for a naval depot than any port on the mainland coast itself.

Fernando Po was certainly more convenient, but it was not healthier. Since 1827, it has developed a notorious reputation for being unhealthy. This reputation is only fading slightly at the moment because there is currently an interval between its epidemics. Fever in Fernando Po, even more so than on the mainland, has periodic outbreaks of a more serious nature than the typical intermittent and remittent fevers found along the Coast. Furthermore, Fernando Po shares with Senegal the questionable honor of having experienced regular yellow fever. In 1862 and 1866, this disease was imported by a ship that had arrived from Havana. Since then, it has not appeared in its distinct South American form and therefore does not seem to have gained the same foothold it has in Senegal. In Senegal a few years ago, all the money voted for the celebration of the *National Festival* <note>original: "Fête Nationale"</note> was, in one district, dedicated by public consent to the purchase of coffins required by an overwhelming outbreak of Yellow Jack <term>Yellow Jack</term><note>A historical colloquial term for yellow fever, named after the yellow quarantine flag flown by affected ships.</note>.

In 1858, the Spanish government—presumably thinking that the slave trade had been suppressed enough, or at least to a point that was sufficiently inconvenient for them—reclaimed Fernando Po. This was much to the horror of the Baptist missionaries who had settled in Clarence <note>Clarence City, later renamed Santa Isabel and now known as Malabo.</note>, apparently under the mistaken belief that the island had been permanently taken over by the English. This mission had received a large grant of land from the West African Company and had gathered a community of Sierra Leoneans and other African artisans and traders. These people were attracted to Clarence by the work provided by the naval station; along with the English traders who also settled...

For similar reasons, these people were the founders of Clarence Town <note>Now known as Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea.</note>. After the Spanish Government declared that only Roman Catholic missions would be supported, the Baptists abandoned their property and withdrew to the mainland at Ambas Bay, where they have remained ever since. Today, Protestantism is represented by a Methodist Mission, which has a sub-branch on the mainland at the Akwayafe River and another on the Qua Ibo.

When the Spaniards resumed possession of the island, they experienced a sudden burst of activity regarding its development. They sent Don Carlos Chacon to take command, accompanied by four Jesuit priests, a secretary, a supply officer, a customs clerk, and a transport ship, the *Santa Maria*, which carried several emigrant families. This attempt to colonize Fernando Po should have at least served the useful purpose of preventing such experiments from ever being tried again with women and children. No houses had been provided for these unfortunate people, despite it being the rainy season, and more than 20 percent of them died within five months. Mr. Hutchinson, who was the English Consul at the time, tells us that: "In a very short time, gaunt figures of men, women, and children could be seen crawling through the streets, with hardly any sign of life in their faces except for a look of sluggish indifference as to how soon it might be their turn to collapse and die. The *Portino*, a steamer, carried fifty of them back to Cadiz; when they embarked, they looked more like living skeletons of skin and bone than living human beings."^1 I quote this not to criticize the Spanish Government, but simply to state a fact: it is a clear example of the disastrous failure of attempts to colonize the West Coast <note>Referring to the West African coast.</note>. Such attempts are still occasionally made today, always with the same tragic results, though in most cases these efforts are now led by religious but misinformed people under Bishop Taylor’s mission <note>William Taylor (1821–1902) was an American Methodist missionary who led self-supporting missions to Africa.</note>.

The Spaniards did not limit their attention only to establishing ready-made colonies on the island. As soon as they had settled in and built their barracks—

I have seen similar rapid growth in Victoria <note>A coastal town in Cameroon, now known as Limbe.</note>, but I prefer to have a robust man and a Consul of Her Britannic Majesty testify to it for me.

<margin>Vertical pencil line marking the first few lines of this paragraph</margin>
Having discussed at length the various immigrants to Fernando Po, we can now turn to the indigenous people, the Bubis. These people are still little known, though they present several interesting problems for ethnologists due to their island isolation and their distinct differences from any mainland groups. This lack of knowledge is largely due to their isolationist nature and their complete lack of interest in commerce. This trait distinguishes them more than any other characteristic from the mainlanders, who—young and old, men and women—regard trade as the primary purpose of life. Mainland Africans take to trade as soon as they can walk and, according to their own accounts, do not even cease trading after death...

### III CLOTHES AND NO CLOTHES

...the way the spirits of distinguished traders still intervene and interfere in market matters. But it is different for the Bubi. A little rum, a few beads, and that is it—then he will turn the rest of his attention to catching porcupines, or the beautiful little gazelles, gray on the back and white underneath, which abound on the island. Any time he has left after this, he spends building houses and making hats for himself. It is only in his completely spare moments that he employs himself in making just enough palm oil from the rich supply of nuts at his disposal to obtain that rum and those beads of his.

He does not want cloth; he completely fails to see what good the material is, for he hates clothes. As a friend of mine observed: "Señora, you will see more bare skin on this island than in a regiment of grenadiers." <note>The speaker likely intended a pun on "bearskin" hats worn by grenadiers.</note> He said this in Spanish, and I had to look it up in a dictionary and then reflect on it afterward; the statement irritated me, for I felt that the man knew enough English to be aware that it would come across as a bad pun. 

Nevertheless, the truth was in it. When you go outside Clarence <note>Now Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea.</note>, you come across the Bubi 
<margin><note>Pencil stroke in margin</note></margin>
conspicuously unclothed—I say "conspicuously" for the benefit of ethnologists—and I have never seen this anywhere else in West Africa. The Spanish authorities insist that the natives who come into the town should wear something, so they 
<margin><note>Vertical pencil line in margin</note></margin>
dress themselves in a piece of cotton cloth. However, before they are even out of sight of the town on their way home, they strip it off and stuff it into their baskets. This shows, as do all other details, how resistant they are to the influence of white culture. 

The Spaniards, like the Portuguese, are very 
<margin><note>Vertical pencil line in margin</note></margin>
strict about clothes and insist on the natives wearing them—usually with all too much success. I shall never forget the yards and yards of cotton the ladies of Loanda <note>Luanda, the capital of Angola.</note> wore; not content with wrapping their bodies like cocoons, they wore about a dozen yards of black cloth over their heads as a *mantilla* <note>original: "mantilla" — a traditional Spanish lace or silk veil worn over the head and shoulders.</note> into the bargain. 

Moreover, this insistence on drapery for the figure is not just for towns. A German officer told me the other day that when his ship had called at Annobón <note>An island province of Equatorial Guinea.</note> a week or so before, they were simply besieged by people crying for "clothes, clothes, clothes." The Annobónese explained that they were all anxious to go across to Príncipe to find employment on the coffee plantations...

### FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS

...hiring conditions, but the Portuguese planters would not hire them while they were in an unclothed state.

<margin>The</margin>
You must not, however, imagine that the Bubi is neglectful of his personal appearance. In his own way, he is quite a dandy. But his idea of decoration tends toward a plaster of "tola" <term>tola: a scented pomade or ointment made from vegetable oil and wood powder</term> over his body, and, above all, a hat. This hat may be an antique European one or a handkerchief tied around the head, but it is more frequently a creation of native manufacture, and great taste and variety are displayed in its making.

They are made of plaited palm leaf—that is all you can safely generalize regarding them—for sometimes they have broad brims, sometimes narrow, and sometimes no brims at all. The same is true of the crown. Sometimes it is thick and domed, and sometimes it is non-existent, with the wearer’s hair aglow with red-tailed parrot feathers sticking up where the crown should be. As a general rule, these hats are heavily adorned with various bird plumes. One chief I knew had a hat resembling a "Dolly Varden" <note>Dolly Varden: a style of women's fashion featuring ornate hats with flowers and ribbons, popular in London's Regent Street in the 1870s</note> creation, which he used to fasten to his hair in a most intelligent way with bonnet-pins made of wood. 
<margin>|</margin>
These hats are also a peculiarity of the Bubi, for none of the mainlanders care at all for hats, except for "display" to wear occasionally. In contrast, the Bubi wears his perpetually, although he has by no means the same amount of sun to guard against, owing to the glorious forests of his island. I am told there is a sound practical reason for his devotion to his hat: it acts as a protection against a beautiful but poisonous green tree snake that abounds on Fernando Po, which has a habit of hanging upside down from the trees. If the snake strikes the hat instead of the head when the wearer is out hunting, it is much better for the wearer.

For earrings, the Bubi wears pieces of wood stuck through the lobe of the ear. Although this is not a decorative habit, it is still less unappealing than that of certain mainland friends of mine in this region, who wear large and necessarily dripping lumps of fat in their ears and in their hair. Around his neck, he hangs "jujus" <term>juju: a protective charm, amulet, or fetish</term> on strings—bits of python backbones, teeth, feathers, and antelope horns—and around his upper arms are bracelets, preferably made of ivory.

<header>III              ORNAMENTS AND COINAGE              59</header>

Often, these bracelets are also made of beads or a circlet of leaves; when on the warpath, the men always wear an armlet of twisted grass. Both men and women wear armlets. In the case of the women, these seem to be put on when they are young, as you can see the flesh bulging out from between them. They are not entirely for decoration, however, as they commonly serve as pockets; men stick a knife under them, while women carry a well-seasoned clay tobacco pipe. Leglets of similar construction are worn just under the knee on the right leg, while around the body you will see belts of *tshibbu*—small pieces cut from *Achatectonia* shells <term>Achatectonia: likely referring to Achatina, a genus of giant land snails</term>—which form the native currency of the island. These shells are also fashioned into veils worn by the women at their weddings.

This native currency is very interesting, for such things are exceedingly rare in West Africa. The only other instance I personally know of a tribe in this part of the world using a native-made coin is that of the Fang <note>original: "Fans"</note>, who use little bundles of imitation axe-heads. Dr. Oscar Baumann, who knows more than anyone else about these Bubis, believes, I think, that these pieces of *Achatectonia* shells may have been introduced in the past by runaway slaves from Angola. These slaves used to flee from their Portuguese owners on São Tomé <note>original: "San Thomé"</note> to the Spaniards on Fernando Po. The villages of the Bubis are located in the forest in the interior of the island, and they are spaced fairly far apart. They are not a coastal people, although each village has its own "beach." This simply refers to the place where the village brings its trade goods; these beaches are usually the dwelling places of the so-called "Portos,"¹ black men who act as middlemen between the Bubis and the white traders.

You will often be told that the Bubis are singularly poor house-builders—indeed, that they build no permanent houses at all—

The Bubi name for white men, *Mandara*, bears a resemblance to the Efik name for whites, *Makara* (that is <note>original: "i.e."</note>, the ruling one), but I do not know whether these two words have any connection.

# FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS — CHAPTER III

...all, but merely rough shelters made of branches. This, however, is a mistake. The shelters of this kind that you encounter are only crude huts built by hunters, not actual houses. The villages are usually quite well-constructed and surrounded by a living hedge of stakes. The houses within this perimeter are rectangular, with walls made of logs set upright. They are topped with thatched roofs built at an extremely steep angle, and the entire structure is typically surrounded by a dug-out trench to drain away surface water. As is common on the West Coast, these houses are divided into two categories: meeting houses and private residences. The meeting houses are much larger. The private houses are very low and sometimes absurdly small, but they are still proper houses—and certainly better than those dreadful Loango grass huts found in the Congo region.

Herr Baumann <note>Dr. Oscar Baumann (1864–1899), an Austrian explorer and ethnographer</note> notes that the houses high up on the mountain have double walls with a space between them. This arrangement likely helps to minimize the extreme drafts typical of an ordinary Bubi house—a very necessary feature in these relatively chilly high-altitude regions. I should note from my own experience that Bubi villages are rarely located directly on the path; like those found along the Calabar River, they are situated some distance away. This is undoubtedly intended to hide their location from strangers, and it works effectively. I have spent many "enjoyable" hours wandering back and forth along a path, trying to determine exactly where it was advisable to dive into the thick forest to reach a village. However, this develops one's powers of observation; after a short time doing this, you learn to recognize individual trees along miles of bush paths as easily as you would recognize shops on your own street at home.

The primary interest in a Bubi man's life is hunting, as he is more of a sportsman than most of the people on the mainland. He has no large game to hunt, with the exception of crocodiles and pythons—which grow to a great size on the island. Elephants, while common on the nearby mainland, are entirely absent from Fernando Po <note>modern Bioko</note>, as are hippopotamuses and the great apes. However, he has a large supply of small gazelles, monkeys, porcupines, and squirrels; and in the rivers, there is a very beautiful otter (*Lutra poensis*) with yellow...

### III TRAPS VERSUS GUNS 61

...brown fur, often quite golden underneath. It is a creature that I believe is identical to the Angola otter.

The Bubis use flintlock guns for hunting, but they primarily rely on traps, nets, and, I am told, slings. I expect the advantages of these latter methods are the same as on the mainland, where a distinguished sportsman once told me:

> “If you go shoot something with a gun, that is all well and good—but you are not certain to get it. No, sir. Those guns make a noise. Very well. Your friends hear that noise and come looking for it, and you have to share what you have killed. Or a bad man hears the noise, and he comes looking, and you won't get a share—you might get killed yourself. Tsk, tsk! <note>original: "Chii ! chii !"—an exclamation of disapproval or warning</note> Traps are best.”

I suggested that the traps might also be robbed. “No, sir,” he said, “the *bian* <gloss>(charm)</gloss> looks after those traps; it is able to make any man who tries to steal from them swell up and burst.”

The Bubis also fish, mostly using basket traps, but they are experts in neither fishing nor handling canoes. Their chief coastal activity is hunting for the eggs of the turtles that lay in the sand from August to October. These eggs—about 200 in each nest—are roughly the size of a billiard ball with a leathery shell. They are highly valued as food, as are the grubs of certain beetles found in the stems of palm trees and the honey from the wild bees that abound here.

Their domestic animals are the usual African varieties: cats, dogs, sheep, goats, and poultry. There are also pigs, which are quite tame in Clarence <note>Clarence City, now Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea</note> and wild in the forest. These pigs are the descendants of those imported by the Spaniards. Not long ago, they became such a terrible nuisance in Clarence that the government issued instructions that any pig without a ring in its nose—meaning those capable of rooting up back gardens—should be shot immediately if found wandering. This proclamation was announced by the government town crier as follows:

> “Listen! Listen! Listen! Listen! <note>original: "I say—I say—I say—I say."</note> If a pig is walking about and there is no iron in its nose, the gun will shoot and kill it immediately! Hear ye! Hear ye!”

However, many pigs with no iron in their noses wandered off and escaped into the interior. They have flourished exceedingly <note>original: "flourished like the green bay-tree," a biblical reference to rapid, lush growth</note>, destroying the Bubi plantations and eating their yams, while the Bubi, in retaliation...

## FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS CHAPTER III

It is a stalemate, for the Bubi enjoys the pig and the pig enjoys the yams, which are of exceptional quality on this island and famous throughout the Bight <note>The Bight of Biafra, now the Bight of Bonny</note>. Now, I am told, the government is strictly discouraging the export of these yams—which used to be a small but steady branch of the Fernando Po trade—in the hope that this will pressure the natives to turn their attention to working on the coffee and cocoa plantations. Hope springs eternal in the human breast, for the Bubi has consistently shown since the 16th century that he has no interest in these industries whatsoever. 

Every now and then, a man or woman will come forward voluntarily to take a job in Clarence <note>Clarence City, now Malabo</note>, agreeing to wear clothes and rapidly learning the routines of a household or a shop. Just when their employer thinks they have found a gem of an employee, and begins to boast that they have discovered an exception to all Bubi behavior—or perhaps that they know how to manage them better than other men—a gap in that man’s domestic arrangements suddenly appears. The Bubi has gone, without a moment's warning and without stealing any of the master's property; they have simply and silently vanished. If sought out, that "treasure" will be found in his or her own village—undressed, comfortable, completely indifferent, and unaware that he or she has lost anything by abandoning Clarence and civilization. It is this behavior that earns the Bubi the reputation of being a bigger fool than he actually is.

For West Africans, their agriculture is of a fairly high standard; the most noteworthy point about it, however, is the absence of cassava. Cassava is grown on Fernando Po, but only by the Portos <term>a term for the Sierra Leonean or West African Creole settlers</term>. The plants cultivated by the Bubis are yams (*Dioscorea alata* <note>original: "Dioscorea alata"—the water yam</note>), koko (*Colocasia esculenta* <note>original: "Colocasia esculenta"—the taro plant</note>)—the taro of the Pacific Islands—and plantains. Their farms are well-maintained, particularly those in the grassland districts near San Carlos Bay. The yams from the mountain districts have the best flavor, but those from the east coast are the largest. Palm oil is used for domestic purposes in the typical ways, and palm wine, both fresh and fermented, is the common native drink. Rum is highly valued, but it is generally used in moderation as a cordial or a special treat, for the Bubi is, like the rest of the West...

### III THE DRINK QUESTION

The African native is by no means a habitual drunkard. He dislikes gin.¹

And I may remark that you will find the same opinion regarding the Duala people on the Cameroon River—based on the undeniable authority of Dr. Buchner, and my own extensive experience on the West Coast confirms this.

Physically, the Bubis are a fairly well-proportioned race of medium height; they are certainly smaller in stature than the Benga or the Kru people, but quite comparable to the Efik people. Indeed, the women are very attractive: their complexion is bronze, and their skin is typical of the Bantu people. Beards are not uncommon among the men, and these, perhaps more than anything else, give their faces a different appearance from those of the Efiks or the Dualas. Indeed, the people who most physically resemble the Bubis whom I have...

---

¹ I am glad to find that my own observations on the drink question entirely agree with those of Dr. Oscar Baumann, because he is an unprejudiced scientific observer who had great experience in both the Congo and Cameroon regions before he came to Fernando Po. In support of my statement, I may quote his own words:
> "The Bubi people are actually very fond of drinking rum; they completely despise gin, but aside from tobacco and salt, rum is one of the most sought-after European items for them. As is well known, a fierce outcry has arisen in Europe against the 'poisoning' of the African by alcohol. While this outcry is almost entirely unjustified for most West African tribes and should be categorized as what is—to use a not very elegant but fitting expression—called 'humanitarian sentimentality,' it is more than pointless regarding the Bubi. It may indeed happen that a Bubi, after selling his palm oil, gets a little tipsy on rum once or twice a year. To speak of 'alcohol poisoning' because of this would be ridiculous, at the very least. I am convinced that many of those gentlemen who rail so loudly in speech and writing against the alcoholism of the natives consumed more spirits in their student years alone than ten Bubis do in their entire lives. The commercial rum—which, as I have often confirmed, is quite diluted but by no means tastes repulsive—is usually just a delicacy to the Bubi, to be enjoyed devoutly, sip by sip. If a worker in our country enjoys a swallow of brandy or a glass of beer to strengthen himself, everyone finds that perfectly normal; yet the Bubi, who must climb about stark naked for days in damp mountain forests, is expected to drink nothing but water!"

Dr. Baumann, the leading authority on the <term>Bubi</term> language, states that it belongs to the <term>Bantu</term> stock.¹ I personally know nothing about it except that it has a harsh sound. Their method of counting is usually based on fives, but they are remarkably poor at arithmetic. In this particular, they differ from the people on the mainland, and especially from their Negro neighbors, who are very good with numbers and surpass the <term>Bantu</term> in this, as they do in most branches of intellectual activity.

<margin>[</margin>However, the most remarkable example of inferiority displayed by the Bubis is their ignorance regarding methods of working iron. I do not know if iron is found in its natural state on Fernando Po, but they have had access to scrap iron for several hundred years. The mainlanders are all familiar with native methods of working iron, although many tribes now depend entirely on European trade for their supply of knives and tools. This difference between them and the Bubis would seem to indicate that the migration of the latter to the island must have occurred at a quite remote period—a time before the iron-working tribes moved down to the coast. It is true that up the Niger River and around Benin and Axim, one can find polished stone axe heads (<term>celts</term>), but these are regarded as strange objects—"thunderbolts"—and are considered suitable only for being ground up and made into medicine. There is no trace in their traditions, as far as I have been able to find, of any time when stone implements were in common use. Certainly, the <term>M’pongwe</term> <note>A Bantu ethnic group of Gabon</note> have not been on the coast for a very long time, as their arrival is still remembered in their oral traditions. 

I have seen the Bubi stone implements twice, but on neither occasion could I secure one. Although I have long been promised specimens from Fernando Po, I have not yet received them. They are difficult to obtain because none of the current towns are situated on truly ancient sites. The Bubi, like most <term>Bantus</term>, move quite frequently—either because the ground is bewitched (demonstrated by outbreaks of sickness) or because another village full of fellow humans, or a dreaded white man establishing a plantation, has come too close to them. 

A Roman Catholic priest in <term>Ka Congo</term> <note>The coastal region of the Congo/Cabinda</note> once told me a legend over which he laughed heartily. It concerned a fellow priest who had ambitiously settled himself one night in the middle of a Bubi village, intending to devote the remainder of his life to quietly but thoroughly converting the inhabitants. The next morning, when he rose, he found himself entirely alone. The people had taken all their portable possessions and vanished to build another village elsewhere. The worthy Father spent some time chasing his flock through the forest, but it was in vain. He returned home disgusted, concluding that the Creator, for some wise purpose, had dedicated the Bubis to the Devil.

The spears used by these interesting people are, even to this day, made entirely of wood. They have such a Polynesian appearance that I intend, at some point, to bring some home and experiment on that learned expert on Polynesian culture, Baron von Hügel, with them—intellectually, please understand, not physically.

Their basket-work is of a high quality. The baskets they make to hold semi-fluid palm oil are excellent and will hold water like a basin. However, I am unsure whether this craft is original or was imported by runaway Portuguese slaves, for they remind me very much of those made by my old friends the Cabindans <note>People from Cabinda, a coastal territory of the Congo</note>, from whom many of those slaves were recruited. I believe there is little doubt that several of their musical instruments share this origin, particularly their favorite one, the *elibo*. This can be described as a wooden bell with several (usually five) sticks inside acting as clappers. These are threaded on a piece of wood jammed into the dome of the bell; they strike the rim, and the sticks protrude just beyond it. These bells are very similar to those you encounter in Angola, but I have not seen the specific double bell of Angola—the *engongui*—on the island, nor does Dr. Baumann mention having seen it. 

The Bubi bell is made from a single piece of wood and is played with both hands. Dr. Baumann says it is customary on bright moonlight nights for two lines of men to sit facing each other and clap—one can hardly call it ringing—these bells vigorously and in rhythm. They accompany this performance with a monotonous song while the delighted women and children dance around them. The learned doctor clearly sees the charm of this practice, but notes that the words of the songs are not "profound" <note>original: "tiefsinnige"</note>, as he has heard men singing "The shark bites the Bubi's hand" for hours—only that over and over again and nothing more. 

This matches my own observations of all Bantu native songs. I have always found that the lyrics of these songs were either the repetition of a phrase like this, or a set of words referring to the recent adventures or experiences of the singer, or the specific quirks of the people present. These often include a very frequent chorus that is old and traditional. I shall never forget a white man coming alongside a ship on which I was once a passenger, quite unconscious that his...

### III MUSIC AND DANCING 67
<sig>F 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

The boatswain was singing a solo: “Here we bring this wretched creature; he’s a very bad man. He does not give us any food or any money; he goes and gets drunk and—” but I will refrain from repeating the rest of the insulting song. However, after each statement, the rest of the crew joined in a chorus that was the native equivalent of “and so say all of us.”

The native tunes used with these songs are far superior, and I expect many of them are very old. They are often full of variety and beauty, particularly those of the M’pongwe and Galwa peoples, whom I will discuss later.

I have no personal knowledge of the dances, but there is nothing in Baumann’s <note>Oscar Baumann (1864–1899), an Austrian explorer and ethnographer</note> description to suggest they are distinct from the mainland dances. I once saw a dance at Fernando Po, but that was among the *Portos* <note>People of Portuguese descent or those influenced by Portuguese culture</note>, and it was my old friend the *Batuco* <note>Batuque, a music and dance genre characterized by rhythmic percussion</note> in all its beauty. However, there is a distinct peculiarity about the locations where the dances are held. Every village has a maintained piece of ground outside it that serves as the dancing place for the village—the ballroom, as it were. These dances must be exceedingly picturesque, as they are mostly held during the nights of the full moon. These maintained grounds strongly remind me of the similar-looking patches of kept grass seen in villages in Ka Congo <note>A historical kingdom in the coastal region of the modern-day Republic of the Congo and Angola</note>. Yet, there is no similarity in their use; the Ka Congo lawns serve a <term>fetish</term> <gloss>spiritual or ritualistic</gloss> purpose, rather than a frivolous one.

The Bubis have an instrument that I have never seen in an identical form on the mainland. It is shaped like a bow with a tight string made of fiber. One end of the bow is placed against the mouth; the player then strikes the string with the right hand using a small round stick, while the left hand scrapes it with a piece of shell or a knife blade. I warn anyone who may think of living among the Bubis that this excruciating instrument is very popular.

The drums used include both the Dualla form—made entirely of wood—and the ordinary skin-covered drum. I think if I list the wooden flutes, I shall have nearly finished describing the Bubi orchestra. I have some doubts on this point because I question whether I may be allowed to refer to a very old, unmounted bullock hide as a musical instrument without bringing down the wrath of musicians upon my head. These stiff, dry hides are highly valued and are played by the

...performers by being shaken as accompaniments to other instruments—they make a noise, and that is, after all, the soul of most African instrumental music. These instruments are all that remain of certain cattle which the Spaniards introduced many years ago, hoping to improve the food supply. They seemed as if they would have thrived well on the island, on the stretches of grassland in the <note>original: "Cordillera"</note> mountain range and the East, but the Bubis, being great hunters, killed them all off.

The festivities of the Bubis—dances, weddings, feasts, and so on—at which this miscellaneous collection of instruments is used together, usually take place in November, during the dry season. However, a Bubi is liable to pour forth his soul in the bosom of his family at any time of the day or night, from June to January; and when he pours it forth on that bow-like instrument, it makes the lonely European long for home.

The Bubi can hardly be said to have divisions of time, but this is a point upon which all West Africans are rather weak, particularly the Bantu. He does, however, have a definite name for November, December, and January—the dry season months—calling them *Lobos*.

<margin>✓</margin>
The <term>fetish</term> <note>The author defines this as the underlying religious and philosophical ideas governing a person's life</note> of these people, although agreeing on broad lines with the Bantu <term>fetish</term>, has many interesting points, as even my limited knowledge of it showed me. It is a subject that would repay further investigation; and since by <term>fetish</term> I always mean the governing but underlying ideas of a person’s life, we will begin with the child. As far as I have been able to determine, nothing happens to him for spiritual reasons when he first appears on the scene. At birth, he receives a name as is usual, which is changed for another upon his initiation into the secret society; this secret society also has, as is common, a secret language. Around the age of three or five years, the boy is decorated, under the auspices of the <term>witch doctor</term> <note>A traditional healer or spiritual leader</note>, with certain scars on the face. These scars run from the bridge of the nose across the cheeks and are sometimes carried up in a curve onto the forehead. They do not use tattooing in the true sense of the word, but they paint themselves, as the mainlanders do, with a red paint made by burning some herb and mixing the ash with clay or oil, and they occasionally—

69
### III SPIRITS AND CHARMS

Whether for <term>ju-ju</term> <note>Traditional West African spiritual or magical systems</note> reasons or for mere decoration, I do not know, but they paint a band of yellow clay around the chest. I know little of the Bubi secret society, nor have I been able to find anyone who knows much more. Hutchinson,1 in his highly entertaining description of a wedding he once attended among these people, suggests that the period of seclusion for the women's society lasts twelve months.

The chief god or spirit, O. Wassa, lives in the crater of the highest peak, and the natives call the peak by his name. Another very important spirit, to whom goats and sheep are offered, is Lobe. He lives in a crater lake on the northern slope of the <note>original: "Cordilleras"</note> mountain range. The grass you sometimes see a Bubi wearing is said to come from this lake and is considered a charm of Lobe's. Dr. Baumann says that the lake at Riabba, from which the spirit Uapa rises, is even more sacred. He describes Uapa as small and residing in a rocky chasm with a slope so steep it can only be descended using bush ropes; during the wet season, he is not accessible at all. If given suitable offerings, he will reveal the future, but only to Bubis. His priest is the King of all the Bubis, whom no white man or <term>Porto</term> <note>A term likely referring to the Portuguese or light-skinned foreigners</note> is ever permitted to see. Baumann also identifies the residence of another important spirit as the grotto at Banni. This is a sea cave, accessible only at low water in calm weather. I have heard many legends about this cave but have never had the opportunity to see it, or to meet anyone who has seen it firsthand.

The charms used by these people are similar in form to those of the mainland Bantu, but their methods of treating paths and gateways are somewhat peculiar. The gateways to the towns are sometimes covered with freshly cut banana leaves. During the religious festival in November, the paths to the villages are blocked with a hedge of grass that no stranger is permitted to pass through.

The government is unusual for West Africa. Every village has its own chief, but the whole tribe obeys one great chief or king who lives in the crater-ravine at Riabba. This individual is called Moka, but I do not know if he is the same man referred to by Rogoszinsky, Mr. Holland, and the Rev. Hugh

### FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS CHAP.

Regarding Brown, who attempted to interview him in the 1870s, I am not certain, for the Bubis are exactly the type of people to maintain the idea of a great king by using a variety of different individuals to represent him. Even the tireless Dr. Baumann failed to meet Moka, though he clearly discovered a great deal about the methods of his administration and formed a very high opinion of his ability. He says that the people owe their current unity and order to this single chief; before his time, the entire island was in a state of internal warfare where murder was frequent and property was insecure. Now, according to the Doctor’s account, their social condition is a model for Europe, let alone Africa.

Civil wars have been abolished, disputes between villages are referred to arbitration, and murder is punished swiftly and surely. If a criminal has fled into the forest and cannot be found, his village is held responsible and must pay a fine in goats, sheep, and tobacco to the value of £16. Theft is extremely rare, as are offenses against the moral code; the Bubis maintain an extremely high standard in these matters, and even small children each have a separate sleeping hut. In the old days, adultery was punished by amputating the offender’s hand. I have personally seen women on Fernando Po who have had a hand cut off at the wrist, but I believe those were enslaved women who had been punished for theft.

The Bubis do keep slaves, but their condition is the mild "poor relation" or retainer form of slavery found in Calabar. This differs from the Dualla system, as Bubi slaves live in the same villages as their masters. Among the Dualla, as among most Bantu slave-holding tribes, the slaves are excluded from the master’s village and live in separate villages of their own. For marriage ceremonies, I refer you to Mr. Hutchinson. Burial customs are exceedingly unusual in the southern and eastern districts, where bodies are buried in the forest with their heads just protruding from the ground. In other districts, the body is also buried in the forest but is completely covered, and a stone structure is erected to mark the place.

Little is known about West African <term>fetish</term> <note>A 19th-century term for traditional West African spiritual and magical systems</note>, and even less is known about the beliefs of these strange people. Dr. Oscar Baumann applied his careful, objective German methods of observation to them, thereby providing us with more valuable information about them than...

...and their island than we would otherwise have. Mr. Hutchinson lived on Fernando Po for many years, serving as Her Britannic Majesty’s Consul. Although his time was consumed by the affairs of the Oil Rivers <note>The coastal region of the Niger Delta.</note> and his dealings with the Portos of Clarence <note>Modern-day Malabo.</note>, he nonetheless made very interesting observations about the indigenous people and their customs. The Polish exile and his brave wife who climbed Clarence Peak, Mr. Rogoszinsky, along with another Polish exile, Mr. Janikowski, roughly complete our list of authorities on the island. Dr. Baumann believes they obtained their information from "Porto" sources—sources that the learned Doctor clearly considers to be more imaginative than factual. However, as you know, all African travelers are prone to dismissing one another’s work from time to time. I must admit that I have primarily dealt with the Portos myself, and my knowledge of the Bubi language is limited to the standard greeting: “Who are you?” “A Porto.” “What is the news?” “No news.” <note>original: “Ipori ?” “Porto.” “Ke Soko ?” “Hatsi soko”</note>

While these Portos are less interesting to the ethnologist than to the philanthropist—being, as they are, the by-products of the philanthropist's efforts—I cannot leave the subject of Fernando Po without mentioning them, as the island's trade depends on them. They serve as the intermediaries between the Bubis and the white traders. The former trust the Portos very little—hardly more than they trust white men. Their view of the Spanish Governor’s position is that he is merely the chief of the Portos. They do not imagine it possible that he has any authority over the Bubis or over Bubi land—which they call *Itschulla*. Baumann says he was once told by a Bubi:

<margin>“White men are fish, not men. They can stay on land for a short time, but eventually they board their ships again and disappear over the horizon into the ocean. How can a fish own land?”</margin>

If coffee and cocoa thrive on Fernando Po as they have already flourished on São Tomé, there is little doubt that the Bubis will become extinct. They refuse to work on plantations, whether for others or for themselves. Consequently, the Portos will become the most important class, as they will take up plantation farming. # FERNANDO PO AND THE BUBIS CH. III

They live in fairly neat houses around the bays, where they collect palm oil from the Bubi people and establish small cacao plantations for themselves. Periodically, they bring these products to the white traders' warehouses <term>factory: a merchant's trading station or warehouse</term> in Clarence <note>Modern-day Malabo.</note>. After spending some time and most of their money in the social excitement of that capital, they return to their homes to recover.

There is also a class of them permanently residing in Clarence; these are the city men of Fernando Po. They are very similar to the Sierra Leoneans of Freetown, though perhaps more agreeable. Their origins are practically identical to those of the Freetown residents. They are the descendants of liberated slaves who were freed during the British occupation of the island, when it served as a naval base for suppressing the slave trade. Others are descendants of Sierra Leoneans and people from Accra who have arrived and settled there since then. They possess some of that "Black gentleman, Sir" <note>original: "Black gennellum, Sar"</note> style, but it is not developed to the same ridiculous extent as seen in the Sierra Leoneans, primarily because they have not lived under British institutions.

The "Fanny Po" <note>A common nickname for Fernando Po.</note> women are famous for their beauty all along the West Coast, and quite rightly so. However, they are not—as they themselves believe—the most beautiful women in this part of the world. At least, not in my opinion. I personally prefer an Elmina woman, or an Igalwa, or a M’pongwe <note>Ethnic groups from modern-day Ghana and Gabon.</note>. But I had better stop and admit that my affections have become very scattered among the Black ladies of the West Coast. No sooner do I remember one lovely creature—whose soft eyes, perfect form, and charming, pretty ways captivated me—than I think of another. 

The Fernando Po women often have a certain amount of Spanish ancestry, which gives their features a decidedly greater delicacy: refined nostrils, mouths that are not too full, a certain gloss to the hair, and a brightness in the eye. However, it does not improve their complexion, and I am told it has a terrible effect on their tempers. Therefore, I think I will remain, for the time being, a faithful admirer of my dark-skinned Ingrimma, the Igalwa woman, with the little red blossoms tucked into her jet-black hair. She has a sweet, soft look and a kind word for everyone, but especially for her ugly husband, Isaac the "Jack Wash" <term>Jack Wash: a common term for a laundryman or washerman</term>.

I will not delay you here with an account of the Oil Rivers <note>The historical name for the rivers of the Niger Delta.</note>. For one thing, they are too vast a subject to summarize; for another, I do not feel I yet know enough to speak authoritatively about them—unless I were simply to follow the usual, well-worn path. Since what I have personally seen and known of the region does not incline me toward that approach, I will wait until I have had more opportunities to observe them.

I have studied the local people, but because their "fetish" <term>A term used by historical travelers to describe traditional West African religious beliefs, rituals, and sacred objects.</term> is so exceptionally interesting, I have moved that discussion to a separate chapter. I did this to keep the text tidy, as the subject is too complex to be scattered throughout the rest of the book. The state of confusion a collector like myself experiences on the West Coast is truly terrible. A single day's notes might contain facts about kraw-kraw <term>A contagious, itchy skin disease common in West Africa, similar to scabies.</term>, the price of onions, the size and number of fish caught, cooking recipes, genealogies, the forms of native oaths, legal cases, market prices, and so on. 

Organizing these notes is a massive undertaking. As for one’s personal memory, it becomes like a ragbag: when someone asks you a question, you dip into it frantically, but you almost always fail to find the specific "fact-rag" you need for several minutes.

# CHAPTER IV

## LAGOS BAR

Thanks to the kindness of Sir Claude and Lady MacDonald, I stayed on the Calabar River from January until May. I collected fish, largely with the assistance of Dr. Whitindale, and insects through the help of Mr. Cooper, who was then in charge of the botanical station. I spent most of my time exploring the river and the forest around Duke Town and Creek Town. However, during this visit to Calabar, I made a point of traveling upriver to see Miss Slessor at Okyon. She allowed me to stay with her, providing invaluable help regarding traditional beliefs <term>original: "fetish"</term> and giving me some of the most pleasant days of my life. 

This extraordinary lady has been in Calabar for eighteen years. For the last six or seven, she has lived entirely alone—at least as far as other Europeans are concerned—in a clearing in the forest near one of the primary villages in the Okyon district. There, she rules as a true "white chief" over the entire region. Her remarkable physical and intellectual abilities have earned her a unique position among the local tribes and won her the profound respect of everyone, both Black and white, who knows her. Her knowledge of the local people—their language, way of thinking, diseases, and challenges—is extraordinary. The amount of good she has accomplished is more than anyone can fully measure. 

When she first went to Okyon alone, she lived in local houses while building her current home with the help of the inhabitants. At that time, the district was feared by the people of Duke Town and Creek Town and was practically unknown to Europeans. Like many surrounding areas still are today, the district was prone to ritual killings at funerals, trials by poison <term>A form of judicial ordeal where a suspect drinks a poisonous substance, such as the Calabar bean, to determine guilt or innocence.</term>, and constant internal warfare. She has eliminated many of these harmful customs. Now, Okyon rarely causes trouble for its nominal rulers—the Consuls in Old Calabar—and trade passes freely through the area to the seaports.

This example of what a single European can achieve offers many important lessons for the administration and development of the West Coast. However, individuals like Miss Slessor are rare. Very few people possess her resilience against the malarial climate, her ability to learn the language, or her deep insight into the African <term>original: "negro"</term> mind. Perhaps, after all, it is no wonder that Miss Slessor stands alone, as she certainly does.

# IV PERPLEXING GEOGRAPHY

After returning down the river, I simply waited until the *Batanga*, my old friend, entered the river again, and then I set out for my beloved South West Coast. The various divisions of the West Coast of Africa are very confusing to a newcomer. Starting from Sierra Leone and heading south, you first pass the Grain Coast, which is also called the Pepper or Kru Coast, or the Liberian Coast. Next comes the Ivory Coast, also known as the Half Jack Coast or the Bristol Coast. Then comes the Gold Coast; then the old Slave Coast, now called the Popos; then Lagos; then "the Rivers"; and below the Rivers, the South West Coast. 

In addition to these names, you will hear references to the "Timber Ports" and the "Windward" and "Leeward" ports. It is confusing when you find a port—for example, Axim—referred to by one competent authority (such as a sea captain) as a Windward port, by the next as a Timber port, and by the next as a Gold Coast port. It is worth studying the matter if you intend to frequent the Bights of Biafra and Benin. As a hint to help your research, I will mention that the Bight of Benin begins at Cape St. Paul and ends at Cape Formosa, while the Bight of Biafra begins at Cape Formosa and ends at Cape Lopez. The Windward Coast is the section between Cape Apollonia and the Sakumo River <note>original: "Secum River"</note>, just west of Accra. At this river, the Leeward Coast begins and terminates at the Volta River.

When I was on the coast in 1893, the Cameroon River was regarded in nautical circles as a "River" <note>Referring to the "Oil Rivers" region of the Niger Delta</note>. Now, unfortunately for me, it is not. Traveling from Calabar to Cameroon is a feat you ought to receive a medal for, because the line of ships that runs from Liverpool to Calabar goes no further than Calabar. In former days, they used to stop at Calabar, then cross to Fernando Po and into Cameroon, stopping steadily at ports all the way down to São Paulo de Luanda <note>original: "Sant. Paul de Loanda"</note>. This was a very convenient and excellent arrangement, but I assume it was not profitable. Consequently, the South West Coast ships—those that stop at ports below Calabar—now stop at Lagos and bypass "the Rivers," going straight to the Cameroon River. So, you see, if you have successfully kept your head clear during this explanation, I had to take a ship heading back toward Europe as far as the Lagos Bar and then catch a South West-bound ship.
