<header>CHAPTER ON THE LAGOS BAR</header>

...outward bound; I assure you that transferring ships at the Lagos Bar makes changing trains at Clapham Junction <note>A famously busy and complex railway station in London.</note> seem simple by comparison. To make this latter point clear to my unfortunate victim—the general reader—I must drag them through a detailed explanation of Lagos and its sandbar.

Lagos is a marvelous example of the combined stubbornness of humanity and nature; it is simultaneously one of the most important export ports on the West African coast and one of the hardest to reach. The town of Lagos sits on an island in the Lagos River—a river prone to dissolving into lagoons and mud—with its sandbar located about two miles out to sea. The total width of the channel through this bar is half a mile, at least on paper. On either side of this channel lie the most dangerous breaking waves in West Africa. Its permanent residents are sharks; while authorities disagree on whether they claim fourteen or forty human lives annually, the truth—like everything else about the Lagos Bar—is uncertain, though certainly grim. 

Even at the best of times, this entrance channel has no more than thirteen feet of water. Although the steamships of the British African and Royal African lines are "noble pedestrians"—thinking nothing of "walking" across a sandbank when necessary, and being as capable of gliding over a dewy lawn as any ocean vessels ever built—I must admit they still require a minimum amount of water to operate. They can sit stranded on a sandbank or mudbank (they prefer mud, I might add) as well as any ship. I have often been aboard when they were engaged in this "pastime," but it undoubtedly causes delays. Consequently, they do not dock at the Lagos pier but instead anchor outside the bar. 

The Lagos Bar is so troublesome that even the specially designed "branch boats"—such as the noble *Dodo* and *Qwarra*, as well as the *Forcados* and others—are liable to get stuck, despite only having a ten-foot draft <term>The depth of water a ship draws</term>. This is because the channel, instead of maintaining its officially reported thirteen-foot depth, often drops to nine feet and is extremely prone to shifting its position. Furthermore, even if a branch boat manages to cross safely, the heavy ocean swell outside—with its massive, slow-moving waves intent on crashing over the bar—

#### IV MRS. S. AND HER CRATES

The waves, resembling coiling snakes under a blanket, cause ships lying sideways to them to swing like pendulums. This movement is so extreme that it prevents the unloading or loading of heavy cargo—and heavy cargo worth £1,566,243 annually must move through Lagos. Because West African trading vessels are resourceful and determined, especially regarding palm oil, they manage this by anchoring in the Forcados River. This river, located 120 miles below Lagos, is an outlet of the Niger River. It has a sandbar you can cross (if you don't mind the ship scraping the bottom slightly) with a depth of seventeen feet, nine inches. Consequently, they anchor just inside the Forcados River and wait for the branch boat <note>A smaller, shallow-draft steamship used to ferry cargo and passengers across dangerous sandbars to larger ocean-going vessels.</note> from Lagos to bring them their heavy cargo. Once it is on board, they head up the coast and stop outside the Lagos Bar, where another unfortunate branch boat brings out the mail and passengers.

After leaving Calabar and stopping at Bonny, the *Batanga* waited as expected in Forcados. Eventually, the branch boat arrived with its cargo and the typical noise. We heard accounts of the latest troubles at the Lagos Bar, which was going through one of its rough periods and was seizing and wrecking many branch boats. We also witnessed the usual scene with Mrs. S. I should mention that Mrs. S. is an attractive and stout black woman and an old acquaintance of mine. She is originally from Opobo and frequently travels to and from Lagos for her own business ventures, which she runs in partnership with another woman. 

Her business usually involves large-scale chicken trading. She goes to Lagos, buys chickens, brings them aboard in crates, and takes them back to Opobo to sell. As a fellow woman, it is not my place to say how much profit Mrs. S. makes, nor would it interest the general public. However, what *does* interest the public (at least those who travel by sea and, for their sins, end up in the Forcados River) is Mrs. S.'s return trip to Lagos with those empty crates and her firm resolve not to pay freight <term>Shipping fees for transporting goods.</term> for them. Wise and experienced chief officers pretend not to see Mrs. S.’s crates, but young and aggressive ones do. They determine that she *will* pay for them and loudly announce this intention all the way from Opobo.

When I am wealthy someday, I will give Mrs. S. purses of gold in the Eastern fashion for the many delightful scenes she has performed for me with those crates in dreary Forcados.

Once these affairs were settled, the *Batanga* left Forcados and proceeded up the coast to stop outside Lagos for mail and passengers. My fate was to transfer to the branch boat that brought these items out. I expected this boat would then take me into Lagos to await the arrival of the southwest-bound ship.

I had been given—as passengers landing at Lagos are properly and customarily given—a course of instruction on the dangers of boarding and leaving branch boats at the sandbar. They made special mention of a gentleman who came down the coast for pleasure and lost a leg to a shark while doing so. They also spoke of the severe type of fever that was currently prevalent.

# IV CROSSING THE BAR

...raging in Lagos. Then, when we saw the branch boat <term>A smaller vessel used to transport cargo and passengers across shallow or dangerous sandbars to larger ships.</term> that was coming out to us get stuck on the bar in the middle of what a German would call a confusion <note>original: "Wirrwarr"</note> of breakers, I admit it took all the fascination of my memories of the Southwest Coast to keep me from giving up the journey and going home comfortably to England on the *Batanga*, as my best friends had strongly advised me to do.

However, the branch boat eventually forced its way over the bar and came panting up, anchoring near us. From it, a Lagos government official climbed onto the *Batanga* in a soaking wet state. He said he had just come out to see how a branch boat could cross the bar at low tide—a noble and enterprising feat that places him alongside Pliny the Elder <note>A Roman author and naturalist who died while observing the eruption of Mount Vesuvius.</note>. He entertained us with a calm, completely unemotional account of how the water had washed right over them, gone down the funnel, and so on—evidently a horribly common experience here. He said the *Eko* (that was our branch boat’s name) was not returning to Lagos until it had delivered the southbound mail and over a hundred deck passengers who were going to the Congo onto the Southwest Coast boat. That boat was expected at any hour in the offshore anchorage <term>Roads: a sheltered area of water near a shore where vessels may ride at anchor.</term>, as its arrival had been telegraphed from Accra. He casually mentioned that he hoped it would not be late in the afternoon, as he had to travel inland the next morning on the government steamer. Well, since things seemed safe and pleasant, I headed for the branch boat, being very carefully lowered over the side in a chair by the winch.

"Take care of yourself," said the crew of the *Batanga*.

"I will," I replied, which shows the futility and vanity of such resolutions; for if other people had not taken care of me, goodness only knows what would have become of me. Once I arrived alongside the *Eko*, I climbed its rope ladder to the deck, and I shall not soon forget that deck. The government official had understated the case; things were in the chaos of a spring cleaning. The waves had not made a "clean sweep" of the boat, but a remarkably dirty one; it would have been better if it had remained stuck among the breakers for another half hour to give the sea nymphs <note>Mythological spirits of the sea.</note> time to tidy up. They had particularly made a mess <term>"Made hay of": to throw into a state of total confusion or disorder.</term> of the brave captain’s cabin, flinging out onto

### LAGOS BAR

On the deck, his socks, hats, and boots were scattered everywhere, and everything was coated in a layer of wet coal dust. On the small lower deck were the unfortunate local passengers. They were silent, which for West African passengers usually indicates seasickness, and every scrap of clothing they owned was soaking wet. Rats ran freely everywhere, and from the dark patch of silence on the main deck, no sound rose except for Mrs. S.’s "*Chei! Chei! Chei!*" <note>Chei: An exclamation of surprise, distress, or disapproval common in West African English/Pidgin.</note> of disgust and disapproval of her surroundings.

The kind German captain—since the *Eko* belonged to a large German trading firm in Lagos and not to the regular steamship companies—did everything possible to make me comfortable. The government official pointed out sights of interest on the distant shore: the lighthouse, the Government House, the Wilberforce Hall, and so forth. He especially noted the small government steamer which, he observed, was building up steam to be ready to take him upriver early the next morning. He seemed to think they were starting a bit too early, as the government is very strict about the "sin" of wasting coal.

As the afternoon wore on, our anticipation for the arrival of the *Benguella* grew until it surpassed all other interests; the *Benguella* became the only thing we truly cared about in life, yet she did not appear. The little *Eko* rolled back and forth, back and forth, as all the loose equipment went "slippery, slop, crash; slippery, slop, crash." Coal dust, soot, and a scorching sun beat down on us steadily. The only variation in the movement was the *Eko* making a violent jerk at her anchor every three or four minutes.

Around six o'clock, a steamer was spotted entering the anchorage <term>Roads: a sheltered area of water near a shore where vessels may anchor.</term>. The experienced captain stated she was not the *Benguella*, and he was right; it was the *Janette Woermann*. As soon as she was settled, her captain boarded the *Eko*, naturally to ask about the prospects for cargo on shore. He appeared as a massive, agile, and powerful Dane, dressed in an exceptionally tight and splendid uniform that ended in a pair of Blucher boots <term>Blucher boots: sturdy, half-length lace-up boots named after the Prussian Field Marshal Blücher.</term>. Every inch of his six-foot-four-inch frame was immaculate, but that was only his outward appearance. In reality, that man was our two guardian angels rolled into one. As soon as he saw us—the depressed, distracted official and the disheveled lady—he took us under his wing, and in a few more

If I were the Caliph of Baghdad, I would have that captain's name—which is Heldt—written in gold letters on ivory tablets, along with a full and detailed account of everything he did for us. He served us dinner with great promptness—an excellent dinner beginning with what I thought was a plateful of hot jam, but which was delicious nonetheless. My companion, however, was not so easily distracted. You cannot turn a man from the higher duties and responsibilities of life so easily. His mind was plagued by the most dismal thoughts and guesses. He regretted coming out on the *Eko*, even though his motive—to see how she would cross the bar at low tide—was a noble one related to his specific official appointment. Not only did he regret that, but he also remembered, with remorse, all the other things he had done which he should not have done. 

Captain Heldt did his best to cheer him up and distract him from brooding over these things and the way coal was being wasted on his account inside the bar. The captain offered him suits of his own clothes to replace his soaked ones; but he refused, saying he felt lost enough already without wearing clothes of that size. Lager beer, cigars, and stories were then tried on him, but with little effect. He did take a certain amount of interest in the captain’s account of how he had severely injured his back and had to navigate his vessel among the shoals of Saint Ann <note>Cape Saint Ann, located off the coast of modern-day Sierra Leone.</note> while lying in great agony for weeks due to an accident in the Grain Coast <note>The coastal region of West Africa, primarily modern-day Liberia.</note> surf. He was also interested in the various accounts of the many ribs the captain had broken in different ways on the high seas, but any...

Captain Heldt tried to cheer him up with more stories, lager beer, and cigars, and finally produced an autoharp <term>A stringed instrument with chord buttons used to play chords by damping other strings.</term>, an instrument at which he was proficient. He was capable of playing not only the march from "Ajax," but also "The Watch on the Rhine" <note>original: "Der Wacht am Rhein"; a German patriotic anthem.</note> and "Annie Laurie." This temporarily distracted my companion from the issue of the coal, and he began to learn how to play the autoharp. He did so quickly, but then he only picked out "Home, Sweet Home" with such intense feeling and sorrow that the instrument was taken away from him. Then we heard long accounts of the region around the Swakop River, where the *Janette* had recently been. Finally, around two o’clock, my companion said sadly, "Here she comes!" And indeed, she arrived. In a short time, the graceful old *Benguella* was duly anchored in the roadstead <term>A sheltered area of water outside a harbor where ships can anchor.</term>, and my two friends took me on board.

I fear none of us felt very enthusiastic. I had never been on her before, so I regarded her as a complete stranger. My companion felt that his situation on shore was now a "hanging matter" <term>A matter of grave consequence or extreme trouble; a metaphor for facing severe professional repercussions.</term> because of those coals, so he was in no hurry to get there. To Captain Heldt, she was a rival vessel. But often those things you expect the least from ultimately give you the most pleasure, as a moralist would...

## IV GOODBYE TO THE BAR

As they say, when you are on the Coast you never know whom you may meet. After quite a bit of trouble in the *Janette’s* boat trying to get my companions to climb the rope ladder to the deck before me, I finally climbed that exciting nautical institution myself. Just as my head cleared the top of the bulwark <term>The extension of a ship's side above the level of the deck.</term>, I saw a man just a yard away, directly ahead, still supervising the hatch—it was my first tutor in Kru English <term>A form of West African Pidgin English used by the Kru people, who were renowned as skilled sailors.</term>. 

He had last seen me in 1893 when I was a complete newcomer going ashore at São Paulo de Loanda <note>Now Luanda, Angola.</note> from the ship *Lagos*, on which he was then an officer. At that time, I was swearing that I intended to go home on the very next boat. Now, seeing me coming aboard in a way that I am sure would have done credit to a Half Jack captain <term>A term for skilled African mariners from the "Half Jack" (Grand-Lahou) region of the Ivory Coast.</term>, he naturally asked for an explanation. However, because I was quite busy with the "palaver" <term>A word used in West Africa to mean a discussion, dispute, or complicated affair; here referring to the fuss of climbing the rope ladder.</term> of the rope ladder, I did not give him one right then and there.

In a short time, I had said farewell with many thanks to my two friends who had taken such care of me at Lagos Bar. My fellow countryman returned on the *Eko*, which—having got its mail and passengers safe and sound onto the *Benguella*—was at last going back into Lagos. I am sure it will be a relief to you to know that none of those expected troubles on shore befell the official. Instead, he lived to earn the gratitude and respect of Lagos and its government for his noble and determined service in managing and surveying that awful bar. 

A few months after our amusing experiences there, the bar became more dangerous than ever, and vessel after vessel was wrecked. He rescued their passengers and crews at the great risk of his own life. Approaching a ship that is breaking up in the surf, in an open boat with a native crew, and rescuing panic-stricken Africans and their belongings while surrounded by such a sea—with its crowd of expectant sharks and the harsh West African climate—is good work for a good man. My fellow countryman did it, and he did it well.

# CHAPTER V

## VOYAGE DOWN THE COAST

->In which the traveler, before leaving the rivers, discusses various dangers; to<-

My voyage down the coast on the *Benguella* was very pleasant and highly informative. Mr. Fothergill, who was the ship’s purser, had lived in the *French Congo* <note>original: "Congo Français"</note> as a merchant in previous years, and I was heading to that same region with a "hold" that was entirely empty of any local knowledge. He was the type of person—often represented among merchants—who lacks the ability so many others along this coast possess (an ability that always amazes me) to live in a district for a considerable time without taking any interest in it, focusing their entire attention only on how much longer it will be before they can leave. 

Mr. Fothergill clearly possessed extensive knowledge and experience regarding the Fernan Vaz district and its native inhabitants. I would say he had perhaps experienced a bit too much for his own personal comfort and pleasure at the time, having been nearly killed and frequently harassed by them. Now, as much as I regret a man’s total lack of local knowledge, I do not wish for anyone to go to such extremes. Mr. Fothergill recounted these incidents calmly and in an unembellished way that gave them a sense of power and conviction. This was somewhat unsettling—though useful—to someone heading into the very district where these events had occurred, for one felt there was no logical reason why one might not person—

personally get involved in similar affairs. I must also acknowledge here how much Mr. Fothergill’s wonderfully accurate descriptions of the unique characteristics of the Ogowé forests helped me later when I dealt with those forests on my own. Every district of the forest has its own particular traits that one needs to understand.

I would like to speak here about the dangers of the West Coast because I worry you might think I am indifferent to them or do not believe they exist. Neither is the case. The more you know about the West Coast of Africa, the more you realize its dangers. For example, on your first voyage out, you hardly believe the stories of fever told by the "old Coasters" <term>veteran European residents or traders on the West African coast</term>. That is because you do not yet understand the type of man who is telling them—a man who faces his death with a joke on his lips.

However, a little experience of your own—especially if you happen to be in a place during one of its periodic epidemics—soon demonstrates that the underlying horror of the situation is real. It is like a rotting corpse that the old Coaster has covered with jokes to hide it, so that it hardly shows from a distance; but when you come to live alongside it yourself, you soon become aware of it. Many men, once they have gone ashore and settled, realize this and let the horror take hold of them. This is a state briefly and locally described as "funk" <term>a state of paralyzing fear or clinical depression caused by the environment</term>, and it is a state that usually ends fatally. You can hardly blame them. 

Why, I know of a case myself. A young man who had never been outside an English country town before in his life was forced by family financial troubles to take a job as a bookkeeper down in the Bights <term>the Bights of Benin and Biafra, coastal regions of the Gulf of Guinea</term>. The "factory" <term>a merchant's trading station or warehouse</term> he was going to was in an isolated, remote place, not in a settlement. When the ship arrived, he was put ashore in one of the ship’s boats with his belongings and a case or two of goods. Only the firm’s "beach-boys" <term>local African laborers</term> were down at the surf. Because the steamer was in a hurry, the ship's officer did not go up to the factory with him; he simply said goodbye and left him alone with what the young man perceived to be "naked savages," but who were actually kindhearted Kru boys <term>an ethnic group from Liberia and Ivory Coast known for their maritime and labor skills</term> on the beach. 

He could not understand what they said, nor they what he said, so he walked up to the house and onto the veranda and tried to find the Agent <term>the head manager of a trading station</term> he had come out to...

was sent out to a firm he was to serve under. He looked into the open-air dining room and shyly around the veranda, waiting for someone to appear. Several locals appeared and spoke at length, but no one was European or spoke an understandable language. In desperation, he took another, bolder walk all the way around the veranda and noticed a strange noise coming from one of the rooms and a massive swarm of flies entering through the shuttered window. Gathering his courage, he went inside and discovered the remains of the European Agent, a large number of rats, and most of the flies in West Africa. He likely contracted a fever afterward; two weeks later, he was rescued by a French boat that the locals signaled, and he is not coming back to the Coast again. Some men would have died instantly from a shock like this.

But most newcomers do not experience a shock of that magnitude. They either die themselves or gradually become accustomed to these situations, eventually viewing death and fever like soldiers on a battlefield. After a hard day's fighting where they have seen their friends and companions fall around them, these soldiers sit around a campfire, laughing and talking, all the while knowing the battle resumes tomorrow and they might not survive the following night. This is not cold-heartedness; it is simply how they cope. Michael Scott described this well in *Tom Cringle’s Log* <note>A popular nautical adventure novel by Michael Scott, first published in 1833</note>, in his account of yellow fever during the war in the West Indies.

While fever is the primary danger—especially for people who live in settlements—it is not the only one. However, since other risks (except perhaps domestic poisoning) are incidental to traveling through the forests or on the rivers among indigenous tribes, I will not dwell on them. A person with common sense can avoid these dangers by staying away from the areas where they occur. Thus, I warn the general reader: if you go to West Africa, it is not because I claimed the place was safe or that its dangers were exaggerated. The cemeteries of the West Coast are filled with the victims of people who claimed that "Coast fever" is actually "Cork fever" <term>an insulting suggestion that the illness was caused by alcoholism rather than the environment</term> and is the victim's own fault—which it is not—and those who claimed that locals will never attack you unless you attack them first. They certainly will attack, on occasion.

<header>WEST COAST RIVERS</header>

My main goal in going to the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note> was to travel above the tidal reaches of the Ogowé River to collect fish; my specific objective on this voyage was to collect specimens from a river north of the Congo. I had hoped this river would be the Niger, as Sir George Goldie <note>Founder of the Royal Niger Company.</note> had offered me excellent facilities to carry out my work there in comfort. However, for certain private reasons, I was reluctant to move from the Royal Niger Protectorate into the Royal Niger Company's territory. Additionally, I did not find the Calabar River—where Sir Claude MacDonald <note>The Commissioner and Consul-General for the Oil Rivers Protectorate.</note> did everything he possibly could to assist me—to be a good river for collecting fish. Since these two rivers failed me (through no fault of their own presiding spirits), my only remaining hope for success lay with the Ogowé, a river on the South West Coast. Everything there depended on Mr. Hudson's attitude toward scientific research in the field of ichthyology <term>the branch of zoology that deals with fish</term>. Fortunately for me, that gentleman chose to take a favorable view of the matter, and he assisted me in every way possible during my entire stay in the French Congo. But before I provide a detailed description of this wonderful part of West Africa, I must give you a brief overview of the general character and "habits" of West Coast rivers to make the subject more intelligible.

There is a consistency in the behavior of West Coast rivers, from the Volta to the Cuanza <note>original: "Coanza"</note>, which is quite charming once you become accustomed to it. Except for the Congo, every truly great river meets the sea with as much mystery as possible. They lounge lazily among mangrove swamps in a "what-does-it-matter-when-one-arrives" and "what’s-the-hurry" style, flowing through numerous interconnected channels. At first glance, each channel looks as much like the others as peas in a pod. They are bordered on both sides by dark green walls of mangroves, which Captain Lugard <note>Frederick Lugard, a British soldier and colonial administrator.</note> vividly described as appearing "as if they had lost all sense of plant-like decency, standing on stilts with their branches tucked up out of the wet, leaving their grim roots exposed in mid-air." Whether it is high tide or low tide, there is little difference in the appearance of the water. Whether the river is broad or narrow, deep or shallow, it looks like a path of polished metal; it is as heavily weighted with stinking mud as water can possibly be, during both the ebb and flow of the tide, all year round.

She describes the characteristic, muddy, and labyrinthine nature of West African river deltas and their mangrove swamps.</summary>

year in. But the difference in the banks, though an unending alternation between two appearances, is eerie.

At high tide, you do not see the mangroves displaying their "ankles" in the way that shocked Captain Lugard <note>Frederick Lugard (1858–1945), a British soldier and colonial administrator influential in the history of Nigeria.</note>. They look most respectable; their foliage rises densely in a wall, irregularly striped here and there by the white line of an aerial root. These roots descend straight into the water from an upper branch as straight as a plumb line, in the strange, deliberate way a mangrove's aerial root does. It maintains that hard, straight line until it gets about two feet above water level, and then it spreads out into blunt fingers with which to dip into the water and grasp the mud. At high water, riverbanks can hardly be said to exist at all. The water stretches away into the mangrove swamps for miles and miles, and you can then travel in a suitable small canoe as far into these swamps as you please.

This is a fascinating pursuit. "For people who like that sort of thing, it is just the sort of thing they like," as the art critic of a provincial town wisely observed regarding <note>original: "anent"</note> an Impressionist painting recently acquired for the municipal gallery. But it is a pleasure to be enjoyed with caution. For one thing, you are certain to encounter crocodiles. Now, a crocodile drifting in deep water, or lying asleep with its jaws open on a sunlit sandbank, is a picturesque addition to the landscape when you are on the deck of a steamer. In that situation, you can write home about it and frighten your relatives on your behalf. 

However, when you are away among the swamps in a small dugout canoe, and that crocodile and its relatives are awake—which they make a point of being at high tide because of the fish passing through—and when he has his foot upon his "native heath" <note>A literary reference to Sir Walter Scott's *Rob Roy*: "My foot is on my native heath, and my name is MacGregor!"</note>—that is to say, his tail within reach of his native mud—he is intensely interesting. You may not be able to write home about him then, as you will be too busy being frightened on your own behalf. Crocodiles can, and often do, snatch at people in small canoes in such places. I have known several locals who lost their lives this way. Some native villages are accessible from the main river by a short cut through the mangrove swamps, and the inhabitants of such villages will occasionally cross this way with small canoes instead of...

...along the permanent channel to the village, which almost always winds. In addition to this unpleasantness, you are likely—until you realize the danger through experience or receive advice from the locals—to get trapped by the tide out in the swamps. The water falls around you while you are away in some deep pool or lagoon, and you find you cannot get back to the main river. You cannot get out and drag your canoe across the stretches of mud that separate you from the river because the mud is too unstable and deep. Sinking into it means staying in it—at least until some geologist of the remote future discovers you in a fossilized state, once that mangrove swamp has become dry land. 

Of course, if you truly want a secure investment in fame and really care about posterity and the future of science, you could jump into the black, batter-like, stinking slime. You can be cheered by the thought of the terrific sensation you will produce 20,000 years from now, and the care your fellow creatures will take of you then in a museum. 

But if you are just an ordinary person of a shy nature, like me, you stay in your lagoon until the tide rises again. Most of your attention is directed to hosting an "at home" <note>A Victorian social term for a formal reception held at one's house; here used ironically to describe being stuck with pests.</note> for crocodiles and mangrove flies, while enduring the fearful stench of the surrounding slime. Whatever little time you have left, you will spend wondering why you came to West Africa at all. You will ask why, after reaching this point of absurdity, you had to "gild the lily" <note>original: "painted the lily and adorned the rose"</note> by being such a massive fool as to go messing around in mangrove swamps. 

This "chatty little incident," as Lady MacDonald <note>Lady Ethel MacDonald, wife of the Commissioner of the Niger Coast Protectorate.</note> would call it, has happened to me twice—but never again if I can help it. On the last occasion, a massive "Silurian" <note>original: "Silurian"; a reference to the prehistoric geological period, used here as a humorous journalistic term for a crocodile.</note>, as *The Daily Telegraph* would call him, chose to get his front paws over the back of my canoe and tried to "improve our acquaintance." I had to retreat to the front of the boat to keep it balanced¹ and hit him on the snout with a paddle. He then withdrew, and I paddled into the very middle of the lagoon, hoping the water there was too deep for him or any of his friends to repeat the performance. Presumably it was, for no...

I have measured them when they have been killed by other people, and they were fifteen, eighteen, and twenty-one feet odd. This was only a pushy young creature who had not yet learned manners.

Still, even if your own specific tastes and pursuits do not take you in small dugout canoes into the heart of the swamps, you can observe the change in the local scenery caused by the flowing of the tide when you are on a vessel stuck on a sandbank—in the Rio del Rey <note>A river and estuary system on the coast of modern-day Cameroon.</note>, for example. Moreover, since you will have little else to focus on except mosquitoes and mangrove flies <term>likely deer flies or horse flies of the genus Chrysops</term> when in such a situation, you may as well pursue the study of the landscape. At the ebb tide, the foliage of the lower branches of the mangroves gradually grows wet and muddy, until there is a wide black band about three feet deep above the surface of the water in all directions. Gradually, a network of gray-white roots rises up, and below this, a slope of smooth, lead-brown slime gradually appears. The effect is not at all as if the water had fallen, but rather as if the mangroves had all at once risen up out of it; and they seem to sink silently back into it again when the flood tide comes. 

However, by using this safer—if still unpleasant—method of observing mangrove swamps, you miss seeing their full structure. Deep within their inner reaches, the mangroves raise their branches far above the reach of the tide line, and the great gray roots of the older trees are always sticking up in mid-air. But, bordering the rivers, there is always a hedge of younger mangroves whose lower branches become submerged.

At various corners along the riverfront, you can see land being created from the water. A mudbank forms, a mangrove seed lands on it, and the process is finished. Well, perhaps not finished, but certainly begun; for if the bank is high enough to be exposed at low water, this pioneer mangrove grows. He has a miserable existence, though. You only have to look at his stunted, spindly form to see this. He is soon joined by a few more bold spirits and they struggle on together, their network of roots catching an abundance of mud and, by good chance, an occasional collection of...

<header>MANGROVES AS ISLAND MAKERS</header>
<sig>V</sig>

...miscellaneous *debris* of palm leaves or a floating tree trunk, but they always die before they reach any significant height. Still, even in death, they collect material. Their bare white sticks remain like a net gripped in the mud, so that these pioneer mangrove "heroes" may be said to have laid down their lives to make that mudbank fit for colonization. Eventually, the time comes when other mangroves can and do colonize it and flourish, steadily extending their territory; then the mudbank joins up with and becomes a part of Africa.

Far away on the inland edge of the swamp—you may travel some hundreds of miles before you reach it—you can see the rest of the process. The mangroves there have risen up and dried the mud to an extent that is more than is good for themselves; they have "over-civilized" that mud, in fact. As a result, the brackish <term>slightly salty</term> tidal waters cannot reach their roots. While these waters are their enemy when too deep or too salt-heavy, they are essential to the mangrove's existence. They have done this gradually, as a mangrove does all things, but they have done it. Down onto that mud comes a whole set of palms from the old mainland, which go through similarly trying experiences in their early colonization days. First, the screw-pines <term>plants of the genus Pandanus, known for their prop roots</term> arrive and live among them; then the wine-palm <term>the Raphia palm</term> and various creepers, and finally the oil-palm. Because the *debris* from these plants is more substantial and creates better soil than dead mangroves, they work faster, and the mangrove is doomed. Soon the salt waters are shut out completely, the mangrove dies, and that piece of Africa is made. 

It is very interesting to enter these regions. Along the riverbank, you see a rich, thick, lovely wall of soft-wooded plants, but behind this, you find great stretches of death—sometimes miles and miles of gaunt, white mangrove skeletons standing on gray material that is not yet earth and is no longer slime. You can sink through its crust into rotting putrefaction. Yet, long after you are dead, buried, and forgotten, this will become a forest of soft-wooded plants and palms, and finally, a forest of hardwood trees. You will find districts of this description in the vast expanses of Kama country <note>The territory of the Kama or Nkomi people in the Ogooué River delta of modern-day Gabon.</note>, for example, and in the rich, low regions leading up to the base of the Sierra del Cristal <note>A mountain range in Gabon and Equatorial Guinea.</note> and the Rumby range <note>The Rumpi Hills in modern-day Cameroon.</note>.

You often hear of the utter lifelessness of mangrove swamps...

...is often commented on; why I do not know, for they are fairly well-populated with wildlife, though the species are relatively few. There are crocodiles—more of them than anyone wants. There are quantities of flies, particularly the large, silent mangrove fly that lays an egg under your skin; the egg becomes a maggot and stays there until it is ready to emerge into the world. Then there are "slimy things with legs crawling on a slimy sea," <note>A reference to Samuel Taylor Coleridge's poem "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner."</note> and plenty of hopping mud-fish <term>mudskippers</term>, crabs, a certain type of mollusk, and various kinds of catfish in the water. They are devoid of birds, except for the flocks of gray parrots that fly over them in the evening, squawking hoarsely. Aside from this squawking, the swamps are silent all day, at least during the dry season. In the wet season, there is no silence day or night in West Africa; there is only the roar of the falling deluge of rain, which is more monotonous and depressing than any silence could be. In the morning, you do not hear the long, low, mellow whistle of the plantain-eaters <term>turacos, a type of African bird</term> announcing the dawn, nor do you hear the "clock-bird" in the evening. You miss the massive choruses of frogs—as large as a Handel Festival performance <note>A massive triennial music festival in London known for its enormous choirs and orchestras.</note>—or the crickets that argue their evening controversy of "she did"—"she didn't" so fiercely on dry land.

But the mangrove swamp follows the general rule for West Africa: the night is noisier than the day. After dark, it is full of noises: grunts from unknown sources, splashes from jumping fish, the peculiar whirring of scuttling crabs, and strange creaking and groaning sounds from the trees. Above all, there is the eerie, strange whine and sighing cough of crocodiles. I shall never forget one moonlit night I spent in a mangrove swamp. I was not lost, but we had moved away from the main river into the swamp so that the villagers from a place with a bad reputation would not encounter us while they were out fishing. We went deep inside to a long pool or lagoon. We dozed off and woke up, seeing the same scene around us twenty times throughout the night. Because of this, the night felt like an eternity <note>original: "æon"</note>, until I felt, in a daze, that I had somehow entered a world that was entirely like this—and always had been, and always would be. Every now and then, a strong musky smell drifted by, which meant a crocodile was nearby, and one

During one check, I found the leg of one of my most valuable men sticking out noticeably over the side of the canoe. I nudged him awake with a paddle and spoke to him about how unwise it was to leave his leg exposed like that in our current situation. He agreed, telling me he had lost a beloved uncle who had been snatched from a canoe by a crocodile in this very swamp. He said his uncle’s ghost had become a kind of malevolent spirit that had been a burden to the family ever since. He believed the ghost must have pulled his leg out—just as I had observed—to make him a victim of another crocodile so he could join him in the spirit world. I thanked him for the information and said it fully explained the situation. I told him I would do my best to prevent another family member from becoming a spirit by striking any arm or leg I saw that "uncle spirit" trying to pull into reach of the crocodiles.

Large regions of mangrove swamps are a defining feature of the West African coast. The first of these lies north of Sierra Leone. After that, they appear in smaller sizes—merely fringes around river mouths—until you reach Lagos. There, you encounter the largest of them all: the swamps of the Niger Delta (comprising about twenty-three rivers in all) and those of the Sombreiro, New Calabar, Bonny, San Antonio, Opobo (both the "False" and "True" branches), Kwa Ibo, Old Calabar (including the Cross, Akwayafe, and Qwa Rivers), and the Rio del Rey. This entire vast stretch of coast is a continuous mangrove swamp. Each river silently carries down an enormous amount of silt-filled water. Every river presents a difficult challenge for navigators due to its complex network of connecting creeks and the sand and mud bars formed at the entrances where the heaviest sediment settles. The lighter mud is carried past the bar, turning the South Atlantic Ocean into a foul-smelling "brown soup," with lines and patches of foam floating on it for miles out to sea.

rivers and in the winding of the creeks—a task difficult even for the most experienced navigator during those thick, wool-like mists called <term>smokes</term> <note>Dense seasonal mists common on the West African coast</note>. These mists hang about the entire Bight from November until May (the dry season), sometimes lasting all day and sometimes clearing three hours after sunrise.

The upper or north-westerly part of the swamp surrounds the mouths of the Niger. It successfully concealed this fact from geographers until 1830, when a series of heroic journeys made by Mungo Park, Clapperton, and the two Landers finally solved the mystery. This problem was as significant—and cost more men’s lives—than even the discovery of the sources of the Nile.

That this should be so may seem very strange to us now that we have been told the answer to the riddle. The upper waters of this great river were known before the time of Christ and were spoken of by Herodotus, Pliny, and Ptolemy. Furthermore, its mouths had been navigated continuously along the seaboard by trading vessels since the fifteenth century, but they were not recognized as belonging to the Niger. Some geographers held that the Senegal or the Gambia was its outlet; others thought it was the Zaire (Congo); and others believed that it did not reach the West Coast at all, but instead merged with the Nile in the middle of the continent, and so forth. 

Yet, when you come to know the swamps, this confusion is not so strange. You may find yourself going up what looks like a massive river—for example, the Forcados, which is two and a half miles wide at the entrance and a genuine part of the Niger. Before you have traveled far up it, great, broad, professional-looking river entrances open on either side. These show wide, mangrove-walled rivers, but two-thirds of them are complete deceptions that will run you aground within half an hour of entering them. A few of them do communicate with other main channels leading to the great upper river, and others are main channels themselves. However, most of them simply interconnect with each other and lead nowhere in particular, and you cannot even explore them because of their shallowness. It is little wonder that the earlier navigators in sailing ships did not get far up them, and that the problem had to be solved by men descending the main stream of the Niger before it begins

Far from it: they do not offer "gentle smiles." Instead, they are known for murdering any unprotected boat crew they happen to encounter, not only for the sake of the sport but to prevent white traders from penetrating the interior—where the goods are produced—and ruining their prices. But I do not need to go into further detail here regarding the discovery of the connection between the Niger and its delta. It is just the usual "bad luck" <term>ju-ju</term> <note>Traditional West African spiritual belief, here used to mean a curse or bad luck</note> associated with all great African rivers. If you find the mouth first, as with the Nile, you have a terrible time finding the source. If you find the upper waters, you have a terrible time discovering the mouth. If you find a section of its middle, like the Congo, you have a terrible time in both directions. Fortunately, the Congo "plays fair" and does not split itself up and dive into a mass of mangrove swamps like the Niger; therefore, that bit of river exploration was at least easier.

The rivers of the great mangrove swamp from the Sombreiro to the Rio del Rey are now known with some certainty not to be branches of the Niger, yet English explorers have much neglected the upper regions of this part of the Bight. I believe the great swamp region of the Bight of Biafra is the largest in the world. In its immensity and gloom, it possesses a grandeur equal to that of the Himalayas. I am not saying it has "beauty"; I admit I see great beauty in it sometimes, but it is evidently not of a popular type, for I can never persuade my companions down in the Rivers to recognize it. Still, it produces a powerful emotion in the bravest among them—even in those who have sailed around the world, who have cruised for years in the Southern seas, know the West Indies by heart, have traveled regularly for years to Rio de Janeiro, and have repeatedly visited where "thy towers, they say, gleam fair, Bombay, across the deep blue sea" <note>A reference to a well-known hymn or poem describing the city of Bombay (Mumbai).</note>.

Raised on stilts above the mud shore, you will see the white-painted factories and their great warehouses for oil; each factory is likely enough to have its flag at half-mast, which does not enliven the scenery either, for you know it is because somebody is "dead again." Throughout and over everything is the torrential downpour of the wet-season rain, coming down night and day with a dull roar. I have known it to rain for six long weeks in Bonny River, exactly as if it were being done by machinery; the only break that came then was a few wet days, after which it settled itself back to work again in a proper West Coast downpour for several more weeks. I imagine that junior clerks in the weather department must be entrusted with the weather of the Bight of Biafra because of its extreme simplicity; their duty is just to turn on several months of wet weather, and then a storm season—one tornado delivered every forty-eight hours; then stop all water supply and turn on the sun; then another storm season as before, and then back to the water tap. But I cannot say I think the weather does them any credit. Storms frequently come twice a day, and they frequently leave the water tap running a month longer than they should. As your eyes take in the characteristics of the Bonny scenery, you notice a peculiar smell—a stronger version of the scent you noticed when approaching Bonny from the sea in the evening. That is the breath of the malarial mud, heavy with fever, and chances are you will be bedridden by tomorrow. If it is near evening now, you can watch the mist take form, creeping, crawling, and gliding out from the side creeks and between the mangrove roots. It spreads across the river, stretching and rolling in a kind of grim play, finally crawling up the ship's side to come aboard and leave a cloak of moisture that grows green mildew over everything within a few hours. 

You will not be much troubled by noise; there is only the sound of the rain—a sound I have known to drive men sick with fever nearly mad—and the occasional depressing cry of the curlews <note>A type of wading bird with a long, slender, down-curved bill and a haunting call.</note> which are common here. This combination is such that after six or eight hours of it, you will be grateful to hear your shipmates start working the winch. I assume you are in a desperate state when you actually enjoy the sound of a winch. And you will say—regardless of your previous experience of the world—"Good heavens, what a place!"

I have been to the Bonny River five times now, and I like it. You always grow to like it if you live long enough for the strange fascination of the place to take hold of you. However, when I first entered it in the wet season of 1893—specifically in August—on a ship commanded by Captain Murray, a sense of horror seized me as I gazed upon the scene. Despite the confidence I had acquired by then in his skill and knowledge of the West Coast, I said to the veteran sailor who was then in charge of my education, "Good heavens! What an awful accident. We have gone and picked up the Styx <note>In Greek mythology, the Styx is the river that forms the boundary between Earth and the Underworld.</note>." 

He was evidently offended and said, "Bonny is a nice place once you get used to it." He then went on to talk about the last epidemic here, when nine out of the eleven residents died from yellow fever in about ten days. ...at the fourth funeral, two young men (who were junior clerks of the deceased man) were so drunk from fear that they fell into the grave before the coffin. "Was that even necessary?" remarked another member of the group, "since those two will likely need graves of their own before sunset tomorrow." The general consensus was that one of those periodic epidemics was "just about due." Aside from the scenery of "a River," for sheer cheerfulness, I recommend the local conversation in its mangrove-swamp regions. Every truly significant West African river has a mangrove-swamp belt which extends inland as far as the tide makes the water brackish <term>slightly salty water where fresh and salt water mix</term>. Its depth and distance from the banks depend on the geography of the country. 

Beyond this belt, there is consistently a region of high forest. Along the riverfront, there are clay cliffs—sometimes high, as in the case of the Old Calabar River at Adiabo, but more often short cliffs, as seen on the Forcados near Warri, and along a long stretch of the Ogowé River through the Kama country. Past the clay cliffs region, you reach a region of rapids caused by the river cutting its way through a mountain range. Such ranges include the Pallaballa, which cause the Livingstone Rapids on the Congo; the Sierra del Cristal <note>original: "Sierra del Cristal" — Crystal Mountains</note>, which create the rapids of the Ogowé and many smaller rivers; and the Rumby and Omon ranges, which create the rapids of the Old Calabar and Cross Rivers.

Naturally, these distinct regions vary in size in different areas. The mangrove swamp might only be a thin fringe at the mouth of the river, or it may cover hundreds of square miles. The clay cliffs might stretch for only a mile or so along the bank, or they might, as on the Ogowé, extend for 130 miles. It is the same with the rapids: in some rivers, such as the Cameroon, there are only a few miles of them; in others, there are many miles. In the Ogowé, there are as many as 500 miles of rapids. These rapids may be close to the river mouth, as in most of the Gold Coast <note>The British colony in West Africa that became the independent nation of Ghana in 1957.</note> rivers, except for the Ankobra and the Volta. Or, they may be far in the interior, as in the Cross River, where they begin about 200 miles inland, and on the Ogowé, where they begin about 208 miles from the sea coast. This depends on how near or remote the [mountains are]...

## CHAPTER VI

### LIBREVILLE AND GLASS

->In which the traveler pauses to explain various things and then gives<-
->some account of the country around Libreville and Glass.<-

I MUST pause here to explain my reasons for providing extracts from my diary, as I have been informed on excellent authority that publishing a diary is a form of literary crime. Such being the case, I must argue in defense of my committing it that—firstly, I have not done it before, for so far I have only given a brief summary <note>original: "*résumé*"</note> of many diaries I kept while visiting the regions I have attempted to describe. Secondly, no one expects literature in a travel book. Thirdly, there are things to be said in favor of the diary format, particularly when it is kept in a little-known and wild region; for the reader finds there notice of things that, although unimportant in themselves, nevertheless go to make up the conditions of life under which men and things exist. The worst part is that these things are not often presented in their due and proper proportion in diaries. Many pages in my journals—which I will spare you—demonstrate this crime perfectly. For example: "Terrible encounter with a crocodile about ten—Kerosene <term>paraffin</term> is good for over-oiled boots—Evil spirits crawl on the ground, hence the high doorframe <term>lintel</term>—Odeaka cheese <note>Dika bread, a foodstuff made from the kernels of the wild mango, *Irvingia gabonensis*</note> is made like this:—" Then follows a long description of the process for making Odeaka cheese.

When a person is out traveling, focused mainly on geography, it is necessary, if they publish their journals, that they should publish them in chronological order. But I am not a geographer. I have to learn the geography of a region I enter in great detail so that I can get around; but my methods of learning it are not the

I have omitted my entire wilderness journal. It is a record of researches into Fetish and of life in the forest and in native villages, and I believe I have a better chance of making this information understood by grouping it together. The African forest is not a place you can accurately describe within reasonable limits by simply chronicling your daily experiences. As a psychological study, the carefully kept journal of a white person would be exceedingly interesting—provided it covered a long period of time and started from the first day they left their fellow whites to live in the Great Forest Belt of Africa among natives who had not been influenced by European culture. However, to the general reader, such a journal would be hopelessly tedious. As for myself, I am not interested in lecturing on my own psychological state, but rather on the general state of affairs in West Africa.

When you first enter the vast, somber twilight regions of the forest, you hardly see anything except the thousands of massive, grey, column-like tree trunks surrounding you and the thin vegetation on the ground below. But day by day, as you become trained to your surroundings, you see more and more, and an entire world gradually emerges from the gloom before your eyes. Snakes, beetles, bats, and beasts populate the region that at first seemed lifeless.

It is the same with the brighter regions, where vegetation is diverse and lush. As you become accustomed to it, what at first seemed to be an inextricable tangle ceases to be so. The different types of plants stand out before your eyes with ever...

You eventually learn that it is easier to weave your way through networks of vines than to avoid them and attempt the softer-looking walls of climbing grasses and curtains of clubmoss <gloss>lycopodium</gloss>. Not only is it easier, but it is also safer; in the grass and clubmoss, there are almost certainly snakes galore, and there is a high chance you might force your way into the private sleeping quarters of a giant python.

There is a similar difference between night and day in the forest. You may have become fairly used to it by day, but then some mishap keeps you out all night, and you see an entirely different world. To my taste, nothing is as fascinating as spending a night out in an African forest or plantation, though I must emphasize that I do not advise anyone else to follow this practice. In fact, I do not recommend life in the African forest to anyone. Unless you are genuinely interested in it and fall under its spell, it is the most awful "living death" imaginable. It is like being trapped in a library full of books you cannot read, while being constantly tormented, terrified, and bored. Yet, if you do fall under its spell, it drains the color out of every other way of life. Still, it is good for a person to experience it, whether they like it or not. It teaches you how very dependent you have been, throughout your previous life, on the familiarity of your upbringing and on your fellow citizens. Moreover, it thoroughly humbles you during the days you spend clumsily stumbling around your new surroundings.

When this first period of adjustment passes, a sense of growing power emerges. The proudest day of my life was the day an old Fan <note>The Fang people of West Central Africa</note> hunter said to me, "Ah! You see." I should mention that he did not say this as a tribute to the hard work I had done to improve my observation skills; rather, he believed it was because a chief had given me a small ivory half-moon charm. Its special purpose was "to make man see Bush" <term>the ability to perceive and navigate the wild African jungle</term>. When you have fully attained that power—a state I do not pretend to have reached yet—you can say, "Put me wherever you like in an...

# VI WHY I WENT TO FRENCH CONGO

Just as it is with the forest, so it is with the minds of the locals. Unless you live alone among the native people, you never get to know them; if you do this, you gradually gain insight into the true state of their "mind-forest." At first, you see nothing but a mess of stupidity and crime; but once you begin to truly see—well, just like in the physical forest—you see things worth seeing. But it is beyond my ability to describe that process, so we will move on to the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>.

My reasons for traveling to this wildest and most dangerous part of the West African regions were perfectly simple and reasonable. I had not found many fish in the Oil Rivers <note>The Oil Rivers was a British protectorate in the Niger Delta, named for the palm oil trade.</note>, and as I have said, my only chance of obtaining a collection of fish from a river north of the Congo depended on the attitude Mr. C. G. Hudson might take toward <term>ichthyology</term> <note>The branch of zoology devoted to the study of fish.</note>. I had met Mr. Hudson in 1893 at Kabinda, when he rescued me from a dire dilemma. He proved himself so reliable that I did not hesitate to depend on his advice. Since those days in Kabinda, he had become a sort of "commercial Bishop"—that is, an Agent-General for Messrs. Hatton and Cookson in the French Congo. In this role, he had the power to let me travel up the Ogowé River, the largest river between the Niger and the Congo. 

In England, this river is mainly known through the works of Mr. Du Chaillu <note>Paul Du Chaillu (1831–1903), a French-American explorer famous for his accounts of gorillas and Pygmies.</note>, who, however, had the misfortune on both of his expeditions to miss actually discovering it. Still, he knew it was there and said so. Based on his reports, other explorers went out to look for it and duly found it, though I will discuss them later. It has been in French possession for nearly forty years now, and the French authorities maintain as much order as one can expect along its navigable waterway. This is a difficult task, considering that the dense surrounding forest harbors and protects several notoriously savage tribes, chief among which are the Fans <note>Now usually referred to as the Fang people.</note>. These Fans are a large tribe that has, within living memory, appeared in the regions known to white men during a migration toward the sea. They are a bright, active, and energetic type of African. Through their aggressive and predatory conduct, they do much to make one stop regretting and mourning the sloth and...

# LIBREVILLE AND GLASS CHAPTER

...lethargy of the other West Coast tribes; but I will speak of the Fans <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group in Central Africa known to the author for their energy and distinct culture.</note> later. I will merely preface my diary by stating that the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note> has a coastline of about 900 miles, extending from the Campo River to a point a few miles north of Landana, with the exception of the small Corisco region claimed by Spain. The borders of the <term>hinterland</term> <note>The inland region lying behind a coast.</note> are not yet defined, except for the Middle Congo. The French possession runs from Brazzaville on Stanley Pool up to the confluence of the Ubangi <note>original: "M'Ubanji"</note> with the Congo, then follows the western bank of the Ubangi. To the North-North-East, the borders are not yet defined, and although the French have displayed great courage and initiative, there are still vast stretches of country in the French Congo that have never been visited by a white man; however, the same may be said to a great extent of the West Coast territories held by England and Germany.

The entire territory that is currently roughly defined may have an area of 220,000 square miles, with a population estimated at anywhere from two to five million people.

The two main outlets for its trade are Gaboon and Fernan Vaz. Gaboon is the finest harbor on the western side of the continent, and for many years it was thought to be exactly what it looks like: the mouth of a great river. In recent years, however, it has been found to be merely one of those large tidal estuaries—like the Bonny River—that go thirty or forty miles inland and then end in a series of small rivers. While under the impression that Gaboon was one of the great waterways of Africa, France made it a headquarters for her West African Squadron and the starting point for exploring the surrounding country. It is said that her attention was first drawn to the importance of Gaboon by reports brought home by the expedition under the Prince de Joinville on the *Belle Poule* <note>original: "Beautiful Hen"</note>—who, in 1840, brought the body of Napoleon from St. Helena for burial in Paris. After de Joinville, the northern end of the Gaboon estuary became officially known by his name, although it is locally called Cape Santa Clara. This was possibly the name given to it by the Portuguese navigator Lopez Gonsalves, who, in 1469, made his great voyage of discovery on this coast, and whose name is still borne by Cape Lopez at the mouth of one of the Ogowé streams.

<page-num>105</page-num>

# VI GABOON AND LOANGO

Fernan Vaz and Cape Lopez are nowadays more important outlets for trade than Gaboon. The trade of the Rembo River and a portion of the main Ogowé trade comes to Fernan Vaz. This followed the discovery of the Ogololé Creek—a natural canal about twelve miles long with a fairly uniform width of fifty-five feet. Its course winds back and forth through the dense forest, and during the rainy season, it is possible to take a small stern-wheel steamboat up and down it. Cape Lopez is the outlet for the Yombas branch of the lower Ogowé, which is also navigable by a small steamboat. The Chargeur Réunis Company <note>A major French shipping company founded in 1872.</note>, subsidized by the government, provides this vessel, the *Éclaireur* <note>French for "The Scout."</note>, to run between Cape Lopez and Njole, the highest point on the Ogowé navigable by ships. The firm of Hatton and Cookson <note>An influential British trading company based in Liverpool with extensive operations in West Africa.</note> used to operate another small steamer that traveled directly between Gaboon and Njole, but unfortunately, it is no longer in service.

Today, Gaboon is merely a storage depot. If it weren't for its magnificent harbor and the fact that the government is already established there in sturdy, permanent buildings, Gaboon would be abandoned. This is because trade at Cape Lopez and Fernan Vaz has increased, while the trade coming down the Gaboon itself has declined. This decline is likely because French efforts have made the trade route via the main stream of the Ogowé safer and easier.

There is now another rival to Gaboon in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>: Loango. Loango owes its importance to the foresight and daring of Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza <note>The Italian-born French explorer who opened up the Congo Basin for France.</note>. When he reached Brazzaville (as it is now rightly called) on Stanley Pool <note>A large, lake-like widening in the lower Congo River.</note>, he saw the possibility of a feasible route through the Niari Valley from the Middle Congo regions to the sea. For de Brazza, recognizing the possibility of a thing is the same as making it a reality. Loango will gradually become the outlet for a very large portion of the Congo trade once the railway along the Niari Valley is completed. 

It has also been suggested that the government's headquarters should be moved from Gaboon to Loango. However, the arguments against this are the high initial expense and the fact that Loango has a poorer anchorage than Gaboon. Nevertheless, things tend to gravitate toward Loango, as it is a more important position from a local political standpoint...

# VI VIVE LA FRANCE 107

He speaks English perfectly, while retaining his French flourishes and conversational ornaments.

The Customs House <note>original: "The Post, *i.e.* Custom House"</note> is situated a hundred yards or so from the trading post <term>factory: a merchant's trading station or warehouse in a foreign country.</term>; like the trading post, it faces the beach. We make our way there over and through the usual debris of a southwest coast beach: water-worn logs, large hard seeds, old tins, and canoes that are drawn up out of reach of the ever-mischievous, thieving sea.

The Customs House is far more remarkable for its eccentricity than its beauty. It is two stories high, with the ground floor serving as the local jail. The officer in charge lives on the top floor and has a long, skeletal wooden staircase with which to communicate with the world below. This staircase is a literal "hen-roost" <note>A very steep, narrow ladder-like staircase.</note>. It is evidently designed to kill people, but why? Individuals wishing to smuggle goods would not be likely to frequent this Customs House staircase, and good people like me, who want to pay our duties, should be encouraged and not killed.

The officer is taking his afternoon nap <note>original: "siesta"</note>; but when awakened, he is courteous and kind. However, he impounds my revolver, making me feel like a criminal just for owning the thing. I am informed that if I pay fifteen shillings for a license, I may have it—provided I fire French ammunition out of it. This seems like a large sum, so I ask Monsieur <note>original: "M."</note> Pichault, our mentor, what I may be allowed to shoot if I pay this? Will it make me free, so to speak, to hunt everything locally? May I daily shoot governors, heads of departments, and junior officers <note>original: "*sous officiers*"</note>? Monsieur Pichault says, "Decidedly not"; I may shoot "hippopotamuses, or elephants, or crocodiles." Now, I have never tried shooting big game in Africa with a revolver, and as I do not intend to start, I leave the weapon in hock. My collecting cases and preservative alcohol <note>original: "spirit"</note>—the items I expected to reduce me to a financial wreck through customs duties—are passed entirely for free because they are for science. Long live France! <note>original: "*Vive la France!*"</note>

This statement gives me the opportunity I have long desired to meet Dr. Nassau, the great pioneer explorer of these regions and one of the greatest authorities on indigenous <term>native: referring here to the local African peoples and cultures.</term> subjects in all their aspects.

Although he has been out here, engaged in mission work, since 1851, he is an exceedingly active man and has a strangely gracious, refined, and courteous manner.

*22nd.*—Uninterrupted investigations of the seashore.

*23rd.*—Monsieur <note>original: "M."</note> Pichault conducts Mr. Huyghens and me into the town of Libreville to be registered.

The road from Glass to Libreville is, at times, very lovely and an impressive piece of work for the country and the climate. Around Glass, the land is swampy—a factor that probably induced the English to settle here when they came to Gabon <note>original: "Gaboon"</note>, for the English love, above all things, settling in or as near as possible to a good reeking, stinking swamp. We pass first along a paved section of road with the swamp on the left hand and, on the other side, a sandy, bush-grown piece of land with local houses on it, beyond which lies the seashore. Whenever the swamp reaches the edge of the shore, an iron viaduct has been built across it. The construction of this road cost the lives of seventy out of every one hundred Tonkinese <term>Tonkinese: Convicts brought from Tonkin, the northern region of modern-day Vietnam, which was then under French colonial rule.</term> convicts engaged in its building. After this swampy stretch, the road runs through sandy land—essentially the shore—with low hills on one side and the beach on the other.

A line of coconut palms has been planted along either side of the road for most of the way. They look beautiful but behave badly, for there is a telephone wire running along them from Libreville to Glass. These gossiping palms—the most relentless chatterers in the plant kingdom are coconut palms—talk to each other by brushing their hard leaves against the wire, just as they did at Fernando Po <note>An island in the Gulf of Guinea, now known as Bioko.</note>, so that mere human beings can hardly get a word in. This irritates the human "atom," <note>A metaphor for the insignificance of an individual person compared to the vastness of nature.</note> who naturally uses bad words toward the wire; I suspect these make up seventy-five percent of all the words that actually get through the patter of the palm leaves.

A two-and-a-half-mile walk brings us to the office of the Director of Internal Administration <note>original: "Directeur de l'Administration de l'Intérieur"</note>, and we wait around...

Courteously inviting us to be seated, he asks for our names, ages, and occupations <term>avocations: here referring to their professions or reasons for being in the colony.</term>. He enters these into a book for future reference and then writes out a permit for each of us to reside in the colony, provided we behave ourselves and obey its laws. These documents are sent upstairs to be signed by the acting Governor. While we wait for them to be returned, the official converses with Monsieur <note>original: "M."</note> Pichault about death, fever, and similar topics. 

Presently, a black man is shown in. He is wearing a blue serge coat, from underneath which the tails of a flannel shirt float over a pair of blue canvas trousers. On his feet is a pair of ammunition boots <term>ammunition boots: heavy, standard-issue military boots.</term> that nearly trip him up. The interpreter says his name is Joseph. 

"Who is your father?" asks the official. The clerk interprets this into trade English <note>trade English: West African Pidgin English used for commerce and administration.</note>. 

"Father?" says Joseph. 

"Yes, father," says the interpreter. 

"My father?" says Joseph. 

"Yes," says the interpreter; "who is your father?" 

"Who is my father?" says Joseph. 

"Take him away and let him think about it," says the officer with a sad, sarcastic smile. 

Joseph is alarmed and offers his mother's name instead. This is of no use; any fool can provide that sort of information. The Government is collecting information of a more obscure <term>recondite: hidden or beyond ordinary knowledge.</term> and interesting nature. Joseph is led away by Senegalese soldiers, boots and all. Since he is going to Boma, in the Congo Free State, the French Government must be taking this trouble to establish his genealogy for purely scientific <term>ethnological: relating to the study of human cultures and origins.</term> purposes.

Now that our stamped papers have arrived, we feel happier and free. But then Monsieur Pichault alarms us by saying, "Now for the Police." We trail off, feeling subdued, to the Palace of Justice <note>original: "Palais de Justice"</note>. There, we are promptly ushered into a room containing a vivacious, animated old gentleman who is incredibly kind and civil, and a powerful, calm young man with a reassuring "he's all right; it's just his way" manner regarding his superior. The chief is dressed in a white shirt and white trousers cut...

Once the formalities regarding us were concluded, the chief made a dash from behind his writing table, clapped his heels together, and bowed with a jerk that caused his trousers to collapse in coils, like the White Knight in *Alice in Wonderland*. My last view of him was a combat with them—I hope a successful one. I also hope their owner, who was leaving for home the next day, is now enjoying a well-earned, honorable rest after his long years of service to his country in the *French Congo* <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>.

*June 24th.—* A day of pouring rain.

*June 25th.—* I visited the Mother Superior and collected shells from the bay beyond Libreville. In the afternoon, I called on the missionary lady, who has now arrived with her young son via a German boat from Batanga. We discussed local religious beliefs <term>fetish: West African spiritual beliefs and the use of charms or ritual objects.</term>. Dr. Nassau told a very pathetic and beautiful story of an old chief at Eloby praying to the spirit of the new moon—which he regarded as a representative of a higher elemental power—to prevent the evil lower spirits from entering his town.

*Sunday, June 26th.—* Mr. Fildes evidently regards it as his duty to devote his Sunday mornings to ladies “assigned to the company,” and he took me in the light boat <term>gig: a light, narrow ship's boat adapted for rowing or sailing.</term> to go up the little river to the east. This river is clearly nothing more than the drainage of the surrounding swamp. The tide just allowed us to pass over the small sandbar, and then we rowed up the river, which is about forty feet across. It runs through a perfect jewel of a mangrove swamp, and the stench is exactly what one would expect—a real *Smell of the Niger Delta* <note>original: "Odeur de Niger Delta"</note>.

As we go higher up, the river channel winds back and forth between walls and slopes of jet-black slime, which is more lightly covered with mangrove bushes than near the entrance. This foul-smelling, soft mud is honeycombed with crab holes. The owners of these—green, blue, red, and black—are walking about sideways on the tips of their toes with that humorous self-importance peculiar to the crab family. I expected...

# VI CATCHING CRABS

I expected only to have to sit in the boat and say “Horrible” every now and then, but that was not the case; my companion, choosing a particularly disgusting-looking spot, said he “thought that would do,” steered the boat toward it, and jumped out with a squelch into the black slime. For one terrifying moment, I thought it was suicide, and that before I could even get the address of his relatives to break the news to them, there would be nothing left but a Panama hat lying on the mud in front of me. But he only sank about a foot or so and then started off—to my horror—calling the boys after him to hunt crabs for me. Now, I had never expressed any desire for crabs; I was merely looking at them, as I always do when out with other white people, noting where they were so I could return alone the next day to collect them. I did not want anyone’s blood, black or white, on my conscience. As soon as I regained my speech, I begged him to return to the boat and leave them alone; but no, “tears, prayers, entreaties, all in vain,” as Ko-Ko <note>A character from Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera *The Mikado* (1885).</note> says. He would not, and he dashed around in the foul-smelling mud regardless of the risk, with his four Kruboys <term>Kruboys: Men from the Kru ethnic group of Liberia and Ivory Coast, frequently employed as skilled sailors and laborers along the West African coast.</term> following him much more cautiously.

The terrified crabs were in a great panic. It seems to be crab etiquette that even when a powerfully built, agile, six-foot-tall young man is charging at you with all his might with a paddle, you must not rush into anyone’s house but your own. Because of this, many crabs were captured; but the matter did not end there. I had never suspected we would catch anything except a deadly fever, and so I had not brought a specimen box with me. Before I could protest, Mr. Fildes’s handkerchief was full of crabs, and mine was too. It was a beautiful sunny morning on the Equator, and therefore it was very hot, and we had nothing to wipe the sweat from our foreheads.

Once all the crabs on this mud bank were either caught or scared back to their holes, we proceeded further up the river. After some more crab hunts, we reached a place where I noticed you did not sink very deep if you kept moving; so I went ashore. We walked toward a gap in the mangroves where some tall trees were growing, and there we encountered some exceptionally lovely mayflies and had a great hunt. They have legs two to three inches long, white at the joints and black in between; a very small body with purple wings belongs to those legs, but you would not suspect this
