Then, in sheer desperation, we targeted the legs and discovered a tiny fly body attached to them, rather than a tiny spider body.

We then made our way onto the slightly higher land bordering the swamp. At the river end of the swamp, there was a belt of palms, and beyond this, a stand of redwoods, acacias, and other trees. Passing through these, we emerged into open, grass-covered country with low, rolling hills. It looked strangely English, with clumps of trees here and there, and densely wooded valleys running between the hills in all directions—a pleasant, comfortable-looking country.

We wandered through a great deal of grass, in which I silently noted there were millions of ticks. We headed for a group of homesteads and chatted with the inhabitants until Mr. Fildes’ conscience pricked him with the realization that he had not given out the cooking supplies for the midday meal. Then we took a shortcut to the boat, which required a lot of hopping through the mud, and so we returned home for a 12 o'clock breakfast.

At breakfast, I found that Mr. Fildes considers it his duty to perform more scientific work, for he asked me to go to Woermann’s farm <note>The Woermann-Linie was a major German shipping and trading company with significant operations in West Africa.</note>. Not knowing where it was, I said yes, privately hoping that the place might not be far away and would be situated in a reasonably dry area. I have lost all reliance on Mr. Fildes’ instinct for self-preservation—an instinct usually strong enough to keep a European on the West Coast from walking even a mile. Along the Windward Coast and in the Oil Rivers, I have always been regarded as insane for my habit of walking, but this gentleman is worth six of me any day—and sixty on Sundays, it is clear.

At 3 o’clock, off we went, turning down the "Boulevard" toward Libreville, and then up a road to the right opposite Woermann’s beach. We followed it through miles of grass over low hills. Here and there were huts that were new to me, and quite unlike the mud ones of the West Coast or the grass ones of the Congo and Angola districts. They are far inferior to the—

# VI BAMBOO HOUSES

...swish <term>a building material made of mud or clay mixed with water and often straw</term> huts of the Efik people, or the Moorish-looking mud ones you see around Cape Coast Castle and similar areas. They are notably inferior to the exceedingly neat Duala huts of Cameroon, but they are better than any other type of African house I have seen.

They are made of split bamboo with roofs made of mats, similar to Efik roofs, but again, of lower quality. I notice that sometimes the sections of the walls are constructed on the ground and then erected. The builder drives a row of strong wooden poles into the ground and then ties the wall sections onto them very neatly with "tie-tie" <term>vines or creepers used as natural rope</term>. The door and window frames and shutters are usually made of planks painted a bright cobalt blue, though occasionally they are red. I suspect that red paint has no business being there, as it looks like the red oxide a European gentleman might have brought out for painting boats.

Sometimes, however, instead of making the sections on the ground with closely set split bamboos, the builder drives unsplit bamboo poles into the earth and lashes the split bamboos to them, alternating between the inside and the outside. Palm-leaf mats are then fixed between these. I suspect this style of architecture is cheaper. Although there are many houses of both types being built on the hills around Glass and Libreville, I cannot say the building work is carried out with much vigor. There are plenty of skeletons of houses standing with just one or two sections tied in place, left as if the builder had gone on strike or simply grown tired of the job.

The stretch of broiling hot grass is taxing but interesting. Some of it is extremely fine and a beautiful yellow-green; I am told this is gathered, dried, and made into pillows. Other types are long and lanky, bearing maroon-colored ears <note>seed heads</note> that turn a gold color when ripe. In either state, it is very lovely when you come across stretches of it on a hillside.

On either side of us, wooded valleys appear like those we saw this morning; away to the east is the line of mangrove swamp fringing the little river we rowed up. To the west are the groves of mango trees around Libreville. Mango trees are only pretty when you are close to them—prettiest of all when you are walking through an avenue of them and can see their richness of color: the deep myrtle-green...

# LIBREVILLE AND GLASS CHAPTER

...leaves, with young shoots of a dull crimson, soft gray-brown stems, and luscious-looking fruit that tastes like turpentine but looks like a glorious gold and crimson nectarine.

We gradually enter a more beautiful type of country and descend into a forest. The tall trees are the typical variety found in high forests, with a majority of acacias. It is a forest of varied forms, though it is flowerless now during the dry season. There are quantities of ferns: hart's-tongues, the type that grows on oil palms, and elk's-horn ferns growing from large brown shields on the trees above. There is also bracken and pretty, trailing lycopodium <term>a type of clubmoss</term> climbing over everything—mostly over the cardamoms that abound in the undergrowth. Here and there are great banks of the most lovely ferns I have ever seen, besides the tree-fern; one is an ambitious climber called, I believe, *Nephrodium circutarium* by botanists. There are also walls of that strange climbing grass and thousands of other lovely things in every direction.

Butterflies and dragonflies were scarce here compared to Okijon, but other flies were more than plentiful.

The roadway is exceedingly good. In the grasslands, however, you are somewhat likely to "stub your toe"—as Captain Eversfield graphically puts it—against lava-like rock, because the grass has overgrown the road, leaving only a single-file path. In the forest, you come across isolated masses of stratified rock, sometimes eight or ten feet high, beautifully overgrown with moss and ferns.

We pass through several villages that Mr. Fildes tells me are Fan <note>The Fan, or Fang people, were frequently described in 19th-century travelogues as being fierce or cannibalistic, though Kingsley’s later accounts often challenged these stereotypes.</note> villages. They are highly interesting, especially after all I have heard about this tribe's bad reputation. Their houses are quite different from the M'pongwe ones we left behind; they are built of sheets of bark tied onto sticks.

In the streets, one frequently sees the characteristic standing drum, painted in white patterns with black or reddish-brown, with a piece of rawhide stretched across the top. One or two talking-drums <term>drums used to mimic the tone and rhythm of spoken language for communication</term> are also usually present.

We cross several pretty streams in the forest, which are carefully bridged with planks. This road, built by the Woermann company, is said to be between six and seven miles long, and its breadth...

# VI A DESERTED PLANTATION
->I 2<-

The road was a uniform nine feet wide and must have cost a great deal of money to construct. It was built for wagons drawn by oxen, which were intended to transport all the produce of the coffee plantation, as well as the timber cut down during the clearing, to Gaboon <note>Now Libreville, Gabon</note> for shipment. A large house was built and a great deal of coffee was planted, but then the enterprise was abandoned by the Woermann firm <note>The Woermann-Linie was a major German trading and shipping company</note>. Now, the entire project—the coffee, the road, and everything else—is rapidly being reclaimed by the jungle.

There is a fair-sized Fan village right at the entrance to the farm which features a large silk-cotton tree. It struck me as strange—having come from Calabar where these trees are frequently surrounded at their roots by spiritual charms <term>Kingsley uses "fetish objects" to describe traditional religious items</term>—to see nothing on this one except a framed and glazed image of the Virgin and Child. Just beyond the Fan town, there is a small river.

By the time we reached this point, it was too late to go any further. I believe that only this concern, supported by the memory of a night when he was forced to walk to Glass <note>A district of Libreville</note> from the farm, prevents Mr. Fildes from crossing to Corisco Bay.

So we turned around and returned in the same order we had arrived: Mr. Fildes led the way, and I followed behind him, moving like clockwork—which was my only chance of keeping up. When we finally reached the “Boulevard,” he wanted to reverse this order, but I refused to go in front without explaining why. I was remembering the terrible state the back of my blouse had gotten into at Fernando Po because of a black bootlace I had been forced to use as a *stay-lace* <term>a lace used to tighten a corset</term>.

27th.—I went up into the tall grass to see if there was anything to be found. There were ticks, plenty of ants, and flocks of very small birds—little finch-like creatures with soft, dull grey-brown feathers, highlighted by a shading of dark green on their backs and small crimson beaks. They have a lovely twittering song and are barely larger than butterflies; butterflies themselves are rare now. I noticed the local boys catch these birds using raw rubber as *birdlime* <term>a sticky substance smeared on branches to trap birds</term>. Down in the wooded hollows, there are many other birds, such as *plantain-eaters* <note>Also known as Turacos</note>, and a bird with a long, soft, rich thrush-like...

### LIBREVILLE AND GLASS DISTRICT

...like a musical note, and the ever-present Wu-tu-tu, known as the "clock bird." It is so named because of its regular habit of calling—from which its native name is derived—every two hours throughout the night, starting at 4:00 PM and ending its shift at 6:00 AM.

Upon my return home, I find that Mr. Hudson has returned from the Ogowé River on the *Mové*. I am happy to say he is unchanged since 1893. He informs me that the good Dom Joachim de Sousa Coutinho e Chichorro has passed away, and that his wife Donna Anna and her sister Donna Maria de Sousa Coutinho—both valued friends of mine—have returned to Lisbon from Kabinda <note>A coastal province and port in modern-day Angola</note>.

*28th.*—I go shell-hunting on the west side of Libreville. After passing through the town and in front of the Espíritu Santo mission station, which is nestled among mango trees, the road runs close to the sea through a beautiful avenue of coconut palms. There is a bridge, and just beyond it the road ends, so I walk along the sandy seashore for about a mile.

The forest borders the sand, rising like a wall of tall trees (not mangroves). Here and there, foul-smelling streams emerge from beneath them, and there are patches of conglomerate rock formed of pebbles and stratified green-gray rock.

Beyond Libreville, there are several small clearings in the forest with native villages tucked into them. The inhabitants seem to be a happy and contented people, mainly devoted to fishing, and they are very polite. On my walk back, I notice the people collecting water from those foul streams; it is no wonder the mortality rate is high in Libreville. This is usually blamed on the inhabitants "living too hard" <term>Kingsley uses the slang "going it" to refer to a lifestyle of hard drinking or reckless behavior</term>, but they could probably "live harder" than they do without killing themselves if they simply stopped drinking this essence of stinking slime.

*29th.*—I went to visit Mrs. Gault and Dr. Nassau. The doctor says the locals have a legend about a volcano located about sixty miles from here.

*30th.*—Mrs. Gault invites me to attend a Bible meeting held by a local woman. I agree and go. Mrs. Sarah, the Biblewoman, is a very handsome, dignified lady who speaks English very well. Besides her, Mrs. Gault, and myself, there are eight or nine local women and two men. I vividly remember Captain ———— being chased by a pig in the outskirts of *Die Grosse Colonie* <note>German: "The Great Colony"</note>, and then there is the risk of ants and such crawling up one’s ankles. Mrs. Gault gives a speech which Sarah translates into M'pongwe; then more hymns follow, the meeting ends, and the ladies settle down for a quiet pipe and a chat. We then stroll off to visit the houses of native Christians. Many houses here are built in clusters around a square, but this arrangement seems to be a mere relic of the past; I find there is no necessary relationship among the people living in the square, unlike in Calabar. And so, home.

*31st.*—I set out at 2:30 PM and walk through the grasslands behind Baraka, and suddenly fall down into a strange place.

Upon sitting up after the shock of an accidental descent of about thirteen feet, I find myself in a wild place. Before me are two cave-like pits, each with a rough wooden seat; behind me is another similar pit or chamber. The space I am in is about three feet wide; to the left, it is closed off by an earthen wall; to the right, it continues as a path down a trench that ends in dry grass.

There is no sign of human habitation. I wonder if these are places of sacrifice, or perhaps spots where the Fang people <note>The original text refers to "Fans," a common 19th-century name for the Fang ethnic group</note>—about whom one hears so much—come to secretly consume human flesh? They are clearly not the remains of an older civilization. In fact, what on earth are they? I investigate and discover they are nothing more than markers' pits for a rifle range.

Disgust, followed by alarm, seizes me. The French authorities might take it into their heads that I am sketching plans of their military works! Visions of imprisonment flash before my eyes, and I flee into more grass and ticks, heading westward until I find a path. Following this, I find myself in a small village. ->### LIBREVILLE AND GLASS CHAP. 118<-

...a head-shaped board mounted on a rough easel, and alongside it, a bundle of stakes. The whole setup was clearly connected with making palm oil and was identical to the device I saw in the distant Fan <note>The Fan (now commonly written as Fang) are an ethnic group found in Gabon and neighboring regions.</note> village on Sunday morning.

Upon investigation, I found that the boiled palm nuts are put into a pineapple-fiber bag, which is hung on the board. Then, stakes are wedged in between the uprights of the easel to squeeze the bag; one stake after another is added to increase the pressure. The oil runs out and flows off the point of the arrow-shaped board into a container placed to receive it.

The next object of interest is a piece of paper stuck on a stick at the far end of the villages. The inscription is interesting, though evidently recent. I found it says, "No thoroughfare." There is a bamboo gateway at this end, so I went through it and found myself, to my surprise, on the Woermann farm road <note>The Woermann-Linie was a major German shipping and trading company with plantations in the region.</note>. I walked down this road, hunting for butterflies.

Presently, I observed an old gentleman with a bundle of bamboos watching me intently. Since I do not know the locals of this country well yet, I felt anxious. After a few minutes, without taking his eyes off me, he crouched in the grass. I remembered the maxim of my great tutor, Captain Boler of Bonny: "Be afraid of an African if you can't help it, but never show it anyway." So, I walked on, intending to pass him with a propitiatory <term>intended to regain favor or reduce hostility</term> *M'bolo*. <note>The M'pongwe greeting; meaning, "May you live long."</note>

As I got alongside him, he hissed out, "Look at this!" <note>original: "Look him"</note> He evidently had something in the grass. Heaven send it is not a snake! But I "looked at it"—it was a lizard! The good soul understood collecting and had meant well from the first. I gave him tobacco and a selection of friendly observations. He beamed, and we went on down the road together, discussing the proper time to burn grass and the differences in practical value for building purposes between the two kinds of bamboo.

Then, coming to a path that clearly runs in the direction of the Plateau at Libreville, and thinking it was time I was heading homewards, I said "goodbye" to my companion and turned down the path. "Do you know the road?" <note>original: "You sabe 'em road?"</note> he asked in a very questioning voice. I said "yes" airily and kept on down it.

The path goes on through grass and then heads for a hollow—I wish it didn't, for hollows are unpleasant at times, and—

-># A WAYWARD PATH<-
->### LIBREVILLE AND GLASS<-

Evidently, something is wrong with this road, and it is not popular, for the grass hangs over it like unkempt hair. The road becomes damp and enters a belt of trees, in the middle of which runs a broad stream with a log laid across it. Congratulating myself on the absence of companions, I ignominiously crawl across onto the road. The path then and there turns around and goes back to the stream again further up—evidently a joke, a "thought-you-were-going-to-get-home-dry-did-you" sort of thing. I wade through the stream and rejoin the road on this side.

Then the wretched path makes a deliberate bolt for the interior of Africa instead of continuing toward Libreville. I lose confidence in it. The Wu-tu-tu <note>This was Mary Kingsley’s nickname for her watch.</note> says it is four o’clock. It gets dark at 6:15 p.m. down here, and I am miles from home, so I begin to wish I had an intelligent companion to guide me as I walk on through the now shoulder-high grass.

Suddenly, another road branches off to the left. "Saved!" I head down it, but then it ends in a manioc <term>Also known as cassava, a starchy root crop.</term> patch with no path out the other side, surrounded by impenetrable bush. Crestfallen, I retrace my steps and continue along my old tormentor, which now attempts to reassure me by doubling back to the left and setting off again for Libreville. I am not deceived; my trust in it has been too seriously undermined. Yes, it is up to mischief again, and it turns itself into a stream. 

There is nothing for it but wading, so I wade; but what will its next manifestation be, I wonder? I begin to doubt whether it is a road at all and suspect it of being only a local devil <note>A reference to local forest spirits or malevolent entities believed to lead travelers astray.</note>, the sort that sometimes appears as a road, sometimes as a tree or a stream, and so on. I wonder what the people at the mission will do if they find I don’t return tonight? They likely wish I were back in Liverpool, at the very least.

After fifteen minutes of knee-deep wading, I suddenly meet a local lady who was at the Bible meeting. She has an excellent knowledge of English, and she stands with her skirt tucked up around her. She is evidently in no hurry and is determined to find out exactly who I am. Recognizing this, I attempt to take charge of the conversation and change its course. 

"This is a nice road," I say, "but it is a little damp." 

"It is watery, ma'am," she says, "but—"

"Does this road actually go anywhere," I interjected, "or is it only a kind of joke?" 

"It doesn’t go anywhere in particular, ma'am," she says, "but—" 

"In a civilized..."

“In a community like this of Gabon,” I said, “it is scandalous that roads should be allowed to wander about in such a loose way.” “That is certainly true,” she agreed; “but, ma—<note>“Ma” was a common respectful form of address for a woman in West Africa.</note>” “You must excuse me,” I answered, “I am in a great hurry <margin>✓</margin> to get back, but I hope to meet you again. Where do you live? I will call on you.” She gave me her address but did not move, and the grass walls on either side of the stream-bed road were high and dense. “My husband,” she said, “worked for H. and C. <note>Hatton and Cookson, a prominent British trading company in West Africa.</note>; he is dead now.” “Dear me, that is very sad; you must have been very sorry,” I answered sympathetically, thinking I had successfully changed the conversation. “We all were; he had ten wives.” “But, ma—” I was damp and desperate, so pushing into the tall grass at the side, I successfully circumnavigated her portly frame. Saying a cheery “goodbye,” I bolted. The uninterrupted question finally came wafting after me on the breeze; but I did not return to discuss the matter. 

Soon reaching drier ground and seeing a path that led toward the boulevard, I hurried down it as quickly as my feet could carry me. Before I realized where I was, I found myself in a network of small irrigation canals running between neatly kept beds of tomatoes, salad greens, etc. A group of Vietnamese <term>Originally "Anamese," referring to people from Annam, a French protectorate in what is now Vietnam.</term> convicts were working busily there. These convicts are deported from the French Cochin-China <note>A former French colony encompassing southern Vietnam.</note> possessions and employed by the Public Works Department in various ways. Those who behave well and survive are given grants of garden plots. They cultivate these in a tidy, meticulously detailed way that is entirely different from the haphazard African methods of doing things. 

They sell their produce to the town residents and live quite prosperously this way. However, the climate of West Africa is almost, if not quite, as deadly to Asian peoples as it is to whites—a fact that has been amply demonstrated not only here, but also in the Belgian Congo <note>Original: "Congo Belge."</note>. There, the railway company conducted a series of experiments with imported labor—experiments that resulted in a terrible waste of human life. None of the imported workers withstood the climate any better than the white men, and you know what that implies. This labor question here is an issue that increases daily with the development of plantation enterprises—

—enterprise, I do not believe will ever be solved by importing foreign labor. Nor is it advisable that it should be, for our European government stops the factors that used to keep the native population down—such as intertribal wars, ritual sacrifices, etc.—and the export of the surplus population as slaves. Therefore, unless ways to support "the indigenous ones," as Mrs. Gault calls them, are developed, Africa will have us to blame for severe bouts of famine. This is because the locals, if left to their own methods, will never farm the land enough to support a large population; furthermore, a vast percentage of the West African soil is very poor, acidic stuff that grows nothing but equally worthless vegetation. From this discussion, you can gather that I finally made it home.

*June 2nd.*—The *Nubia* <note>A steamship of the African Steamship Company.</note> is in, but she will not stop at Batanga, so Mrs. Gault is stuck here until another steamer arrives. The *Nubia* lost all her heavy anchors further south, where the crew reports the Calemma <term>The powerful Atlantic surf or ground swell characteristic of the West African coast.</term> is exceptionally bad this year.

*3rd.*—I went alone for a long walk to the bend of the mangrove-swamp river to the east. It smelled terrible, but it was most interesting, offering a miniature version of the conditions of life in a mangrove swamp. Leaving this, I headed northwest along local paths across stretches of grass growing on rolling hills and down through wooded valleys. Each valley had a small stream or a patch of swamp where giant arums <note>A family of plants including many tropical species like the calla lily or elephant ear.</note> and other water plants grew. I passed through Fan <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group of Central Africa.</note> villages, each consisting of just one straight street with a clubhouse at either end. In the forest, I met a hunter carrying home a deer he had shot; in addition to his musket, he carried a couple of long, tufted spears of an ancient style. He was very talkative, and I gave him some tobacco while we discussed hunting. Upon parting, I gave him some more tobacco because he kindly gave me a charm to help me see things in the forest. He was pleased and said, "You very nice," "Goodbye," "Good day," "So long," and "Good night." This was very kind of him, as these phrases were evidently all the friendly English greetings he knew. You often hear the locals in Gabon say "So long"; it always sounds quite charming. They have, of course—

## CHAPTER VII

### THE OGOWÉ

->Wherein the traveler provides extracts from the logbooks of the *Mové* and the *Eclaireur* <note>Two steam launches used for river travel.</note>, and an account of the traveler’s first meeting with “those fearsome Fans” <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group in Central Africa known at the time for being warlike.</note>; also, a stern warning to all young people who neglect their study of the French language.<-

*June 5th, 1895.*—I set off on the *Mové* at 9:30 AM. The passengers include Mr. Hudson, Mr. Woods, Mr. Huyghens, Father Steinitz, and myself. There are plenty of African deck-passengers; I do not know their respectable names, but they are clearly very much married men, for there is quite a brightly colored little crowd of ladies to see them off. They greeted me as I passed down the pier and began asking questions. I said to them hastily: “Farewell, I am off upriver,” because I noticed Mr. Fildes approaching me, and I did not want him to start a conversation about local social gossip. I expect that matter is settled now, or very nearly so.

There is a fair amount of gentle commotion among the African group, and the *Mové* decisively sets off before even half of the good advice and well-wishes for the African husbands are brought aboard. She is a fine little vessel—much better than I expected. The accommodations I have been given are excellent: a long, narrow cabin with one bunk and almost everything one could wish for, even including a copying press. The food is excellent, the company charming, and the captain and engineer are real assets. The saloon is square and spacious for the size of the ship, and most things, from rowlocks <term>U-shaped fittings on the side of a boat that hold oars in place.</term> to teapots, are kept under the seats in proper nautical style. 

We stopped at the guard-ship <term>A vessel stationed to supervise or protect a port or coast.</term> to present our papers, then steamed ahead out of the Gabon estuary to the south, rounding Pongara Point while staying close to the land. About forty feet from the shore, there is a clear, deep channel for vessels with a light draught <term>A shallow depth of water needed for a boat to float.</term>. If you do not take this channel, you must make a wide turn out to sea to avoid a reef. Between four and five miles—

Below Pongara, we pass Point Gombi, which is equipped with a lighthouse—a bright and noticeable structure by day as well as by night. It is perched on a small hill near the end of a long stretch of low, sandy ground. It is painted with black and white horizontal stripes which, along with its overall shape, give it the appearance of a pagoda.

Next to it stands a white house with a red roof for the lighthouse keeper, and a storage building for the oil. The light is either flashing, revolving, or stationary—at least when it is actually lit. One must be precise about such details; my information comes from what I have been told, and amounts to the description above. I cannot offer any personal experience because I have never passed it at night, and seen from Glass <note>The commercial district of Libreville, Gabon.</note>, it appears to be a steady light. Most lighthouses on this coast stop performing fancy tricks like flashing or revolving quite soon after they are established. Seventy-five percent of them are not lit half the time anyway. "It’s the climate," people say. However, you can depend on Gombi to be lit at night, and I have no hesitation in saying it is visible for seventeen miles out to sea. The hill on which the lighthouse stands is a grass-covered sand cliff, roughly forty or fifty feet above sea level.

As we round Point Gombi, the weather becomes noticeably rough, especially during lunch. The *Mové* handles it better than her passengers and pushes steadily along past the wooded shore, behind which a distant range of blue hills is visible. Silence falls over the African passengers, who lie down on the deck and suffer. All the items from under the saloon seats slide out and dance together, playing "puss-in-the-corner" <note>A traditional children's game; used here to describe loose objects sliding across the deck.</note> as loose gear often does when the sea is rough.

As night falls, the scene becomes increasingly picturesque. The moonlit sea shimmers and breaks against the dark shore; the black forest and the hills are silhouetted against a purple sky dusted with stars. At my feet, the engine-room stoke-hole <term>The space in front of a ship's furnace where the stokers stand.</term> is lit by the rose-colored glow of the furnace. By the great wood fire, I can see the two nearly naked Krumen stokers <term>Krumen: An ethnic group from the West African coast (Liberia/Ivory Coast) famous for their skills as sailors and ship laborers.</term>, their skin shining like polished bronze from sweat as they throw logs of red wood into the fire that look like freshly cut chunks of flesh. At last, we anchor for the night just inside Nazareth Bay, because Nazareth Bay requires daylight to navigate, being full of low islands and sandbars. We crossed the Equator this afternoon.

*June 6th.*—We set off at daybreak into Nazareth Bay. The navigators showed great anxiety; soundings were taken on both sides of the bow with long bamboo poles painted in stripes. We go “slow ahead” and “hard astern” successfully until we round a large island, but there we remain stuck until four o’clock high tide. When the water rises, we get off safely and steam triumphantly but cautiously into the Ogowé River. The shores of Nazareth Bay are fringed with <term>mangroves (coastal trees with tangled roots that grow in salty water)</term>, but once in the river, the scenery soon changes. The waters are walled on either side by a forest rich in bamboo, oil palms, and wine palms. These forest cliffs seem to rise straight up out of the mirror-like brown water. Many of the tallest trees are covered with clusters of brownish-pink young shoots that look like flowers, and others are decorated by my old enemy, the <term>climbing palm (a thorny, vine-like palm tree)</term>, which is now bearing clusters of bright crimson berries. The great brown river stretches away unbroken, looking like a broad road of polished bronze. Behind us, the *Mové’s* <term>screw (propeller)</term> leaves a trail like a streak of frosted silver in the water. Just about six o'clock, we reach the *Fallabar*, the ship that preceded the *Mové* in working the Ogowé. It is now a <term>hulk (a decommissioned ship stripped of its engines and used for storage)</term>, serving as a depot for the firm of Hatton and Cookson. She is anchored at the entrance of a creek that leads to Fernan Vaz; some say it is a six-hour journey, while others say it takes eight hours by canoe. Everyone agrees that there are plenty of mosquitoes.

The *Fallabar* looks grimly picturesque and is about the last place where a nervous person would want to spend the night. One half of her deck is reserved for fuel logs; the other half contains wooden stores for goods and a room for the African sub-trader in charge of them. I am certain there must be scorpions that crawl out of those logs and into the living quarters, and God only knows what else one might imagine coming up the creek or rising out of the floating grass or the seemingly endless forest. I am told she was a fine steamer in her day, but those in charge did not account for how quickly the Ogowé water rots metal. Consequently, her hull rusted through before her engines were even a quarter worn out. There was nothing left to do but fill her with concrete and turn her into a depot. In this role, she is very useful, because during the height of the dry season, the *Mové* cannot get through the creek to supply the company's factories at Fernan Vaz.

Later, I heard a great deal about the *Fallabar*, which seems to have been a famous—or rather, notorious—vessel. Everyone claimed her engines possessed immense power, but I believe this was merely a local legend. # VII SHIPS CLIMBING TREES
127

...if those *Fallabar* engines could have been sent to Chatham dockyard, people would mention that “you could not get any speed out of her.” All who knew her sadly admitted that “she wouldn’t steer.” Consequently, she spent most of her time on the Ogowé River stuck on a sandbank or in the brush. All West African steamers seem to have an obsession with the jungle and suffer from the delusion that they are supposed to climb trees. The *Fallabar* had this affliction severely because of her poor steering abilities, combined with the temptation offered by the magnificent forest, the rapid currents, and the sharp turns of the creek district. She failed to climb them, of course—they all do—but it was not for lack of trying. I have seen many West Coast vessels stuck in trees, but never more than fifteen feet or so above the water.

The trade of this lower part of the Ogowé, from the mouth to Lembarene—a distance of about 130 miles—is virtually non-existent. Above Lembarene, however, you come into contact with the rubber and ivory trade.

This *Fallabar* creek is famous for mosquitoes. In the evening, the African passengers made elaborate and visible preparations for their onslaught by tying their sturdy <term>chintz</term> <note>a multicolored printed cotton fabric</note> mosquito nets to the <term>stanchions</term> <note>upright posts or supports on a ship</note> and the cook-house. Their arrangements were constantly interrupted by the white engineer causing a commotion among them. This was because if too many people gathered on one side, the *Mové* would <term>list</term> <note>lean to one side</note>, which causes her boilers to burn unevenly. Both the conversation and the atmosphere are full of mosquitoes. The consensus among the experienced travelers with us is that, after the lower Ogowé, New Orleans is the worst place for them in the world.

The day ended with magnificent, dramatic beauty. Directly ahead of us, the moon rose through a bank of dull, brownish-grey mist—a great crimson orb casting a blood-red reflection across the still, oil-smooth river. Directly behind us, the sun sank into the mist, an even larger crimson orb. Once it had vanished from sight, it sent up flashes of amethyst, gold, carmine, and vibrant green before leaving the moon in undisputed possession of the deep purple sky.

The forest and river were absolutely silent, but there was a pleasant chatter and laughter from the African crew and passengers further forward, which made the *Mové* seem like an island of life in a land of death. I retired to my cabin to get under the mosquito curtains to write. One by one, I heard my companions enter the adjacent saloon and say to the watchman: “Do you know six o'clock? When the long hand reaches that spot and the short hand reaches that spot, wake me in the morning.” Then they would leave the saloon—silence—then another would say: “Do you know five o'clock? When the long hand reaches that spot and the short hand reaches that spot, wake me in the morning.” Again, an exit—silence—then: “Do you know half-past five? When the long hand—” Oh, if I were a watchman! In any case, that five-o'clock caller will have the entire ship's company awake in the morning.

*June 7th.*—Everyone was woken up in the morning by the commotion resulting from the five-o'clock caller being roused. It is a glorious morning. The scene is the complete reverse of last night. To the east, the forest shows a deep blue-purple, set against a background that changes as you watch it—from the colors of daffodils and amethyst to a rose-pink—as the sun rises through the night mists. The moon sinks down into the mist, her pale face flushing crimson as she descends; then the yellow-gold sunshine arrives, glorifying the forest and gilding the great sweep of tufted papyrus growing along the bank. The mist vanishes, though little white flecks of it linger among the water reeds and lie in the dark shadows of the forest trunks. The air is full of the long, soft, rich notes of the plaintive warblers, and the noise resulting from the *Mové* taking on firewood, which arrives in canoe loads from the *Fallabar*.

Father <note>original: "Père"</note> Steinitz and Mr. Woods are busy preparing their respective canoes for their journey to Fernan Vaz through the creek. Their canoes are very fine ones, with a remarkably <term>clean run aft</term> <note>a streamlined hull design toward the stern (back) of a boat</note>. The Father’s boat is a proper traveling canoe, featuring a small bamboo platform at the back covered with a hood of palm thatch. Underneath it, you can make yourself quite comfortable and keep yourself and your belongings dry, unless a particularly heavy rainstorm occurs.

### VII A FOREST OF FLOWERS
<sig>K</sig>

...river at full speed. The river seems broader above the *Fallabar* <note>A decommissioned vessel used as a factory or stationary post</note>, but this is mainly because it is temporarily free of islands. Much of the bank we have passed on the south side since leaving Nazareth Bay has been the shoreline of islands, with a channel running between the islands and the true southern bank.

The day soon turned overcast and looked threatening, in the deceptive way of the dry season. The climbing plants here are more magnificent than any I have ever seen before. They form massive veils and curtains over and between the trees. They often hang so straight and flat—in stretches twenty to forty feet wide and thirty to seventy feet high—that it seems incredible that no human hand has trained or pruned them into such perfect shapes. Sometimes these curtains are adorned with large, bell-shaped, brightly colored flowers; at other times, they feature delicate sprays of white blossoms. This forest exceeds all my expectations of tropical abundance and beauty. It belongs to another world compared to the forest of the Upper Calabar, which, despite its own beauty, seems plain and dull by comparison. There, you certainly feel a sense of grimness and vastness; here, you find that same scale but with the addition of superb color. This forest is a Cleopatra <note>Symbolizing exotic beauty and luxury</note> compared to which Calabar is merely a Quaker <note>A reference to the Religious Society of Friends, known for their historical preference for plain, unadorned clothing</note>.

The forest does not rely solely on flowers for its brightness. Many types of trees have young shoots in shades of crimson, brownish-pink, and creamy yellow. In addition, there is the refreshing appearance of the local West African trees, which typically have white trunks. These are often splashed with pale pink lichen and vermilion-red fungus, which is enough on its own to keep the massive amount of vegetation from becoming a monotonous green.

All day long, we steam past constantly changing scenes of loveliness. The individual parts remain the same, yet the overall effect is always different. It is probably wrong to call it a symphony, yet I know no other word that better describes the scenery of the Ogowé. It is as full of life, beauty, and passion as any symphony Beethoven ever composed; the themes change, interweave, and return. There are *recurring themes* <note>original: "leit motifs"</note> here as well. You see the papyrus plants ahead, and you know that when you pull alongside them, you...

But as the *Mové* passes, her wake <note>original: "wash"</note> sets it undulating in waves across its vast expanse, showing it is only riding at anchor. You know that after a patch of grass, you will soon see a small red clay cliff with a village perched on its top. The inhabitants, dressed in their blue and red cloths, stand by to shout and wave at the *Mové*, or run as fast as they can <note>original: "legging it like lamp-lighters," referring to the speed of men who hurried to light streetlamps</note> from the back streets and the plantations to the riverfront just to be there in time. Through all these changing scenes, there is always the presence of the vast, wild forest and the swift, deep, silent river.

At almost every village we pass—and they are frequent after the *Fallabar* <note>A decommissioned vessel used as a stationary trading post</note>—there is a showy display of firewood piled either on the bank or on posts driven into the mud in front of it. In their own unrefined way, they are silently saying, “Try our famous wood; best value for your money”—meaning tobacco and other trade goods—to the *Mové* or any other small steamer that might come along hungry for fuel.

Mr. Hudson is immersed in accounts all day. I stare at the forest, while Mr. Huyghens watches the engines. The captain spends most of his time on top of the sun deck; however, every twenty minutes or so, everyone except Mr. Hudson and Mr. Huyghens goes down into the rear storage area <term>afterhold</term>. If Mr. Hudson were not on board, I would go down too, just to see what on earth they have down there. When the Krumen <note>West African sailors and laborers, often from the Kru ethnic group of Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire</note> return, they carry pails of dirty water. Mr. Hudson, kindly fearing I will think the *Mové* is leaking badly, explains that the water comes from something connected to the propeller, caused by the condition of the watertight seal <term>packing</term>. Then the captain appears with his arms full of canned food. The engineer arrives empty-handed but looking content. Rosa, Mr. Hudson’s devoted servant, follows with boots and boot-cleaning supplies. I wish to goodness I could go down there; perhaps I would find hairpins and ammonia, both of which I desperately need—especially the ammonia for these mosquito bites.

### VII THE SS. ÉCLAIREUR

We stopped for a few minutes this afternoon at Ashchyouka, where an enterprising young Frenchman rowed out to us in a canoe. He has established and maintained a coffee plantation in this remote region, which I am glad to hear is just now starting to produce a harvest. After leaving Ashchyouka, high ground appeared to the northeast. At 5:15 p.m., for no reason obvious to the inexperienced observer, the *Mové* began whistling like a large ocean liner. A few minutes later, a trading post <term>factory</term> belonging to the Woermann line appeared on the hilly north bank; then, just beyond and behind it, we saw the Government Post, and then Hatton and Cookson’s trading post, all situated in a row. 

Opposite Hatton and Cookson’s, a charming little stern-wheel steamer was docked against the steep clay bank of Lambaréné Island as we came into sight. However, she immediately pulled away in a perfect curve, leaving a trail of frosted silver on the water as she headed downstream. I learned later that she was the *Éclaireur* <note>French: "Scout" or "Pathfinder"</note>, the stern-wheeler that operates on the Ogowé River for the Chargeurs Réunis Company <note>French: "United Shippers"</note>. This company is subsidized by the government, and when the *Mové* whistled, the *Éclaireur* was just finishing loading 3,000 logs <term>billets</term> of wood for fuel. She travels up from Cape Lopez using a mix of wood and coal as far as Njole and back to Lambaréné; from Lambaréné down to the sea, she runs entirely on wood. 

In a few minutes, we took her spot close to the bank and tied up to a tree. The white engineer shouted to the Black engineer, "Tom-Tom: Pull out some of that fire and open those drains immediately!" The stokers used hooks to pull the glowing logs onto the iron deck in front of the furnace door and threw water over them. The *Mové* released a cloud of oily steam toward the bank, nearly scalding some of the local admirers gathered there. I suspect the ship felt spiteful because they had been admiring the *Éclaireur*.

After a few minutes, I was escorted onto the wide veranda of Hatton and Cookson’s trading post, where I sat down under a lamp, ready to admire the wild beauty of the scenery until dinner. This plan was not carried out; in the twinkling of an eye, I was bitten all over my neck and realized there were far too many mosquitoes and sandflies in the scenery to permit any kind of peaceful reflection. Never—

# THE OGOWÉ CHAPTER

Never have I seen sandflies and mosquitoes in such appalling quantities. With a wild ping of joy, the latter made for me, and I retired promptly into a dark corner of the porch, swearing horribly—but only internally—and fought them off. Mr. Hudson, the Agent-General, and Mr. Cockshut, the Agent for the Ogowé, walked up and down the beach in front, presumably talking about cargo and appearing unconscious of the mosquitoes; but by and by, while we were having dinner, they got their share. I behaved exquisitely, and was quite lost in admiration of my own conduct. I was busily deciding in my own mind whether I should wear one of those plain ring halos or a solid plate one, in the style of Cimabue <note>original: "à la Cimabue." Cenni di Pepo (Cimabue) was an Italian painter; Kingsley is jokingly comparing her stoicism to that of a saint in a medieval painting.</note>, when Mr. Hudson said in a voice full of reproach to Mr. Cockshut, “You have mosquitoes here, Mr. Cockshut.” 

Poor Mr. Cockshut did not deny it; he had four on his forehead and his hands were covered with them, but he said, “There are none at Njole,” which we all felt was an absurdly weak excuse, for Njole is some ninety miles above Lambaréné, where we are now. Mr. Hudson said this to him bluntly, and feeling he had utterly crushed Mr. Cockshut, he turned on me. Failing entirely to recognize me as a suffering saint, he said directly and irritably, “You don’t seem to feel these things, Miss Kingsley.” Not feel them, indeed! Why, I could cry over them. Well! That is all the thanks one gets for trying not to be a nuisance in this world.

After dinner, I went back to the *Mové* for the night, for it was too late to go round to Kangwe and ask Madame Jacot, of the Evangelical Mission <note>original: "Mission Evangelique"</note>, if she would take me in. The air was thick with mosquitoes, and after saying a few suitable words to them, I dashed under the mosquito net and slept, lulled by their shrill yells of frustrated rage.

*June 8th.*—In the morning, I was up at five. There was great activity on the beach. The *Mové* was simultaneously taking on wood fuel and discharging cargo. A very active young French pastor from the Kangwe mission station was around looking for the mission’s cargo. Mr. Hudson kindly made inquiries as to whether I might go over to Kangwe and stay with Madame Jacot. He said, “Oh, yes,” but as I found he was not Monsieur Jacot, I did not feel justified in accepting this statement without having personal confirmation from Madame Jacot herself; and so, leaving my luggage with the

# VII FIRST STAY IN KANGWE

Since the *Mové* <note>The steamer *Mové*</note> was staying, I got them to allow me to go around with the captain and his cargo to Kangwe. This was about a forty-five-minute paddle around the upper part of Lambaréné Island and down the broad channel on the other side. Kangwe is beautifully situated on a hill, as its name suggests, on the mainland and the north bank of the river. Madame Jacot most kindly said I could stay, even though I knew I would be a terrible nuisance, because there was no room for me except Monsieur Jacot's beautifully neat, clean, and tidy study. I went back in the canoe to fetch my luggage from the *Mové* and said goodbye to Mr. Hudson. He gave me a great deal of valuable advice, which was later very useful to me, and many equally good warnings. If I had listened to them, I would have been able to avoid many, if not all, of my mishaps in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>.

I camped out that night in Monsieur Jacot's study, wondering how he would feel when he came home and found me there; he was currently away on one of his usual evangelizing tours. Fortunately, before Monsieur Jacot returned, Madame Jacot let me have the room where the girls belonging to the mission school usually slept, much to my relief.

<margin>✓</margin>
I will not bore you with my diary entries from my first stay at Kangwe. It is simply a list of the collection of fish, etc., that I made, and a record of the continuous, never-failing kindness and help I received from Monsieur and Madame Jacot. It also records my attempts to learn from them the peculiarities of the region, the native people, and their language and customs, all of which they both know so well and manage so admirably. Every day, I saw what it is possible to achieve even in the wildest and most remote regions of West Africa. I realized there is still one heroic type of human being whose praise has never been adequately sung: the missionary's wife. Despite all the drawbacks and difficulties of the draining climate, the lack of trained domestic help, and the addition of two small children of her own—Edmond the <term>sententious</term> <note>Given to moralizing in a pompous or formal manner.</note>, aged five, and "Roger the Great," aged eighteen months and teething with phenomenal speed and vigor—along with a group of school children from the Fan and Igalwa tribes, Madame Jacot kept that mission house as clean, tidy, and well-ordered as if it were in Paris.

# THE OGOWÉ CHAPTER

One of the main comforts I had at Kangwe was the perfect English spoken by both Monsieur and Madame Jacot. Only I know how much that meant to me, because I cannot speak a word of French. Nor could I give you specific dates until I left Kangwe on the *Eclaireur*, for it is one of my disastrous habits—well known to my friends on the Coast—that whenever I am happy, comfortable, and content, I lose all track of the date, the time of day, and my hairpins. "It’s the climate." 

However, I kept my fetish notes <note>Kingsley's ethnographic notes on local religious beliefs and "fetishes."</note>, except for two days when my right elbow was out of commission as a result of my first visit to a Fan <note>The proper way to spell this tribe's name is Faung, but as they were called "Fans" by the first writer to describe them, Paul Du Chaillu, I will keep that name. They are also referred to as the M'pangwe, the Pahouines, the Fam-Fam, the Osheba, and the Ba-fann—the latter being a plural form.</note> fireside. It happened this way: 

Down on the river bank, about a mile and a half below Kangwe, lies Fula, a large Fan village. On that unlucky day, I passed through Fula with all the fanfare <note>original: *éclat*</note> of Wombwell’s traveling circus <note>Wombwell’s Traveling Menagerie was a famous 19th-century touring animal show.</note>. After being escorted by half the population for about half a mile or so beyond the town, and feeling nervous about the Fans based on information I had received, I decided to return to Kangwe by another road, if I could find one. 

I had not gone far on my search before I saw another village. Having had enough "village work" for one day, I made my way quietly up into the forest on the steep hillside overhanging that village. There was no path up there, and while going through a clump of *shenja* <term>Shenja: A type of tall, sharp-edged sword-grass or sedge common in the region.</term>, I slipped, slid, and finally fell right through the roof of an unprotected hut. 

I don’t know what the unfortunate inhabitants were doing, but I am fairly certain they were not expecting me to "drop in," and a scene of great confusion followed. My knowledge of the Fan dialect at the time consisted only of the word *Kor-kor* <note>A common greeting or expression of goodwill.</note>, so I said that in as charming a tone as possible. I explained the rest using three pocket handkerchiefs, a bundle of tobacco, and a knife which, luckily, I had stored in what my sailor friends would call my "after-hold"—my pockets. I also said I would pay for the damage. Although this important message had to be delivered in trade English <term>Trade English: A simplified Pidgin English used for commerce between Europeans and West Africans.</term>, they seemed to understand; when I pointed to the roof and mimicked writing a "book" <note>In West African Pidgin, a "book" referred to any written document, such as a receipt or a formal promise of payment.</note> for it, the master of the house...

# VII. BOARDING THE *ÉCLAIREUR*

He said "Um," and then grabbed an old lady, pointing first to her and then to the roof. He clearly meant that I had caused equal damage to both, and that she was just as valuable as the roof. Wishing to travel further up the Ogowe, I took the opportunity to board a river boat belonging to the *Chargeurs Réunis* <note>A French merchant shipping company.</note> during one of its trips up to Njole.

*June 22nd.*—The *Éclaireur* <note>French for "Scout" or "Pathfinder."</note> is a charming little stern-wheel steamer, kept in exquisite condition. She has an upper and a lower deck. He is a tremendously lively person who has survived blackwater fever <term>a severe complication of malaria</term> four times while out in the bush with nothing to live on but manioc <term>a starchy root also known as cassava</term>, a diet that would be much easier to die on under those circumstances. He describes Monsieur S— with his pince-nez <term>eyeglasses clipped to the bridge of the nose</term>, the Doctor, and, above all, the rapids of the Ogowé. He rolls his hands round and round each other and dashes them forward with a descriptive sound effect of "Whish, flash, boom, boom, bump," and then comes what clearly represents a terrifying struggle for life against overwhelming odds. I truly wish to goodness I knew French; since I want to see these rapids myself, I cannot help feeling anxious and worried at not fully understanding this dramatic performance regarding them. 

There is another passenger said to be the engineer's brother, a quiet, gentlemanly man. The captain argues violently with everyone: with Mr. Cockshut on the subject of the shameful waste of money in maintaining the *Mové* and not shipping all goods by the *Éclaireur*, "isn't that so?" <note>original: "n'est-ce pas ?"</note>; and with the French official on goodness knows what, but I imagine it will be "pistols for two and coffee for one" <note>A humorous reference to a duel fought at dawn.</note> by morning. When the captain feels himself being defeated in an argument, he shouts for support to the engineer and his brother. "Isn't that so?" <note>original: "N'est-ce pas ?"</note> he says, turning furiously to them. "Yes, yes, certainly," <note>original: "Oui, oui, certainement"</note> they say dutifully and calmly, and then he, refreshed by their support, dashes back into his controversial fray. 

He even tries to start a row with me regarding the English merchants at Calabar, whom he asserts have sworn a kind of blood oath to ship by none but British African Company's steamers. I cannot stand for this, for I know my esteemed and honored friends the Calabar traders would ship by the *Flying Dutchman* <note>A legendary ghost ship that can never make port.</note> or the devil himself if either of them would take the cargo at 15 shillings per ton. We have, however, to stop this argument for lack of a shared language, to our mutual regret, for it would have been a magnificent fight.

It flows in quietly from the east-southeast—a broad, quiet river here with low banks and two islands (Walker’s islands) visible just at its entrance. Further upstream, it flows through mountainous terrain. At Samba, the furthest point reachable by boat, there is a stunningly beautiful waterfall where the entire river pours over a low cliff, encircled by a natural amphitheater of mountains. It takes the *Éclaireur* two days of steaming from the mouth of the Ngunie to reach Samba when the water is high enough. However, at the peak of the long dry season, neither she nor the *Mové* can make the trip because of sandbanks; as a result, Samba is cut off until next October. 

The Hatton and Cookson company has factories <note>Trading posts or warehouses.</note> at Samba, because it serves as an outlet for the rubber and ivory trade from Achango land. This trade is managed by the Akele tribe, a powerful and difficult people to deal with. From what I can gather, they remain in the same state as they were when Paul Du Chaillu <note>A famous 19th-century French-American explorer of Central Africa.</note> made his remarkable journeys among them. 

While I was at Lambaréné waiting for the *Éclaireur*, a notorious chief attacked and looted a sub-factory on the Ngunie. The wife of the African trading agent put up a brave resistance while her husband was away on a trading expedition, but the chief ordered her to be seized, beaten, and thrown into the river. An appeal was made to the Doctor, who was then the Administrator of the Ogowé—a powerful and helpful official. He soon arrived with a small gunboat <term>cannonier</term>, bringing Mr. Cockshut with him to defend the honor of the French flag, under which all these factories operate. 

Once they arrived at the scene of the incident, they sent a message to the chief, inviting him to come down and discuss the matter <term>palaver</term>. Being a fool, the chief arrived with two of his headmen and some followers. Only he and his headmen were allowed into the room, while three or four Senegalese soldiers guarded the door. The three white men—the Doctor, the captain of the gunboat, and Mr. Cockshut—each tackled one of the men. After a significant struggle, they wrestled them to the ground and bound them. The injured woman was then brought in and given a *kasanguru* <note>A whip, often made of hippopotamus hide, used for punishment.</note>, with which she personally "thanked" the chief with all her might. The banks of the Ogowé River just above Lambaréné Island are low. The forest is broken only by village clearings, and it seems to press in on them, ready to reclaim the land if the inhabitants ever stop their struggle against it. The blue mountains of Achango land appear as a distant range to the east-southeast. Behind us, the high ground of Lambaréné Island gradually fades into the distance.

Soon we pull up alongside a large village street with four tall houses that rise a story above the others, which are all single-story. Over the side and into the canoes they go. The boats rock wildly and wobble away quickly toward the bank, frightening the passengers because they are wearing their best clothes and fear that the *Éclaireur* will start moving and capsize them with its wake.

Upon reaching the bank, the new arrivals disappear into crowds of wives and relatives, and the dogs into fighting clusters of local dogs. What a happy, happy day! The men who have gone ashore have been away working for the government and trading posts on year-long contracts; they are now safely home with their families again, bringing back not only themselves but all the goods they received as pay. The remaining passengers below still shout to their departing friends; I do not know exactly what they are saying, but I expect it is the <term>Fan: an ethnic group of Central Africa, also known as the Fang</term> equivalent for "Be sure to write. Take care of yourself. Yes, I will come and see you soon," and so on. While all this is happening, the *Éclaireur* quietly slides down the river with the current, drifting broadside as if it could smell its stable at Lambaréné. I find this is its constant habit whenever the captain, the engineer, and the helmsman are all busy standing in a row along the railing shouting over the side, which happens whenever we have passengers to land. Once its drifting is noticed after the last canoe load has left for the shore, the ship is turned around and sent back upriver at full speed. Just as this is being done, the local inhabitants greet the captain with a ceremonial gun salute. I am quietly leaning against his cabin door at the time when—*bang!*—comes his answering salute from inside, just three and a half inches from my right ear. I was stunned for several minutes. The captain was apologetic; he "did not know I was there." I was apologetic too; I knew he was there, "but I did not know he was going to fire his gun." "He is forgiven." "Isn't that so?" "Yes, yes, certainly," <note>original: "N'est-ce pas?" "Oui, oui, certainement"</note> I say, quoting the engineer. Peace is restored.

We continue upstream, occasionally stopping at small villages to land passengers or at small trading posts to unload cargo, until evening falls. He looks like only a boy, but he is actually twenty years old. He is French and worked for the firm of Hatton and Cookson first; then he joined Woermann’s, who have put him in charge of this post. The isolation for a white man must be terrible; sometimes two months pass without him seeing another white face except his own in the mirror. When he does see someone else, it is only during a fleeting visit like the one we are paying him now. To make the most of this, he stays on board for dinner. While waiting for dinner that night, as I sat at the lounge table, I saw a strange sight on the couch opposite me. Is a fever coming on? Or is it because some brain cells were permanently shaken out of place by the shock of that gun blast this afternoon? I did not mention it to my fellow passengers, who did not seem to notice it, for fear of being mocked; instead, I watched it secretly during dinner. It did not move or multiply, nor did it have a glowing halo. These were all good signs, but still, it could not possibly be a black silk <term>chimney-pot hat: a tall silk top hat</term>. Yet, after all, it was, and it belonged to the captain. How, why, or when he got it, I do not know—neither do I know exactly what he and the passengers are doing with it now that I have retired to my cabin, which is next to the lounge. 

I am quite sure that the French official is the ringleader of the proceedings, for I recognize his voice; he is currently singing tunes I have heard at the <note>The Jacots were French Protestant missionaries at Lambaréné.</note> Jacots’ as hymns. I am convinced, however, that they are not being used as hymns now, because you do not dance a version of a Highland fling—which I can tell is happening from the vibrations reaching me—to hymns; nor do you greet them with shouts of laughter. I wish—no, of course I don’t, for it involves neither <term>fetish: traditional West African spiritual objects or beliefs</term> nor fish. Moreover, during the intervals filled with loud conversation, I am perfectly sure I hear the French official trying to convince the others that I am an English officer in disguise, acting as a spy. This makes me feel embarrassed and anything but flattered. I wish to goodness I knew French, or knew how to flirt with that French official just enough to dispel his illusion.

*June 23rd.*—We set off steaming upriver early in the morning. The land ahead appears mountainous. Quite suddenly, the banks grow higher. Here and there in the forest are patches that look like regular, hand-made plantations.

# VII UMBRELLA TREES

...ations, which they are not, but are only patches of <term>engombie-gombie: the Musanga cecropioides or umbrella tree</term> trees, indicating that a native town once stood at this location. Whenever land is cleared along here, this tree sprouts up all over the ground. It grows very rapidly and has large leaves somewhat like a sycamore leaf, only much larger. Because these leaves grow in a cluster at the top of a straight stem, they give the plant an umbrella-like appearance. Consequently, the natives use the same name for both the tree and an actual umbrella; however, I cannot determine whether they think the umbrella resembles the tree or the tree resembles the umbrella. I am always getting myself confused over this sort of thing in my attempts "to contemplate phenomena from a scientific standpoint," as <note>Kingsley was commissioned by researchers at Cambridge to collect biological specimens and ethnographic data during her travels.</note> Cambridge ordered me to do. I will give up that habit. "You can't do that sort of thing out here—it’s the climate," so I will content myself with stating the fact that when a native comes into a store and wants an umbrella, he asks for an *engombie-gombie*.

The consistent height of the individual trees in one of these patches is striking, and it happens because they all start growing at the same time. I cannot figure out other details about them to my satisfaction, for one very rarely sees them in the wild bush; furthermore, they do not bear a fruit that the natives collect and use, only to then throw away the seeds around their homes. Regardless, there they are: all the same height and the same color, apparently allowing no other vegetation to make any progress among them. 

However, when I carefully investigated these *engombie-gombie* patches, I found that there were a few of the massive, slower-growing forest trees sprouting up amongst them. In time, when these reach a sufficient height, their shade kills off the *engombie-gombie*, and the patch is reclaimed by the great forest from which it came. The frequency of these patches arises from the nomadic habits of the primary tribe in these regions, the <note>The Fans (now usually referred to as the Fang people) are an ethnic group native to equatorial Africa.</note> Fans. They rarely occupy one village site for any considerable time. This is due, first, to their wasteful method of collecting rubber by cutting down the vine—which soon wipes it out of a district—and second, to their quarrelsome nature. So, when a village of Fans has exhausted all the rubber in its district, or has made the area too hostile to remain in due to "rows" <term>rows: heated arguments or disputes</term> with other villages, or has...

When a village has been properly bombarded and burned for an attack on traders or for disrespecting the French flag in any way, its inhabitants simply move to another district and build a new village. Bark and palm thatch are cheap, and moving house is effortless. When you are an unsophisticated Fan cannibal, you do not require a <term>pantechnicon: a large van used for moving furniture</term> to pack up your one or two mushroom-shaped stools, knives, cooking pots, and a <term>calabash: a container made from a dried gourd</term> or two. If you are wealthy, perhaps you will also have a chest for clothes, but as a general rule, all your clothes are on your back. 

So, the wives simply pick up the stools, the knives, the cooking pots, and the chest, while the children toddle off with the calabashes. You, of course, carry the gun, for whether awake or asleep, a Fan never parts with his weapon. And there you are—"finished," as Monsieur Pichault would say—and before your new bark house is even built, the <term>engombie-gombie: the umbrella tree (Musanga cecropioides)</term> begins to grow where your house once stood. 

Now and then, for lack of nearby neighboring villages to quarrel with, one end of a village will pick a fight with the other end. The weaker faction then leaves and builds itself another village, keeping a sharp eye out for any member of the stronger faction who might conveniently wander into their neighborhood to be killed and eaten. Meanwhile, the *engombie-gombie* grows over the houses of the abandoned end, making it look like a plantation belonging to the remaining half of the village. 

I once heard a newcomer argue eloquently that the Fans were slandered. "They say," he said, with a grand wave of his arm toward such a patch of trees, "that these people do not farm the soil—that they are not industrious—that the few plantations they do make are poorly maintained—that they are only a group of wandering hunters and cannibals. Look there at those magnificent plantations!" I did look, but I did not change my opinion of the Fans, for I recognize my old friend, the *engombie-gombie*, when I see it.

This morning the French official seems sad and melancholy. I suspect he has a <note>“Monday head” is a reference to a phrase used by Rudyard Kipling, meaning a hangover or a sluggish, foggy feeling at the start of the work week.</note> "Monday head," but he perks up as the day goes on. As we continue, the banks turn into hills, and the broad river—which has been showing stretches of sandbanks in every direction—now narrows. It shows only neat little beaches of white sand in shallow places along the bank. The current is terrific. The *Éclaireur* <note>The *Éclaireur* (meaning "Scout") was the stern-wheel steamer on which Kingsley traveled.</note> labors heavily and uses all...

### VII ARRIVE AT NJOLE

The river is so strong that the boat must use all the power she has to fight her way up against it. Masses of black, weathered rock in great boulders appear along the exposed parts of both banks, left dry by the falling waters. Each bank is steep, and many large trees, stripped and bare, hang down from them. They are held back from being swept away by the rushing current only by their roots and an entanglement of woody vines <term>bush-rope: a common West African term for lianas or climbing vines</term>, forming a great white fringe along the banks. The hills become higher and more abrupt, and the river runs between them in a gloomy ravine, winding back and forth. We catch sight of a patch of white sand ahead, which I mistake for a white-painted house, but immediately after rounding a bend, we see the houses of the Talagouga Mission Station. 

The *Éclaireur* <note>original: "The Scout"</note> immediately has a hysterical fit on her whistle to startle Monsieur Forget and get him to dash off in his canoe to meet her at once. Apparently, he knows the ship and does not hurry but comes on board quietly. I find there will be no place for me to stay at Njole, so I decide to continue on the *Éclaireur* and use her as a hotel while there; afterward, I will return and stay with Madame Forget, if she will have me. I consult Monsieur Forget on this point. He says, “Oh, yes,” but he seems to have recently lost something of great value and isn't quite sure where. It was just his manner, I suppose. 

When Monsieur Forget has received his mail, he leaves and the *Éclaireur* continues; indeed, she has never really stopped, for the water here is too deep to anchor, and the terrific current would promptly whisk the steamer down out of the Talagouga gorge if she stopped fighting it. We run on up past Talagouga Island, where the river broadens out again a little, but not much, and reach Njole by nightfall. We tie up to a tree by the Dumas trading post <term>factory: a merchant's trading station or warehouse</term> beach. There is the usual uproar, but as Mr. Cockshut says, there are no mosquitoes. The mosquito belt ends abruptly at O' Soamokita.

*June 24th.*—Mr. Cockshut, who went ashore last night, kindly comes on board and asks me if I will go ashore to his branch trading post. I say yes and go, but once ashore, I decide not to disrupt the domestic arrangements of Hatton and Cookson by staying in the trading post. Besides, I see a real road before me to the left—the first road I have seen for months. I tell Mr. Cockshut I will go for a walk; he seems

### VII AN ACCLIMATIZATION GARDEN <note>original: "A JARDIN D’ACCLIMATATION" — A garden used for the purpose of introducing and adapting foreign plants and animals to a new environment.</note>

...river. The road continues into the valley, as pleasant as ever, if not more so. How wonderful it would be if our government along the Coast had the same enterprise and public spirit as the French, and built such roads on the slim chance that a stray traveler might arrive by steamer once every ten years and want a walk. 

I notice some extremely neat huts built by the Igalwa people <note>The Igalwa are an ethnic group from the lower Ogowé region of Gabon.</note>. The people are sitting on the bright, clean ground outside them, weaving mats and baskets. "Hello to you all," I say. "Hello," <note>original: "Mboloani" and "Ai Mbolo," greetings in the Omyene languages.</note> they reply, and they stop their work to stare at me. I see large wire enclosures on the left side of the road and investigate them. I find they are inhabited by animals—goats, sheep, chickens, and so on. This is clearly an acclimatization garden. It is no wonder the colony is not profitable if it invests in this sort of thing 206 miles inland, where there is simply no public to pay admission fees. 

While contemplating these things, I hear a terrible hiss. Snakes? No, geese. A massive fight ensued. Good, old-fashioned long skirts are truly wonderful for Africa! I make it through the geese and continue in good order, though moving quite quickly down the road. I turn a sharp corner past some native houses and encounter a turkey cock—a terrifying confrontation. I flee forward down the road, which is still going strong, now heading in a northerly direction and seemingly going on forever. I hope to goodness there will be a turn I can take to get back without having to return through this ferocious farmyard. 

Intent on finding such an exit, I walk about thirty yards further down the road. I hear shouts coming from a grove of banana trees on my left. I know they are directed at me, but it is not always wise to respond to shouts. I expect it is just a local person with a limited knowledge of English, eager to ask about my family history; therefore, I speed up. 

The shouts grow louder: "Madame Gacon! Madame Gacon!" Out of the banana grove comes a large, stout, pleasant-looking gentleman, dressed in an undershirt and a divided skirt. Since white people must be acknowledged, I walk carefully toward him through a plantation of young coffee, apologizing humbly for trespassing on his land. He smiles and bows gracefully, but—horror!—he knows no English, and I know no French. It was a "very inexplicable and very interesting" <note>original: "très inexplicable et très interessante"</note> situation, as I later heard him remark. The worst of it is that he is clearly dying to know who I—

We sit down opposite each other at a table and wait for the interpreter who is being fetched. The house is built low to the ground in the native style, but it is beautifully maintained and arranged with an artistic flair that is quite as unexpected as the rest of my surroundings. On the walls, I notice sets of pictures depicting terrifying incidents from Algerian campaigns and a copy of that superb portrait of Monsieur de Brazza <note>Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza (1852–1905) was a French explorer and the colonial founder of the French Congo.</note> wearing Arab headgear. 

Soon the Black attendants who had been sent to find one of the plantation workers—someone supposed to know both French and English—return with the "interpreter." That young man is a fraud. He does not know English—not even "Coast English" <note>A form of West African Pidgin English used for trade.</note>—and all he has inside his head is a deep ignorance made worse by terror. After one or two failed attempts and some frantic scratching at both of those areas that an African seems to regard as the source of intellectual inspiration, he bolts out the door. *A terrible situation!* <note>original: "Situation terrible!"</note> My host and I smile wildly at each other, and both wonder in our respective languages what—in the words of Mr. Squeers <note>A character from Charles Dickens's *Nicholas Nickleby*.</note> mentioned in the classics—we "shall do in this here most awful go." 

We are both going mad with the strain of the situation when the engineer’s brother from the *Éclaireur* <note>A French steamer that navigated the Ogowé River.</note> walks in. ...I am sure he told the planter something like this: “Calm yourself, my friend; we picked up this curiosity at Lambaréné. Now, although the engineer’s brother would not admit it, he knew English. So, I told him how the beauty of the road had lured me onward, how interested I was in coffee-planting, and how much I admired the magnificence of this plantation and all the enterprise and energy it represented.

“Yes, yes, certainly,” <note>original: "*Oui, oui, certainement*"</note> he said, and translated my words. My friend the planter seemed charmed; it was the first sign of anything approaching reason he had seen in me. He offered me sugar water <note>original: "*eau sucrée*": a common French beverage of the time made by dissolving sugar in water.</note> more kindly than ever. I must see the plantation, “the whole plantation” <note>original: "*toute la plantation*"</note>. 

So, presently, the three of us went out and thoroughly toured the grounds. It was the most well-ordered, well-cultivated plantation I have ever seen, and a very noble monument to the knowledge and industry of the planter. For two hot hours, these two perfect gentlemen showed me over it. I also behaved well; for though my petticoats were ample, they did not prevent insects and "critters" <term>catawumpuses: a playful term for various biting insects or strange creatures</term> of all sorts from crawling up my ankles and feeding on me as I stood in the long grass. This grass had been very wisely cut and laid around the young trees for mulching <term>mulching: the practice of placing organic material around plants to preserve moisture and improve the soil</term>. 

This plantation is of great extent, covering the hillsides and the valley bottom; portions of it are just now beginning to bear fruit. The whole place is kept as perfectly as a garden, which is amazing considering it is the work of one white man with a staff of only eighty unskilled native laborers. The coffee planted consists of three kinds: the Elephant berry, the Arabian, and the San Thomé.
