The ferns were evidently being carefully tended among some coffee plants. It was highly exciting, and I tried to learn more about them. It seemed unlikely—even in this center of enterprise—that they had been brought from the Australasian region just "for show" <term>original: "for dandy"; meaning for ornament or vanity</term>, and I had never encountered them in my travels except on the island of Fernando Po. Unfortunately, my friends thought I wanted to keep them and shouted for men to bring tools and dig them up. I had a brisk little skirmish with the men, driving them away from their prey with the point of my umbrella, while squawking "Kor Kor" like an agitated crow. When they finally understood that my interest in the ferns was scientific rather than piratical, they called the men off. They explained that the ferns had been discovered in the wilderness when the land was being cleared for the plantation.

Ultimately, with many bows and my most sincere thanks, we parted—luckily beyond the reach of the geese. I returned down the road to Njole, where I found Mr. Cockshut waiting outside his factory <term>a merchant's trading post and warehouse</term>. He insisted on taking me to the Post to see the Administrator. From there, he said I could board the *Éclaireur* from the Post beach, as the ship would be moving there from Dumas’ factory. We set off up the road that skirts the riverbank, which consists of a low clay cliff overgrown with vegetation except where it has been cleared for beaches. The road is short but exceedingly pretty. On the side opposite the river is a steep bank where a cocoa plantation is growing. 

Lying out in the center of the river, you can see Njole Island. It is a low, sandy island, wooded not only with wild bush but also with orange and other fruit trees. Formerly, the Government Post and the trading factories were situated on the island, but now only their trees remain for various reasons—one being that the island is often underwater during the rainy season. Everything is now situated in a rambling but picturesque line on the northern bank of the mainland. First comes Woermann’s factory, then Hatton and Cookson’s, and then John Holt’s; these last two are close together with a shared beach in a style that is quite friendly for factories, which usually barricade themselves firmly against their next-door neighbors. Then comes Dumas’ beach, a small native village, the cocoa patch, and finally the Post at the up-river end of the European settlement—an end to European civilization, I am told, for a distance of five hundred miles. <header>VII THE FRENCH ADMINISTRATOR</header>

The Post is a small river flowing into the Ogowé. On its far bank sits a small village belonging to a chief who, having heard of the glories of the Government, came down to see it—like the Queen of Sheba in spirit, if not in personal appearance. He has been so charmed by what he found that he has stayed here just to gaze at it.

Although Mr. Cockshut forced the Administrator of the Ogowé out of his bath, that gentleman is exceedingly amiable and charming. He is all the more pleasant to me because he speaks good English. Personally, he is large, handsome, exuberant, and energetic. He shows me around with gracious enthusiasm, pointing out all kinds of things: large gorilla teeth and heads, native spears, and guns decorated with brass nails. While we are in his study, he explains that the little model canoe full of Kola nuts <term>seeds containing caffeine, used as a stimulant</term> is his supply to help him stay up all night to work. 

Then he takes us outside to see the new hospital. In his capacity as Administrator—acting while the professional Administrator is away on leave in France—he has granted this hospital to himself in his capacity as a Doctor. He shows us the captive chief and headman from Samba, who are busily quarrying a clay cliff behind the building to enlarge the government plateau. He also points out the former ministers of the ex-King of Dahomey <note>The Kingdom of Dahomey was a major regional power until its colonization by France in the 1890s</note>. They have been deported to Njole and seem comfortable, employed in various non-menial occupations. 

Next, we walk down a small avenue of cacao trees in full fruit and head to the left, where there is an encampment of Adoomas <term>an ethnic group from the upper Ogowé known for their skill as canoeists</term>. They have come down as a convoy from Franceville and are preparing to return with another group under the command of our lively fellow passenger. I am sorry to see that he will have a difficult time regarding his accommodations; he will be traveling in those narrow, shallow canoes currently tied to the bank, with no other white man to talk to. He will certainly be a conversational blessing to Franceville when he arrives. The Adooma encampment is very picturesque, as they have set up their bright-colored chintz mosquito nets to serve as tents.

There are lovely *odeaka* trees <term>also known as Dika nut or wild mango trees</term> that form a gateway like a triumphal arch leading from the river to the Post’s beach. Under them, the doctor speaks in a most interesting way on all sorts of subjects. We continue waiting for the *Éclaireur* <note>original: "Éclaireur"; French for "Scout" or "Pathfinder"</note>, which is still down at Dumas’ beach even though it is past four o'clock. I feel almost frantic for delaying the doctor, but neither he nor Mr. Cockshut seem to be in the least hurry. 

At last, I can stand it no longer. The image of the Administrator of the Ogowé is too painful to imagine: exhausted, yet chewing kola nuts <term>seeds containing caffeine, used as a stimulant</term> to stay awake all night while he finishes his reports to go down on the *Éclaireur* tomorrow morning. Therefore, I say I will walk back to Dumas’ beach and board the *Éclaireur* there, hoping to free the Administrator from his social obligations so he can return to his work. 

It is no use! He insists on coming down to Dumas’ with Mr. Cockshut and me. Off we go; just as we reach Dumas’ beach, the *Éclaireur* starts off with a shriek, heading for the Post beach. So I say goodbye to Mr. Cockshut and return to the Post with Dr. Pélessier. He sees me on board, and to my immense relief, he stays on board for a good hour and a half talking to other people. Thus, it is not my fault if he has to stay up all night.

*June 25th.*—The *Éclaireur* has to wait for the Administrator until ten o'clock because he has not finished his mail. At ten, he comes on board like a friendly whirlwind, as he is traveling to Cape Lopez himself. I am saddened to see them also carrying a French official on board who is very ill with fever. He is the engineer of the gunboat <note>original: "cannonier"</note>, and they are taking him down to Cape Lopez. They hope to find a ship there to take him to Gaboon and to the hospital on the *Minervé*. I later heard that the poor man died at Achyouka, in the Kama country, about forty hours after leaving Njole.

We finally get away and move rapidly downriver, aided by the powerful current. The *Éclaireur* must stop at Talagouga to pick up planks from Mr. <note>original: "M."; abbreviation for Monsieur</note> Gacon’s sawmill. As soon as we pass the end of Talagouga Island, the *Éclaireur* ties its whistle cord to a support beam and breaks into a series of screaming fits, as only that ship can. The goal is to prompt Mr. Forget or Mr. Gacon—or better still, both—to come out in their canoes with the wood ready for her, because the ship cannot anchor in such deep water.

Gacon comes along among the trees on the bank and laughs at her. A rope is thrown to him, and the laboring *Éclaireur* is tied to a tree close to the bank. The water here is deep enough to moor an ocean liner, though there are many rocks. 

In a few minutes, M. Forget and several canoes full of beautiful red-brown mahogany planks are on board. Once the business is finished, I say goodbye to the captain and head to the shore in a canoe with M. Forget.

# CHAPTER VIII

## TALAGOUGA

->Concerning the district of Talagouga, with observations and advice on catching snakes.<-

Mrs. Forget received me with great kindness and hospitality. She, along with her husband, their infant daughter, and Mr. and Mrs. Gacon, represent the Evangelical Mission <note>original: "Mission Évangélique"; referring to the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society active in the French Congo.</note> and the white race at Talagouga. Mrs. Gacon is the lady the planter mistook me for; when I saw her sweet young face and masses of pale gold hair, I felt highly flattered. Either 그 planter must be very short-sighted, or the color of my hair must have misled him—not that mine is pale gold, but rather the color of hay. I do not know how he made the mistake. Mrs. Forget is a truly beautiful French woman, with pale, transparent skin and perfect, large dark eyes; she possesses an indescribable charm, grace, and liveliness in conversation. It grieves me to think of her being wasted in this savage wilderness, surrounded by its deadly, fever-laden air. Oranie Forget—also known as the baby—is also charming, though I am not generally an admirer of infants her age (she is only a few months old). I am not saying this because she flattered me by liking me—all babies and children tend to do that—but she has great style. I have no doubt she will grow up to be a beauty too, though it would have been an absolute certainty if she had taken after her mother.

The mission station at Talagouga is perched on a rocky hillside that rises so abruptly from the river that there is barely room for the narrow footpath running along the riverfront. When you are on the Forgets’ veranda, it feels as if you could easily tumble right off it into the dark, deep, rushing Ogowé River. I suggested this to Mrs. Forget as

It would be a terrifying future for Oranie <note>The infant daughter of the Forgets mentioned on the previous page.</note>, but her mother has considered the danger and enclosed the veranda with wire. To enter the house, you climb a steep flight of steps. The front of the building is raised on poles about fifteen feet above the ground, while the back is built directly against the hillside. This slope is comprised mostly of massive quartz boulders, as the Talagouga mountains form the western end of the Sierra del Cristal range. Once you walk through the house, you encounter more stairs, these being carved directly into the hillside rock. They lead to the kitchen on the right and to the storehouses; to the left, they continue upward to the church, which sits even higher on the face of the hill.

...strong wooden framework from which the bell is hung. To the right of this structure is another, consisting of a roof supported by bare poles. At its lower end, there is a small raised platform <term>daïs</term> where a table and chair stand. The yellow clay floor slopes steeply uphill, and the pews consist of round, relatively thin poles, neatly mounted on stumps about ten inches from the ground. I would have thought those pews were perfect for an African congregation, but I am told I am wrong. They say that even the Elders fall sound asleep on them, quite comfortably—I suppose like bats. I do not mean they hang upside down, you understand, but rather that they use a similar kind of muscular reflex, with their legs gripping the pole-pew while they sleep. 

Beyond the church, the hillside is split by a ravine, and a beautiful, clear stream runs out of the dense forest growing within it. The stream has been dammed further up because it is harnessed to M. Gacon’s sawmill. The construction of this dam, the installation of the two large water-wheels and the saw, and the building of the shed that covers it—indeed, all the work connected with the project—has been done by M. Gacon with his own hands. Not only has he dammed the water and built his sawmill, but he still works hard at it daily, cutting hundreds of fine redwood planks for the mission's use. He ships them on the *Éclaireur* <note>original: "*Éclaireur*" (The Scout); the mission's stern-wheel steamer.</note> using unsteady little canoes in this dangerous section of the river, and keeps a large supply of them under his house—a bamboo building that was once the Talagouga church. All of this has been achieved with no assistance other than unskilled native labor. You might understand a little of what this means if I were to write down the details from June to January, and then if you were to come out here and try such a job yourself to finish your education. 

Across the other side of the ravine and high up, the house built by Dr. Nassau <note>Dr. Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), a pioneer American missionary and physician in Gabon.</note> is perched where he first established mission work on the Upper Ogowé. The house is now in ruins; but in front of it, as a symbol of how fleeting European life is in West Africa, is the grave of Mrs. Nassau. Located among great white blocks of quartz rock, its plain stone looks like the one firm, permanent, human-made thing in the area. Below the grave, down the hill, are some houses inhabited by the native employees of the station. Passing these and continuing down toward the river, you come to a wooden bridge spanning...

...the mill-stream. Crossing this, you find yourself back on the path that passes in front of Mr. Gacon’s house. Passing this, you come to the house inhabited by the girls in the mission school, overseen by the attractive Imgrimina, wife of Isaac the <term>Jack-Wash</term> <note>A term for a laundryman or person in charge of washing clothes.</note>. A few more steps bring you to the foot of the Forgets’ <note>The family of the missionary, Mr. Forget.</note> veranda staircase. The path continues a little beyond this to the east, onto a slightly broader, level piece of ground, behind which the hillside rises. It ends abruptly at another ravine with another, smaller stream. Beyond this, the hills descend directly into the river. On this small, flat piece of ground, there are a few more native houses belonging to the Bible-readers and others. 

Up on the hillside above them hangs a garden, which appears to be held in position by a large number of sturdy wooden pegs driven into the ground. These are actually intended to keep the artificially leveled beds of soil, and the plants within them, from being washed down into the river by the torrential rains of the wet season. The gardener claims that all sorts of things are growing in those beds, but Mrs. Forget declares there is nothing there but a kind of salad green. It is a very nice salad; I believe it to be dandelion, and there is plenty of it. Perhaps Mrs. Forget could be more resigned to it. 

On the other hand, I agree with her and fail to see why the gardener’s salary should be continually raised, as he desires. I also do not see exactly what connection his stomach problems have with the fact that the tomato plants produce nothing, nor why he should be paid more because of them; for strange abdominal symptoms are very common among all the West African tribes. My own opinion about that garden is that there are too many plantains in it and too much shade. 

The entire station is surrounded by a dense, dark, and menacing forest. In front of it runs the dark, rapid river, which is profoundly deep but no more than 400 yards wide at this point. On the opposite side, there is another hillside similarly covered in forest, unbroken by any clearing except for one small spot higher up than the mission, where there is a small native town and a small branch of the <term>factory</term> <note>In this context, a "factory" refers to a trading post or warehouse owned by the British firm Hatton and Cookson.</note> belonging to Hatton and Cookson.

Talagouga is magnificent, but its scenery is undoubtedly grim, and its name, meaning "the gateway of misery," seems applic—

...able.<note>original: "Otal a ma gouga" — Mr. R. B. N. Walker believes this name means "hardship" or "privation."</note> It must be a melancholy place to live; the very air feels heavy and silent. I never saw the trees stirred by a breeze the entire time I was there; even the broad plantain leaves seemed to stand sleeping day in and day out, motionless. This is because the mountains shelter the area at both the front and back; on either side, promontories extending from both banks create a narrow, winding gorge for the river channel. The only sign of movement you see is in the Ogowé River; if you look at it, you can see that despite its dark, quiet surface, it is sweeping past at a terrific speed. One large gray rock sticks up through the water just below the mission beach, and from it flows a constant silver streak caused by the obstruction it presents to the current. 

Every now and then, you will notice a canoe full of wild, naked, or nearly naked people—silent because they are Fans <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group of the Congo Basin.</note>, and they do not sing like the Igalwas <note>The Galwa people.</note> or M'pongwe <note>The Mpongwe people.</note> when in their canoes. They are either paddling very hard and creeping slowly upstream against one of the banks, or simply keeping the canoe's head straight and traveling rapidly downstream. Occasionally, you will hear the labored thumping of the engines of either the *Mové* <note>original: "Mové" — French for "Moved" or "Movement."</note> or the *Éclaireur* <note>original: "Éclaireur" — French for "Scout."</note> before you see the vessel or hear the warning shriek of their whistles. You can watch as a ship comes upriver, fighting its way toward Njole, or see it heading downriver, slipping past like a dream in a few seconds—and that is all. 

My first afternoon was enough time to see the station. Mr. Jacot reports that there are thirty-two buildings on the property, but he is a stickler for the truth and counts every cook-house and shed. There are only three buildings deserving of the name "house": the Gacons', the girls' dormitory, and the Forgets'.

Mrs. Forget took wonderful care of me. I looked at my clean, tidy, and comfortable room with dread until I discovered an attached bathroom where I will be able to make a terrible mess with fish and other specimens without disgracing myself or my country. And to my inexpressible joy—there are "no mosquitoes," yet there is still a curtain. I mentioned before that I had heard they disappeared after reaching O Soamokita, but when I see people hanging mosquito nets over their beds, I always have my doubts. Besides, around here you will always find people who deny having mosquitoes if they can do so without committing blatant perjury—

jury; if they cannot deny it—as was the case with Mr. Cockshut at Lambarene—they try to change the subject or claim that other places are worse. Because of this blissful absence of irritation, I slept deeply during my first night at Talagouga. However, I was woken by awful sounds in the morning—at 5:30 AM—and sat straight up in bed "at once" <note>original: "one time" — West African English (Pidgin) meaning "immediately" or "instantly."</note>. As the sound grows louder and continues, a flash of reason replaces this first impression. It is the morning service in the church, and the locals are simply singing hymns. In later days, the sound always caused the same physical shock, but the mental shock eventually faded, crushed under the weight of knowing the sound's true origin.

I spent my second day talking to Madame Forget. Her English is perfectly good, although she tells me she resisted learning it quite stubbornly out of patriotic motives. I must say, I truly admire the spirit of patriotic fire in the French. I do not mean to imply for one moment that I, as an Englishwoman, suffered from it in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>. They always gave me the greatest help in traveling through their territory and showed me every kindness. Of course, there was no reason why they should not, for they have no reason to be anything but proud of the great things they have achieved here and the admirable way this noble province of theirs is administered. 

The French Congo is a very different thing compared to the Belgian Congo <note>original: "Congo Belge"</note>, a part of the world I shall not wander into again until it becomes the French Congo—and that won't be long. I now soothe my pride as an Englishwoman with the knowledge that if a Frenchwoman were to travel to any of our West Coast settlements, she would receive as warm and helpful a welcome as I have received here. I will even be a bit petty and say she would do more "harm" <note>The author is likely joking about the romantic havoc charming French women might wreak on the local bachelor population.</note> in the English settlements than I ever did in the French ones. Think of Madame Jacot, Madame Forget, or Madame Gacon going into Calabar, for example; why, there wouldn't be a whole heart left in the place within twenty-four hours!

# TALAGOUGA CHAPTER

...a mutual friendship grew between us. I admire him sincerely. His personal appearance, his grand manner, and the orderly way he lives his life—going down regularly to one particular stone at the river’s edge to wash, attending every meal during the day, and going to roost on one specific door-top—command admiration and respect. But he behaved cruelly toward me. He bullied me out of my food at mealtimes, always ending in a fight where he would hold onto my finger with his beak like a vice. I know he regards me as a defeated slave. He took as his rightful due my many rescues of him from behind a tilted wall mirror, behind which he constantly fell, dazzled by the vision of his own beauty as he flew up in front of the glass. There is another common pigeon domesticated at Talagouga, but he was a nobody, and "Monsieur" <note>French: "Mister" or "Sir"—the name given to the dominant pigeon.</note> let him know it, despite several rebellions on his part. There were also two very small, very black kittens which were being carefully, but unfortunately unsuccessfully, nursed, as their mother had abandoned them.

M. Forget did not think I would have much chance of obtaining fish for specimens. He said that although the Fans <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group of Central Africa.</note> catch plenty, they do not care to sell them, as fish is the main source of food in this region where other food is scarce. Nevertheless, he said he would try to persuade them to bring some to me. His efforts were so successful that that afternoon several Fans arrived with specimens. For these I paid, as I usually do when starting to trade in a new district, <term>fancy prices</term> <note>highly inflated prices used to encourage locals to bring more items.</note>. This ruse was so successful that I was soon at my wits’ end for bottles and preservatives. I might have obtained <term>trade gin</term> <note>a low-quality, cheap gin often used as currency in West Africa.</note>, but there is not enough alcohol in trade gin to preserve specimens. Again, M. Forget came to the rescue and gave me a bottle of medical alcohol from the dispensary.

I had a terrible fright during my second night at Talagouga. I went to bed feeling quite secure because there had been no mosquitoes the previous night. I was awakened between 2:00 and 3:00 AM by sharp pain from puncture wounds on my chest, finding the mosquito netting completely down and smothering me. My first fear was that I had brought a mosquito or two of the Lambarene <note>spelled "Lembarene" in original</note> strain up to—

I struggled my way out from behind the mosquito netting and stepped on a cold, flabby thing which kindly said "Croak"—identifying itself as a harmless frog and relieving my second fear, which was that it might be a snake. I then had a frustrating search for matches in the pitch dark; I knocked over half the items in the room before I found them. When that was done and I got the candle lit, I found a large black cat sitting and smiling on my bed. Guessing she was the mourning mother of those suffering, abandoned kittens, I moved her off and tied the mosquito net to the ceiling again. I then took her inside the net with me to finish my night's rest, for I feared if I left her outside she would cause another sharp reminder of those Lembarene mosquitoes <note>Lembarene is a town in Gabon where Kingsley had previously stayed; she is humorously comparing the noise of the cat/kittens to the annoyance of mosquitoes.</note>. The frog, having caught its breath again, hopped about the floor all night, croaking to its outdoor relatives about the unprovoked attack that had been committed against it.

I spent the following days purchasing fish from the local people, who brought them in large quantities. There were mostly two varieties, and of course, they wanted very high prices for them. However, I confess I rather enjoy the playful negotiation of bartering against their attempts to overcharge me. My trading with them served as an introduction to one another, so when we met during the long, climbing walks I used to take while hunting for beetles in the forest behind the mission station, we recognized each other and were not particularly shocked or frightened.

That forest around Talagouga was one of the most difficult landscapes to navigate that I have ever encountered, for it was dense and there were no forest paths. No Fang <note>original: "Fan"; an ethnic group of Central Africa.</note> village feels the need to walk to another Fang village for social visits, and all their trade travels up and down the river in canoes. No doubt there are forest paths some miles inland, but I never came across one, so they must be quite far away. Neither did I encounter any villages in the forest; they all seem to be located on the riverbank in this area.

The views from the summits of the steeply shaped hills around Talagouga are incredibly magnificent and provide a good sense of the direction of the Sierra del Cristal <note>The Crystal Mountains, a mountain range in Gabon.</note> range in this district. To the east, the higher portions of the ranges were visible, just—

Beyond Njole lies a closely packed series of strangely shaped summits of a beautiful purple-blue color. These peaks run indefinitely to the north-northwest and southeast. When the day was clear, one could see the mountains of Achangoland far to the south-southeast; based on their shape, they were evidently of the same formation, though they did not follow the same direction as the range of the Sierra del Cristal. 

The hills I personally had to deal with were the western flanking hills of the Sierra—all masses of hard black rock with veins and blocks of crystalline quartz. Between the gaps in the rocks was the rich organic soil <term>vegetable mould</term> created by hundreds of thousands of years of falling leaves and timber. The undergrowth was very dense and tangled among the great gray-white trunks of the high trees. The young shoots of this undergrowth were interesting; they were not as often rose-colored as those around Lembarene, but in the denser parts, they were usually a pale creamy-white or a deep blue. 

I was foolish enough to imagine that a soft, delicate-leaved plant with white shoots had a most fragrant scent of its own. However, I soon found the scent actually came from the civet cats, which are abundant here and seem to prefer this shrub particularly. It is quite strange how intense an aversion the Africans have to this scent, and they grimace and spit whenever they encounter it; their dislike is shared by the elephants. I once saw an elephant put his trunk against one of these scented bushes, rip it up in a second, and flee into the forest with an "Oh Lord! Burn some brown paper! A handkerchief, please!" <note>Burning brown paper was a traditional Victorian remedy used to mask foul odors or to revive someone who felt faint.</note> expression all over him. The natives, knowing this, use civet in elephant hunting, as I will describe some day. 

The high trees were of various kinds—acacias, redwood, African oak, a little ebony, and *odeaka*, along with many other species for which I still do not even know the native names. One tree which I know well by sight produces a vividly yellow wood of great beauty when cut. Now and again on exposed parts of the hillside, one comes across great piles of fallen timber that have been blown down by tornadoes. These trees are either flat on the ground—in which case snakes and scorpions hide under and among them, making climbing over them slippery work—or they are thrown sideways and left hanging against their fellows, covered with a gorgeous drapery of climbing, flowering plants. In such cases, they present to the tiny human observer...

# VIII SNAKES IN A CLEFT STICK

...a wall made up of strong tendrils and climbing grasses, through which the "said atom" <note>The author, referring to herself as a small speck in the vast forest.</note> has to cut its way with a machete and push into the crack so made, getting, meanwhile, covered with red driver ants and the like, and having sensational meetings with blue-green snakes, dirty green snakes with triangular horned heads, black cobras, and boa constrictors. I never came back to the station without having been frightened half out of my wits, and with one or two of my smaller terrifiers in cleft sticks to preserve in bottles. When you get the hang of it, catching a snake in a cleft stick is perfectly simple. Only mind you have the proper kind of stick, split far enough up, and keep your attention on the snake’s head—that’s his business end—and the tail which is whisking and winding around your wrist does not matter. There was one snake, by the way, for which it was impossible to tell which was his head in the forest. The natives swear he has one at each end; so you had better "Leave them alone" <note>original: "Lef ’em"</note>, even though you know the British Museum would love to have him, for he is very venomous; one of the few cases of death from snake-bite I have seen was from this species.

Several times, when further in the forest, I came across a trail of flattened undergrowth for fifty or sixty yards, with a horrid musky smell that demonstrated it had been the path of a boa constrictor, and nothing more.

It gave me more trouble and terror to get to the top of those Talagouga hillsides than it gave me to go twenty miles in the forests of Old Calabar, and that is saying a good deal; but when you reached the summit, there was the glorious view of the rest of the mountains, stretching away, interrupted only by Mount Talagouga to the Southeast by East and the great, grim, dark forest, under the lowering gray sky common during the dry season on the Equator. One had no glimpse or hint of the Ogowé River up here, so deep down in its ravine does it flow. A person coming to the hilltops close to Talagouga from the North or North-Northwest and turning back in his track from here might be utterly unaware that one of the great rivers of the world was flowing, full and strong, within some 800 feet of him. There is a strange sense of secretiveness about all these West African forests; but I never saw it so marked as in these that—

I very rarely met any natives in this region; those I did encounter were hunters—large, agile men who focused all their grooming efforts on their hair. On two occasions, I ran some risk because these hunters stalked me, mistaking me for game. "Goodness gracious, man, what a fine thing it would have been for an Englishwoman to be shot by mistake for a gorilla by a cannibal Fan, of all people!" <note>original: "Hoots toots, mon, a verra pretty thing it would hae been for an Englishwoman to hae been shot in mistake for a gorilla by a cannibal Fan of all folks"</note> was the commentary of a Scottish friend. I escaped, however, because these men get as close as possible to their prey before firing. When they realized their mistake, they were not such incompetent sportsmen as to kill me just because I was something unusual. We stood and stared at each other, exchanged a few words in our respective languages, and parted. One thing that struck me significantly in these forests was the absence of signs of spirit worship <term>fetish worship</term>, which are so prevalent in Calabar. There, one constantly encounters trees worshipped as the homes of spirits and small huts built over offerings to forest souls.

Thanks to the kindness of Monsieur Forget, I had the opportunity to visit Talagouga Island. The French Government has granted this island to the Evangelical Mission <note>original: "Mission Évangélique"</note>. Because of the inconvenience of being precariously perched on a hillside, the missionaries intend to move from their current location and settle on the island shortly.

Talagouga Island is situated in the middle of the river, about halfway between the current mission beach and Njole. It is a mile long and averages about a quarter of a mile wide. The upriver end consists of a low, rocky hill, and the island tapers downriver from there, ending in a charming little white sandbank. At the upper end, there is a reef of black rocks that the Ogowé River strikes against. Its brown surface turns white with agitation at being interrupted while in such a tremendous hurry to reach the South Atlantic. When traveling upriver to the island in a canoe, hugging the bank, I had a better chance to see details than I did when on the *Éclaireur* <note>The river steamer (French for "Scout") Kingsley used for transport.</note> with its distracting activities. The first object of interest was Talagouga Rock. Seen at close range, its gray, rough, weathered head rises—much worn by water—some twenty feet above the dry season water level. Heaven knows how far down it extends...

Until a few years ago, it was regarded as the boundary between the regions of Gabon <note>original: "Gaboon"</note> and the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>. However, this division has now been abolished; there is no longer a separate Gabon, as the entire province is now the French Congo. Consequently, Talagouga Rock holds no official status and is left to the worship it receives as the dwelling place of an *Ombuiri* <term>a local nature spirit or guardian deity</term>. 

On the edge of the riverbank, adjacent to Talagouga Rock, is a small swamp. Beside it stands another gigantic monolith which, assuming Talagouga Rock stands twenty feet above the water, must be between fifty and sixty feet high. This stone receives no worship at all. However, if that massive, Stonehenge-like structure were located in the Oil Rivers <term>the Niger Delta region</term>, it would be considered a major *ju-ju* <term>a spiritual object or fetish</term>. Its base would be wrapped in scraps of white cotton cloth <term>calico</term>, with bottles of gin placed before it, along with bowls made of gourds <term>calabashes</term> filled with hard-boiled eggs and heaven knows what else. That rock is wasted on these Bantu people; that is what happens when one is magnificent at the wrong time and place. 

Opposite Talagouga Rock, on the other bank, the Fan village of Talagouga is perched on top of a small clay cliff. It contains a branch trading post <term>sub-factory</term> belonging to the Hatton and Cookson company, managed by a man from Sierra Leone. A little further up on the north bank, Monsieur Forget pointed out a spot in the forest where, a year or two ago, the unusual dwarf people <note>referring to the Pygmy groups of the region, such as the Akowa</note> had a village. None of them are there now, as they wander back and forth through the forest, never remaining in one spot for more than a few months. They are scattered in small communities throughout the forests of the French Congo, but their primary home seems to be among the Bakele tribe in Achangoland.

Instead, I regard it as a blessing in disguise; to my way of thinking, the Ogowé River water—exposed to the air and moving with a swift current—is safer to drink than *a decoction of African earth* <note>original: "decoc terræ Africano"; Kingsley means spring water is like a tea brewed from the soil</note>—spring water, I mean.

They originally agreed to do this in exchange for the wood, but it has since occurred to them that they would also like to be paid wages. These West African tribes are sweet, unsophisticated children of nature; little thoughts like these are constantly arising in their minds. On all sides—missionary, governmental, and trading—I am told these Fans are exceedingly treacherous and that you can never trust them to hold to a bargain. I must say this is not the case with other African tribes I have encountered. In the Oil Rivers <term>the Niger Delta</term>, for example, when a deal <term>original: "jam"</term> is made, it is made, and they will stick to it—except perhaps for the timing—more honorably than twenty percent of white men would. I spent the rest of my time at Talagouga trying to find a way to reach the rapids above Njolé <note>A town on the Ogowé River that served as a major colonial outpost</note>. I had become increasingly determined to see them after observing the unusual types of fish at Talagouga and the differences between them and the fish at Lambaréné. For a while, no one I spoke to thought the plan was feasible. However, M. Gacon eventually thought it could be managed. I offered a reward of 100 francs to anyone who would lend me a canoe and a crew, and I agreed to pay all expenses, including food and wages. 

M. Gacon had a good canoe and could spare two English-speaking Igalwas <note>The Igalwa are an ethnic group from the lower Ogowé region, known for their skill as boatmen and translators</note>. One of them had traveled part of the way with Messrs. Allégret and Teisserès during their journey to Franceville, across to Brazzaville, and down the Congo two years earlier. He also thought we could recruit six Fans <note>The Fan (or Fang) people were the dominant ethnic group in the area, frequently described by European travelers of the era as fierce and cannibalistic</note> to complete the crew. I was delighted and packed my small suitcase <term>portmanteau</term> with a few items, gathered some goods for trade, wound my watch, checked the date, and borrowed three hairpins from Madame Forget. 

But then, disappointment struck. Upon my return from the bush that evening, Madame Forget told me that M. Gacon now said it was "impossible." The Fans near Talagouga refused to go past Njolé at any price because they were certain they would be killed and eaten by the up-river Fans. Internally wishing the entire tribe to a place where the temperature is even higher than this climate <note>Kingsley is humorously suggesting they go to Hell</note>, I went with Madame Forget to speak with M. Gacon. We talked it over, and finally, M. Gacon thought he could get me two more Igalwas from the Hatton and Cookson <note>A major British trading firm operating in West Africa at the time</note> post across the river. After sending a message across, we found this was possible. I now felt committed to the plan and steeled my courage—which was no easy feat, given all the information I had gathered regarding the dangerous rapids of the River Ogowé.

Away we went, still damp from the rain we had come through, but drying nicely as the day progressed and feeling cheerful about the food.

The Ogowé is broad at Njole, and its banks are not mountainous like they are at Talagouga. But as we continued, it soon narrowed, and the current ran more rapidly than ever. We were soon surrounded by the mountain range again. Great masses of black rock appeared among the trees on the hillsides and under the fringe of fallen trees that hang from the steep banks. Two hours after leaving Njole, we were facing our first rapid. Great gray-black masses of smooth rock rose up out of the swirling water in all directions. These rocks had a peculiar appearance that puzzled me at the time, but as I eventually grew used to it, I accepted it quietly and admired it. When the sun shines on them, they have a soft, light blue haze around them, like a halo. The effect produced by this—combined with the forested hillsides and the little beaches of glistening white sand—was one of the most perfect things I have ever seen.

# IX COLLAR WORK

...point in question, yelling and shouting at the tops of our voices. M’bo said, “Jump for the bank, sir,” <note>original: "sar"</note> and I “jumped up,” followed by half the crew. What banks they were! There were sheets, walls, and rubbish heaps of rock, all mixed up with fallen and standing trees. I shall not forget one appalling corner, for I had to jump at a rock wall and hang onto it in a manner more suited to an insect than an insect-hunter. I then had to scramble up it into a dense forest that was heavily cluttered with boulders of all sizes. 

I wonder whether the rocks or the trees were there first? There is evidence for both. In one place, you will see a rock on the top of a tree, with the tree creeping out from underneath it; in another place, you will see a tree on the top of a rock, clasping it with a network of roots and getting its nourishment—goodness knows how. These are by no means soft, digestible sandstones, but uncommonly hard gneiss and quartz. These rocks have no intention of breaking up into crumbly <term>friable</term> small pieces; they only take on a high polish when they are vigorously sanded and scoured <term>canvassed</term> by the Ogowé River. 

While I was busy climbing across these rocky points <term>promontories</term>, the crew would be shouting and hauling the canoe around the point by using the strong chain fixed to the bow for such emergencies. When this was done, we got back in and paddled away until we met our next affliction.

M’bo had advised that we should spend our first night at the same village where Mr. <note>original: "M." We thought it would be better to stay at a village a little further up so as to make tomorrow’s work shorter, as we wanted to reach Kondo Kondo. ## CHAPTER IX

...dramatic entertainment as an answer, which was typical for these lively and excitable <term>Fans</term> <note>The Fang people of West Africa, whom Kingsley frequently refers to as "Fans."</note>. One chief, however, soon settled down to specific details. He began his remarks by commanding silence with the shout, "Azuna! Azuna!" <note>A Fang exclamation meaning "Listen!" or "Attention!"</note> and his companions grunted their approval of his observations. He took a piece of plantain leaf and tore it into five pieces of different sizes. He laid these along the edge of our canoe at various intervals. While doing this, he told M’bo many things—mostly scandalous—about the character of the villages these bits of leaf represented, except, of course, for piece A, which represented his own village. 

The distance between the pieces was proportional to the distance between the villages, and the size of the pieces corresponded to the size of each settlement. He recommended that we only visit village number four. When he had finished, I gave our kind informants some heads of tobacco and many thanks. Then M’bo sang them a hymn with the help of Pierre; Pierre sang half a line behind him in a different key, but was every bit as flat. The Fans seemed impressed, though any crowd would be struck by my crew’s hymn-singing, unless they were residents of a school for the deaf. We then said our farewells and elaborately thanked the villagers for their kind invitation to spend the night there on our way home. We shoved off and paddled away in great style, just to show those Fans what <term>Igalwas</term> <note>The Igalwa are an ethnic group from the lower Ogowé region, known for their skill as boatmen.</note> could do.

We had not gone 200 yards before we encountered a current coming around the end of a rock reef that was too strong for us to hold our position in, let alone move forward. I was ordered onto the bank and obeyed. It was a low stretch of rugged, messy boulders and rock fragments, carelessly piled together and evidently underwater during the rainy season. As I scrambled along, the men yelled, shouted, and hauled the canoe. The villagers, seeing that we were becoming entertaining again, came running at full speed after us—young and old, male and female, not to mention the dogs. 

Some kind souls helped the men haul the boat, while I did my best to amuse the others by accidentally diving headlong into a thick clump of willow-leaved shrubs from a large rock I had carefully climbed. They cheered my performance loudly and then assisted my efforts to extricate my—

# IX A LOVELY AFTERGLOW

...myself, and during the rest of my scramble they kept close to me, competing keenly for the front row in hopes that I would do something like it again. But I refused the *encore* because, bashful as I am, I could not help but feel that my last performance was carried out with all the superb, reckless abandon of a Sarah Bernhardt <note>A world-famous French stage actress known for her highly dramatic and emotional style.</note>, and a display of art of this caliber should satisfy any African village for at least a year. At last, I got across the rocks onto a lovely little beach of white sand. I stood there talking, surrounded by my audience, until the canoe overcame its difficulties and arrived almost as scratched as I was. Then we again said farewell and paddled away, much to the grief of the natives; after all, they don't get a circus visiting up above Njole <note>N'Djolé, a town in Gabon that served as a key trading post on the river.</note> every week, poor dears.

Now, there is no doubt that the chief’s plantain-leaf chart was an ingenious idea and a credit to him. There is also no doubt that the <term>Fang mile</term> is a bit like an "Irish mile"—a matter of nine or so of those used by ordinary mortals <note>An idiom referring to a distance that is much longer than a standard mile.</note>. Even allowing for this, I am bound to say I don't think he put those pieces of leaf far enough apart. We paddled a long way before we reached village number one mentioned in that chart. We went on even longer until we came to village number two. Village number three appeared high up on a mountainside soon after, but it was getting dark and the water was becoming rougher. The hillsides grew higher and higher into nobly shaped mountains, forming a ravine with their steep, forest-covered sides. In the gathering gloom, it looked like an iron alleyway for the foaming Ogowé <note>The Ogooué, the principal river of Gabon.</note>. 

We anxiously looked for village number four, but we never saw it. Instead, the darkness surrounded us, appearing to drift onto the river from the forests and the side ravines, where it had been sleeping for some hours like a sailor with his clothes on in bad weather. We paddled on, looking for signs of village fires but seeing none. The <term>Earth Spirit</term> <note>original: "Erd-geist." A reference to the spirit from Goethe's *Faust* that represents the living forces of nature.</note> knew we wanted something, and seeing how we personally lacked it, thought we needed beauty. Being in a kindly mood, it gave it to us, sending the lovely, lingering flushes of its afterglow across the sky. As it faded, the sky became a divine, deep purple velvet that no one has dared to paint. Great stars came out, blazing high above us, and the darkness around us was be-gemmed with fireflies; but...

# IX THE RAPIDS OF THE OGOWÉ

We were not as satisfied with these things as we should have been; what we really wanted were fires to cook by and dry ourselves by, and other comforts of that kind. The <note>original: "Erd-geist"</note> Earth-spirit did not understand, and so it left us once the evening light had faded. There was only enough starlight to see the spraying foam of the rapids ahead and around us, but not enough to see the massive trees that had fallen from the bank into the water. When the rapids were not too noisy, we could listen for these, because the dark current rushes through their branches with an impatient “lish, swish” sound. However, when a rapid was roaring right alongside us, we ran into those trees and got ourselves battered, facing dangerous moments while trying to get back on our course. Every now and then, we struck large rocks protruding from the black water—grim, solitary figures that seemed to be standing silently, watching their fellow rocks fight noisily in the arena of the white water.

Still, we pushed on, poling and paddling. Around 8 <term>P.M.</term>, we came to a bend—a dangerous one. We were unable to leap onto the bank and tow the boat around because we could see neither the details nor the exact position of the shore. I think we felt a natural reluctance to jump toward the kind of terrain we had experienced that afternoon, especially with only the help of a compass viewed briefly by the flickering light of a <term>lucifer match</term> <note>An early type of friction match.</note>. Even that would not have told us how many dozens of feet of dense trees lay between us and the land, so we did not attempt it. One must be careful at times, or nasty accidents may follow. 

We fought our way around that corner, yelling defiance at the water, and handled the following bends with <note>original: "vi et armis"</note> sheer force, occasionally breaking a pole. Around 9:30, we entered a violent rapid. We fought it inch by inch. The canoe jammed itself on some rocks just beneath the surface. We shoved it off and over them, but it tilted over and threw us out. Since the surrounding rocks were just level with the water, we survived and righted the boat. We got back into it and drove it forward relentlessly. It struck again and bucked like a wild horse, and we fell in heaps upon each other, but stayed inside that time—the men by the help of their agile feet, and I by gripping the vine-rope lacing which ran around the rim of the canoe. # IX A RUSH DOWN STREAM

...which I did not understand when I left Talagouga. We quickly gathered ourselves and pushed the canoe back into the current once more. A heavily strained pole and a paddle both snapped with a "smash." We spun round and round in a wild whirlpool which, in a carefree and maliciously playful way, threw us tail-first back into the main current. It was at this moment that the great advantage of these canoes—having both ends shaped exactly the same—became clear. At this juncture, all we had to do was rotate on our axis and start fresh, using what had been the front as the back.

Naturally, we were defeated. We could not go upriver any further without the help of our lost poles and paddles, so we had to head downriver to find shelter anywhere we could. Down we went through the white water at a terrifying speed. While we had been snagged among the rocks, the arrangement of our crew had been altered, with Pierre joining M’bo at the front. However, this precaution was ruined when we were spun around. Our situation remained precarious until we entered another whirlpool, where we managed to maneuver ourselves so that we were facing the right way again. 

This only took a few minutes since whirlpools were everywhere. Then M’bo and Pierre, using our remaining poles, stood at the front to push us away from the rocks as we rushed toward them. Meanwhile, those of us with paddles in the middle of the boat helped steer and, when necessary—which happened with lightning speed—slapped the whirlpools with the flat side of our paddles to break their force. Cook crouched in the back, focusing entirely on steering. 

It was an excellent plan in theory, and undoubtedly the safest one in practice, but it didn’t exactly work out brilliantly, even though everyone did their best. We charged headlong toward massive rocks—structures twenty to fifty feet above the water. Those of us in the middle paddled backward and splashed furiously; M’bo and Pierre took the impact on their poles. Sometimes we managed to graze the side successfully and fly past; other times, we didn't. When the impact was too great for M’bo and Pierre, they were thrown back onto me, flattening me against the bundles of cargo. Because the cargo was now tied down tightly, it couldn’t shift any further back, but the impact of the canoe’s bow hitting the rock certainly caused chaos. The rest of the crew tumbled forward onto the bundles, onto me, and onto each other. We were shaken up together so many times that night that it is a wonder...

It seemed a miracle to me, considering the rush, that we sorted ourselves out correctly, each with our own particular legs and arms. And although those of us in the middle of the canoe flapped our paddles very energetically, our attempts to break the whirlpools were no more successful than M’bo and Pierre’s efforts to fend off the rocks. We danced many a wild waltz that night with the waters of the Ogowé River.

As unpleasant as going through the rapids was, we fared no better when the current pulled us into the dark, deep water. For sheer, all-around inconvenience, nothing compares to crashing full speed in the dark into the branches of a fallen tree at the pace we were traveling—with a crash, swish, and crackle, you find yourself stuck, with a branch pressing against your chest, your hair being torn out, and your clothes ripped to ribbons by other branches, all while the treacherous river tries to drag the canoe out from under you. I expect we would have been an amusing sight for any hard-hearted onlookers, but there were no onlookers. Nor could we form a "cooperative society" to share a laugh at our own ridiculous situation, as we usually did when there was enough light to see it. After more than an hour of these experiences, we ran hard onto a large, black reef of rocks. The canoe was wedged so firmly that, in our exhausted state, we could not move it. We wisely decided to “leave it” <term>lef ’em: West African Pidgin English for "leave it" or "let it be"</term> and see what could be done about finding food and a fire for the rest of the night. Our eyes, now adjusted to the dark, noticed a large mass of land looming out of the river very close to us. We later discovered this was Kembe Island. The rocks and foam on both sides stretched away into the darkness, and high above us against the starlit sky, the peaks of the mountains of the Sierra del Cristal <note>Spanish: "Crystal Mountains"</note> stood out clearly.

Our most pressing question now was whether this rock reef was connected well enough to the island for us to reach it. Stopping our guesswork, we tied the canoe very firmly to the rocks. This seemed a bit unnecessary since she was jammed tight and immovable, but you can never be too careful with any kind of boat. We then set off among the boulders. I would climb up onto a flat rock table and then fall off the other side

# IX WE REACH A VILLAGE

I scrambled onto rocks again, which were covered with varying amounts of water. Then I would find a patch of "singing sand" beneath my feet, only to suddenly plunge back into more water—into deep or shallow, broad or narrow pools among the rocks. From there, I climbed over more rocks, and so on. My companions, judging by the noises they made, were clearly going through the same ordeal, but we remained quite cheerful because the likelihood of reaching land seemed to be increasing. 

Most of us ended up in deep channels of water that occasionally cut between this rock reef and the riverbank. M'bo was the first to find a sure way forward; he was, and I hope still is, absolutely remarkable at this kind of work. I stayed close to M'bo, and once we reached the shore and the rest of our wanderers had gathered, we decided, "The chances are there is a village around here," and set off to find it. 

After a lively struggle through a forest cluttered with rocks—where the vegetation grew in a tangled, matted mess on a steep hillside at a 45-degree angle—M'bo spotted the glow of fires through the tree trunks away to the left. We headed toward the light, guided by the sound of a drum. Seen through the lattice of the tree trunks, the scene was very picturesque. The village was merely a collection of huts built from palm mats, which were very low and cramped. In its tiny street, which was about sixty feet long and twenty feet wide, there was a series of small fires. 

The villagers themselves, however, were the most striking features of the scene. Their nearly naked bodies were painted bright red <note>original: "vermilion"</note> all over, and they were dancing enthusiastically to a rhythmic drumming beat, played energetically by an old man on a tall, black-and-white painted drum. They explained that because they had been dancing when we arrived, they had failed to hear us. 

M'bo secured a—well, I do not exactly know what to call it—for my use. I imagine it was the remains of the village club-house. It had a certain amount of palm-thatch roof and part of its left side remained, but the rest of the structure was just bare, weathered poles with shreds of palm matting hanging from them here and there. Truly, if it had not been for the roof, one would not have known whether one was inside or outside of it. The floor was packed earth, and in the middle of it was a pile of white ash and the usual two bush lights <term>bush lights: torches typically made of resinous wood or bundles of oily palm fiber</term>, laid down with their burning ends propped up off the ground with stones. They were emitting, as is...

### THE RAPIDS OF THE OGOWÉ

They had their usual rather sickly but not altogether unpleasant smell. Volumes of smoke found their way out through the thatch, leaving a rich, oily varnish of a bright, warm brown color on the inside of the roof. They give a very good light, provided someone keeps an eye on them and knocks the ash off the end as it burns gray—the "bush lights" version of being trimmed <note>original: "snuffed"</note>. 

Against one of the lattice-like sides hung a drum covered with raw hide and a long, hollow section of a tree trunk, which served as a cupboard for a few small articles. I noticed all these details as I sat on one of the hard wood benches, waiting for my dinner, which Isaac was preparing outside in the street. 

The atmosphere of the hut was oppressive, despite its excellent ventilation. The smell of the torches, my wet clothes, and the natives who crowded into the hut to look at me created a very unpleasant combination. The people were clearly very poor, and they had very little clothing. The two headmen wore ragged old French military coats. They were quite satisfied with their appearance, however, and evidently felt that these coats put them in touch with European culture; they lectured the others on the habits and customs of the white man with great self-confidence and superiority. 

I found that the majority of the villagers were Adoomas, most of whom already had a slight acquaintance with this interesting animal <note>The "white man"</note>. They had settled on Kembe Island about two years ago. Then the Fans <note>The Fan or Fang people, known at the time for being a warlike and cannibalistic tribe</note> came and attacked them, killing and eating several people. The Adoomas fled to the French authority at Njole and remained under its protection until the French came up, punished the Fans, and burned their village. 

Once things had quieted down and the Fans had gone off to build a new village to replace their burned one, the Adoomas returned to Kembe Island and their plantain patch. They had only done this a few months before my arrival and had not yet had time to rebuild, which explained the dilapidated state of the village. I am told they are a Congo region tribe whose country lies southwest of Franceville. As I have already mentioned, they are the tribe used by the French authorities to take convoys up and down the Ogowé to Franceville.

<header>IX A NIGHT SCENE</header>

...ville, more to keep this route open than for transport purposes. The rapids make it impossible to take heavy supplies this way, and with good luck, it is a thirty-six-day journey from Njole. The practical route is by way of Loango and Brazzaville. The Adooma people told us that the convoy traveling with the lively government official had run into trouble at the rapids. They spent five days at Kondo Kondo, dragging the empty canoes up using ropes and chains, and carrying the cargo by land until they had passed the worst of the rapids before repacking. They added that the rapids were at their worst right now and shared stories of a poor young French official who had drowned there last year—indeed, they were just as encouraging as my white friends <note>Kingsley is being ironic here regarding the grim warnings she received from both Europeans and locals.</note>. As soon as my dinner arrived, they politely left. I heard the devout M’bo holding a religious service for them in the street, complete with hymns. Once that was over, they returned to their drumming and dancing, staying up quite late, as it was already 11:10 PM when we first arrived at the village.

While the men were getting their food, I stood guard over our few possessions. When they arrived to tidy up my hut, I walked down to the shore along a path we had carefully avoided when arriving at the village. It was a very steep, slippery little path, but it was the one the locals used to reach their canoes, which were tied up among the rocks. The moon was rising, illuminating the sky, but it had not yet cast its light down onto the foaming, rushing Ogowé in its deep ravine. The scene was divinely beautiful; on every side, the peaks of the Sierra del Cristal rose out of the shapeless gloom. Tomanjawki, on the far side of the river and surrounded by neighboring peaks, looked its most magnificent, its silhouette sharp against the sky. In the higher valleys, where the dim light shone faintly, one could see wreaths and clouds of silver-gray mist settling, basking lazily or rolling back and forth. Olangi seemed to stretch all the way across the river, its great, blunt mass blocking all passage. Meanwhile, to the northeast, a prominent cone-shaped peak was visible, which I later learned was named Kangwe. In the darkness around me flitted thousands of fireflies—

shadows, and out beyond this pool of total darkness, the white foam of the rapids flew by unceasingly; there was no sound except for their thunder. The majesty and beauty of the scene fascinated me, and I stood leaning with my back against a rock pinnacle, watching it. Do not imagine it gave rise, in what I am pleased to call my mind, to those complicated, poetic reflections that natural beauty seems to inspire in other people’s minds. It never works that way for me; I simply lose all sense of human individuality and all memory of human life—with its grief, worry, and doubt—and I become part of the atmosphere. If I have a heaven, that will be mine. I truly believe that if I were left alone long enough with a scene like this—or on the deck of an African liner in the Bights <note>The Bight of Benin and the Bight of Biafra off the Atlantic coast of West Africa.</note>, watching its funnel and masts swinging back and forth in the great, long, leisurely roll against the sky—I would be found soulless and dead. But I never have the chance for that. 

Tonight, my absent *Kras* <term>In Fanti culture, a 'Kra' is a soul or life force that can leave the body during sleep.</term>, as my Fanti friends would call them, were sent hurrying back to my body, badly frightened, by a terrifying shriek that tore through the sound of the Ogowé and into the silence of the hills. I woke with a shudder and found myself sore and stiff, but I moved quickly toward the shriek, imagining that some of our hosts had speared a member of the crew—a foolish and unfounded suspicion for which I apologize. 

What had actually happened was that my men, thinking it wiser to keep an eye on our canoe, had come down, built a fire near it, and set up their mosquito nets as tents. One of the men, exhausted from the day's work, had sat down on one of the three logs whose ends—pointed toward a common center where the fire burns—make up the universal stove of this region. He was smoking one last pipe before going to bed, but sleep overcame him, and the wretched fire had crept along the log beneath him and suddenly burned him. The shriek was his way of announcing that fact. Having learned this, I left the victim sitting in a cooling, medicinal pool of water and climbed back to the village, where the inhabitants, finally tired, were going to sleep. I found that M’bo had hung my mosquito net over one of the hardwood benches; crawling cautiously under it, I lit a small lamp and read myself to sleep with my damp, falling-apart copy of Horace <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus, the Roman lyric poet.</note>.

# IX UP STREAM AGAIN

I woke at 4:00 AM lying on the ground among the plantain stalks, having fallen out of the house due to a reckless movement. Thank goodness there are no mosquitoes. I do not know how I escaped the rats that swarm here, running about among the huts and the inhabitants in the evening with a tameness that is shocking to see. I went back to sleep until six o'clock, when we started getting things ready to go upriver again. We carefully provided ourselves with a new stock of poles and paid a local man to come with us and help us fight the rapids.

In the daylight, we now saw that the widest part of the river channel was the south-southwest branch; this was the one we had been swept into, and it was almost completely blocked by rocks. The other branch to the north-northwest was more open, and the river rushed through it in a terrifying, swirling mass of water. Had we been caught in this, we would have been swept past Kembe Island and "gone to glory" <note>A Victorian idiom meaning to die or be destroyed.</note>. Whenever the shelter of the spits of land or the reefs was enough to allow the water to deposit its sand, strange-shaped sandbanks appeared, as perfectly formed as if they had been smoothed by human hands. They rise above the water in a slope, with the low end or "tail" facing against the current; the downstream end terminates in an abrupt miniature cliff, sometimes six or seven feet above the water. You will find that they are the same shape even when they do not have their heads above water by getting stuck on them in a canoe—which I did several times, with a kind of automatic dedication to scientific research that is peculiar to me. Your best way of getting off is to push forward in the direction of the current, while carefully preparing for the shock of suddenly dropping off the cliff’s end.

We left the landing-place rocks of Kembe Island around 8:00, and no sooner had we set afloat than, in the blink of an eye, we were swept sideways right across the river to the north bank. We then became engaged in a heavy fight with a severe rapid. After passing this, the river is mostly uninterrupted by rocks for a while, and it is silent and swift. When you are ascending such a section, the effect is strange; you see the water flying by the side of your canoe as you vigorously drive your paddle into it with short, rapid strokes, and you immediately imagine you are traveling at the speed of a North-Western express <note>A reference to the fast, prestigious trains of the London and North Western Railway.</note>; but you just raise your eyes, my friend, and

Look at the riverbank, which appears to be standing almost still, and you will realize that you and your canoe are also barely moving. All your efforts only allow you to crawl at the speed of a crushed snail, while it is actually the water that is rushing past. It is a very strange and unpleasant realization.

Beyond that stretch of fast, silent water, we reached the Sengelade Islands, and here the river changes its course from a north-northwest to south-southeast axis to a straight north and south flow. After overcoming a dangerous rapid that our guide from Kembe Island called "Unfanga," we seemed to enter a lake enclosed by mountains. By staying close to the left bank, we made great progress for twenty restful minutes. This lulled us all into a false sense of security, and my crew began singing M'pongwe songs. These songs described how they return to their homes to see their wives, families, and friends. They included teasing descriptions of their friends' personalities and flaws, which caused bursts of laughter from those among us who recognized the references. They also sang about how they go to their storage trunks, take out their clothes, and put them on. Each man performed a solo with a long, boastful list of these possessions, and then his companions joined in a hearty chorus to express their admiration and amazement at his wealth and status. 

Next, they sang about how—being dissatisfied with the last dollar's worth of goods they bought from "Holty's" <note>John Holt & Co., a major British commercial trading company in West Africa.</note>—they had decided to take their future business to Hatton and Cookson <note>Another prominent British trading firm operating in the region.</note>, or *the reverse*. Then came the chorus, praising the wisdom of such a decision and celebrating the excellence of the chosen company's goods. 

These M'pongwe and Igalwa <note>Ethnic groups from the Gabon region known for their involvement in river trade and navigation.</note> boat songs are all quite beautiful and have very complex melodies in a minor key. I do not believe there are any ancient lyrics to them; I have tried hard to research them, but I believe only the tunes—which are limited in number and distinct from each other—are very old. The singer improvises the words on the spot. They are only restricted in the sense that specific themes are tied to certain tunes: for instance, the domestic list of possessions—whatever the specific details might be—would always be sung to one fixed tune, while trade information would be sung to another, and so on. In these parts, a "good singer" is a man who can improvise the best song—the most impressive, or the most

It is amusing; I have mentioned a similar state of affairs elsewhere regarding the Ga, Krumen, and Bubi peoples. In all these cases, the melodies are intended only for the voice, not for instrumental performance. The instrumental music consists of that remarkably developed series of drum patterns—the attempt to understand which has occupied much of my time and led me into strange company—and the many tunes played on the *'mrimba* <term>a traditional African musical instrument, often a xylophone or thumb piano</term> and the harp with strings made of orchid roots. I believe these instrumental melodies are entirely distinct from the vocal songs. And these peaceful tunes my men were now singing were, in their flowery elaboration, very different from the rhythmic chant they used while fighting the rapids: "So Sir—So Sur—So Sir—So Sur—Ush! So Sir," and so on.

The rocks, however, were of the flat-topped variety, rather than those dangerous, closely packed pinnacles that rise straight up from deep water, where a canoe is easily wedged and split apart. We, standing knee-deep in water with a current strong enough to nearly sweep us off our feet, pushed and shoved the canoe until it was free. Getting back on board, we returned across the river singing "So Sir" to confront that current again. We succeeded; at the head of the current, we found a rapid and noticed a village clearing on the mountainside—the first sign of human life we had seen all day.

Past this rapid, we were treated to still water, while the main current of the Ogowé rushed along the southern bank. On our side, there were sandbanks with graceful slopes and abrupt ends. The foam, thrown off the rushing main current into the quiet water in flakes and balls, created a strange and beautiful effect. These whirled through the eddies, rushing back and forth as if still driven by a frantic speed. Since there was no current to carry them downstream, they eventually drifted into sheltered bays. There, they came to a standstill, appearing bewildered and lost, as if trying to remember where they were going or where they had come from. The foam itself was a yellowish-white, with a spongy, solid quality to it.

In a small bay we passed, we saw eight native women. They were clearly <term>Fans</term> <note>The Fang people of West Africa, known to Kingsley for their distinct culture and appearance</note> based on their bright brown complexions and the many brass bracelets and armlets they wore. They likely had anklets as well, but we could not see them because the women were busy waist-deep in the foam-flecked water, focused on dismantling a wooden fish trap. We stopped to chat and watched them collect fish in baskets; I even acquired some specimens. Then, after shouting our goodbyes once we were a polite distance away, in the proper civil manner, we resumed our journey.

The middle of the Ogowé here is crowded with high rocks. Standing grimly above the foam, they look like a regiment of strange, powerful creatures braving the current. Their straight faces point upriver, while their smoother curves trail downstream, appearing like black cloaks being blown backward. Across on the other bank rose the dark, forested ridges of Tomanjawki. Our channel was

The arched opening to a large cave lies on the south bank. The mountain-side is a single mass of rock covered by dense, unbroken forest, and the entrance to this cave is situated right on the upper wall of the south bank’s promontory. Since we are sheltered from the current here, we rest and examine it at our leisure. The river flows into it, and you can easily enter during this season; however, during the peak of the rainy season—when the river level would be about twenty feet or more higher than it is now—I doubt you could. They told me this place is called Boko Boko and that the cave is very long, extending level for some distance into the hill before ascending and emerging near a mass of white rock that appears as a tiny speck high up on the mountain.

If you paddle into it, you go "very far," and then "the water ends" <note>Original: "no more water live"</note>. You must then get out and travel up the tunnel—which is sometimes wide, sometimes narrow, sometimes high, and sometimes so low that you have to crawl—to exit at the other end.

One French gentleman has completed this feat, and I am told he found many, many bats, hedgehogs, and snakes. They could not tell me his name, which I much regretted. Since we had no supply of <term>bush lights</term> <note>Torches usually made of bundles of resinous wood</note>, we went no further than the entrance. Indeed, strictly between ourselves, even if I had possessed every torch in the <term>French Congo</term> <note>Original: "Congo Français"</note>, I personally would not have enjoyed going further. I am terrified of caves; the very thought of them sends a chill down my spine.

We crossed the river to see another cave entrance on the opposite bank, where there is a narrow stretch of low, rock-covered land at the foot of the mountains, which is likely underwater during the rainy season. The mouth of this other cave is low, situated between tumbled blocks of rock. It looked so suspiciously like a shortcut to the underworld that I felt even less enthusiasm for exploring it than I did its neighbor across the water—even though they told me no man had ever gone down "those things." Likely, that much-honored Frenchman who explored the other cave agreed with me that if one truly wanted to go from the Equator to <term>Hades</term> <note>The Greek underworld; a reference to Hell</note>, there were more pleasant ways to get there than this. # IX PAST THE OKANA RIVER

...rocks being responsible for the whirlpool we met outside the gateway of Boko Boko.

The scenery above Boko Boko was exceedingly lovely, with the river shut in between its rim of mountains. As you travel up, the view opens out in front of you and closes in behind; the closely-set, chaotic mass of mountains alters in form as you view them from different angles. One exception is Kangwe—a blunt cone that is clearly the remnant of some great volcanic eruption. The sandbanks appear again wherever the current shifts and leaves calm water, their bright, glistening color providing a contrast to the scene.

For a long period, we paddled along the south bank and passed a steep, narrow valley. Its upper end seems blocked by a finely shaped mountain, almost as conical as Kangwe. The name of this mountain is Njoko, and the name of the clear, small river that occupies the entire valley floor is the Ovata. Our peace did not last long, and we were soon again in the midst of a bristling forest of rock. However, the current was not dangerously strong because the riverbed rises into a ridge, which is too high for much water to flow over at this time of year. In the wet season, though, this must be one of the most dangerous places. This ridge of rock runs across two-thirds of the Ogowé, leaving a narrow, deep channel by the north bank. When we had moved our canoe over the ridge—mostly by standing in the water and lifting her—we found the water deep and fairly quiet.

On the north bank, we passed the entrance of the Okana River. Its mouth is narrow, but the natives told me it is always deep, even at the height of the dry season. It is a quite substantial river, flowing inland to the north-northeast. Little is known about it, except that it narrows into a ravine before expanding again. Its banks are densely populated by the Fans <note>The Fang people of West Central Africa</note>, who send down a considerable amount of trade and have a fearsome reputation. In the main stream of the Ogowé, below the Okana’s entrance, is a long rocky island called Shandi. As we were crossing the ridge and paddling near the Okana’s entrance, my ears recognized a new sound. We knew the rush and roar of the Ogowé well enough, and we could usually identify which particular obstacle was causing its headlong rush...

We seemed to be looking into the heart of the <note>original: "Sierra del Cristal"; translation: Crystal Mountains</note> range. One mountain—whose name I do not know, unless it is what is sometimes recorded as *Mt. We soon passed this lovely scene and entered the walled-in channel, creeping up what seemed to be an endless slope of black water. We then moved through some whirlpools and a rocky channel to the sand and rock shore of our intended island, Kondo Kondo, along whose northern side the *Alemba* roared like thunder. 

We secured our canoe in a little cove among the rocks and landed, quite stiff, tired, and very damp. This island, when we were on it, must have been about half a mile long. However, during the long wet season, a large part of it is submerged. Only the higher parts—great heaps of stone where a long, branched, willow-like shrub grows—are above or nearly above water. The Adooma man from Kembe Island especially drew my attention to this shrub. He told me his people who worked the rapids always regarded it with a loving respect. He said it was the only thing that helped a man when his canoe was overturned in the dreaded *Alemba*.
