# IX THE ALEMBA RAPID

We found ourselves wedged among the rocks on Kondo Kondo. The main part of the island consists of sand, with slabs and flat tables of polished rock protruding through it. In between these rocks grew thousands of beautiful lilies; their white flowers possessed a very strong scent of vanilla, and their bright, light-green leaves looked lovely against the glistening pale sand and the black-gray rock. I do not know how they survive the long periods of submersion they must endure. The locals tell me they begin to sprout as soon as the water level drops and leaves the island exposed. They grow and flower very quickly, continuing to bloom until the <note>Now spelled Ogooué; the principal river of Gabon.</note> Ogowé rises again and <term>rides roughshod: to act or move with overwhelming force without restraint</term> sweeps over Kondo Kondo for months.

While the men were building their fire, I walked across the island to see the great Alemba rapid, of which I had heard so much, located between the island and the north bank. More talented writers than I must praise its glory and grandeur. Its appearance was unlike anything I have seen before, and its voice was unlike anything I have heard. The other rapids cannot be compared to it; they are wild, headstrong, and malicious enough, but the Alemba is not like them. It does not struggle, writhe, and brawl among the rocks, but instead moves in a majestic, leaping dance—a triumphant stretch of waltzing foam.

The beauty of the night on Kondo Kondo was superb. The sun set, and the afterglow flashed across the sky in crimson, purple, and gold, leaving the heavens a deep violet-purple. Great stars hung in the sky like moons until the moon itself arose, illuminating the sky long before its beams reached us down in this valley. As she rose, the mountains hiding her face grew sharper in outline and a deeper shade of black. Meanwhile, the mountains opposite were just bright enough to reveal the wisps and floating veils of bluish-white mist upon them. When at last—and for only a short time—the moon shone directly down on the savage foam of the Alemba, she transformed it into a soft silver mist. Fireflies flickered on all sides, appearing as if they had come to see if our campfire was a large relative of their own; they and ourselves were the only representatives of animal life. When the moon had set, the sky remained lovely, still lit by the stars and appearing to be glowing from within. However, it shared none of...

### CHAP. IX.

The moon shared its light with us, and we sat around our fire surrounded by absolute darkness. Cold, clammy drifts of mist—so thick they felt almost solid—encircled us. Every now and then, cold, faint gusts of wandering wind arrived, feeling eerie and grim beyond description.

I cannot give you the individual names of the mountains around and above Kondo Kondo, though I was told what they were. In my last shipwreck before reaching Kondo Kondo, I lost my pencil. My notebook, even if I had possessed a pencil, was unfit for recording native names; it had become a pulpy mass because I had kept it in my pocket after leaving the Okana River to be ready for any <term>submergences: the act of being submerged or pulled underwater</term>. I also had several fish and a considerable amount of water in my pocket as well, so I am grateful that I have even a single note remaining.

I will not bore you further with the details of our ascent of the <note>Now the Ogooué River in Gabon.</note> Ogowé rapids. I have described it enough already for you to understand the kind of work such a journey requires. I have no doubt that if I could have given you a more vivid picture of them, you would join me in admiring the spirited courage of those few Frenchmen who traverse them while on official duty. Personally, I deeply regret that I did not have the good fortune to meet the French official again whom I had the pleasure of meeting on the *Éclaireur*. He would have been truly magnificent in his description of his voyage to Franceville. I wonder how he would have "portrayed" his experience of unpacking canoes and his time on Kondo Kondo; incidentally, we came across many of the ashes from his expedition’s <term>attributive: belonging to or associated with a specific person or group</term> fires. Well! He must have been a welcome addition to Franceville, and I hope also to the good fathers at Lestourville, for those places must be quite somber for Parisians.

Descending large rapids is always and everywhere more dangerous than ascending them. When you are going up and a whirlpool or eddy jams you against the rocks, the current actually helps push you off—though certainly only with the intent of dashing your brains out and smashing your canoe on another set of rocks it has ready further down. But for the moment, it helps. Once you are off, you take control and disrupt its plan. Conversely, when going down, the current works against your ability to back off the rocks. M’bo had a series of prophetic visions about what would happen to us on our way down, based on both his own memories and local tradition.

## IX GLOOMY PROPHECIES

I tried to comfort him by pointing out that, if any one of his prophecies were fulfilled, it would save our friends and relatives all funeral expenses; and, unless they went and wasted their money on a memorial window, that ought to be a comfort to our well-regulated minds. M'bo did not see the logic in this, but he was too good a Christian to be troubled by the disagreeable conviction held by other members of my crew—namely, that our souls, if not released from this world by funeral rites, would have to hover forever over the <term>Ogowé: Now the Ogooué River in Gabon.</term> near the scene of our catastrophe.

A funny incident happened to us one evening. The canoe jammed among a cluster of rocks, and we were all thrown into the water. Mine was extremely inconvenient—a smooth, pillar-like rock that I could barely cling to, along with the French flag, which always stayed with me during these upsets. It took quite a while to regroup the party, as the darkness of the night meant each of us could only see the foam churning around our own particular rock. The roar of the rapids also made it difficult to communicate our positions or decide on a plan of action. 

However, because that clumsy canoe swung broadside against the rocks, it did not drift away downriver. When Pierre reached it, he said it was trying to climb sideways over them "like a crab." Seven of us got back in, but we could not find the eighth person and were starting to fear the Ogowé had claimed another victim. Then, above the roar of the rapids, we heard an agonized howl singing the strains of that fine hymn, "Our haven is in Heaven" <note>original: "Notre port est au Ciel"</note>—a local favorite because of its noble tune. We joyfully went and rescued the singer from his rock, then dashed downriver toward further troubles and disasters. 

The route we had to take coming down was different from the one we took going up. Going upstream, we stayed as close as possible to the safest bank, dodging behind every rock we could to take advantage of the shelter they provided from the current. Going downstream, the rocks and the banks—now lined with fallen trees—turned from friends into enemies. Therefore, we worked as hard as we could to stay in the very center of the fastest part of the current to avoid them. The most spectacular part of the entire journey was the descent below the Alemba, where the massive <term>Ogowé: The Ogooué River in modern-day Gabon.</term> lunges forward like a tiger for about half a mile, I imagine, before crashing into a reef of rocks below. # IX. KEEP THE BOW STRAIGHT

Looking out from the rocks in the upper rapid, it gives you—or perhaps I should only say it gave me—a strange, sinking feeling in the pit of my stomach to see that expanse of black water, gleaming like a polished sheet of metal, sloping steeply downward. Your only task is to keep the bow of your canoe straight—absolutely straight, mind you—because any failure to do so will send you straight to the grave, rather than into the messy but survivable chaos of the lower rapid’s rocks. These lower rapids are among the worst during the dry season; perhaps they are in the wet season as well, because the river channel makes a sharp, elbow-like turn here that makes the Ogowé River churn dangerously.

I hope to see the Ogowé during the rainy season next time; there must be many more of these vast sheets of water then, covering what are currently rocky rapids. Imagine what it would be like to descend over that ridge above Boko Boko! However, I don’t imagine it would ever be possible to travel upriver when the water is at its peak, especially with a crew as small as ours was when we performed our reckless comedy in front of King Death, in his amphitheater within the Crystal Mountains <note>original: "Sierra del Cristal"</note>.

# CHAPTER X

## LAMBARÉNÉ <note>original: "Lembarene"</note>

->In which an account is given of the episode of the *Hippopotame* <note>original: "Hippopotame"; a small river steamer named "The Hippopotamus"</note>, and<-

Upon my return to Talagouga, I found both of my good friends sick with fever—M. Forget was very ill indeed. Fortunately, the *Éclaireur* <note>original: "Éclaireur"; meaning "The Scout"</note> came upriver with the Doctor Administrator on board; he came ashore and prescribed medicine, and within a few days, M. Forget was doing better. I said goodbye to Talagouga with much regret and boarded the *Éclaireur* when she returned from Njole, taking all my specimen bottles and belongings with me. 

I found no other passengers on board. The captain’s English had improved considerably, and he remained as pleasant, cheerful, and ready for a fight as ever. However, he had a preoccupied manner and a most peculiar set of new habits, which I discovered were shared by the engineer. Both of them would make rapid dashes to the railing, nervously scan the river for a minute, and then return to their tasks, only to dash back to the railing again. Their behavior during breakfast was nerve-wracking. After hastily taking a few mouthfuls, the captain would drop his knife and fork and simply hurl his sturdy, sailor-like frame through the nearest door onto the deck. A minute later he would be back, and with just a shake of his head to the engineer, continue his meal. Shortly afterward, the engineer would leap from his seat; being much thinner than the captain, he would fly through the doorway with even greater speed, then return, shake his head at the captain, and resume eating. This kind of excitement is infectious, and I wondered whether I should show some sympathetic friendliness by leaping from my own seat and hurling myself onto the deck through the nearest door as well.

# CH. X A SMOOTH RUN DOWN

But although there are plenty of doors—as four enter the saloon from the deck—I do not see how I can perform this task aimlessly, and I cannot imagine what on earth they are both trying to achieve. So, I confine myself to what was considered a "woman’s true sphere" <note>Kingsley is using irony here to comment on Victorian social expectations.</note> and assist in a humble way by catching the wine and Vichy water bottles, glasses, and plates of food. These items are put in danger during every "performance" by the members of the "nobler sex," who keep dashing off with a considerable portion of the large tablecloth wrapped around their legs. At last, I can stand it no longer, so I ask the captain point-blank what is the matter. "Nothing," he says, leaping out of his chair and flying out of his doorway; but upon his return, he tells me he has a bet of two bottles of champagne with the Woermann <note>The Woermann-Linie was a major German shipping company operating in West Africa.</note> agent for Njole regarding who shall reach Lambaréné <note>original: "Lembarene"</note> first. The German agent had started off some time before the *Éclaireur* <note>original: "Éclaireur"; the name of the steamer, meaning "The Scout"</note> in his little steam launch.

During the afternoon, we run smoothly along. The steady rhythm of the engines shows what a very different experience coming down the Ogowé is compared to going up against its powerful current. Every now and again we stop to pick up cargo or discharge cargo that was carried past its stop, and the captain's mind becomes eased because he has received no news of the Woermann launch passing downriver. He shares this thought with the engineer: it is impossible she could have passed the *Éclaireur* since they started; therefore, she must be somewhere behind them at a sub-factory <note>A smaller trading post subordinate to a main trading station.</note>. "Isn't that so?" <note>original: "N'est-ce pas?"</note> "Yes, yes, certainly," <note>original: "Oui, oui, certainement"</note> says the engineer. By these considerations, the engineer is also calmed, and he feels he may do something else besides scanning the river like "Sister Anne" <note>A reference to the fairy tale *Bluebeard*, in which Sister Anne stands on a tower looking for help to arrive.</note>. 

What that "something else" is puzzles me. It evidently requires secrecy, and he avoids being detected. First, he looks down one side of the deck—no one is there. Then he looks down the other—no one is there. Good so far. I then see that he has put his head through one of the saloon portholes; no one is there. He hesitates for a few seconds until I begin to wonder whether his head will suddenly appear through my own porthole; but he regards this as an unnecessary precaution, and I hear him enter his cabin, which sits next to mine. There is silence for some minutes. "He is writing home to his mother," I think to myself, as I continue sewing a new braid trim around the bottom of a worn—

# CAPTURE OF A HIPPOPOTAMUS

Breathless excitement! Surely they will get it now. Alas, no! Just when it is within reach of the canoe, a fearful shudder runs through the buoy. It throws up its head and sinks beneath the current. A feeling of shock comes over all of us. The canoe crew, ready and eager to grasp the approaching help, gaze blankly at the circling ripples where it sank. In a second, the captain knows what has happened. That heavy hawser <term>a thick rope used for mooring or towing a ship</term>, which had been let out after it, has dragged it down; so he hauls it back on board.

The *Éclaireur* <note>The Scout</note> now moves close enough to the hippo-anchored canoe for a rope to be thrown to the man in her bow; he catches it and hangs on gallantly. Saved! No! Oh, horror! The lower deck hums with fear that, after all, they will not taste that delicious hippopotamus chop. The man who caught the rope is nearly jerked out of the canoe when the strain of the *Éclaireur*—contending with the hippopotamus's weight—travels along the line. However, his companion behind him grips him by the legs and is, in turn, grabbed by another. The crew, holding on to each other with their hands and to their boat with their feet, save the man with the rope and the entire situation. Slowly bobbing toward us comes the hippopotamus, which is soon hauled on board by the triumphant winners.

My esteemed friends, the captain and the engineer, who of course have been below during this hauling, now rush onto the upper deck, each coatless and carrying an enormous butcher’s knife. They dash into the saloon, where a noisy sharpening of these instruments takes place on the sharpening steel belonging to the saloon's carving knife, and then they head back downstairs. The captain had had enough of it, he said, but the engineer stuck to the task with a courage I profoundly admire. He saw it through and then retired to his cabin; he scrubbed himself with sand and canvas first, and then soaked and saturated himself in Florida water <term>a popular 19th-century American cologne used for refreshing and masking odors</term>. The flesh gladdened the hearts of the crew and the lower-deck passengers, as well as the inhabitants of Lembarene, who received portions <term>originally "dashes," a West African term for gifts or small payments</term> of it upon our arrival there. Hippo meat is not to be despised by either Black or white men; I have enjoyed it far more than the stringy beef or tasteless goat meat one gets down here.

I stayed on board the *Éclaireur* <note>original: "Éclaireur," French for "The Scout"</note> all night; for it was dark when we reached Lembarene, too dark to travel around to Kangwe. The next morning, after taking my leave of her—I hope not a final one, for she is a most luxurious little vessel for the Coast, as the food on board is excellent and the company varied and charming—I went around to Kangwe. Monsieur and Madame Jacot received me back most kindly, and they both looked all the better for my having been away. Monsieur Haug and a young missionary from Baraka, who had come up to Lembarene for a change of air after a fever, were busy preparing to go up to Talagouga in a canoe. I was very glad of this, because M. Haug, at any rate, would be of immense help to Madame and Monsieur Forget while they were in such bad health; however, during his absence, M. Jacot had enough work to keep five men busy.

I remained for some time in the Lembarene district and saw and learned many things. I owe most of what I learned to M. and Mme. Jacot, who knew a great deal about both the local people and the district, and I owe much of what I saw to having mastered the art of managing a native canoe by myself. I am certain this “recklessness” of mine did not deserve the severe criticism it has been subjected to, for my performances gave immense amusement to others (I can hear Lembarene’s shrieks of laughter even now) and to myself they gave great pleasure.

# A TRIAL TRIP
<sig>X</sig>

In the afternoon, I thought Monsieur and Madame Forget were safely taking their siestas <term>midday naps</term>. Oranie was with Madame Gacon. I knew for certain where Madame Gacon was; she was with Monsieur Gacon. I also knew he was up in the sawmill shed, out of sight of the river, because I could hear the soft *thump, thump, thump* of the large water-wheel. There was, therefore, no one to keep me out of trouble. I was too frightened to go into the forest that afternoon because, on the previous afternoon, I had been stalked like a wild beast by a cannibal savage, and I am a nervous person. Besides, and above all, it is quite impossible to watch other people—even if they are only "naked savages"—gliding about in canoes without wishing to go and glide about yourself. So, I went down to where the canoes were tied by their bows to the steep bank. Finding a paddle—a broken one—I untied the smallest canoe. Unfortunately, this boat was about fifteen feet long, but I did not then realize the disadvantage of having such a "long-tailed" canoe; I found out shortly afterward.

The points of land extending into the river on each side of the mission beach create a small stretch of calm water between the bank and the current of the Ogowé, which runs like a mill-race. I wisely decided to stay in the calm water until I had figured out how to steer—steering being the most important thing. I got into the bow <term>the front of the boat</term> of the canoe and pushed off from the bank successfully. Then I knelt down—planning to learn how to paddle while standing up later on. So far, so good. I quickly learned how to steer from the bow, but I could not pick up any speed. Intent on gaining speed, I reached the edge of the calm water; then, showing more wisdom, I turned around to avoid the main current. I was as proud as a peacock, you understand, for having figured out how to turn around. At that moment, the current of the greatest equatorial river in the world grabbed my canoe by its tail. We spun around and around for a few seconds like a teetotum <term>a four-sided spinning top used in games of chance</term>, while I steered with all my might. Then, the current humiliatingly dragged the canoe downriver, tail-first.

Fortunately, a large tree was temporarily stuck against a rock in the river just below the sawmill beach. The canoe crashed into that tree, and I held on. Pulling my paddle inside, I hauled the canoe back into the calm water...

...again, with the help of the branches of the tree, which I was in deadly terror would break off the rock and insist on accompanying me and the canoe, via Kama country <note>The region inhabited by the Enenga and Galwa people along the Ogowé</note>, to the Atlantic Ocean. But it held, and when I had gotten safe against the side of the pinnacle rock, I wiped a sweating brow and searched my mind for any bit of information regarding navigation that would be applicable to the management of long-tailed Adooma <note>The Adouma people are renowned as the best canoeists on the Ogowé River</note> canoes. 

I could not think of any for several minutes. Captain Murray has given me a vast amount of advice at one time or another regarding the management of vessels, but those vessels were all assumed to have steam power. However, since he had been the first man to take an ocean-going steamer up to Matadi on the Congo, through the terrifying currents that swirl and fly in Hell’s Cauldron, he knew about currents. I remembered he had said regarding taking vessels through them, “Keep all the headway you can on her.” 

Good! That hint, reversed, will fit this situation perfectly, and I’ll keep all the *tail-way* I can off her. Feeling now as safe as only a human being can feel who is backed up by a sound principle, I was cautiously crawling to the back end of the canoe, intending to kneel in it to look after it, when I heard a terrible shouting on the bank. 

Looking there, I saw Madame Forget, Madame Gacon, Monsieur Gacon, and their associated crowd of mission children, all in a state of frenzy. They said many things in unison. “What?” I said. They said some more and added gestures. Seeing I was wasting their time since I could not hear, I pushed the canoe from the rock and made my way, mostly by steering, to the bank close by. Then, after tying the canoe firmly, I walked over the millstream and various other obstacles toward my anxious friends. 

“You’ll be drowned,” they said. 

“Good heavens!” I said, “I thought that half an hour ago, but it’s all right now; I can steer.” 

After much conversation, I calmed their fears regarding me. Having received strict orders to keep in the stern <term>the back of a boat</term> of the canoe—because that is the proper place when you are managing a canoe alone—I returned to my studies. I had not, however, calmed my friends’ interest in me, and they stayed on the bank watching.

<page-num>199</page-num>
# X AMATEUR CANOEING

I discovered, first, that my training in steering from the front was useless; second, that it worked perfectly if you reversed the technique. For example, when you are in the bow <term>the front of the boat</term> and make an inward stroke with the paddle on the right-hand side, the bow moves to the right. However, if you make an inward stroke on the right-hand side while sitting in the stern <term>the back of the boat</term>, the bow then moves to the left. Do you understand? 

Having grasped this law of physics, I crept along upriver. But, by Allah! before I had gone twenty yards, that wretched current of the "Great River" <note>The Ogowé River; the author likely uses "&c." to refer to its full local titles</note> grabbed the nose of my canoe, and we spun around like a top again as merrily as ever. My audience on the bank screamed. I knew what they were saying: "You'll be drowned! Come back! Come back!" I heard them, but I paid no attention. If you listen to advice during a crisis, you are lost; besides, I couldn't have "come back" just then even if I had wanted to. 

However, I managed to get back into the calm water through some very flashy, high-quality steering. Yet steering, as fine as it is, is not everything you need and desire. You also want speed, and so far—except when caught in the clutches of the current—I had not achieved any. 

Perhaps, I thought, the source of speed in a canoe lies in its center; so I crawled on my knees into the middle to experiment. It was a total failure; the canoe began drifting sideways down the river, like Mr. Winkle's horse <note>A reference to a character in Charles Dickens’s "The Pickwick Papers" who struggles to control a horse that stubbornly moves sideways</note>. Shouts of laughter came from the bank. Both my front-end and back-end training were completely useless in the center. Seeing that I was entirely out of place there, I crept back into the bow. In a few more minutes, I steered my canoe perfectly among the other boats by the bank and tied it up. 

Madame Forget ran down to meet me and assured me she had not laughed so much since she had been in Africa, although she had been frightened at the time that I might capsize and drown. I believe her, for she is a sweet and gracious lady. I can see now, as she pointed out, that the sight of me spinning around like a top, all while trying to steer in an elaborate and flashy way, was incredibly funny. 

She also gave a most amusing account of how, when she started looking for me to offer me tea—a charming habit of hers—she could not see me among my specimen bottles. She asked the little black boy where I was. "There," he said, pointing to the tree hanging against the rock...

# LAMBARÉNÉ CHAPTER

...out in the river. Seeing me stuck in a canoe against the rock, and knowing the danger and depth of the river, she became alarmed.

Well, when I arrived at Lambaréné, I naturally continued my canoeing studies, trying to achieve real speed. My efforts were successful, and I can honestly and truly say that there are only two things I am proud of—one is that Doctor Günther <note>Albert Günther (1830–1914), a prominent zoologist at the British Museum who studied Kingsley's fish specimens</note> has approved of my fish collection, and the other is that I can paddle an Ogooué canoe. Speed, style, steering, and everything else—"just the same" <note>original: "All same for one," a West African Pidgin English phrase meaning "exactly the same"</note> as if I were a local Ogooué African. It is a strange, mismatched pair of achievements, but I often wonder what other people are truly most proud of; it would be an unusual and rewarding subject to investigate.

Madame Jacot gave me every possible help with my canoeing. She is a remarkably sensible woman and recognized that, since I was always getting soaked anyway, I ran no extra danger of getting wet in a canoe. Furthermore, because it was the dry season, there was a vast stretch of water opposite Andande beach that was quite shallow. Therefore, she didn't see any risk of me drowning.

The sandbanks were showing their yellow tops in every direction when I returned from Talagouga. Right across from Andande, a large, graceful palm frond was sticking up out of the water. It had been planted in the top of a favorite sandbank, and every day children would visit it in canoes to see how much longer they would have to wait for the sandbank’s appearance. A few days after my return, it emerged, and within two more days, there it was—acres and acres of it—looking like a vast golden carpet spread across the center of the clear water. The water is clear on this side of Lambaréné Island because the river flows fairly slowly here, giving the mud time to settle. On the other side of the island, the Ogooué rushes past a dark brown color, as the main current is diverted that way by a bend just below the entrance of the Ngounié River.

There was great rejoicing. One canoe after another, filled with boys and girls, headed to the sandbank. Some fished around its edges while others brought their laundry there, all of them playing and singing. I have rarely seen a more beautiful sight than those...

<page-num>201</page-num>
-># DEATH OF M. JACOT<-

...on that sandbank—the cheerful, dark figures dancing or lying stretched out upon it. There were brightly colored patchwork quilts and chintz mosquito nets that had been washed and spread out to dry; viewed from Kangwe <note>The site of a Protestant mission station on a hill overlooking the Ogooué River in Gabon</note> on the hill above, they looked like beds of vibrant flowers. At night, when the moon was out, groups of dancers would gather there with torches, spinning, mingling, and separating until you might imagine you were watching a dance of stars.

They started their activities very early on that sandbank and kept them up very late; all the while, a soft murmur of laughter and song drifted from it. Oh, if the goal of life were simply happiness and pleasure, Africa should be sending missionaries to us instead of us sending them there—but fortunately for the world's progress, happiness is not the ultimate goal.

One thing I remember that struck me deeply regarding the sandbank was how much pleasure Madame Jacot found in taking her work out onto the veranda where she could see it. I knew she did not care for the singing and dancing. One day she said to me, "It is such a relief."

"A relief?" I asked.

"Yes," she said. "Don't you see that until the sandbank appears, there is nothing but forest, forest, forest, and that still stretch of river? That bank is the only piece of open ground I see all year, and it only lasts a few weeks until the wet season arrives. Then it disappears, and there is nothing but forest, forest, forest for another year. It has been two years since I came to this place; I don’t know how many more it will be before we go home again."

I am deeply saddened to say, for my poor friend’s sake, that her life at Kangwe was nearing its end. Soon after my return to England, I heard of her husband's death from malignant fever <note>Likely a severe case of malaria or yellow fever</note>. Monsieur Jacot was a fine, powerful, energetic man in the prime of life. He was a teetotaler <term>a person who never drinks alcohol</term> and a vegetarian; although he was constantly traveling back and forth through his district on his missionary work, he was never foolishly reckless. No one would have expected him to be the first of us to die—those of us who used to sit around his hospitable table. His delicate wife, his two young children, or I would have seemed far more likely candidates. His loss will be a lasting one to the people he risked his life to save (in his view). The local people held him in the greatest affection and respect, and his influence

His influence over them was considerable, far deeper than that of any other missionary I have ever seen. His death is also a great loss to those African scholars who are studying the culture or the languages; his knowledge of both was extensive, particularly regarding the little-known languages of the Ogooué district. When I left, he was busily employed in compiling a dictionary of the Fang <note>The original text uses "Fan."</note> language and had many other linguistic works in progress. His work in this field would have been highly valuable, for he was a man with a university education, well-grounded in Latin and Greek, and thoroughly acquainted with both English and French literature. Although born a Frenchman, he had been raised in America. He was also a skilled musician. In the evenings, he and Madame Jacot would sing old French, Swiss, and English songs in their rich, full voices; if you stepped quietly out onto the veranda, you would often find it crowded with a silent African audience, listening intently.

The amount of work M. and Madame Jacot used to complete was amazing to me. I believe the Ogooué Protestant mission is sadly understaffed; its missionaries are not content to follow the typical Protestant approach in West Africa—namely, sitting quietly and keeping house with just a few local children indoors to do the housework, while maintaining a school and a small church nearby for Sunday services. Instead, the representatives of the *Mission Évangélique* <note>original: "Mission Évangélique" — Evangelical Mission</note> travel back and forth throughout the district surrounding each station to perform missionary work among some of the most dangerous and unrefined tribes in Africa. They frequently spend two weeks at a time away from their homes, traveling the waterways of a wild and perilous country. In addition to going themselves, they send trained locals as evangelists and Bible readers, and they must supervise these trained locals closely, which involves a considerable amount of worry and strain. The work at the stations in the Ogooué districts is heavy because once you have cleared the land and finished the buildings, the job is by no means over; you must constantly fight the Ogooué forest back, just as a Dutchman fights the sea. However, the primary cause of labor is the mission store, which, in this exhausting climate, is more than enough work for one man alone.

<page-num>203</page-num>
<header>NATIVE FINANCE</header>
<sig>X</sig>

Payments on the Ogooué <note>The original text uses "Ogowé."</note> are made in goods; the natives do not use any currency equivalent, except in the unusual case of the Fang <note>The original text uses "Fans."</note> people, which does not affect general trade and which I will discuss later. They do not even use the brass bars and *cheetems* <term>A specific type of imported cloth used as currency in the Bight of Biafra.</term> that are used in Calabar, or cowries as in Lagos. To speed up and simplify this trade in goods, a written or printed piece of paper is used—essentially a check—which is called a "bon" <note>French for "voucher" or "good for."</note> or "book." These "bons" are "gooded"—that is, cashed—at the store. They represent three amounts: 
- Five *fura* <term>A local unit of value based on the franc.</term> equal one dollar.
- One *fura* equals one franc.
- A *desu* <term>Likely derived from the French "dix sous," representing ten sous.</term> equals fifty centimes, or half a *fura*. 

The value given for these "bons" is the same whether from the government, commercial traders, or the mission. Although the Evangelical Mission <note>original: "Mission Évangélique"</note> does not engage in trade—meaning they do not buy produce to sell for a profit—its representatives have a great deal of business to manage through the store, which functions practically as a bank. All the native evangelists, Black teachers, Bible-readers, and laborers at the stations are paid with these *bons*. Additionally, when any mission representative is away on a journey, food purchased for themselves and their canoe crews is paid for in *bons*. These are brought in by the natives at their convenience and exchanged for goods at the store. 

Therefore, for several hours every weekday, the missionary must dedicate himself to store work. Store work here is by no means merely "playing shop." It is very hard, tiring, and exasperating work when you have to handle it fully as a trader, where you must purchase produce at a price that leaves a reasonable profit margin after accounting for storage, customs duties, shipping expenses, and so on. However, it is enough to test the patience of any saint even when you are only running the store to pay out on *bons*, missionary-style <note>original: "à la missionary"</note>. This is because every class of article used in trade—and there are hundreds of them—has a fixed and recognized value. The trouble arises because different articles have the same value; for example, six fishhooks and one pocket handkerchief have the same value. Alternatively, you can make up that value with matches <note>original: "lucifer matches"</note>, pomade <note>original: "pomatum"</note>, a mirror, a hair comb, tobacco, or bottled scent.

Now, if you are a trader, some of these articles cost you more than others, even though they have an identical value to the local people. Consequently, it is to your advantage to pay with what we

Take gunpowder as an example. There is no profit on gunpowder for the trader in the *French Congo* <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>, but the native always wants it because he can make a huge profit on it from his fellow Black people in the bush. Consequently, it pays the trader better to pay out his *voucher* <gloss>bon</gloss> in Boma checks and similar currency rather than in gunpowder. This is a constant source of argument and persuasion. 

However, whether the native is turning in a bundle of rubber or an ivory tusk, or merely cashing a *voucher* <gloss>bon</gloss> for a week’s bush catering, he is—in the *French Congo* <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>—incapable of deciding what he wants when it comes down to it. He enters the shop with a *voucher* <gloss>bon</gloss> in his hand, perhaps with the idea in his head that he wants fish-hooks—"*jupes*" <note>Possibly a local trade term or a corruption of the French word for "skirts."</note>, he calls them. But, confronted with the visible temptation of hair ointment <term>pomatum</term>, he hesitates and scratches his head violently. 

Surrounding him are ten or twenty other natives in a similarly wavering state of mind, yet all are anxious to be served immediately. As a result of that stimulating head-scratch, he remembers that one of his wives told him to bring some matches <term>lucifer matches</term>, another wanted cloth for herself, and a third knew of some rubber she could buy very cheaply, using tobacco, from a Fang <note>original: "Fan"</note> woman who had stolen it. This rubber he knows he can take to the trader’s store and sell for high-quality handkerchiefs, gunpowder, or rum—items he cannot get at the mission store. 

He finally chooses something and takes it home, and likely enough brings it back a day or so later, somewhat damaged, desiring to exchange it for some other article or articles. Remember also that these Bantu, like other Black people, think out loud in a booming voice. Like Mr. Kipling’s camel <note>A reference to Rudyard Kipling’s poem "Oonts," which describes the camel as smelling "most awful vile."</note>, he "smells most awful vile." If he is a Fang man, he accompanies his observations with violent, dramatic gestures. Regardless of the customer’s tribe or sex, the customer is sadly, sadly liable to pick up any portable object within reach during the uproar of his companions and hide it in his armpits, between his legs, or, if his cloth wrap is large enough, inside that.

<page-num>205</page-num>
<header>MISSION SCHOOLS</header>
<sig>X</sig>

Imagine the anxieties of a Christian minister who is forced to act as a storekeeper under these circumstances—likely while suffering from a fever and with parasitic fleas <term>jiggers</term> in his feet. Even when the store is closed, the goods inside require constant vigilance to protect them from mildew and white ants.

In addition to the work at the store, the schools for both boys and girls are a constant source of labor and worry. It is considered useless to try to gain any real influence over the children unless they are removed from the influence of the local customs that surround them in their village homes. Therefore, the schools are boarding schools; consequently, the entire care of the children, including feeding and clothing them, falls upon the missionary.

The French government has made matters more difficult by decreeing that the children must be taught French. The law does not require that missionary work be conducted in French, but it mandates that if any foreign language is taught, that language must be French first. The missionaries generally oppose this because of the great difficulty in teaching the natives such a delicate and highly complex language. Africans pick up English faster than any other foreign language.

I do not like to think that my esteemed friend Donna Maria de Sousa Coutinho is right when she says this is "because it is so much more like their own savage tongue." Instead, I attribute this facility in learning English to the universal use of "Trade English" in the surrounding villages. Indeed, I believe that if the missionary were left alone, he would not teach any European language at all. He would instead limit himself to using the native languages in their phonetically written forms. Africans learn to read these very quickly, and the missionary can then restrict their reading to those books he deems suitable for his congregation—namely, the Bible, the hymn-book, and John Bunyan’s *The Holy War*.

The native does not see things in this light. Half the time, he comes to the schools only to learn what he calls "sense"—that is, the White man’s ways and language, which will enable him to trade more effectively. Native interpreters are occasionally "deceitful above all things and desperately wicked," <note>A reference to the biblical verse Jeremiah 17:9.</note> making the just administration of the country under these conditions almost impossible.

You may ask, "Why should the government official not learn the native language like the missionary?" I believe government officials who are settled in one place like missionaries on the Coast should indeed do so. However, if you enforced this rule in the French Congo, where government officials are frequently moved from place to place, only polyglots like Mezzofanti <note>Cardinal Giuseppe Mezzofanti (1774–1849) was a famous Italian linguist who reportedly spoke dozens of languages fluently.</note> would be eligible for appointments. In my limited experience, I have met representatives there from tribes speaking Shekani, Balungi, M'benga, M'billo, M'pongwe, Bakele, Ncomi, Igalwa, Adooma, Ajumba, and Fan, and there are plenty more. Furthermore, none of these tribes are neatly confined to distinct districts; therefore, you cannot simply teach an unfortunate official one language and then keep him in one place where he could use it. Certain districts have a majority of certain tribes, but that is all. The Fan people are everywhere in the northern districts of the Ogowé; however, among them, in the districts below Lambaréné, you will find Igalwa and Ajumba villages side by side, likely with a Bakele village just across the stream. Above Talagouga, until you reach Boué, you could get along with the Fan language alone; however, there is no government rule requiring language skills there because, aside from keeping the Ogowé River open to the French flag, the area is not interfered with. Then, when you reach Franceville above Boué, there is an entirely different group of languages—Okota, Batoke, Adooma, and others—along with the Middle Congo languages. To require a knowledge of all these languages would be absurd and would necessitate a massive increase in the number of officials.

<header>TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION</header>
<sig>X</sig>

[They assist] the mission ladies with sewing, washing, and ironing; in other respects, they have an uncommonly pleasant and easy time. They bitterly regret that this time is over when they go to their husbands—for every one of them has a husband.

It is strange that no government here provides technical instruction. All the governments support mission schools through grants, but the graduates produced by these schools are, at best, only fit to be clerks. The rest of the world seems to have a surplus of clerks already, and Africa does not need clerks yet; it needs planters. I do not mean just plantation laborers, for I am certain, based on the self-taught native planters I have seen in Cameroon, that intelligent Africans could do an immense amount to develop the country's resources. The Roman Catholic mission at Landana does great work by providing agricultural instruction in improved methods. However, most other technical mission stations limit their focus to teaching carpentry, bricklaying, blacksmithing, tailoring, bookbinding, and printing. With the exception of the first two, Africa does not yet urgently need to be taught these trades.

Even teaching sewing, washing, and ironing is a bit premature. The kind Mme. Jacot will exhaust herself for months teaching a <term>Fan</term> <note>The Fan (now commonly called Fang) are a large Bantu ethnic group found in equatorial Africa.</note> girl how to make a dress. The girl will learn eagerly and enjoy the finished dress so much that it breaks one's heart to know her future. When her husband soon takes her back to his village, despite the two dresses the mission gave her, she will be reduced to wearing a bit of filthy rag. This rag will serve as her dress, sheet, towel, and dishcloth. Even if her husband were willing to provide more cloth for her to practice her dressmaking skills, he would not dare to do so. Men are men and women are women the world over; what would his other wives, his mother, and his sisters say? Furthermore, washing and ironing are merely "parlor tricks" when your husband does not wear a shirt and household linens do not exist, as is the case among the <term>Fans</term> and many other African tribes. There are other things these women could be taught that would be of much greater benefit to them and those around them.

[...leaf-cloth, and though the cooks] should be men, yet all the cooking among the natives themselves is done by women. It is done abominably badly in all the Bantu tribes I have ever encountered; and the Bantu are in this particular—and indeed in most particulars—far inferior to the true Negro, although I must admit this is not the conventional view. The Negroes generally cook very well, and at times they are truly inspired when it comes to palm-oil chop <note>A traditional West African stew made with palm nut oil, meat or fish, and vegetables.</note> and cooking fish. This is not the case with the Bantu, whose methods desperately need improvement, as they use the easiest and laziest possible ways of preparing food. 

Their food supply consists of plantains, yams, coco-yams, sweet potatoes, corn, pumpkins, pineapples, and okra; fish, both fresh and smoked; and meat of many kinds—including human flesh in certain districts—as well as snails, snakes, crayfish, and the large, maggot-like larvae of the rhinoceros beetle and the *Rhyncophorus palmatorum* <note>The African palm weevil, whose larvae are a common food source.</note>. For sweets, sugar cane is abundant, but it is only eaten raw <note>original: "au naturel"</note> by chewing it. For seasoning, there is a type of bark that tastes like an onion—a distinctly spoiled <note>original: "passé"</note> onion, but powerful and long-lasting, especially if it has been used in one of the rough, native-made earthenware pots. 

These pots look very primitive; they are unglazed, lidless bowls. They withstand fire wonderfully well, but you must tolerate, as best you can, the flavor of the aforementioned bark that clings to them, as well as the taste of the smoke that enters them during cooking over an open wood fire. They even impart a soot-like color to your own white rice. Using all these varied materials, the natives of the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note> forests produce a dull, indigestible diet in a dirty, careless, and wasteful manner. 

Yams, sweet potatoes, okra, and corn are not cultivated or used as much as they are among the Negroes. The daily food consists almost entirely of plantains—picked while green, peeled, and the tasteless, starchy interior baked or boiled—and the widely distributed manioc <term>manioc</term> <note>Also known as cassava.</note>, which is prepared in the usual way. I have rarely seen the sweet or non-poisonous manioc cultivated because it produces a much smaller yield and takes much longer to mature. The poisonous variety is the one in general use; its large, dahlia-like roots are soaked in water to remove the toxins, and then dried and grated, or more commonly beaten into a kind of dough in a wooden trough...

<page-num>209</page-num>
-> MANIOC MEAL <-
<sig>X, P</sig>

...that looks like a model canoe, along with wooden clubs that I have seen curiosity hunters happily taking home as "war clubs" to frighten their families with. The thump, thump, thump of this manioc beating is one of the most familiar sounds in a bush village. When the meal is beaten up, it is used for thickening broths, or it is rolled into bolsters about a foot long and two inches in diameter. These are then wrapped in plantain leaves, tied around with tie-tie <term>vines or strips of bark used as cordage</term>, and boiled—or more properly speaking, steamed. A number of the rolls are arranged in a brass skillet—a "kettle," Mr. Hudson <note>Likely a reference to a local missionary or colonial official</note> persists in calling it; but, much as I respect his statements, I cannot blindly accept this one. Any woman knows a kettle must have a spout, and these utensils are spoutless and round, with a handle across the top, looking for all the world like the skillet I make jam in back in England—a skillet, I repeat. A small quantity of water is poured over the rolls of plantain, a plantain leaf is tucked tightly over the top to prevent the steam from escaping, and the whole affair is balanced on three cooking-stones over a wood fire. It is left there until the contents are done—or more properly speaking, until the lady in charge of it has delusions on the matter, and the bottom rolls are a trifle burnt or the whole batch is insufficiently cooked.

This manioc meal is the staple food, the equivalent of bread, all along the coast. As you travel, you are perpetually encountering new names for this food: *fou-fou* on the Leeward Coast, *kank* on the Windward Coast, *m’vada* in Corisco, and *agooma* in the Ogowé. However, an acquaintance with it demonstrates that it is all the same thing—manioc. If I ever meet a tribe that refers to "buttered muffins," I shall know what to expect and so will not get excited.

It is a good food when it is properly prepared; but when a village has soaked its soil-laden manioc tubers in the exact same pool of water for years, the water in that pool becomes a trifle strong. Both the water and the manioc acquire a smell which, once smelled, is never to be forgotten. It is something like the smell of bad paste with a dash of vinegar, but it far surpasses those things, having qualities of its own that have no civilized equivalent.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of West African culinary practices, specifically focusing on the health impacts of a manioc-heavy diet and the methods used to prepare fish and meat in the interior regions.</meta>

<page-num>210</page-num>
# LAMBARÉNÉ CHAPTER

The diet is largely responsible for that severe and frequent disease known as "cut-belly" <term>likely dysentery or acute abdominal pain</term> and several other unusual disorders, possibly even sleeping sickness <term>Trypanosomiasis</term>. The natives themselves say that a diet consisting too exclusively of manioc <term>cassava</term> produces dimness of vision, ending in blindness if the food is not varied. The poisonous principle <note>Manioc contains cyanogenic glycosides which must be removed through thorough soaking and fermenting; if the water is already saturated, the toxins remain.</note> cannot be properly soaked out in saturated water, and the meal, when it is prepared and cooked, has the same sour, acrid taste you would expect from its smell.

The fish is boiled or wrapped in leaves and baked. Dried fish, very appropriately known as "stink-fish," is much preferred; this is either eaten as it is or added to stews as seasoning, as are snails. Meat is eaten either fresh or smoked, boiled or baked. By "baked," I always mean buried in the ground with a fire lit on top, or wrapped in leaves and buried in hot embers.

The smoked meat is poorly prepared; it is simply hung in the smoke of the fires, which hardens it and blackens the outside quickly. However, when the lumps are taken out of the smoke, cracks soon appear in them, and the interior begins to spoil and, needless to say, becomes maggoty. If it is kept in the smoke—as it often is to keep it away from dogs and driver ants—it acquires the pleasant taste and texture of a piece of old tarpaulin. I have gone into this wilderness cooking here in detail so that you may understand why, on the Coast, when a man comes in and says he has been living on local food <term>native chop</term>, we say "Good gracious!" and hand out our best tinned goods on the spot.

I may be judging the coastal tribes too harshly if I include them with the wilderness tribes in my culinary indictment, so I confine my accusations to the Fans and up-river tribes, with whose cooking methods I have been more in contact. When on the coast, I have been either in European houses or in those of educated natives who have, at any rate, partially adopted European ways of cooking. I must say that among the Mpongwe and Igalwas, I came across a bright ray of intelligence—nay, I will say genius—in the matter of Odeaka cheese <term>Odika: a paste made from the kernels of wild mango seeds, often called "African dika butter"</term>. It is not actually cheese, but, as the schoolboy said concerning the author of the *Iliad* <note>A common 19th-century joke: "The Iliad was not written by Homer, but by another man of the same name."</note>, it is something else of the same name; but it is good.

<header>REASONS FOR POLYGAMY</header>
<sig>P 2</sig>

...and I will sing its praises when I talk of the M'pongwe. Now, I must ask the surviving reader, who has waded through this lengthy discussion on cookery, if something should not be done to improve the degraded condition of Bantu cooking culture? This is not for his physical pleasure alone, but because his current methods are bad for his morals and drive the man to drink. Furthermore, these methods assist in keeping him stuck in the practice of polygamy, which the missionaries say is an exceedingly bad practice for him to follow.

The relationship between these two subjects may not seem very clear on the surface, but connections between customs very rarely are. I well remember Monsieur Jacot coming home one day to Kangwe from an evangelizing visit to some nearby Fan towns. He said he had been given a new reason for polygamy that afternoon: it enabled a man to get enough to eat. This sounds sinister coming from a notoriously cannibalistic tribe, but the explanation is simply that the Fans are an exceedingly hungry tribe and require a great deal of providing for. 

It is their custom to eat about ten times a day when in a village. The men spend most of their time in the <term>palaver-houses</term> <note>Community meeting houses used for social gatherings and legal discussions</note> at each end of the street, and the women bring them bowls of food of one kind or another all day long. When the men are away in the forest hunting for rubber or elephants and have to cook their own food, they cannot get quite as much to eat. However, when I have come across them on these expeditions, they halted quite regularly every two hours to have a substantial snack. The massive feast they all indulge in after a successful elephant hunt is a thing to see—once.

There are other reasons, besides cooking, which lead to the prevalence of this custom. One is that it is totally impossible for one woman to do all the work of a house—looking after the children, preparing and cooking the food, processing the rubber, carrying it to the markets, fetching the daily supply of water from the stream, cultivating the plantation, and so on. Perhaps I should say it is impossible for the slow African woman; I once had an Irish <term>charwoman</term> <note>A woman employed to do housework or cleaning</note> who drank, yet she would have done a whole week's work of an African village in an afternoon, and then been quite fresh enough to knock some of the nonsense out of her husband's head with that of

...the broom, and throw a kettle of boiling water or a kerosene lamp at him if she suspected him of flirting with other ladies. That woman, who deserves fame in the history of her country, was named Harragan. She attained immortality some years ago by falling down the stairs one Saturday night from excitement arising from "*the Image's*" (Mr. Harragan’s) conduct; but we have no Mrs. Harragans in Africa. The African lady does not care a traveling tinsmith’s curse <term>travelling whitesmith's execration</term> <note>A phrase indicating a trivial or common oath; a "whitesmith" is a worker in white metal, such as tin</note> if her husband flirts, as long as he does not go and give the cloth, etc., that should be hers to other women. "The more wives, the less work," says the African lady; and I have known men who would have preferred to have only one wife and spend the rest of their money on themselves in a civilized way, but were driven into polygamy by the women. Of course, this state of affairs is most common in non-slave-holding tribes like the Fan. But then there is that custom which, as far as I know, is common to all African tribes—and I suspect to Asiatic ones as well—which is well known to ethnologists, and which once caused a missionary to say to me:

> "A blow must be struck at polygamy, and that blow must be dealt with a feeding bottle."

He was a practical man, so there are a couple of gross <note>A gross is 144 items</note> of Alexandra feeding bottles <note>A popular 19th-century baby bottle with a long rubber tube, which the missionary hoped would reduce the long period of breastfeeding that often restricted a mother's labor and contributed to the social structure of polygamy</note> at a place on the Coast; but they don't sell, and the missionary has returned to America.

Now polygamy is, like most other subjects, a difficult thing to form an opinion on if, before forming that opinion, you actually study the facts and implications of the case. It is therefore advisable to follow the usual method employed by the majority of people: just take a prejudice of your own and bolster it with the so-called opinions of people who share that same prejudice. This method is absolutely essential to forming an opinion on the subject of polygamy among African tribes that will be acceptable in "enlightened" circles. Polygamy is the institution which, above all others, governs the daily life of the native. It is, therefore, the one that the missionaries—who enter into this daily life and not merely into commercial and legal matters like the trader and the government official—are constantly confronted with and hindered by. They hesitate to cast out women from their homes who have lived and worked for them for years—and not just for them, but often for their fathers before them. I know of one case in the Rivers region that is almost tragic if you put yourself in the man's position. An old chief, who had three wives, deeply and vividly believed that being barred from Holy Communion meant eternal damnation. The missionary had thoroughly instructed him on the details of this damnation, and the chief did not like the prospect at all. On the other hand, he did not like to turn away the three wives he had lived with for years. He found that the matter could not even be settled by compromise. He could not simply send away two wives and go to church to be married with hymns and orange blossoms to the third, because the women stood together. Not one of them would marry him if it meant the other two had to leave. Consequently, the poor old chief worried himself into a hammock and bothered anyone else he could get to listen to him. 

His white trader friends told him not to be such a complete fool. Some of his fellow Black chiefs said the missionary was quite right. They suggested the best thing for him to do would be to hand over the three old wives to them and go marry a young girl from the mission school. Personally, they were not yet bothered by moral objections to polygamy. Of course, they assumed that since he was a "missionary man" now, he would not think of accepting payment for his wives. Therefore, they offered to do their best, as friends, to help him out of his difficulty. Other fellow Black chiefs, who were less influenced by European culture, simply said, "What kind of foolish talk <term>palaver</term> <note>palaver: a long discussion, dispute, or negotiation, often between different cultures</note> is this?" and spat repeatedly. The poor old man felt the heat of hellfire, cried out "Yo, yo, yo," and beat his hands against the ground. It was a moral disaster of the highest order. 

Still, do not imagine the mission field is full of such distressed old chiefs. Although the African is often indecisive, he is also very clever, particularly at avoiding inconvenient moral principles. Many sharp-witted old chiefs turn on their pastors and ask pointed questions regarding the biblical patriarchs <note>The leaders of the tribes of Israel in the Old Testament, such as Abraham and Jacob, who often had multiple wives</note>. I have heard more than one frustrated pastor question the wisdom of introducing the Old Testament to the locals. Many a young man hesitates

He knows he would not be allowed to beat her, and he knows that she would be aware of this and might misbehave in any number of ways. She might also report all his minor failings to the mission, getting him into trouble with the missionary, whose high opinion he values. He is clever enough to realize that he enjoys more favor as an interesting potential convert than he would as a Church member subject to "discipline" <note>Ecclesiastical punishment or censure for breaking church rules.</note>.

The most difficult cases involving polygamy for the missionary are those concerning boys trained in the mission school who marry girls from the same background. For a time, they live according to Church laws; then they maintain the appearance of following them while abandoning them in their hearts. During this transition period—where the missionary fights a difficult and losing battle for these souls against their inherited sensuality and laziness—they sink into a state that, in my view, seems worse than if they had never encountered a missionary at all. However, I will not delve into the destabilizing effects of mission training here, because my opinions on that matter do not apply to the work of the *Mission Évangélique* <note>The Evangelical Missionary Society of Paris.</note>. Their influence on the locals has been, and remains, entirely positive. Considering their limited financial resources, the amount of work they have accomplished is remarkable to anyone who has seen other missions, and they are not subject to the usual criticisms leveled at missions in general.

Missionary work on the Ogowé was first established by Dr. Nassau, the great pioneer and explorer of these regions. He was representing the American Presbyterian Society; however, when the French government mandated that schooling be conducted in French, the stations on the Ogowé—Lembarene (Kangwe) and Talagouga—were transferred to the *Mission Évangélique* of Paris. They have since been managed by its representatives with great devotion and energy. For my own reasons, I am generally unsympathetic toward Christian missions; therefore, my admiration for this particular mission does not stem from the typical praise—that they are doing "great and holy work" regardless of how it is managed. Instead, I respect the *Mission Évangélique* based on the actual results I have seen...

# X LEMBARENE ISLAND

...as the perfection of what one might call a purely spiritual mission.

Lembarene is, strictly speaking, a district that includes Adânlinan lângâ and the Island, but the name is locally used to denote the large island in the Ogowé River, whose native name is Nenge Ezangy. However, for the sake of the general reader, I will keep to the everyday term of Lembarene Island.

Lembarene Island is the largest of the islands on the Ogowé. It is about fifteen miles long from east to west, and a mile to a mile and a half wide. It is hilly and rocky, consistently covered with forest, and several small, permanent streams run from it on both sides into the Ogowé. It is situated 130 miles from the sea, at the point just below the entrance of the N’guni River, where the Ogowé begins to divide into that network of channels through which—like all great West African rivers except the Congo—it chooses to enter the ocean. The island, as we mainlanders at Kangwe used to call it, was a favorite haunt of mine, particularly after I returned from Talagouga and decided I was competent enough to control a canoe. I do not mean that I was cut off from it before; for M. Jacot and M. Haug were always willing to send me across in a large canoe with the mission boys to paddle. The boys were always ready to come because it meant a "dash" <term>A tip, gift, or small payment common in West African trade and service.</term> and the amusement of going to what was the local equivalent of Paris. However, there was always plenty of work for them at the mission station, so I did not like taking them away. Therefore, once I could get there alone, I went more frequently.

From Andande, the beach at Kangwe, the width of the arm of the Ogowé to the nearest village on the island was about the same as that of the Thames at Blackwall. One half of the way was calm water, while the other half was positioned broadside against a stiff current. My favorite canoe at Andande was about six feet long, pointed at both ends, and flat-bottomed so that it floated on top of the water. Its freeboard <term>The distance between the waterline and the upper edge of the boat's side.</term> was only about three inches when empty. The poor thing had seen its share of trouble, for it had a hole at one end large enough to put your hand through. In order to navigate it successfully, you had to squat in the other end, which sank...

He introduced himself as Samuel and volunteered the statement that he was "a very good man." We settled ourselves in the canoe: he took the bow, I sat in the middle, and a Mrs. Samuel sat in the stern. Mrs. Samuel was a powerful, attractive lady and a diligent, tireless paddler. Mr. Samuel was none of these things, but a former Bible reader <term>A layperson employed by missions to read scripture to the community.</term> with an amazing knowledge of English, which he spoke in a curious, high-pitched, distant sort of voice; and that man’s greatest flaw was curiosity. 

"Are you a Christian, ma’am?" he asked. 

I asked him if he had ever met a white person who was not. 

"Yes, ma’am," said Samuel. 

I said, "You must have been spending time with people you shouldn't know." 

Samuel, fortunately lacking a comeback for this, paddled on with his long paddle for a few seconds. "Where is your husband, ma’am?" was the next conversational bomb he threw at me. 

"I don't have one," I answered. 

"Don't have one?" said Samuel, paralyzed with shock. As Mrs. Samuel, who did not know English, gave a vigorous shove with her paddle at that moment, Samuel was nearly jerked head-first into the Ogowé River, and we took on about two bucketfuls of water. He recovered himself, however, and returned to the attack. 

"You don't have one, ma’am?"

"I am not a trader," said Samuel, refusing to fall into my trap to change the subject. "Why don't you have one?"

# X A SAD CASE

The canoe was difficult to handle, but he landed me at Andande safely and received his dollar.

On my next trip, which took place the following day, I decided to go to the factory <term>A merchant's trading station or warehouse</term> by myself—it is located on the other side of the island—and I did so. I obtained some goods to trade for fish and heard from Mr. Cockshut that the poor young agent at Osoamokita had committed suicide. It was a tragic thing. He was, as I have mentioned, a bright, intelligent young Frenchman; but living in such isolation, surrounded by aggressive and tiresome tribes, the psychological pressure of his responsibilities had been too much for him. 

He had suffered significantly from fever, and the very kind head agent for Woermann’s <note>A prominent German shipping and trading company active in West Africa</note> had sent Dr. Pélessier to see if he should be sent home for medical reasons. However, he told the doctor he felt much better, and since he had no family at home to return to, he begged the doctor not to send him away. The doctor, to his later regret, gave in. No one who has not visited Africa can understand how terrible the life of a white man is in one of these remote factories, with no white society and nothing to look at, day in and day out, but the same set of objects—the forest, the river, and the beach. In a place like Osoamokita, you cannot leave these surroundings for months at a time, and you soon come to know every plank and stone by heart. 

I felt completely miserable as I started home again, heading toward the end of the island to go around it and down to Andande. I paddled for some time before I noticed that I was making absolutely no progress. I doubled my efforts and crept slowly toward some rocks sticking out of the water, but I could not pass them, as the main current of the Ogowé River swirled violently around them against my canoe. Several passing canoes full of natives gave me advice in Igalwa <term>A language spoken by the Igalwa people of the Gabonese coast</term>; but facts were facts, and the Ogowé was too strong for me. 

After about twenty minutes, an old Fan <term>The Fan (or Fang) people are an ethnic group in the Ogowé region</term> gentleman came down the river in a canoe and gave me advice in the Fan language. I managed to get him to take me in tow—that is to say, he got into my canoe and I held onto his, and we headed back downriver. I then realized his intention was to take me across to that disreputable village, half-Fan and half-Bakele <term>The Bakele (or Kélé) people of Gabon</term>, which is situated on the main bank of the river opposite the island. I did not go to the island the next day, but instead went down below Fula. I spent the time watching the fish playing in the clear water and the lizards and birds on the high, rocky banks. However, on my next journey around to the factories, I ran into another and even worse disaster. I set off early one morning; thinking the only difficulty lay in getting back up the Ogowé <note>The Ogooué River</note>, and having developed a theory that this could be minimized by keeping very close to the island bank, I never gave a thought to the dangers of going downriver. By then I had picked up speed, and my canoe shot out beyond the rocks at the end of the island and into the main stream. 

It took me a second to realize what had happened, and another to find that I could not pull the canoe out of the current without capsizing it, nor could I force it back up against the flow. There was nothing to do but keep the canoe's head straight now that it had bolted. A group of local ladies, who had followed my progress with much interest, shouted observations which I believe were: "Come back, come back; you’ll be drowned!" 

"Good-bye, Susannah, don’t you weep for me," <note>A humorous reference to the lyrics of the popular 19th-century American song "Oh! Susanna"</note> I courteously retorted. I flew past them, the factory beaches, and everything else in general, keenly watching for a chance to steer my canoe into a side channel, as if pulling off a main railway line. 

I finally found an opening—a spit of land projecting from the island with rocks sticking out of the water in front of it. This disrupted the current, and after a few wild turns and a close call when my terrified canoe almost tried to climb a rock, I reached slack water and took a moment to rest. <header>THE IGALWAS</header>
<sig>x</sig>

After an hour of steady paddling, I met three large canoes going upriver. They took me as far as Fula, from where a short paddle landed me at Andandé only slightly late for supper, convinced that it is almost as safe and far more amusing to be born lucky than wise.

Now that I have described my circumnavigation of the island, I will proceed to describe its inhabitants. The upriver end of Lambaréné Island is the most populated. A path around the upper part of the island passes through a succession of Igalwa villages and past the Roman Catholic missionary station. The slave villages belonging to these Igalwas are located further down the north face of the island, opposite the Fang <note>original: "Fan"</note> town of Fula, which I have already mentioned. It strikes me as remarkable that the Igalwa, like the Duala <note>original: "Dualla"</note> of Cameroon, keep their slaves in separate villages; but this is indeed the case, though I do not know the reason for it. These Igalwa slaves cultivate the plantations, bring vegetables and fruit up to their owners’ villages, and perform the daily housework.

The interior of the island consists of high, rocky, heavily forested hills, interspersed here and there with a stream or a swamp. The higher ground is toward the upriver end; downriver, there is a lower strip of land with small hills. I imagine this was formed by deposits of sand and other debris <note>original: "&c."</note> catching among the rocks and connecting what were once several isolated islands. There is no big game or gorillas on the island, but it is home to a peculiar and awful house ant. It is much smaller than the driver ant but has a venomous, painful bite. Its only redeeming quality is that its primary food is white ants <term>Termites</term>, which are consequently kept in check on Lambaréné Island, despite flourishing destructively on the mainland banks of the river in this area. I never tired of going to watch those Igalwa villagers, nor, I think, did the Igalwa villagers ever tire of observing me. Although the physical conditions of life were practically identical to those on the mainland, the way the Igalwas dealt with them—that is <note>original: "i.e."</note>, their culture—was distinct from the culture of the mainland Fang.

The Igalwas are a tribe very closely related to, if not ethnically identical with, the Mpongwe, and the culture of these two tribes is on a level with the highest native African civilizations.

<header>### LAMBARÉNÉ CHAPTER</header>

<margin>✓</margin>
African culture, I may remark, varies just as much as European culture in this regard: there is as much difference in the way of life between, say, an Igalwa and a Bubi of Bioko <note>original: "Fernando Po"</note> as there is between a Londoner and a Laplander <note>Now usually referred to as the Sami people</note>.

The Igalwa builds his house of bamboo, like those of the Mpongwe <note>original: "M'pongwe"</note>, and surrounds himself with European-made articles. The neat houses—fitted with windows, wooden shutters to close at night, and a solid pine <term>original: "deal"</term> door (a door made by a carpenter)—stand in sharp contrast to the ragged, ant-hill-looking structures of the Akkas, or the bark huts of the Fang <note>original: "Fan"</note>, which have no windows and only an extra-wide piece of bark to slide across the hole that serves as a door. 

On entering an Igalwa house, you will see a four-legged table, often covered with a bright-colored tablecloth, on which stands a water bottle and two clean glasses. Around you, you will see chairs—Windsor chairs. These houses usually have three or more rooms, and a separate enclosed little kitchen built nearby. In the kitchen, you may observe European-made saucepans in addition to the ever-present skillet. 

Outside, along the clean sandy streets, the inhabitants are seated. The Igalwa is truly great at sitting; the men pursue a policy of deliberate inactivity, interrupted occasionally by leisurely weaving a fishing net. The end of the net is hooked onto the thatched roof rather than held by a stirrup. The ladies are employed in manufacturing items belonging to a "higher culture"—I refer, as Mr. Micawber <note>A famously long-winded character from Charles Dickens’s novel "David Copperfield"</note> would say, to bedspreads and pillowcases. These are the most magnificent patchwork bedspreads and pillowcases. Every now and then, you will see a mosquito net <term>original: "mosquito-bar"</term> being made. Of course, these are not made of netting or muslin because of the terrifying strength and ferocity of the Lambaréné strain of mosquitoes, but of sturdy, floral-patterned chintz. You will notice that these items are often being sewn with a sewing machine. 

Here and there, you will see a misguided woman making a Mother Hubbard dress. Forgive me, but I must speak out on the subject of "Hubbards"; I promise to avoid offensive language, no matter what the effort costs me. A Hubbard <term>A loose, shapeless, high-necked dress introduced by Christian missionaries to enforce Western standards of modesty</term> is a female garment favored by every mission from Sierra Leone to the Belgian Congo <note>original: "Congo Belge"</note>, so please understand I am not criticizing...
