<header>### THE MOTHER HUBBARD <note>original: "THE HUBBARD"</note></header>
<meta>x at top left</meta>

...the Evangelical Mission <note>original: "Mission Évangélique"</note> in this matter. I believe these issues are among the factors causing the well-known lethargy of girls trained in the missions. These garments should be abolished for their own sake, quite apart from their appearance—which is enough to make them a punishable offense. 

Their design is as follows: a yoke fits around the neck and shoulders and fastens at the back with three buttons (two of which are usually missing). Short, stunted sleeves stick out from this yoke. Around the lower edge of the yoke, level with the armpits, a flounce is sewn on with many gathers, falling all the way to the wearer's heels. 

Sometimes this flounce is sewn on with a chain-stitch machine, which led to a dreadful accident I once witnessed on the Leeward Coast. In church, a child looking for amusement during the pastor's long, spontaneous prayer happened upon a white thread sticking out from the back of the yoke of a Mother Hubbard dress <term>A long, loose, shapeless dress introduced by missionaries</term> worn by the woman in front of her. The child pulled it out by the yard. Naturally, when the unsuspecting victim stood up, the entire functional part of her outfit collapsed to the floor. 

This is only an occasional danger, but the garment's constant habit is to fall forward and sweep up dirt whenever the wearer leans over. It gets into the fire, the cooking, and everything else, hindering all quick movement. These garments are usually made by sewing circles in Europe. I cannot imagine what idea the pious ladies in England, Germany, Scotland, and France have of the African physique, but they evidently believe it closely resembles a tub. 

I was once helping to unpack a shipment from the mission. "Why have they sent out these frilled covers for palm-oil barrels <term>original: "puncheons"</term>?" I asked my esteemed friend, the lady missionary. 

"Don’t be more foolish than you can help," she replied. "Don’t you see the sleeves? They are Mother Hubbards." 

I was silenced; but even she admitted it was frustrating that the people back home made them like that—especially since their delusions about the African figure weren't limited to Mother Hubbards, but extended to shirts and chemises <term>A woman's basic undergarment or simple dress</term> as well. There is nothing quite like measurements in ethnology <note>The study of the characteristics of different peoples</note>, so I took some. I found one garment with a length of thirty inches and a width <term>original: "breadth of beam"</term> of forty-two inches; another with a length of thirty-six...

This makes their broad, long heads appear as if they have two horns above them. They are very flattering to these dark but beautiful ladies—truly, I believe they are the most beautiful women I have ever seen on the Coast. They are very dark, darker than many of their neighbors and always darker than the Fang <note>original: "Fans"</note>. Although their skin lacks the velvety texture of the true Negro, it is not too shiny; instead, it is fine and usually unblemished. Their figures are gracefully rounded, and their hands and feet are small—almost as small as those of a high-class Calabar woman. Their eyes are large, lustrous, soft, and brown, and their teeth are as white as the sea foam and are not disfigured by filing.

The traditional dress for both men and women is the cloth wrap, or <term>paun</term> <note>A "paun" (from the Portuguese "pano") is a rectangular piece of fabric worn as a wrap-around garment.</note>. Men wear it by rolling the top edge around the waist. In addition, they frequently wear a singlet or a flannel shirt worn *in the African style* <note>original: "more Africano"</note>, letting it flow freely. Wealthy men will wear a European coat and hat, and men associated with the missions or trading stations occasionally wear trousers. The overall appearance of the men is not particularly striking when all is said and done, so we will return to the women. They wrap the upper hem of these cloths under their armpits, which is a graceful style of drapery, though it requires constant adjustment. The cloth is about four yards long and two yards deep. There is always a border, or false hem, along the edge made of <term>turkey red twill</term> <note>A durable cotton fabric dyed a bright red using a complex process involving madder root and oil.</note> or some other colored cotton fabric that contrasts with the main body of the <term>paun</term>. 

In addition to the cloth, they wear a European shawl when possible. This is either a thick cotton one printed with Chinese-style patterns in dull red on a dark background—this type is wrapped around the upper body—or, what is even more highly valued, a bright, light-colored, fancy wool shawl. Pink or pale blue are preferred. This is carefully folded into a roll and placed over one shoulder entirely for show <note>original: "for dandy"</note>. I am grateful to say they do not favor hats. When they wear anything on their heads, it is a handkerchief folded like a shawl. The base of the triangle is tied around the forehead just above the eyebrows, and the ends are carried around...

...over the ears and tied behind over the point <note>original: "apex"</note> of the triangle formed by the handkerchief, with the three ends then arranged like a fan at the back. Add to this costume a sober-colored silk parasol—not one of those green or red, tent-like, brutally masculine, knobby-handled umbrellas, but a delicate, ladylike parasol. When carefully rolled up, it is carried handle-forward right in the center of the head, also for style <note>original: "dandy"</note>. Then add a few strings of turquoise-blue beads, or imitation gold ones, worn around the shapely throat. I would bet on my Igalwa or M’pongwe beauty against any of those South Sea Island young ladies we hear so much about nowadays, thanks to Mr. Stevenson <note>Robert Louis Stevenson, who wrote extensively about his life and the people of the South Pacific in the late 19th century.</note>—even though those women may be draped in fragrant flowers, whereas African women very rarely use flowers for decoration. The only time I have seen African women wearing them as ornaments has been among the Igalwa, who occasionally pin pretty, small, round, bright red blossoms into their jet-black hair in a most attractive way. I wonder why Africans do not wear flowers more often, as both men and women are very fond of perfumes.

The common claim that African women age—"go off," I believe, is the technical term—very early is, I am certain, incorrect in many cases. Look at those Sierra Leone "mammies" <note>A term of respect for elder or influential West African women.</note>—slightly stout, I admit, but undeniably charming. And the Calabar women, although they belong to a very plain-looking tribe, show very little change over twenty years one way or the other. As for the women here in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>—well! I know one who is at least forty-five, and yet she is currently regarded by a French official—a judge, no less—as a beautiful woman <note>original: "une belle femme"</note>.

The Igalwa are a proud people, one of the noble tribes like the M’pongwe and the Ajumba. The women do not marry into lower-class tribes, and within their own tribe, their options are quite restricted because they are forbidden from marrying any relatives on the mother’s side. This well-known system of tracing lineage only through the mother—mother-right <note>original: "Mutter-recht"</note>—is more highly developed and complex among the Igalwa than among any other tribe I have personally encountered. Brothers and cousins on the mother’s side are grouped into a single class of relationship and are called by one name: *Ndako*.

A father’s responsibility regarding authority over his own...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of social structures among the Igalwa and M’pongwe peoples, focusing on the role of the maternal uncle in the family, marriage customs, and the conditions for divorce.</meta>

<header>MARRIAGE CUSTOMS</header>

the father's connection to the children is very slight. The truly responsible male relative is the mother’s eldest brother. Permission to marry must be obtained from him for either a girl or a boy. The gift required for a girl’s marriage must be given to him and the mother. Should the mother die, the responsibility for raising the children falls on him, not the father. They move to his house, and he treats and regards them as closer and dearer to him than his own children. Upon his death, after his own brothers from the same mother, they become his heirs. <note>This describes a matrilineal social structure known as the avunculate, where the maternal uncle holds primary authority over his sister's children and serves as their legal guardian.</note>

Marriage among the Igalwa and M’pongwe is not a direct purchase. Instead, a gift of a fixed price is given to the girl’s mother and uncle. Other conciliatory <term>propitiatory</term> gifts are also made, but these do not count legally. They do not necessarily have to be returned if marital disputes lead to a divorce—a very frequent occurrence in this society. Igalwa women are lively and devoted to fashion, and they often nag their husbands. On many occasions while walking on Lambaréné Island, I have seen a woman stand in the street and tell her husband exactly what she thought of him while he took shelter inside the house. The scene reminded me of the slums of London. When the husband loses his temper—which he inevitably does sooner or later, being a man—he beats his wife, or his wives if they have all ganged up on him. This crisis usually happens at night. While staying on board the *Mové* or the *Éclaireur* <note>The *Mové* and *Éclaireur* were steamers used for transport and trade in West Africa during this period.</note> moored at the landing place on Lambaréné Island, I have heard screams and cries of a most miserable nature. A husband may beat his wife without consequence as long as he does not draw blood. If he does, no matter how little, his wife leaves for her relatives. In that case, the gift he gave for her is returned, the marriage is annulled, and she can remarry as soon as she is able.

Her relatives are only too happy to have her back. Although the marriage gift must be returned, they get to keep the conciliatory offerings. Furthermore, they know that more conciliatory offerings and another marriage gift will be gained from the next set of suitors. Of course, this only happens with the younger women. Older women generally nag less, and moreover, they usually have children who are willing and able to support them.

<header>### LAMBARÉNÉ CHAPTER</header>

If they do not have children, their situation is very desolate, as is the case for all elderly childless women in Africa.

Infant marriage is now popular among the Igalwa, and to my surprise, I find it has been introduced and adopted quite recently. Their own explanation for this cultural decline is that in the last generation—some of the old people even claim to have known him—there was an exceptionally ugly and deformed man who could not find a wife. This was because the women then, just like the men now, were great admirers of physical beauty. Being very clever, this man came up with the idea of getting betrothed to a girl before she could choose for herself. Knowing a family where a "blessed event" was likely to occur, he gave expensive gifts to the right people and reserved the coming infant if it should be a girl. It was a girl, and so, say the Igalwa, the custom began. Nowadays, although they do not engage their wives as early as the founder of the custom did, they have adopted infant marriage as a social institution.

For the sake of <term>ethnology</term><note>the study of the characteristics of various peoples and the differences and relationships between them</note>, I asked carefully about what courting methods were used previously. They said that people used to marry because they loved each other. I think other ethnologists will investigate this further, for we might find a real "golden age" here, which in other human races is lost in the mists of time, predating even ancient <term>kitchen middens</term><note>prehistoric refuse heaps consisting of shells, bones, and other waste</note> and the Cambrian rocks. My own opinion on this matter is that the earlier courting methods of the Igalwa required a certain amount of effort from the man—something an Igalwa man finds repulsive. It required him to dress himself up and likely fight that "impudent scoundrel" who was also courting her. Above all, it meant serenading her at night on the native harp—with strings made from the tendrils of a certain orchid—or on the <term>marimba</term><note>a percussion instrument consisting of a set of wooden bars struck with mallets</note>, surrounded by swarms of mosquitoes. Any custom that involved being outside at night among the swarms of those Lambaréné mosquitoes would inevitably disappear, no matter what that custom might be.

The Igalwa are one of the coastal tribes that are dying out. In addition to Lambaréné Island, their villages are scattered along the banks of the Lower Ogowé River and on the shores and islands of *Elivã Z’onlange* <note>Lake Azingo</note>. On the island they are, so far, undis-

->**ODEAKA CHEESE**<-

...disturbed by the <term>Fang</term><note>historically referred to as "Fan"</note> invasion, they laze their lives away like lotus-eaters. Their slaves work their large plantations and bring them magnificent yams, ready-prepared <term>agooma</term><note>a thick porridge or paste made from mashed starchy vegetables like yams or cassava</note>, sweet potatoes, papayas, and so on—not forgetting that delicacy, <term>Odeaka cheese</term><note>also known as dika bread or odika; a rich, oily paste made from the seeds of the wild mango tree (*Irvingia gabonensis*)</note>. This is not exclusively their own invention, as the <term>Mpongwe</term><note>an ethnic group living primarily in the Gabon Estuary</note> and the <term>Benga</term><note>a coastal ethnic group of Gabon and Equatorial Guinea</note> use it as well. 

It is made from the kernel of the wild mango, a remarkably beautiful tree of great size with a stately spread of foliage. In its appearance and growth habit, I can only compare it to our Irish, or evergreen, oak, though it is a more perfect version of that fine tree. Its leaves are a softer, brighter, and deeper green. In the proper season (August), it is covered with flowers—not showily like the real mango, which has large spikes of bloom that look like giant heads of <term>mignonette</term><note>a fragrant garden plant with small flowers</note>—but with small, yellow-green flowers tucked away under the leaves. These fill the air with a soft, sweet perfume before falling onto the bare, shaded ground below to create a thick, plush carpet. 

I am no botanist, so I do not know if it is truly a mango tree at all, but the fruit resembles a mango in outward appearance. It is even more similar on the inside, as it has a disproportionately large pit. These pits are cracked open and the kernels are removed. The kernels are spread in the shade for a short time to dry; then, they are pounded into a pulp with a wooden pestle. This pulp is placed in a basket carefully lined with plantain leaves and left in the sun, which melts it into a stiff mass. The basket is then taken out of the sun and set aside to cool. Once cool, the "cheese" can be turned out of the basket, keeping its shape. It can be preserved for a long time if wrapped in leaves and cloth and hung up inside the house. It looks like <term>almond rock</term><note>a type of hard toffee or brittle made with almonds</note> and is easily cut with a knife; however, at any point, it will quickly melt back into an oily mass if left in the sun.

The local people use it as a seasoning in their cooking, using it to stuff fish and plantains and so on. They also use it to prepare a type of <term>sea-pie</term><note>a layered dish of meat or fish and vegetables, traditionally cooked in a pot</note> they make with meat and fish. To make this—which is well worth doing, especially with hippopotamus or other coarse meat—reduce the wood fire to embers and shape plantain leaves into a kind of bag or cup. Small pieces of meat should then be packed in layers with red pepper and...

# LEMBARENE CHAPTER X

...<term>Odeaka</term><note>A rich, oily paste made from the kernels of the wild mango tree (*Irvingia gabonensis*), also known as dika bread.</note> spread in between. The tops of the leaves are then tied together with fine plant fibers <term>tie-tie</term><note>Flexible vines or strips of bark used as cordage.</note>, and the bundle is placed directly on the glowing embers without using a pot of any kind, while the cook ensures there is no open flame. The meat is cooked and a superb gravy is formed before the protective plantain leaves are burned through—plantain leaves can withstand a surprising amount of heat. This dish is truly excellent, even when prepared with boa constrictor, hippopotamus, or crocodile. It makes the former quite palatable, though it does not remove the musky flavor from the crocodile; I know of nothing that will.

The Igalwa have been under missionary influence since 1874, when Dr. Nassau founded the mission station at Kangwe <note>Dr. Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921) was an American Presbyterian missionary and ethnologist; Kangwe was a mission station on the Ogooué River near Lambaréné.</note>. Due to this influence, they are often able to read and write, and perhaps possess a somewhat more refined culture. Nevertheless, this influence has not yet deeply penetrated their social institutions.

The major and important difference between the <term>fetish</term><note>A term used by 19th-century writers to describe West African traditional religions and spiritual systems.</note> of the Mpongwe, Igalwa, and Ajumba and that of the surrounding tribes lies in their conception of a certain spirit called Mbuiri. As is common among the Bantu peoples of Southwest Africa, they believe in a great god—the creator—who made all things but now no longer takes an interest in the things he created. Their name for this god is Anyambie, which sounds to my ears like *an-lyin-lah* when pronounced (with very soft 'l' sounds). The name is derived from *Anyima* (a spirit) and *Mbia* (good). Unlike other versions of the creator god in these religions, this god has a deputy or minister who is a deity he created and to whom he leaves the management of affairs. This god is Mbuiri (or Ombwiri), and he is of great interest to students of comparative religion. He has never been a man, nor can he ever be born as one, but he can merge his own personality with those of human beings. He can similarly imbue the souls of things that we white men consider inanimate, such as rocks and trees.

The Mpongwe know that his residence is in the sea, and some of them have seen him as an old white man, not made of flesh—

<page-num>229</page-num>
### THE SPIRIT MBUIRI
<sig>X</sig>

His color is white, but a chalky white. There is another important point here, but it would require a whole volume to explain, so I must pass over it. Mbuiri’s appearance in a physical form signifies bad luck—not death for the person who sees him, but misfortune of a severe and widespread nature. The failure of a trading venture or the destruction of a village or a family is attributed to Mbuiri’s actions. Yet he is not considered an evil god or a devil, but rather an avenger or a punisher of sin. The Mpongwe view him as the Being to whom they primarily owe the good things and successes of this life, and as the only Being with the power to control the many truly malicious spirits that exist in nature.

The different elements he uses to shape human destiny bear his name when he employs them. When acting through water, he is Mbuiri Aningo; in the weather, he is Mbuiri Ngali; in the forests, he is Mbuiri Ibaka; when appearing as a dwarf, he is Mbuiri Akkoa, and so on.

The major difference between Mbuiri and the lesser spirits is this: the lesser spirits cannot take physical form except through external objects; Mbuiri can. He can become visible simply through his own will. Other spirits must inhabit something to be seen. This is an extremely complex aspect of <term>fetish</term><note>A 19th-century term for West African traditional religious systems and spiritual objects.</note> that took me weeks to understand. I believe I can say one more thing about Mbuiri, though I do so cautiously: among the Mpongwe and their parent tribes—the now rapidly disappearing Ajumba and their relatives, the Igalwa—Mbuiri is a distinct, single entity. However, among neighboring tribes, he represents a class of spirits. That is <note>original: "i.e."</note>, there are hundreds of Mbuiri or Ombwiri—one for every notable place or thing, such as a rock, tree, forest thicket, or dangerous spot in a river. Had I not observed a similar situation regarding Sasabonsum <note>A powerful, often malevolent forest spirit in Ashanti and broader Akan mythology.</note>—a completely different type of spirit on the Windward Coast—I would have had even more difficulty finding the key to what initially seemed like a mass of conflicting details regarding this important spirit, Mbuiri.

There is one other very important point in Mpongwe <term>fetish</term>;

...and that is that human souls exist before birth as well as after death. As far as I have been able to discover, this is a doctrine held universally by <term>West African</term> tribes. However, among the <term>M’pongwe</term>, there is a variation that aligns remarkably well with an idea I found regarding reincarnated diseases among the <term>Okÿon</term> tribes. Malevolent minor spirits are capable of being born with what we might call a person's soul, just as they can enter a soul during sleep. 

For example, an <term>Olâgâ</term> may be born with a man, and that man will consequently be born mad. At any point in his life, under certain conditions, he may become possessed by an evil spirit—such as an <term>Onlogho Abambo</term>, <term>Iniembe</term>, or <term>Nkandada</term>—and become insane or ill. But if he is born mad or sickly, it is believed that one of the evil spirits, such as an <term>Olâgâ</term> or an <term>Ibambo</term> (the soul of a man who was not buried properly), was born with him.

The rest of <term>M’pongwe</term> <term>fetish</term><note>A 19th-century term for traditional West African religious systems and spiritual objects.</note> is generally similar to that of other tribes, so I have moved those details to my general collection of notes on the subject. <term>M’pongwe</term> <term>jurisprudence</term><note>The theory or philosophy of law; a legal system.</note> is founded on the same principles as <term>West African</term> law in general, but it is so elaborate that it would be a disservice to provide only a brief sketch. It requires a massive, dedicated study.

# CHAPTER XI

## ON THE WAY FROM KANGWE TO LAKE NCOVI.

->In which the traveler sets out for the bush again and wanders into a new lake and a new river.<-

*July 22nd, 1895.*—Left Kangwe. The four Ajumba^1 men did not show up early in the morning as had been planned, but arrived about eight o'clock in pouring rain. I decided to wait until two o'clock; this will still give us time to reach their town of Arevooma before nightfall and might perhaps give us a chance of arriving there dry. 

We start at two. The kind Madame Jacot comes down to Andande beach to see us off, accompanied by Edmond. I am sorry to say that Monsieur Jacot has a bad bout of fever, but he insists that he will be fine tomorrow. As he is a person whom one instinctively trusts, and is also a disciple of Kühne <note>Louis Kühne (1835–1901), a German hydrotherapist known for his "natural" healing methods.</note>, there is nothing more to be done. So I depart, though I feel anxious for Madame Jacot. 

I have a terrible headache myself, worsened by the conviction that I am in for a heavy bout of fever. However, as an Aduma canoe is one of the most comfortable things in or out of Africa, this is no reason for delay. We travel downriver on the Kangwe side of Lambaréné Island and pause in front of the Igalwa slave town, which is on the island and nearly opposite the Fan town of Fula on the mainland bank. Our purpose is to stock up on yams and plantains—and we obtain magnificent specimens of both. Then, when our—

<header>FROM KANGWE TO LAKE NCOVI</header>

Our canoe is laden with them to such an extent that it would get us into trouble under the Merchant Shipping Act <note>The Merchant Shipping Act regulated the loading and safety of British vessels; Kingsley humorously notes their canoe would be considered dangerously overloaded.</note> if it were enforced here. Off we go again. Every canoe we meet shouts a greeting and asks where we are going. We say, “Rembwé”—and they say, “What! Rembwé!”—and we say, “Yes, Rembwé,” and paddle on. I lay among the luggage for about an hour, not taking much interest in the Rembwé or anything else, except for my own headache. However, this soon lifted, and I was able to take notice of my surroundings just before we reached the Ajumba town called Arevooma. 

The sandbanks stretch across the river here and are nearly level with the surface. Consequently, our entire cargo of yams has to be thrown overboard onto the sand, from which they can be collected by wading out to them. The canoe, lightened this way, is able to go a little further, but we are soon stuck fast again. The crew has to jump out and shove her off about once every five minutes, and then they must look lively about jumping back into her again as she shoots over the edges of the sandbanks.

When we reach Arevooma, I find it is a very prettily situated town on the left bank of the river. It is clean and well-kept, and composed of houses built on the Igalwa and M’pongwe <term>Igalwa and M’pongwe plan: A traditional architectural style using local materials like bamboo and palm.</term> plan, with walls of split bamboo and a palm-thatch roof. I must admit I did not much care for these Ajumbas when we started, but they are evidently going to be kind and pleasant companions. 

One of them is a gentlemanly-looking man who wears a grey shirt; another looks like a genial Irishman who has accidentally turned black—very black—and is distinguished by wearing a singlet <term>singlet: A sleeveless undershirt.</term>. Another is a thin, elderly man who is notably silent. The remaining one is a strapping, big fellow, as black as a wolf’s mouth, with immense muscular development and wearing many <term>fetish charms: Objects believed to have spiritual power or to provide protection.</term> hung about him. The first two I mentioned are Christians; the other two are pagans. I will refer to them by their characteristic traits, for their honorable names are very similar when you hear them and, as is common among Africans, are rarely used in conversation.

"Grey Shirt" places his house at my disposal, and both he and his exceedingly pretty wife do their utmost to make me comfortable. The house lies at the west end of the town. It consists of one room inside, but has, I believe, a separate cooking shed. In the veranda in front, they have placed a table and an <term>ivory bundle chair: A prestige chair, often constructed with multiple supports or decorated with ivory.</term>.

# XI AN OPEN-AIR SERVICE

...and a gourd of water. I am also treated to a calico tablecloth and most thoughtfully screened off from the public gaze with more calico so that I can have my tea in privacy. After this meal, to my surprise, Ndaka appears. He is certainly one of the very ugliest men—black or white—I have ever seen, and I imagine one of the best. He is currently on holiday from Kangwe, overseeing the settlement of his deceased brother’s affairs. His late brother was a prominent man in Arevooma and a pagan, but Ndaka, the Christian Bible-reader <term>Bible-reader: A layperson, often local, trained by missionaries to read and explain the scriptures to the community.</term>, seems to get along perfectly with the family. He is holding a meeting tonight outside his brother’s house and comes with a lantern to fetch me so I may attend. Of course, I have to go, regardless of my headache.

Most of the town was there, mainly as spectators. Ndaka and my two Christian boatmen manage the service between them; between the hymns and the mosquitoes, the experience is somewhat miserable. We sit in a row in front of the house, which is brilliantly illuminated. Our own lantern on the ground before us acts as a rival attraction to the house lamps inside for the "high society" of African insects. In the usual manner of the insect world, they insist on blaming us for their own stupidity in getting singed and sting us in revenge. Meanwhile, we slap at them vigorously while howling hymns in the dreadful Igalwa and M’pongwe way. Aside from an English picnic, the most uncomfortable thing I know is an open-air service in this part of Africa. 

The service being over, Ndaka takes me through the house to show off its splendors. The intense brightness of its lighting comes from two hanging lamps purchased from Messrs. Woermann <note>Messrs. Woermann: The Woermann-Linie, a prominent German shipping and trading company influential in West Africa at the time.</note> at five dollars each, burning Devoe’s patent paraffin oil <term>paraffin oil: Kerosene.</term> in them. This is not an advertisement; it is simply that no other firm sells this type of lamp around here, nor can you find any other kind of paraffin oil anywhere along the Coast. The most remarkable feature of the house is the floor, which is made of split, woven bamboo, the likes of which I have never seen before. It sags under your feet in an alarming way, as it is raised about three or four feet above the ground. I am haunted by the fear that I will fall through it, hurting myself and causing a great deal of trouble for others to get me out. It is a beautiful piece of craftsmanship—

FROM KANGWE TO LAKE NCOVI     CHAP.

The craftsmanship is excellent, and Arevooma has every reason to be proud of it. Having admired these things, I go—exhausted and still suffering from a headache—down the road with my host, who carries the lantern. We walk through an atmosphere that seems to consist of 45 percent solid matter in the form of mosquitoes. Then, wishing him goodnight, I shut myself in and humbly light a candle. The furniture of the house consists mainly of boxes containing the wealth of **Gray Shirt**, including clothes, mirrors, and other items. One corner of the room is filled with large <term>calabashes: dried, hollowed-out gourds used as containers</term> full of some kind of liquor. There is also a chair made of ivory bundles, a hanging mirror, several rusty guns, and a considerable collection of china basins and jugs. Evidently, **Gray Shirt** is rich.

The most interesting article to me right now, however, is the bed. It is hung with a clean, sturdy, chintz <term>mosquito bar: a mosquito net or curtain</term>, spread with clean calico, and adorned with pillows covered in patchwork. I take off my boots and put on my slippers; in this country, it never pays to go without boots entirely at any time. One cannot risk getting mosquito bites on the feet while on a journey, because the rubbing of a boot against a bite always produces a sore. When a sore develops in "Gorilla country," it is there to stay.

No sooner have I carefully brushed all the mosquitoes out from under the netting and settled into bed than a cat scratches and mews at the door; I have to get out of bed to let her in. She is evidently a pet, so I take her onto the bed with me. She is a very nice cat—sandy-colored and fat. If I held the <note>original: "opinion of Pythagoras concerning wild fowl" — A reference to Shakespeare’s *Twelfth Night*, where the character Feste discusses Pythagoras’s theory of the transmigration of souls (reincarnation).</note> belief of **Pythagoras** regarding the souls of animals, I would have no hesitation in saying she possessed the soul of <note>Dame Juliana Berners (born c. 1388) was the legendary author of works on hunting, hawking, and heraldry.</note> **Dame Juliana Berners**, given the wholehearted devotion to sport she displays. She repeatedly dashes out through the flaps of the mosquito net after rats. Amid squeals from the rats and curses from her, she kills them among the china collection. Then she returns to me, triumphant and expecting congratulations—accompanied by mosquitoes—and purrs and kneads my chest until she hears another rat.

*Tuesday, July 23rd.*—I am woken by violent knocking at the door in the early gray light of dawn. The knocking is so forceful that two large centipedes and a scorpion drop onto the bed. They had evidently been tucked away among the folds of the mosquito net all night. Well, "where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise."

# XI AJUMBA WAYS AND GAMES

"...otherwise," particularly along here. I get up without delay and find myself feeling quite well. The cat neatly knocked a basin of water into my bag during her nocturnal hunts; and when my tea arrives, I am informed that a man "died" during the night, which explains the gunfire I heard. I inquire what he died of and am told, "His luck just ran out, and then he died." His widows are having their faces painted white by sympathetic lady friends and are dressed in their oldest, dirtiest clothes—and very few of them at that. Still, they seem to be taking things in a resigned spirit. These Ajumba seem like pleasant people. They play with their pretty brown children in a charming way. Last night, I noticed some men and women playing a game new to me, which consisted of throwing a hoop at each other. The goal was to get the hoop to fall over your opponent's head. It is a cheerful game. There are many houseflies about—and during the early morning, it rains gently; but soon after we are afloat in our canoe, it turns into a soft white mist.

We continue paddling westward down the broad, quiet waters of the O'Rembo Vongo. I notice great quantities of birds here—large hornbills, vividly colored kingfishers, and, for the first time, the great vulture I have often heard of. I will take its skin home before I even mention its approximate wingspan.¹ There are also noble—

## FROM KANGWE TO LAKE NCOVI CHAPTER

There were white cranes and flocks of small black and white birds that were new to me. They had heavy, razor-shaped bills that reminded me of the puffins found in Devon. However, the hornbill is perhaps the most striking in appearance. It is the size of a small, or perhaps a good-sized, hen turkey. Gray Shirt says that the flocks, which consist of eight or ten birds, always have an equal number of males and females, and that they live together "white man's fashion"—meaning each couple stays together. They certainly do a great deal of courting. The male fills out the wattles on his neck like a turkey and spreads out his tail with great pomp and ceremony, though he does so very awkwardly. 

To see hornbills on a bare sandbank is a solemn sight, but when they are dodging about in the <term>hippo grass</term> <note>thick, tall grass common in African river systems</note>, they drop the ceremony and instead roll and waddle. My guide said they were looking for snakes and the small sand-fish found close under the bank. Their hilarious way of dropping their jaws—or rather, opening their bills—when they are alarmed is quite comical. I think this has something to do with their hearing, for I often saw two or three of them in a line on a long branch, stretched up to their full height with their great eyes opened wide and their beaks agape, evidently listening for something. Their cry is very strange and could only be mistaken for a local horn. Although there seems to be little variety in the sound to my ears, there must be more to theirs, for they will carry on long conversations with each other across a river. I believe they even stay up half the night to gossip.

There were plenty of <term>plantain-eaters</term> <note>also known as Turacos</note> here as well. Although their screech was as appalling as what I have heard in Angola, the Ajumba did not regard them as birds of bad omen, as people do in Angola. Still, by no means all the birds here only screech and squawk; several of them have very lovely notes. There is one that always gives a series of infinitely beautiful, soft, rich-toned whistles just before the first light of dawn appears in the sky, and at least one that has a prolonged and very lovely song. In Gaboon, I was told this bird is called <term>the red-winged sounder</term> <note>original: "Telephonus erythropterus"; now commonly known as the Black-crowned Tchagra</note>. I expect an ornithologist would enjoy himself here, but I cannot—and will not—collect birds. I hate to have them killed at all, and particularly in the barbaric way these natives kill them.

# XI LESSONS IN GEOGRAPHY

The broad stretch of water looks like a long lake. In all directions, sandbanks are showing their broad yellow backs, and more will be appearing soon, for it is not yet the height of the dry season. We are constantly running aground on banks that will be completely above water by next month. These canoes are built, I believe, more with an eye toward handling sandbanks comfortably than anything else; however, they are not yet specialized enough for getting off them. Their flat bottoms enable them to glide onto the banks and sit there without either capsizing or cutting into the sand, as a canoe with a keel would. The trouble comes when you are trying to get off the steep edge of a bank, and this usually results in the boat capsizing. So far, my Ajumba friends have only tried to address this difficulty by tying the cargo down.

I try to study the geography of this region conscientiously. Fortunately, I find Gray Shirt, Singlet, and Pagan can speak <term>trade English</term> <note>a form of West African Pidgin English used for commerce</note>; for my interpreter’s knowledge of that language seems confined to “Perhaps,” “It is better so,” and “Lord, Lord, help me”—a useless vocabulary. None of them, however, seem to recognize a single name on the chart. This is not necessarily a criticism of the chart or its makers, who probably obtained their names from the Mpongwe and Igalwa tribes instead of the Ajumba, as I am trying to do. 

Geographic research in this region is fraught with difficulty, I find, because different tribes call the same place by different names. I am sure the Royal Geographical Society ought to include among their “Hints to Travellers” a recommendation that every traveler in this area should carefully learn every separate native word, or set of words, signifying “I don’t know.” I have come across four villages and two rivers out here solemnly recorded with various forms of this statement as if it were their native name. Really, I think the old Portuguese way of naming places after saints, etc., was wiser in the long run, and it was certainly more pleasant to the ear. My Ajumba guides, however, know about Ngambi and the Vinue all right, as well as <term>Elivã z’Ayzingo</term> <note>Lake Azingo</note>, so I must try to get cross-bearings from these.

We have an addition to our crew this morning—a man who wants to go and find work at John Holt’s <term>sub-factory</term> <note>a smaller branch of a trading post</note> away on the Rembwé River. He has been waiting a long while at Arevooma,

### FROM KANGWE TO LAKE NCOVI

I am told we are unable to get across "because the road is now blocked between Ayzingo and the Rembwé by those fearful Fans."

"How are we going to get through that way?" I ask, with natural feminine alarm.

"We are not, sir," says Gray Shirt.

This is what Lady MacDonald would call a "chatty little incident"; my hair begins to stand on end as I remember what I have been told about these Fans <note>The Fang people, known at the time for their fierce reputation and rumored cannibalism</note> and the signs I have already seen of those rumors being true while on the Upper Ogowé. Now we are going to try to pass through the heart of their country, far from any French station and without the protection of the French flag. Why did I not obey Mr. Hudson's orders not to go wandering about so recklessly! Regardless, I am committed now, and fortune favors the brave. The only question is: do I personally belong to that class? 

I ask for more details. It seems Pagan thinks he can rely on the friendship of two Fans he once met and did business with, and who now live on an island in Lake Ncovi. Ncovi is not marked on my map and I have never heard of it before, but that is where we are headed now.

Each man has brought his best gun, loaded to the muzzle and tied to the baggage I am leaning against; the muzzles stick out on either side of my head. The flintlocks are covered with cases, or sheaths, made of the black-haired skins of gorillas, leopard skins, and a beautiful bright reddish-brown skin that I do not recognize. They say it is "bush cow" <note>The African forest buffalo</note>—though they call half a dozen different things "bush cow." These guns are not the "gas-pipes" <note>Cheap, low-quality trade guns often sold to locals</note> I have seen further north, but decent rifles that have had the rifling filed out and the locks replaced by flintlocks to convert them into muzzle-loaders; many of them have beautiful barrels. 

I discover the Ajumba name for the beautiful shrub with long bunches of red, yellow, and cream-colored young leaves at the ends of its branches is *obāa*. I also learn that in their language, "ebony" and "monkey" share the same name. The forest on both banks is very lovely. Enormously high green columns are formed by climbing plants that have taken over lightning-struck trees. In one spot, it truly looks as if someone had spread a massive green coverlet over the forest to keep it dry. No high ground is visible in any direction. Pagan tells—

# XI SANDBANK PALAVER

He tells me the extinguisher-shaped juju <term>an amulet or fetish used in West African traditional religions</term> filled with medicine and made of iron is to prevent drowning—the red juju is "to keep one's feet on the path." There is a beautiful effect of a gleam of sunshine lighting up a red sandbank until it glows like the Nibelung gold <note>The Rhinegold from Germanic mythology, famously featured in Richard Wagner’s operas</note>. Indeed, the effects are Turneresque <note>Resembling the atmospheric, light-filled landscapes of the painter J.M.W. Turner</note> today owing to the mist and the sun playing in and out of it.

This bank provides evidence of this also being the case in the wet season, for a fringe of uprooted trees hangs from it into the river. We pass Seke, a town on the north bank, exchanging the usual remarks regarding our destination. The river seems absolutely barred with sand again; but as we paddle down it, the obstructions resolve themselves into spits of sand from the north bank and the largest island in mid-stream, which also has a long tail, or train, of sandbanks trailing downriver. Here we meet a picturesque series of canoes, laden with fruit and trade goods, being poled upstream; one man has his pole over one side, the other with his pole over the other, forming a St. Andrew’s cross <note>An X-shaped cross</note> as you meet them head-on.

This is a most luxurious, charming, and pleasant trip. The men are standing up, swinging their long, rich redwood paddles in rhythmic motion in perfect time to their elaborate, melancholy boat song, sung in a minor key. We were nearly lost with all hands. A sandbank palaver <term>a West African term for a discussion, dispute, or in this case, a difficult situation</term>—just as we were going over the end of it, the boat slipped sideways over its edge. The river is deep here, with a bottom of sand and mud. This information may be interesting to a geologist, but I hope I shall not be converted by circumstances into a human sounding apparatus <note>A device used to measure water depth; here, Kingsley refers to herself accidentally falling in to gauge the depth</note> again today. The next time the boat strikes a bank, I shall get out and push from behind.

We are now skirting the actual north bank, and not the shore of an island or islands as we have been for some time previously. A lovely stream falls into this river over cascades. The water is now somewhat rough, and the width of the river is great, but it is soon crowded again with wooded islands.

Patches and wreaths of a lovely, vermilion-flowering vine <term>bush rope; a type of tropical climbing plant or liana</term> decorate the forest, and every now and then we see clumps of a plant that displays a yellow and crimson spike of bloom, which is strikingly beautiful. We pass a long tunnel in the bush that looks quite dark as you gaze down it—it is evidently the path to a local village. The south bank is covered with hippo grass <term>Vossia cuspidata; a tall aquatic grass found in tropical Africa</term> where the receding waters have exposed it. There are a terrible number of mangrove flies <term>biting flies of the Tabanidae family, such as horse-flies or deer-flies</term> about, even though we are more than a hundred miles above the mangrove belt.

The river broadens again, tending west-southwest, with a wide, flattened island in the middle surrounded by tributary sandbanks. The navigable channel lies along the south bank of the river. Gray Shirt tells me this river is called the O’Rembo Vongo, or "Small River," to distinguish it from the main stream of the Ogowé which flows past the south side of Lambaréné Island—as I know only too well after my previous canoe adventure. Lake Azingo now lies due north, and the native mahogany is called "Okoumé" <term>Aucoumea klaineana; a significant timber tree in West Africa</term>. 

We pass a village called Welli on the north bank. It looks like a collection of gypsy caravans perched on poles. I suspect that village knows what it is like to be swamped by the rising river; it looks as if it had hastily retreated onto stilts in the middle of the night. From their current rickety condition, I am certain they will only last through the next wet season, and then some unfortunate spirit will be blamed for the collapse. I also learn that this is the birthplace of my friend Kabinda, the carpenter at Andande. 

Now, if some of these good people I know would only distinguish themselves, I might write a sort of county family history of these parts; but they do not, and I suspect they will not. For example, the entrance—or should I say the exit?—of a fairly broad little river lies just off the south bank. If you travel up this river, which runs southeast, you reach a good-sized lake; in this lake, there is an island called Adole. Then, from the other side of the lake, there is another river that falls into the main stream of the Ogowé. However, that is not the point of the story; the point is that on the island of Adole, Ngouta the interpreter first saw the light of day. Why he ever did—there or anywhere—only Heaven knows! I know I shall never want to write his biography.

# XI A STRANGE CEMETERY

Wanderegwoma is an Igalwa town, notable for a large number of fine white ducks and a cluster of Indian bamboo. My informants say, "No white man has ever lived in this place," so I suppose the ducks and bamboo were imported by some African trader who was born here. We got stuck on a sandbank—I jumped out and shoved from behind, leaving Ngouta to manage the balancing act in the stern. I am told, once we re-embarked, that this O’Rembo Vongo divides into three streams just below here. One flows into the main Ogowé opposite Ayshouka in Nkami country—Nkami territory begins at Ayshouka and stretches to the sea—another flows into the Ngumbi, and a third into the Nunghi, both of which are in Ouroungou country. Lake Ayzingo now lies to the northeast, according to Gray Shirt’s gesture. On this river, there is another broad, low island with gold-colored banks that shine brightly; it seems to block the entire channel, but there is actually a passage for canoes along both banks.

At this point, we turn into a river on the north bank that runs north and south; the current is flowing very swiftly toward the north. We head down into it, and since it is well past time for a meal <term>chop; West African pidgin for food or a meal</term>, we push the canoe onto a sandbank in this new river, which I am told is the Karkola. After having my tea, I wander off. Behind our high sandbank—which, like all the other sandbanks currently above water, is becoming overgrown with hippo grass <term>Vossia cuspidata; a tall aquatic grass</term>, the favorite food of both the hippopotamus and the manatee—I find a forest. Entering it, I notice a series of strange mounds or heaps made of branches, twigs, leaves, and dead flowers. Many of these heaps are recent, while others have fallen into decay. 

Investigation reveals they are burial sites. Among the *debris* <note>original: "débris"</note> of an older mound, there are human bones; from one of the newer ones, a stench emerges along with a hurried, incredibly busy line of ants, demonstrating the process of decay. I must admit I thought these mounds were some kind of bird or animal nest. They appear entirely inhuman in this desolate stretch of forest. Leaving the mounds, I go down to the water’s edge at the sandbank and find many pools of various sizes, each surrounded by a rim of dark red-brown sediment that can be lifted off the sand like a skin.

# FROM KANGWE TO LAKE NCOVI — CHAPTER XI

On the surface of the water is a film of exquisite, iridescent colors, like those on a soap bubble but darker and brighter. Along the sandy banks of the river, there are thousands of those beautiful little fish with a black line on each side of their tails. They are perfectly tame, and I feed them crumbs from my hand. After making every effort to scare the unknown object containing the food—these "gallant bulls," a full two inches long, sidle up and snap at my fingers—they come and feed right in my palm. I could have caught them by the handful if I had wished. There are also many of those strange, semi-transparent, yellow-spotted little sand-fish with cup-shaped pectoral fins, which I see they use to make their astoundingly long leaps. These fish have a more nervous and distrustful nature; they hover around my hand but will not come into it. Indeed, I do not believe the other bold little fellows would allow them to. They have grand butting matches among themselves, which end with a most comical tail fight. Each combatant spins around and engages in a slapping match with its adversary using its pretty, red-edged tail—the red rim around the tail and gill covers turns a deep claret color <note>claret: a deep purplish-red color, similar to the wine</note> with fury. I could not figure out how points were scored in these fights, as no one seemed a single scale the worse for it.

The men, having finished their rest and their pipes, call out for me, and we set off again. The Karkola ¹ soon widens to about 100 feet; it is clearly very deep here. The right bank (the east) is forested, while the left is low and covered in shrubs. One patch looks as if it were being cleared for a plantation, but no village is visible. A large rock appears on the right bank, which is a change from the usual clay and sand, and soon the entire character of the landscape changes. We come to a sharp turn in the river where it shifts from a north-south direction to east-west, and the current is very swift. The river channel winds against a large bank of sword grass and then widens to the width of the Thames at Putney <note>The River Thames at Putney, London, is approximately 200–300 yards wide</note>. I am told that a river branches off from here to the west toward the Ouroungou country, and so I imagine—

# XI ISLANDS AND HIPPOS

The Karkola River eventually flows into the Nazareth River. We travel along the eastern banks, which are covered in short grass with a few scattered trees along the ridge. High ground is visible in the distance to the south-southwest and southwest. Then, we suddenly turn into a wide river or stretch of water, heading north-northeast. On the opposite bank, atop a small, steep cliff, is a Fan village. "It is all Fan territory now," says Singlet in a tone that sounds far from pleased <note>Fan: also known as the Fang people, an ethnic group in Central Africa</note>.

We are now in a strange, wild, and lonely part of the world. It looks like a lake or a wide stretch of river filled with sandbanks; some are bare, while others are developing into permanent islands because of the floating coarse grass growing on them. Any piece of this grass torn away by the current, a passing canoe, or hippos floats downstream and takes root wherever it lands. Like most floating things in these parts, it usually lands on a sandbank. It then grows much like couch grass <note>couch grass: a common, fast-spreading weed with long, creeping roots</note> does in England, forming a network that traps all kinds of floating *debris* for the sandbank it has claimed. Thus, the sandbank "rises in the world." When the water rises during the rainy season, it drowns the grass; but when the level drops, the grass grows back from the roots. Gradually, the sandbank turns into an island and encourages actual trees and shrubs to take root, and its future is then secured.

We travel alongside a large, newly formed island of this type where the sword grass is about ten or fifteen feet high. It doesn't have any trees yet, but it likely will by next season. The grass is trodden down into paths by hippos, and just as I realize who the road-makers are, they appear in person. One huge bull, hearing us, stands up in the grass about six feet away. He stares calmly, then lets out a yawn a yard wide and grunts his news to his companions. Some of them—there is clearly a large herd—get up and stroll toward us with all the "flowing grace" of **Pantechnicon vans** <note>Pantechnicon van: a large furniture removal van, originally horse-drawn</note> in motion. We steer our paddles hard to the right and move away from that bank. These hippos always look to me as if they were either the very first or the very last creatures ever created. At present, I cannot decide whether Nature was practicing her "apprentice hand" <note>Nature's 'prentice hand: a reference to Robert Burns' poem "Green Grow the Rashes, O"</note> on them in her earliest stages...

...youth, or whether, having grown thoroughly tired of making delicately beautiful antelopes, corals, butterflies, and orchids, she just said: "Goodness! I am completely exhausted by this fussy work. Here, just put these other internal organs into big bags—I can’t be bothered anymore."

Having finished our quick trip across to the bank of the island on the other side, we searched for seclusion. Hoping that "out of sight" would mean "out of mind" to the hippos, we shot down a narrow channel between sandbanks that were almost islands. Those sandbanks, if you can believe it, are covered with examples—as fine a set of specimens as you could wish for—of the West African crocodile. These interesting animals are also taking their afternoon naps, lying sprawling in all directions on the sand with their mouths wide open. One immense old female has a family of lively young crocodiles running over her, clearly playing like a group of kittens. The heavy musky smell they give off is most repulsive, but we do not stand up and make a scene about it. We feel hopelessly in the wrong for intruding into these family scenes uninvited, so we apologetically use our poles to move along rapidly, not even singing. The speed at which the canoe travels down that channel would be a wonder to the Henley Regatta <note>Henley Regatta: a prestigious rowing event held annually on the River Thames in England</note>. 

When we are out of earshot, I ask Pagan whether there are many gorillas, elephants, or bush-cows <term>bush-cow: the African forest buffalo (*Syncerus caffer nanus*)</term> around here. "Plenty, too many," he says. It occurs to me that the cornfields are growing golden-green back in England; soon, a picture that fascinated me in my youth in the *Fliegende Blätter* <note>original: *Fliegende Blätter* (Flying Leaves); a popular German satirical magazine</note> rises in my mind. It represents "**Friedrich Gerstaecker on his travels**" <note>original: *Friedrich Gerstaecker auf der Reise*. Gerstaecker (1816–1872) was a well-known German author of travel and adventure stories.</note>. That brave man is depicted stomping on a serpent—one unknown to Mr. Boulenger <note>George Albert Boulenger (1858–1937), a prominent zoologist at the British Museum</note>—while he attempts to club a most lively savage with the butt end of his gun. This savage, accompanied by a bison, is attacking him from the front. A terrifying and clearly enthusiastic crocodile is grabbing the tail of the explorer's coat, and the explorer says, "**Hurrah! That will make another splendid article for the *General Gazette*!**" <note>original: "Hurrah! das gibt wieder einen prächtigen Artikel für Die Allgemeine Zeitung." *Die Allgemeine Zeitung* was a major German newspaper at the time.</note>. I do not know where in the world Gerstaecker was supposed to be at the time, but I imagine it was somewhere like this. 

My vigorous and lively conscience also reminds me that the last words a most distinguished and valued scientific friend said to me before I left home were: "Always take measurements,

The expanse of water here is vast, dotted in every direction with sandbanks and islands, and it seems to be framed uniformly by low, swampy land. Beyond that, to the north, rounded hills appear blue in the distance. On one of the islands is a little white house which, I am told, was once occupied by an African trader working for John Holt <note>John Holt: A prominent British merchant and founder of a major West African trading company</note>. It looks like a desolate place for any man to live, and the way the crocodiles and hippos must have climbed onto the garden grounds in the evening could not have enhanced its charms for the average cautious person. My men say, "No one lives in that place now." The trading post <term>factory: a merchant's trading station or warehouse in a foreign country</term>, I believe, has been abandoned for some commercial reason. Behind it is a large clump of dark-colored trees. The rest of the island is now covered with hippo grass, which looks like a beautifully kept lawn. We stop for a short rest at another island, which is also a strange spot in its own way; it is covered with a grove of only one kind of tree, which has a twisted, distorted, grayish-white trunk and dull, lifeless-looking, hard green leaves.

I learned that these good people—as if to make the geographical confusion even worse—call a river by one name when you are going upstream and by another when you are coming downstream. It is just as if you called the Thames "the London" when you were going upriver and "the Greenwich" when you were coming down. The banks all around this lake or lagoon seem to consist entirely of light-colored sand and clay. We pass out of it and into a channel where the current flows north. As we enter the channel between banks of sand overgrown with grass, a superb white crane is seen standing on the sandy edge to the left. Gray Shirt tries to get a shot at it, but the bird—alarmed by our unusual appearance—lifts itself up with one of those graceful preliminary bows and, after one or two initial flaps, spreads its broad wings and sweeps away, with its long legs trailing behind it like a figure on a Japanese screen. Of course, if Providence had taken the trouble to keep us off the bank or remind Gray Shirt to uncock his weapon, the accident would not have happened at all—but foresight is not one of Providence's usual traits. Still, when it did happen, Providence certainly rose to the occasion. I might have had the back of my head blown out, and the men might have been killed. The river we entered zigzags about and then takes a south-south-east course. It is dotted with islands slightly higher than those we passed earlier, thinly covered with forest. The place seems alive with birds; flocks of pelicans and cranes rise before us out of the grass, and every now and then a crocodile slides off the bank into the water. They look remarkably like old logs, especially when you see one letting itself roll and float down the current. Despite these points of interest, I began to wonder where in this lonely land we were to sleep tonight. Ahead of us were miles of distant mountains, but in no direction was there the slightest sign of human habitation. Soon we passed out of our channel into a lovely, strangely melancholy, and lonely-looking lake—Lake Ncovi, my friends tell me. It is exceedingly beautiful. At first, there was no sign of human habitation; and despite its beauty, there was something about the place I was almost going to call repulsive. The men evidently felt the same as I did. Had anyone told me that the air lying on the lake was poisonous, or that a path to absolute death lay among its forests, I would have said, "It looks like it." But no one said anything, and we only looked around uneasily until the easy-going Singlet <note>One of Kingsley's crew members, named for his attire</note> made the unfortunate observation that he "smelled blood." <note>A common African sensation among the locals when alarmed, somewhat similar to our feeling of "someone walking over our grave."</note> We all called him an utter fool to relieve our tension and made our way toward the second island. When we got near enough to see the details, a large village appeared among the trees on its summit, and a steep low cliff, overgrown with trees and creeping plants, came down to a small beach covered with large, water-washed gray stones.

There was evidently some kind of disturbance going on in that village, which involved a great deal of shouting. We headed straight for the beach and drove our canoe among the outlying rocks. The scene did not look restful, nor were these Fan people personally pleasant. Every man among them—no women were present—was armed with a gun. They loosened their shovel-shaped knives in their sheaths as they approached, evidently regarding a fight as being just as likely as we did. They drew up in silence about twenty paces from us. Pagan and Gray Shirt <note>Kingsley's crew members, referred to by these nicknames</note>, who had joined him, held out their empty hands and shouted the name of the Fan man they had claimed to be friends with: "Kiva-Kiva." 

The Fans stood still and talked angrily among themselves for several minutes. Then, Silence <note>Another of Kingsley's crew members</note> said to me, "It will be bad trouble if Kiva does not live in this place," in a tone that suggested he thought this unpleasant possibility was almost a certainty. The Passenger <note>An unnamed member of the traveling party</note> showed unmistakable signs of wishing he had taken a different boat. I rose from my seat in the bottom of the canoe and leisurely strolled ashore. I said "M'boloani" <note>A standard greeting; "Hello to you all"</note> to the line of angry faces in an unconcerned way, even though I knew well that etiquette required them to greet us first. They grunted, but did not commit themselves further. 

A minute later, they parted to allow a fine-looking, middle-aged man to come forward. He was naked except for a twist of dirty cloth around his waist and a bunch of leopard and wildcat tails hanging from his shoulder by a strip of leopard skin. Pagan rushed toward him as if he were going to clasp him to his broad chest, but he held his hands just short of touching the Fan man's shoulders in the usual way. He said in the Fan language, "Don't you know me, my beloved Kiva? Surely you haven't forgotten your old friend?" 

Kiva grunted with emotion and raised his hands, holding them just off Pagan's shoulders, and we breathed a sigh of relief. Then Gray Shirt rushed at the crowd and went through great demonstrations of affection with another gentleman whom he recognized as a Fan friend of his own, and whom he had not expected to meet here. I looked around to see if there were any Fans from the Upper Ogowé <note>The primary river of the region in Gabon</note> whom I knew and could approach, but I could not see any I recognized from previous experience. Based on their individual appearance alone, I did not feel inclined to perform even this fashionable imitation of an embrace. Once peace was proclaimed, conversation became general. Gray Shirt brought his friend over and introduced him to me, and we shook hands and smiled at each other in the conventional way. Pagan’s friend, who was introduced next, was more alarming. He held his hands for half a minute just above my elbows without quite touching me, though he meant well. From the violence and intensity of the shouting and gestures, you would have thought we were about to be torn to shreds immediately; however, not a single hand actually touched me. As I, Pagan, and Gray Shirt walked up to the town in the middle of the throng, the crowd opened in front of us and closed in behind, clearly half-frightened by my appearance. 

The uproar redoubled in volume when we reached the town because the women, the children, and the dogs joined in. Every child in the place, as soon as they saw my white face, let out a howl as if they had seen the Devil himself <note>original: "his Satanic Majesty"</note>—horns, hooves, tail and all—and fled headlong into the nearest hut. I fear, from their continued screaming, that they had fits. 

The town was incredibly filthy. The remains of a crocodile they had been eating two weeks ago, piles of fish guts <term>offal: the internal organs and discarded parts of an animal</term>, and the remains of an elephant, hippo, or manatee—I really cannot say which, as decomposition was too far advanced—combined to create a truly impressive stench. As is typical in a Fan town, the bark huts stand in unbroken rows, but here there are three or four streets instead of just one. 

The palaver house <term>palaver house: a communal building used for meetings and negotiations</term> is in the innermost street. We went there, noticing that the village view looked across toward the other side of the lake rather than the direction from which we had come. I told the Ajumba <note>An ethnic group from the Gabon region serving as Kingsley's guides and boatmen</note> to explain that we wanted hospitality for the night and wished to hire three carriers for tomorrow to go with us to the Rembwé River.

It was a very different dwelling from Gray Shirt’s residence at Arevooma. I was as tall as its roof ridge and had to stoop low to get through the doorway. 

Inside, the hut was fourteen or fifteen feet square and unlit by any window. The doorway could be closed by pushing a broad piece of bark across it, held in place by two horizontal sticks. The floor was sand, like the street outside, but dirtier. In one spot, there was a fire whose smoke found its way out through the roof. In one corner of the room was a rough wooden bench; judging by the few filthy cloths and a wooden pillow on it, I saw that it was the bed. There was no other furniture in the hut except for some boxes, which I assume held my host’s worldly possessions. 

From the bamboo roof hung a long stick with hooks on it, made by cutting off branching twigs. This was evidently the hanging wardrobe. On it hung a few charms <term>fetish: an object believed to have supernatural powers or inhabited by a spirit</term> and a beautiful ornament made of wildcat and leopard tails. These were tied to a square piece of leopard skin with a small mirror in the center, surrounded by dozens of common shirt buttons. Among the tails hung three little brass bells and a brass rattle. These bells and rattles are not only for show <note>original: "for dandy"</note> but serve to scare away snakes when the ornament is worn in the forest. A fine strip of silky-haired, young gorilla skin served as the strap to sling the ornament from the shoulder. 

Gorillas seem well-known around here. I saw one old lady in the crowd outside who had a necklace made of sixteen gorilla canine teeth strung on pineapple fiber. Gray Shirt explained to me that this is the best house in the village, and my host is the most renowned elephant hunter in the district.

We then returned to the canoe. Its occupants had been getting uneasy about how affairs were going “on top” because of the uproar they heard and the length of time we had been away. The only white man who had been here before in living memory was a French officer who paid Kiva six dollars to take him somewhere, I was told—but I could not find out when this happened, or what became of that Frenchman.¹ It was a long time ago, Kiva said, but these people have no definite way of expressing the duration of time; nor do I believe they have much of a mental concept of it. Nevertheless, their ideas—as is usual with West Africans—are far more advanced than their language allows them to express.

All the supplies were brought up to my hut, and while Ngouta prepared my tea, we started the porter negotiations <term>palaver: here, specifically referring to the bargaining over payment for carriers</term> again. The Fans received my offer—starting at two dollars more than Monsieur Jacot said would be enough—with utter scorn and every dramatic gesture of disagreement. One man, pretending to catch Gray Shirt’s words in his hands, threw them to the ground and stomped on them. I adopted a relaxed, take-it-or-leave-it attitude and simply watched. A woman stepped out of the crowd toward me and held out a mass of slimy, gray abomination on a piece of plantain leaf: smashed snail. I accepted it and gave her some fishhooks. She was delighted and her companions were excited; she put the hooks into her mouth for safekeeping. I quickly explained in my best Fan language that I did not require any more snails, so another woman tried to see if a pineapple would work. There might be no end to this, so I turned to business and asked what she would sell it for. She did not want to sell it; she wanted to give it to me as a gift. So, I gave her more fishhooks. All the while, the negotiation <term>palaver: a long discussion or negotiation</term> for porters continued without ceasing. I went out and offered to take the place of Gray Shirt and Pagan, knowing they must want their food <term>chop: West African pidgin for food or a meal</term>, but they refused the relief. They also said I must not raise the price; I was already offering too high a price now, and if I were to increase it once, the Fans <term>Fan: the Fang people of West Central Africa</term> would only think I would keep on increasing it, thereby making the negotiation even longer to talk through.

“How long does a negotiation usually take to talk through around here?” I asked. 

“The last one I conducted,” said Pagan, “took three weeks, and that was only a small price negotiation.” 

“Well,” I said, “my price is for a start tomorrow—after then, I have no price—after that, I go away.” 

An hour later, however, the deal was struck <note>original: "the jam made" refers to the breakthrough in negotiations</note>, and to my surprise, I found that the three richest men in this town of M’fetta had personally taken up the contract: Kiva, my host; Fika, a fine young fellow; and Wiki, another noted elephant hunter. These three Fans, the four Ajumba, and the Igalwa man, Ngouta, will, I think, be enough. 

Moreover, I imagine it is safer not to have an overwhelming majority of Fans in the party, as I know we shall have considerable stretches of uninhabited forest to cross. The Ajumba say that the Fans will kill people—that is, the black traders who venture into their country—and cut them up into neat pieces, eating what they want at the time and smoking the rest of the bodies for future use. Now, I do not want to arrive at the Rembwé River in a smoked condition, even if my fragments were neatly cut. Furthermore, I am traveling in a different direction than I claimed when leaving Kangwe, and there are so many ways to account for death in these parts—leopards, capsized canoes, elephants, etc.—that even if I were traced, well, nothing could be done by then anyway. Therefore, I will only take three Fans. One must reduce "dead certainties" to the level of "sporting chances" in this region, or one can never make any progress.

# XI A NIGHT PADDLE

The Fang men said they only knew the route to a large Fang town called Efoua, where no white man or black trader had ever been. They knew there was a path from there to the Rembwé River because the people of Efoua take all their trade goods to the Rembwé. They said they would come with me the entire way if I would guarantee their safety if they encountered conflict <term>war: in this context, local inter-village disputes or ambushes</term> on the road. I agreed to this and arranged to pay them at Hatton and Cookson’s <note>Hatton and Cookson was a prominent British trading company in West Africa during the 19th century.</note> branch factory on the Rembwé. They replied, "Look at my mouth and it is sweet, so the negotiation is settled" <note>original: "Look my mouth and it be sweet, so palaver done set" is a West African Pidgin English expression meaning the terms are satisfactory and the deal is final.</note>. By the light of the torches <term>bush lights: torches made from resinous wood or bundles of grass</term> held by the women, we organized every load. I had to unpack my jars of fish specimens to balance the weight of the packs. Each load was then wrapped into a sort of cocoon using forest vines <term>bush rope: strong, flexible climbing plants used as natural cordage</term>.

I was finally left in peace at about 11:30 P.M. After clearing some clothes off the bench, I threw myself down and tried to get some sleep, as the Fang men said we were to start before dawn. Sleep was impossible—mosquitoes! lice!!—so at 12:40 A.M., I got up and slid aside my bark door. I found Pagan asleep under his mosquito net <term>mosquito bar: a mosquito net or canopy</term> outside, across the doorway. However, I managed to get past him without waking him from his dreams of negotiations—which he was still talking about aloud—and scouted the town. The inhabitants seemed to have talked themselves out and were sleeping heavily. I went down to our canoe and found it safe, pulled high up on the stones among the Fang canoes. I then slid a small Fang canoe into the water and, taking a paddle from a cluster stuck in the sand, paddled out onto the dark lake.

It was a wonderfully lovely, quiet night with no light except for the stars. One immense planet shone pre-eminent in the purple sky, casting a golden path across the still waters. Many large fish leaped out of the water, their glistening silver-white scales flashing so that they looked like swinging swords. Some bird was making a long, low booming sound far off on the forest shore. I paddled leisurely across the lake to the right bank. Seeing some large glow-worms crawling on the ground, I drove the canoe onto the bank among some tall grass <term>hippo grass: *Vossia cuspidata*, a coarse aquatic grass</term> and got out to catch them.

While I was busy with this hunt, I felt the earth quiver under my feet and heard a soft, heavy rustling sound. Looking around, I realized I had stumbled right into a hippopotamus banquet. I made—

I counted five of the immense beasts around me, so I quietly returned to the canoe and shoved off. I stole along the bank, paddling silently with the blade submerged, until I thought it was safe to head across the lake toward my island. I reached the end opposite the village; finding a tiny rocky bay with a soft patch of sand and no hippo grass, the memory of the conditions in the Fan hut made a bath seem advisable. Furthermore, there was no collection of porcelain <note>Kingsley frequently referred to her glass specimen jars and scientific equipment as her "china" or "crockery."</note> in that hut, and I knew it would be a long time before I had another chance. So, I went ashore again and, after carefully scouting the area to ensure no human was living nearby, I enjoyed a peaceful wash.

Drying oneself with a cummerbund <term>cummerbund: a wide sash worn around the waist, often used by travelers as a multi-purpose cloth</term> is not exactly a joy, but it can be done if you set your mind to it. As I was finishing my dressing, I saw a strange thing happen. A violet ball the size of a small orange came down through the forest on the opposite bank of the lake. When it reached the sandy beach, it hovered back and forth close to the ground. Within a few minutes, another ball of similarly colored light approached from behind one of the islets, and the two wavered to and fro over the beach, sometimes circling each other. 

I set off toward them in the canoe, thinking—as I still do—that they were some new kind of luminous insect. When I reached their beach, one of them retreated into the bushes and the other flew away over the water. I followed in the canoe, for the water here is very deep; just as I thought I had nearly caught it, it dove into the lake. I could see it glowing as it sank until it vanished in the depths. I hurried back, fearing that if my absence with the canoe were discovered it might cause trouble. By 3:30 AM, I was safely back in the hut, though I was not as comfortable as I had been on the lake. 

Shortly before five o'clock, my men began to stir and I had my tea. I did not tell them about my adventure, but I asked what those lights were. "Akom," said the Fan man, and pointing toward the shore of the lake where I had been during the night, they said, "They came from there; it was an 'Aku'"—or <term>devil bush</term> <note>In West African colonial-era parlance, a 'devil bush' refers to a sacred grove or a place where spirits are said to reside, often associated with secret societies.</note>. I regretted more than ever that I had not secured one of those two phenomena. What a delight a real devil, properly preserved in raw alcohol, would have been to my scientific friends!
