# XI A TRAP FOR HIPPOS

...approaching in a separate canoe. We stopped at the island next to M’fetta to buy some more aguma <term>aguma: a staple food made from cassava, typically prepared as dense, doughy rolls</term>. The inhabitants were very interested in my appearance; they ran along the stony beach as we paddled away and stood at the end of the shore until we were out of sight among the many islands at the northeastern end of Lake Ncovi. 

The scenery is rugged. There are no terrifying cliffs or towering mountains to make it what one usually calls "wild" or "romantic," but it has a distinct character all its own. This northeastern end features beautiful sandy beaches on the southern side in front of the forested bank; they lie like smooth ribbons along the level shore and curve into scallops around the headlands where the hills descend into the lake. The forest on these hills—or mountains, for they are part of the Sierra del Cristal <note>A mountain range in Western Equatorial Africa, primarily in modern-day Gabon</note>—is very dark in color, and the undergrowth appears thin. 

We soon reached a narrow but deep channel flowing from the east into the lake. We traveled up it, winding our way into a valley between the hills. After going up the channel a little way, we found it completely fenced across with sturdy stakes. A gap was left open in the middle, wider than the spaces between the other stakes. Poised over this opening was a spear with a bush rope <term>bush rope: strong, flexible climbing vines used locally as cordage or rope</term> attached, weighted at the top of the handle with a large lump of rock. The entire mechanism is held in position by a bush rope arranged just below the water level so that anything passing through the opening would trigger the spear to drop. 

This was a trap for hippopotamuses or manatees. It is similar in structure to those one sees set in the hippo grass <note>A tall, aquatic grass (likely *Vossia cuspidata*) that serves as a primary food source for hippos</note> near villages and plantations. These traps serve the double purpose of protecting the vegetable supply and adding to the meat supply of the inhabitants. We squeezed through the stakes carefully so as not to set the trap off and found that our little river led us into another lake, much smaller than Ncovi. 

It is dotted with islands of fantastic shapes, all wooded with tall trees of a uniform height. Because there is little or no undergrowth among them, their pale gray trunks look like clusters of columns supporting a dark green ceiling. The forest comes down the steep hillsides to the water's edge in all directions, and a dark, gloomy-looking herb grows out of the black slime and water in a ribbon in front of it. There is another channel leading out of this...

## CHAPTER XII

### FROM NCOVI TO ESOON

*Regarding the journey from the island of M’fetta to an uncertain destination in suspicious and difficult company, the consequences of that journey, and accounts of the Great Forest and its inhabitants.*

I will not bore you with the specific details of my diary regarding our journey by land, because the small, water-damaged notebook from this period is mostly filled with reports on legal disputes, for reasons I will explain later. Furthermore, while traveling through this region, I was usually too exhausted at night to write anything more than cryptic entries like: “5 S., 4 R. A., N.E Ebony. T. 1—50, etc.”—notes that need further detail to be understood, which I will now provide.

Our first day’s march was very long. There was no “path” in the usual sense of the word. For hour after hour and mile after mile, we traveled through the deep gloom of the Great Forest’s undergrowth. The pace set by the Fans <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group of Central Africa</note>—who are by far the fastest Africans I have ever encountered—exhausted the Ajumba. The Ajumba are essentially canoe men; though they had been full of energy even after their incredibly long day of paddling from Arevooma to M’fetta, this land trek wore them out. Ngouta, the Igalwa interpreter, felt completely drained <term>pumped: an archaic slang term for being exhausted or out of breath</term> and said as much very early in the day. 

I deeply regretted bringing him; due to a combination of nervous exhaustion from our experiences at M’fetta and a slight chill, he had almost completely lost his voice, and I feared he would fall ill. The Fans, however, were clearly in their element in the forest, moving over fallen trees and rocks with a graceful, easy stride. The only thing that saved us “weaklings” was the Fans’ appetites; every two hours they sat down to have a snack of a pound or so of meat and aguma <note>A starchy, dough-like food often made from cassava</note>.

...each, followed by a pipe of tobacco. We would catch up with them during these stops. Ngouta and the Ajumba would sit down and rest with them; I would join them for a few minutes to rest and chat, but then I would continue alone to get a head start. I received a "good start" in the other sense of the word—a real shock—on the afternoon of the first day while descending into a ravine.

At the bottom, I saw a herd of five elephants wading and rolling in the mud. I am certain that, due to some misunderstanding among the Fates, I was granted a series of magnificent hunting opportunities meant as a special treat for some favorite Nimrod <note>Nimrod: A biblical figure described as a "mighty hunter," here used to refer to any legendary or skilled hunter</note> of those three goddesses. I know exactly how I should have behaved: I should have felt my favorite rifle fly to my shoulder, carefully aimed at the finest specimen, and fired. The noble beast would have stumbled forward, recovered, and—leaving a trail of blood behind—crashed away into the forest. Then I would have tracked it and either delivered the final blow <term>quietus: a finishing stroke or death blow; from the Latin "quietus est," meaning "he is at rest"</term> with one well-aimed shot, or been charged by it, with the elephant passing completely over my prone body. Either ending is considered "good form" in hunting stories, but such things never happen to me, and they never will. 

(In this instance, I quickly remembered that your only chance when charged by several elephants is to dodge around trees, constantly moving downwind <note>Downwind: being in a position where the wind blows from the animals toward the person, preventing the animals from smelling the intruder</note> until they lose your scent and sight, then to lie still for a while before heading home.) It was clear from the total indifference of these massive creatures that I was already downwind, so I only had to focus on dodging. I immediately ducked behind a tree—thinking perhaps a "dodge in time saves nine"—and lay down. 

Since they still showed no awareness of my presence, and because I was fascinated by the novelty of the scene, I crept forward from tree to tree until I was close enough to have hit the nearest elephant with a stone. Clumps of mud, sent flying by their stamping and wallowing, landed with a "flap, flap" among the bushes covering me.

One large bull had a fine pair of roughly forty-pound tusks that were remarkably straight; another had one large curved tusk and one broken one. If I were an elephant, I think I would prefer straight tusks; they must be more effective weapons that way.

<header>XII ELEPHANTS IN SINGLE FILE</header>
<sig>S 2</sig>

However, there seems to be no set way for elephants to behave here. Some of them lay right down like pigs in the deeper part of the swamp; some drew up trunkfuls of water and sprayed themselves and each other; and every one of them enjoyed a good rub against a tree. When they finally had enough, they all strolled off against the wind, as elephants often do <note>This is foolish, because the local people always attack them from behind.</note>. I do not know why they do this, because they clearly know the difference; they always carry their trunks differently when they are going against the wind compared to when they are going with it. I suppose one could call it arrested mental development <note>This is the typical explanation used by Europeans for anything they do not understand about the behavior of an African native.</note>. 

They strolled through the bush in single file <term>Indian file: a line of people or animals traveling one behind the other</term>, occasionally breaking off a branch, but leaving remarkably little disturbance <term>dead water: a nautical term used here to describe the trail or wake left behind by a moving body</term> considering their massive weight and size. One laid his trunk affectionately on the back of the one in front of him, which I believe is the elephant equivalent of walking arm-in-arm. When they had gone, I stood up and turned around to find the men. I stepped right on Kiva’s back then and there, squarely and fully, and fell sideways down the steep hillside until I caught myself among some roots.

It turned out that Kiva had come forward after his meal, ahead of the others. Being a born hunter and seeing the elephants, he had crawled down to watch them just as I had. He said he had not expected to find me there. I do not believe he gave me a single thought while in the presence of these fascinating creatures, and so he ended up being stepped on. I suggested to him that we should stack the baggage and go on an elephant hunt. He shook his head reluctantly, saying "Kor, kor," like a depressed crow, and explained that we were not strong enough. There were only three Fans—the Ajumba and Ngouta did not count—and furthermore, we had not brought enough ammunition because the luggage had to be carried. The ammunition we did have had to be saved for game other than elephants, as we might encounter conflict before we reached the Rembwé River.

We had by now joined the rest of the party, and were all soon splashing about <term>squattering: splashing or wading through water or mud</term> on our own account in the elephant bath. The footing was terribly bad—like a ploughed field—

The experience was like an exaggerated, terrifying nightmare. It nearly pulled my legs out of their sockets, and to this hour I cannot tell you whether it is better to step directly into an elephant's footprint—which is essentially a small pond about the size of the seat of a Madeira wicker armchair—or whether you should try to balance yourself on the rim and stride hopefully toward the other side. By now, the footprints and the hollows where the elephants had been rolling were filled with water, and the mud underneath was hard and slippery in places. 

Despite my determination to remain calm and dignified while traveling among these dangerous savages, I couldn't help but burst out laughing. It was an irresistible sight to see the stout, powerful Pagan suddenly turn himself into a four-legged animal as he slipped, while Gray Shirt balanced on one heel and waved his other leg in the air—signaling to everyone present that he was about to fall down. No one made such a fuss <term>palaver: a long and idle discussion; here used to mean a great deal of trouble or commotion</term> about "taking a seat" as Gray Shirt did; I fell down repeatedly myself without making nearly as much noise about it. 

I imagine that majestic elephant hunter, the Great Wiki, would have crossed safely and with dignity, but the man in front of him spun around and threw his arms around the Fan man, and they both crashed to the ground together. The heavy load on Wiki’s back drove them both into the mud like a pile driver. Eventually, we made it through, and after I climbed up the other side of the ravine, I saw the Fan guides let the Ajumba people go on ahead while they stayed behind, busy searching their bodies for something.

I followed the Ajumba, but before I caught up with them, I felt a terrible pricking irritation. Upon inspecting the affected area, I discovered a tick of enormous size with its head buried in my flesh. Investigating further, I found three more. It was incredibly difficult and painful to remove them, as they don't just cause irritation at the bite site; they send a shooting pain, similar to rheumatism, up from the spot. After finishing my "operations," I continued on and came upon the Ajumba in a state of undress that would have been more appreciated by Praxiteles <note>Praxiteles was a renowned ancient Greek sculptor famous for his lifelike nude statues.</note> than by the general public today. They had also discovered the elephant ticks on themselves. I moved past them and got a good start on the next stage of the journey.

By this time, shortly after noon on the first day, we had entered a mountainous and rocky country, and also encountered...

<header>XII A PRIMEVAL FOREST</header>

...a track—one you had to keep your eye on or you would lose it in a minute, but still a guide for direction.

The forest trees here were mainly ebony and great hardwood trees <note>original: "Diospyros and Copaifera mopane"</note>, with no palms except for my old enemy: the climbing palm, *calamus*. As usual, it went on its long excursions, climbing up one tree and down another. Whenever it caught a gleam of sunshine, it would burst into a plume of fronds; in the middle of each plume was a single long spike sticking straight up, which was an unopened frond. It runs along the ground over anything it meets, whether rock or fallen timber; its long, dark-colored, rope-like stem is simply covered with thorns. The length of some of these climbing palms must be immense. One tree I noticed that day had a long, straight, rope-like palm stem hanging from its summit, a good one hundred and fifty feet above us. Interested, I went to it and tried to track it to its root, only to find it was a loop coming down from another tree. I had no time to trace it further, for they climb up a tree and travel along the surrounding treetops, taking an occasional dip before heading up again.

The character of the entire forest was very interesting. Sometimes for hours we passed among thousands upon thousands of gray-white columns of uniform height—about 100 to 150 feet. At the top of these, the boughs branched out and interlaced, forming a canopy or ceiling. This dimmed the light of even the equatorial sun to such an extent that no undergrowth could thrive in the gloom. The reality of the struggle for existence was evident here in plain terms. However, unlike in our climate, it was not primarily a struggle against the weather, but rather a deadly internal war caused by overpopulation. 

Now and again we passed among the vast trunks of buttressed trees, some enormous in girth. From their distant summits hung great bush-ropes <term>bush-ropes: thick, woody vines or lianas characteristic of tropical rainforests</term>. Some were as straight as plumb lines, while others were coiled and intertwined with each other until one could imagine they were watching some mighty battle between armies of giant serpents, frozen at its peak by a magic spell. All these bush-ropes were as bare of leaves as a ship’s wire rigging, but many were covered in thorns. I was very curious as

...to how they climbed straight up, and investigation showed me that many of them were carried upward as a tree grew. The only true climbers were the *calamus* <note>rattan palm</note> and the rubber vine (*Landolphia*), both of which use hooked gear to climb.

Some stretches of this forest consisted of thin, spindly-stemmed trees of great height. Among these stretches, I always noticed the remains of some forest giant whose death—caused by lightning or because its superior height gave the demonic tornado winds an extra grip on it—had allowed sunlight to penetrate the lower regions of the forest. Then, the seedlings and saplings, which had for years been starved of light, shot upward. They seemed to know that their only chance lay in reaching the forest canopy level as quickly as possible. They had no time to thicken their trunks, nor time to grow side branches or any such luxuries. Up, up to the light they raced, and the one among them who reached it first won this game of life or death. Once it reaches the top, it spreads its crown of upper branches and blocks the life-giving sunshine from its competitors, who then wither and die or continue a stunted existence, waiting for another chance—sometimes for centuries. Tens of thousands of seeds must perish before they ever get their chance, but the way the seeds of African hardwoods are packed in specially durable cases is truly wonderful. Indeed, the ways of Providence here are remarkable in their strange, dual intention to both preserve and destroy; but on the whole, as Peer Gynt <note>The protagonist of Henrik Ibsen's 1867 play</note> truly observes, <note>original: "Ein guter Wirth—nein das ist er nicht."</note> "A good host—no, that He is not."

We saw this influence of light on a large scale as soon as we reached the open hills and mountains of the Sierra del Cristal and had to cross those fearful, avalanche-like timber falls on their steep sides. The worst of these lay between Efoua and Egaja, where we hit a part of the range that was exposed to the southeast. These falls were evidently caused by tornadoes, which from time to time have hurled down gigantic trees. Their hold on the shallow soil over the layers of hard bedrock was insufficient, despite all the anchors they had in the form of roots and buttresses, and all the rigging in the form of bush ropes <note>large, woody vines or lianas</note>.

<header>XII A BAD FALL 263</header>

Down they had fallen, crushing and dragging along with them those nearby or tied to them by great, tough climbing vines.

Crossing these fallen trees was dangerous, not to mention abrasive work. Someone from our party was always falling through the gaps; and I found it quite uncomfortable when I tried it myself in a fall above Egaja. I fell ten or twelve feet through crashing, creaking timber, and then landed heavily on a pile of rotten, wet *debris*, surrounded by more snakes and centipedes than anyone could possibly want, even if you were a specimen collector. You had to stay there while Wiki—who was a very discerning expert—selected a vine from the surrounding forest that he considered the right tool for the job. Then, you were hauled back up through the branches you had snapped the wrong way during your fall.

"The Duke" <note>One of Kingsley’s carriers, nicknamed for his mannerisms</note> had a bad fall, dropping twenty feet or so before hitting the rubbish heap. Meanwhile, on one occasion, it took us half an hour to rescue Fika, who had fallen through while carrying a heavy load on his back. Just as we had pulled him to the top and he was able to cling to the upper branches, Wiki—who had been supervising the operation—slipped backward and fell through himself. The vine we had been using to haul them up was too worn out by the weight to be used again, so we pulled Wiki out using the first vine we could pull down and cut. When Wiki emerged, he complained that we were reckless and knew nothing about forest vines, which just shows how ungrateful an African can be. 

The sweat runs down my nose whenever I think of it. The sun was out that day; we were positioned right on the Equator, and the air was thick with the foul-smelling vapors from the swamps that border and cross the mountain chain. We were already hot enough without those smells, due to the intense effort of hauling these 168 to 182-pound <term>twelve to thirteen stone</term> men back up to our level, combined with the strenuous exercise of climbing over the fallen trees ourselves.

When we reached the cool forest beyond, it was delightful. This was particularly true if it happened to be one of those lovely stretches of forest that are gloomy at ground level, but suggest a world of blossoms, fragrance, and beauty far above us—an upper world we saw as little of as earthworms see of a flowerbed. <header>FROM NCOVI TO ESOON          CHAP.</header>

The ground was strewn with large, fallen blossoms—thick, wax-like, glorious cups of orange, crimson, and pure white. Each flower was a handful in size, proving that some of the trees around us were displaying their glorious colors to the sky alone. Scattered among them were clusters of pure, stephanotis-like flowers, which indicated that the spindly lianas <term>bush-ropes</term> were actually rubber vines that had burst into bloom upon reaching the sunlight. We encountered these flowers in nearly every type of forest along our route, as rubber trees are abundant here.

I will bore you no longer with descriptions of the different kinds of forest; suffice it to say, I have spared you several. The local people have distinct names for seven different forest types, and I believe that number could easily be expanded to nine.

A sort of friendship soon developed between the Fans <note>The Fang people of West Africa</note> and me. We both recognized that we belonged to the same category of people: those with whom it is better to share a drink than to pick a fight. We knew we would have killed each other if given enough incentive, so we both took care to ensure that no such incentive arose. The Fans treated Gray Shirt and Pagan—their trading partners—with a sort of independent courtesy. However, they didn't care a bit for Silence, Singlet, the Passenger, or especially Ngouta. I have little doubt that if it hadn't been for the three of us, they would have killed and eaten these very amiable gentlemen with no more remorse than an English sportsman feels when shooting rabbits. On their part, the others hated the Fans and never missed a chance to tell me, "These Fans are very bad men."

I must also mention another member of our group: a Fan gentleman with the manners of a duke and the habits of a scavenger <term>dustbin</term>. He joined us entirely uninvited and never asked for payment; I think he simply wanted to witness the excitement, join in any fights that might break out, and generally scavenge what he could. He was clearly a man of some status, judging by the way the others treated him. Moreover, he carried a magnificent gun with a gorilla-skin sheath for its lock, its stock decorated throughout with brass nails. His outfit consisted of nothing but a small, dirty rag around his waist. Whenever we pushed through dense undergrowth or waded through a...

<header>XII  A DANGEROUS LESSON</header>
<page-num>265</page-num>

Through the swamp, he wore that thin strip of cloth tucked up scandalously short. Whenever we were sitting down in the forest having one of our casual meals, he always sat next to me and took possession of my tin cup. Then he would fill his pipe, and turning to me with the easy grace of an aristocrat, would say what may be translated as: "My dear Princess, could you favor me with a match?" <term>lucifer: an early type of friction match</term>

I used to say, "My dear Duke, I would be delighted," and give him one already lit.

I did not dare trust him with the whole box, as I was personally convinced he would have kept it. I asked him what he would do if I were not there with a box of matches; in response, he produced a forest buffalo's horn <term>bush-cow: the West African forest buffalo</term> with a neat wooden lid secured with vine-twine <term>tie-tie: sturdy climbing vines used as cordage</term>. From inside it, he produced a flint and steel and demonstrated his method. Unfortunately, because of his scanty clothing, all of his lordship’s small possessions were kept in the same pineapple-fiber bag slung across his shoulder. These possessions, though few, were as dangerous to the body as a million pounds is said to be to the soul, for they consisted largely of gunpowder and snuff. Their separate containers leaked and their contents mixed together, so the demonstration of Fan fire-making methods ended in a sudden, minor explosion. The "Professor" and his pupil sneezed uncontrollably for ten minutes, and a cruel world laughed until it nearly died for twenty. Still, that bag, despite all its failings, was a marvel for its carrying capacity.

The first day in the forest we came across a snake <gloss>1</gloss>—a beauty with a fresh, velvety skin patterned in red-brown and yellow, about three feet six inches long and as thick as a man's thigh. Ngouta encountered it hanging from a branch and recoiled backward like a lobster; among his many weaknesses, Ngouta had a deep-seated horror of snakes. All the natives of the Ogooué region hold this snake in great dread. They claim to have remedies for the bites of other types of snakes, but for this one, they have none. If, however, a native is bitten by one, he usually conceals the fact that it was this particular species and tries to take whatever chance the traditional healer’s medicine may provide. The Duke stepped—

Moving forward, with a single blow he flattened the snake's head against a tree using his gun butt. He then folded the snake up and stuffed as much of it as possible into his bag, while the rest hung dangling out. Ngouta, unable to keep up with the Duke because his Grace's pace was so brisk, moved to the very back of the party. He did this so that others would be killed first if the snake returned to life, as he suspected it would. He fell into other dangers because of this caution, but I cannot chronicle all of Ngouta's afflictions without making this book as long as an old-fashioned, oversized volume <term>folio: a large book format made of large sheets of paper folded once</term>. We had the snake for supper—that is to say, the Fan guides and I did. The others would not touch it, even though a good snake, properly cooked, is one of the best meats one can find out here; it is far better than the African chicken.

The Fans also did their best to educate me in every way. They told me their names for things, while I told them mine, adding in a few colloquial phrases as a "bonus" <term>dash for top: a West African English term for a tip or extra gift</term>, such as: "Dear me, now," "Who would have thought it," "Nonsense, my dear sir," and so on. By the time I left them, they had run these phrases together into single words, and they had a pleasantly wild sound to them, especially "dearmenow." Therefore, I must warn any linguist <term>philologist: a person who studies the history and structure of languages</term> who visits the Fans to be careful not to assume any word longer than two syllables is of native origin. I found several European words already slightly altered in use among them, such as "*Amuck*"—a mug, and "*Alas*"—a glass or tumbler. I do not know whether their word "*Ami*"—used for a person being addressed or spoken of—is French in origin or not. It may come from "*Anwĕ*"—the M'pongwe <note>The M'pongwe are an ethnic group in Gabon.</note> word for "You" or "Ye." As a rule, they use it when addressing a person after the phrase they always use to open a conversation: "*Azuna*"—meaning "Listen" or "I am speaking."

They also showed me many things, such as how to light a fire using the soft inner tissue <term>pith: the soft, spongy cellular tissue in the stems of plants</term> of a certain tree. This was useful to me later in life, but they rather overdid this branch of instruction in various ways. For example, Wiki had, as I mentioned before, a mania for climbing vines <term>bush-ropes: lianas or sturdy climbing vines used as cordage</term> and a marvelous eye and knowledge of them. From among the thousands surrounding us, he would pick out one of such peculiar flexibility that you could wind it around anything like a strip of cloth, yet it was as strong as a thick cable <term>hawser: a thick rope used for towing or mooring a ship</term>. Or he would find another which has...

<header>XII GORILLAS AT HOME</header>

...a certain stiffness, combined with a slight elastic spring, which was excellent for hauling with the ease and accuracy of a lady picking out a particular twisted strand of embroidery silk from a multicolored, tangled ball. He would go into the bush after these vines while other people were resting, especially seeking the variety that is bright yellow when split, very supple, and excellent for tying around loads.

On one occasion between Egaja and Esoon, he returned from one of these searches and wanted me to come see something very quietly. I went, and we crept down into a rocky ravine; on the other side lay one of the outermost Egaja plantations. When we reached the edge of the cleared ground, we lay down and wormed our way with elaborate caution through a patch of Koko <note>Koko: Colocasia esculenta, a tropical root vegetable also known as taro or coco-yam</note>. Wiki went first, and I followed in his trail.

After about fifty yards of this, Wiki sank flat, and I saw before me—some thirty yards off—five gorillas busily pulling down plantains and committing other raids: one old male, one young male, and three females. One of the females had a young one clinging to her, which had beautiful, wavy black hair with just a slight kink in it. The big male was crouching on his haunches with his long arms hanging down on either side, the backs of his hands on the ground and the palms facing upward. The oldest female was tearing apart and eating a pineapple, while the others were at the plantains, destroying more than they actually ate.

They kept up a sort of whinnying, chattering noise, quite different from the sound I have heard gorillas make when enraged, or the sound they make when they are—as the natives call it—“dancing” at night. I noticed that their arm reach was immense. When they moved from one tree to another, they scuttled <term>squattered: moved awkwardly or shuffled along</term> across the open ground in a most inelegant style, dragging their long arms with their knuckles downward. I estimate the big male and female were each over six feet tall. The others were likely between four and five feet. I reached out and laid my hand on Wiki’s gun to prevent him from firing; he, thinking I was about to fire, gripped my wrist.

I watched the gorillas with great interest for a few seconds,

...until I heard Wiki make a peculiar little sound, and looking at him, I saw his face was twitching in a terrifying way as he gripped his throat violently with his hand.

"Heavens!" I thought, "this gentleman is going to have a seizure; we are completely lost this time." He rolled his head back and forth and then buried his face into a heap of dried debris at the base of a plantain stem, clasped his hands over it, and let out an explosive sneeze. The gorillas dropped everything, stood up for a second, and made a strange sound between a bark and a howl. Then the females and the young male started for home. The old male rose to his full height—it struck me at the time that he was at least ten feet tall, but for scientific purposes, allowances must be made for a lady’s emotions—and looked straight toward us, or rather, toward where that sound came from. Wiki fell into a fit of high-pitched sneezes the likes of which I have never heard. Evidently, neither had the gorilla; doubtless thinking—as one of his black human relatives would have thought—that this phenomenon favored a Duppy <note>Duppy: A West African and Caribbean term for a ghost or restless spirit</note>, he went after his family with amazing speed the moment he reached the forest. He disappeared just as they had, swinging himself along through the trees from bough to bough in a way that convinced me that, given the necessity of getting around in tropical forests, humanity has made a mistake in letting our arms become shorter. I have seen many wild animals in their native habitats, but never have I seen anything to equal gorillas going through the bush; it is a graceful, powerful, superbly perfect hand-trapeze performance.¹

After this sporting adventure, we returned—as I usually return from a sporting adventure—without measurements or a specimen. Our first day’s march, though the longest, was the easiest, though fortunately I did not know this at the time. Based on my walks on the Woermann road <note>Woermann road: Roads or paths associated with the Woermann-Linie, a prominent German shipping and trading company in West Africa</note>, I judge it was well over twenty-five miles. It was easiest, however, because for the greater part of it...

But although elephants, leopards, and pythons give you a feeling of alarm, they do not produce that feeling of horrible disgust that an old gorilla causes because of its hideous appearance.

<page-num>269</page-num>
<header>XII A FORCED MARCH</header>

...the way through the gloomy forest. All day long, we never saw the sky once.

During the earlier part of the day, we were steadily climbing uphill, occasionally making a small descent and then climbing again, until we reached what was apparently a long ridge; from there, we could look down on either side into deep, dark, ravine-like valleys. Twice or thrice we descended into these to cross them, finding a small or large swamp at the bottom with a river running through its center. All those rivers flowed toward Lake Ayzingo.

We had to hurry because Kiva—who was the only one among us who had been to Efoua—said that unless we did, we would not reach Efoua that night. I said, "Why not stay in the bush?" <term>bush: the wild, uncultivated forest</term> having developed no love for spending a night in a Fan <note>The Fan people, now usually called the Fang, were an ethnic group Kingsley traveled with; at the time, they were often feared by outsiders as cannibals.</note> town after my experience at M’fetta. Moreover, the Fans themselves were not entirely sure that our whole party might not spend the evening at Efoua—once we did arrive—simmering in its cooking pots.

Ngouta, I should remark, had no doubt on the subject at all; he keenly regretted having left Mrs. N. <note>Likely Mrs. Nassau, a missionary Kingsley had stayed with.</note> and sincerely missed the store at Andande. But these Fans are a fine, adventurous tribe and decided they would risk it; besides, they were almost certain they had friends at Efoua. In addition, they showed me trees scratched in a way that was a massive exaggeration of the condition of my own cat’s favorite table leg at home, proving there were leopards in the vicinity. I kept moving, as it was my only chance, because I found that I grew stiff if I sat down. They always carefully told me which direction to go when they sat to rest; with their superior pace, they soon caught up to me and then passed me, leaving me, Ngouta, and sometimes Singlet and Pagan behind. In our turn, we would overtake them, with the difference being that they were sitting down when we did so.

About five o’clock, I was ahead and noticed a path which I had been told I would encounter and must follow. The path was slightly faint, but by keeping my eye on it, I could see it. Eventually, I came to a place where it vanished, but it appeared again quite clearly on the other side of a clump of undergrowth. I took a shortcut toward it, and the next thing I knew, I was in a heap, fallen onto a pile of spikes,

It is at these times you realize the blessing of a good thick skirt. If I had paid attention to the advice of many people in England—who ought to have known better and did not follow it themselves—and adopted masculine garments, I would have been impaled to the bone and finished. Instead, except for a good many bruises, here I was with the fullness of my skirt tucked under me, sitting on nine ebony spikes about twelve inches long in relative comfort, shouting loudly to be hauled out. The Duke came along first and looked down at me. I said, “Get a <term>bush-rope</term> <gloss>a strong, flexible climbing vine used as rope</gloss> and haul me out.” He grunted and sat down on a log. The Passenger came next, and he looked down. “Are you killed?” <note>original: "You kill ?"</note> he asked. “Not much,” I said; “get a bush-rope and haul me out.” “I can't do it,” <note>original: "No fit," a common West African Pidgin English expression of the era</note> he said, and sat down on the log. 

Presently, however, Kiva and Wiki came up. Wiki went and selected the one and only bush-rope suitable to haul an English lady of my exact complexion, age, and size out of that one particular pit. Such ropes seemed rare around there, judging by the time he took; I was just wondering what method would be best to use to climb the smooth, yellow, sandy-clay, inward-curving walls when he finally arrived with it. I was out in a twinkling and felt very much ashamed of myself—until Silence, who was then leading the way, disappeared through the path before us with a despairing yell. 

Each man then pulled the skin cover off his <term>gun lock</term> <gloss>the firing mechanism of a musket</gloss>, carefully checked to see if things there were all right and ready, and loosened his knife in its snake-skin sheath. Then we set about hauling poor Silence out, binding him up where necessary with cool green leaves; for he, not having a skirt, had been considerably "frayed at the edges" by those spikes. 

Then we closed ranks, for the Fans <note>The Fang people</note> said these pits indicated we were in the immediate neighborhood of Efoua. We tested the ground as we went into a thick plantain patch, through which we could see a great clearing in the forest and the low huts of a large town. We charged into it, going right through the guard-house gateway at one end in single file, as its narrowness required, and into the street-shaped town, forming ourselves into as imposing a looking party as possible.

# XII RECEPTION AT EFOUA

In the center of the street, the people of Efoua regarded us with much amazement. The women and children cleared out of the way into the huts and watched us through the door-holes. There were only a few men in the town; we later learned that the majority were away hunting elephants. However, there were enough left to form a crowd in a ring around us. Fortunately, the friends of Wiki and Kiva were present, and we were soon lost in another fog of words. It was not as bad as the confusion at M’fetta; indeed, Efoua made a favorable impression on me from the start. For one thing, it was much cleaner than most Fan towns I have visited.

As a result of the discussion, one of the chiefs had his house cleared out for me. It consisted of two rooms that were almost bare of everything except a pile of boxes and a small fire on the floor. There were some little bags hanging from the roof poles and a general supply of insects. The inner room contained nothing but a hard plank bed, raised from the dirt floor on four short pegs.

I shook hands with the chief and thanked him, then directed that all the loads should be placed inside the huts. I must admit my good friend was a villainous-looking savage, but he behaved with great hospitality and kindness. From what I had heard of the Fan people, I decided it was best not to give him a present immediately. Instead, I based my claim on the rights of a friendly stranger seeking hospitality. When I saw that all the baggage was stowed away, I went outside and sat in the doorway on a rather rickety, mushroom-shaped stool in the cool evening air. I waited for my tea, which I wanted desperately. Pagan came up as usual for tobacco to buy <term>chop</term> <gloss>food</gloss>; after I gave it to him, I and the two chiefs had a long chat, with Gray Shirt acting as an interpreter. Of course, the first question was: why was I there?

I told them I was on my way to the factory of H. and C. on the Rembwé River. <note>H. and C. refers to Hatton and Cookson, a prominent British trading firm in 19th-century West Africa.</note> They said they had heard of "Ugumu"—their name for Messrs. Hatton and Cookson—but they did not trade directly with them. Instead, they passed their trade goods to towns closer to the Rembwé, which they described as "swindling, bad towns." They got the idea stuck in their heads that I was a trader—a sort of <term>bagman</term> <gloss>a traveling salesman or commercial agent</gloss> for the firm. Gray Shirt could not convince them otherwise, so one of their majesties went off and returned with—

I had twenty-five balls of rubber, which I bought to promote good will, subsequently <term>dashing</term> <gloss>giving as a gift or tip</gloss> them to Wiki, who turned them in at Ndorko when we arrived there. I also bought some elephant-hair necklaces from one of the chiefs’ wives by trading my red silk tie for them, along with one or two other items. I realized that fish-hooks would not be of much value because Efoua was not near any large body of water; so, I kept the fish-hooks and traded handkerchiefs and knives instead.

One old chief was exceedingly eager to do business, and I bought a meat spoon, a plantain spoon, and a gravy spoon from him. Then he brought me a lot of junk I did not want, and I told him so, announcing that I had finished trading for the night. However, the old gentleman was not to be discouraged. After an unsuccessful attempt to sell me his cooking pots, which were roughly made of clay, he gestured energetically that if I would wait, he had something to sell that Gray Shirt described as "very good." He went across the street and disappeared into his hut, where he evidently conducted a thorough search for the precious item. One box after another was brought out into the light of a bush torch held by one of his wives, and there was a heated discussion between him and his family of the "I’m sure you had it last," "You must have moved it," "I never touched the thing" variety. 

At last it was found, and he carried it across the street to me very carefully. It was a bundle of bark cloth tied very securely around something with <term>tie-tie</term> <gloss>traditional rope made from vines or plant fibers</gloss>. When this was removed, it revealed a layer of rag that was unwound from around a central object. *What could this be?* I wondered. It was surely some rare and valuable object, hopefully connected to <term>fetish worship</term> <gloss>traditional religious practices involving sacred objects</gloss>, and I watched its unpacking anxiously. In the end, however, it revealed—to my disgust and annoyance—an old shilling razor. The way the old chief held it out, and the high price he asked for it, was enough to make anyone believe I was in such desperate need of the thing that I was at his mercy regarding the cost. I waved it away with haughty scorn; then, feeling moved by the expression of agonized bewilderment on his face, I <term>dashed</term> <gloss>gave as a gift</gloss> him a belt that delighted him, and went inside to have tea to soothe my ruffled feelings.

### XII AN UNPLEASANT DISCOVERY

The chiefs made furious raids on the crowd of spectators who pressed around the door and stood with their eyes glued to every crack in the bark walls of the hut. The next-door neighbors on either side could have made a comfortable fortune for their old age by charging for seats as if for a circus. Every hole in the side walls had a human eye peering through it, and I heard new holes being bored in all directions; so I strongly suspect the chief, my host, must have found his palace quite drafty. I felt perfectly safe and content, however, even though Ngouta suggested the charming idea that “Perhaps these M’fetta Fan people have sold us.” The only serious question I had to face was whether I should take off my boots or not; they were soaking wet from wading through swamps and other terrain, and my feet were very sore. But on the other hand, if I took those boots off, I felt certain that I would not be able to get them back on again the next morning, so I decided to leave them on.

As soon as all my men had come in and settled themselves in the inner room for the night, I curled up among the boxes with my head on the tobacco sack and dozed.

After about half an hour, I heard a commotion in the street, and looking out—for I recognized the chief's voice performing a solo part followed by a chorus—I found him in legal difficulties over a murder case. An *alibi* was proven for the time being; that is to say, the prosecution could not bring forward witnesses because of the elephant hunt. I went back for another nap, and the town at last grew quiet. Waking up again, I noticed a powerful smell in the hut—exacerbated by being shut up, I suppose—and it had an unmistakably organic origin. Knocking the ash off the end of the smoldering bush-light <note>a traditional torch made of resinous wood or plant fibers</note> that lay burning on the floor, I investigated and tracked the smell to those bags. I took down the largest one and carefully noted exactly how the <term>tie-tie</term> <gloss>traditional rope made from vines or plant fibers</gloss> had been wrapped around its mouth, for these details are important and often mean a great deal. I then shook its contents out into my hat for fear of losing anything of value. They were a human hand, three big toes, four eyes, two ears, and other portions of the human body. The hand was fresh; the others were only "so-so" and shriveled.

Replacing them, I tied the bag up and hung it up again. I subsequently learned that although the Fans will eat their—

fellow friendly tribespeople, yet they like to keep a little something belonging to them as a memento. I learned about this touching trait in their character from Wiki; and, although it is to their credit under the circumstances, it is still an unpleasant practice when they hang the remains in the bedroom you occupy, particularly if the family’s loss in your host’s household has been recent. I did not venture to wander around Efoua, but I slid the bark door aside and looked out to get a breath of fresh air.

It was a perfect night, and there were no mosquitoes. The town, enclosed on every side by the great cliff of the high, dark forest, looked very wild in the starlight. Its low, crudely built bark huts stood in two straight rows, closed at either end by a guardhouse. In both guardhouses, a fire was burning, and the forms of sleeping men were visible in their flickering glow. Nothing was moving except for the goats, which are always brought into a special house built for them in the middle of the town to keep them safe from the leopards that roam from dusk to dawn.

Dawn found us awake; I prepared my tea, while the rest of the party had their food <term>original: "chop"; West African pidgin for a meal</term> and rebound the loads with Wiki’s fresh, flexible vines <term>original: "bush-ropes"</term>. Kiva amused me greatly; during our march, his clothing was extremely minimal, but when we reached the towns, he took garments from his bag and dressed himself so splendidly that I feared the charm of his appearance would involve me in one of those dreadful "wife disputes" <term>original: "wife palavers"; legal disputes regarding marriage or adultery</term> which experience had taught me to dread. Every morning, he always devoted some time to repacking his things. I gave a large tip <term>original: "dash"</term> to both chiefs, and they accompanied us very politely to the edge of their first plantations. We then said our goodbyes, with both sides expressing hope that we would meet again. They gave us many warnings about the immoral and depraved character of the other towns we would pass through before reaching the Rembwé River.

Our second day’s march was significantly worse than the first, for it led across a series of steep hills with deep ravines between them; every ravine had its swamp, and every swamp its river. <header>XII FROM BOG TO BOG</header>
<sig>T 2</sig>

...the dry season. We encountered examples of the three main types of West African bogs. The large, deep swamps were the easiest to handle because they create a clearing in the forest; this allows the sun to reach the surface and bake a crust, which you can walk across if you move quickly. Based on my experience with bogs in Devon <note>Devon is a county in South West England known for its treacherous peat bogs on Dartmoor and Exmoor</note>, I knew that speed was our best hope, and I suspect I earned one of my nicknames among the Fan people for my performance on these. The Fans crossed easily with a rapid, gliding stride, but the other men were too cautious. While they hesitated, trying to find a safe spot for their next step, the ground beneath them would sink with a "glug" sound. Furthermore, they tended to huddle together, which was more weight than the crust could support. The stout man we called "Pagan" and the "Passenger" <note>Two of Kingsley's traveling companions</note> gave us quite a task in one bog when they both sank in close to each other. Some of us cut tree branches and grabbed handfuls of tough canna leaves <term>large-leaved tropical plants</term>, while others threw them around the sinking victims to create a makeshift raft. Then, using vines <term>original: "bush-rope"</term>, we eventually hauled them out.

The worst kind of swamp, and the most common in this area, is the deep, narrow variety. These have no surface crust because they are too heavily shaded by the forest. The slopes of the ravines are also usually covered with an undergrowth of *shenja* <note>A type of tropical plant, likely a species of Costus or similar monocot with tough stalks</note>, which is beautiful beyond description but terrible to trek through. I quickly learned to dread seeing the man in front of me head downhill, or doing so myself, because it meant that within the next half hour we would be struggling through a patch of *shenja*. I believe few sights can compare to their beauty, with the golden sunlight filtering through the high forest branches onto their perfectly shaped, tough, dark green leaves, making them appear as if they were sprinkled with golden sequins. Their long green stalks, which support the leaves and carry small clusters of crimson berries, curve gracefully in every direction, and the entire plant is remarkably free of insects. However, once you have said that, you have said everything there is to say in favor of *shenja*. Those long stalks are as tough as twisted wire, and their graceful curves form a dense net that reaches up to your shoulders. Furthermore, the tough green leaves are incredibly slippery when they lie on the ground. It is not pleasant going down

It is even less pleasant, however, climbing up the other side of the ravine once you have made it through the swamp. You have to fight your way upward among jagged rocks through this hard, tough network of stems; it exhausted all of us except for the Fans.

These narrow, shaded swamps caused us a world of trouble and took up a great deal of time. Sometimes the leader of the party would make three or four attempts before finding a ford, wading in until the black, batter-like mud came up to his neck, then turning back and trying in another place. Meanwhile, the rest of the party sat upon the bank until the ford was found, feeling it was unnecessary to throw away human life needlessly. They believed that the more men there were paddling about in that swamp, the greater the chance of finding a hole in the bottom; and when such a hole is found, the discoverer is likely to leave his bones in it. If I happened to be in front, the duty of finding the ford fell to me, as none of us had personal knowledge of these swamps after leaving Efoua. I was too intimidated by the Fans, and too nervous and uncertain of the character of my other men, to dare show any cowardice <term>original: "show the white feather"</term> regardless of what happened. The Fans took my behavior as a matter of course, having never traveled with white people before or learned that some of them require being carried over swamps and rivers and so on. I suppose I might have taken things easier, but I was like the immortal Schmelzle <note>A reference to the protagonist of Jean Paul’s "Army-Chaplain Schmelzle's Journey to Flätz," a humorous tale about a man paralyzed by his own excessive caution and psychological fears</note> during that carriage journey he made on his way to Flætz <note>A fictional town in Jean Paul’s story</note> during a thunderstorm—I was afraid to be afraid. I am very certain I would have fared very differently if I had entered a region occupied by a powerful and fierce tribe like the Fans coming from certain districts on the West Coast. In those places, the inhabitants are used to seeing white people who are incapable of personal exertion, requiring to be carried in a hammock, or wheeled in a stroller <term>original: "go-cart"</term> or a Bath chair <note>A three-wheeled wheelchair steered by the occupant, common in the 19th century</note> through the streets of their coastal towns, depend—

<header>XII A SEVERE DOSE OF STEEL</header>

This is not the case in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>, and I had behind me the prestige of a group of white men. For a native to say to them, "You shall not do such and such a thing," or "You shall not go to such and such a place," would only mean that those very things would certainly be done. I soon found that the name of Hatton and Cookson’s agent-general for this district, Mr. Hudson, was one to conjure with among the trading tribes. Furthermore, although the Ajumba's knowledge of white men had been limited, those they were accustomed to seeing were impressive individuals. Mr. Fildes, Mr. Cockshut, M. Jacot, Dr. Pélessier, Father <note>original: "Père"</note> Lejeune, M. Gacon, Mr. Whittaker, and that lively French official were not men whom anyone, black or white, would willingly provoke. 

In addition, there was the memory among the black traders of "that white man MacTaggart," whom an ambitious trading tribe near Setta Khama had had the audacity to attack. They shot him, towed him behind a canoe, and slashed him all over with their knives; yet he survived and confronted them again in a way that must have pathetically astonished those simple savages, considering the considerable effort they had put into killing him. Of course, it was difficult to live up to these standards, and I do not pretend to have succeeded—or rather, I doubt I would have succeeded had a real strain been put upon me.

I am particularly sure that I would never thrive under the treatment Mr. MacTaggart habitually receives. I had the pleasure of meeting him on my way home recently and found him quite recovered from another "overdose of steel." About six weeks earlier, he had gone with various other white men on a perfectly peaceful mission into a town. After receiving them kindly and holding a palaver <term>a formal discussion or negotiation</term>, the treacherous inhabitants attacked Mr. MacTaggart with sharpened machetes as the party was returning to their boats. They sliced off the top of his head and took a large chip out of the back of it. Then, evidently knowing the resilience of their man, they proceeded to carry him away in his stunned condition into the bush on a door. Once there, they planned to finish beheading him to make a Ju Ju <term>a fetish or protective charm, often involving spiritual power</term> out of his head. By securing Mr. MacTaggart’s head, they hoped to achieve this goal while also removing him from his current area of activity: the prevention of gin smuggling. Their plan seems excellent in theory, but I would not bet any money on its success, even if they had been able to carry him away on that door—which, thanks to his companions, they were not. It is almost as risky to be famously brave among a West African tribe as it is to be famously holy in the East. 

I know of another case where a tribe desired to collect the head of a gentleman for their Ju Ju house <note>A shrine or place of worship in West African traditional religions, often associated with charms or fetishes.</note>. In that instance, it showed a high degree of devotion on their part, for it would have caused them serious domestic inconvenience to have removed their entire set of tradesmen at one fell swoop. It showed even more of a high-order artistic feeling, for the head in question is a very handsome one. Although they command my respect as a fellow collector for the care they took in trying to "collect the specimen" by shooting it in the legs, from any other standpoint, I am very glad they failed. 

This idea of the advantage of possessing a great man’s head is somewhat like the Eastern custom I remember reading about in one of Richard Burton’s <note>Sir Richard Francis Burton (1821–1890), the famous British explorer, linguist, and writer.</note> memoirs. He was once among some very pious Easterners, disguised as a dervish <note>A member of a Muslim religious order known for their poverty and austerity.</note>. He was enjoying such a high level of admiration from them that he felt safe and content, until one day a native friend came to him secretly and advised him to flee. The friend said it was "because the people of this city are desirous of having the shrine of a very holy man among them—both because of the spiritual advantages it bestows, and the temporal ones arising from pilgrims coming to the town from other places to visit it. They have decided that you are so very holy, wise, and learned in the Koran <note>The central religious text of Islam.</note> that you will do." Burton left.

But to return to that forest in gorilla country: I was told that all the rivers we crossed on the first, second, and third days flowed into one or another of the branches of the Ogowé. This shows that the long slope of land between the Ogowé and the Rembwé tilts toward the Ogowé. The stone that formed the mountains was the same hard black rock that I had found on the Sierra del Cristal <note>A mountain range in Gabon, West Africa.</note> by the Ogowé rapids. However, in this vicinity, it did not contain those great masses of white quartz...

# XII PICKING OUR WAY

...which are such a prominent feature from Talagouga upward in the Ogooué valley. The mountains here were not nearly as high, but they had the same abrupt shape. They look like very old parts of the same range, worn down to stumps by the erosive forces of the torrential rain and sun, and the dense forest growing upon them. They had not been subjected to frost, of course; however, I noticed that rocks were often split in a similar way by small roots that had entered tiny crevices and, through gradual growth, enlarged them into cracks.

I have already mentioned our troubles with the fallen timber on these mountains, and these difficulties were at their worst between Efoua and Egaja. I suffered a good deal from thirst that day, as unboiled water is my <term>ibet</term> <note>Kingsley uses the local term "ibet" to refer to a taboo or a strictly forbidden thing; here, she refers to her rule against drinking unboiled water to avoid disease.</note>, and we were all nearly exhausted from the "athletic sports" required since leaving Efoua. We knew only one thing for certain about Egaja: none of us had a friend there, and the town had an especially evil reputation. Consequently, we were not feeling very cheerful when, toward evening, we reached its outermost plantations. Our arrival in the vicinity was announced when Silence <note>One of Kingsley's porters.</note> stepped squarely onto a sharp ebony spike driven into the narrow path, hurting himself. Fortunately, after we passed this first plantation, we came across a camp of four young men collecting rubber. I convinced one of them to carry Silence’s load and lead us into the town as we continued through more plantations.

Nothing is more tiresome than a path that leads into a plantation, because it disappears in the cleared ground or splits into many smaller paths running through the crops. No West African path goes straight through a stream or a plantation and comes out directly on the other side, so you have a difficult time finding it again.

Our new friend, the rubber collector, saved us from a great deal of "fine, varied walking," as I noticed he led us out via a path nearly at a right angle to the one by which we had entered. He then fell into a pit half-full of thorns—a pit he claimed he didn't know was there, proving that an African guide can indeed tell the truth. Once he climbed out, he handed back Silence's load and...

He left us to spend the rest of his evening by his forest fire picking thorns out of his skin, while we proceeded to wade across a swift, somewhat deep river. This river crossed the path he told us led into Egaja. We then traveled across another section of forest and headed downhill again. "Oh, bless those swamps!" I thought, "here is another one." But no—not this time. Across the bottom of the steep ravine, stretching from one side to the other, lay an enormous tree serving as a bridge. It was positioned about fifteen feet above a river that rushed beneath it over a bed cluttered with boulders. I assessed the situation at a glance; then and there, I would have traded that bridge for any swamp I have ever seen—yes, even for a certain <term>bush-rope bridge</term> <note>A suspension bridge made from woven vines or lianas.</note> in which I once became tangled like a buzzing fly in a spider's web. I was terribly tired, and my legs trembled under me after the falls and stresses of the earlier part of the day. My boots were also slippery from being soaked in water.

The <term>Fans</term> <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group Kingsley was traveling among.</note> went into the river and half-swam, half-waded across. All the <term>Ajumba</term> <note>A group of people from the Ogooué region serving as Kingsley’s porters.</note>, except for Pagan, followed them, and Ngouta managed to get across with their assistance. Pagan thought he would try the bridge, and I decided to watch how it worked. He made it about three yards along when he slipped; however, he caught the tree with his hands as he fell and hauled himself back to my side again. Then he went down the bank and through the water. This was not exactly designed to boost my confidence. I knew by now that I had to cross by the bridge, for I saw I was not strong enough in my exhausted state to fight the current. If only the wretched log had kept its bark, it would have been better; but it was bare, smooth, and round, and a slip meant death on the rocks below. I rushed across it and reached the other side safely. Because of this, poor Pagan was teased by the others about his failure; they claimed they had only gone through the water to wash their feet.

When we reached the other side, it did not seem much worth the effort. It was a swampy fringe at the bottom of a steep hillside, and after a few yards, the path turned into a stream or a backwater of the river. It was bordered with thick, <term>pleached</term> <note>Branches or vines that are densely intertwined or woven together.</note> bushes and covered with liquid water on top of half-liquid mud. Now and again, for a change, you had a foot of water on top of extremely slippery, harder mud, and then—

# XII WE ENTER EGAJA

We cheerfully tumbled sideways into the bushes or simply sat down. When the path wasn't following its usual treacherous course, it was riddled with holes. In fact, I suspect the bottom of those holes was the actual ground level, as the path was nearly as full of holes as a fishing net. It was very strange to see the man in front, who had been wading knee-deep just a moment before, suddenly drop down until the water was around his shoulders. Getting out of these slippery pits—which were sometimes a tight fit—was difficult.

However, that is the path you must take if you aren't wise enough to stay at home: a small stretch of swamp overgrown with shrubs, bordering the river on one side and running up the mountainside on the other.

At last, we reached a sandy bank, and on that bank stood Egaja. It was a town with an evil reputation even among the <term>Fan</term> <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group Kingsley was traveling among, often described in colonial accounts as fierce warriors.</note>, but it was where we had to stay, for better or worse. We entered the town through its <term>palaver house</term> <note>A communal building used for public meetings, negotiations, and legal discussions.</note> and soon encountered the usual argument.

I had detected signs of trouble among my men throughout the day. The <term>Ajumba</term> <note>A group of people from the Ogooué region serving as Kingsley’s porters.</note> were tired and dissatisfied with the Fans. Meanwhile, the Fans were in high spirits, openly rude to Ngouta, and eager for me to stay in this "delightful" locality to go hunting with them and various other "choice spirits." They assured me they could easily get these characters to join us at Efoua. Ngouta kept his distance from them, and I was worried about him because of his cold and his lost voice. 

I kept the peace as well as I could. I explained to the Fans that I didn't have enough money with me now because I hadn't expected such magnificent opportunities to be available when I started. I promised to come back next year—a promise I hope to keep—and told them that then we would go and have a grand time. This state of the party was a dangerous one in which to enter a strange Fan town, as our safety depended on us remaining united. 

When the first burst of shouting at Egaja began to settle into something reasonable, I discovered that a villainous-looking man—smeared with soot and draped in a fragment of genuine ancient cloth—was a head chief in mourning. He placed a house at my disposal; it was quite a mansion, for it had no fewer than four rooms. The first one was almost

The house was entirely occupied by a bed frame that was being assembled inside because the door was too small to fit it through. 

This had to be removed before we could get in with the baggage at all. While this removal was being carried out—causing as much damage to the house and the bed as if it were a moving day in England—the other chief arrived. He had been sent for, as he was away down the river fishing when we arrived. I saw at once that he was a far superior man to any of the chiefs I had yet met. It was not just his clothing, remarkable as it was for the district—consisting of a gentleman’s black frock coat (the kind included in a <term>ivory bundle</term> <note>A collection of European trade goods, including clothing and tools, exchanged for ivory.</note>), a bright blue felt sombrero hat, and an ample cloth of <term>Boma check</term> <note>A specific type of patterned trade fabric popular in West Africa.</note>—but his face and general bearing were distinctive, powerful, and intelligent. I knew that Egaja, for better or worse, owed its reputation to this man, and not to the sensual, brutal-looking one I had met first. He was exceedingly courteous, ordering his people to bring a stool for me and one for himself, and then a fly-whisk to battle the evening cloud of sandflies. I had Pagan come and act as interpreter while the rest were stowing the baggage and other supplies. After the usual compliments, I said, “Tell the chief that I hear this town of his is a 'thief town.'”

> “Better not, sir,” says Pagan.
> “Go on,” said I, “or I’ll tell him myself.”
> So Pagan did. It was a sad blow to the chief.
> “A thief town? This highly respectable town of Egaja! A town whose moral conduct in all matters (<term>Shedule</term> <note>Likely a local term referring to customary law, etiquette, or social regulations.</note>) was an example to all towns—called a thief town! Oh, what a wicked world!”

I said it was indeed a wicked world, but I would reserve my opinion as to whether Egaja was a part of that wicked world or a star-like exception until I had experienced it myself. We then discussed many matters, and I gathered a great deal of interesting <term>fetish</term> <note>A term used by 19th-century travelers to describe West African traditional religious beliefs, charms, and spiritual practices.</note> information from the chief. This was valuable to me because this entire district had not been in contact with white culture. Altogether, the chief and I became great friends.

I felt I could not treat it and then eat my tea afterward, so I ordered one of the small, canoe-shaped tubs used for mashing <term>manioc</term> <note>Also known as cassava, a starchy root vegetable that is a staple food in West Africa.</note> to be brought and filled with hot water. After adding a heavy dose of <term>Condy’s fluid</term> <note>A disinfectant solution made of potassium permanganate, commonly used in the 19th century.</note> to it, I made her sit down and soak her entire arm in it while I went to have my tea. 

As soon as I was finished, I went outside and asked some of the many women standing around to hold <term>bush-lights</term> <note>Torches made from resinous wood or bundles of grass.</note> while I examined the patient. The entire hand was a mass of yellow pus streaked with <term>sanies</term> <note>A thin, watery discharge from a wound or ulcer, often containing both blood and pus.</note>. Large ulcers were eating into the forearm, and there was a large <term>abscess</term> <note>A localized collection of pus caused by infection.</note> in her armpit. I lanced the <term>abscess</term> immediately. The old lady then terrified me by gently slumping over; I thought she was dying, but I soon realized she had simply fallen asleep. 

I thoroughly washed out the <term>abscess</term>. Having obtained a large quantity of baked <term>plantains</term> <note>A starchy fruit similar to a banana, usually cooked before eating.</note>, I made a large poultice of them mixed with boiling water and more Condy’s fluid in the tub. I placed her arm directly into this mixture. After propping her up and covering her with cloths I took from her son, I left her to nap while I investigated the history of the injury. It turned out that about forty-eight hours earlier, she had been wading along the riverbank catching <term>crawfish</term> <note>Freshwater crustaceans resembling small lobsters.</note> and had been stung by “a fish like a snake.” I suspect the ulcers were a long-standing <term>palaver</term> <note>In this context, a long-term problem or medical issue.</note>. 

The creature had badly torn her hand, and the pain and swelling were so severe that she hadn’t slept for a moment since it happened. Once the poultice grew cold, I removed her arm, cleaned it again, and wrapped it in a dressing. I had the old woman carried—still asleep—into her hut. After waking her briefly to give her a dose of that powerful medicine, <term>pil. crotonis cum hydrargi</term> <note>original: "pil. crotonis cum hydrargi"; a pill made of croton oil and mercury, used as an extremely potent and harsh laxative.</note>, I saw her tucked into her own wooden bed for the night, where she fell fast asleep again. 

The chief was very eager to have some pills as well, so I gave him a few with strict orders to take only one at a time. I knew that taking just one would teach him never to exceed the dose far better than any lecture I could give him, no matter how long I talked. # XII A CASE IN BANKRUPTCY

The situation had calmed down, and the debt had been renewed for the time being. However, the creditor had not gone to sleep. Instead, he sat up reflecting on the matter and recalled many instances—all cited in full—of how Kiva had failed to pay his debts. He also remembered that Kiva’s maternal brother and maternal uncle had done the same. Consequently, he decided to foreclose immediately on the debtor's estate. Since the estate was represented by and consisted of Kiva himself, he intended to seize his person and eat him.

It is always fascinating to observe the seeds of our own institutions existing within the culture of a supposedly "lower" race. Nevertheless, it is exhausting to be dragged out of one’s sleep in the middle of the night and thrust into such a study. This was evidently a vestige of an early form of Bankruptcy Court. In this case, the court that clears a man of his debt was represented by the knife and the cooking pot. The "whitewashing"—as I believe we call it <note>A legal term used at the time for the discharge of a bankrupt person, effectively "cleaning" their financial record.</note>—was also present, though it was not the debtor who was whitewashed. Instead, the creditors covered themselves in white clay to celebrate the removal of their enemy from his sphere of deceitful activity. This reversal may stem from the fact that whitewashing a debtor who was about to be cooked would be unwise, as the clay would boil off the meat and ruin the gravy. There is always a fragment of sound sense underlying African traditions. When I went out, Kiva was tied up and talking incessantly; everyone else was doing the same, and a woman was preparing white clay in a pot.

I suppose I should have rushed at him, cut his bonds, and started killing people with a revolver before fleeing into the bush with my party. However, my group clearly had no intention of fleeing; they were tucked up in the hut, pretending to be asleep and uninterested in the affair. Although I could have abandoned them without a second thought just then, I could not so easily flee into the bush alone with Kiva and leave my fish specimens <note>Kingsley was an accomplished scientist who traveled to West Africa to collect fish and insect specimens for the British Museum.</note> behind. Therefore, I shouted for Azuna <note>One of Kingsley's Fan companions and carriers.</note> to come to the "Bankruptcy Court" and found a Fan who spoke trade English to interpret for me. From him, I learned the outline of the proceedings as stated above. Hatton and Cookson was my great authority <term>original: "Ju Ju"</term>, and it was to their sub-factory on the Rembwé River that I was traveling. # XII A QUESTION OF CHARACTER

...recently gone through with. Not that I doubted for one minute that his representatives would have honored my credit <note>original: "book," referring to a written note of credit or IOU common in the West African trade</note>; for the generosity and helpfulness of West African traders is boundless and patient. But I did not like to take advantage of it, all the more so because of a feeling that I might never survive the journey to refund the money. So at last, I paid the equivalent value of the coat out of my own trade goods; and the affair was regarded by all parties as satisfactorily closed by the time the gray dawn was rising over the forest wall. I went back inside and slept in snatches until I got my tea about seven o'clock, and then turned out to hurry my party out of Egaja.

This I did not succeed in doing until past ten. One argument followed another among my men; but I was determined to get them out of that town as quickly as possible, for I had heard so much from perfectly reliable and experienced people regarding the treachery of the Fan <note>The Fang people.</note>. The chief was very anxious for me to stay and rest, but since his mother was doing wonderfully well and the other women seemed to quite understand my directions regarding her care, I did not feel inclined to risk staying. The old lady’s farewell to me was peculiar: she took my hand in both of hers, turned it palm upwards, and spat on it. I do not know whether this is a common form of greeting among the Fan; I suspect not. Dr. Nassau, who explained it to me when I saw him again at Baraka, said the spitting was merely an accidental by-product of the action, which actually consisted of blowing a blessing. Having encountered this custom twice afterward, I am certain from my own observation that he is right.

The two chiefs courteously escorted us out of the town as far as the point where the river crosses the outgoing path again. The chief in the blue hat gave me some charms "to keep my feet on the path," and the chief in mourning lent us his son to guide us through the lines of fortifications protecting the plantation. I gave them each an equal <term>dash</term> <note>A West African term for a tip, gift, or gratuity.</note>. In answer to their question about whether I had found Egaja to be a "thief-town," I told them that to call Egaja a town of thieves was total perjury, for I had not lost a single thing while I was there. We parted with mutual expressions of respect and hopes for another meeting in the near future.

The defenses of the fine series of plantations at Egaja on this side were extremely intricate, judging by the zigzag course our guide led us through. He explained that they had to be this way because of the character of the towns located toward the Rembwé River. We continued into the gloom of the Great Forest again—that forest which seemed to me to have no end. In a lazy, dazed state of mind, I expected to wander through it by day and stop at night in some noisy, primitive town for the rest of my life.

We climbed one hill, moved around its summit, performed our usual acrobatics over various fallen logs, and descended into a ravine as we always did. But at the bottom of that ravine, which was extremely steep, ran a small river free from swampland. As I was wading through it, I noticed a detail that distinguished it from all the other rivers we had crossed. Right then and there, I sat down on a boulder in the middle of the stream and pulled out my compass. Yes, by God! <note>original: "by Allah!"</note> It is flowing northwest and is heading, just as we are, for the Rembwé River. I climbed out the other side of that river with a lighter heart than when I entered, and I shouted the news to the men. They yelled and sang as we continued on our way.

All along this stretch of country, we had seen quantities of rubber vines, and between Egaja and Esoon, we came across large amounts of rubber being collected. Evidently, there was a large camp of rubber hunters working very busily in the district. Wiki and Kiva did their best to teach me the trade. Along each side of the path, we frequently saw a ring of sturdy vine rope, propped up on pegs about a foot to eighteen inches off the ground.
