# XII HOW BLOOD FEUDS BEGIN

inland for it. When a Fan town has exhausted the rubber in its vicinity, it migrates with all its possessions to a new part of the forest. Young unmarried men are the typical rubber hunters. Parties of them venture into the forest, wandering through it and camping under shelters made of branches at night for a month or more at a time during the dry seasons, until they have gathered a sufficient quantity. They then return to their town, where the women process the rubber. Finally, it is sold either to a white trader, in districts where one is within reach, or to an M'pongwe trader who travels around buying it along with collected ivory and ebony, much like a traveling peddler in Norfolk. In districts like those I was in, which are remote from the M'pongwe traders, the Fan people carry the rubber to the nearest town that has contact with a black trader and sell it to the inhabitants; they, in turn, resell it to the next town until it finally reaches him.

This passing down of rubber and ivory creates a series of commercial complications between the various towns. These disputes are as significant as "woman palavers" <term>palaver</term> <note>A term used in West Africa to denote a dispute, negotiation, or lengthy legal argument.</note> for causing trouble. It is the custom of these Fan people to require a life for a life, and they regard any one life as being as good as another. Furthermore, the rubber trade and disputes over wives are closely intertwined. A man seeking to kill someone regarding <note>original: "in re"</note> a wife palaver knows his best chance of taking a life from the village he holds a grudge against is to catch one of that village's men while he is out alone hunting for rubber. 

So he does this, and then the men from the victim's village lie in wait for a rubber hunter from the killer's village. Then, of course, the men from the killer's village lie in wait for rubber hunters from the first victim's village. Thus, the blood feud continues through the generations, so that if you happen to come upon the affair, you cannot see the beginning or the end of it. Frequently, the people involved have entirely forgotten what started the killing in the first place. Not that this discourages them in the least. Truly, if Dr. Nassau <note>Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), an American missionary and doctor who studied West African customs.</note> is right and these Fan people are descendants of Adam and Eve, I expect the feud between Cain and Abel is still being kept alive among them.

Wiki, who was an expert on bush rope <term>bush rope</term> <note>Vines or lianas used as cordage.</note>, gave me much information regarding rubber, showing me various other vines besides

->FROM NCOVI TO ESOON CHAPTER<-

...the true rubber vine. Its juice is mixed with the actual sap by the collector while in the forest to add weight—a matter of great importance, because rubber is purchased by weight. The second type of adulteration is performed by the women in the villages when the collected sap is handed over to them to prepare for the markets.

This preparation consists of boiling the sap briefly in water and adding a little salt; this causes the gummy part to separate and settle at the bottom of the pot, where it looks like a thick cream. The water is carefully poured off this deposit, which is then removed and molded, usually by hand. However, I have seen it poured into molds made of small calabashes with a stick or piece of iron passing through, so that when the rubber has set, the rod can be withdrawn. Since a hole is left behind, the balls can be threaded onto a stick—usually five to a stick—for the convenience of transport. It is during this molding process that most of the adulteration occurs. Down by the side of many of the streams, there is a white, chalky-looking clay which is brought into the villages, pulverized, and then hung over the fire in a basket to achieve a uniform, smoky blackness. It is then worked into the rubber as it is being formed into balls. Additionally, a large chunk of Koko, <term>*Arum esculentum*</term> <note>Also known as taro or cocoyam, a starchy tuber.</note> (Koko is better than yam, I should note, because it is heavier), which is also smoked to approximately the right color, is often placed in the center of the rubber ball. In fact, anything is put there that is hopefully regarded as likely to deceive the white trader.

I once overheard a long discussion between two women. "I always add plenty of clay to my rubber," said the first. "I think," said the second, "a bit of yam is better, with just a coating of rubber on the outside; then it bounces very well when Mr. —— throws it on the floor." They did not convince each other of the superiority of their individual methods, but they became very friendly over the foolishness of a mutual friend, who had used both clay and yam in her rubber to such an extent that when Mr. —— "threw it on the floor, it just went splat." Mr. —— then cut the ball open and "threw" both pieces at her head—an action that actually raised Mr. —— in their estimation, as it demonstrated "commercial intelligence," a quality universally admired.

# XII INGENUITIES OF ADULTERATION

down here. The adulteration <term>adulteration</term> <note>The practice of making something poorer in quality by adding another substance.</note> is so widespread that most traders must cut every ball open. Even Kinsembo rubber must be cut, though one would think it difficult to hide anything inside it. This variety is packaged in clusters of small bits, shaped like little thimbles by rolling pinches of rubber between the thumb and finger. Yet the “simple children of nature” who collect it and bring it to the “swindling white trader” hit upon an ingenious idea: they took small pieces of wood shaped like thimbles, dipped them in rubber, and added them to the clusters as excellent weight-fillers.

When first produced, pure rubber looks like putty and has the same dusky-white color. However, the balls become almost inky in color because they are kept in baskets inside smoky huts and in wicker-work cages submerged in muddy pools. This is done so they can soak up as much waste and moisture as possible to increase their weight before they pass into the hands of the traders.

# CHAPTER XIII

## FROM ESOON TO AGONJO

->In which the Traveler describes the beauties of the route from Esoon to N’dorko and provides an account of the local Swamps.<-

Our next stop was Esoon. They received us with the usual noise and commotion, but were friendly enough. I liked the town because the people there actually knew of the Rembwé River. They did not just wave their arms in the air toward some random direction and say, “Far, far away, many bad people live on 그 side,” as the people in other towns had done. 

Of course, they still insisted on the "bad people" part of the legend. However, I was becoming quite indifferent to the moral character of my new acquaintances. I felt certain that for pure, murderous villainy, several of my old Fan <note>The Fan (or Fang) people: an ethnic group in Central Africa whom Kingsley grew to admire for their strength and skill, despite their reputation for cannibalism.</note> companions—and even my own traveling party—would be hard to beat. Yet, every one of them had treated me well. I am glad to see from my diaries that I realized this at the time. In my Cameroon journal, I found an entry: “I wish to God the Fans were in this country; I have been searching in vain for a cannibal tribe to spend time with, but there isn't one around here.” But that is another story. 

Esoon made me understand that of all the wicked places <note>original: "Sodoms and Gomorrahs"</note> in the world, the town of Egaja was by far the worst. They could hardly believe we had survived traveling through there. Even so, Egaja had treated us well. However, I was less interested in Esoon’s opinion of the country we had already survived than in the information they had about the territory we still had to navigate to reach the Big River. By this time, the "Big River" no longer referred to the Ogowé, but to the Rembwé. 

I was curious about some details regarding the criminal career of Chief Blue-hat of Egaja, but only as a friend. My primary focus was reaching one of the Hatton and Cookson <note>A major British trading company operating in West Africa during the 19th century.</note> sub-factories <term>sub-factories</term> <note>Secondary trading posts or warehouses managed by agents of a larger merchant company.</note> located there. But—strictly between ourselves—I had no more idea which town that factory was in than a kindergarten student would.

# CH. XIII "BLOOD WAR ON THE PATH"

...as a Board School <note>Board Schools: Primary schools established in England and Wales after 1870, providing basic education to the working classes.</note> child does. I did not mention this fact; and a casual observer might have thought that I had spent my youth in that factory <note>Factory: In this historical context, a "factory" refers to a merchant's trading post or warehouse, not a manufacturing plant.</note>, given how I directed my inquiries toward finding the shortest route to it. 

The people of Esoon shook their heads. "Yes, it was close," they said, "but it was impossible to reach Uguma's factory." 

"Why?" I asked. 

"There is a blood war <note>Blood war: A localized feud or conflict between villages or families, often involving retaliatory killings.</note> on the path." 

I said it was no war of mine. But Esoon said that such was the appalling depravity of the next town on the road, that its inhabitants lay in wait during the day with loaded guns and shot anyone coming up the Esoon road on sight. At night, they tied strings with bells across the road and shot upon hearing them ring. No one had been killed since the first party of Esoonians was fired on from a distance, because no one had gone that way since. However, the neighboring town had been heard by people who had been out in the bush at night, firing down the road when the bells were tinkled by wild animals. Clearly, that road was not yet truly healthy.

The Duke—who, as I have said before, was a fine, courageous fellow ready to engage in any undertaking—suggested that I should go up the road alone by myself first, a mile ahead of the party. He thought the next town might not shoot on sight if they noticed I was something "strange." I might then explain things, and the rest of the party would follow. 

"There is nothing like dash and courage, my dear Duke," I said, "even if one displays it through a deputy. This plan does you great credit. But as my knowledge of this charming language of yours is limited, I fear I might create the wrong impression in that town. They might think I had kindly brought them a present of eight edible heathens—meaning you and the rest of my followers, you understand." 

My men saw that this was a real danger, and this was the only way I could see to excuse myself. It is at such a moment as this that the "giant's robe" <note>Giant's robe: An allusion to Shakespeare’s Macbeth ("Now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him, like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief"), suggesting she feels ill-fitted for the heroic role of an explorer.</note> gets between your legs, so to speak, and threatens to trip you up. Going up a forbidden road and exposing yourself as a target to ambushed natives would be "jam and fritters" <note>Jam and fritters: A Victorian colloquialism meaning something easy, pleasant, or a "piece of cake."</note> to someone like Mr. MacTaggart <note>Mr. MacTaggart: Likely a reference to a bold contemporary official or explorer known for his bravado.</note>, for example; but I am not up to that level yet. 

So, I determined to leave that road strictly alone and bypass the next town by a road that leaves Esoon heading West-Northwest. This path joined the Rembwé River by N'dorko.

I was told to follow the riverbank until I reached the sub-factory <note>Sub-factory: A smaller branch of a trading post or warehouse.</note>. Later experience did not make me feel inclined to recommend this plan, but at the time in Esoon, it seemed pleasant enough.

A few of the more highly cultured inhabitants here could speak a little trade English <note>Trade English: An early form of West African Pidgin English used for commerce between Europeans and local tribes.</note>; they had been to the Rembwé and were quite intelligent about the whole situation. They had seen white men before. A village they had formerly occupied closer to the Rembwé had been burned by Europeans because of something that had happened to a Catholic priest who visited it. Naturally, none of them were personally involved in this sad affair, so they could give no details about what had happened to the priest. They also knew "the *Mové*," <note>Mové: Likely a reference to agents of the British trading firm Hatton & Cookson, or a specific vessel known in the region.</note> which served as a great bond between us. 

"Was I a wife of those *Mové* white men," they inquired—"or those other white men?" 

I politely said those *Mové* men were my tribe, and they should have known it by looking at me. They discussed my points of resemblance to "the *Mové* white men," and I am ashamed to say I could not help smiling, as I clearly recognized my friends from the very lively description of their appearances and habits given by a spirited Esoonian woman who had certainly met them. 

I became so content and happy under these soothing influences that I actually took off my boots—a habit I had quite lost—and had them dried. I wanted to have them rubbed with palm oil, but I found, to my surprise, that there was no palm oil to be had; the tree was either absent or scarce in this region. So, I had to be content with having them rubbed with a piece of animal fat instead. 

While among the women of Esoon—a bold set of girls—I chaperoned my men with the vigilance of a dragon. Like the Mikado of Japan <note>The Mikado: A reference to the 1885 comic opera by Gilbert and Sullivan; Kingsley paraphrases a song from the character Ko-Ko.</note>, I decreed "that whosoever leered or winked, unless connubially linked, should forthwith be beheaded"—or rather, have their pay "chopped" <note>Chopped: A West African Pidgin term for eaten or consumed; here, it means their wages would be docked or withheld.</note>. Since they were beginning to look forward to their wages, they were careful, and we made it through Esoon without any of my men ending up in jail. This was no small feat, considering that every man had a "past," to put it mildly. Fika remained behind here, and the others promised to bring back his pay bundle on their return journey home. I think Fika heard...

# XIII MANGROVES AHEAD

There were rumors in Esoon of some gentlemen he had met before and was not keen to meet again, who were currently at N’dorko. Therefore, I parted with him and left Esoon in peace, after providing appropriate gifts <term>Dashes: A common West African term for tips, bribes, or customary trade gifts given to facilitate travel or business.</term>.

Esoon is not situated like the other towns, which are usually closely surrounded by a swamp and the forest; instead, it is built on the side of a fairly well-cleared ravine among its plantain groves. When you are on the southern side of the ravine, you can see Esoon looking as if it were hanging on the hillside before you. You then pass through a plantation, down into the little river, and up into the town—which consists of one long, broad, and clean-kept street. Leaving Esoon, you continue up the hill through another plantation to the summit. Immediately after leaving the town, we headed westward; when we reached the top of the next hill, we were greeted by a view that showed we were dealing with a different type of country. The hills to the west are lower, and the valleys between them are broader and less heavily forested—or rather, I should say they are forested with smaller types of timber.

Throughout the early part of the day, our paths took us up and down hills and through swamps and small rivers, all flowing toward the Rembwé. About the middle of the afternoon, we reached the top of a high hill after a terrible struggle through a massive windfall <term>Timber fall: A large area where many trees have been blown down or felled, creating a difficult obstacle for travelers.</term> of the first magnitude. Four of us had fallen into it—myself included, of course. There, I saw a sight that made my heart stand still. Stretching away to the west and north, winding in and out around the bases of the now isolated, mound-like hills, was that unmistakable black-green forest swamp of mangroves. This was undoubtedly the edge of the Rembwé River, which evidently reaches much further inland than the mangrove belt on the Ogowe River. This is logical and to be expected, though it surprised me at the time; for the great arm of the sea called the Gaboon is actually a fjord, just like the Bonny and Opobo rivers, with several rivers flowing into its head. This fjord brings seawater much further inland. In addition to this, the two rivers that flow into this Gaboon—the Como (Nkâmâ) and the Rembwé—along with several smaller rivers, both bring down a smaller volume of fresh water. Furthermore, they do not flow with anything like the violent, tide-resisting speed of the Ogowe. As my brother would say, "It’s perfectly simple if you think—"

...about it;” but thinking is not my strong point. Anyhow, I was glad to see the mangrove belt. I was all the happier because I did not then know how far inland it was from the sea, and also because I was foolish enough to think that a long line I could see, running east and west to the north of where I stood, was the Rembwé River. As we soon found out, it was not. 

Cheered by this pleasing prospect, we marched on, forgetful of our scratches, down the side of the hill and its lower slopes until we reached the edge of the swamp. We skirted this for about a mile, heading northeast. Then we ventured into the swamp to reach what we had assumed was the Rembwé River. "Nature was at its ghastliest," as *Chambers’s Magazine* <note>original: *Chambers’s Magazine*, likely referring to *Chambers's Edinburgh Journal*, a popular 19th-century periodical.</note> once put it—offending the local sensibilities with that description of the Oil Rivers <term>Oil Rivers: The coastal region of the Niger Delta, named for the palm oil produced there.</term> scenery. 

We found ourselves at the edge of that open line we had seen from the mountain. We weren't standing—because you don’t even attempt to stand on mangrove roots unless you are a born fool, and even then, you won't stand for long. Instead, we were clinging like so many monkeys to the network of aerial roots <term>Aerial roots: Roots that grow above the ground or water, common in mangrove trees to help them breathe in waterlogged soil.</term> surrounding us, staring blankly at a lake of ink-black slime. It was half a mile wide and several miles long. We could not see where it ended to the east or west, for it lay like a decaying serpent twisted between the mangroves. 

It never entered our heads to try to cross it. When a swamp is too deep for mangroves to grow in it, "No bottom lives for those damned things," <note>original: "No bottom lib for them dam ting"</note> as a Kruboy <term>Kruboy: A member of the Kru people of West Africa, frequently employed as sailors or laborers on European expeditions.</term> once said to me regarding a similar feature of the landscape. 

We simply looked around to see which direction we should take. Then I observed that the roots, aerial and otherwise, were coated in mud and had no leaves on them for at least a foot above our heads. Next, I noticed that the surface of the mud before us was quivering, and here and there it showed swellings that rose in one place and fell in another. 

An experienced "coaster" <term>Coaster: A European who had spent significant time living or working along the West African coast.</term> like me didn't need to look at that sort of thing twice to know what it meant. Feeling it was a situation more suited to Mr. Stanley <note>Henry Morton Stanley (1841–1904), the famous explorer known for his expeditions in Central Africa.</note> than myself, I attempted to imitate his leadership methods and addressed my men. 

"Boys," I said, "this miserable hole is tidal, and the tide is coming in. Since it took us two hours to reach this 'blessed' swamp, it’s time we started..."

I deeply regretted that my ancestors had prematurely given up their grasping tails for four limbs—particularly when two of those limbs are stuck in boots and are not enough to enable one to navigate a mangrove swamp network of slimy roots rising out of the water, with swinging lines of aerial roots coming down to the water *in the mangrove style*, <note>original: *à la mangrove*</note> with anything approaching safety. About four o’clock, we reached some more plantations. Passing through these, we found a path running northeast and followed it. I must say the forest scenery here was superbly beautiful. Because of the steepness, the sharp drops, and the changing curves of the ground, the sun was able to reach the soil along this mountainside cliff next to the mangrove swamp. Meanwhile, the soft, steamy air rising from the swamp enveloped everything; although the smell was unpleasantly strong to us, it was clearly very beneficial for the plants. There were lovely wine palms and raffia palms that looked as if they had been grown in a greenhouse; their feathery foliage was so delightfully green and lush. These were mixed with giant redwoods and beautiful, dark, glossy green lianas <term>climbing, woody vines found in tropical forests</term>, blooming with wreaths and garlands of white and mauve flowers, which gave the scene a magnificent wealth of beauty and color. Even the monotony of the nearby mangrove belt added a certain charm to it, like a frame around a painting.

As we continued, the ridge turned north, and the line of mangroves narrowed between the hills. Our path now ran east, deeper into the forest, and the cool shade was delightful after the heat we had experienced earlier in the day. We crossed a lovely little stream that cascaded down the hillside; then our path dipped into a beautiful valley. Through the trees, we caught glimpses of an amphitheater of blue, mist-veiled mountains forming a crescent in front of us and on all sides—except to the west, where the mangrove swamp lay. I shall never forget the extreme beauty of that valley: the foliage of the trees surrounding us, the delicate wreaths and garlands of climbing plants, and the graceful, delicate fronds of the palm trees interlacing with one another. Through them all, one could see a background of soft, pale, purple-blue mountains and forest. As a practiced eye could tell, they were not actually far away, but the mist made them appear so. The mist has a way of suggesting immense space without losing the beauty of the details. Those misty African forests have the same marvelous, distinctive quality that Turner <note>Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775–1851), a famous English Romantic painter known for his landscapes and his mastery of light and atmospheric effects like mist and fog.</note> captures in his...

As for me, while I was at the start of the submerged bridge, debating whether it was better to walk on a slippery log bridge one could see or one that was hidden, I was knocked off by that relentless fate that insists I gain personal experience with fluvial and paludial <term>pertaining to rivers and marshes</term> ground deposits. Consequently, I took a dive headfirst, and can now inform the world that there are between fifteen and twenty feet of water on either side of that log. I thoroughly went in on one side and came up on the other. I suspect the log is dum <term>a type of palm tree (Hyphaene thebaica)</term> or ebony, and it is about fifty feet long; in any case, it is a type of wood that does not float. N'dorko was quite close, and the plantations we saw before us were its outermost fields. However, the locals spoke of a swamp—a "bad swamp." In our overconfidence, we thought they meant the one we had just forded, and leaving them to rest, we continued on our way. Half a mile further on, we were wiser and sadder, for then we stood on the edge of one of the largest swamps I have ever seen south of the Rivers <note>The "Rivers" refers to the Oil Rivers district of the Niger Delta region in West Africa.</note>. There were islands, great banks of screw pine, and groves of wine palm <term>Raphia vinifera, a palm tree common in West African swamps</term> with their lovely fronds reflected in the still, mirror-like water. The reflection was as vivid as the reality, and most remarkable of all was a plant,<sup>1</sup> new and strange to me, whose pale-green stem rose out of the water and then spread into a flattened surface, thin and in a peculiarly graceful curve. This flattened surface had leaves growing from it that were the size, shape, and color of lily of the valley leaves. Until I saw this thing, I had considered the wine palm to be the queen of grace in the plant kingdom, but this new beauty quite surpassed her.

Our path went straight into this swamp over the black rocks forming its rim, in an authoritative, no-alternative, "Come-along-this-way" style. Singlet, who was leading and carrying a heavy load of bottled fish and a gorilla specimen, went at it bravely. He disappeared before our very eyes as we followed close behind, sinking then and there down through the water. He came up, thank goodness, but his load is down there now—more’s the pity. Then I said we must wait for the rubber carriers who were coming this way to show us the path; and so we sat down on the bank—a tired, miserable, and bedraggled-looking row—until they arrived. When they came up, they did not plunge in immediately; instead, they leisurely began a most nerve-wracking set of preparations, taking off their clothes and forming them into bundles which, to my horror, they placed on top of their heads. # XIII A COLLAR OF LEECHES

...were followed by the women and by our party, and soon we were all in up to our chins.

We spent two hours and fifteen minutes crossing that swamp. It took me an hour and forty-five minutes; I managed quite well by following the rubber-carriers <note>Men employed to carry harvested wild rubber, a major export from West Africa at the time.</note> closely, only going completely underwater twice. Other members of my group were less fortunate. One man, finding himself getting out of his depth, grabbed a palm frond and pulled himself into even deeper water; he had to perch among the palms until a special rescue party of the tallest men went and "plucked" him like a flower. Another man got himself very tangled and scratched because he tried to take a shortcut through some screw pines. He didn't know the screw pine's little habits,¹ and he also required a special relief expedition. 

When we finally emerged, every one of us was horribly infested with leeches. We had a ring of them around our necks like **astrakhan collars** <note>A type of curly fur made from the pelts of Karakul lambs.</note>, and our hands were covered with them. The depth of the swamp was very consistent; at the ford, we went in up to our necks and climbed onto the rocks on this side out of water that was just as deep.

Knowing that you do not like me to go into details on such matters, I will limit my comments regarding the leeches to the fact that it was very lucky we had some **trade salt** <term>salt used as a form of currency or for barter</term> with us. It was a most comical sight to see us salting each other; but in spite of the salt’s effective action, I felt quite faint from the loss of blood. We all looked like a ghastly sight as we made our way toward **N'dorko**. Of course, the bleeding did not stop immediately, and it attracted flies and—but I am starting to go into details, so I will stop.

We had to pass across the first bit of open country I had seen for a long time—a genuine patch of grass on the top of a low ridge, which is bordered by swamp on all sides except the eastern one, where we were heading. Shortly after passing through another farm, we saw brown huts and...

# FROM ESOON TO AGONJO

Within a few minutes, we were standing in the middle of a ramshackle village. At the end of the village, through a high stockade with a gateway smeared with thick clots of blood, we saw our long-desired Rembwé River. I headed straight for it, paying little attention to the commotion our arrival caused. I passed through the gateway to the riverbank and rang the alarm bell violently. I stood on the steep, black, muddy bank, surrounded by a noisy crowd. It is a large river, but it does not compare to the Ogowé in either width or beauty. What beauty it possesses is similar to the Niger Delta: black, mud-filled water fringed everywhere by mangrove swamps. 

I soon returned to the village and asked for Ugumu's factory <term>a merchant's trading station or warehouse</term>. "This is it," said an exceptionally dirty but handsome and polite man. He spoke perfect English, though he was a pure-blooded African. "This is it, sir," he said, pointing to one of the huts on the right side, which was just as squalid as all the others. "Where is the agent?" I asked. "I am the agent," he replied. You could have knocked me over with a feather. 

"Where is John Holt's factory?" <note>John Holt & Co. was a major British trading company operating in West Africa.</note> I asked. "You have already passed it; it is up on the hill," he said. This showed that Mr. Holt’s local factory was no larger than Ugumu’s. At this point, a tall, thin, very dark man appeared. He had an irregularly shaped face the size of a tea tray and looked like a character from a theatrical pantomime of the ***Arabian Nights***. He dashed through the crowd, shouting, "I'm for Holty! I'm for Holty!" 

"This is my business; you go away," said the first agent. Fearing my two agents would fight and hurt each other—making them both useless to me—I firmly asked, "Do you have any rum?" 

The first agent looked disappointed, while "Holty's" agent looked triumphant. "Rum, for sure!" he said. I gave him a five-franc piece <note>A silver coin used as currency in French colonies and widely accepted in West Africa at the time.</note>, which he looked at with great pleasure. He put it in his mouth and ran like a lamplighter <note>An idiomatic expression meaning very fast.</note> toward his store on the hill. 

"Do you have any tobacco?" I asked the first agent. He brightened up. "Plenty of tobacco, plenty of cloth," he said. I then told them to go buy chop <term>West African pidgin for food or a meal</term> and make themselves comfortable. They were highly...

“Besides,” I said, “Mr. Glass (I knew the head Rembwé agent for Hatton and Cookson was a Mr. Glass), you only have cloth and tobacco. I have promised to pay the Fans in whatever they choose, and I know for certain they want gunpowder.” 

“I am not Mr. Glass,” said my friend. “He is up at Agonjo; I only handle small trades for him here.” 

Success! But where was Agonjo? To make a long story short, I found that Agonjo was an hour’s paddle up the Rembwé and was the place where we were actually supposed to have arrived. There was some trouble again about sending a message because of a local conflict <term>war palaver: a negotiation or dispute involving local tribal warfare</term>; but I finally managed to deliver a pencil note, along with my letter of introduction from Mr. Cockshut, to Sanga Glass.

No white person of any kind had crossed over from the Ogowé River for years, and none had ever arrived at N’dorko. Just as one gentleman decided which goods he would accept as payment, and we began to look into another gentleman's preferences, the first man’s mind would change completely. Mr. Glass was clearly an expert at this business, but it was past 11:00 p.m. before we finished writing out the orders. Kiva came along to ensure that the bundles for his fellow Fans were prepared satisfactorily.

Because the canoes were small, we formed quite a procession. Mr. Glass and I shared one paddled by two small boys. How we ever made it up the Rembwé that night, I do not know; although neither of us was heavy, the canoe was meant for only one person, and the water lapped over the edge in an alarming way. If any of us had sneezed—or if it had been daylight, when two or three mangrove flies would have joined the party—we certainly would have sunk. However, everything went well. Upon arriving at Agonjo, Mr. Glass very kindly opened his store. By the light of lamps and lanterns, we selected goods from his varied and ample supply and handed them over to the Ajumba and Kiva. Everyone was satisfied except for three of the Ajumba.

The three—Gray Shirt, Silence, and Pagan—quietly explained to me that they found the prices on the Rembwé so little better than the prices at Lambarene <note>Lembarene: A major trading post on the Ogooué River where Kingsley began her trek</note> that they would rather receive their pay from Mr. Cockshut than risk carrying it back through Fan territory. # CHAPTER XIV

## BUSH TRADE AND FAN CUSTOMS

In which the traveler, having encountered the black traders, discusses these men and their way of life. She describes the difficulties and dangers involved in the barter they carry on with the forest dwellers, and some of the reasons why this trade is so beloved and pursued by both the black trader and the local people. I spent a few lazy, pleasant days at Agonjo. Mr. Glass did everything he could to make me comfortable, even though he was suffering from a nasty bout of fever just then. His efforts were capably supported by his wife, an exceptionally attractive Gaboon woman with charming manners and an excellent talent for cooking. The third member of the staff was the store-keeper, a clever fellow. I suspect he was a Loango based on his sharp features and slender build, though I do not know his tribe for certain. What I do know is that he can sing *“Partant pour la Syrie”* <note>original: "Partant pour la Syrie"—a popular French patriotic song about a crusader, which served as an unofficial anthem during the Second French Empire</note> with intense power and a piercing sadness in the middle of the night. However, I do not record this as a discovery of my own; it was common knowledge to every living soul within a half-mile radius of the factory <term>factory: a merchant's trading post or warehouse in a foreign country</term>.

We encountered mosquitoes here again. Someone ought to study the local distribution of mosquitoes in the French Congo <note>original: Congo Français</note> instead of just saying harsh things about them. I leave that work for a nobler soul than mine, but to assist them, I note the fact that they are simply dreadful throughout all of the Kama and Ouroungou regions. Up at Lembarene, which is above the Kama country, they are even worse, and they remain so until you reach Osamokita; there they finally cease.

# CH. XIV FLAPPISTS AND CRUSHERS

...from troubling us—although there is still a stretch of flat country and a supply of stagnant water in the form of small lakes. I say this regretfully, but science demands the truth. I once had a pleasant little theory that worked well in the Niger Delta: that you never had mosquitoes if you had a water supply with a four-knot current, unless you bred those mosquitoes yourself in tanks or barrels. According to the theory, the larvae were washed away by the current. But although the Ogowé River has a current twice that strength at Osamokita and there are no mosquitoes there, there are still those lakes in the forest behind it. So, anyone who can patch that theory up and make it work again is welcome to it. 

Regarding mosquito distribution again, there is a nearly solid fog of them from Kangwe to Arevooma, and from Arevooma on to Lake Ncovi. At Lake Ncovi, they—well, there is no use in my writing down my opinion of the mosquitoes at Lake Ncovi because no one would print it. When we left Ncovi and ventured deep into the forest, we missed them and were no longer troubled by them until we reached Agonjo, where there is no four-knot current. 

But I will not return to that theory; I will merely mention a peculiarity I have observed in mosquitoes since I have been in such close contact with them in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>. It is that they evidently feed on oil; many hundreds that I have crushed have left quite a pool of oil—I presume it is palm oil, but it may be animal fat. I should remark before leaving this subject that there are two schools of thought in this district that argue extensively over the merits of their different methods for destroying mosquitoes: the "Flappists" and the "Crushers." I am a Crusher, believing it is better to allow the vermin to get a grip, with his entire mind focused on blood, and then to descend on him quietly but firmly with a finger. As for those heretics, the Flappists, they always hurt themselves and frequently fail to catch their prey with their more flamboyant methods.

During my first night in Agonjo, I really thought I was getting another chance to secure a valuable specimen of *spectra domestica*—or the common domestic ghost <note>original: "spectra domestica"—a humorous pseudo-scientific Latin name the author uses for a ghost</note>. I believed it to be the ghost of a carpenter because it made a continuous sawing noise in the bamboo wall beside my bed, but once again I was disappointed: it was only the usual rat. This enterprising rodent was indeed a fellow collector; it had stolen the bladder from...

Staying at one of these African trading posts <term>factory: a merchant's trading station or warehouse</term> is extremely interesting because you are right at the foundation of the trade. On the Coast, for the most part, white traders deal with African middlemen. These middlemen have obtained their goods from the local bush people who collect and prepare them. Here, in the African trading post, you see the first stage of the export trade: the bartering of collected goods between the collector and the middleman. I will not go into every detail regarding it. What I saw merely confirmed the opinion I formed from my other experiences. This opinion was further strengthened by what I had seen during the previous months while living among the bush people who collect these goods. My view is that the native person is not cheated—no, not even by a fellow African trader. I will pause here just to sing a song of praise <note>original: "pæan"</note> to a very unpopular group: the African middleman as he exists on the South West Coast. 

It is impossible to understand how dismal the lives of these men are in these remote posts unless you have lived in one yourself. It is no use saying, "they know no better and so do not feel it." They *do* know several things that are better. They are very social men who fully appreciate the joys of a coastal town. Their aim, object, and end in life is, in almost every case, to amass a fortune that will allow them to live in a town, host a dance twice a week, hold card parties most nights, and dress themselves so that the local men might envy them and the women might love them. If you were of a trusting nature and listened to their accounts of the dreadful state of trade and the awful, unprecedented losses they have suffered—from overturned canoes to raids and robberies by "those awful bush savages"—you would view the African trader with admiring awe. You would see him as the man who has finally solved the great commercial problem of how to run a shop and live off the losses. Not only live, but build for himself—

I am not of a trusting nature, and I take those "losses" with a heavy discount; I know most of the remaining funds have come out of my friend the white trader's pockets. Still, I can never feel the righteous indignation that I ought to feel when I see the black trader "down in a seaport town with his Nancy," <note>original: "Nancy" — a reference to a sweetheart, popularized in the comic operas and poems of W. S. Gilbert.</note> and so on, as Sir W. S. Gilbert classically says, because I remember those bush factories <term>factory: a remote trading post and warehouse</term>.

Mr. Glass, however, was not a trader who made a fortune by losing the fortunes of other people, for he had been in the firm's employ for many years. He had certainly risen to the high post and position of being in charge of the Rembwé district, but he was not living a wild, extravagant life <note>original: "giddy-flying"</note> at Gaboon. His accounts of his experiences were fascinating. He had spent many years, long ago, away up the still little-known Nguni River in a factory in contact with the lively Bakele people; then in a factory among the Fans and Igalwa on the Ogowé; and now among the Fans and Skekiani on the Rembwé. His stories told vividly of the joys of first starting a factory in a wild district. 

The way your customers, for the first month or so, enjoy themselves by trying to frighten you—the trader—out of your wits and your goods, and into giving them inflated prices for things you are trading for, and for things of no earthly use to you or anyone else! During this period, the trader's existence is marked by every kind of unpleasantness except boredom. He is spared from that by the presence of a mob of noisy, dangerous, thieving savages all over his property all day long. They invade his cook-house to put some disgusting thing into his food as a trade charm; they help themselves to any movable property they see; and they make themselves at home to the extent of sitting on his dining table. At night, those customers proceed to sleep all over the premises so as to be ready to start shopping in the morning. The trader is doomed if he gives in to this and tolerates the invasion, for there is no chance of that house ever being his own again. In addition to the local flies and other pests on the tablecloth, he will always have several large black gentlemen sharing his meals. If he raises prices just to get through some extra conflict, he is a lost man, for the Africans can under-

understand prices going up, but never prices coming down; and since time is no object to them, they will stop trading altogether to wait for better rates. When this happens, the district's economy is ruined, and the trader is ruined along with it, because he cannot increase the price he receives for the goods he has already purchased.

What that trader must do is become a "Devil man" <term>Devil man: a term used to describe a person of formidable will, perceived by the locals as possessing a supernatural or overwhelming authority</term>. They always kindly said they recognized me as one, which is a great compliment. He must show no weakness, possessing a character that I would describe as a combination of the best traits of Cardinal Richelieu, Brutus, Julius Caesar, Prince Metternich, and Mezzofanti <note>original: "Mettzofante" — Giuseppe Mezzofanti (1774–1849) was a famous Italian cardinal and hyperpolyglot renowned for his ability to speak dozens of languages.</note>, the latter being necessary to handle the various native languages involved in the business. He must expel those troublesome customers not only from his house but from his yard, and strictly adhere to the principle of "No admittance except on business." This causes a great deal of unpleasantness, and the trader’s nights are then brightened by lively war-dances held just outside his stockade. The accompanying songs announce that the customers intend to climb over the stockade, raid the store, and cut the trader "into bits like a fish." Sometimes they actually do come—and then it is the end—but usually they do not. Gradually they settle down and develop a great respect for the trader as a "Devil man," and they conduct business on sound terms during the day. However, they will continue to sneak over the stockade at night in ones and twos to steal until the end of time.

At Agonjo, Mr. Glass, his wife, and the person who sang "Departing for Syria" <note>original: "Partant pour la Syrie" — a French patriotic song popular during the Second Empire</note> used to take turns keeping watch. This was necessary because it was the habit of these local "children of nature" <note>Kingsley uses this phrase ironically to describe the cleverness and pragmatism of the local people.</note> to sell a log or two of ebony during the day, and then come back to steal it at night. They would then take it down to the next factory <term>factory: a merchant’s trading post and warehouse</term> and sell it there—similarly stealing it back, bringing it back to the first place, and reselling it, and so on, *from the beginning* <note>original: "da capo" — a musical term meaning to repeat from the start</note>. Consequently, it turns out that a man might live for quite a long time on just a few logs <term>billets: small logs or thick pieces of wood, in this case, ebony</term> without any real exertion or hard work. To them, stealing is a beloved pastime—a kind of game in which you only lose if you are caught.

Moonlight nights are fairly restful for the bush trader, but when the night is pitch black or pouring with rain, he has to be very active and alert. He must be particularly vigilant on storm nights <term>tornado: in West Africa, this refers to violent squalls or thunderstorms</term>—a most uncomfortable sort of weather in which to attend to business, I assure you.

<header>XIV TRADERS: ENGLISH AND FOREIGN</header>

The factory at Agonjo was typical. The house is a fine specimen of the Igalwa style of architecture, mounted on poles above the ground. The space under the house is used as a store for barrels of rubber and logs of ebony. This arrangement allows the trader to hover over these precious possessions, day and night, like a sitting hen over her eggs.

Near the house are the sleeping quarters for the shore laborers and the kitchen. In front, in a position clearly visible from the veranda and set well back from the defensive wall, are large piles of red barwood logs. The entire clean, sandy yard containing these items and various others is surrounded by a sturdy stockade. Its main side faces the riverfront; at high tide, the water laps at its base, and at low tide, it exposes a shore of black mud in front of it. Although I cite this factory as a typical example of a Black trader's establishment, it is a specimen of the highest class. Because it is associated with the firm of Messrs. Hatton and Cookson, it is well-maintained and fully stocked. Firms differ greatly in this regard. Messrs. Hatton and Cookson, like Messrs. Miller Brothers in the Bights <note>The Bights of Benin and Biafra, coastal regions of West Africa</note>, take every possible care of the people who serve them, down to the Kruboys <term>Kruboys: Krumen from Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, traditionally employed as sailors and laborers along the West African coast</term> working on their shores, providing ample and high-quality rations and good housing. 

But this is not the case with all firms on the Coast. I have seen factories belonging to Swedish houses beside which this factory at Agonjo is a palace, even though those are European factories. The unfortunate white men in them are expected by these firms to live on local food <term>chop: a West African Pidgin English term for food or to eat</term>—an expectation the agents never actually meet, for they usually die. African laborers, however, do not suffer much at the hands of such firms. The Swedish agents are a quiet, gentlemanly set of men, in the best sense of that much-misused term. They do not employ a large staff of African helpers on their shores like the English houses do, so the two or three Kruboys on a poorly-provisioned beach can fend for themselves fairly well. There is always a nearby village, and in that village there are always chickens; there are crabs on the shore and fish in the river. For the rest of his diet, the Kruboy flirts with the local women.

This is a hundred times more dangerous and a thousand times more uncomfortable, and it is a thoroughly unhealthy occupation. The journeys these bush traders make are often remarkable, and they deserve great credit for the courage and enterprise they display. 

Certainly, they run less risk of death from fever than a white man would. On the other hand, their color gives them no protection, and their chance of being murdered is significantly higher. Furthermore, the white colonial authorities cannot avenge their deaths in the way they would the death of a white man. These murders usually take place far away in some forest region, in a district no white man has ever penetrated. When the account of it reaches the main trading station or the coastal town where the man lived—for many of them are not attached to any specific factory but trade on their own account—it usually comes in the form of a statement that "So-and-so died of a disease." 

The relatives of the deceased never believe this, but the Government naturally feels disinclined to launch a highly expensive expedition—which is almost certain to cost the life of any white man who accompanies it—on a month-long march through trackless swamp and bush. They would be doing this on the slim chance of discovering at the end of their quest that the trader really did die of a disease, or finding that the village where he died is utterly deserted, the natives having gone for a picnic in the surrounding forest upon hearing of the expedition's approach.

You will naturally ask how it is that so many of these men survive "to lead a life of sin," as a missionary once described their coastal town life to me. This question struck me as requiring an explanation. The result of my investigations, and the answers I have received from the men themselves, show that there is a reason why the natives do not succumb every time to the temptation to kill the trader and take his goods. This reason is twofold: first, all trade in West Africa follows definite routes, even in the wildest parts; and so a village...

315

XIV A FEMALE BODYGUARD [centered]

A village far away in the forest, but located on a trade route, knows that as a general rule, a trader will appear twice a year to purchase its rubber and ivory. If he does not appear around the expected time, that village becomes uneasy. The women are impatient for their new clothes, and the men are nearly frantic for want of tobacco. When the situation reaches a crisis, they make inquiries about the trader from one village to the next down the road. If it is discovered that a specific village has killed the trader and stolen all his goods, a major <term>palaver</term> <note>A long discussion or negotiation, often used here to describe a serious legal or social dispute between tribes or villages.</note> naturally ensues. Things are made extremely difficult—even by the standards of equatorial Africa—for that village by the husbands without tobacco and the wives without clothes. Herein lies the trader’s chief safety: the village is not the least bit afraid or hesitant to kill him, but they are afraid of their neighboring villages and do not wish to be killed by them.

However, the trader is not yet entirely safe. There is still a gap in his defenses, and this can only be closed in one way: by having wives. You see, although a village cannot safely kill him and seize all his goods, they can still safely allow him to die of a "disease" and take a portion of them, passing on enough merchandise to the other villages to keep them quiet. Now, the most common "disease" in the African bush originates in the cooking pot. To ensure that what goes into the cooking pot is safe and wholesome—which is the crucial point, as the earthen pots themselves do not produce poison—you must have someone devoted to your health to manage the cooking. And who can do this better than a wife?

Consequently, a trader has a wife in every village along his entire route. I personally know one gentleman whose wives are spread across 300 miles of country, in addition to a main household in a coastal town. This system of carefully managed alliances gives the Black trader a security that nothing else can. Naturally, he marries into influential families in each village, and all of his wife’s maternal relatives regard him as one of their own and look after him and his interests. A so-called "civilized" man might ironically doubt that security could be found in women—especially so many women—but the security is there, and only there, and it rests on a solid foundation. Remember, the position of a traveling trader’s wife in a village is one that grants the lady significant prestige; therefore, a discreet husband...

As I am assured by Black ladies, the more domestic husband is prone to such behavior.

I fear you may now be falling into the opposite error. After wondering how any Black trader survives, you might now wonder why any Black trader ever gets killed, given all these safeguards and wives. But there is yet another danger that no number of wives or local rivalries can protect him against. This danger arises from the nomadic habits of the bush tribes, notably the Fan. When a village has made up its mind to move to a different district—either because they have made the current area too hostile through quarrels with neighboring villages, because they have exhausted the local "trade stuff" (meaning the rubber and ivory within reach of their current location), or because another village has raided them and stolen all the supplies they were saving to sell to the Black trader—the village resolves to enjoy one last treat in their old home. They decide to pull off a commercial stroke <note>original: "coup"</note> in one fell swoop. Thus, when the Black trader arrives with his boxes of goods, the village kills him, eats some for supper, smokes the rest of the meat, takes his goods, and departs to found new homes in another district.

The bush trade I have sketched above is the trade conducted with the Fans. In the districts on the southern banks of the Ogowé River, the main features of the trade and the trader's life are the same, but the details are more intricate. This is because the Igalwa trader from Lambaréné, Fernan Vaz, or Njolé deals with another set of trading tribes rather than dealing first-hand with the original collectors. The Fan villages on the trade routes may, however, be regarded as trade depots, for the trade goods of the more remote villages filter through to them. Therefore, the difference is really merely technical, and in all villages alike, the same sort of thing occurs.

The Igalwa or M'pongwe trader arrives with the goods he has received from the white trader. There is great rejoicing and much noise as his chests, bundles, and <term>demijohns</term> <note>Large, narrow-necked bottles often encased in wickerwork, used for spirits or oils.</note> are brought up from the canoe. ->XIV PRICES AND PROFITS<-

After a great deal of talk, the goods are opened. The chiefs of the village take their pick and divide these items among the principal men of the village. They pay for them in part with their stored supply of collected rubber or ivory and take the rest on credit, promising to collect enough rubber to pay the balance during the trader’s next visit. Consequently, the trader has many outstanding debts in each village which are liable to become bad debts, and this is where his primary loss occurs. Each chief takes a certain agreed-upon value in goods as a commission for himself—<term>nyeno</term>—giving the trader, in exchange for this, a recognized bond to help him collect the debts owed by his village. He uses this *nyeno* to buy trade goods from villages that are not located on the main trade route. Among the Fan people, the men who have obtained the goods wait to trade them for rubber with the general public and the bachelors of the village, in a way I will explain shortly. In tribes such as the Ajumbas, Adooma, and others, the men who have the goods travel as traders among various remote tribes, similarly paying their *nyeno*. Thus, by the time the goods reach the men who actually produce the materials, only a small portion of the original goods is left, though their price has necessarily risen.

Still, it is quite absurd for a casual white traveler—who may have only visited the terminus of a trade route—to complain about the low value the collector gets for his materials compared to the price they fetch in Europe. The collector is often erroneously described as the "producer," which gives him a false halo of being one who "earns by the sweat of his brow." In reality, before those materials even reach the factory <note>In this context, a "factory" refers to a merchant's trading station or warehouse on the coast.</note> of the coastal settlement, they must support a whole series of middlemen traders. At first, it appears negative that this should be the case, but this is the reality along the west coast of the continent, except in the districts controlled by the Royal Niger Company. With courage and enterprise, they have pushed far inland and established contact with the great interior trade routes. This performance has sparked keen animosity in the hearts of the coastal trader tribes who have been supplanted—an animosity which, like most resentment in Africa, is not concerned with the truth. The tribes that have seen the trade of the Bight of Biafra <note>A bay off the coast of West Africa, located within the Gulf of Guinea.</note> passing through their hands have been accustomed to making a seventy-five percent profit on it, according to the German Government (who are also pushing inland), and they resent being deprived of this. Consequently, peace does not exist <note>original: "so palaver no live"</note>.

We will now examine the reason why a man from the interior <term>bush man</term> is motivated to collect goods to sell among the Fan people: the high cost of the women in the tribe. A Fan living in the interior is forced to marry within his own tribe because, across much of the territory they occupy, there is no other tribe nearby to marry into. Even a Fan living in villages that have contact with other tribes has little chance of finding a "cheaper" lady. This is because in the French Congo <term>Congo Français</term> and the adjacent country to the north (Batanga), there is a rigid social hierarchy <term>aristocracy</term> that can be summarized as follows: all the other tribes look down on the Fans, and the Fans look down on all the other tribes. This social hierarchy has sub-divisions: the M'pongwe of Gaboon are the elite circle; next come the Benga of Corisco; then the Bapoka; and finally the Banaka. This system of hierarchy is maintained by the women. For instance, a M'pongwe lady would never dream of marrying into one of the lower tribes; she is restricted to her own tribe, and even then faces many internal restrictions. A Benga lady would marry a M'pongwe or a Benga, but not a Banaka or a Bapoka, and so on with the others. However, none of them would marry a Fan. As for the men, they would, of course, marry any woman from any tribe if she had a pretty face or good trade connections—if they were permitted to do so. That is simply how men are. To the southeast, the Fans are in contact with the Achille, Bakele, and Dakele—which are practically one and the same tribe and a tribe...

She knows exactly how much debris you can mix into a ball of rubber without the white trader or the African factory trader instantly detecting it.

In certain more dangerous districts, the traveling bush trader must accept rubber without inspecting it, as doing so would offend the sensitive feelings of his Fan friends. However, in these areas, he carefully keeps the price low to compensate for this risk. When a young Fan man has married his wife legally through the "cash system," he takes her to meet his relatives and shows her off, and they give small gifts to help the couple establish their household. 

But the young man cannot settle down yet, for his wife will not allow him to. She has no intention of working herself to death by doing all the housework alone; consequently, he continues collecting—and she continues preparing—trade goods. Eventually, he becomes wealthy enough to buy other wives—some of them young children, while others are widows who are no longer necessarily old. 

It is not until he is well into middle age that he acquires enough wives, usually six or seven. It takes a long time to collect enough rubber to purchase a wife, and he does not gain a foothold in the ivory trade until he has achieved a certain status in the village and established his own plantations. If elephants are found raiding these crops, he is entitled to a percentage of the ivory taken from that herd. Occasionally, he may come across a dead elephant, but that is merely a stroke of good luck; in his early days, he must depend on rubber and ebony. 

He exchanges these goods with the wealthy men of his village for a very peculiar and interesting form of currency—<term>bikěi</term>—small iron pieces shaped like axe-heads. These are tied into bundles called <term>ntet</term>, with ten pieces to a bundle, because the price of a wife must be paid in <term>bikěi</term>. One cannot pay with rubber, ivory, or general goods. These <term>bikěi</term> circulate as common currency among the Fan for other trade items as well, but I do not believe they trade <term>bikěi</term> outside of the tribe. It is likely that no one else would accept this form of currency. Thousands of these <term>bikěi</term>, bundled into <term>ntets</term>, go toward the price of a wife. You will not find *bikĕi* <term>small iron ornaments used as currency</term> near Libreville among the Fans who live in a semi-civilized state—or, more accurately, in a state where their traditional culture is disintegrating. You must go into the "bush" <term>the remote interior wilderness</term> to find them.

I thought I noticed a certain similarity between *bikĕi* and the early Greek coins I saw at Cambridge, which were shaped like the front halves of cattle. I have little doubt that before the introduction of the rubber, ebony, and ivory trades—which are relatively recent in these districts—the items used for barter among the Fans were iron implements. Since the Fans are skilled blacksmiths, it is consistent with well-known examples of other cultures regarding stone tools that these items, which were important in ancient times, should survive and be used for such an old and significant matter as marriage. They thus become *ju-ju* <term>objects or concepts with spiritual or supernatural power</term>. Indeed, while all legitimate West African marriage may seem like a simple matter of trade to a casual observer, it is never just that; it always involves a spiritual element.

Now that we have seen how a Fan man marries, we might as well examine the rest of his domestic life. His difficulty lies not only in accumulating enough *bikĕi* but also in finding a woman he is legally permitted to marry. No amount of *bikĕi* can justify a man marrying his first cousin or his aunt. Since kinship among the Fans is recognized through both the father and the mother—unlike the Igalwa people, who only recognize the mother's blood relatives—there is a vast number of aunts and cousins whom he is forbidden from marrying.

But once he has overcome these many difficulties, navigated his family connections, and married, he seems to be a better husband than the men from more "civilized" tribes. He is willing to help with any task, provided it does not require him to leave his gun outside the village gates. He will help chop firewood or prepare food for the goats, and he will happily carry the baby while his wife performs these tasks. In the bush villages, he always escorts her to be nearby in case of leopards or other local dangers. When he is inside the village, he sets his gun down within easy reach and builds the house or combs out plant fibers to...

Fan pottery, although rough and sun-baked, is artistic in form and decorated, for the Fan people ornament all their work. The articles they make consist of cooking pots, palm-wine bottles, water bottles, and pipes; however, not all water bottles or pipes are made of pottery. I wish they were, particularly the former, for they are occasionally made of beautifully woven fiber coated with a layer of a certain gum with a foul taste, which it imparts to the water in the vessel. They say it does not do this if the vessel is soaked for two days in water, but it does, and I suspect it contaminates the stream it is soaked in as well. The pipes are sometimes made of iron very neatly. I imagine they would be hot to smoke, but I have no personal knowledge of this. One of my Ajumba <term>an ethnic group from the Ogowé River region</term> friends bought one of these pipes when we were in Efoua, and that pipe was, intermittently, a curse to the party. Its owner soon learned not to hold it by the bowl, but by the wooden stem when smoking it; the other lessons it had to teach, he learned more slowly. He tucked it, when he had finished smoking, into the folds of his cloth <term>a wrap-around garment</term>, until he had three serious fires raging around his waist. And to the very end of our journey, after having his last pipe at night with it, he would lay it on the ground before it was cool. He learned to lay it out of reach of his own cloth, but he and his fellow Ajumbas persisted in always throwing a leg onto it shortly after, and there was another argument.

The Fan basket-work is sturdily made, but very inferior to the Fjort <term>an ethnic group from the Loango coast</term> basket-work. Their nets are, however, the finest I have ever seen. These are made mainly for catching small game, such as the beautiful little gazelles (*Ncheri*) with dark gray skins on the upper part of the body, white underneath, and satin-like in smoothness all over. Their form is very dainty; their little legs are no thicker than a man’s finger, the neck is long, and the head is adorned with little pointed horns and broad round ears. The nets are tied to trees in two long lines which converge at a sharp angle, with the bottom part of the net lying on the ground. The fiber from which these nets are made has a long grain and is exceedingly strong. I once saw a small bush cow <note>likely a forest buffalo, Syncerus caffer nanus</note> caught in a set of them and unable to break through; on another occasion, I saw a leopard caught. The leopard, however, carried his section of the net away with him, along with a good deal of vegetation and sticks to boot. In addition to nets, this fiber is made into bags for carrying items while in the wilderness, and into the water bottles already mentioned.

The ironwork of the Fan people deserves special notice for its excellence. The anvil is a large piece of iron which is embedded firmly in the ground. Its upper surface is flat and pointed at both ends. The hammers are solid cones of iron, with the upper part of the cones extended to provide a good grip; the blows are struck directly downward, like the action of a pestle. The bellows are of the typical African style, carved from a single piece of solid but soft wood. At the upper end of these bellows, there are two chambers hollowed out of the wood and then covered with the skin of an animal from which the hair has been removed. This skin is bound firmly around the rim of each chamber with <term>tie-tie</term> <note>strong, flexible vines or plant fibers used as cordage</note>, and the top of the skin bag is gathered and tied to a small stick to provide a convenient handle. The straight cylinder, ending in the nozzle, has two channels burned into it which connect to each of the chambers respectively. Halfway up the cylinder, three series of holes are burned from the outside into the air passages: one series on the upper surface and a series on each side. This ingenious arrangement provides a constant current of air from the nozzle when the bellows are operated by a man sitting behind them, who rapidly and alternately pulls up the skin cover of one chamber while pushing down the other. In order to make the apparatus stable, it is lashed to sticks driven into the ground in a way that keeps the bellows at an angle, with the nozzle directed toward the fire. Since wooden bellows like these would soon catch fire if placed directly in the flames, the nozzle is inserted into a cylinder made of clay. This cylinder is made sufficiently large at the end where the bellows' nozzle enters for the air to

The Fan bellows only differ from those of the other iron-working West Coast tribes in that the channels from the two chambers are carved into a single piece of wood throughout their entire length; in other bellows I have seen, the two channels join together just above the nozzle. Additionally, the Fan people decorate the bellows with spearhead patterns, the points of which are directed toward the fire; they seem to believe this helps the work. Their forge is the same as other forges: a round cavity dug into the ground. Their fuel is also charcoal. Their other smithing tool consists of a pointed piece of iron, with which...

<header>XIV IVORY EATERS</header>

...he carves out the patterns that he places on the handles of his swords, and so on.

I must now speak briefly about the most important commodity with which the Fan tribe deals, namely ivory. Their methods of collecting this are varied, and the handles of your table knives could tell many a wild story if their ivory once passed through Fan hands. For ivory is everywhere such an evil thing that the quest for gold seems like a parlor game by comparison; and when its charms seize a tribe like the Fans, "the outcome is often fatal" <note>original: "conclusions pass their careers," a Shakespearean reference suggesting a disastrous or final end</note>. A very common way of collecting a tusk <term>tooth: ivory tusks were commonly referred to as "teeth"</term> is to kill the person who owns one. Therefore, to prevent this catastrophe from happening to you when you possess one, it is considered advisable—unless you are a powerful person in your own village—to bury or sink the tusk and say nothing about it until a trader enters your district or you find a chance to smuggle it quietly to him. Some of these private stashes of ivory are kept for many years before they reach a trader’s hands. About a third of the ivory you see being loaded onto a ship bound for Europe is dark from being stored this way; some tusks are a lovely brown, like a well-stained meerschaum pipe <note>a soft white mineral used to make tobacco pipes, which turns brown with use</note>, while others are quite black and gnawed by that strange little creature—often heard of and blamed, yet little known in ivory ports—the ivory rat.

This squirrel-like creature was first brought to Europe by Paul du Chaillu <note>a famous 19th-century French-American explorer</note>, and as far as I know, no further specimens have been secured. I obtained two, but I am ashamed to say I lost them. Du Chaillu called it the *ivory-eating squirrel* <note>original: "Sciurus eborivorus"</note>. Its most notable feature, as might be imagined, is its teeth. The incisors in the upper jaw are long and set closely together; those in the lower jaw are even longer. Since the lower teeth always seem to tuck behind the upper ones, I wonder how the creature ever manages to close its mouth. The feet are hairless and somewhat like those of a squirrel. The tail is long and marked with horizontal bars, and it is not carried over the back. There are very long, stiff bristles over the eyes and on both sides of the mouth. The damage these little creatures do to buried ivory is immense because, for some mysterious reason, they seem to prefer the flavor of the points of the tusks, which are the most valuable part.

Ivory obtained through murder, however, is considered "private" ivory. The public ivory trade among the Fans is carried out in a different way...

---

This method is more in line with European ideas of a legitimate trade. Most of this ivory comes from dead elephants. In this region, there are specific places where elephants are said to go when they are dying. One such place pointed out to me in a particular district was a large swamp in the forest. The swamp was clearly deep in the middle, because no plants or trees grew out of its dark waters. Its shores likely sloped down steeply, as there was only a narrow band of swamp plants around the edge. It is possible that during the rainy season, when most of the surrounding area is flooded, elephants might wander into this natural trap and drown. When the water dries up, their bodies are discovered. Once the location is known, local people who are aware of the spot search it regularly for ivory. I asked whether these places where the elephants came to die always contained water, but they said no. In one district, they described a valley or a round depression nestled among the mountains. Naturally, the local people were unwilling to take a stranger to these "ivory mines." Similarly, any white person who has caught—as anyone in contact with the trade inevitably does—"ivory fever," is just as reluctant to reveal the locations.

The Fan people collect some of their ivory from live elephants, but I must admit that their hunting method is disgracefully unsportsmanlike. When a herd of elephants is discovered by rubber hunters or because they have been raiding plantations, the entire village—men, women, children, infants, and dogs—goes into the forest. They stalk the great beasts toward a suitable ravine, taking care not to frighten them. Once they have gradually guided the elephants into the right spot, they cut down trees and roughly weave them together with bush rope <term>strong, flexible vines or lianas used as rope</term> to create a massive enclosure. They still take care not to startle the elephants into a stampede. The fence itself is not strong enough to stop an elephant, but it is made effective by being smeared with certain substances. The elephants hate the smell of these so much that when they approach the fence, they turn back in disgust. It goes without saying that this mixture is prepared by the witch doctors <note>the author's term for local spiritual and medical practitioners</note> and its ingredients are a secret, though I was able to identify a few of them. Then, poisoned plantains are placed within the enclosure...

During this time, the crowd of men and women spend their days around the enclosure, ready to turn back any elephant that may attempt to break out, going back and forth to the village for their food. They spend their nights in small shelters made of branches by the enclosure, watching even more vigilantly than by day, as the elephants are more active at night, which is their usual feeding time. 

During this entire time, the <term>ritual specialist (witch doctor)</term> is hard at work performing incantations and making charms with the goal of finding the proper time to attack the elephants. In my opinion, his decision fundamentally depends on his knowledge of how poisoned the animals are, but his own version is that he receives his information from the forest spirits. 

When, however, he has settled on the day, the best hunters slip into the enclosure and take up safe positions in trees. The crowd outside sets light to the prepared fires and makes the loudest uproar possible, firing upon the staggering, terrified elephants as they attempt to break out. The hunters in the trees fire down on them as they rush past, as the fatal point at the back of the skull is well-exposed to them.

When the animals are nearly exhausted, those men who do not possess guns dash into the enclosure. The men who do have guns reload and join them, and the work is then completed. One elephant hunt I happened upon at the final stage had taken two months of preparation; although the plan sounds safe enough, a great deal of danger remains despite all the drugging and <term>charms (ju-ju)</term>. Eight elephants were killed that day, but three burst through everything, sending energetic spectators flying and squashing two men and a baby as flat as botanical specimens.

The subsequent proceedings were impressive. All the people gorged themselves on the meat for days, and great chunks of it were smoked over fires in every direction. Dr. Nassau tells me that the ivory gained from one of these hunts is divided as follows: "The <term>ritual specialist (witch doctor)</term>, the chiefs, and the family on whose land the enclosure is built—and especially the household whose women first discovered the animals—decide in a council how to divide the tusks and the share of the meat to be given to the crowd of outsiders. The next day, the tusks are removed, and each family represented in the gathering cuts up and distributes the meat." In the hunt I saw completed, the elephants had not been discovered in a plantation by women, as in the case Dr. Nassau describes above. Instead, they were found by a party of rubber hunters in the forest some four or five miles from any village. Therefore, the ivory that would have been allotted to the plantation owner in the former case went, in this instance, to the young rubber hunters.

I have already spoken of the method of catching game in traps. Such are the pursuits, sports, and pastimes of my friends, the Fan people. I have been teased considerably by both whites and blacks about my fondness for this tribe. However, as I like Africans in my own way—not <note>original: "à la Sierra Leone"—referring to the Westernized African society of Freetown, which Kingsley often contrasted with the interior tribes.</note> in the style of Sierra Leone—and since these Africans possess more of the qualities I like than any other tribe I have met, it is only natural that I should prefer them. They are brave, and so you can respect them, which is an essential element of a friendly feeling. They are, on the whole, a fine race, particularly those in the mountain districts of the <term>Sierra del Cristal</term> <note>The Crystal Mountains in modern-day Gabon.</note>, where one continually sees magnificent specimens of human beings, both male and
