<page-num>329</page-num>
# XIV NEVER LOSE YOUR HEAD

The women's color is also a light bronze. Many of the men have beards, and albinos are rare among them. The average height in the mountain districts is five feet six to five feet eight inches, and the difference in stature between men and women is not great. Their faces are very bright and expressive, and once you have been among them, you can never mistake a Fan for anyone else. 

But it is in their mental characteristics that their difference from the sluggish, dying-out coast tribes is most marked. The Fan is full of fire, temper, intelligence, and energy. They are very teachable but rather difficult to manage and quick to take offense, and they are utterly indifferent to human life. I should mention that other people, who should know them better than I do, say they are treacherous, thieving, murderous cannibals. I never found them treacherous; but then, I never trusted them, remembering one of the maxims of my great teacher <note>Captain Boler was a well-known English trader and Head Agent for the African Association in the Bight of Biafra.</note> Captain Boler of Bonny: “It’s not safe to go among bush tribes, but if you are such a fool as to go, you needn’t go and be an even bigger fool by being careless—you’ve done enough just by going.” And Captain Boler’s other great maxim was: “Never be afraid of a Black man.” “What if I can’t help it?” I asked. “Don’t show it,” he said. To these precepts I humbly add another: “Never lose your head.” 

I may remark that my favorite form of literature is accounts of mountaineering exploits, though I have never seen a glacier or a permanent snow-capped mountain in my life. I do not care at all how badly they may be written, or what form of <term>clumsy and haphazard</term> <note>original: "bumble-puppy"</note> grammar and composition is employed, as long as the writer walks along the edge of a precipice with a sheer drop of thousands of feet on one side and a sheer wall on the other. Better still, I love when they crawl up an <term>arête</term> <note>original: "arête"—a sharp mountain ridge</note> with a precipice on either side. 

Nothing on earth would persuade me to do either of these things myself, but they remind me of parts of the country I have traveled through. In those places, you walk along a narrow line of security while gulfs of murder loom on each side. In exactly the same way, you are as safe as if you were in your easy chair at home, as long as you find sufficient solid ground. In a bush village inhabited by murderous cannibals, that ground is not found on rock, but on the ideas within those men’s and women’s minds. These ideas, which I believe you will always find, are what give you safety.

### BUSH TRADE AND FAN CUSTOMS

It is not advisable to toy with their beliefs or attempt to wipe them out simply because you consider them superstitious; and never, never shoot too soon. I have never had to shoot, and I hope I never will. In such a situation, a lone white person without troops for backup faces certain death if they resort to violence. However, this risk would not discourage me if I were forced to act; it simply makes me more inclined to walk around an obstacle than to become nothing more than a bloodstain against it—provided this can be done without losing one’s self-respect, which is the source of one’s power in West Africa.

As for waving a revolver around and threatening to fire, I consider it total idiocy. I have never tried it myself, so I speak from a prejudice rooted in the feeling that there is something cowardly about it. You should always have your revolver loaded and in good order, with your hand on it when things are getting intense. In addition, carry an exceptionally good bowie knife rather than a folding knife. With a folding knife, you have to struggle to get it open—a difficult task in a country where everything rusts at the joints—and they are liable to snap shut on your own fingers. The best type of knife is a bowie with a shallow, half-moon curve cut out of the back near the tip, with that depression sharpened to a cutting edge. <note>This describes a "clip point" blade, common on classic bowie knives.</note> A knife is essential because after wading neck-deep through a swamp, your revolver is neither useful nor ornamental until you have had time to clean it. Yet, the chances are you may travel across Africa, or live there for years, and never need either. It is just like the case of the gentleman who asked if a revolver was necessary in Carolina. The answer he received was: “You may be here one year, or you may be here two and never want it; but when you do want it, you’ll want it very badly.”

The cannibalism of the Fan people, although a common habit, is not—in my opinion—a danger to white people, except for the trouble it causes when trying to prevent one's Black companions from being eaten. The Fan is not a cannibal for sacrificial or religious reasons like the Negro <note>The author distinguishes between the ritualistic practices she attributes to coastal tribes and the dietary cannibalism of the interior Fang people.</note>. He approaches it with a kind of common sense. He says that human flesh is good to eat—very good—and he wishes you would try it. Oh dear, no—he claims he never eats it himself, but the people in the next town certainly do. He is always very defensive about it...

# CHAPTER XV

## DOWN THE REMBWÉ

->Explaining how the traveler descends the *Rembwé* River, experiencing various excursions and alarms in the company of a Black trader, and returns safely to the coast. This includes an account of the geography of this region, the *Gaboon* and its main tributaries <term>affluents</term>.<-

Leaving Agonjo seemed like it would be almost as difficult as getting there. However, since the accommodations were comfortable and the company was fairly good, I was not anxious. I admit the local scenery resembled the Niger Delta a bit too much to be perfectly beautiful—nothing but long lines of mangroves and the muddy river drifting almost imperceptibly toward the sea, with nothing else in sight. Mr. Glass, however, did not view the situation so calmly. I weighed on his commercial conscience because I had arrived from the bush, and he saw profit in me. Therefore, I was a trade product—a new type of commodity that should be processed and developed. He found himself unable to do this; although he had secured the "first shipment," so to speak, and had it safely stored, he could not ship it out, and he felt this was a personal failure.

He complained loudly and often that his firm had not provided him with a large sailing canoe and a suitable crew to handle this new line of business. I did my best to comfort him, pointing out that even the most enterprising company could not be expected to provide such expensive equipment on the extremely slim chance of ladies arriving from the wilderness <term>per bush</term> at Agonjo—at least, not until the trade in "ladies" was well established. But he refused to see it that way and kept dwelling on the subject, wrapped up—poor man—in a heavy overcoat and a muffler, because

I feel fairly certain that even if firms like Hatton and Cookson, or any other company, were to run a weekly line of luxury steamboats with brass bands and red-velvet lounges up and down the Rembwé River, there would not be enough white passenger traffic to pay for the coal. This is especially true for my route, which had never been taken by even a Black trader before. However, I am not thinking of taking out a patent for it; for one thing, I am sure it would never become popular enough to cover the initial expenses, and for another, the relatives of people who might attempt to use it at any time of year except the brief window when it is navigable would likely sue me for damages.

I next tried to convince Mr. Glass that any canoe would be sufficient for me to travel down. "No," he said, "just any canoe will not do." He explained that when you travel down the Rembwé to 'Como Point, you enter a rough, dangerous stretch of water called the Gaboon. It has a confusing set of currents caused by the tides and the merging flows of the Rembwé and 'Como rivers. He believed it was unlikely a river canoe could survive there for any significant amount of time. He considered it impossible to make progress below 'Como Point by paddling alone. There was no choice but to use a large sailing canoe, and there was no large sailing canoe available. I think Mr. Glass found a bit of comfort in the fact that John Holt's sub-agent was just as unable to find transport for me as he was.

At this point in the affair, a highly dramatic figure entered. He dashed up onto the veranda, slapped the fragile Mr. Glass between the shoulders, and threw his own massive frame into a chair. <header>XV CAPTAIN JOHNSON, ALIAS OBANJO</header>

He evidently intended to present the image of a reckless, jovial sea captain. There was a <term>“Hello-my-Hearty”</term><note>A stereotypical nautical greeting used by sailors.</note> atmosphere coming off him from the top of his hat to the soles of his feet, like the scent off a flower. However, it did not require a genius at judging character to see that beneath and behind this was a very different sort of man. If I should ever want to embark on a wild and dangerous career up a West African river, I shall start it by hiring Captain Johnson. He struck me as being one of those men—of whom I know only five—on whom I could rely; if he and I went into the deep wilderness together, at least one of us would come out alive and have gained something substantial from the venture. This is a great deal more than I could say, for example, of Ngouta, who was still with me because he desired to see the wonders of Gaboon and buy a hanging lamp. I will not start that hanging lamp <term>palaver</term><note>A West African term for a long discussion, negotiation, or dispute.</note> here, however, but I will remark that Ngouta persisted in believing he was still surrounded by danger at Agonjo.

Captain Johnson’s attire deserves special comment and admiration. However disconnected the two sides of his character might be, his clothes perfectly reflected both of his natures. When we first met, he wore a huge sombrero hat, a spotless singlet, and a suit of clean, well-tailored <term>dungaree</term><note>A sturdy cotton fabric, often blue, used for work clothes.</note>. He cut an uncommonly picturesque and powerful figure in them, with his finely built, strong physique and handsome face. His face was always full of expression, but his sharp, small eyes were constantly watching the effect his friendly smiles and hearty laughter produced. The eyes were the eyes of Obanjo; the rest of the face was the property of Captain Johnson. I do not mean to say that they were the eyes of a wicked man, but you did not have to look twice at them to see they belonged to a man who was courageous in the African manner—full of energy and resource, keenly intelligent, self-reliant, and that sort of thing.

I left him and the sophisticated Mr. Glass together to discuss the <term>palaver</term> of transporting me, and they talked it over at great length. Obanjo was thinking of taking his goods down to Gaboon. The only drawback was that this "noble vessel" was not yet finished; but that did not discourage any of us, except for Mr. Glass. He seemed to think his firm would hold him financially responsible for my value if I were to get lost. However, the next morning Obanjo arrived with his vessel, and after saying farewell to my kind host, Mr. Sanga Glass, I departed.

The boat had the potential to be a fine vessel, though she was roughly carved out of an immense hardwood tree. Her lines were good, and her design was like that of the large sea-canoes from the Bight of Panavia <note>The Bight of Pannavia, an area on the coast of modern-day Cameroon.</note>. Way up at the front was a roughly made pole mast, European in style, which carried a long <term>gaff</term><note>A spar or pole used to support the top edge of a sail.</note>. It lacked <term>shrouds and stays</term><note>Ropes or cables used to support and steady a mast.</note>, and my impression was that the mast would be snapped off if we encountered even half a tornado. That was until I saw our sail and realized that the fabric would tear into threads instantly if it met even a light breeze. The sail was actually a bed quilt that had evidently been in the family for years; although it had been carefully patched in places with scraps from the captain’s old <term>dungarees</term><note>Sturdy cotton work clothes.</note>, in other unpatched spots it gave "free passage to the winds of Heaven." I should mention that such "canvas" does not exactly help the speed of a boat. Between this sail and the number of trading stops we made, I believe I earned the credit for making a record trip down the Rembwé—the slowest time ever recorded by a white person.

Fixed across the stern of the canoe was the usual platform made of bamboo, level with the <term>gunwale</term><note>The upper edge of the side of a boat.</note>. Now, this kind of platform is an excellent idea when it is fully finished. You can store endless items under it, and a hood of palm-thatch is usually built over it to create a very comfortable cabin, five or six feet long and about three feet high in the center. You can curl yourself up inside and, if you like, hang a mat across the opening for privacy. However, we had not progressed that far on our vessel yet; in fact, the platform had only just been fixed in place. I assure you that a bamboo platform is a very unstable place to sit when it is in this stage of construction. I arranged my belongings to make a reclining couch on it in the Roman style and was extremely comfortable until we were nearly out of the Rembwé and entering the Gaboon.

<page-num>337</page-num>
<header>XV A TRYING SITUATION</header>

Then began some exciting times. By now, our noble vessel had developed a significant tilt because of our cargo, which was poorly packed. This made my seat on the bamboo platform about as restful as the slanted surface of a highly polished writing desk. Furthermore, the rough and choppy sea gave our boat the strangest variety of movements imaginable. She rolled from side to side, which made it precarious for anything sitting on the bamboo platform, though that was at least a predictable and natural motion. In addition to this, she had a violent, sudden kick that I suspect the wretched thing intended to be a pitch. No human being could anticipate or prepare for it; it frequently threw loose belongings overboard into the Gaboon waters or onto the mismatched heap of goods in the bottom of the canoe itself. This caused Obanjo to repeat, with great intensity and emotion, curses he had learned years earlier when he served as a boatswain on a trading steamer along the coast. It was fortunate for my character, you must understand, that I have usually traveled on ships belonging to the British African or Royal African lines while voyaging along this West African coast. Since the owners of those ships forbid the use of profanity on board, goodness only knows what words I might have otherwise remembered and used myself in the Gaboon estuary.

We departed from Agonjo with all the shouting, bustle, and general display of expert seamanship that Obanjo could manage. An optimistic person might have expected us to reach a significant destination by nightfall. I did not expect that; however, neither did I expect that after we had traveled only five miles <note>The author uses the phrase "a mile and only four," mimicking the style of old English ballads.</note>, we would pull up and anchor at a small village for the night. Yet that is what we did, as the captain went ashore to look for cargo and hire more crew members.

There were lively celebrations on shore that night, and the captain returned to the boat around 2:00 a.m. He brought some rubber, piassava <term>piassava</term><note>A stiff, fibrous product from palm trees used for making rope and brushes.</note>, and two new crew members whose appearance made them perfect additions to our vessel; for I have never laid eyes on a more suspicious-looking group than our crew. One enormously powerful man looked like the embodiment of a terrifying pirate from a storybook, and I respected Obanjo for the way he kept them under control. We

<header>DOWN THE REMBWÉ CHAPTER</header>

We had now also acquired a small dugout canoe to serve as a tender <term>a small boat used to support or service a larger vessel</term>, and a large fishing net.

At about 4 a.m. in the moonlight, we started drifting downriver on the tail end of the land breeze. As I noticed Obanjo wanted to sleep, I offered to steer. After putting me through an examination in practical seamanship and passing me, he gladly accepted my offer. He handed over the tiller, which stuck out across my bamboo platform, and went to curl himself up, falling sound asleep among the crew in less time than it takes to write about it. On the other nights we spent on this voyage, I had no need to offer to steer; he handed over charge to me as a matter of course. As I prefer the night to the day in Africa, I enjoyed it. Indeed, as much as I have enjoyed life in Africa, I do not think I ever enjoyed it as fully as I did during those nights drifting down the Rembwé. 

The great, black, winding river had a pathway of frosted silver in its center where the moonlight struck it; on each side were the ink-black mangrove walls, and above them, the band of starry and moonlit heavens that the mangroves allowed one to see. Forward rose the shape of our sail, transformed from improvised bedsheets into something glorious; and the little red glow of our cooking fire provided a single note of warm color against the cold light of the moon. 

Three or four times during the second night, while I was steering along the south bank, I found the mangrove wall thinner. Standing up, I looked through the network of their roots and stems at what seemed like acres upon acres of polished silver plains—more examples of those awful slime lagoons, one of which, before we reached Ndorko, had so very nearly "collected" <note>This refers to an earlier incident where Kingsley nearly fell into or became trapped by the dangerous mud of the lagoons.</note> me. I watched them with a kind of fascination as we leisurely slipped past. 

On the second night, toward dawn, I had the great joy of seeing Mount Okoneto away to the southwest, first shining in the moonlight and then catching the colors of the dawn before they reached us down below. Ah me! Give me a West African river and a canoe for pure pleasure. Drawbacks, you say? Well, yes, but where are there not drawbacks? The only drawbacks on those Rembwé nights were the series of terrible frights I got by steering into tree shadows and thinking they were mud banks, or trees

Fortunately, I never woke the watchmen, but I bravely steered the boat away from the shadows on my own every time, and I called myself a fool instead of being called one by others. My sailor friends complain that I was frightened by mere shadows, but I ask them to consider this before they judge me: have they ever steered an awkward canoe with a bed-sheet for a sail down an unknown river at night by the light of the moon? Between my own ideas about the proper way to take a vessel around a bend and the struggle to keep the wind in that bed-sheet sail, it is a miracle to me that I did not wreck the ship or cause damage to the African coast.

By daylight, the scenery along the Rembwé was certainly not as beautiful, and one could sleep through it without feeling any regret. It was monotonous, but not quite vast enough to be considered grand. Every so often we reached villages, each built on a mound of clay and sandy soil—likely the end of a point of land extending into the mangrove swamp that bordered the river. We stopped at every village we saw to talk with the residents and try to find cargo to trade in the usual manner. 

We had an especially lively time at one particular village. Obanjo had a wife and a home there, as well as a large herd of goats, some of which he wanted to bring with us to sell at Gaboon. It was a pleasant-looking village with a clean yellow beach that most of the houses overlooked, but it had extensions further inland. Being quite lazy, I did not go ashore, but instead watched the performance from the bamboo platform. The entire herd of goats entered from the right side of my "stage" and ran wildly across the scene, disappearing on the left. Two minutes passed. Then Obanjo and his brave crew entered from the right, ran as fast as they could across the front, and disappeared on the left. There was a loud commotion behind the scenes. Five minutes passed. The goats entered from the right again as before, followed by Obanjo and his company as before, and so on from the beginning <note>original: "da capo"</note>. It was more like a stage fight I once saw between the armies of Macbeth and Macduff <note>Characters from William Shakespeare's play *Macbeth*</note> than anything else I have ever seen before or since. However, our production on the Rembwé was better staged, with more <term>extras</term>, more noise, and all that sort of thing. I assure you, it was a very spirited performance.

The villagers and I, who were not personally involved in catching the goats, acted as the audience and cheered enthusiastically. While I was busy shouting “Encore” <note>French: "Again" or "Once more"</note> during the third round, I was quite shocked to hear a well-spoken, clearly educated voice say in perfect English:

“It is a most amusing sight, madam, isn’t it?”

Now, you do not expect to hear things called “amusing sights” on the Rembwé River; so I turned around and saw standing on the bank where our canoe was moored what appeared to be an English gentleman. It seemed as if, through some misfortune, he had turned black all over, lost his trousers, and been forced to replace them with a very decorative tablecloth. The rest of his wardrobe was in excellent condition, including the usual white denim coat, white shirt and collar, a very neat tie, and the felt hat favored by white gentlemen in this region. Taking a large, strong cigar from his lips with one hand, he gracefully raised his hat with the other and said:

“Please excuse me, madam.”

I said, “Oh, please, continue smoking.”

“May I?” he asked, offering me a cigar case.

“Oh, no thank you,” I replied.

“Many ladies do nowadays,” he said, and then asked me whether I “preferred Liverpool, London, or Paris.”

I said, “Paris; but there are nice things in both the other cities.”

“Indeed, that is true,” he said; “they have many very respectable works of art in St. George’s Hall.” <note>A Neoclassical building in Liverpool known for its concert halls and law courts.</note>

I agreed, but said I thought the National Gallery was preferable because there you could find such a fine representative collection of works from the early Italian schools <term>Early Italian schools: Refers to Renaissance painters from the 13th to 15th centuries.</term>. I felt I had to match this man’s level of conversation, whoever he was. Having regained my composure, I was holding my own in our cultured discussion when Obanjo and the crew arrived, carrying goats. Obanjo abruptly dropped his goat into the hold and took off his hat, giving his very best bow to my new acquaintance, who acknowledged the greeting with a delightfully condescending air.

“Introduce me,” said the gentleman.

“I cannot,” said Obanjo.

# XV PRINCE MAKAGA

"I’m sorry, madam," said the gentleman, "I didn't bring my card-case with me. One hardly expects to need one in such a remote region; my name is Prince Makaga." <note>Makaga is an honorable title that only one man—the bravest and best hunter in the tribe—may hold. The role of the Makaga is to lead dangerous missions. For example, if someone murders a fellow villager and the murderer’s town refuses to hand him over (which usually happens, as they consider it shameful to surrender someone who has sought refuge), it is the Makaga’s duty to lead the best men from his village to attack the town protecting the murderer and destroy it along with its inhabitants. (Source: *Du Chaillu's Explorations and Adventures in Equatorial Africa, 1861, p. 393*).</note>

I told him that I was also without a card-case for the same reasons as his, but I gave him my name and address. Meanwhile, Obanjo had gotten everyone on board, including one crew member he had literally dragged back by the leg. We shoved off, and with many bows, we and the Black gentleman parted ways. As soon as we were out of earshot from the shore, I asked, "Who is he, Obanjo?" 

Obanjo laughed and explained that he was a M'pongwe gentleman who had previously worked as an agent for one of the large European companies in Gaboon and had visited Europe several times. Thinking he could earn more money on his own, he had left the company to start trading throughout this district. At first, he made a great deal of money, but many of the people he had given goods to on credit <term>trust: a system where goods were advanced to local traders on credit, often leading to debt issues</term> had recently failed to pay him back. He was likely up here now trying to settle some of those debts. Obanjo clearly thought he was too much of a refined, "white-glove" gentleman to handle the rough business of the inland trade, and he believed this was the usual result: a man was often ruined by going to Europe. I generally agree with him on that point, but Prince Makaga had a sophisticated manner without the obvious arrogance usually found in men who have been "home" to Europe.

We had another cheerful little incident that afternoon. After a few minutes' conversation with Obanjo, one of the men carefully sank his canoe, while the other simply let his drift away, and both joined our crew. I saw they were Fans <note>The Fan (or Fang) people are an ethnic group from Central Africa known during this period for their skill in hunting and reputation as fierce warriors.</note>, as indeed nearly all the crew were, but I did not think much of the occurrence at the time. 

Our "tender"—the small canoe—had been sent out as usual with the big black man and another <term>A. B.: an "Able-bodied Seaman," a term for an experienced sailor</term> to fish. One of our main activities was fishing hard all the time with a large net. The fish caught—sometimes a bushel or two at a time, almost all grey mullet—were then brought alongside, split open, and cleaned. We then all had as many as we wanted for supper. The rest we hung on strings over our fire to be smoked—though often quite insufficiently—to prevent them from rotting. Obanjo intended to sell them during his next trip up the 'Como River; since the 'Como has fewer fish than the Rembwé, they would sell for a high price there. We always kept an eye out for opportunities like this. I can proudly say we were not some gilded floating hotel or a ferry boat like those Cunard or White Star liners; we were just a solid trading vessel that wasn't ashamed to turn a profit and wasn't afraid of hard work.

Well, just after we had leisurely entered a new stretch of the river, our fishing canoe—which we had left behind to haul in the net and rejoin us—came around the corner after us, propelled at an incredible speed. The occupants, especially the big black sailor, were shouting something in terror-stricken voices. 

"What?" said Obanjo, springing to his feet. 

"The Fans! The Fans!" shouted the men in the canoe as they shot toward us like agitated chickens scurrying toward a hen. In another moment, they were alongside and tumbling over our <term>gunwale: the upper edge of the side of a boat</term> into the bottom of the vessel, still crying, "The Fans! The Fans! The Fans!" 

Then, through energetic questioning and colorful language—the kind that might make the air smell of sulfur—Obanjo drew out the information. It seemed that about 40,000 Fans, armed with knives and guns, were coming down the Rembwé with the intent to kill and slay us, and they were expected to arrive in an instant. <header>XV A RACE FOR LIFE</header>

"The rudder!" he shouted to me, "take her into the middle of the stream and keep the sail full." It occurred to me that perhaps a position underneath the bamboo platform might be safer than staying on top of it, where I would be exposed to every scrap of old iron and whatever else—according to native testimony—would soon be flying through the air from those Fan guns. Moreover, I had not forgotten having previously been shot in a similar situation, though I was in better company then. 

However, I did not say anything; nor, between ourselves, did I quite believe the threat from those Fans. So, regardless of danger, I grasped the helm and sent our gallant craft flying before the breeze down the heart of the great wild river. (That is the poetic way to put it; for the sake of scientific accuracy, it could be translated as "crawling toward the middle"). 

Meanwhile, Obanjo performed feats of great valor all over the vessel. He hauled up the mainsail, rallied his cowardly crew, and brought out the sweeps <term>sweeps: long, heavy oars used to propel a barge or sailing vessel in calm water or for steering</term>—specifically, one old oar and four paddles. With this assistance, we solemnly plodded away from danger at a pace so slow that nothing but a Thames dumb barge <note>A "dumb barge" is a flat-bottomed freight boat without an engine or sails, moved only by the tide or by being towed.</note> going against the current could possibly fail to overtake us. 

Still, we did not feel safe, and I suggested to Ngouta that he should get up and help; but he refused, stating that he was a married man. Obanjo, cheering the paddlers with inspiring words, leaped with the agility of a leopard onto the bamboo platform at the stern. He stood there with his gun loaded and cocked to face the approaching enemy, looking like a statue of himself erected at public expense. 

The trouble with this, however, was that while Obanjo’s face was toward the coming foe, his back was toward the crew. They immediately began to sink back down into the bottom of the boat, paddles and all. As second in command, seeing this, I gave them a few inspiring words, and Obanjo shouted a few even more powerful ones at them over his shoulder, and so we kept the paddles moving.

Soon, a Fan canoe came darting around the corner. It carried a woman in the bow, weeping and wringing her hands, while another woman, howling in sympathy, paddled the boat. Obanjo, using colorful language, demanded to know why they were following us. The woman in the bow cried, "My son! My..."

Consequently, the young rascal had run away without permission in a canoe and was suspected of having joined the well-known Obanjo. Obanjo admitted he had the boy (as more armed canoes were coming around the corner) and said that if the mother would come and fetch her son, she could have him. # XV NAUTICAL PROBLEMS

Having been successfully picked up by Obanjo, the boys thought they were safe. However, after this incident, the second boy judged that they were not out of danger yet. He believed his family would be coming after him very shortly, for he said he was a more valuable and important boy than his companion, and his family was an uncommonly fierce group. We felt not the least bit of anxiety to make their acquaintance, so we put on speed in our "gallant" vessel and kept the paddles moving. Since no more Fan people were in sight, our crew kept working bravely. Meanwhile, Obanjo—now in a boisterous mood and flushed with victory—said things to the crew about the way they had collapsed when those two women in a canoe came around the corner. His words must have stung their pride, but they never winced; instead, they laughed merrily at the joke against themselves. We never saw the other boy’s family, and so we took him safely to Gaboon, where Obanjo found him a good job.

I cannot say exactly how much actual danger there was compared to the immense amount of fear shown on our boat. It never occurred to me that there was any danger at all, but on the other hand, the crew and Obanjo evidently thought it was a perilous place. My status as a white person would have offered no protection, for the Fan people would not have suspected a white woman was on such a canoe. They might have fired on us if they had been unduly irritated and not handled by Obanjo with that fine mixture of intimidation and smooth-talking of which he is such a master.

Whatever the true nature of the affair may have been, however, it had one good result: it got us out of the Rembwé River and into the Gaboon estuary. Although at the time this seemed a doubtful blessing, it did represent progress. By this time, I had mastered the main ways our vessel was incompetent: 

*A.* We could not go against the wind. 
*B.* We could not go against the tide. 

While we were in the Rembwé, there was a state we will designate as *C*—the tide coming one way and the wind another. In this state we could make progress: backwards if the wind blew against us too strongly, but toward the sea if it did not and the tide was running down. If the tide was running up and the wind was blowing down, then we moved seaward "softly, softly" <note>This is a common West African English expression meaning slowly and carefully.</note> alongside the mangrove bank, where the current of the tide is weakest. However, when we got down past 'Como Point, our situation changed.

<page-num>346</page-num>
# DOWN THE REMBWÉ CHAPTER

We encountered a situation there that I will call *D*—a truly chaotic mix of sea and river activity. To the north, the 'Como, the Boqué, and two other smaller but significant streams were, along with the Rembwé, pouring their waters down in swirling, intermingling, and clashing currents. Pushing against them, making the chaos even worse, came the tide. The tide in the Gaboon is swift and powerful, and it is irregular; it rises eight feet during spring tides <note>The highest tides, occurring after a new or full moon.</note> and two and a half feet during neap tides <note>The lowest tides, occurring during the first and third quarters of the moon.</note>. The wind had died down as well, as it was evening. In this region, it is common for the wind to blow from the land from 8:00 P.M. until 8:00 A.M., moving from the southwest to the east. Then comes a lull—either a completely dead, hot, brooding calm or light, frustrating breezes and drafts that blow a few hot, panting breaths into your sails and then die. After that, the sea breeze comes up from the south-southwest or northwest, sometimes early in the forenoon and sometimes not until two or three o'clock. This breeze blows until sunset, followed by another even hotter calm.

Fortunately for us, we arrived at the head of the Gaboon estuary during this calm, because if we had had to deal with the wind, we would have been finished. There were one or two wandering gusts of wind; the first one made our bedspread <note>original: "counterpane"</note> give up its ambitious career as a sea sail. It came loose from its gaff <note>The spar that holds the upper edge of a fore-and-aft sail.</note> and draped itself over the crew, as if to say, "I've had enough of this sailing; I'll be a bedspread again." We performed a great deal of varied and spirited navigation, the details of which I won't dwell upon, simply because it was successful. We spun in circles once or twice, taking on water all the while, and then returned to the south bank backwards.

We wisely stayed at that bank for the night. So far, our encounter with the Gaboon had resulted in our sail being wrecked, Ngouta getting seasick, and me becoming exasperated. Since our noble vessel had just demonstrated its disastrous "kicking" power for the first time, I had quite a struggle with my belongings on the bamboo platform. A basket designed for catching human souls—given to me as a farewell gift by a valued friend who is a witch doctor—contained the few things in life I actually cared about: specifically, my brush, comb, toothbrush, and pocket handkerchiefs. This basket went over the stern, while I—

I was recovering this with my fishing line (its quality was so excellent that, I am happy to say, it floated). Meanwhile, a black bag containing my blouses and other essentials drifted away to leeward <note>The side sheltered from the wind; downwind.</note>. Obanjo recovered that bag, but in the meantime, my small portmanteau <note>A large traveling bag or suitcase that opens into two equal parts.</note>—which contained my papers and trade tobacco—slid off to leeward. Since it also held geological specimens from the Sierra del Cristal, a massive mountain range, it would have surely sunk if not for the large black man <note>original: "the big black"</note> who grabbed it. All my bedding—six Equetta cloths given to me by Mr. Hamilton on the Opobo River before I traveled south—managed to get away, but they were eventually picked up with the fishing line, wet but safe. After this, I did not attempt any more "Roman reclining couch" luxuries. Instead, I stowed all my loose gear under the bamboo platform and spent the night on top of it, dozing fitfully with my head on my knees.

When morning broke, I looked out toward the sea and saw the welcome shapes of König and Perroquet Islands in the distance. They looked, as they usually do, like two lumps of cloud that had dropped onto the wide Gaboon River. I felt that I was finally nearing something worth reaching: Glass <note>A district in Libreville, Gabon, which was a center for European trade.</note>. Though it was still out of sight, I knew it lay to the west of those islands on the northern shore of the estuary. If anyone had given me the choice between being in Glass within twenty-four hours from the mouth of the Rembwé, or being in Paris or London in a week, I would have chosen Glass without a moment’s hesitation. Although I generally dislike West Coast towns, there are exceptions; of all those exceptions, the one I like most is undoubtedly Glass, Gaboon. Its charms seemed very great on that damp, chilly morning after a night spent on a bamboo platform in an unfinished native canoe.

I should probably provide a brief sketch of the local geography at the head of the Gaboon estuary, as I seem to be the next English traveler to follow Mr. Winwood Reade <note>Winwood Reade (1838–1875), an English explorer and philosopher who traveled through West Africa.</note>, who was here in 1863. He traveled up the estuary and into the 'Como River, which he ascended as far as the rapids—rapids caused, as is typical in this country, by the rocks of the Sierra del Cristal. I hear from local sources that above these rapids, the 'Como is formed by a series of smaller...

# DOWN THE REMBWÉ CHAPTER

...streams originating in the mountain range. The 'Como flows into the Gaboon on its northern bank, at its eastern end, and is likely its largest tributary. A short distance upstream, the 'Como—or more correctly, the Nkâmâ—is joined on its southern bank by the Boqué or Bakwe. Their combined flow, named the Olomb'ompolo, enters the Gaboon. On the wide peninsula of land that separates the mouth of the 'Como from the Rembwé, there are two other smaller rivers. The mouth of the Rembwé is about one and a half miles wide and is located on the southern bank of the eastern end of the Gaboon. This southern bank is a long, low stretch of sandy land between thirty-five and forty miles long; it contains numerous native Mpongwe <note>A Bantu ethnic group indigenous to the Gaboon estuary region.</note> villages, but no European settlements at all. It ends at Pongara Point, the western seaward tip of the estuary, which is over nine miles away from Cape Santa Clara, the western tip of the northern shore.

Like the 'Como, the Rembwé is said to originate in the Sierra del Cristal <note>The Crystal Mountains of West Africa.</note>. It is navigable as far as a place called Isango, which is past Agonjo. Just above Agonjo, it is joined by a tributary on its southern bank and flows through mountainous country where its course is blocked by rapids for anything but small canoes. Obanjo did not seem to think this mattered, since there was little trade in that area and no particular reason why anyone would want to go further upstream. Furthermore, he said the natives there were an "exceedingly bad lot," though Obanjo usually holds a low opinion of the interior <term>bush</term> <note>Deeper inland regions, away from coastal or urban settlements.</note> natives in these regions. In any case, they are Fans—and *Fans are Fans*. <note>The Fan (or Fang) people were often described by 19th-century explorers as fierce and warlike.</note>

However, he was eager for me to join him on a trading voyage up another river—a notorious one—in the nearby Spanish territory <note>Present-day Equatorial Guinea.</note>. The idea was that I would buy goods at Glass <note>A district in Libreville, Gabon, known for European trading houses.</note> and we would travel together so he could use them to buy ivory in the interior. I anxiously asked where my profits would come from. Obanjo, who had suspected all along that I had trade motives, craftily said, "Why did you come across from the Ogowe? You say you want to see this country. Well, I say come with me! I will show you much country, many men, elephants, leopards, and gorillas. Oh, plenty of things! Then you ask, 'Where is my trade?'" I grandly denied having any trade motives. Then he said:

# XV DECLINING TRADE

"You should come with me up there," he said. I replied that I would think about it later; for the time being, I had seen enough men, elephants, gorillas, and leopards, and I preferred to enter wild districts under the French flag over any other. I am still considering taking that voyage, but I will not "march through Coventry" <note>A reference to Shakespeare’s *Henry IV, Part 1*, meaning to be seen in public with a disgraceful or ragtag group.</note> with the crew we had on the Rembwé—and that is final, as Sir John Falstaff says. Imagine for yourselves, my friends, the delightful situation of being upriver, surrounded by greedy savages with a canoe full of valuable goods, and having only a crew to defend them who possessed the kind of "fighting spirit" our men had demonstrated. Obanjo might be fine, I suppose; but imagine if he were shot and you were left with over 250 pounds <term>eighteen stone odd</term> <note>One stone equals 14 pounds; eighteen stone is approximately 252 pounds.</note> of him on your hands, in addition to your other little worries. There is little doubt such an excursion would be eventful and highly interesting, but I am certain it would be a failure from a commercial perspective.

Trade, however, even when conducted in a safer and more sensible way than our proposed scheme, is declining on the Rembwé and 'Como. European firms no longer find it profitable to station white agents at the trading posts <term>factories</term> <note>In this context, "factories" refers to trading stations or warehouses where "factors" (agents) conducted business.</note> on the Rembwé at Agonjo and Isango, or on the 'Como at N'enge N'enge, although they still keep the posts running under the management of Black agents. N'enge N'enge, a large island located just inside the mouth of the 'Como near its meeting with the Boqué, still has a white missionary representative from the American Presbyterian Mission. This was the first mission to begin working in the Gaboon, Ogowé, and Batanga regions. The station at N'enge N'enge is still connected to the mission's headquarters at Baraka, as it was not handed over to the Evangelical Mission <note>original: "Mission Evangélique"</note> of Paris along with the Ogowé stations. But aside from this mission station and the missionary tours conducted by the energetic Roman Catholic priests, the upper Gaboon region is rarely visited by European commercial ventures. Occasionally, that very hardworking little vessel—the gunboat stationed at Libreville—travels upriver to see whether the natives are behaving properly or to correct their errors.

The reason for the decline of trade in this particular district is, I suspect, not—as some suggest—the impoverishment...

The decline of the country's export trade is not because resources are exhausted, but arises from the Fang <note>Originally "Fan"; the Fang people were migrating into the region during this period.</note> invasion disrupting established systems, and also from the trade being diverted to the Ogowé River. This is due to the enterprising way the French have opened up that river since the 1860s. Before the sixties, the Ogowé was virtually only a legend in the local languages. Now, French enterprise has made it a practical trade outlet for a large portion of some of the richest land in West Africa, and the trade from the upper Rembwé has been drained in that direction. This is a very similar case to that of Bonny <note>A major trading port in the Niger Delta.</note>, where trade has pitifully fallen away in recent years, being drained toward Opobo by the superior ability and power of the Opobo chiefs.

Trade is fascinating to me, but crossing the nine-mile-wide, rough Gaboon estuary in an unfinished canoe with an inefficient bedspread <term>counterpane</term> for a sail holds no such charm; nonetheless, I return out of duty to this unpleasant subject. We started very early in the morning. We reached the other side just as night was falling <note>original: "entangled in the trailing garments of the night."</note>. During that sweltering hot day, I was thankful for one thing: that if Sister Ann was looking out across the river—as was her invariable way of spending spare moments—she would never imagine I was in a canoe that performed such audaciously bad maneuvers. It missed its turns <term>missed stays</term>, stalled head-to-wind <term>got into irons</term> <note>A sailing term for when a vessel loses forward momentum while heading into the wind, making it impossible to steer.</note>, and in general behaved in a way that should have cost her captain his certificate. 

Just as night fell, however, we reached the northern shore of the Grand Gaboon at Dongila, just off the mouth of the 'Como River. We were still some eleven miles east of König Island, and even further from Glass, but being on the same side of the river felt like good progress. The shoreline here is very rocky, so we could not go close alongside but instead anchored out among the rocks. At this place, there is a considerable village and a station of the Roman Catholic Mission. When we arrived, a nun was down on the shore with her school children, who were busy catching shellfish and generally enjoying themselves. Obanjo went ashore in the small boat <term>tender</term>, and the holy sister kindly sent an invitation through him for me to come ashore and spend the night. However, I was exhausted and felt quite unfit for polite society after the long, sweltering day and being soaked by the water that had splashed on board. Moreover, I learned...

# XV INVOLUNTARY IMMERSION

She could not speak English, and in my current state, I hesitated to try and piece together some French from memory. I felt quite certain I would be completely misunderstood by the gentle, clean, and tidy lady, and she might label me as a typical example of an Englishwoman; thus, I would disgrace my country. If I had been able to get dressed up, I would have gone ashore, but as it was, I wrote her a note explaining the situation and thanking her.

We anchored off Dongila all night because of the tide. I cast off everything—Dongila, the canoe, and all—a little after midnight. Obanjo and almost all the crew stayed on shore that night, and I rolled myself up in an Equetta cloth <note>A type of local woven textile common in the region.</note> and went soundly and happily to sleep on the bamboo platform, leaving the canoe pitching slightly. Around midnight, either a change in the tide or some inherent flaw in the canoe caused it to swing around softly, and the next thing I knew, I was in the water. I had expected this to happen for a long time, so I was not surprised, though I was extremely annoyed. Needless to say, I was dripping wet when I climbed back on board. So, in the darkness of the night, I retrieved my portmanteau <term>a large traveling bag or trunk that opens into two equal parts</term> from the hold and thoroughly tidied myself up. The next morning we set off early, coasting along toward Glass <note>A commercial district of Libreville where European trading houses were located.</note>. Arriving safely there, I attempted to look as unconcerned as possible. I vaguely hoped Mr. Hudson would be away in Libreville, for I was nervous about meeting him; I knew that since he had carefully left me in the safe hands of Madame <note>original: "Mme."</note> Jacot with many instructions to be careful, there were many events in my journey that would not meet with his approval. It was a vain hope! He was waiting on the pier. He did not approve. He had already heard of most of my exploits.

The agent for the German trading firm at Lambaréné <note>Originally "Lembarene."</note> had come to Libreville a few days earlier in the "legitimate" way—that is, down the Ogowé River in a small steamer, then onto a mail boat at Fernan Vaz, and from there to Libreville. He had brought news that I was reported to have left Kangwe, heading toward the Rembwé. Knowing I was supposed to reach Agonjo, Mr. Hudson had most kindly sent a surf-boat with a good crew up the Rembwé to pick me up. We never saw this surf-boat as we came down. I expect we were weaving around some corner or another in search of trade, or perhaps hiding away in a swampy creek.

# CHAPTER XVI

## FRENCH CONGO <note>original: "CONGO FRANÇAIS"</note>

->In which a hymn of praise in honor of the great Ogowé explorers is sung by the<-
->Traveler, to which is added a great deal of very dense information<-
->on the general geography of the French Congo.^1<-

Before leaving the Ogowé region, I must attempt to give you a general summary <note>original: "résumé"</note> of its geography. My own journals, kept while I was there, contain this information in such a scattered state that no one—unless they were an expert on this part of Africa—would understand their full significance. It would take an enthusiastic expert indeed to go through the trouble of piecing the information together.

My reason for going into these geographical details at all is that I believe no region in Africa—certainly no region of equal importance—is so little known in England.

The history of the exploration of the upper regions of the Ogowé can be found in the life of one man: the greatest of all West African explorers, Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza <note>M. de Brazza (1852–1905) was an Italian-born French explorer who opened up the Congo basin for France.</note>. It is impossible for anyone to fail to regard him with the deepest respect once they know from personal experience the nature of the country and the danger of the native populations he has dealt with—and continues to deal with—as he restlessly but wisely pushes forward to expand the territories of his country.

Walker, I have since my return received a list of these names spelled according to their native pronunciation. Thinking they may be valuable to future travelers, I will occasionally include them in footnotes.

<header>FRENCH CONGO <note>original: "CONGO FRANÇAIS"</note> CHAP. XVI</header>

adoption, France. Indeed, it takes someone who has personally experienced Africa to fairly estimate the value of certain pieces of work from what I might call an artistic standpoint. The "armchair explorer" may be impressed by the sheer length of an explorer's red-line route on a map. However, someone familiar with the region knows that some of those long red lines are very easy to achieve in Africa—thanks to the efforts of previous travelers, or to what one of my German friends once poetically called the "lamb-like stupidity" <note>original: "lamblike-calfheadedness"</note> of the natives, or because the terrain is naturally easy to cross. In other regions, a short red line represents four hundred times the work and danger, requiring four thousand times the courage, perseverance, and tact. We might call these regions "difficult spots."

I do not mean to diminish the value of extensive travel in Africa—far from it. Its value is enormous and so obvious that I don't need to dwell on it. However, the man who combines both—who makes his long red line pass through vast areas of difficult terrain—deserves special admiration. When, in addition to traversing these lands, he gains and maintains authority over the native people, uniting the districts and making his country's flag both respected and feared there, he is truly a great man. Such a man is de Brazza. Henry Morton Stanley <note>Stanley (1841–1904) was a Welsh-American explorer famous for finding David Livingstone and for his controversial role in establishing the Congo Free State for King Leopold II of Belgium.</note> might have been such a man as well, were it not for matters I will not discuss here, as they would lead us into a debate regarding the Congo Free State.

Pierre de Brazza’s first journey into the interior^1 of the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note> took place between 1875 and 1878. Accompanied by Dr. Noël Ballay and Alfred Marche, he reached the upper waters of the Ogowé River and then pushed eastward and northward. He discovered two new rivers, the Alima and the Licona, both of which he suspected were tributaries of the Congo River. He immediately recognized the importance of these rivers to the French colonies; through them, access could be gained to the Congo River above the Livingstone Rapids, which were the major barrier to navigation. He convinced the authorities in France of this and was commissioned by the French Committee of the African Association and

# XVI DE BRAZZA

[De Brazza was commissioned] by the Government to make a second journey in order to trace the Alima River to the Congo; to establish civilizing stations, one on the Ogooué <note>original: "Ogowé"</note> and one on the Congo; and to cultivate friendship with the native tribes throughout the region.

The Chambers [of the French Parliament] voted a grant toward the expenses, and he left France for Africa on December 27, 1879. M. Ballay, his companion on the first journey, remained behind to complete the preparations for the exploration, specifically the equipping of a steamer that was to be used for navigating the Ogooué and the Alima. When this steamer was ready in sections, M. Ballay was to bring it out and join de Brazza. In the story of every major expedition, there is always a steamer transported in sections, and such a steamer is invariably a burden that costs men's lives; de Brazza's steamer was no exception to the rule, but more on that later.

Two Europeans went out with de Brazza: M. Noguez and M. Michaud. Upon landing on the coast, he organized his expedition at Gaboon and ascended the Ogooué. The most difficult part of the journey was the stretch from Lambaréné <note>1</note> to Boué, due to the Fan people living all along this region and the rapids found throughout much of it. These rapids had to be navigated through the Crystal Mountains <note>original: "Sierra de Cristal"</note> because the wildness of the riverbanks made portage <term>the carrying of boats or goods overland</term> impossible. Once these mountains are passed, however, there is an open, park-like country where porters can be employed. At that point, you are no longer at the mercy of the swift, raging river that makes this portion of the voyage from Njole to Boué a particularly grueling experience. Beyond the Crystal Mountains, de Brazza made contact with the Okanda and Adouma <note>original: "Adooma"</note> tribes, people who were less ferocious and more helpful than the Fans. De Brazza gained great influence over these two tribes, arranging with them the regular system of communication with Njole that continues to this day, with the Adoumas transporting supplies up and down through the region of the rapids.

The native name for the island is Ezangé-nenge. In 1866, the name Lambaréné was held by one of the three Inlenga villages just below the confluence with the Zélé lake or lagoon.</note>

Two or three days' journey east from Franceville, the landscape <term>original: "nature of the country"</term> changes. The clay soil of the Ogooué <note>original: "Ogowé"</note> basin and its lush, wooded, moist valleys are replaced by a sandy, arid, hilly region, with groups of palm trees appearing here and there near the villages.

This is the appearance of the country that forms the watershed between the Ogooué and the tributaries of the Upper Congo. On both the northern and southern banks of the Congo, I found this same type of terrain <term>original: "make of country"</term> further toward the sea, in the Pallaballa mountains above Matadi.

De Brazza remarks that it is a striking <term>original: "singular"</term> fact that these narrow, sandy stretches of land are everywhere inhabited by the same tribe: the Bateke. He notes that they are reputed to be cannibals, though he suggests this reputation is likely mistaken.

<header>CONGO FRANÇAIS CHAP.</header>

After crossing the Leketi—a southern branch of the Alima River—his route took him across the Achicuya plateau. This elevated region sits about 2,600 feet above sea level and is separated from another similar plateau (the Aboma) by the Mpama River. (Mpama means "Ox.")

The chief of Achicuya welcomed the traveler warmly, and he received a similar welcome upon reaching the Abooma tribe. He describes these people as the handsomest and bravest he had encountered; it was from them that he learned about the Congo River and the powerful King Makoko, whose authority the Abooma recognize.

Leaving the Abooma district, he traveled along the Lefini River (which Mr. Stanley called the Lawson). Just as he was finishing the construction of a raft to descend the Lefini, messengers arrived from King Makoko with friendly greetings and offers of help. This greatly assisted his progress. He descended the Lefini on his raft with the king’s envoy as far as Ngampo. From there, he traveled overland for two days across an uninhabited plateau.

He states that his march over the sun-scorched plateau was exhausting. That two-day journey must have been a "choice spot" <term>original: "choice spot," used ironically to mean a particularly difficult place</term> if, as I suspect, this plateau was formed like those truly horrible Pallaballa mountains. Those mountains contain a massive amount of mica, which glitters in the sun like diamond dust and dazzles the eyes. Lacking vegetation, they reflect the burning heat in a scorching way, creating a layer of shimmering hot air. The entire desolate, hideous scene vibrates before your eyes, much like the air over a line of gas jets. I will never forget my own brief experience in the Pallaballa range. Nowhere else in West Africa have I encountered a place that so perfectly matched my idea of the infernal regions <term>original: "infernal region," meaning hell</term>. Even at night, the earth all around you exhales a heavy, hot breath from the heat it absorbed during the day.

It is no surprise that Monsieur <term>original: "M."</term> de Brazza "began to find fault with his guide, Makoko’s envoy, just before eleven o’clock on the second night after a forced march." Fortunately, shortly afterward, he came in sight of the Congo River. "It appeared like an immense..."

<header>KING MAKOKO</header>
<sig>XVI</sig>

...sheet of water, the silver sheen of which contrasted with the somber hue of the lofty mountains around. Toward the northwest, the waterline extended to the horizon, and the river swept in a noiseless, slow current past the foot of the hills below."

His first objective on reaching the banks of the Great River <note>The Congo River</note> was to establish peaceful relations with the Apfuru and other tribes of the Ubangi nation. The principal tribe of this family are the Alhialumo, "sailors of the Congo," who are born, live, and die with their families on board the fine canoes in which they carry on their trade in ivory and other goods between the Alima and Stanley Pool. This was the case during de Brazza's first visit. Now I am informed that this trade route has been considerably diverted.

De Brazza addressed himself to Ngampey, their chief, who seemed inclined to be friendly. "Choose," de Brazza said, "between the cartridge and the flag I send you. One will be the sign of a war without mercy; the other, a symbol of a peace as profitable to you as to us." He gave the tribes on this side time to think over their answer and went on to meet King Makoko.

De Brazza states here that he felt his rights of priority and those of France were now clearly established over the entire region between the Ogowe, the Equator, and the Congo. He next wished to extend this influence over the left bank of the Congo to the north, as far as the confluence of the Djue River to the south of Stanley Pool. In this part of the country, the plateaus are more fertile and better cultivated than those in the interior, and the population is denser and equally peaceful. "Since the Muslim element <note>original: "Mussulman element"</note> is unknown in this region," says de Brazza, "European civilization need not expect to encounter the hostility, hatred, and fanaticism which force the French, for example, to advance only with armed forces from the Senegal to the Niger. There is nothing to be feared there except the natural opposition of the natives to whatever is new."

Makoko received him with all available magnificence. De Brazza remained twenty-five days with the chief and for a longer period in his provinces; he "could not have been better treated."

In the end, a treaty was concluded by which the king placed his territories under the protection of France and ceded a tract of land along the shores of the Congo, to be selected by Monsieur de Brazza. The treaty was ratified on an appointed day in the presence of all King Makoko's subordinate chiefs. Upon its completion, the high priest <note>Original: "grand fetish master"; a spiritual or ritual leader</note> put a little earth in a box and presented it to de Brazza, saying, “Take this earth and carry it to the great chief of the whites. It will remind him that we belong to him.” De Brazza then planted the French flag in front of Makoko’s house, saying, “This is the symbol of friendship and protection which I will leave with you. Wherever this emblem of peace waves, France is present, and she will ensure that the rights of everyone it protects are respected.”

I do not hesitate to say that, as far as the French Congo is concerned (though I have no experience with other French territories), this grand statement is true. Although de Brazza achieved a great victory for France that day, Makoko also benefited, for he saved himself from the Congo Free State <note>The Congo Free State was the personal colony of King Leopold II of Belgium, notorious for its extreme colonial brutality.</note>.

Soon after signing this treaty with Makoko, de Brazza left him and attended a meeting with the Ubangi chiefs at Nganchuno on the Congo. The chiefs arrived in an unsettled state of mind and initially showed great opposition to concluding a treaty. They expressed their mistrust because of a previous white traveler <note>Likely a reference to Henry Morton Stanley, whose 1877 expedition was marked by several violent conflicts with local tribes.</note> who had shot a member of the tribe and escaped down the river too quickly to be pursued. However, after a second major meeting, a peace treaty was arranged, and war was "buried." This ceremony involved each chief and every member of de Brazza's small party burying a weapon in a hole, over which a fast-growing tree was then planted. French flags were distributed among the chiefs, and the treaty was definitely agreed upon.

De Brazza then set off to choose the site for a station on the Congo. He traveled five days down the river to the west into Stanley Pool, finally selecting Ntamo, now known as Brazzaville. He formally took possession of this site under his agreement with Makoko and raised the French flag there on October 1, 1880. <meta>catchword: Its</meta>

<page-num>361</page-num>
<header>XVI BRAZZAVILLE</header>

The selection of this site has faced significant criticism, but it is clear that it holds a strategic commanding position. Without the cooperation of Brazzaville, no one can travel from the Upper to the Lower Congo *by way of* <note>original: "via"</note> the river. The Livingstone Rapids of the Congo, which begin to the west of the city, are indeed permanent obstacles to steamships navigating the Congo for about 200 miles; yet they do not block canoe transport because the banks of the Congo, unlike those of the Ogowé, allow for portage <term>the practice of carrying watercraft or cargo over land between two navigable waters</term>.

It must be admitted that these rapids of the Congo are a major challenge. The waters collected by the great river in its drainage area of 1,600,000 square miles pass through a narrow channel 170 miles long, carved by the water through the rocks of the Pallaballa range. The river descends 1,000 feet through violent stretches of rushing water, interrupted by thirty-two distinct cataracts. However, to overcome these, a railway is currently being built from Matadi to Stanley Pool; for the courage and skillful navigation of Captain Murray proved that it was possible to take an ocean-going steamship through the whirlpools of Hell's Cauldron to Matadi, which is near the base of the final cataract, the Yellala, and 120 miles from the sea. It is certain that the Congo Free State <note>The private colony of King Leopold II of Belgium</note> must soon be divided among the colonial powers in Africa. When that happens, the long stretch of territory from Brazzaville to the Ubangi confluence—which France already possesses thanks to Monsieur de Brazza—will give France control over the entire Middle Congo region. This is the district that funnels its trade into the Congo for the 1,000 miles separating the Livingstone Falls from the Stanley Falls.

Access to the right bank of the Congo at Stanley Pool is undoubtedly easier; however, those southern regions not currently held by the Congo Free State belong to Portugal. Portugal would have little hope of acquiring a tract of land when its rival for it is France. Portugal has already been almost entirely pushed out of the Congo region, which its great explorer Diogo Cão discovered in 1482. Nevertheless, Portugal still holds the southern bank of the Congo from the sea to a location (Nkoi) just below Matadi, and a very large amount of the Congo trade flows into its territory because—

Along the way, he met Mr. Stanley <note>Henry Morton Stanley</note>, who received him warmly.

From the mouth of the Congo, he sailed to Gaboon, arriving at Libreville on December 15, 1880. A bitter disappointment awaited him there, which—as one might expect—involved that steamer. Neither de Ballay <note>Dr. Noël Ballay, a French explorer and associate of de Brazza</note> nor the steamer had arrived. This must have been an incredibly frustrating setback, one that would have caused many people to abandon the entire project. He had sent 770 men and 44 canoes downriver, promising them various amazing displays of the white man’s power and plenty of work; instead, there was neither. De Brazza admitted he felt pained to find himself so poorly supported. Although he had personally fulfilled everything he had set out to do, instead of returning to Europe to recover from his exhaustion, he was forced to hurry back into the interior. He needed to bring reinforcements to the men left in charge of the two stations he had founded—one 500 miles away and the other 800 miles away.

He set out for the interior again with a party reinforced by two French sailors, Guiral and Amiel, as well as several native carpenters, gardeners, and others. While traveling up the Ogowé River for the third time, his canoe capsized at the Boué Falls. He became very ill after spending a long time working in the water to recover his luggage. When he arrived at Franceville in February 1881, he found 100 native people successfully settled and working in various trades. The gardens were well-tended, and the settlement was self-sufficient. 

Despite everything, de Brazza still had not lost faith in that steamer, and he began preparing a way to transport it once it finally arrived. There were seventy-five miles of portage <term>carrying boats or goods overland between two waterways</term> between the Franceville station and the point where the Obia and Lekiba rivers meet the Alima. This was the spot chosen to begin navigating the Alima River. With the help of 400 laborers supervised by Michaud, Guiral, and Amiel, they cleared a path to transport the sections of the steamer.

The organization of a transport service was then undertaken, a task of some difficulty due to the jealousies of the tribes regarding the profits from carrying goods over different sections of the route. He brought news to de Brazza that Ballay was being detained at Gaboon and that the steamer had construction defects that would prevent it from joining the expedition for a long time.

Mr. de Brazza then resolved to leave Franceville in the charge of Mr. Mizon and go off on an entirely new exploration. By now, after three voyages up and down them, he was aware that the rapids of the Ogowé are not exactly a safe or pleasant route to Franceville, particularly for heavy goods. He returned to his old idea, which he had been forced to abandon testing when leaving Brazzaville in 1880: namely, that a safer route to the sea-coast than the Ogowé provides existed down the Niari valley. Through this expedition, M. de Brazza claimed a territory one-third the size of France as an addition to his previous discoveries. It was in the hands of France, and the route by way of the Niari was the best path to it and the best line for a railway; he argued that the French should undertake this project as the most effective way to open up the country.

The construction of this railroad has been undertaken. The fact that it has not yet been completed stems, I believe, from the belief that the Congo Free State <note>The territory then under the personal sovereignty of King Leopold II of Belgium</note> will shortly fall into the hands of France. At that point, the route up the Congo River—with a railway to bypass the Livingstone Rapids—would be the best and shortest way to Brazzaville and the Middle Congo region in general. However, until that day comes, France has done much to utilize the Niari valley route, and regular convoys now use it to reach the interior. With his characteristic insight into African geographical issues, de Brazza recognized that the Sanga River was more likely to provide a route to the central Sudan <note>original: "Soudan"</note> from the Congo than the seemingly more significant Ubangi <note>original: "M'ubungi"</note> River. Camfurel was the first person dispatched to chart the course of the Sanga, but he and his expedition were completely destroyed. Furneaux was sent next and managed to travel several days' journey beyond the Sanga rapids before he encountered conflict; one white man and seventeen black men of his party were killed. He then returned to de Brazza, who personally ascended the river as far as the rapids and established a station there that is now frequented by African traders. I should note that as proof he had reached an inland trade route, he encountered traders carrying passports from Algeria on the Mediterranean, which he then countersigned. Some of these people accompanied him, and when he returned to Brazzaville, horses from the Sudan were photographed next to a steamship on the Congo.

He reported that as soon as one left the Ogowe <note>original: "Ogowé"</note> forests to the north, the region became exceptionally healthy, and none of the expedition members suffered from illness. He also noted that this country is abundant in cattle and horses. The lieutenant must have been crossing highlands for part of the journey between the Ogowe and the Niger. However, I suspect that the claim of the country being healthy for white men is only because there are no white men there to die and contribute to a mortality rate. I do not believe that any part of Africa between the Zambezi and the Sahara is healthy for white men.

A railroad is currently under construction to open a route from the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note> to Lake Chad, following the course of the Sanga River. When completed, this will establish a series of markets that will be of great importance due to the wealth of the region they will serve. It should become the primary trade route for ivory and other commerce throughout north-central Africa. 368 FRENCH CONGO CHAPTER

Unless Providence, in the form of death, or Sir George Goldie—de Brazza’s only rival in administrative skill in West Africa—intervenes, he will succeed in uniting the French Congo with the French Sudan. De Brazza has accomplished so much and done it so well that I, as a woman, may be excused for the sentimental hope that he lives to see his structure of power completed.

After outlining the work of de Brazza the finisher, we must turn to the work of Du Chaillu, the pioneer of geographical knowledge in this region. However, I will only briefly summarize Du Chaillu’s work because his books are available to English readers and are not hidden in the scattered journals of geographical societies, as are the reports on de Brazza.

Anyone interested in the African forest region should read Du Chaillu’s works carefully. In them, you will find a series of wonderfully vivid pictures of life—both of man and beast—and of the country itself, with its dense, gloriously beautiful, gloomy forests and its wild rivers. These descriptions remain as true today as the day Du Chaillu wrote them. Upon his return to England, great doubt was cast on his accounts; however, I have no hesitation in saying that while I was in that region, I never encountered anything that discredited Du Chaillu’s narrative as a whole. 

The conclusions he drew from what he saw are a separate matter, as no two West African travelers ever agree on their interpretations. But his descriptions of the land and the animals are truthful—yes, including those gorillas. I know places where the gorilla population is just as dense as he describes and the individuals just as large. Furthermore, his accounts of the indigenous people and their customs are recognizable to anyone with personal knowledge of the area. I am glad to say I am not alone in this opinion. One of the greatest authorities on this matter, Dr. Nassau—who was on the coast at the same time as Du Chaillu—states that nothing Du Chaillu relates is outside the realm of possibility in this country. No more could be said of any traveler from the school of which Du Chaillu, Dr. Barth, Joseph Thomson, and Livingstone are masters—and of which I am a humble member. We do not have a group of white companions with us to confirm our statements and say, "Yes, yes, certainly, Sir" <note>original: "Oui, oui, certainement, Monsieur"</note>, as the engineer and his brother used to say to their captain on the *Éclaireur*; but we

<header>XVI DU CHAILLU</header>

...have great compensations for this. We do not have terrible arguments with each other in difficult locations in Africa, or upon our return home, and we can say to our critics: “Have you been there? No? Then go there—or to whatever place you may happen to believe in—and until then, shut up.” Mr. Winwood Reade accepted this kind of answer from Du Chaillu and traveled down to the regions of the Panavia Bight and Gaboon with a predetermined intent to prove Du Chaillu was wrong; and I must say I think he utterly failed. He did not follow Du Chaillu’s route throughout by any means, doing little more than going behind Corisco Bay and up the Gaboon estuary and the Como River—a very good piece of work, and charmingly described in his book *Savage Africa*—but he was not in the areas rich with gorillas in either location.

Du Chaillu’s journeys may be divided into two main groups, one of which is described in his first book, *Explorations and Adventures in Equatorial Africa* (1861). During this journey, he ascended the Muni River as far as the Osheba <gloss>1</gloss> country, and the Como and Boqué rivers as far as the Sierra del Cristal. He marched overland from the Gaboon estuary to the rivers of the Ogowé Delta and performed a great deal of work throughout this vast, dangerous network. He traveled up and down the N'Poulounay <gloss>2</gloss> and the O’Rembo and reached the upper waters of the Ngunie, moving back and forth among the tribes of the Sierra del Cristal and the mountains of Achangoland. On his second journey, made in 1864–1865, he was entirely in regions south of the Ogowé. He entered Fernan Vaz, followed the O’Rembo for a short distance, and then headed east-by-south, crossing the Ngunie at a point south of the spot he had reached when he first discovered the river in 1858. From there, he continued into the mountains of Achangoland, where he was attacked and forced to make a very hurried retreat to the ocean.

He reached Orongo, a little above Osoamokita, definitely proving that the Gaboon estuary was not a mouth of the Ogowé and was quite disconnected from it.

From those days until the time of de Brazza, the most important explorer on the Ogowé was Mr. R. B. N. Walker. Mr. Walker reached Lope—the furthest point reached until de Brazza’s 1889 journey—and, in addition to this, he conducted many exploratory expeditions in the region.¹ 

Next came the missionary journeys of Dr. Nassau, who was well-established at Talagouga,² with his house and church already built when de Brazza arrived in 1879. Since de Brazza opened up the district, the only travelers I know of who have passed through the region up the Ogowé rapids are Messrs. <note>original: "MM."</note> Alegret and Tesseris. They made a journey all the way up the Ogowé and out onto the Congo to select sites for mission stations. I am indebted to these gentlemen for many photographs of native peoples on the Upper Ogowé.
