### FRENCH CONGO CHAPTER <note>original: "CONGO FRANÇAIS CHAP."</note>

...at a place called Lestourville, close to Franceville, established in memory of a Governor who died, are now the outposts of Christianity in these West African regions. The main results of these travels on the Ogowé may be summarized as having shown that the Ogowé is one of the great rivers of Africa. It is the largest river between the Niger and the Congo and the largest strictly equatorial river in the world, with its course lying fairly neatly along the equator for over 700 miles. It has a catchment basin roughly computed—for its basin is not yet thoroughly explored—at 130,000 square miles, and its discharge of water into the Atlantic is, according to the season, between 360,000 and 1,750,000 cubic feet per second.

Its main tributaries are, in order of importance, the Ngunie, entering on its south bank, and the Ivindo and the Okanda, both of which enter on its north bank.

The Ogowé is, on the whole, more similar in nature to the Congo than to the Niger, except that unlike the Congo, it has an immense delta. This delta begins at Lambaréné, just below the point where it receives the waters of the Ngunie River. The delta region is tremendously interesting in terms of its flora, fauna, and <term>fetish</term> <note>Traditional spiritual practices and religious objects.</note>; however, it lacks commercial trade. Its main population consists of malaria microbes and mosquitoes, and it is extremely damp. Indeed, the entire delta and the country from the Gaboon to Sette Cama¹—except for the strange bubble-shaped mountains like Mount Sangatõ, Mount Mandji, and Mount Okoneto—are underwater when the Ogowé and its neighboring rivers flood during the "long wet" season. The lakes in the Lambaréné district, Elivã Ayzingo and the even larger Elivã z’onlange, along with the entire string of lakes along the O’Rembo, Ungo, and Vinue, overflow into the forest. The Sierra del Cristal <note>The Crystal Mountains.</note> cuts the course of the Ogowé just above Njole, forming the region of the rapids. There are 500 miles of these rapids, making navigation impossible in any other craft...

It was first opened as a trading station by Henry Walker in 1849, who traded from a ship. His brother, R. B. N. Walker, established a factory on the shore there in 1857. The natives have a bad reputation to this day.

<header>XVI THE OGOWÉ</header>

...[nothing] but a canoe, and it is highly perilous work in that, I assure you from personal experience. When you get above the rapids, the river is not of much use except for canoes until you reach Franceville. Beyond Franceville, it is only navigable by canoes during the wet season; however, you do not need the Ogowé there, as it is in contact with the great rivers flowing across it into the Congo.

Below the rapids, however, the Ogowé is a grand waterway, as far as waterways go on the West Coast. You can travel up its main stream to Njolé for over 200 miles, and up its tributary <term>affluent</term> <note>A stream or river that flows into a larger river or lake; a tributary.</note>, the Ngunié, as far as Samba, where there are lovely falls. Above these falls and a series of rapids, the Ngunié would again be accessible to small steamboats, but there are none there at present.

In addition to the main stream of the Ogowé, you can—with the exercise of great care and the assistance of good fortune—navigate a small steamboat into Lake Ayzingo and Lake Z’onlange during the wet season. You can also enter the main stream of the Ogowé from the ocean via two side creeks that run down to Fernan Vaz. The current of the Ogowé is extremely swift, particularly above Lambaréné, and during the wet season, the river rises eighteen to twenty feet in the Talagouga narrows. This rise begins a month before the wet season is fully established here, likely because the rains start earlier on the upper waters of the tributaries that join above Njolé—the Okanda and the Ivindo.

The southern region of the delta is more water-eroded than the northern part. The stretch of land to the north, between the Ogowé delta and the Gaboon, is bordered along the seashore and the estuary by a kind of sand rampart. This barrier holds back the floodwaters of the wet season, creating a morass that is almost impossible to navigate during this period. The human population of this region is sparse; those who do live there reside in villages on the steep, bubble-shaped hills that rise in isolation here and there. This region is very little explored. The main stream of the Ogowé, entered either from Nazareth Bay or from Fernan Vaz, serves as the highway to and from the interior; the unhealthiness and lack of trade in this vast, swampy forest belt offer...

<meta>This page continues the description of the Ogowé River region in the French Congo, moving from the geography of the waterways to the landscape of the riverbanks and the intense weather patterns of the rainforest.</meta>

<page-num>374</page-num>
<header>FRENCH CONGO CHAPTER</header>

...there is little reason to travel around in it. Along the banks of the main waterways passing through the region, the villages are all situated in similar spots: perched on top of a clay bank or a small cliff. Behind these, the land slopes steeply down into what becomes a swamp during the rainy season. On every side rises the massive forest, draped in <term>lianes</term> <note>Woody climbing plants or vines found in tropical forests.</note> and supported by white trunks. One could say it rises on all sides without exception, even facing the broad river; for across the water stands another cliff of trees, and the forest and sky are mirrored back in the deep, dark water. This is all the world consists of for the inhabitants of these villages. They are born, live, and die seeing nothing but this universe of forest, river, and sky—and only a small portion of the sky, which they can see above the river—with no break except for sleep.

The only variety they experience is brought by the seasons: the gloomy dry season, when the wind drifts softly up the river in the morning and back down the river in the evening; and the tornado seasons, with their bursts of earth-shaking thunder and lightning that strikes the forest in great forked splashes. During these times, howling, shrieking, and moaning winds rush through the woods with devastating force, claiming as many victims among the giant trees as even the lightning does.

Watching a massive tornado pass through a high forest is a sight to behold, but it is anything but pleasant to experience. There is a heavy, brooding, suffocating heat when the great storm seems to press its hot chest down against the very ground. A sensation of depression and misery creeps over you, and every living thing clearly feels dread for what they know is coming. This apprehension turns into terror when the storm breaks and sweeps toward the sea with all the frenzy of its demonic power and the roar of its rain. Behind it lie the corpses of many of the grandest trees. Some are scorched by lightning and left standing, transformed in a moment from lush living things into gaunt skeletons. Others are thrown down, with all their magnificent foliage and <term>bush-rope</term> <note>A local term for thick, woody tropical vines used like rope.</note> stripped away by the wind's force, which has twisted them around and pulled them straight out by the roots. These are things 100 to 200 feet high, yet they are pulled up just as you would pull out a root of <term>groundsel</term> <note>A common, easily uprooted weed.</note>! The storm flings them crashing among their fellows, leaving them as wrecks to rot.

<page-num>375</page-num>
<header>XVI THE WET SEASON 375</header>

Then comes the wet season. Here, it is not like the wet season in the Rivers <term>The "Rivers" refers to the Oil Rivers, the delta region of the Niger River.</term>, which is one grim, torrential waterfall. Instead, there are daily heavy sheets of rain interspersed with intervals of bright sunshine and accompanied by heavy, steamy heat. During this time, the Ogowé River becomes muddier every day. Its swift current carries along bits of the riverbank with trees still growing on them, surrounded by tangled masses of grass and driftwood. These form the well-known "floating islands" that mariners often encounter miles out at sea off this coast.

Every day, the river rises higher against the banks, overflowing the lowest sections into the deeper parts of the forest. This flooding threatens to destroy the clay or mud cliffs and the villages perched upon them. Often, the river carries out this threat, tearing down parts of the clay banks, swamping and sweeping away the fragile houses, and ruining the nearby plantations of plantains.

Between the Kama country <note>Sometimes spelled Camma country. The native name is Akama. The tribes living in it are known as the Nkâmi, or frequently the Ncomi.</note> and the Ouroungou country, the channel of the Ogowé is, fortunately, broad. This allows the swollen waters to flow easily into the low-lying, uninhabited parts of the forest. If this were not the case, those clay cliffs would suffer far more than they do now, and the villages would be even more unstable places to live. In the Talagouga gorge, the current is much more fierce because the waters are hemmed into a narrower channel and the banks are made of the hard rocks of the Sierra del Cristal. Here, even though the water rises twenty or thirty feet above the dry-season level, it does not cause the same destruction seen in the clay bank region.

The long wet season <note>In the local language, the long wet season is called Nlyanja.</note> begins in September and lasts until the end of January, reaching its greatest intensity in November and December. In February, there is a short dry season, followed by a short wet season that lasts until May. From May until September is the long dry season <note>In the local language, the long dry season is called Enomo.</note>. However, these seasons cannot be relied upon with the same certainty one might have regarding the weather on the Gold Coast or in the Rivers. That said, the long dry season and the long wet season generally live up to their names.

One peculiarity of the dry season is that it is the coolest season...

<meta>This page continues the description of the climatic shifts in West Africa, transitioning from the description of the Ogowé River's flooding to the broader seasonal patterns found between Cameroon and Angola.</meta>

<page-num>376</page-num>
<header>FRENCH CONGO CHAP.</header>

The sky, often overhung with gray, threatening clouds, belongs to a climate that extends from just below Cameroon to Angola—that is, to the edge of the Kalahari Desert, where there are no wet seasons. It seems very strange and peculiar to someone coming south from the Bights <term>The Bight of Benin and the Bight of Biafra, large bays along the West African coast.</term>, where the dry season is the hot season and the wet season is the cooler one. One of the many difficulties of traveling down the West African coast is that you are certain to get your timing for the seasons wrong somewhere. 

It is not as difficult for me as it is for some people, because I actually prefer the wet season and have made my peace with the climate. However, a person with a preference for dry seasons has a miserable life of it, and I must fairly admit that such a preference is the more sensible one to have. I know an American gentleman who "reckoned he would conquer West Africa," but ultimately "reckoned West Africa had conquered him." He became so frustrated by the fact that different seasons occurred at different times in different parts of the Coast that he described the entire West African climate as "a fried eel." Why he said "fried," I do not know. In this Coast climate, we do not fry; we stew—and I consider his statement harsh. 

Of course, we have the worst climate in the world, and we are proud of it. Someday I will write a ten-volume work that will be a complete guide to the whole subject. It will be what my German friends would call the essential handbook for West African travelers, and it will let them know what to expect, as well as when, where, and how. But in the meantime, I may note that both the wet and dry seasons have their advantages. 

If you want to travel far up a river without having many opportunities to study the various ways your boat can get wrecked on sandbanks, you must go during the height of the wet season. Of course, this usually results in your returning, or attempting to return, during the dry season. Once you have traveled any distance into the interior, you typically start your return journey at full speed, pursued by greedy and ferocious cannibals. In such a situation, the fact that you get stuck on sandbanks an average of three times per mile causes considerable anxiety. 

If you wish to travel into the interior on foot, you must choose the dry season because of the swamps. A truly bottomless swamp is impassable in the wet season. In the dry season, it develops a crust over it which, with proper precautions, can be crossed, while the shallow swamps can be waded through. And all the rivers are—

[These rivers are] navigable by canoe during the dry season, even if they are too shallow for steamers; besides, canoes are the most comfortable way to travel in the entire world. The preference for small steam launches is a mystery to me. I cannot imagine what joy any sane person, who is not in a rush, could find in one. I have had some experience with them, and those experiences were among the worst I have ever endured. I remember one time when I tried to navigate a small launch through a creek that, while deep, was choked with water grass. You could not raise a sail because there was no wind strong enough to penetrate the grass, which grew in a thick mass about ten feet higher than your funnel <term>the smokestack of the steam engine</term>. # FRENCH CONGO CHAPTER

If anyone can suggest a better solution, I would be absolutely delighted to hear it, for it was exhausting work, and these difficult spots are quite common in West African rivers. I also remember another steam launch—the *Dragon Fly*. She had been built to burn coal, but since no coal was available, she had to burn wood. Wood, as my nautical friends would say, fills a ship up to capacity <term>referred to in the original as "blows a ship out"</term>. To store enough wood to travel even twenty miles, you had to stack wooden logs everywhere: all over the deck, on top of the sun-deck, and so on. This was done to such an extent that there was no room for passengers, and the gunwale <term>the upper edge of the boat's side</term> was nearly underwater. 

Furthermore, you always ran aground on sandbanks—often several of them—so the wood was completely burned up before you reached your destination. Consequently, you had to return by drifting with the current and using poles. If I had been forced to continue traveling in her, we would have spent most of our lives chopping wood in damp forests. However, I am far too anxious a person to venture into the interior on the *Dragon Fly* with her crumbling boiler.

Then there was a patented launch that was supposed to move, theoretically, by the explosion of small quantities of gunpowder. However, the commercial gunpowder we had did not seem to suit her, so she adopted a policy of "masterly inactivity," making terrifying noises in her machinery. The fastest trip she ever made was straight to the bottom of the river—and she certainly accomplished that using the commercial powder. 

I admit I am prejudiced against launches. The heat of the West Coast climate is quite enough for me without sitting next to a massive hot water bottle in the form of a boiler. A canoe, however, is a vessel you can take almost anywhere. It is therefore better for general work, unless you have a deep enough channel to accommodate a steamer of a respectable size.

In addition to grassy creeks and sandbanks, the obstacles to navigating the side streams of the Ogowé and its neighboring rivers include papyrus swamps—which are beautiful but difficult to pass through—and large floating masses of water lettuce <note>original: "*Pistia stratiotes*"</note>. It looks very much like a well-grown cabbage lettuce. It is quite charming to look down a creek filled with it, as the beautiful, soft green creates a perfect scene against the dark forest rising from the banks. <meta>This page continues the author's description of "river-lettuce" and how its root system creates hazards for navigation, as well as the formation of floating islands.</meta>

up another lettuce. If you go up that creek eighteen months or so later in a small launch, the plant winds those roots around your propeller. The fierce current of the wet season—when the main river scours the creeks and the creeks develop strong currents of their own from the increased water—wreaks great havoc on these lettuce beds. Large patches of them are cut off from the main mass. These patches float downriver, and as soon as they reach calm water or snag on a rising sandbank, they collect all the other floating debris that comes their way and begin to form islands. The grass soon chokes out its companion, the lettuce, and makes the island habitable for other plants; thus, you have a floating island. These floating islands possess a strange fascination, and I never saw as many of them in any river as I did in the Ogowé. It is unsettling to one’s general ideas of natural order to see what looks like solid land solemnly drifting past you down the river as if it were out on business. Or, if you are in tidal waters and stationed at a fixed point, to see it approach you, linger, and then retire. One of the largest of these floating islands I saw was in the Karkolá River. It had been caught in an eddy created by another stream entering the river, and it kept circling slowly and quietly.

I have not described even half the difficulties of navigating a tropical river in the forest region, because they are so numerous, and many of them cannot be guarded against. There are logs that, because of their density <term>specific gravity</term>, float just beneath the surface and strike you unexpectedly; even those logs that float on the surface are nasty things to encounter on a pitch-black night. I well remember the various "joys" we encountered once while traveling down the Ogowé in the dark in a small canoe. For half the journey, the canoe was like a horse in a steeplechase jumping over floating logs. Sometimes the boat refused its fences <note>A metaphor comparing the canoe's collision with logs to a horse refusing to jump a hurdle in a race.</note> entirely and simply rammed them. Sometimes it would climb up them and tip over on the other side. Even my experienced native companion admitted that it was difficult to tell—during the resulting "aquatic sports" the crew was forced to indulge in—which was the bottom of the canoe and which was a plain, natural log. Sometimes the boat would clear its log-fence in a single, impressive leap; but then, as it came down on the other side, it would sink too deep and fill with water and

# XVI TAKING THE TIMBER

...foundered, so the only solution was to push the logs away with a pole. Some of those logs, by the way, had strange ways about them. One, when poked on its end as it floated toward us, opened its front section and bit the pole with such a grip that the man using it let go instantly. Yes, I suppose it was a crocodile—nevertheless, African vegetation is a strange thing indeed.

You would naturally think that, despite sandbanks with cliff-like edges downstream, sections of the continent floating around, and logs that may or may not be liable to bite, you had at least one thing left to rely on—the bank. But that bank might be solid, or then again, as the captain of the late steamship (*ss.*) *Sparrow* would say, it might not be. For example, a friend of mine who got stuck in a launch on a sandbank up a river creek brought out a heavy rope <term>hawser</term> and, winding it around some mangroves on the bank, proceeded “to pull her off in no time” using the steam winch. The boat did not move an inch, but the African continent did: the entire section of the bank gave way, and the trees came crashing down on the boat with a rush, burying everyone and everything in branches and leaves. As he said, we were “like the Babes in the Wood after the robins had been along, but on a massive scale” <note>A reference to the traditional English folktale "Babes in the Wood," in which robins cover the bodies of abandoned children with leaves</note>; he also stated, as we climbed onto the top of our structure of fallen trees, that “Africa was a rotten continent.”

## CHAPTER XVII

### THE LOG OF THE *LAFAYETTE*

->During a voyage undertaken to the island of Corisco, to which is added some account of the present condition of the island and its inhabitants, and also of that of Cape Esterias and things in general, as is the author's custom.<-

As soon as I returned to Glass <note>A district in Libreville, Gabon, where European traders and missionaries were established</note>, I naturally went to talk with Doctor Nassau <note>Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), a prominent American Presbyterian missionary and ethnologist</note> about Fetish <term>traditional West African religious and spiritual practices</term>. We spoke at length, and I found our conversation very beneficial. In one of these talks, the doctor mentioned that there were lakes in the center of the Island of Corisco, and that those lakes contained a great many fish. These fish were always and only caught by the local women during specific, set seasons. Needless to say, I felt it a solemn duty to go and investigate this personally. Equally needless to say, Doctor Nassau gave me every possible assistance, which took the form of lending me a small vessel called the *Lafayette*. She had been in his possession for a long time but had been little used in recent years; still, she was a fine, seaworthy boat. So, with a crew led by the Doctor’s personal assistant <term>factotum</term>, Eveke, who was a native of that island, along with a few of his friends, we set sail.

We left Libreville at 8:00 A.M. to get the full advantage of the wind and tide. Doctor Nassau kindly came down to the wharf to see us clear away. We then headed for the guard-ship to pass our papers, but we did so in a very unseamanlike way. We lowered our gaff <term>a spar used to support the top of a sail</term> too soon, and consequently had to row alongside the ship quite ignominiously. The offshore breeze was blowing strongly this morning, and the tide was running out like a mill-race <term>a very fast current of water</term>, so the *Lafayette* flew toward the sea.

...gallantly. Libreville looks very bright and pleasing—with its red roofs and white walls among the surrounding wealth of dark green mango trees. However, we soon leave it behind, passing along in front of the low, rolling hills, all densely covered with forests, out toward Cape Clara—or Cape Joinville, as some maps call it—which marks the end of the northern shore of the Gabon estuary. 

When we reach the Cape, we find a fairly rough sea running. Eveke, whose seamanship I am beginning to view with suspicion, allows the boat to jibe <term>a sailing maneuver where the stern of the boat crosses the wind, causing the sail to shift sides rapidly</term>, and I am knocked into the bottom of the boat by the boom and stay there. There is nothing like entering into the spirit of an experience like this if you intend to enjoy it; after all, that is the wisest thing to do out here, for there is nothing between enjoying it and dying from it. The sun is broiling hot; everything one has to sit on or hold onto is as hot as a burning brick, and there is no cabin, nor even a storage locker, on our craft. So, I prop myself up against my collecting box and lazily take stock of the things around me while I write.

My crew is a diverse group of Mpongwe <note>An ethnic group native to the Gabon estuary region</note>, who are dark-skinned but not particularly handsome. One gentleman, however, evidently thinks he is, as he has a beautiful pair of carefully tended whiskers—a rare feature for an African. He also wears a pair of kerseymere <term>a fine, twilled woolen cloth</term> trousers that are far too tight for him. But a man with whiskers "just like a white man's" must dress the part, and trousers are scarce in this country. 

Our cargo consists of two bags of salt, several bags and boxes of sand for ballast, several bottles of drinking water, a bundle of bedding (a loan from the Doctor), and a deck chair (a loan from Mr. Hudson). Since the *Lafayette* has no deck, the chair is "not required on the voyage" and remains folded. I observe with anxiety that the cargo is not packed in a way that would meet the approval of Captain Murray <note>A reference to a professional standard of naval order</note>, and I decide to get dunnage <term>loose material used to support and protect cargo in a ship's hold</term> and organize it properly at the first port we visit. It is impossible to shift the cargo in this sea. The crew drinks the water in such quantities that there will be a tragedy at sea if we become becalmed. We sail close to the shore from Cape Clara to Cape Esterias—a fine, sandy, rock-strewn coast backed by magnificent wilderness—for eight miles. The land then falls away, as Esterias is the southernmost point of Corisco Bay. Close to Cape Esterias

I see the familiar village built of bark that indicates the presence of the Fan people <note>The Fang people, an ethnic group of Central Africa</note>. Upon spotting this, we change our course and set one that appears to be heading toward Brazilian ports.

The *Lafayette* speeds along through a heavy sea. From my position at the bottom of the boat, I can see nothing but her large white mainsail and her mast, with its shrouds and stays <term>the ropes or cables used to support a ship's masts</term> standing out clearly and rocking back and forth against the hard blue sky. I see only the white crests of the waves as they dance by. I hear nothing but the most pleasant sounds in the world—the rustle of the sail and the swish of the waves as they play alongside the vessel. Now and then, the lazy, laughing conversation of the African crew is added to these sounds; occasionally, a particularly active wave splashes its crest over us. Soon the entire crew drifts off to sleep, and Eveke joins them. I rouse myself and take hold of the main sheet and the tiller to keep her on course. I feel as if I am being baked to a cinder by the sun, but there is no help for it, and some of the experience is quite pleasant. 

About four o’clock, I see two masses of land on the horizon. I wake Eveke, and he seems surprised that I do not know what they are. “That’s Corisco and Banã, sir,” he says. As I hand the navigation back over to him, I explain to Eveke that not everyone was fortunate enough to be born on Corisco, and the fact that he enjoyed this advantage is why he is the pilot now. I sit back down in the bottom of the boat and carefully look over the side, mindful of that previous boom palaver <term>referring to the earlier incident where the author was struck by the boat's boom; "palaver" here means trouble or a fuss</term>. We head for the larger and most western piece of land, and soon we can see the details of its rolling, dark-green forests. When we get within a mile, Eveke asks me to wake the man in front of me. I stir him firmly but gently with a chart, for I know what waking these men can lead to sometimes. When he rouses, I order him to wake the others. In a few minutes they are all more or less awake, even the lookout. They wash their mouths with sea-water and then resume their laughing, talking, and water-drinking.

We run into a small, wooded bay with a sandy shore. As I have found is Eveke’s habit, we lower our gaff <term>a spar used to support the top of a sailing vessel's four-sided sail</term> too early and drift toward the shore in the customary way: slowly and stern-first. At last, the *Lafayette*, finding that everything has been left to her, says: “Look here, you fellows, if you don’t help..."

<header>XVII CORISCO</header>

"I won’t play," the wind seems to say, as it stops and the boat begins to swing broadside to the waves. So the oars—or sweeps, as I should call them, for we have evidently returned to fourteenth-century seamanship—are brought out, and in a few minutes we are bumping violently on the shore. We let go the anchor, make everything secure, and go onto the land. Once ashore, the crew—with the exception of myself and the pilot—indulge in a dance to stretch their cramped limbs. 

As no inhabitants appear, Eveke runs up into the little village facing us and hunts a few of them out. They come and stare at us in a dull, sluggish way, very different from my friends, the lively Fans <note>The Fang people, whom Kingsley had stayed with previously</note>. Eveke has enthusiastic greetings for them—especially for the young women. He hastily informs me that he is related to them. I hope he is. He says most of the people are away at the farms, which is no great loss to me, because Eveke wastes enough time on the ones we have already found, and they seem like a grumpy lot for Africans. 

The only question they ask us is: "Do you have any tobacco?" Corisco is nearly out of tobacco because the weather has been too rough lately for them to cross over to either Eloby or Cocco Beach, where the factories <term>In this context, trading posts or warehouses for merchants</term> are located, to get more. They are pleased by our positive answer and sit down in a line on a large log, smiling at us in a quiet way while we unload the things we need from the *Lafayette* and finish securing her for the night. This being done, Eveke and I set off for his father’s house—his father, the Reverend Mr. Ibia <note>Originally spelled Ibea; Ibia j'Ikeke was a prominent Benga clergyman and educator</note>, being the only representative of the American Presbyterian mission currently on Corisco Island.

I have heard much of the strange variety of scenery to be found on this island: how it contains, in miniature, rivers, lakes, forests, prairies, swamps, and mountains; and our walk demonstrates the absolute truth of that statement. Since the tide is now nearly in, we cannot walk along the beach the whole way, which is a mercy—for that beach is made of the softest, whitest sand imaginable where it is dry; and where it is wet, the sand is a soft, pinkish dove-gray. Furthermore, it is piled with seaweed in various stages of decay, into which you sink past your ankles with every exhausting step. On its surface, you see centipedes crawling and, needless to say, plenty of sandflies. When we come to a point of any...

Leaving one of the many small bays or indentations in the coastline where the sea breaks, we climb up the bank and turn inland. Still ankle-deep in sand, we walk through what feels like a museum of physical geography. First, we see a sample of grassland, then follow a lane of thickly intertwined bushes, then descend into a forest with a small, currently nearly dried-up swamp in its depths. We then emerge onto an open heath that has recently been burned and is covered with dead ferns and scorched oil palms. Next, we pass through a village back into the grass, and then return to the beach to trudge through seaweed across another bay. We then circle some remarkable rocks, climb into a forest, cross more grass, more bushes, and more beach, and go up among a cluster of coconut palms and more grass. This is followed by a long stretch of path where one side is a thick hedge that is encroaching in a way that requires energetic pruning, for the bushes lean so far across the path that you also have to lean at an angle of nearly 45° toward the other side. I begin to lose hope, my boots being full of sand, and I fear we shall never finish seeing all these "specimens" before nightfall. There is such an air of elaborate completeness about this museum, and we have not even started on the glacier or river departments. However, at length, we see what seems to be the entrance to an English park, and coming up to it, we find a beautiful avenue of mango trees.

Corisco evidently suffers severely during the dry season. The dry, sandy soil is thickly covered with dead leaves. At the end of the avenue, there is a pretty wooden house, painted white, with its doors and window frames painted a bold, bright blue. Around it are a cluster of similar outbuildings, each mounted on poles: the little church, the store, and the house for the children in the mission school. A troop of children rush out and greet Eveke enthusiastically. One of them, I am informed, is his brother, and he begins to chatter away in Benga <note>A Bantu language spoken by the people of Corisco and the surrounding coast</note>. I send Eveke off to find his mother, thinking he would like to have his greetings with her unobserved. After a few minutes, she comes forward to greet me—a pretty, bright-looking lady whom it is hard to believe is old enough to be Eveke’s mother; and not only Eveke’s, but the mother of a group of strong young women who come forward with her.

# XVII A NATURAL BREAKWATER

...and the grandmother of other strapping young women mixed in among them. I really must try to find out which is which. Until I do, it will perhaps be diplomatic to treat them all as her daughters. Mrs. Ibea insists, in the kindest way possible, that I take possession of her own room. She says Mr. Ibea is away on an evangelizing visit to the mainland at Cape St. John (the northern extremity of Corisco Bay) and intends to call at Eloby Island. He may not be back for several days, so she promptly gives me tea and <term>alligator pears (avocados)</term>, both of which are exceedingly welcome.

The views from the windows of my clean and comfortable room are very beautiful. The house stands on a high promontory called Alondo Point, which is the turning point between the south and west sides of the island, and it almost overhangs the sea. A reef of rock runs along the foot of the cliff for about a mile, where the sea breaks constantly. The great rollers of the South Atlantic, meeting their first obstacle here since they left Cape Horn and the Americas, fly up in sheets of foam with a never-ending thunder. I go to bed early, thankfully observing that the bright mosquito curtain is entirely "for dandy"—meaning it is decorative and not actually needed for defense. <note>Kingsley notes that there were no mosquitoes to defend against at this location.</note>

Since my main object in visiting Corisco is to obtain specimens of fish from the lakes in the center of the island, I set to work by starting immediately after breakfast for the bay we reached last night, which I will call Nassau Bay in the future. I travel along the same varied path I took yesterday. Eveke slept at the village in the bay among his relatives so that he could, he says, keep an eye on the *Lafayette*. When I find him, he tells me that only women can catch the lake fish, and that they always catch them in specific baskets. Since these baskets have to be manufactured, they cannot be ready today. 

Having heard that Corisco is famous for shells, and having seen nothing on any of the many beaches on the southern side of the island more <term>conchologically</term> <note>relating to the scientific study of shells</note> charming than half a dozen dilapidated whelks, I ask where the main deposits of shells are located. Eveke says there is any quantity of them on the other little islands: Laval to the south and Baña to the southeast in Corisco Bay. To his horror, I tell him I will go to those islands now, and we gather our scattered crew together and—

We got the *Lafayette* moving and sailed over to some sandbanks first, whose tops are exposed at low tide. They are beautiful stretches of dove-colored sand, but there was apparently not even a <term>whelk</term> <note>a type of predatory sea snail</note> as far as shells are concerned. Thousands of little white tubes stick up through the sand; they appeared empty at first. However, after a few minutes—once I had moved away from the noisy crew and it was quiet—I found that when the foam wet the sand, some lovely little sea anemones looked out from the tops of the tubes.

After a time, I rejoined the crew and found they had dug up a few <term>olive</term> and <term>harp shells</term>, but nothing remarkable. I hurt Eveke’s feelings by saying I considered Corisco a disappointment as a place for collecting shells. He solemnly assured me that during the wet season, which has calmer seas than the dry season, the sandbanks are covered with thousands of shells when the sun shines on them. However, based on his description, I think they are mostly olive shells. 

We crossed from the sandbank to Laval, a small rocky island with a patch of shrubs on its summit. From its edges—which are too small to be called shores—I collected some sponges. Then we moved on to Baña, a larger island inhabited only by rats, which is why it is sometimes called Rat Island; however, I found no more shells there. Before I returned to Corisco, Eveke solemnly promised that the women with their fishing baskets would be ready early tomorrow.

I got up and hurried off early to Nassau Bay, but the women were not ready. I waited for two hours, sitting on the steps of a local’s house, which was built in the European style and located at the upper end of the village. I noticed two other houses like this one between here and Alondo, each prominently positioned across the street. Finally, Eveke arrived and said, “The women are causing trouble. They won’t have the baskets ready today; they will definitely have them ready tomorrow, but not today.” 

Silently cursing Eveke and the ladies, I went to see how the landscape was formed along the southern shores of the island. I walked along the dove-colored sand, bordered on my right by the wall of spray from the surf and on my left by low-growing bushes. These were flowering profusely with long sprays of white, intensely sweet-scented flowers, similar to <term>mimosa</term>. Behind these rose the tall vegetation of a miniature forest. # XVII CAVES OF CORISCO

...to a local village. Although hidden behind trees, its presence is revealed by the canoes—three or four of them are pulled high up, out of the surf's reach, under a cluster of coconut palms that usually serve as a gateway to these paths. About a mile further along—perhaps a little more—the land tapers into a point that forms the eastern end of Nassau Bay. This is the largest bay on the southern side of the island and the only reasonably safe place to anchor along all of Corisco's shores. This point is made of the same kind of rock as the one that juts out to form the bay's western end.¹ The rocks are incredibly strange and picturesque. The action of the surf has hollowed them out from below until the upper part overhangs like a ledge of snow. In several places, masses of rock jut out past the others, weathered into bizarre shapes that look remarkably like the heads of giant lizards or sea serpents, stretching out and gazing toward the African mainland. 

Some of these rocky points have trees growing along their "necks," resembling a bristling mane. The lower part of the rock has been eroded into a hollow, within which groups of caves have formed. These create an interconnected network in places, with stone pillars rising from floor to ceiling. On the floor are perfectly beautiful, clear pools of seawater. The rock they are hollowed out from is a soft gray-green. A type of <term>zoophyte</term> <note>an invertebrate animal that resembles a plant, such as a sea anemone or coral</note> of an exquisite bright mauve or pink-violet color grows in a wide band around the upper edges. In the water, shimmering with light reflected from the cave roof, seaweeds float in tangled strands—the softest, most beautiful blend of golden browns, greens, and reds imaginable. 

These little caves are true gems of beauty. Only the sudden realization that the tide is coming in fast forces me to tear myself away. I return across the bay, passing where the *Lafayette* is anchored, and head toward Alondo. After trekking for a mile over a difficult path of rotting seaweed, I round a small point and find a group of wild, rude children. They yell and dance around me, appearing half-terrified but entirely hostile. They spit at me and shout, "Frenchy no good," "Frenchy no good," in broken English and equally poor Spanish. At first I think, "Well, France is no concern of mine," but I...

—I instantly receive a sharp reprimand from my conscience. It reminds me that since I chose to place myself under the protection of the French flag above Njole <note>original: "Njole"; a French administrative and trading post on the Ogooué River in what is now Gabon</note>—and a great protection it undoubtedly was—I must, in turn, protect that flag from insult when it flies on the *Lafayette* in foreign waters. Furthermore, my Viking blood is stirred by such treatment, and I decide to give those children a proper lesson immediately. I am especially annoyed by a male albino about fourteen years old, who is dressed in the remains of an old salt sack; he wears it just as it was, turned upside down over him.

Unfortunately, holes have been crudely cut in the bottom and sides of it to allow for his unnecessary head and arms. But at that very moment, I catch sight of a sweet-looking nun sitting on the rocks and doing needlework. I approach her and exchange pleasantries, but I do not complain about her "flock." She must be perfectly aware of how they are behaving, and I am certain she is too gentle to deal with them, even if she disapproves. Besides, my knowledge of Spanish consists almost entirely of expressions of thanks and greetings—phrases which, as a rule, you need most when dealing with Spaniards.

Finding she knows no English, I bow and take my leave. I head around the rocky point that forms the end of another shallow bay, making a show of looking tired and weak. The yelling pack, led by the albino, follows me around that rocky point. There, things happen to those children that make them prefer the nun’s company to mine. I continue on, but to my dismay, I find the sea spraying and churning in a roaring cauldron of rocks at the tip of the next point, making it impossible to pass. 

There is no inland path I can reach without going back past the place where I left the nun. I feel understandably shy about doing this because the albino boy has run off, leaving his sack behind with me. I do not know the Spanish idiom for "Please, ma'am, it just came off in my hand," although that idiom undoubtedly exists. Spain has parlor maids and wine glasses, and I am sure they use this phrase every time they grip one end of a glass like a vice and twist the other off while washing it. Unfortunately, she does not know any English, but I "shed" a box of <term>lucifer matches</term><note>An early type of friction match.</note> upon her. I do this wishing to show that I mean well, and knowing that one of the great charms of a white person to a local is this habit of "shedding" things. It is their custom to hang around a traveler in their wilderness in the hope that something will be shed, either intentionally or unintentionally. I suspect this is not for the mere sake of the article itself, but from a sort of sporting interest in what the next item shed will be. 

I know it is my chief charm to them, and they wait around wondering whether it will be matches, leaf tobacco, pocket handkerchiefs, or fishhooks. When the flow of items slows down, they bring me various articles for sale to try to get me back into "working order" again. This particular old lady is glad to have her matches, and they seem to brighten her spirits; she begins to understand that I want something. After unsuccessfully trying to offer me a bunch of plantains and a <term>paw-paw</term><note>Papaya fruit.</note>, she goes and fetches a healthy young woman. This woman soon understands that I am looking for Mrs. Ibea’s house, and she and the old lady immediately escort me down a grass path and through several "galleries of specimens of physical geography" <note>Kingsley’s humorous way of describing difficult, rocky terrain that looks like a geological museum display.</note>. 

We are soon joined by two pretty young girls and wind our way back to the shore again, reaching the far side of the rocky point that had driven me inland. The elders then depart after a mutual exchange of compliments and thanks, while the young women continue on with me. What a lovely sight they are, with their soft dark skin, lithe, graceful figures, pretty brown eyes, and teeth as white as the surf showing between their laughing lips as they dance along before me. I cannot help but think what a comfort they would be to a shipwrecked sailor, and how much he would enjoy the company.

I find the tide has come in too far for there to be any beach left at all, so I strike out onto an inland path. These Corisco paths require some understanding to navigate successfully. They all seem to start with the mere intention of taking you around a headland because the tide happens to be in; but, like all African paths, once they have begun, only <term>Allah</term><note>Arabic for God</note> or <term>Sheitan</term><note>Arabic for Satan or the Devil</note> knows where they will lead. Their presiding spirits might quote *Kipling* and sing, "<note>original: "God knows where we shall go, dear lass, and the deuce knows what we shall see"</note> God knows where we shall go, dear girl, and the devil knows what we shall see," to the traveler who follows them. 

There is one thing, and only one thing, you can safely predict about an African path: it will never follow the shortest line between any two points. A Corisco path turns away from the beach and springs inland, saying to you, "You want to go around that corner, do you? Well, just come and see some of our famous scenery while you’re here!" It then takes you through a miniature forest, a small swamp, and a field of tall grass. "It’s a pity," says the path, "not to stop at so-and-so’s village since we’re so close to it," and off you must go through a patch of grass and a plantation to the village. "We must hurry up and get back to that beach again. I’ll be blessed if I hadn't nearly forgotten what I came out for!" the path continues; and then it plunges back onto the beach, landing you about fifty yards from where you left it just to bypass that little headland.

At last, we reach Alondo, and I give my guides buttons, spools of thread, pocket handkerchiefs, fishhooks, and matches. We part as friends; they go to show off their treasures in their village, giving rise to the hope that I might get lost on Corisco again, soon and often. Meanwhile, I go to have tea and a chat with Mrs. Ibea. I tell her that Eveke had said this morning, when I last saw him, that he was coming home in the evening; however, he does not show up. His mother says she "expects he is courting his mother-in-law." 

Regarding this as a potentially fascinating example of local custom, I force my sleepy eyes open and listen in the interest of science. As it turns out, it isn't a complex custom—but merely a strange piece of local morality. It seems his sweetheart is a housekeeper for a man on the mainland who is always talking about leaving the district but never actually does so, so the marriage is perpetually postponed. I hope that man won't try the patient...

# NATIVE TRADER KILLED

XVII

the affection of the engaged couple for too long, for I imagine it might lead to some internal health problems.

I heard many details regarding Corisco family affairs—one very sad story about how a young man, who was a native trader for one of the German trading houses up the Cameroons River, met his death a short time ago. The firm had decided to <term>close the factory</term><note>In this historical context, a "factory" was a merchant's trading post or warehouse where a "factor" (agent) resided to conduct business.</note> at the place where he was stationed, a move the natives of this region cannot tolerate. Having an established factory removed from their midst brings them ridicule and contempt from their neighbors. "You are a fine town, indeed," the scornful say. "You cannot even keep a factory! Bah!" Furthermore, a factory in a town is a source of entertainment and convenience, not to mention being profitable for the locals. 

Well, this unfortunate young Benga man was left behind by the white men to oversee the final removal of the goods and bring them down the river; and while he was faithfully attending to these matters, the local natives attacked and killed him, and "cut him up like a fish into small pieces and threw them into the water," according to Mrs. Ibea. These native sub-traders lead very risky lives, traveling defenseless with goods among the fierce tribes on this southwest coast. They are frequently killed and robbed; the only thing that prevents this from happening even more often is that the commercial instinct of the inland tribes warns them that it would completely destroy trade. 

In Corisco Bay, the River Muni—a name given to it by early Portuguese navigators from the native word for "take care"—is notoriously unsafe. This is especially true because there is no settled European authority over it, as France and Spain are at odds regarding the ownership of the stretch of coast from Cape Esterias to Batta. This conflict undoubtedly had much to do with those children’s behavior this afternoon; for Corisco Island and the Elobey Islands are Spanish possessions, and are governed by a Vice-Governor who reports to the Governor of Fernando Po. I remember being led to believe during a previous trip that the Vice-Governorship of Elobey was a sort of retirement home for Spanish officials who had lost their minds, or perhaps that the office was held by London County Councillors in disguise. One of the Vice-Governors was truly remarkable for his domestic legislation, and nothing

However, the place was only made habitable at all because the Governor had a habit of forgetting the orders he had issued within a day or so. At one time, there was a decree that all lights on the island had to be out by 10:00 P.M.; since the West Africans are fond of late hours, this bored them terribly. Shortly after, there was another rule that all goats had to be kept tied up. This nearly exhausted the locals as they ran themselves ragged trying to catch them. I believe the goats liked it, regarding it as a kind of game, though they made an awful bleating which kept the lightless Africans awake. I do not know what the present Governor is like. Perhaps he would have seen fit to regard me as a <term>filibuster</term><note>A filibuster was a person engaging in unauthorized military expeditions into a foreign country or territory to foster a revolution or annexation.</note> arriving under the French flag with the intent of annexing Corisco to Gabon, and might have sent me off to prison at Fernando Po. That is what happened to Mr. Ibea once because of some religious dispute <term>palaver</term><note>In this context, a 'palaver' refers to a long discussion, dispute, or negotiation.</note> he got into with the two Catholic priests who are on the island.

These priests and, I believe, three nuns are now the only living white people on the island. There are a tragic number of deceased white people in the two cemeteries; in the early 1850s, when the American Presbyterian Mission began its work on this coast, they believed the risk of fever for white ministers would be lower on this island. Since it is separated from the mainland by about twenty miles of sea, they thought they could establish a station here and live in relative safety while they trained locals to go and do the work on the mainland. However, Corisco Island behaved like every other West Coast "sanatorium," proving that it was no healthier than the neighboring country. After several ministers died and most of the others suffered severely from fever, they decided to move to the continent. There, they could carry on their work directly and would not be much worse off than they were on the island.

Dr. Nassau, whom I have already mentioned, and Mrs. Hogden, whose husband is buried on Corisco, are the surviving members of the early days of the American Presbyterian Mission. When the Mission moved to the continent, the Doctor, in his own way <note>original: "*more suo*"</note>, made some wonderful journeys hundreds of miles into the interior where no white man had been before, and where in many places no white man has been since. I am quite aware that Dr. Nassau was the first white man to send home...

My frustration comes entirely from the justifiable irritation a student of <term>fetish</term><note>Kingsley used "fetish" to refer to the traditional religious systems and magical practices of West African cultures.</note> feels when realizing there is only one "copy" of all this knowledge. That "copy" is the man himself, and it will disappear with him before we—who cannot achieve what he has—can learn even half of what he knows.

I got up very early, ate a quick breakfast, and walked to Nassau Bay, filled with pleasant expectations for a day of good fishing in those lakes. When I arrived at the village, I found I needn't have hurried, so I sat down for my usual wait.

At last Eveke, who had been making a great show of activity to get the women ready to go, succeeded. Or, more accurately, I suspect the women who were already prepared and inclined to start on their own simply did so. Several men accompanied the party. We left the village by a path that goes around the right side of the plank house, immediately plunges into a small ravine, crosses a dried swamp, climbs a hill, and opens onto a prairie—all within about twenty minutes. The prairie had recently been burned and was a stretch of blackened green, with the remains of a few singed or charred trees rising from it.

These burned lands are interesting, though they leave one in a terrible mess. I now understand the reasoning behind what the locals have often told me: that if you burn the grass too soon, or when there is no wind, you kill it permanently. If you wait until it is "very dry," it is fine and does not die. This is because the grass grows in many bulb-like tufts at the base; when the outer and upper parts...

...are quite dry, they catch fire. Fanned by the wind, the flames lick up the dry material and sweep onward with great speed, leaving the moist heart of the grass tuft relatively unharmed. This heart then sends out fresh green leaves when the tropical storms of the wet season arrive. However, if you burn the grass too early or without a breeze, the outer layer—not being dry enough to burn quickly—simply smolders. Because the heat lasts longer, it kills the inner part of the plant.

Some of the low-growing, bamboo-like palms behave the same way. But if there happens to be a lot of dry grass or their own fallen leaves piled up close to the stem, their vital core just above the root gets damaged, and they either die or make very poor recoveries. I do not know if this is the case on Corisco, but in other places I have visited, there is always a "fire-doctor." By using <term>ju-ju</term><note>A West African term for traditional charms, spells, or the supernatural power associated with them.</note>, which is often backed by sound common sense and local knowledge, he decides exactly which day is the proper time to set the grass on fire.

We walk across this prairie into a small woods mainly made up of beautiful wild fig trees. Their "muscles" show through their bark much like the ribbed trunks of our own beech trees, except the wild fig stems are whitish-grey and twisted into picturesque branches. From there, we emerge onto another prairie, larger and unburnt. During our entire walk from the village, we have been yelling in long, rhythmic howls for the women, whose presence is necessary for the proper conduct of our fishing. A female representative from each village is expected to attend to ensure the fish are divided correctly. I cannot find any <term>fetish</term><note>Kingsley’s term for the traditional religious and magical belief systems of the region.</note> reason at the root of this custom. I believe it is restricted to women because of the African men's aversion to work, and the requirement for representatives from each village is based on the Africans' mutual distrust of one another.

Most notably, and frustratingly, we howl for En-gou-ta-a-a, but Engouta does not come. So, we throw ourselves down on the deliciously soft, fine, golden-brown grass in the sun and wait for the latecomers, smoking, laughing, and sleeping. Whenever any of these activities bores us, we stand up and howl "Engouta" again. After about two tedious hours of this, and...

# XVII CORISCO CONFLAGRATIONS

Once my companions have been settled for a while, completely content to sleep peacefully, I hear a crackling sound like a volley of miniature guns. Looking toward the place where the sound is coming from, I notice a cloud of bright blue smoke rising above a fast-moving wall of crimson fire. I get up and quickly mention this to my sleepy companions—giving those in a deeper sleep a helpful kick—and make a direct run for the bushes ahead of us. The others follow my lead with a speed I would not have expected from them. However, despite some very impressive and energetic sprinting, three members of the party get scorched. They spend the rest of the afternoon sitting in mud holes, soothing themselves with the cool black slime.

The fire swept across our section of the prairie, driven by the breeze, and died out very quickly when it reached the green woods. Shortly afterward, the missing members of our group, including Engouta, arrive. These women explained that "some foolish man had been burning" a patch of land on the other side to plant <term>manioc</term><note>Also known as cassava, a starchy root crop that is a staple food in tropical regions.</note>. The whole island is busy planting now before the rainy season begins. A few days ago, the man thought the fire was out and safe, but it wasn’t, and the strong breeze fanned it back up. "People should be careful with fire," I say self-righteously, and they all agree with me—the scorched ones most enthusiastically.

A short climb down into the woods where we are currently located brings us to the lakes. There is a small chain of them; they are simply basins of various sizes in the rock layers, and each has a thick lining of black mud. The water level is at its lowest now since it is the end of the dry season. I believe the water they contain is collected rain from previous rainy seasons.

As far as I can tell, no streams flow into or out of them, though there may be both during the rainy season. The women refuse to fish in one of the lakes, saying it is too deep. It is likely a deep crevice in the rock, similar to the one you see as you pass the enclosed grounds of the Catholic Mission at Evangelanda. I suspect these lakes are prevented from evaporating—unlike the one at the mission during the dry season—because they are shielded by the dense, tangled undergrowth of the small woods that fill the hollow of the island's interior where they are situated.

Even with this, I believe the lakes would dry up if the dry season were also the hot season, as it is on the Gold Coast. Most of these lakes have a surrounding rim of rock. If you are a fisherman, you jump from there down into absolute black slime up to your knees; you then waddle, splash about, grunt, and generally frolic until you reach the shallow remains of the water. If it is one of the larger lakes, you and your companions drive in two rows of stakes that cross each other at roughly right angles in the center of the lake.

Once this is done, the women—carrying specially made baskets that look like bed pillows with one side open—form a line with their backs toward the banks and their faces toward the water inside the enclosure. The other women go into the water by the stakes and splash with their hands, feet, and sticks as hard as they can, while (it goes without saying) shouting loudly the whole time. The terrified fish flee from them into the baskets and are scooped up by the <term>peck</term><note>A dry measure equivalent to 8 quarts or a quarter of a bushel.</note>. In smaller pools of water, the stakes are not required, but the rest of the process is the same: some women stand with their backs to the bank, holding the openings of their baskets just under the water, and scoop up the fish fleeing from the beaters in the middle.

A typical day's fishing yields twelve to fourteen <term>bushels</term><note>A unit of volume equal to 8 gallons, used here to measure the quantity of fish.</note>, and the catch is divided among the representatives and distributed to the various villages. A massive fish dinner follows in the evening, and any remaining fish are smoked and kept as condiments and treats until the next fishing season arrives.

I was told on the island that this fishing happens every year in August—that is, after the crops are planted and just before the <term>tornado rains</term><note>The heavy squalls and storms that mark the transition between seasons in West Africa.</note> begin. On the mainland, the tradition is that it happens here every two years in August. I imagine this was the case in the old days; however, I heard that this formal system of fishing with representatives and so on was a relatively recent development. It supposedly began because of the fear that the fish would be wiped out by constant and unorganized fishing. Corisco would not accept this view at all, insisting that the practice had been handed down from ancient times, implying it was of infinite antiquity. But despite all this formality, after all I had experienced, and all my

<center>### A BITTER DISAPPOINTMENT</center>
<sig>XVII</sig>

After all that walking and waiting, those miserable fish turned out to be nothing more than African mud-fish—a creature I truly despise. Whenever I ask native fishermen for fish, they bring me these; if I start catching fish for myself, nine times out of ten, this is what I catch. It was a bitter disappointment, as I had hoped to find some rare species or a highly distinct <term>form</term><note>A biological variation or subspecies adapted to a specific environment.</note> in the fresh water of this small island, located some twenty miles from the mainland shore. 

But that is typical of Africa: it presents you with familiar objects when you least want them—like finding a common razor in the heart of <term>Gorilla-land</term><note>A reference to the dense interior forests of West Africa, specifically the Gabon region.</note>—and then confronts you with the unfamiliar, such as elephants and buffaloes, when you are out for a quiet stroll armed only with a butterfly net. This is to say nothing of finding snakes in your bed or scorpions in your boots and sponges. One’s view of life becomes quite distorted; I do not believe I would be the least bit surprised to see a herd of hippos stroll onto the tracks out of one of the railway tunnels at Notting Hill Gate station. West Africa is undoubtedly bad for one’s mind.

I did not travel completely around all the lakes, as I had to watch the fishing. Finally, realizing there was only this one kind of fish to be had and seeing that it was getting late, I began my long, weary walk back to Alondo. Upon arriving, I found that Mrs. Ibea had tea waiting for me and that Mr. Ibea had returned from his missionary trip to Cape St. John and Eloby. He is a magnificently built man with broad shoulders, a member of the Benga people of the highest caliber, and full of energy and enthusiasm. I found it difficult to believe his claims regarding his and Mrs. Ibea's ages; I still suspect he added at least ten years to the truth.

I had less difficulty accepting his views on local social issues, especially those that align with my own. We spoke about the Fan—the main subject of local conversation and a significant topic among white residents throughout this region.

In this part of the world, the expansion of this great tribe is displacing the older inhabitants of the land. Mr. Ibea says that one of the first white members of the American Presbyterian Mission, who arrived on this coast some thirty years ago, made a journey into the interior behind Batanga. At the furthest point of that journey, he heard reports of the approaching Fan tribe, who were even then migrating westward. From what he heard, he concluded...

On his return to Corisco, he prophesied that before another ten years had passed, they would have to deal with the Fan people in the coastal districts. Both the locals and the Europeans laughed at him; however, before those ten years were up, the Fans had crossed the borderlines of the M'pongwe and Igalwa territories. Unfortunately, the prophet did not live to see the realization of his prophecy.

At this present time, the Fans have reached the seashore itself in a few places. They are busy learning how to handle a canoe on the open and deep sea. They are not yet as proficient in this art as the M'pongwe or Benga, who are great masters of the craft, but they are progressing well in their studies. They are a tireless and courageous race, which is the primary element in any people's success. 

It is very evident to an observer that the Fans on the Ogowé River are relatively recent arrivals, and that when they first came, they brought no experience in dealing with a large, rapid river. However, they tackle it bravely and are improving. In addition to the causes of decline that the presence of the Fan brings upon the coastal tribes, there are many other factors contributing to the latter's extinction. It always seems like a wonder to me that we have as many traces of early man as we do, especially when one sees here in Africa how one tribe completely sweeps out another. The displaced tribe vanishes like the foam of a broken wave into <term>eternity</term> <note>original: "*Ewigkeit*"</note>, leaving nothing behind after a century to show they ever existed.

Here, the Dualla and the M'pongwe—both tribes now becoming extinct on their own account—have traditions of having migrated down to the seaboard from nearly the same region where the Fans are now swarming. The inhabitants of <term>Fernando Po</term><note>An island off the coast of Central Africa, now known as Bioko.</note>, the so-called Bubi, who are probably the oldest race now on the coast, also remember the arrival of the M'pongwe. They say these M'pongwe drove them out of the districts around Gaboon. 

How long ago this happened is impossible to say, owing to the absence of physical monuments and the African's vague perception of time. However, I am sure from many conversations that you may set a limit of 500 years as the absolute maximum for the very oldest <term>Negro</term><note>A historical term used in the 19th century to describe people of Black African descent.</note> or <term>Bantu</term><note>A major linguistic and ethnic group in Africa.</note> historical tradition. Indeed, I highly doubt whether any Bantu tradition would even reach that far. I specify "historical" traditions because religious traditions may be of intense...

ancient times, being handed down from generation to generation unaltered for immense periods of time. For example, a child would be told that a dangerous spirit lived in the river rapids or lurked in the forest, and that it would be wise for him to keep an eye on it for his own safety. But who would bother to tell him that a chief with such-and-such a name once lived where the Engombie-Gombie trees <note>Likely a local name for a species of African tropical tree</note> have been overshadowed again by the great forest? The chief is dead. The village is dead; "the matter is settled," <note>original: "palaver done set"</note> and so historical tradition fades away like smoke.

Even the invasion of another tribe, such as the Fans, for instance, does not greatly affect religious tradition. This is because it is not, on the whole, a war-like invasion. They move down in entire villages among the older tribes, hear the local gossip regarding spirits, take it into their vast treasury of beliefs, and pass these traditions on to their children. Meanwhile, the tribe that originally told them these things has moved West, away from them. This is because the Fans have cleared the best forest areas and covered them with their own plantations; they catch all the fish, secure all the trade, and occasionally eat respectable people. Furthermore, they steal from the older tribes continually and make such a racket—having perpetual arguments among themselves and with the respectable villages of the older tribe—that the older tribe is forced to the conclusion that no decent people can live near those filthy, frightening Fans. Consequently, they move closer to Lembarene or Libreville.

In addition to these reasons for a tribe leaving its old districts, there are others that remove tribes from earthly districts entirely. Among these are smallpox and the sleeping sickness <note>original: "sleep disease"</note>. The former is most common in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>, where it is given the vividly descriptive name of "the spotted death" among the natives. The latter appears in its worst form in Kacongo and Angola, where entire villages are depopulated by it at intervals. The outbreaks of these maladies—indeed, of all maladies in West Africa—take the form of epidemics and seem to be periodic. I have collected much material, but not yet enough to make deductions regarding the length of time between these outbreaks. The natives all along the coast from Calabar to the South will tell you: "It..."

"...is when the crabs come up the river," which actually means when the crayfish come down the rivers; but that is just their simple, unobservant way of describing it. This swarming of the crayfish occurs about every five years, and for days the river water is crowded with them, so that you can scoop them out by the basketful. The locals do this while singing and playing drums, and they then eat huge quantities of them. They smoke and preserve another portion—in what they consider a "dried" state—to make sauce; and the largest portion of all they throw into heaps to rot around their homes.

There are many other causes for the extinction of tribes besides these—so many, in fact, that one begins to wonder how any coastal tribes over a hundred years old still exist.

Mr. Ibea himself says that there are not more than 2,000 members of his own tribe left today, and that those who currently represent it are physically much weaker than the old men he remembers seeing when he was a boy.

These Benga were once an extremely powerful and proud tribe. Now, they have little left but their pride. In the old days, they were very busy waging war on their neighbors, hunting elephants, working as crew members on whaling vessels, and selling other people as slaves to slave ships, and so on. The Benga were very active in the slave trade, and they remain slave owners today; but their glory has vanished, and in a few more years, the Benga themselves will have gone to join the ghosts of the tribes that preceded them in this land. They will leave behind no sign—not even a flint arrowhead—to show they ever existed; for their wooden tools and their iron weapons will rot like rags in the hot, damp earth; and then it will be over.

Mr. Ibea and I became quite depressed about this. He agreed it was partially the Benga’s own fault; he said they had recently adopted bad habits, including child marriage <term>infant marriage: the practice of betrothing or marrying children at a very young age</term>. This struck me as strange because, as I have already mentioned, the Igalwa people—who are also dying out—have only recently adopted this custom. He says that forty years ago it was completely unknown among the Benga, and that in former days, both men and women were frequently over fifteen or twenty before they married. Now the old men buy young girls, both as wives for themselves and...

<header>XVII EFFECTS OF CIVILIZATION</header>

for their infant sons. Mr. Ibea then blamed rum, though he admitted they had plenty of it during the prosperous old days of whaling and slaving. In fact, he said he believed the primary reason for their extinction was the inactivity that had overtaken the tribe now that their motivations for action were gone; for in Africa, inactivity is death. He explained that as a Christian minister, he knew it was for the best that the old, warlike, and bloodthirsty Benga spirit was broken. However—well, I think he felt much as I do when I hear my own countrymen discussing the "wickedness" of war or the need to limit our growing population, and so on. The only difference is that I feel it even more strongly than Mr. Ibea does, as I am not a Christian minister and am more of a "savage" than he is.

Nothing is more striking when studying the decline of these native tribes than the direct role that civilization and reform play in accelerating it. The greatest threat to an African tribe's survival is the person who arrives and says: "Now you must become civilized, attend school, stop all your terrible behaviors, and settle down quietly." The tribe complies, for Africans are teachable and cooperative. The women and some young men find happiness and satisfaction in the novelty of European clothing and frequent church services. However, the older men and the more adventurous young men soon become bored with these things and find the restrictions irritating. Consequently, they either turn to excessive drinking, pine away until they die, or return to their traditional customs. The African treats his religion much like anyone else. Once he becomes slightly educated—one might even say "scientific"—he strips his religion of all its unpleasant aspects. He quickly discards its version of Hell (which, in <term>Fetishism</term> <note>A 19th-century term for traditional West African religions centered on the power of charms or "fetishes."</note>, is represented by immediate rather than future punishment). Next, he discards strict Sabbath-keeping and dietary restrictions. He is left with only the enjoyable parts, such as dancing and polygamy, which is very harmful for him. I mention these points only to emphasize to people back home the importance of including vocational training in missionary work. By instilling a sense of discipline and providing manual labor, such training will save the African from these relapses, which currently bring shame to—

I am not certain that one must accept Mr. Ibea’s opinion and categorize child marriage among the causes of tribal extinction, because this custom is common among many tribes that are still flourishing; among these Fang people, it is practiced regarding the women. This, I think, is the earliest stage of the custom.

The island of Corisco is three miles long, north to south, and averages one and three-quarter miles in width. Its northwest point is located at latitude 0°, 58' North and longitude 9°, 20' East. I have gathered a great deal of information from local traditions, maritime charts, and personal experience—the latter being, of course, largely derived from the positions of rocks and sandbanks encountered while navigating personally. Therefore, I will set down the general results of my studies here.

Corisco Island is situated in the middle of Corisco Bay and is the furthest seaward of the islands in the bay. It is surrounded by a shallow bank, irregular in outline, which extends in some places two and a half miles offshore. In addition to this extensive shoal, there are several detached rocky patches off the northeast shore of the island. Off the northeast point lie the Corisco Banks; the outer patch has three and a half <term>fathoms</term> <note>A unit of length equal to six feet, used to measure the depth of water.</note> of water and is located three miles offshore. On the outer large patch, one may find twelve feet of water, but I personally found the bottom at two feet. On the inner and larger patch, the depth averages three feet. There are boat channels among both these patches. Mr. Ibea’s accounts of his experiences among them during the many voyages he has made to and from the mainland—along with the strong current that runs around Cape St. John—are thrilling, but they are not the sort of stories that would induce anyone to make Corisco a center for yachting.

Laval Island, which I mentioned above, is about 200 yards long, but it makes the most of itself with its rocks and trees and stands high above the water. It is located one mile south of Corisco Island. It has a line of sandbanks to the north and northeast where the sea breaks. The *West Coast Pilot* <note>A British Admiralty publication providing navigational directions for mariners.</note> says there is only a passage for canoes between it and Corisco Island. This is not the case, for you can take a small schooner between them, though I do not advise it because of the rock reef running out from Alondo Point.
