# XVII LAVAL AND BAÑA BANKS

...and two miles to the south. About a mile southeast of Laval, there is a reef which, when I was on Corisco, was a constant line of foam.

Laval Bank lies southwest by south-three-quarters, three and a half miles from Laval Island. It consists of rock and sand. There is good fishing near it, but the sea breaks over its crest furiously. It stretches two miles north and south and is one and a half miles wide, according to the *Pilot* <note>Referring to the *West Coast Pilot*, a standard British Admiralty navigational guidebook for the region.</note>. I passed through it on my return voyage to Gaboon and believe it is two miles wide in many places; as it was then the rough season in these seas, the bank revealed its full extent.

Baña Island is a quarter of a mile long and is lower in elevation than Laval. It is located five miles south of the southeast end of Corisco Island—that is, Alondo. Its surrounding rocky base is visible in places at low tide, and one large rock that is never submerged is visible about a mile out to sea, to the west by south.

But Baña Island is nothing compared to Baña Bank, which supports Obanjo's—I beg his pardon, Captain Johnson's—statement that "half of those infernal Corisco Bay islands live underwater." <note>original: "half dem dar 'fernal Corisco Bay Islands lib under water." This is written in a West African pidgin or dialect commonly used by local guides and sailors at the time.</note>

This bank is nine miles long, running in an east-by-north to west-by-south direction, and averages three and a half miles in width. The depths across it are very shallow and variable. The eastern part of the bank is called the Crown Sand, and a section of it <term>dries</term> <note>In nautical terms, a feature "dries" when it is exposed above the water at low tide.</note>, as I went shell-hunting there myself. About two miles southeast by east-three-quarters-east of Baña—that is, toward the mainland—there is another patch of the Crown Sand which dries, called the East Sand; here I collected some sponges and *Gorgonia* <note>A genus of soft corals, commonly known as sea fans.</note>. After attempting to provide a conscientious account of Baña Bank, I noticed that my friend, the *West Coast Pilot*, gives up and pathetically pleads with the reader to be very careful if they choose—or are forced—to enter Corisco Bay. I believe these dry patches of the Crown Sand must be near the end of the bank; for Captain Porter, who knows this stretch of coast well, tells me there is a passage for vessels leading out of Corisco Bay by Oranda Point toward Cape Esterias, provided they do not <term>draw</term> <note>Draft: the depth of water a ship requires to float.</note> more than two <term>fathoms</term> and know the way. however, this passage is no longer in use.

I do not know why Little Eloby Island should be the one that is inhabited. Big Eloby is a fine, promising-looking island. I was told by a Benga man on Cape Esterias that it was once inhabited, but there was a war and the inhabitants were killed or carried off as slaves, and it has not been recolonized since.

I have had no personal experience in navigating the northern part of the bay, but according to the *Pilot* <note>Referring to the *West Coast of Africa Pilot*, a standard British Admiralty navigational guidebook.</note>, it has its drawbacks. According to the people who have to work there, these hazards are by no means fully detailed in the charts. It was in this bay that the ship *Benguella* struck something. I cannot be more specific because some of my friends who should know say it was a wreck—the old wreck of the *McGregor Laird*; others, who also should know, say it was rocks. Regardless, she suffered a massive gash right then and there. Nothing but the fine seamanship of Captain Eversfield ever got her up into the Cameroon River and successfully beached and repaired her there. During her recovery, she was the sanctuary for the unfortunate white residents of Cameroon while the mutiny of the Dahomeyan soldiers took place ashore in 1894.

There is another wreck not marked on the chart, just off Alondo, the southeast point of Corisco Island; it is that of the schooner *Elfie*, belonging to the American Presbyterian Mission.

When you look at Corisco Bay on a map, it seems to be an ideally formed harbor, and I once heard it strongly recommended as a suitable site for a coaling station. However, a glance at its chart will show you it is only a subtle, rock-filled trap for vessels, even as imperfect as the chart is. Its width is thirty-five miles south by west and three-quarters west. This line touches the eastern end of Corisco Island, and eastwards of it, the bay is fourteen miles deep.

# XVII SIERRA DEL CRISTAL

Two rivers flow into Corisco Bay: the Muni and the Moondah. The latter flows behind Libreville. There is a creek with an entrance on the right bank near the mouth of the Moondah; it runs southeast behind Cape Esterias and nearly connects with the Gaboon estuary. The connection is so close that it can be used as a shortcut from Libreville to Corisco Bay by dragging a boat across the narrow strip of intervening land.

The Muni is longer and more significant than the Moondah; its outlet is to the north, opposite Little Eloby Island on the mainland shore. On a map, it looks like a typical African river turned upside down, as its upper course splits into several streams rather than its lower course. Both of these rivers, like many others in this region, originate in the Sierra del Cristal <note>The Crystal Mountains, a mountain range running parallel to the Atlantic coast of Gabon and Equatorial Guinea.</note> range, a massive belt of mountainous country whose eastern boundaries remain unexplored.

A few large rivers cut through this range from sources beyond the mountains, such as the Ogowé and the combined streams of the Mbam and Sanaga (which reach the Atlantic as the O'Bengo and the Boungo). The mountains surrounding the Ogowé are the best-known parts of the Sierra del Cristal. The Ogowé provides a 500-mile path through the range, as I have partially described. Its main tributary, the Nguni, cuts through the mountains again from Samba toward the southeast, while the Okanda's course—as far as that river has been explored—runs through the heart of the range toward the northeast. This range is of ancient volcanic origin, consisting of parallel ridges that follow the continent's coastline. It generally runs from the northwest to the southeast. It reaches almost to the beach behind Batanga, where the beautiful little Loway River drops from a twenty or thirty-foot cliff onto the shore itself.

This mountain range makes the coast from Cameroon to Landana far more beautiful than the rest of the West African coast—excepting, of course, the spectacular Ambas Bay, which is unique and incomparable to the rest of the shoreline. These western ridges of the Sierra provide a beautiful purple-blue background to the magnificent...

A band of forest runs behind the bright yellow sands of the seashore, which are bordered on the seaward side by a white wall of surf. The mountains forming this backdrop have distinct outlines and fantastic shapes. Notably, the mountain behind Batanga, when seen from the sea, takes the exact shape of a kneeling elephant. It stands 1,707 feet high, and I am told there is another mountain of almost identical shape at the same latitude on the East African coast. Sir Richard Burton <note>A famous 19th-century British explorer and geographer.</note> was the first to ascend it; since then, Mr. Newberry of Batanga has also climbed it. He tells me that the view from the summit toward the east reveals a mountainous landscape stretching as far as the eye can see. 

Several other peaks in this range have been measured and are visible from the sea; some are even higher than Mount Elephant. The Mitre, located inland from Cape St. John, is 3,940 feet high. The tallest of a stretch of hills called the Seven Hills—which actually belong to a single range—reaches 2,786 feet. Mount Alouette stands at 3,415 feet, yet none are as visually striking in form as Mount Elephant.

Behind Corisco Bay, the range trends inland in a direction nearly perpendicular to the shore, heading southeast by south. However, the specific details of its peaks remain unknown, as this district is largely unexplored. The range appears to turn even further eastward behind Cape Esterias. It runs toward and joins that part of the Sierra del Cristal <note>The Crystal Mountains</note> which intersects the course of the Ogowé River at Talagouga, about 170 miles from the sea. In the Ogowé delta region, only a few isolated, bubble-shaped hills exist, such as Mount Sangataõ. 

When I reached the western flank of this range while traveling across from the Ogowé to the Rembwé, I was about 140 to 150 miles inland. The main chain of this section lay to my east. The Rembwé River cuts through a portion of the range just above Agonjo, though the Rembwé itself originates within these mountains. The Como River, which joins the Rembwé at Como Point to form the Gaboon estuary, is said to rise inland behind this range; like the Muni, it is formed by the convergence of several streams. Obanjo <note>Likely a local guide or trader accompanying the author.</note> told me when I was at Ajongo that the range continues from there in a north-northeasterly direction. However, white men have little to no personal knowledge of the upper reaches of the Como.

Those traders who know the inland tribes describe them as savage and treacherous. The Fans <note>Now commonly known as the Fang people.</note> are migrating down through this part of the country to the beach all along the coast from Batanga to the Gaboon estuary. I cannot offer much hope that they will enlighten or improve the manners and customs of the older inhabitants regarding trade, but they can teach them a thing or two worth knowing in terms of activity and courtesy. There is no reason to doubt that they will suffer the same decline that previous migrants to the coast have experienced, for they will live under similar conditions; and Mr. Ibea and I agree again that there is something hostile to human life—whether black or white—in the immediate coastal region of West and Southwest Africa as far down as the Congo. The interior tribes also share our opinion. Many times, I and others have been told by interior tribes that there is a certain air which comes from the sea that kills men—that is simply their way of describing it. I call it malarial swamp fever <note>original: "Paludisme Malariæ." *Paludisme* is the French term for malaria, derived from the Latin *palus*, meaning swamp.</note>, which is just my way of putting it; and, of course, I imagine that it comes from the rotting, reeking swamplands and lagoons, and not from the sea. Regardless, white men and black men feel it, suffer, and die.

# CHAPTER XVIII

## FROM CORISCO TO GABOON

The log of the *Lafayette* on its return voyage from Corisco to Gaboon, giving some account of Cape Esterias and its inhabitants; to which is added a full and detailed account of a strange sailing maneuver, first carried out by this voyager and not included in any published manual on the art of seamanship in the known world.

*August 8, 1895.*—The weather is still very rough. The two-mile spit of rock running seaward from Alondo Point is a white stretch of flying foam, and its roar and thunder shake the rocky cliff on which the house stands. Mr. Ibea thinks, however, that we should reach Cape Esterias by nightfall—presumably because we are all sober. He tells me an entertaining story of how he "started from Corisco on just such a day as this" in a boat owned and commanded by a native who was drunk at the start and became even more so. In addition to himself and this disreputable person, there were some women and a crew of four or five men. "Shortly afterward," says Mr. Ibea, "we capsized <note>original: "upset"</note>, and I had to swim around and put them all back into the boat again. I hadn't had them in for even half an hour before he overturned the boat again, and I once more had to pull them out of the water." 

Mr. Ibea is a magnificent swimmer and a fine, spirited sailor. I wish he were coming with me instead of Eveke—leaving Eveke to look after church duties <term>pastoral matters: religious or missionary work</term>. But I know this is not possible, and the weather may be worse tomorrow, so I am setting off. I shall spend my time trying to keep the *Lafayette* from capsizing, for I cannot swim around like ten storybook Newfoundland dogs or like Mr. Ibea, gathering people from the South Atlantic waves and putting them back on board this or any other vessel. So I take a grateful farewell of Mrs. Ibea and the—

# CHAPTER XVIII

### WAITING FOR THE TIDE

...family at large. Mr. Ibea and his younger son—who has been chattering away in the Benga <note>A Bantu language spoken by the Benga people of Equatorial Guinea and Gabon.</note> language ever since I arrived on the island—accompany me a short distance, and then we part.

I notice that the sea is rough, and the lagoons behind the beaches smell even worse than usual. It is no wonder the mission found this place just as unhealthy as the mainland! The fine sand blows in the wind, stinging my face—in fact, it is poor weather. However, I have had enough of walking back and forth along this sandy beach while Eveke woos his future mother-in-law. In order to gain more time for his courtship, he attempts to scare me with talk about the weather.

I arrived at Nassau Bay and had the usual task of hunting for Eveke and the crew in the village, which caused the usual delays. We are waiting for the tide to turn on Eveke’s advice. I am certain it would have been better to have set out before the slack water <term>the period of relatively still water at the turn of the tide</term>, so that we would have had the full tide to reach Esterias. However, I let him have his way and wait patiently in a wooden house built in the European style, which I learn belongs to Eveke's uncle. It does not look as though it is lived in very often.

It is fairly clean; the interior walls are painted white, while the door and window frames are a bright cobalt blue. Cobalt blue, by the way, seems to be a major feature on this island. I wonder whether a cargo of it was once salvaged from a shipwreck, or if it is a specific commodity used for making payments? One rarely sees any other color of paint. There is another small village I have passed through daily while here, where every house door is painted with blue and white stripes, diagonal bands, straight lines, and checkerboard patterns; it serves as well as names and numbers for that village.

This system would be far better for postmen and people going out to dinner than the method used in a distant London suburb I know. There, the naming of the villas seems to have been done by a gardener, giving the average person a difficult time. The houses are named after trees, and the memory of which particular shrub your friend lives at often vanishes just as you find yourself facing the front gates of "The Bays," "The Lilacs," "The Elms," "The Oaks," "The Laburnums," and so on. This house belonging to Eveke’s uncle needs no name or—

# CHAPTER XVIII

### FROM CORISCO TO GABOON

...house has a number to distinguish it from the neighboring bamboo huts. You could not miss it even in a London fog, for if you were to enter the village street, you would be bound to run into it, as it stands right across the top of the road.

The interior is well-furnished. In the room where I am waiting for the tide to turn, there are two chests of drawers, a real dining table, nine chairs, another table, three mirrors, and a large wooden bedstead of the local style—essentially a wooden bench without sides, but with a headboard and footboard. One usually sees this type of bedstead sitting out in the sun in the street. I can see four of them right now in the broad village street below me, placed there for the purpose of forcing the excess parasites <note>Likely referring to bedbugs or lice, which were common in wooden furniture and killed by exposure to hot sunlight.</note> to leave. On the bed in this room lies a pile of messy, dirty clothes, giving it the appearance of being the only thing in the house that is actually used. The rest seems to be "just for show." On the table, scattered haphazardly together, are glass scent bottles, a hanging lamp, and framed color prints of English farmyard scenes. Among them is an old album full of faded photographs, evidently once the prized treasure of some white man who is now dead; for had he been living, he would never have parted with it, after pasting those little English wild roses and bits of heather and bluebells next to the pictures.

At last, Eveke rushes up, pretending to be busy with one of those sudden bursts of activity that he fakes, which never fool anyone but himself, and we all go aboard. Yesterday, I met a lady on the shore who asked me if I would take her to Gaboon. I said, as any captain would, "I would be delighted, my dear"; and here she is, sitting on top of the cargo with her head in exactly the right position to be bashed in or knocked off by the boom <term>the horizontal pole at the bottom of a sail used to control its position</term>. She has brought five bundles, a tin box, a gallon of limes, and a husband. 

In fact, things are in such a mess on board that before we weigh anchor, I decide to organize the cargo myself, as becomes a student of Captain Murray <note>Likely Captain hooker of the Bakana, or another merchant captain who taught Kingsley the practicalities of West African maritime life.</note>. No African man knows how to pack cargo properly; I say this irritably, based on my experiences with canoes. The *Lafayette’s* "hold" is in a condition that would turn the hair of any British African official on the Coast white, even if he only caught sight of it through a telescope. It looks very much like a rubbish heap; the lady passenger’s belongings, my own, the crew’s, the deck gear...

The chair, the bundle of bedding, and the boxes of sand used for ballast were all thrown together haphazardly. For dunnage <term>loose material used to protect cargo</term>, there were parcels of the men's aguma <note>A local West African food, usually a thick paste made from mashed cassava or yams.</note> and neat little packets of salt, wrapped in plantain leaves and tied with tie-tie <term>sturdy local twine or rope made from vines</term>. There was also an untidily wrapped bundle of yams, pieces of which had slipped out of the plantain leaves and escaped the tie-tie; these were now rolling around, mixed in with almost everything else. 

At first, I thought Mr. Hudson's clean, tidy deck chair was underneath everything. I could just see a corner of it sticking out from under a box of sand, much like Mr. Pecksniff's feelings <note>A reference to the hypocritical character Seth Pecksniff from Charles Dickens's novel *Martin Chuzzlewit*.</note>, or the Princes in the Tower <note>The young sons of King Edward IV, who were traditionally believed to have been smothered with pillows in the Tower of London in 1483.</note>—except it was certainly not pillows that were smothering it. Upon making a spirited rescue of the chair, I discovered, however, that Dr. Nassau’s bedding was the item actually sitting in the bilge water <term>dirty water that collects in the bottom of a ship's hull</term>. 

During these operations, I jumped forward onto what I imagined was a pile of the crew's clothes. "Oh! That's my husband," cried the lady passenger, "you are going to really hurt him!" <note>original: "you fit to hurt him proper"</note> He knocked me over onto the cargo and groaned quite a bit, talking about compensation. But I said he had "come at the shipper's own risk" and that I had "no liability," so he settled down again. 

When I had finished stowing the cargo, we set out to sea with Eveke at the helm. I found I was expected to sit surrounded by a ring of alligator pears <term>avocados</term> and bananas, as if I were some kind of roast joint garnished for the dinner table, instead of a West Coast skipper. Because the *Lafayette* has neither a cabin nor a locker, it is extremely difficult to keep tidy. No matter what one does, there is unavoidably an "all the coals loose on deck, half the rails below" <note>A nautical idiom describing a messy, disorganized, or poorly maintained ship.</note> look about her. I stowed the pears under the end support, where there is a hole with a decorative woodwork carving around it but no door; consequently, those charming fruits persisted in rolling back out as soon as I had put them in. 

"Oh, the sea is a dog's life for a man," as my sailor friends say. Meanwhile, Eveke took us out of Nassau Bay through the Baña Bank, and then he went to sleep, leaving me in charge. My lady passenger is truly a "lady passenger"—frightened of the sea and dissatisfied with the accommodations. I have stowed her with great care in the bottom of the boat, on the bedding placed athwart-ships <term>positioned across the boat from side to side</term>, and she is grateful for the attention. However, she says "the vessel is not big enough" and continues eating excruciatingly sour limes in a

The way she sleeps sets my teeth on edge. Half her suffering comes from her disastrous habit of falling asleep; then her head falls "thump" off the seat she is leaning against and cracks against the ribs of the boat’s side. I put my leather photograph case where she usually hits her head, but she misses it seven times out of ten during her descent.

The sea is rough, and all afternoon we struggle to sail against the wind. The *Lafayette* behaves playfully, like a duck washing itself—dipping its bow and shaking water out over its stern. A lot of water comes on board one way or another: over one side on one tack, over the other side on the next, and always over the bow. The man with the whiskers is a skilled sailor—the only one worth his salt—and he manages the jib <term>a small triangular sail at the front of the ship</term>. The others just sleep, eat, talk, and pick at the jiggers <term>parasitic sand fleas that burrow into the skin</term> in their feet, which they picked up on Corisco where the insects are everywhere.

The weather is a bit thick, so we do not see the mainland until four o'clock, and it becomes clear to me that we will not reach Cape Esterias tonight. Eveke pilots us close to the shore, and we sail through the long line of breaking waves caused by the massive rock reefs that fringe the coast. These reefs extend out to sea in an irregular cone shape, stretching north and north-northeast from the blunt headland that ends at Akanda Point in the northwest and Cape Clara in the south. Cape Esterias extends further into the sea than Akanda and marks the actual southeast boundary of Corisco Bay. However, the stretch from Akanda to Cape Clara (also known as Joinville) defines the headland separating Corisco Bay from the Gaboon Estuary, where the mouth of the Moondah River is located. "The sun's rim sinks, the stars rush out, at one stride comes the dark" <note>A quotation from Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner."</note> and it finds us still bobbing around in the breaking waves. 

Half an hour after sunset, the wind stops with the suddenness typical of coastal breezes in this region. Although we could barely make progress when we had the wind—since it was blowing almost directly against us—we can certainly do nothing without it. Therefore, we steer the *Lafayette* onto a strip of sand between rock reefs that were "breathing heavily" with the tide, just north of Akanda Point.

# XVIII BECALMED

I remember lounging in a deck chair on the deck of the 2,000-ton *Rochelle* in 1893, while Captain Harrison bore all the anxiety regarding our location and navigation, and I lazily wondered what it was like ashore here. The stretch of land looked so desolate and wild: a long line of surf, a long line of dove-colored sand, and a long line of green shrubs, backed by a low, dark forest. We soon lost sight of it on the *Rochelle*, as she swung out west to give its dangers a wide berth. I never imagined then that I would ever be in a situation so perfectly suited for gaining detailed knowledge of all these features—the surf, rocks, sand, beach and all—as I am in right now. We lower our gaff <term>the spar that supports the top of a sail</term> and anchor as firmly as we can. Then, leaving two men and the lady passenger in the boat, the rest of us jump over the side into the surf and wade ashore to stretch our limbs and pick up firewood. We do not stay long because we are afraid of the *Lafayette* dragging her anchors. Please do not mention this in "British African" circles, but as we back her stern-first onto the sand, we need a hand-line for soundings <term>measuring the depth of the water</term> to find a suitable sandbar to settle on. I give "Whiskers" my fishing line; its lead sinker works very well, except we do not have time to remove the fish hooks. Consequently, when he swings the lead to take a cast in the proper style, those hooks catch right in the cargo. I cut them loose with a pocketknife with commendable speed. Meanwhile, Eveke handles the sail, and when danger becomes imminent, I energetically take soundings over the stern with my umbrella. It is magnificent, but it is not navigation; still, it works well.

We wade back to the *Lafayette*, climb on board, and start to prepare our supper in the dark, for by now the last light has faded from the sky and we have no artificial light. Unfortunately, I have packed my food in my specimen collection box, so I attempt to eat a very interesting piece of dead-wood fungus in place of a biscuit. Giving this up, I decide to focus my attention on my one surviving tin, the opening of which costs me skin and blood. I am not surprised, though I am disappointed, to find that it contains only vegetables for making soup, as I have had experience with this type of canned product before. This particular tin is part of the shipment so kindly sent by Mr. Hudson to my rescue on the—

There is plenty of bottled water for the men, but unboiled water is my "ibet" <term>a personal taboo or something forbidden, likely for health reasons</term>. There are always minor unpleasant things like this in African travel.

The lady passenger is groaning quite a bit and eating those incredibly sour limes and the biscuits I had given her in large quantities this afternoon, hoping to distract her from her constant comments about the height of the Atlantic waves. She soon falls asleep, as I can tell by the sound of her head cracking against the ribs of the boat. In my dual role as captain and stewardess, I look for her head among a bunch of bananas, an iron pot, and a photography case. Moving the other items aside, I settle her head comfortably on the banana bunch and wrap her up completely in my thick rug and shawl. She is only wearing one thin cloth, and the waves washing overboard soaked it through long ago.

After their supper of provisions I had rescued from the dunnage <term>loose packing material or debris in the hold</term>, the men light their pipe. I say "pipe" intentionally, because they only had one—an object about the size of a large laundry boiler <term>originally "washing copper," a large vat used for boiling clothes in communal housing</term>. It requires an entire leaf of tobacco, rolled up and placed in horizontally, with three broken wooden matches <term>lucifer matches</term> placed in the center hole. Of course, they put a folded plantain leaf on top to keep it from burning too quickly. They pass it from one person to the next while making their arrangements for the night. 

These arrangements consist of draping the mainsail across the boom like a tent; they then crawl under this and go to sleep on the cargo. They want to set up a tent for me using the jib <term>a small triangular sail</term> because they say it is very dangerous to sleep in the light of the rising moon, but I do not feel like sleeping, so I refuse. Sharing their tent with them is a large ram that Mr. Ibea is sending to Gaboon. That sheep has sharp, scimitar-shaped horns and restless habits; I can see that he constantly does things that hurt the sleepers and wake them until they groan. I sit up by the rudder watching the black, heaving ocean. It is too rough for the weak moon to brighten, except when the water rises in angry white foam and surf over the sandbanks and rocks. I watch the dimly moonlit sky, with clouds flying in the constant upper wind from the equator, and the motionless black line of the forest. Soft white mist rolls low there, creeping and crawling out from between the tree trunks from the lagoons behind the sand-ridged beach. 

The mist stretches out from under the bushes over the sand toward the sea—now raising itself up into peaks, now crouching down upon the sand, and sending out long white arms or feelers toward the surf. It then draws them back as if it were some spirit-possessed thing, poisonous and malignant, that wanted to reach us and yet is timid and frightened of the surf's thundering roar and spray. After about an hour, however, it overcomes its alarm and comes curling out in a white wall. During the rest of the calm before the dawn wind arrives, it wraps itself around us, smelling damply like a rotting corpse.

I do not think this sort of mist is healthy, but it is often supremely lovely and always fascinates me. I have seen it play the weirdest, wildest tricks many times in many places in West Africa. When caught out by nightfall, I have walked hurriedly through it for miles in the forest while it has mischievously hidden the path at my feet from the helpful light of the moon, swishing and swirling around my moving skirts. I have seen it come out of the forests and gather on the creek before and around me when I have been out at night in canoes. As we glided gradually toward the breeze-swept river, the mist formed itself into a great ball that rolled before us, alongside us, or behind us. It showed dimly in the shadows and appeared ghostly white in the moonshine, bursting into thousands of flakes if the river breeze it met was too strong for it; if the breeze was not, the ball simply melted away into the sheet of mist that lay sleeping on the broad river itself. Now and again, you will see it in the forest stretch up a gradually lengthening—

It has weird ways, this mist of the West Coast. I have often, when no one has been near to form opinions about my silliness, played with it, scooping it up in my hands and letting it fall again, or swished it about with a branch when it lay at a decent level of three or four feet from the ground. I have seen it rise out of the Bimbia flats and cover the Great Cameroon as though it said, "Ah, you are <note>Grand Mungo is a local name for Mount Cameroon.</note>Grand Mungo, but I am grander—I am Death."

*August 10th.*—The morning breaks gray, cheerless, and chilly; the sea looks angry and wicked. For half an hour, while the crew are getting things ready, I comb my tangled hair and reflect on the problem, "Why did I come to Africa?" This done, we weigh anchor and push off at about 5:30 A.M. From then until 1:45 P.M., we travel near the shore on the land breeze, moving among the <term>rollers</term> <note>Large, heavy waves that do not break until they hit the shore or shallow water.</note>. I do not mention this as the proper course to take, but give it as an example of the impossibility of getting a black crew to sail out of the smell of land; they always like to hug the shore, as both my own experiences and those of sympathetic friends with whom I have exchanged stories demonstrate. Whatever the shore may be like, they cling to it. Poor Mr. S., traveling from Gaboon to Eloby, was once taken far up the Moondah River because of this persistent habit, and other adventurers have fared no better.

The shore from Akanda to Cape Clara is one that any white sailor would give a wide berth. Immediately south of our anchorage, it begins to rise into small vertical cliffs overhung by brush and trailing plants, between which the cliff face shows strange-looking slabs of white clay and rock. The sea crashes furiously against them at high tide, and at low tide, it leaves a very narrow beach heavily scattered with immense boulders. By 1:30 P.M., we find we cannot get around Cape Esterias, so we head for the shallow <term>lee</term> <note>The side sheltered from the wind.</note> of its northern side. There is a narrow sandy beach here, with plenty of rocks on it, and a nearly vertical and extremely slippery path leading up to a conspicuously European-style house built of planks. We secure the *Lafayette* safely and all go ashore.

Furthermore, she explains that because of its European planks, the showy house is regarded by these kind people as automatically <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> the appropriate and proper place for me to stay during whatever time I choose to remain at Cape Esterias.

Its ambitious builder and owner apologizes for its unfinished state. Indeed, when I see it up close, I realize it only has its walls up and its roof on. It is perched about four feet above the ground on poles, and the owner has not yet decided what kind of stairs he will build to reach the veranda. He has purchased an old, ready-made set of stairs and has also built a bamboo ladder himself, with its rungs tied to the uprights—it goes without saying—using <term>tie-tie</term> <note>Traditional West African cordage made from vines or plant fibers.</note>. Having done this, he has both ladders lying on the ground next to each other while he carefully considers the advantages of each. Of course, the extra excitement of my unexpected arrival makes him even more unable to decide between their rival merits. I put his mind at ease by ignoring both; I swing myself up onto the veranda and enter the house.

The furniture consists of wood shavings, tools, the frame of a local bedstead, and a bag of something that clearly serves as a bed. The owner proudly shows off the charms of the establishment. He mentions that he intends to paint the interior walls white, with the door and window frames a bright blue. I recognize the familiar cobalt blue in a pot. I approve of the idea—not that it is a new style on this coast, but it is better than plain white or <term>dunduckety</term> <note>An archaic term meaning a dull, dingy, or brownish-yellow color.</note> mud-colored paint, which are the only other popular color schemes for home decorating. It is also miles ahead of using varnish, which acts like "sticky flypaper" <note>original: "catch ’em alive oh" — a Victorian-era term for sticky insect traps.</note> for all kinds of insects, as well as for your clothes when you hang [them up]...

The next room—though there are only two in the house—is particularly well-supplied with windows, having three of them. From the two windows facing north, there is a lovely view of wooded valleys and low hills, seen across a charming, bright foreground of a banana plantation. The east-facing window overlooks the various activities behind the houses on one side of the little village—a view full of interest for an <term>ethnologist</term> <note>A scientist who studies the cultures and characteristics of different peoples.</note>. However, at this moment, I am far too wet and tired for the profound contemplation of science or scenic beauty. Therefore, I close all three windows with their wooden shutters—there is no glass, of course. Having retrieved my <term>portmanteau</term> <note>A large traveling bag made of stiff leather that opens into two equal parts.</note> and a European pudding basin—decorated with a vibrant combination of blue, maroon, and <term>gas-green</term> <note>A bright, yellowish-green color common in 19th-century dyes.</note>—I fill it with water. To my joy, Agnes has provided a towel, and I proceed to wash and dress in the dark. 

Meanwhile, I hear a great uproar in the next room; the entire settlement seems to be busy and talking about their work! Upon re-entering the other room, I find that one kind local resident has lent me a four-legged table, and another has provided an ivory bundle chair. The population of Cape Esterias has been energetically employed in hauling and hoisting furniture onto the stairless veranda and into the house, or standing by to give advice on how it should be done. Agnes also adds a strip of new <term>calico</term> <note>A plain-woven cotton cloth.</note> to serve as a tablecloth. I am exceedingly grateful, but oh, how stiff, bruised, and tired I feel! After having some food and a cup of sugarless and milkless coffee, I excuse myself. I go and lie down on a most "luxurious" bed: a bag made of old salt sacks and filled with damp seaweed. It is perhaps a bit over-populated with fleas, but it is very enjoyable to lie there on the plank floor.

It is 5 o’clock when I wake up, and I am still thirsty. Not wanting to bother Agnes for more coffee and being deathly afraid of drinking untreated water, I ask her for a <term>paw-paw</term> <note>A papaya fruit.</note>. She brings me some unripe ones, explaining "that those nasty boys have eaten all the ripe ones"—such is the universal nature of boys! I regretfully decline the hard fruit, and as they attract...

I feel it is my duty to go and pay my respects to the Mission; Agnes completely agrees, and off we go among the scattered bamboo houses. She tells me she is building one of them, which is currently just a frame, for herself.

The Roman Catholic Mission, the only representative of white men here, is on the southern face of Cape Esterias. Its buildings consist of a small residence and a large church. The church has a concrete floor and wooden benches. The white walls are decorated with a row of framed religious prints, and there is a pretty altar with its array of bright brass candlesticks. Above the altar stands a painted and gilded figure of the Virgin Mary and Child. Every part of the place is fresh and clean, showing the loving care with which it is maintained. As I pass the residence, the missionary sees me and sends one of his African attendants to bring me inside. He leads me onto the porch, where I am most warmly received by the <term>Père</term> <note>French for "Father," the title for a priest.</note> in charge. He has practical views on hospitality and is eager for me to have wine and many other things he can barely afford to spare from his own supplies. I thankfully limit my requests to some sugar and a loaf of excellent bread, but he insists on giving Agnes a tin of beef and a lot of oranges for me. Since I cannot speak French and he cannot speak English, I do my best to express my gratitude for his kindness and take my leave.

Agnes, who is very proud of the Mission, tells me there is only one <term>Père</term> and one <term>Frère</term> <note>French for "Brother," a member of a religious order who is not a priest.</note> stationed here, but she says “they are very good—exceptionally good.” They educate the children, teaching them to read French and other subjects. Should a child display any talent, they are sent to Gaboon to receive further training in the technical schools there, which are connected to the headquarters of the Mission. *August 11th.*—Agnes wakes me from my <term>thalassic</term> <note>Relating to the sea; here referring to her mattress made of dried seaweed.</note> couch and suggests attending Mass at 5:30 a.m. It seems like a very appropriate suggestion, so I follow it. "What is the matter?" I ask. She whispers something. "Hail Mary," I say, hastily joining the congregation's chorus, and add in a whisper, "I cannot hear you; say it very softly." She then lets out a hissing whisper, full of earnest meaning but impossible to understand in its details. "Hail Mary" comes again, and I—fearing I am doing something terribly wrong somehow—answer anxiously, "What?" In this context, a "Jack wash" refers to someone who does laundry.</note> "Hail Mary," I say, along with the congregation.

In addition to this wandering madman, there is a local one at Cape Esterias who is quite the largest black man I have ever seen. He must be nearly seven feet tall, and his muscular development is such that he looks very heavily built for his height. They tell me he is a slave who was brought here in his youth—as are most Benga slaves—from one of the Fernan Vaz tribes. He is quite harmless and hardworking, but completely mad; the local explanation is that "some witch has stolen one of his souls." 

I have seen it stated that insanity is almost unknown among Africans; I can truly say I have never stayed for any length of time in a district among them without encountering several cases of it. In the Rivers region—indeed, among all the true Negro tribes—it is customary to kill those who are insane. On the South-West Coast, insanity usually takes the form of a malignant melancholy, and they often kill themselves. 

Among the Kacongo and Bas-congo <note>Groups from the Lower Congo region.</note> tribes, this suicide is at times almost an epidemic. It is customary there, when a man shows symptoms of its onset—such as by hanging himself around the place without rhyme or reason, or by trying to knock his brains out against a post—for a family council to be held. The complete foolishness of his behavior is then pointed out to him by his relatives, as only relatives can point it out. Should he still persist in attempting to kill himself after this—spoiling things and disturbing people—the task is taken out of his hands, and his relatives

It swung around with a flourish and then came down with a heavy thud onto and into the broken sea, sending sheets of water over us and into the boat. We all baled water as hard as we could and prepared for another performance; however, to my intense relief, we saw the whale blow a few minutes later a good distance away, and then give another flourish—a most charming spectacle on the horizon. As they relaxed their baling, my crew said this is a common occurrence in Corisco Bay at this time of year, as it is the whales' courting season.

I will not enter Corisco Bay again in canoes or small craft while any of that wretched foolishness is going on.

The *Minerve* is an old ship of the line <term>ship of the line</term> <note>A large, powerful naval warship used in the "line of battle" formation.</note> moored off Libreville to serve as a guard ship, a supply depot, and a hospital. She sits naturally high out of the water. The hospital is on her gun deck; the officers' quarters and the exercise ground for the sailors and marines are on the main deck; and above this is yet another structure topped with cisterns. Their taps project over the side—why, I do not know, unless they attach hoses to them, for I have never been on board her or had her layout explained. Over everything is a roof made of palm-leaf mats, in the traditional West African "Coast" style. The whole structure—as the novelist Clark Russell <note>William Clark Russell (1844–1911), a famous author of nautical fiction.</note> would say—towers high into the air, sitting at just the right height above the cisterns for the lively *Lafayette* to get her precious spar <term>spar</term> <note>A general term for a mast or boom supporting a sail.</note> caught in the nozzle of one of those taps. Of course, it was a joke the boat could not resist trying. I want it clearly understood that I am not saying a single word against the dignified and stately *Minerve*. The only mistake she was ever guilty of was once breaking from her moorings and drifting away during a heavy tornado—to the horror of the people in Glass <note>A district and trading center in Libreville.</note> and Libreville—drifting...

The belief in the effectiveness of such stations <note>referring to land-based sanatoriums</note> is one of the most dangerous illusions common on the West Coast. I have even heard recently that this government is considering closing the floating hospital to build one on land, which likely will not achieve a record as successful as the wards of the *Minerve* currently maintain.

After our incident with the authorities, we pull ourselves together and arrive at Hatton and Cookson’s Wharf with a deceptive flourish; I am glad to reach it and return to the comfort, society, and safety associated with it.

## CHAPTER XIX

### FETISH

->In which the traveler cautiously attempts to approach the subject of<-
->Fetish, providing a classification of spirits and some account of the<-
->Ibet and Orundas.<-

Having already provided an account of my personal experiences with an African tribe in its original state—that is, in a condition unaffected by European ideas and culture—I will now attempt a rough sketch of the African way of thinking and the challenges of studying it. This study is my primary reason for traveling to West Africa. Since 1893, I have been gathering information about Fetish in its native environment. I use the common terms "fetish" and "ju-ju" because they have a specific, established meaning for us—a conventional but useful one. Neither word is native to Africa. "Fetish" originates from the word used by early Portuguese explorers to describe the objects they believed the natives worshipped. They were wise enough to recognize a similarity to their own small images and relics of saints: *Feitiço* <note>Portuguese: "charm," "sorcery," or "spell"</note>. "Ju-ju," on the other hand, is French, deriving from their word for a toy or doll <note>original: "joujou"</note>. Thus, it is not as appropriate as the Portuguese name, because the native image is neither a doll nor a toy. It has much more in common with the image of a saint, as it is not worshipped for its own sake or valued for its beauty, but only because it serves as the residence or occasional home of a spirit.

---

¹ Some authorities believe it comes from *gru-gru*, a Mandingo word for a charm, but I respectfully doubt whether *gru-gru* did not actually originate from *ju-ju*, which is the native attempt to pronounce the French *joujou* <note>French: toy</note>.

430 FETISH CHAPTER

Stalking the wild West African idea is one of the most charming pursuits in the world. Quite apart from the intellectual aspect, it has a high sporting interest; for its pursuit is as filled with difficulty and danger as grizzly bear hunting, yet the climate in which you carry out this pursuit—as vile as it is—is warm, which to me is almost a necessity of life. Personally, I prefer it to elephant hunting. I shall never forget the pleasure with which, while in the forest among the Fan people, I "netted" one reason for the supposed advantage of possessing a white man’s eyeball. As I wrote it down in my water-worn notebook, I saw how it connected to the reason why it is considered advisable to cut off the heads of important men in the Niger Delta. Above all, I ask you to understand that I make no claim to a thorough knowledge of Fetish ideas; I am only on the threshold. "I do not know everything, yet much is known to me" <note>original: "Ich weiss nicht all doch viel ist mir bekannt"</note>, as Faust said—and, like him after he said it, I still have a great deal to learn.

I do not intend to weary you here with more than a small portion of even my current knowledge. I have vast collections of facts that I keep only to compare with those of other "hunters of the wild idea," and which, in their present state, are worthless to the <term>cabinet ethnologist</term> <note>A scholar who studies cultures through books and reports rather than field research.</note>. Some of these may be outright lies; some may be merely individual mental quirks; others may have an underlying concept that I do not yet understand.

The difficulty of gaining a true understanding of the native's actual ideas is great and varied.

In places on the Coast where there is, or has been, significant missionary influence, the trouble is greatest. In the first instance, the natives carefully conceal things they fear will bring them ridicule and contempt, even though they still hold those beliefs in their innermost hearts. In the second instance, you encounter a set of traditions that are Christian in origin, though they are frequently altered almost beyond recognition after being held for years within the mindset of the African. For example, there is a beautiful story currently circulating among the Cabinda people. In the African version of the story, God initially made all men black, and then He crossed a great river and called for men to follow Him. The wisest, bravest, and best men plunged into...

<summary>Kingsley describes the intellectual "sport" of studying West African beliefs and explains the difficulties of fieldwork, particularly how missionary influence leads to the concealment or syncretism of native traditions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous page's discussion on the difficulties of understanding African beliefs, specifically illustrating how foreign influences can blend into local folklore and the challenges posed by West African languages.</meta>

...the great river and crossed it; the water washed them white, so they became the ancestors of the white men. But the others were too afraid and said, “No, we are comfortable here; we have our dances, our drums, and plenty to eat—we won’t risk it, we’ll stay here.” They remained in their original home, and from them come the black men. To this day, the white men come to the bank on the other side of the river and call to the black men, saying, “Come, it is better over here.” 

I suspect there is little doubt that this story is a modified version of a parable preached to the Cabindas during the time the Jesuit Fathers held great influence among them. This was before the Portuguese expelled the Jesuits from the lower Congo regions for political reasons more than a century ago. The Cabindas have entirely forgotten the story's origins—saying simply, “it is an old story”—and they maintain the tradition much like a neighboring tribe that continues to ring old bells every morning and evening. Those bells once belonged to a long-forgotten Jesuit monastery. “Our fathers did it”; so <term>the matter is settled</term> <note>original: "palaver done set"</note>.

### XIX NATIVE LANGUAGE AND NATIVE MIND

In the “bush”—where the people have had little or no contact with European ideas—investigation is easier in some ways, yet a different set of difficulties arises. The most obvious challenge people usually point to is the language barrier. My brother recently mocked me, as is his habit, saying, “What a great advantage it was—that strange power African travelers all seem to have for discussing the most obscure metaphysical questions with the locals! When he was in Singapore, however, things were different—if you carefully said, ‘<term>Go to the Mercantile Bank</term>’ <note>original: "Pergi ka Mercantile Bank"</note>, there was a good chance your rickshaw driver would take you to the waterworks instead.” 

But the truth is that West African languages are not difficult to learn. Nevertheless, there is an immense number of them, and at their best, they are very imperfect means of communication. No one who has spent time on the West African Coast can fail to recognize how the native language falls short of the native mind behind it—and the wordiness and repetition a speaker must therefore use to make their thoughts understood.

The one great advantage is the widespread use of that peculiar...

# FETISH CHAPTER

This language, "Trade English," is not only used as a means of communication between whites and blacks but also between natives who speak two distinct languages. On the southwest coast, you will find individuals in villages far from the sea or a trading station who know it. This is because they have learned it and employ it in their dealings with the coastal tribes and traveling traders. It is by no means an easy language to pick up. It is not a jumble of bad words and broken phrases; rather, it has a definite structure, unique verb forms, and uses no genders. There is no grammar book for it yet. One of the best ways to learn it is to listen to an experienced second mate managing the unloading or loading of cargo over a ship’s hatch. No, my friends on the Coast, I have not forgotten—and even though you did not mean to be helpful, that was one of the best tips you ever gave me.

Another good way to learn is through the careful study of examples that display the highest style and the most correct phrasing. Therefore, I have included the letter provided by Mr. Hutchinson, as it is one of the best examples of Trade English I know.

> “To the Father at the Stamp Office—
> 
> Oh Father, please, I beg you to tell those people for me; let the Sierra Leone <note>original: "Sally-own"</note> people know. Please. Very well.
> 
> I live on Pademba Road. A boy lives on the other side, just as those two doctors live across from your Stamp Office. Very well.
> 
> That boy is far too arrogant <note>original: "head big too much"</note>. He says he is in the Militia Band. He has a very long brass instrument with parts that go 'flip-flap,' which they call keys. Very well. Hah! That boy can blow!—shhh!—in the morning, at noon, in the evening, and in the middle of the night—it is all the same—he lets no one sleep. That is not all; there is more! A boy from Bonny lives nearby, and he likes to blow the bugle. When those two troublesome <note>original: "woh-woh"</note> boys blow those things, the noise is far, far too much.
> 
> When a white man blows that instrument and someone is sleeping, he can stop; why can’t those boys do the same? Those boys blow every day—even on Sunday they blow. When I hear <note>original: "yerry"</note> them blow on Sunday, I wish that bugle would go down their throats, or that they would blow their own brains out <note>original: "blow them head-bone inside"</note>.”

# XIX TRADE ENGLISH

> I beg you to tell all those people about that thing those two boys are blowing. It's so bad that Robert Armstrong <note>original: "Amtrang Boboh"</note> has a bad fever. Even my sister <term>titty: sister or young girl</term> cannot sleep at night. That noise is going to kill my two children <term>pickin: children</term>, oh!
> 
> ->The argument <term>plabba: palaver/dispute/matter</term> is finished. Goodbye, Father.<-
> ->Crashey Jane."<-

Now, for the beginning student, let us consider this letter. The complaint in Crashey Jane’s letter concerns two boys who are torturing her morning, noon, and night—on Sundays and weekdays—by blowing a "very long brass thing" as well as a bugle. The way she dwells on their stamina must bring a sympathetic pang for this African sister to the hearts of many London householders who live next to a girls' school or a musical family. As the saying goes, "one touch of nature <note>A reference to Shakespeare's *Troilus and Cressida*: "One touch of nature makes the whole world kin."</note>," etc. "Father" <note>original: "Daddy"</note> is not a term of rude familiarity, but one of esteem and respect. The "Stamp Office" <note>original: "Tampin Office"</note> is a respectful name for the office of the *New Era* newspaper, where this letter was originally published. "The boy's head is too big" <note>original: "Bwoy head big too much"</note> means the young man is filled with conceit because he is associated with the "Militia Band" <note>original: "Militie ban"</note>. You will find that "extremely bad" <note>original: "woh woh"</note> is used by all the natives in the Bights to mean something very poor or wicked. I believe it is a native term, connected to the root *Wo*—meaning power, etc.; however, Mr. Hutchinson may be right in suggesting it means "a capacity to bring double woe."

"Robert Armstrong" <note>original: "Amtrang Boboh"</note> is not the name of some uncivilized savage, as the uninformed might think; far from it. It is "Bob Armstrong" reversed and slightly altered, and it refers to the Honorable Robert Armstrong, the stipendiary magistrate of Sierra Leone, etc.

"Very well" <note>original: "Berrah well"</note> is a phrase used whenever the speaker thinks they have succeeded in presenting their statement effectively. They essentially pause, look back at it, say "Very well" in admiration of their own skill, and then proceed.

"Children" <note>original: "Pickin"</note> are kids.

"Bonny boy" <note>original: "Boney bwoy"</note> is not a local living skeleton, but a native from the Bonny River region.

"Sierra Leone" <note>original: "Sally own"</note> refers to the colony.

"Blow the top off their heads" <note>original: "Blow them head-bone inside"</note> means to blow their minds or the top of their skulls off.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Trade English" (West African Pidgin), moving from a specific letter by "Crashey Jane" to a broader analysis of the language's logical structure, the "grandiloquent" style of educated West Africans, and the mental flexibility required for Europeans to understand African thought processes.</meta>

# FETISH CHAPTER

I have a collection of Trade English letters and documents, for it is a language that I regard as exceedingly charming. It really requires study, as you will see by reading Crashey Jane's letter <term>epistle: a formal or instructive letter</term> without the aid of a dictionary. It is, moreover, a language that will take you unexpectedly far in Africa, and if you do not understand it, you may find yourself in some difficult situations. One important point that you must remember is that the African is logically correct in his answer to a question such as, "You have not cleaned this lamp?" He says, "Yes, sir"—which means, "Yes, you are right; I have not cleaned the lamp." It is not a denial of your accusation. He always uses this form, and it is liable to confuse you at first, as are many other phrases, such as "I look him, I no see him." This means, "I have been searching for the thing but have not found it." If he really meant he had looked upon the object but had been unable to reach it, he would say: "I look him, I no catch him," and so on.

There is another class of letters written by Africans who have had a high degree of school teaching, and these are very fine literature—quite as fine as that of the "Indian Baboo" <note>A 19th-century term, often used patronizingly by the British, for an educated Indian person who used highly formal or "grandiloquent" English.</note> and with more ability and energy in them. They are usually written in truly exquisite handwriting and abound in grandiloquence <term>grandiloquence: a lofty, extravagant, or colorful style of speech or writing</term>. I will not quote any here, except for a phrase written in a letter I heard read out before the Court of the Chiefs at Bonny by young George Peppel <note>A member of the royal family of the Kingdom of Bonny, a powerful trading state in the Niger Delta.</note> regarding a quarrel then going on between him and his brother. "The subject," George eloquently stated, "has now become so delicately distended as to require the united wisdom of the wisest heads in Bonny for its solution." I like the phrase "delicately distended" very much. I know so many subjects in England that are in this condition because of the quantity of "gas" <note>Likely referring to empty talk or "hot air."</note> that has been put into them.

The difficulty of the language is, however, far less than the set of difficulties involving your own mind. Unless you can make your mind flexible enough to follow the African idea step by step, you will not succeed in your goal <term>bag your game: a hunting metaphor meaning to achieve an objective</term>, however much care you may take. I heard an account the other day—I have forgotten where—of a representative of Her Majesty in Africa who went out for a day of antelope shooting. There were plenty of antelope around, and he stalked them with great care; but always, just before

### XIX PRIMITIVE CULTURE

When he got within range of the game, they saw something and fled. Knowing that he and the boy behind him had been making no sound and could not have been seen, he stalked on, but always with the same result; until, happening to look round, he saw the boy behind him was supporting the dignity of the Empire as a whole—and this representative of it in particular—by steadfastly holding aloft the consular flag. Similarly, if you go hunting for African ideas while ostentatiously waving the flag of your own religion or opinions over you, you will likewise end up with a very poor catch.

A few hints regarding your mental preparation when starting this pursuit may be useful. Before starting for West Africa, discard all your notions about sun-myths and the worship of elemental forces. In my opinion, you should also discard the notion—although it is fashionable—that human beings first developed the concept of the soul's origin from dreams.

I went out with my mind full of the conclusions of every book on ethnology <term>ethnology: the study of the characteristics of various peoples and the differences and relationships between them</term>, German or English, that I had read during fifteen years. Being a devoted Cambridge person, I was particularly confident that from Mr. Frazer’s book, *The Golden Bough*, I had obtained a nearly universal key to the underlying ideas of native custom and belief. But I soon found this was very far from the truth. His idea is a true key to a certain number of facts, but in West Africa, it only applies to a limited quantity.

I am not saying you should not read ethnology—by all means, do so. Above all things, read—until you know it by heart—*Primitive Culture* by Dr. E. B. Tylor. Regarding that book, I may say that I have never found a fact that contradicted the carefully formulated, broad-minded conclusions of this greatest of ethnologists. In addition, you must know your Westermarck on *Human Marriage*, your Waitz's *Anthropology* <note>original: "Anthropologie" (German)</note>, and your Topinard—not that you should expect to go measuring people’s skulls and chests as this last-named authority expects you to do. No self-respecting person, black or white, likes that sort of treatment from a complete stranger, and if you attempt it, you will make yourself disliked in West Africa. Add to this a knowledge of all A. B. Ellis’s works; Burton’s *Anatomy of Melancholy*; Pliny’s *Natural History*; and

...as much of Aristotle as possible. If you have a good knowledge of the Greek and Latin classics, I think it would be an immense advantage—an advantage I do not possess, for my classical knowledge is fragmented. In its place, I have a knowledge of Native American dogma <term>dogma: a principle or set of principles laid down by an authority as incontrovertibly true</term>, a dogma which, by the way, seems to me much closer to the African type than Asiatic forms of belief.

Equipped with these tools of observation, and with a little hard work and care, you should be able to process the messy collection of facts you will soon acquire in the "mill of your mind" and turn them into a paper. I then advise you to present the results of your collection to some great thinker; they will write an opinion on it that their broader and clearer vision makes them more fit to form.

You might ask, "Why not bring these home in their raw state?" You must indeed bring them home in a raw state for reference purposes, but in that state, they are of little use to a person unfamiliar with the conditions that surround them in their native homes. Also, very few African stories focus on only one subject, and they hardly ever stick to a point. Take this legend from Fernando Po <note>modern-day Bioko, an island in Equatorial Guinea</note>. Winwood Reade (*Savage Africa*, p. 62) records it and says he heard it twice. I have heard it in various forms four times—once on Fernando Po, once in Calabar, and twice in Gaboon. So it is evidently an old story:

> “The first man called all people to one place. His name was Raychow. ‘Hear this, my people,’ he said, ‘I am going to give a name to every place; I am King in this River.’ One day he came with his people to the Hole of Wonga Wonga, which is a deep pit in the ground from which fire comes at night. Voices spoke to them from the Hole, but they could not see anyone. Raychow said to his son, ‘Go down into the Hole’—and his son went. The son of the King of the Hole came to him and challenged him to a spear-throwing contest. If he lost, he would be killed; if he won, he would return in safety. He won—then the son of the King of the Hole said, ‘It is strange you should have won, for I am a spirit. Ask whatever you wish,’ and the King’s son asked for a remedy for every disease he could remember; and the...”

The spirit gave him the medicines, and when he had done so, he said, “There is one sickness you have forgotten—it is the Kraw-kraw <term>Kraw-kraw: a contagious skin disease, typically scabies</term>, and from that you shall die.”

“A tribe named Ndiva was then strong, but now none remain (Winwood Reade says four remain). They gave Raychow’s son a canoe and forty men to take him back to his father’s town. When he saw his father, he did not speak. His father said, ‘My son, if you are hungry, eat.’ He did not answer, and his father said, ‘Do you wish me to kill a goat?’ He did not answer. His father said, ‘Do you wish me to give you new wives?’ He did not answer. Then his father said, ‘Do you want me to build you a fetish hut <term>fetish hut: a shrine or small building used to house ritual objects and spirits</term>?’ Then he answered, ‘Yes,’ and the hut was built, and the medicines he had brought back from the Hole were put into it.

“‘Now,’ said the son of King Raychow, ‘I am going to make the Moondah River flow into the Orongo’ (the Gaboon River); so he went and dug a canal, and when this was finished, all his men were dead. Then he said, ‘I will go and kill a river-horse <term>river-horse: a hippopotamus</term> in the Benito.’ He killed four, and as he was killing the fifth, the people descended from the mountains against him. So he performed a ritual on his great war-spear and sang:

> My spear, go kill these people,
> Or these people will kill me;

and the spear went and killed the people, except for a few who got into canoes and fled to Fernando Po <note>modern-day Bioko</note>. Then their King said, ‘My people shall never wear cloth until we have conquered the M’pongwe,’ and to this day, the people of Fernando Po go naked and hate the M’pongwe with a special hatred.”

Now, this is a noble story—there is "a lot of fine confused feeding in it," as the Scotsman said of boiled sheep’s head <note>A common 19th-century anecdote suggesting the story is rich and full of various interesting, if disorganized, elements</note>.

You learn from it:
A. The name of the first man, and also that he was driven by a desire for topographical nomenclature <term>topographical nomenclature: the naming of geographical places and features</term>.

B. You hear of the Hole Wonga Wonga, and this is most interesting because to this day—aside from the story—the natives tell of a hole that emits fire. Dr. Nassau says it is always described as being north of Gaboon; but so far, no white man has any knowledge of an active volcano there.

Although the district is of volcanic origin, the crater of Fernando Po <note>modern-day Bioko</note> may be the one referred to in the legend because the king’s son was sent home in a canoe. However, I do not believe it is the same place, because "the Hole" <note>the spirit world entrance mentioned previously</note> is known not to be on Fernando Po; furthermore, according to local tradition, the Hole has a river running from it or very close to it.

C. The **kraw-kraw** <term>kraw-kraw: a contagious skin disease, typically scabies</term> is an extremely common disease. No one has a remedy for it, presumably because Raychow’s son forgot to ask for one.

D. The son’s silence in response to questions is notable. One often finds that people who have been among spirits temporarily lose the ability to ask for what they want and can only respond when the correct question is asked.

E. The sudden way in which Raychow’s son is inspired to become a civil engineer, just when he has a magnificent opportunity to pursue a career as a doctor, is merely the typical impulsiveness of young men who do not realize where their true advantages lie. The fact that the men died after digging a canal is quite normal, and modern experiences support this; men who dig canals in West Africa die in great numbers, whether they are black, white, or yellow. Thus, one cannot help but believe in the existence of those men, although it is remarkable that a black man would have been enterprising enough to attempt canal digging at all. There is no other known case of this to my knowledge. A remarkable fact, however, is that the Moondah River comes so close to connecting with the Gaboon estuary by way of one creek that you can actually drag a boat across the small intervening strip of land.

F. This is a hunting story that appears somewhat unexpectedly, to be sure; however, the Benito River is within an easy distance north of the Moondah, so the geography is accurate.

G. The inhabitants of Fernando Po still harbor a particular hatred for the M’pongwe. Both they and the M’pongwe share this account of one tribe driving the other off the mainland. Regarding the **Bubis**<sup>1</sup>—the name for the inhabitants of Fernando Po—the term arose from a confusion in the minds of sailors visiting the island. <header>XIX AFRICAN CHARACTERISTICS</header>

...ing—these Bubis are undoubtedly a very ancient African race. Their culture, though it presents some remarkable aspects, is on the whole extremely primitive. They never wear clothes unless forced to, and their language relies so heavily on gestures that they cannot communicate with each other in the dark.

I provide this as an example of African stories. It is far more coherent and stays on point in a much more organized way than most others. These stories are very interesting when you know the location and the tribe they originate from. However, I am certain if you were to bring home a pile of stories like these and dump them onto any distinguished ethnologist <note>a scientist who studies the characteristics of different peoples and their relations to one another</note>, without labeling them with the culture of the tribe they belong to, their living conditions, and so forth, you would overwhelm him with the apparent contradictions of some and the complete pointlessness of others. He would likely abandon ethnology and hurriedly devote his remaining years to trying to collect a million postage stamps just to accomplish something definite before he died. Remember, you must always keep your original material—carefully noted at the time of the event—with you, so that you can explain *why* something is the way it is: because of this, and this, and this.

<margin>✓</margin> However good the equipment you bring for your work may be, you will initially find it very difficult to realize that it is possible for the people you are among to truly believe things in the way they do. You cannot spend much time with them before recognizing that these Africans often possess remarkable mental sharpness and a great deal of common sense; there is nothing truly “child-like” about their mindset at all. Observe them further, and you will find they are not at all a flighty or mystical people. They are not dreamers or poets. You will also notice—and I hope you look closely, for in my view this is the most significant difference between their mindset and our own—that they are notably lacking in all mechanical arts. Unless under the direction and instruction of white people, they have never produced even a low-quality piece of cloth, pottery, a tool, a machine, a house, a road, a bridge, a picture, or a statue. Furthermore, none of them possess a written language of their own invention. A careful study of the things a man, whether black or

...fails to do, whether for good or evil, usually gives you a truer understanding of the man than the things he succeeds in doing. When you fully realize this mental sharpness on one hand and this mechanical inability on the other, both of which exist in the people you are studying, you can move forward. Only, I beseech you, proceed carefully. 

You may find an easy "key" that explains the reasoning behind a series of facts, such as these: a Benga <note>a member of the Benga people of Gabon and Equatorial Guinea</note> spits on your hand as a greeting; you see a man who has been marching through the scorching sun all morning with a heavy load, yet upon entering a village and putting his load down, he elaborately sneaks around in the shadow of the houses instead of simply crossing the street; you encounter a tribe that cuts its dead into small pieces and scatters them far and wide; and another tribe that thinks a white man’s eyeball is a most desirable thing to possess. 

When you have found the key to these things, do not drop your collection work and go home shouting, "I know all about Fetish," because you don't. The key to the facts above will not explain why it is considered advisable to kill a person who is making Ikung <term>Ikung: likely a reference to a specific ritual or a state of spiritual taboo or power</term>; or why you should avoid a silk-cotton tree at night that has red earth at its roots; or why hair combings and nail parings should be carefully preserved; or why a speck of blood that falls from your body should be cut out of wood—if it has fallen on that—and destroyed, or, if it has fallen on the ground, should be stamped and rubbed into the soil with great care. This second set of facts requires an entirely different key.

I must also warn you that your own mind requires protection when you send it tracking "the savage idea" through the tangled forests, dark caves, swamps, and fogs of the African intellect <note>original: "Ethiopian intellect," a 19th-century term for African mental processes</note>. The best protection lies in recognizing how untrustworthy human evidence is regarding the unseen—and even the seen—when it is viewed by someone who already has an explanation for a phenomenon before it even occurs. 

For example, take a person who, believing in ghosts, sees a white figure in a churchyard. He bolts home, has a fit, and upon recovering, states he has seen a ghost and provides details. To him, he *has* seen a ghost, and therefore he is telling the truth. However, another person who does not believe in ghosts sees the same thing, runs toward it, and finds that its component parts are merely a boy and a bedsheet.

# THE AFRICAN POINT OF VIEW
## XIX

Do not applaud this individual, for he is quite conceited enough as it is; yet when he says the phenomenon was merely a boy and a bedsheet, he is also telling the truth—and not much more of the truth than the first observer. After all, inside the boy, there is a real ghost that drove him to do the thing. I know many people have doubts as to the existence of souls in small boys of this class, holding that they contain only devils; but according to a mass of testimony, devils can become ghosts. Great as the protection to the mind is to keep it, as Hans Breitmann <note>A character in the dialect poems of Charles Leland, representing a German-American persona</note> says, "still skeptical," I warn you that, even with all precautions, the study of African metaphysics is bad for the brain when you carry it on among the weird, often unaccountable surroundings and depressing scenery of the "Land of the Shadow of Death"—a land that stretches from Gorée <note>An island off the coast of Senegal, once a major center of the Atlantic slave trade</note> to Luanda <note>The capital of modern-day Angola</note>.

The fascination of the African point of view is as sure to linger in your mind as malaria lingers in your body. Never again will you be able to achieve the gay, happy self-assurance regarding the Deity and the Universe held by those people who stay at home, whom *The Saturday Review* <note>An influential London weekly newspaper established in 1855</note> so aptly called "the suburban agnostics." You will always feel inclined to ask people of this class, "Yes; well, what is Force? What is Motion? And above all, tell me, what is this 'Matter' you talk of so glibly? And if so, why?" And the suburban agnostic looks down on you and says pityingly, "Read Schopenhauer <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), a German philosopher known for his atheistic pessimism</note> and Clifford <note>William Kingdon Clifford (1845–1879), an English philosopher and mathematician who wrote on the "ethics of belief"</note>," as if he were prescribing you pills. This revolts you, and you retort, "Read Kant <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), a German philosopher who sought to bridge the gap between rationalism and empiricism</note> and Darwin," and the conversation disappears into a fog of words.

The truth is, the study of natural phenomena humbles any man's conceit if it is done honestly and not by selecting only those facts that fit his preconceived or ingrained notions. And, to my mind, the wisest way is to get into the state of mind of an old marine engineer who oils and sees that every screw and bolt of his engines is clean and well-watched. He loves them as living things, caressing and scolding them himself and defending them, with stormy language, against the insults of the silly, uninformed outside world, which persists in regarding them as mere machines, a
