Even I, with my animistic mindset, was severely reprimanded the other day in Cameroon by a superior but kindred spirit in the form of a First Engineer. I had thoughtlessly repeated some scandalous gossip against the character of a naphtha launch <note>A small motorboat powered by a naphtha engine, a precursor to gasoline engines</note> in the river. "Nonsense!" he said furiously. "She is perfectly fine, and she would run from June to January if those blithering fools would just leave her alone." Naturally, I apologized.

The religious ideas of the West Africans—that is, the people in the region from the Gambia to the Cameroon area, extending roughly to the Rio del Rey <note>An estuary on the border of modern-day Nigeria and Cameroon</note>—differ considerably from the religious ideas of the Bantu tribes of the South-West Coast. (The Bakwiri <note>An ethnic group living on the slopes of Mount Cameroon</note> appear to have religious ideas more like the Bantu than the West Africans, although physically they seem closer to the latter). The Bantu are vague on religious subjects. To someone accustomed to West African beliefs, the Bantu give the impression that they once held the same set of ideas but have forgotten half of them; the beliefs they do retain do not have the same hold on them that the corresponding (or superimposed Christian) ideas have over the West Africans. However, the Bantu are just as focused on the subject of witchcraft, and their witchcraft differs far less from West African witchcraft than their religious ideas do.

Witchcraft is a wonderful thing in its own way. In Africa, I constantly encounter ideas and methods of procedure that are identical to those found in Irish, Devonian <note>From Devon, England</note>, and Semitic witchcraft, but this subject is too large to enter into here.

The concept of "God," in the sense we use the word, is essentially the same in all the Bantu tribes I have met on the coast: a non-interfering and therefore negligible quantity. He goes by various names: Anzambi, Anyambi, Nyambi, Nzambi, Anzam, Nyam, Ukuku, Suku, and Nzam. However, a better investigation shows that the "Nzam" of the Fang people <note>original: "Fans"</note> is practically identical to "Suku" south of the Congo in the Bihe country, and so on.

They regard their god as the creator of man, plants, animals, and the earth, and they hold that having made them, he takes no further interest in the matter. But this is not the case with the crowd of spirits with which the universe is populated; they take...

<page-num>443</page-num>

<header>XIX INFERIOR SPIRITS</header>

The spirits take only too much interest in human affairs, and the Bantu person wishes they would not. He is constantly saying so in his prayers, a large percentage of which boils down to: "Go away; we don't want you. Do not come into this house, this village, or its plantations." He knows from experience that the spirits pay little attention to these rebukes. Since they are the beings who must be dealt with, he develops a system through which they may be managed, used, and understood. This system is what we call <term>witchcraft</term>.

Since I am not writing an exhaustive work on <term>Fetish</term> <note>A term used by Kingsley to describe West African traditional religions and spiritual objects</note> here, I will set <term>Nzam</term> <note>A name for the supreme deity among certain Bantu groups, such as the Fang</note> aside and turn to the inferior spirits. These are almost all malevolent. Sometimes they can be coaxed into displaying respectable feelings, like generosity and gratitude, but you can never trust them. No, not even if you are a well-established <term>medicine man</term> <note>A traditional healer and spiritual practitioner</note> yourself. Indeed, they are particularly dangerous to medicine men, just as lions are to lion tamers. Many a professional practitioner, in the prime of his career, is consumed by his own particular <term>familiar</term> <note>A spirit supposed to attend and obey a person, often believed to reside within the person’s body</note>, which he must keep inside himself whenever he has not sent it out to affect others.

I am indebted to the Reverend Doctor Nassau <note>Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), an American missionary and physician who spent decades in West Africa and wrote extensively on its cultures</note> for a vast amount of valuable information regarding Bantu religious ideas. No one is as qualified as he to provide this information, for no one else knows the West Coast Bantu tribes with such thoroughness and sympathy. He has lived among them since 1851 and is perfectly fluent in their languages and culture; he applies a remarkably clear, powerful, and highly-educated intelligence to his study of them.

I shall therefore carefully label the information I have received from him so that it is not confused with my own observations. My own deductions might be wrong, but Dr. Nassau’s are beyond question.

He says the origin of these spirits is vague. Some of them come into existence by the authority of <term>Anzam</term> (whom you should understand to be the same god I mentioned earlier as having many names), while others are self-existent. Many are clearly the souls of deceased human beings who, "in the future that surrounds them," retain their human needs and feelings. The Doctor assures me he has heard—

<page-num>444</page-num>

# FETISH CHAPTER

Dying people, with their final breaths, often threaten to return as spirits to take revenge on their living enemies. Dr. Nassau could not tell me if there was a set duration for the existence of these human souls as spirits, but two <note>original: "Congo Français"</note> French Congo natives from different tribes—the Benga and Igalwa—told me that once a family had completely died out, its spirits eventually died as well. Some, though certainly not all, of these spirits of human origin undergo reincarnation, as is also the case among the Negro Effiks. The Doctor told me he once knew a man whose plantations were being devastated by an elephant. He advised the man to shoot the beast, but the man said he did not dare because the spirit of his dead father had passed into that elephant.

The number of these spirits is infinite, and their powers are as varied as the human imagination can conceive. Classifying them is therefore a difficult task, but Doctor Nassau thinks this can be done fairly thoroughly into the following categories:

1.  Human disembodied spirits—***Manu***.
2.  Vague beings, well-described by our word "ghosts"—***Abambo***.
3.  Beings somewhat like <term>dryads</term> <note>In Greek mythology, spirits or nymphs that inhabit trees</note> who resent any intrusion into their territory, whether it be their rock, their promontory, or their tree. When passing the residence of one of these beings, the traveler must move silently or use some ritual invocation with a bowed or bared head. They must also leave some symbol of an offering or tribute, even if it is only a pebble. You occasionally come across large trees that have fallen across a path which have small heaps of pebbles, shells, and other items placed upon them by previous passers-by. This class is called ***Ombwiri***.
4.  Beings who act as agents in causing sickness, and who either aid or hinder human plans—***Mionde***.
5.  The Doctor says there seems to be another class of spirits somewhat akin to the ancient <term>household gods</term> <note>original: "Lares and Penates," the protective spirits of the home in ancient Roman religion</note>. These belong specifically to the household and are passed down through the family by inheritance. In their honor, a bundle of finger bones or other bones, nail clippings, eyes, brains, and similar remains are secretly kept. These are accumulated from deceased members over successive generations.

<page-num>445</page-num>

# XIX. TRANSMIGRATION OF SOULS

Dr. Nassau says this happens “secretly,” referring to this custom existing in non-cannibalistic tribes. I saw similar bundles among the cannibalistic Fan people and the non-cannibalistic Adooma, hanging openly in the thatch of their sleeping quarters.

6. He also mentions a possible sixth class—which might just be a function of the other classes—consisting of spirits that enter animal bodies, usually leopards. Sometimes the spirits of living humans do this, and the animal is then guided by human intelligence, using its strength to serve the temporary human owner. In other cases, a non-human soul enters the animal, as is the case with *Ukuku*. <note>A powerful spirit associated with a secret society among the Benga and other West African tribes</note>

It is difficult to classify spirits by their functions because different classes of spirits are often used for the same tasks. For example, I have found that one witch doctor <note>A traditional healer or religious leader in West African cultures</note> might have influence over one class of spirit, while another doctor controls a different class, yet both will perform the same work. Despite this, I believe spirits must be classified by their functions; since they cannot be weighed or measured, and very few ever appear in physical form.

All authorities seem to agree on certain characteristics, one being that individual spirits within the same class vary in power: some are strong for their type, while others are weak.

Their power is limited in nature; no single spirit is all-powerful. Their effectiveness is confined to specific types of action, and all of them can be influenced or made to serve human desires through proper incantations. This can be an advantage to humans, but it also has drawbacks: you can never truly trust a spirit, even if you have paid a large sum to a famous medicine man to trap a powerful one in a *ju-ju* or *monde*—as these charms are called by various tribes.

The method of creating these charms is very similar among both Bantu and <term>Negro</term> <note>Kingsley uses this historical term to refer to West African ethnic groups distinct from the Bantu-speaking peoples</note> peoples. I have elsewhere described the—

You call in the medicine man, or the <term>oganga</term> <note>A traditional healer, diviner, or priest in various Central African cultures</note>, as he is commonly called among the tribes of the French Congo. After various ceremonies and processes, the spirit is persuaded to reside within an object that then becomes subject to the will of its owner. According to Doctor Nassau, the objects most frequently used are antelope horns, large snail shells, and large nut shells.

Among the <term>Fan</term> <note>The Fang people of Central Africa</note>, I found that the most common charm case was shaped like a small sausage and neatly made of pineapple fiber. The contents served as the home for the spirit or power, and the outside was colored red to flatter and please it—since spirits always prefer red.

The substances placed inside these charms consist of all sorts of unpleasant materials; on the seacoast, these often include a high percentage of bird droppings.

<page-num>XIX 447</page-num>
<header>THE BLOOD IS THE LIFE</header>

...intended to be attractive—attractive enough to induce it to leave its present home and come reside within the charm.

In addition to this attractive substance, I find there are other materials included that relate to the specific task the spirit is intended to perform for its owner. For example, charms made either to influence a person to be well-disposed toward the owner, or the even larger category made with the intent to harm other human beings against whom the owner holds a grudge, must contain some part of the person being targeted—their hair, blood, nail clippings, etc. If those are unavailable, the charm must contain their most personal belonging, something that carries their scent—a piece of an old loincloth, for example.

This belief in the ability to gain power over people by using their blood, hair, or nails is found everywhere. You will find it in Devon <note>A county in South West England known for its local folklore and "charms"</note> and as far away as Cathay <note>An archaic name for China</note>. I am told that in some parts of the Chinese Empire, they have small ovens specifically to burn their nail and hair clippings. The fear of these personal remains falling into the hands of malicious people is ever-present among West Africans. The Igalwa and other tribes will allow no one but a trusted friend to cut their hair, and clippings of nails and hair are carefully burned or thrown into a river. Even blood from a small cut or a nosebleed is most carefully covered up and stamped out if it falls on the ground. Dr. Nassau says, “If it falls on the side of a canoe or a tree, the spot is carefully carved out and the wood chip destroyed.” Blood from a woman’s wound is viewed with great horror. This likely has something to do with the fact that drawing blood is considered grounds for divorce among the Igalwa. A man of the <term>Fan</term> <note>The Fang people of Central Africa</note> told me that a man in the village, who was so weak from some unknown cause that he could hardly crawl, had fallen into this state because he had seen the blood of a woman who had been killed by a falling tree. The underlying idea regarding blood is, of course, the ancient one: that the blood is the life.

In Africa, "life" means a spirit; therefore, released blood is a released spirit, and released spirits are always forcing themselves into people who do not want them. In the case of the young Fan man, the prevailing opinion was that the weak spirit of the woman had entered him. I could not help being reminded of the

<page-num>448</page-num>

It is a saying one often hears from a person in England who has witnessed a tragedy: "I cannot get the horror of it out of my sight." To an African, this "horror" would signify a spirit emanating from the object or event itself.

Charms are created for every occupation and desire in life—loving, hating, buying, selling, fishing, planting, traveling, hunting, and so on. Although they usually take the form of objects filled with a mixture in which the spirit resides, there are other varieties as well. For example, a powerful love charm is made from the water the lover used for washing; when mixed into the drink of the beloved, it is believed to soften even the hardest heart. A similar type of friendship-compelling charm is found on the Ivory Coast, and I am told it is also used in the Batanga regions <note>A coastal region in modern-day southern Cameroon</note>. This is obtained upon the death of someone you truly cared for—such as a father or mother—by removing the head and suspending it over a heap of "chalk" (the name given here to the white earth found in riverbeds). The head is left to drip onto the chalk for as long as possible. This saturated chalk is then mixed into the food of anyone you wish to have think kindly of you and trust you. 

A Bassa man <note>An ethno-linguistic group in Liberia and Cameroon</note> told me this charm was "extremely effective on the white trader" <note>original: "was good too much for the white trader"</note> and compelled him to offer an "excellent price" <note>original: "good price too much"</note> for palm oil and other goods. That statement reminded me of a friend who once told me that when he first arrived on the Coast, he had "his insides practically raked out of him" by the illness caused by the charms his local cook fed him to benefit the cook’s friends. That man now employs a cook from Accra <note>A city in modern-day Ghana; Accra cooks were often prized by Europeans for their professional training</note>, and I trust he now lives a life of healthy, icy, unemotional calm.

Certain types of charms—such as those designed to prevent drowning, being shot, or being spotted by elephants—are worn on a bracelet or necklace. A newborn child begins with a health-knot tied around the wrist, neck, or waist, and its collection of charms continues to grow throughout the rest of its life. However, this collection does not reach unmanageable sizes, because some charms inevitably fail to work.

That is the problem with charms and prayers. What you desire may—and frequently does—happen in a strikingly direct way, but at other times it does not. In Africa, this failure is believed to occur...

<page-num>449, XIX</page-num>
<header>UNCERTAINTY OF CHARMS</header>

...from the bad character of the spirits; their gross ingratitude and fickleness. You may have taken every care of a spirit for years, providing it with food and other offerings that you needed for yourself, wrapping it in your own cloth on chilly nights while you went cold, placing it in the only dry spot in the canoe, and so on. Yet after all this, the wretched creature is capable of being manipulated by your rival or enemy and lured away, leaving you with nothing but the empty vessel it once inhabited.

Suppose, for instance, you find that you have been capsized and half-drowned, and your canoe-load of goods has been lost three times in a single week. Your paddles are always breaking, and the number of snags in the river is abnormal. You conclude that your canoe charm has stopped working. You then go to the medicine man who supplied it to you and complain. He argues that it was a perfectly good charm when he sold it to you and that he has never had any complaints before, but he promises to investigate the matter. After doing so, he either says the spirit has been lured away from the home he prepared for it by the incantations and gifts of others, or he claims the spirit is dead—killed by a more powerful spirit of its own kind in the employ of one of your enemies. In any case, the small object you used to house the spirit is now useless, fit only to be sold to a white man as "**a great curiosity!**" The sooner you provide him with enough money to obtain a new and even more powerful spirit—which is naturally more expensive—the safer you will be, especially since your misfortunes clearly suggest that someone desires your death. You grumble, of course, but seeing the situation from his perspective, you pay up. The medicine man then busily sets to work with incantations, dances, gazing into mirrors or basins of still water, and preparing various concoctions to create a new protective charm for you.

As I have already mentioned, human eyeballs—particularly those of white men—are considered powerful charms. Dr. Nassau <note>Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), an American Presbyterian missionary and ethnologist who spent decades in Gabon and wrote extensively on West African religions and customs.</note> says he has known graves to be robbed for them. I suspect this is done to secure the "*man who lives in your eyes*" for the service of the village. Naturally, since the white man is regarded as a superior being, his spirit would be of high value if enlisted into its service. A similar idea regarding the possibility of seizing the spirit of a dead man exists among the Negroes, and the heads of important...

<header>FETISH CHAPTER</header>

The heads of chiefs in the Calabar districts are usually removed from the body after burial and kept secret for fear that the head—and therefore the spirit—of the dead chief should be stolen from the town. If it were stolen, it would not only be a great advantage to its new possessor, but also a great danger to the chief's former town, because the spirit would know all the unique <term>ju-ju</term> <note>A term used by Europeans to describe West African spiritual objects, charms, or the system of religious beliefs themselves.</note> related to it. Each town has a specific one kept exceedingly secret in addition to the general charms, and this secret one would then be in the hands of the new owners of the spirit. It is for similar reasons that the brave General MacCarthy’s <note>Sir Charles MacCarthy (1768–1824), a British governor killed during the First Anglo-Ashanti War; his skull was reportedly kept as a trophy by the Ashanti.</note> head was treasured by the <term>Ashantees</term> <note>The Ashanti people of modern-day Ghana.</note>, and so on.

Charms are not all worn upon the body; some are placed in the plantations and hung there, ensuring a swift and miserable end for any thief who comes stealing. Some are hung around the bows of a canoe, others over the doorway of a house to prevent evil spirits from entering—acting as a sort of tame watch-dog spirit.

The entrances to the long, street-shaped villages are frequently closed with a fence of saplings, and you will see these sapling fences hung with <term>fetish</term> charms to prevent evil spirits from entering the village. Sometimes, in addition to charms, you will see the fence decorated with leaves and flowers. I tried to find out whether these leaves were intended as a residence or for the amusement of the protecting spirits, or whether they were traps for the evil spirits attempting to enter the town. Both reasons were given to me, though the latter was stated most definitely. 

Bells are frequently hung on these fences, but I do not think they are ever used for spiritual reasons. At Ndorko, on the Rembwé River, there were many guards against spirit visitors, but the bell—which was carefully hung so that you could not pass through the gateway without ringing it—was a guard against thieves and human enemies only. It was entirely of native manufacture, shaped very much like the cow-bells my friends bring home from Switzerland and having the same hoarse note. I was informed, when at Lembarene, that down in a corner of the Lake of Islands there was a group of <term>Fans</term> <note>The Fang people of Central Africa.</note> who could not get out because they had quarreled, *in their own way* <note>original: "more suo"</note>, with a village of fellow Fans who guarded the canoe entrance to that corner. These guards kept a sharp lookout by day to ensure the imprisoned ones did not escape.

<page-num>451</page-num>
<header>XIX SACRIFICIAL RITES</header>

and by night, they stretch a line hung with bells from stake to stake, so that the slightest touch of a canoe against it sets the bells ringing and puts the captors on alert. The general opinion was that unless the government intervened, the imprisoned <term>Fans</term> <note>The Fang people of Central Africa.</note> would gradually be killed and eaten by their fellow tribesmen, and then there would be a brief peace in that region. I must say, they seem to be quite a group down in Eliva Z'onange, for they had eaten a returning convert from the Catholic mission a few weeks before I reached Lambaréné. However, this is merely <term>chop palaver</term> <note>West African Pidgin English for "talk about food" or "matters concerning eating."</note>, for the cannibalism of the Fan is not a sacrificial cannibalism like that of the Niger Delta tribes; therefore, we will set that aside and return to the subject of gateways.

Frequently, a sapling is tied horizontally near the ground across the entrance. Dr. Nassau could not tell me why, but he says it must never be stepped on. When smallpox—a deadly plague in these regions—is raging, or when there is war, these gateways are sprinkled with the blood of sacrifices. For these sacrifices, and for the payment of heavy blood fines and similar debts, goats and sheep are kept. They are rarely eaten for ordinary meals, and these West Coast Africans all have a complete horror of the idea of drinking milk; they consider this custom to be a filthy habit and say so in very blunt language.

The villagers eat the meat of the sacrifice, as that part has nothing to do with the offering to the spirits. The sacrifice to the spirits is the blood, for the blood is the life.¹

Besides the few spirits that the <term>Bantu</term> <note>A general term for the various ethnic groups in sub-Saharan Africa who speak Bantu languages.</note> believes he has brought under control through his charms, he must also worship the uncontrolled "army of the air." This he does through sacrifice and incantation.

The sacrifice is the standard practice of killing something valuable as an offering to the spirits. In these southwest coast regions, the value of the offering certainly has a regular relationship to the significance of the favor requested from the spirits. It is a sort of bow or taking off one's hat to him. Some gifts, the Doctor says, are supposed to be actually used by the spirit.

In some part of the long single street of most villages, a low hut is built in which charms are hung, and near which a consecrated plant grows—a lily, a <term>euphorbia</term> <note>A type of succulent plant, often called spurge.</note>, or a fig tree. In some tribes, a rudely carved figure, generally female, is set up as an idol before which offerings are laid. I saw at Egaja two figures about two feet six inches high in the house placed at my disposal. They were left in it during my stay, except that the rolls of cloth (their source of power) which were around their necks were removed by the owner-chief; I will speak elsewhere of the significance of these rolls.

Incantations may be divided into two classes: supplications similar to our idea of prayers, and certain <term>mystical</term> <note>cabalistic</note> words and phrases. The supplications are addresses to the higher spirits. Some are even made to Anzam himself, but the spirit of the new moon is the one most commonly addressed to keep the lower spirits from causing trouble.

Dr. Nassau gave me many instances from his wealth of knowledge. One night, when he was staying at a village, he saw a venerable chief standing out in the open street who addressed the spirits of the air and begged them,

> "Do not come into my town;"

At another time, in a different village, a man’s son had been wounded. A bleeding artery that the Doctor had closed had reopened, and the hemorrhage threatened to be fatal. “Notice,” the Doctor said in his striking manner, “these were clearly prayers—appeals for mercy and agonizing protests—yet there was no praise, no love, no gratitude, and no confession of sin.” I replied that, given their underlying beliefs, I did not see how it could be otherwise. We had one of our minor disagreements. I will always be grateful for his great tolerance of me. I am certain this was because he felt I recognized that there was a coherent logic in the minds of the people he loved enough to risk his life for. He hoped to benefit and ennoble them, and I did not—as many others do—dismiss them as mindless brutes who took pride in a pointless cruelty that would shame a devil.

Regarding the mysterious words and phrases—things that had long been difficult for me to understand—the Doctor was very helpful. He explains that some of these words and phrases are made up by the individuals themselves, while others are ancient terms passed down from ancestors. These are believed to be effective even though their original meanings have been forgotten. He says they are used at any time as a defense against evil—such as when a person is startled, sneezes, or stumbles. Idols are relatively rare in the French Congo <note>Historical region in Central Africa, now mostly Gabon and the Republic of the Congo</note>, but where they are used, the people hold the same view as the West African tribes—specifically, that these are objects where spirits reside or haunt, but they are not inherently divine in their physical form. The spirit living in them, as well as in the charms and plants regarded as spirit dwellings, must be appeased with offerings of food and other sacrifices. In the Fetish <term>Fetish: An object believed to have supernatural powers, or a spirit inhabiting a physical object</term> huts mentioned earlier, you will see dishes of plantains and fish left until they rot. 

Dr. Nassau says that only the life or "essence" of the food is consumed by the spirit; the physical form of the vegetable or meat is left behind to be removed once its vitality has departed. The Calabar <note>A coastal city and region in present-day Nigeria</note> people told me that spirits often take the form of lizards—which are abundant in this country—and come to eat the food. They always seem to doubt whether the offering has reached its destination unless some animal has eaten it. 

However, as I mentioned before, the West African people are more precise in their ideas, and their gods and spirits are viewed as very practical individuals. In contrast, the Bantu people are more vague. Furthermore, there are not as many lizards in the French Congo, so perhaps the local thinkers are forced to be more spiritual in their ideas about sacrifice.

In cases of emergency, a fowl and its blood are placed at the door of the Fetish hut. When a plague is expected, or an attack by enemies, or when a prominent man or woman is very ill, goats and sheep are sacrificed. The blood is placed in the Fetish hut as well as on the gateways of the village. 

Among the Fan <note>The Fang people of Central Africa</note>, these sacrifices are made with a very uniquely shaped knife; I obtained a fine specimen through the kindness of Captain Davies. It is shaped like the head of a hornbill and is quite different from the knives commonly used by the tribes, which are either long, leaf-shaped blades sharpened on both edges, or broad, trowel-shaped, almost triangular daggers. All Fan knives are excellent weapons, superior to the knives of all other coastal tribes I have encountered, but the sacrificial knife is clearly distinct. Du Chaillu <note>Paul Du Chaillu (1831–1903), a French-American explorer famous for his travels in West Africa</note> illustrates one in his book, calling it a tomahawk. There are several other implements used by this cannibal tribe illustrated by Junker that bear a great resemblance to the objects the Fan people use for similar purposes. I am strongly inclined to think that these two tribes are, if not identical, at least very closely related. The same dwarf people, the pygmies, are found in the Mangbetu region and are also fairly common in the forests among the Fans; furthermore, the northeastern and eastern boundaries of the Fan territory are not yet known.

I found, to my great interest, the same superstition in the French Congo that I first encountered in the Oil Rivers <note>A region in the Niger Delta, named for the palm oil it produced</note>. I cannot fully explain its meaning, but I believe it to be a form of sacrifice. In Calabar, every individual has a certain forbidden thing or things. These prohibitions involve either specific types of food or specific ways of eating. In Calabar, this prohibition is called <term>Ibet</term> <note>A ritual taboo or personal prohibition, similar to the concept of "totem" or "taboo"</note>. When a man gives up his <term>Ibet</term> due to the influence of European culture, he is seen by devout <term>ju-juists</term> <note>Practitioners of traditional West African religions or "juju"</note> as leading a reckless and immoral life. Even an unintentional violation of the <term>Ibet</term> is considered very dangerous. 

For example, when buying a slave, the purchaser always asks what the slave's <term>Ibet</term> is. This is because if the slave were given his <term>Ibet</term> to eat, he would become ill. Once, while I was staying with my esteemed friend Miss Mary Slessor <note>A famous Scottish missionary to Nigeria</note> at Okyön, a small boy arrived among her many patients with a severely "sick foot." When asked how it had happened, instead of giving the usual answer—that he had "picked up medicine on the road" <note>An expression meaning one has been cursed by a charm placed on a path</note>—the boy said he had broken his <term>Ibet</term>. # FETISH CHAPTER

When a child is born, some of the elderly female relatives meet together and determine, through their magic, what the child’s *Ibet* <term>a lifelong personal food taboo</term> will be throughout their life. Once they have determined this, it is made known and the child must adhere to it.

Special days are set aside by each individual; on these days, he eats only the smallest quantity and the simplest quality of food. No one is allowed to eat with him, nor may any dog, chicken, or other animal feed on the crumbs, and no one is permitted to watch him while he eats. I suspect the *Ibet* is eaten on this day, but I have not verified this; I only received a statement from an unreliable source that supported the idea.

Dr. Nassau told me that among the tribes of the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>, certain rites are performed for children during infancy or youth. In these rites, a prohibition is placed upon the child regarding the eating of a specific food item or the performance of certain acts. “It is difficult,” he said, “to understand the exact purpose of the ‘*Orunda*’ <term>a sacred prohibition or taboo</term>. Certainly, the prohibited item is not evil in itself, for others besides the restricted individual may eat or use it as they please. Most of the natives blindly follow the customs of their ancestors without being able to give any reason for its existence <note>original: "raison d'être"</note>. However, from those best able to provide a reason, you learn that the prohibited item is a sacrifice ordained for the child by its parents and the medicine man <note>original: "magic doctor"</note> as a gift to the spirit governing its life. The forbidden thing is removed from the child’s common use and is made sacred to the spirit. Therefore, any use of it by the child or man would be a sin, which would provoke the spirit’s anger in the form of sickness or other misfortune. This can only be atoned for through expensive ceremonies or gifts to the medicine man who intercedes for the offender.”

Anything may be an *Orunda*, provided only that it is connected with food; I have been able to find no definite rule for how it is selected. The Doctor said, for example, that “once when on a boat journey, and camped in the forest for the midday meal, the crew of four had no meat. They needed it. I had a chicken but ate only a portion and gave the rest to the crew. Three men ate it with their cassava <term>manioc</term> meal, but the fourth would not touch it. It was his *Orunda*.” “On another journey,” said the Doctor, “instead of all my crew leaving me...”

### XIX ORUNDA AND IBET

...left me respectfully alone in the canoe to have my lunch while they went ashore to have theirs, but one of them stayed behind in the canoe; I found his *Orunda* <term>a sacred prohibition or taboo</term> was that he could only eat over water when on a journey by water.” “At another place, a chief, at whose village we once anchored in a small steamer, was given a glass of rum. He had a piece of cloth held up before his mouth so that the people might not see him drink, which was his *Orunda*.”

I know some ethnologists will think this last case should be classified under a different category, but I believe the Doctor is right. He is well aware of the existence of the other class of prohibitions regarding chiefs. I have seen plenty of chiefs myself along the Rembwé River who have no objection to drinking in public <note>original: "coram publico"</note>, and I have no doubt this was only an individual *Orunda* of this particular Rembwé chief.

Great care is required in these matters because a person may do or abstain from doing the same thing for various reasons.

The word *Orunda* means prohibition, according to the Doctor. In the Efik language <note>original: "Effik"</note>, I found the word *Ibet* <term>a lifelong personal food taboo</term> meant a command, a law, or an act of abstinence.

IT is exceedingly interesting to compare the ideas of the Negroes with those of the Bantu. At present, I have a more definite knowledge of the former, but I have gained enough knowledge of the West Coast Bantu to be able to begin a regular comparative study of these two similar, but by no means identical, sets of ideas.

I believe you find the earliest forms of both religion and witchcraft among the Negroes. I hope, during some future stay on the Bantu border, to study the subject more thoroughly, for it is one of great interest to students of mental evolution.

The mental state of the lower classes of both races seems very close to that other great boundary that separates humans from the great apes <note>original: "anthropoid apes"</note>. I believe that if we had the evidence—or rather, if we could understand it—we would find little or no gap in mental evolution within this ancient, undisturbed continent of Africa.

There is one point regarding evolution, and only one, on which I am a bit unorthodox <term>heterodox</term>. That is the dogma that all human beings originally descended from a single pair who appeared somewhere in Asia, and that their descendants then migrated across the earth, adapting themselves, their religion, their cooking, and their culture to new environments, changing into all sorts of colors and developing unique traits of no

# CHAPTER XX
## WITCHCRAFT AND BUSH-SOULS

I am aware, of course, that the South-West Coast tribes have all migrated from a region in the northeast. That region seems to be perpetually throwing off tribe after tribe, all of which move west and eventually die out in the swampy lands of the West Coast. However, we also know—and have known for hundreds of years—enough about the regions beyond those from which the South-West Coast tribes (the Duala, Mpongwe, Benga, and Fan) have come during modern times to be certain that these interesting and striking-looking groups of humans did not arrive by wandering all the way from Asia. I am not trying to establish an African Garden of Eden to rival the Asiatic one; I am simply stating that I agree with the French ethnologists and suspect there were several different points of origin for the human race.

Be that as it may, one thing about the Negro and Bantu races is very certain: their lives are dominated by a profound belief in witchcraft and its effects.

Among both groups alike, the rule is that death is regarded as a direct consequence of the witchcraft of some malicious human being, acting by means of spirits over which they have, by one means or another, obtained control.

To all rules, there are exceptions. Among the Calabar people <note>The Efik and other ethnic groups of the Cross River region in modern-day Nigeria</note>, who are very definite in their opinions, I found two classes of exceptions. The first arises from their belief in a bush-soul. They believe every person has four souls: *a*, the soul that survives death; *b*, the shadow on the path; *c*, the dream-soul; and *d*, the bush-soul.

This bush-soul always takes the form of an animal in the forest—never a plant. Sometimes when a man falls ill, it is because his bush-soul is angry at being neglected. A witch-doctor <term>traditional healer or diviner</term> is called in; having diagnosed this as the cause of the illness, he advises the administration of some kind of offering to the offended soul. When you wander through the forests of the Calabar region, you will frequently see small miniature huts containing these offerings. You must not confuse these huts with those of similar construction that you are continually seeing in plantations, or near roads, which

**Ebumtupism** is rare, and if you happen to possess this gift, it is discovered by the presiding elders during your initiation into the secret society of your tribe. When it is discovered, the presiding elders strongly advise that you should enter the medical profession and become a **witch doctor** <term>A traditional healer or diviner who treats spiritual and physical ailments</term>, as this profession is a lucrative one. However, the training for it is extremely expensive for your parents, as it must be conducted by an established witch doctor. If you are discovered to be an **Ebumtup**, your parents usually make sacrifices—much like parents everywhere, whether Black or White—and you proceed with your studies.

But to return to the bush-soul of an ordinary person: if the offering in the hut works well on the bush-soul, the patient recovers, but if it does not, he dies. However, diseases arising from disturbances in the temperament of the bush-soul are very likely to be stubborn, even when treated by the most eminent practitioners. This is because the bush-soul never realizes that by injuring you, it endangers its own existence. For when its human owner dies, the bush-soul can no longer find a safe place and goes mad, rushing back and forth. If it sees a fire, it rushes into it; if it sees a crowd of people, it rushes among them until it is killed. When it is killed, it is "finished" for that soul <note>original: "finish" — likely a reference to the French "fini," used by the French official M. Pichault</note>, as M. Pichault would say, for it is not an immortal soul.

The bush-souls of a family are usually the same for a man and for his sons, and for a mother and for her daughters. Sometimes, however, I am told all the children take the mother’s, and sometimes all take the father’s. They may be almost any kind of animal; sometimes they are leopards, sometimes fish, or tortoises, and so on.

<header>REINCARNATION</header>

bush-souls. On the other hand, a man may be a quiet, respectable citizen, devoted to peace and his own physical safety, and yet he may have a sadly flighty and disreputable bush-soul which will get itself killed or damaged, causing him death or continual ill-health.

There is another way by which a man dies aside from the action of bush-souls or witchcraft; he may have had a severe illness from some cause in his previous life and, when reincarnated, part of this disease may be reincarnated with him. He will then ultimately die of it. There is no medicine of any use against these reincarnated diseases.

The idea of reincarnation is very strong in the Niger Delta tribes. It exists, as far as I have been able to find out, throughout all Africa, but usually only in scattered cases. However, in the Delta, most—I think I may say all—human souls of the "surviving soul" class <term>The aspect of the human spirit believed to persist after the death of the physical body</term> are regarded as returning to the earth again, undergoing a reincarnation shortly after the proper burial of the soul.

These two exceptions from the rule—that all deaths and sickness are caused by witchcraft—are, however, of minor importance. The vast majority of death and sickness is held to arise from witchcraft itself, more particularly among the **Bantu** <term>A major linguistic and ethnic group inhabiting Central and Southern Africa</term>.

Witchcraft acts in two ways: namely, by charming something out of a man, or charming something into him. The former method is used by both West African and **Bantu** peoples, but is decidedly more common among the West Africans. There, the witches are continually setting traps to catch the soul that wanders from the body when a man is sleeping. When they have caught this soul, they tie it up over the cooking fire on a canoe, and its owner sickens as the soul shrivels.

This is merely a regular line of business, and not an affair of individual hate or revenge. The witch does not care whose dream-soul gets into the trap and will restore it upon payment. Also **witch-doctors**—men of unblemished professional reputation—will keep asylums for lost souls; that is, souls who have been out wandering and found on their return to their body that their place has been filled by a **Sisa** <term>A lower-class, often wandering or malevolent spirit</term>, a low-class soul I will speak of later. These doctors keep

#### FETISH CHAPTER

...souls and administer them to patients who are lacking them.

But there are other witches, either wicked of their own accord or hired by people motivated by hatred toward individuals. In these cases, a trap is carefully set and baited for the soul of the specific person they wish to injure. Concealed in the bait at the bottom of the pot are knives and sharp hooks that tear and damage the soul, either killing it instantly or mauling it so badly that it causes the owner to fall sick upon its return to him. I knew of a case involving a **Kruman** <term>A member of the Kru people of West Africa, often employed as sailors or laborers</term> who, for several nights, had smelled the savory scent of smoked crayfish seasoned with red peppers in his dreams. He became anxious, and the headman decided that a witch had set a trap baited with this delicacy for his dream-soul, intending to cause him grievous bodily harm. Consequently, great care was taken over the next few nights to prevent his soul from wandering abroad.

My attention was drawn to the case by snorts, snores, and thumps from the **Kruman** that were even more violent than usual. I went to see what was wrong with the man, privately deciding that what he needed was a dose of my favorite pill. I found him under a blanket with his nose and mouth tied over with a handkerchief. It was a sweltering hot night, and the man was as drenched in sweat as if he had been dragged through a river. I suggested his muzzle should be removed, but after being informed of the situation regarding his soul, I naturally did not interfere.

The practice of bewitching objects *into* a person is by far the most frequent method among the **Bantu** <term>A major linguistic and ethnic group in Central and Southern Africa</term>; this explains why post-mortem examinations are so prevalent among them—a practice I never encountered among the Negroes <note>In the context of the 19th century, the author distinguishes between "Bantu" and "Negro" ethnic groups based on linguistic and cultural observations</note>.

I believe the idea that the majority of deaths arise from witchcraft is quite true, provided one interprets "witchcraft" as "poison." In a dull sort of way, the local people sometimes understand it this way too. This is shown by the fact that they generally regard the best remedy for being bewitched as a strong laxative <term>A medicine used to encourage bowel movements; a purgative</term> and an emetic <term>A substance that causes vomiting</term>, accompanied, of course, by the appropriate ceremonies.

The belief in witchcraft causes more African deaths

### TERROR OF WITCHCRAFT

...than anything else. It has killed and still kills more men and women than the slave trade. Its only rival is perhaps smallpox—the "Grand Kraw-Kraw" <term>A local term for a severe skin disease or smallpox; "Kraw-Kraw" originally referred to a type of contagious skin eruption similar to scabies</term>, as the **Krumen** <term>The Kru people of West Africa, historically known for their skills as sailors and laborers</term> graphically call it.

At almost every death, a suspicion of witchcraft arises. The witch-doctor <note>A traditional healer or diviner tasked with identifying those responsible for using harmful magic</note> is called in and proceeds to identify the guilty person. Then, woe to the unpopular men, the weak women, and the slaves; for the accusation will fall upon some of them. This means an ordeal <term>A method of determining guilt or innocence by subjecting the accused to dangerous or painful tests, such as consuming poison</term> by poison or fire. If these point to guilt—as they usually do by their very nature—a terrible death follows: slow roasting alive, gradual mutilation before the throat is mercifully cut, or being tied to stakes at low tide so that the rising water drowns them, along with any other death human ingenuity and hate can devise.

The terror in which witchcraft is held is interesting, despite all its horror. I have seen mild, gentle men and women turned by it in a moment into embodied fiends, ready to tear apart and destroy those who, a second before, were their nearest and dearest. Terrible is the fear that falls like a spell upon a village when a person of high status—a "big man" or "big woman"—is known to have just died. Even the men catch their breath and grow pale around the lips. Then everyone, particularly those belonging to the household of the deceased, engages in the most demonstrative display of grief. Long, low howls creep out of the initial silence—those blood-curdling, infinitely melancholy, wailing howls that, once heard, can never be forgotten.

The men tear off their clothes and wear only the filthiest rags. The women, particularly the widows, remove their jewelry and almost all their clothing; their faces are painted white with chalk, their heads are shaven, and they sit crouched on the earth inside the house in an attitude of abasement. Their hands rest on their shoulders with the palms facing downward, not crossed across the chest unless they are going out into the street.

Meanwhile, the witch-doctor has been sent for, if he is not already present, and he sets to work in different ways to find out who is guilty of causing the death.

Whether the methods vary by tribe or by the individual witch-doctor, I cannot say for certain, but I suspect it depends largely on the individual.

->## FETISH CHAPTER<-

Among the Benga people, I saw a <term>witch-doctor</term> <note>A traditional healer or diviner responsible for identifying those using harmful magic</note> going around a village ringing a small bell, which was intended to stop ringing outside the hut of the guilty person. Among the Cabinda (Fjort) people, I observed two witch-doctors on different occasions attempting to find witches. One did so by repeatedly taking the lid on and off a small basket while reciting the names of everyone in the village. When the lid refused to come off at the mention of a person's name, that person was condemned. The other Cabinda doctor first tried casting nuts upon the ground while also repeating names. That method apparently failed. He then resorted to another: rubbing his flat palms against each other. When his palms refused to meet at a certain name and his hands began to move wildly, he had found his man.

If the accused person denies their guilt and does not demand an <term>ordeal</term> <note>A physical test used to determine guilt or innocence</note>, they are tortured until they not only confess to the crime but also name their accomplices in the murder. Remember, in African eyes, this witchcraft is considered murder. It is not merely the performance of the parlor tricks seen among modern spiritualists.

If the accused demands the ordeal, as is usually the case, they typically must drink a poisonous mixture. Among all the Bantu tribes I am familiar with, this is made from <term>Sass wood</term> (the word "sass" means bad; for example, "sass water" means rough water, "sass surf" means dangerous surf, etc.). It is a liquid extract made from the freshly harvested bark of a large, hardwood forest tree that has a tall, unbranched trunk ending in a crown of branches with small leaves. Among the Calabar tribes, the ordeal drink is of two kinds: one made from the <term>Calabar bean</term> <note>Physostigma venenosum, a highly toxic legume</note>, and the other being the powerful juju drink <term>Mbiam</term>, which is also used when taking oaths.

In both the sass-wood and Calabar bean drinks, the only chance for the accused lies in bribing the witch-doctor. This ensures that the sass-wood drink is allowed to settle before it is administered, or that the accused receives a very heavy dose of the bean; both arrangements tend to trigger an immediate vomiting effect, which is taken as proof of innocence. If this effect does not happen quickly, you die a miserable death from the effects of the poison—a process often cut short by others who kill you as soon as your lack of violent sickness decides your guilt.

-># MBIAM OATH FORMULA<-

The use of the bean is entirely for <term>witch palaver</term> <note>Legal disputes or trials concerning accusations of witchcraft</note>; but it is the most respected and dreaded of all oaths, and from its decision there is only one appeal—an appeal open to all condemned persons, but rarely made—the appeal to <term>Long ju-ju</term> <note>A famous and powerful oracle and judicial shrine, specifically the one at Arochukwu</note>. This Long ju-ju means almost certain death and, before that, a severe frightening that is worse to a West African mind than mere physical torture.

I was able to obtain the Mbiam oath formula in the upper districts of the Calabar River. One version of it runs as follows, and it is recited before swallowing the drink made of filth and blood:

> "If I have been guilty of this crime,
> "If I have gone and sought the sick one's harm,
> "If I have sent another to seek the sick one's harm,
> "If I have employed anyone to make charms or to <term>cook bush</term> <note>To prepare traditional herbal medicines or harmful magical concoctions</note>,
> "Or to put anything in the road,
> "Or to touch his cloth,
> "Or to touch his yams,
> "Or to touch his goats,
> "Or to touch his fowl,
> "Or to touch his children,
> "If I have prayed for his harm,
> "If I have thought to harm him in my heart,
> "If I have any intention to harm him,
> "If I ever, at any time, do any of these things (recite in full),
> "Or employ others to do these things (recite in full)
> "Then, Mbiam! *You* deal with me."

This form I have provided was for use when a man was sick and things were generally going badly for him, for it is not customary in cases of disease to wait until death occurs before making an accusation of witchcraft. In the event that Mbiam is administered after a death, this long and complicated oath would be worded very carefully to suit the case, and the clauses regarding future intentions would be omitted. In all cases, whenever it is used, the greatest care is taken that the oath be recited in full, as oath-takers are sadly prone to "kiss their thumb," as it were—particularly women who are taking the Mbiam for accusations of adultery in conjunction with the boiling oil ordeal. Indeed, so unreliable is this class of offenders, or let us rather say this—

class of suspected persons, and notes that someone usually recites the oath on their behalf.

There is only one way to escape the penalties and hardships of these witchcraft accusations: fleeing to a sanctuary. There are several sanctuaries in French Congo. The primary one in the Calabar district is at Omon. Mothers of twins, widows, thieves, and slaves flee there, and they are safe if they reach it. However, attempting to flee is considered a confession of guilt. Since no one is ever certain if the accusation will target them, people hope for the best until it is usually too late. Furthermore, traveling anywhere more than a day's journey is difficult in West Africa. Consequently, the killings continue, and it is common for ten or more people to be executed because of one man’s illness or death. Thus, across vast regions, the death rate exceeds the birth rate. In fact, some smaller tribes have been nearly eradicated this way. In the Calabar district, I have heard of entire villages voluntarily taking the bean <note>The Calabar bean (Physostigma venenosum), used as a poisonous ordeal to determine guilt</note> because another village had accused the whole community <note>original: "en bloc"</note> of witchcraft. It is almost a mania among these people. Miss Slessor <note>Mary Slessor (1848–1915), a famous Scottish missionary to Nigeria who worked to stop the killing of twins</note> has often told me how, during a dispute, one person would accuse another of witchcraft; the accused would then rush off in a blind rage and swallow the bean.

The witch doctor is not always the reason people are subjected to the ordeal or torture. In Calabar and the Okÿon districts, all of a deceased man’s widows must undergo an ordeal.

The night after the death, they must appear before a gathering of chiefs and the local crowd in a cleared area where a fire is burning. A chicken is tied to each widow's right hand. If the bird fails to cluck when it sees the fire, the woman is found guilty of bewitching her late husband and is punished accordingly.

Among the Bantu, although many wives are killed due to witchcraft accusations—with some almost certain to become victims—there is not the same mass slaughter of women and slaves intended to accompany the soul of the deceased as is found among the Negroes <note>The author uses "Negroes" here to distinguish West African Guinea Coast ethnic groups from the Bantu-speaking peoples to the south</note>.

### xx POST-MORTEM EXAMINATIONS

Dr. Nassau <note>Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), an American missionary and physician who wrote extensively on West African customs and folklore</note> told me about an interesting case he had observed. He once met an Akele chief who showed him a string of shells, horns, and wildcat tails which he claimed could deflect bullets. Although the doctor was well known as an excellent marksman, the Akele chief challenged him in a friendly way to shoot at him with a rifle. To test him, the doctor pointed the rifle at him from a distance of just a few paces, but the Akele man never flinched. "Of course," the doctor said, "I did not fire." Two years later, while hunting, that same man was charged by a wounded elephant and gored by its tusks. His attendants drove the beast away, and the terribly wounded man survived just long enough to accuse one of his wives and several slaves of bewitching his gun and causing his death. Based on this accusation, four people were killed. A clever ethnologist might trace the origins of the excuses modern European sportsmen make about their guns back to this, recognizing similar survival instincts in them.

In cases where the cause of death is uncertain—that is, in all cases not resulting from actual physical violence where blood is visible—the Bantu of the Southwest Coast perform post-mortem examinations. This practice is notably common among the tribes of the Cameroon and Batanga regions. The body is cut open to search the internal organs for some sign of the path taken by the "injected" witch.

I am told that the spirit most often eats the lungs. If the deceased was a witch doctor, it is believed—as I mentioned before—that his familiar spirit has eaten him from the inside. He is then opened with the intention of capturing and destroying his "witch." In 1893, in a village in Kacongo, I saw five unpleasant-looking objects displayed on sticks. They were the livers and lungs—essentially the <term>plucks</term> <note>The heart, liver, and lungs of an animal or person</note>—of witch doctors. The inhabitants informed me that these were the "witches" that had been found inside them during post-mortems and subsequently secured.

Mrs. Grenfell <note>Patience Grenfell, the wife of the famous missionary and explorer George Grenfell</note>, of the Upper Congo, told me that same year—when I had the pleasure of traveling with her from Victoria to Matadi—that a similar practice was common among several of the Upper Congo tribes.

Again in 1893, I encountered another instance of this post-mortem practice. A woman had dropped dead at a factory <note>In this context, a "factory" refers to a European trading post or warehouse in West Africa</note>...

beach at Corisco Bay. The locals could not understand it at all. They were frustrated by her behavior:

> "She was not sick, she did not complain, she showed no symptoms, and then she suddenly died." <note>Original: "She no sick, she no complain, she no nothing, and then she go die one time."</note>

The post-mortem examination revealed a burst aneurysm. The native verdict was, "She bewitched herself"—in other words, she was a witch consumed by her own <term>familiar</term> <note>an animal-shaped spirit or supernatural entity believed to serve a witch</note>.

The general opinion held by people living near a river is that the spirit of a witch can take the form of a crocodile to carry out its work. Those who live away from large rivers or in districts like the *French Congo* <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>, where crocodiles are not very aggressive, believe that the witch takes the form of a leopard. Nevertheless, the crocodile spirit form is still believed in within the *French Congo*, and even more so in Kacongo. This is because the crocodiles of the Congo are very fierce and numerous, claiming as many human lives as they do in the Niger Delta and the estuaries of the Sierra Leone and Sherbro Rivers.

One witch-doctor I know in Kacongo had a strange professional method. When he had identified a witch or a bewitched person through his hand-rubbing rituals and other techniques, he always gave the unfortunate person an <term>emetic</term> <note>a medicine or substance that causes vomiting</note>. He always claimed to find several small, live crocodiles in the resulting vomit. The stories of the natives in this region are full of accounts of people who have been carried off by "witch crocodiles" and kept in underground places for years. I often wonder if this idea arose from the crocodile's well-known habit of burying its prey on the riverbank. Sometimes it will tear a limb off its victim immediately, but it frequently buries the body whole for a few days before eating it. The body is always buried if the crocodile leaves it for later.

I have a most profound respect for the entire medical profession, but I must confess that its African representatives are somewhat experimental in their methods of treatment. An African doctor is not always a witch-doctor as well, but he usually is. Female doctors are numerous. They are somewhat dangerous when it comes to pharmacy, but they do not often attempt surgery; so, on the whole, they are safer, for African surgery is extreme. Dr. Nassau cited the worst case of it I have ever heard of.

# HEROIC SURGERY

->XX<-

A man had been accidentally shot in the chest by another man with a gun on the Ogowé <note>a river in Gabon, West Africa</note>. The native doctor who was called in made a vertical incision into the man’s chest, extending down to the last rib. He then cut diagonally across and actually lifted the wall of the chest, groping among the vital organs for the bullet, which he successfully extracted. The patient died. No anesthetic was used.

I also encountered a minor operation. A man had broken the ulna <note>the thinner and longer of the two bones in the human forearm</note> of his left arm. The native doctor found a piece—a very nice piece—of bamboo and drove it through the muscles and <term>integuments</term> <note>the natural outer coverings, such as skin and membranes</note> from the wrist to the elbow. He then encased the limb in plantain leaves and bound it tightly and neatly with <term>tie-tie</term> <note>strong, flexible vines or bark used as rope for binding</note>. When I saw the arm and hand some six or seven months after the operation, they were quite useless and were withering away.

Many of their other methods, however, are better. The Dualla <note>an ethnic group from Cameroon</note> doctors are truly skilled at using poultices to extract foreign substances, such as bits of iron cooking pots. These fragments are a very frequent type of foreign object found in people here because they are commonly used as bullets. Both Black and white residents tell almost incredible stories about the effectiveness of these poultices. I heard of one case from a reliable source concerning a man who had been shot in the thigh with fragments of an iron pot. The white doctor extracted several pieces and said he had removed them all, but the man continued to suffer and could not walk. At his request, a native doctor was called in and applied a poultice. In a few minutes, the doctor removed it, and on its surface were two pieces of jagged iron pot. They had probably been hidden in the poultice when it was applied; regardless, the patient recovered rapidly.

Baths accompanied by massage are highly regarded. These baths sometimes consist of hot water with a few herbs thrown in. At other times, they are prepared by digging a hole in the earth and filling it with a quantity of herbs, bruised cardamoms, and peppers. Boiling water is then poured plentifully over these ingredients. The patient is placed in the bath and covered with the parboiled greenery; a coating of clay is then placed over everything, leaving only the head sticking out. The patient remains in this bath for several hours, or even up to an entire day.

I saw this form of bath used by the M’pongwe and Igalwa peoples, and it is undoubtedly effective for many diseases, notably for that curse of the Coast, rheumatism, which afflicts both Black and white people alike. Massage, kneading, and hot baths are, I think, the best native remedies. Additionally, a plaster made of crushed <term>grains-of-paradise</term> <note>the seeds of Aframomum melegueta, a West African spice often used in traditional medicine</note> mixed with clay and applied to the forehead is often very useful as a remedy for malarial headaches or "brow ague." However, apart from these, I have never seen any trace of a truly valuable drug in any of these herbal remedies.

The natives of Calabar are notably behind in their medical methods, depending more on <term>juju</term> <note>traditional spiritual or magical beliefs and practices</note> than the Bantu peoples do. In a case of rheumatism, for example, instead of prescribing a hot bath, the local practitioner will "woka" his patient. He claims to extract pieces of iron pots, millipedes, and other objects from the painful area, even when there is no wound. In cases of dysentery, he may "extract" bundles of shredded palm leaves. He asserts that these things have been inserted into the patient through witchcraft. His conduct can hardly be considered professional; moreover, because he then proceeds to diagnose who bewitched these items into the patient’s body, his practice is highly dangerous to the patient’s friends, relatives, and neighbors as well.

The strangest thing I ever heard of being "bewitched" into a man was told to me by a most intelligent Igalwa man—a Christian and a very trustworthy person. His statement was confirmed by another man, who was equally reliable but not a Christian. They said that a relative of theirs had been bewitched two years previously. An <term>emetic</term> <note>a substance used to induce vomiting</note> was administered, and a strange little animal appeared, which grew with visible speed. An hour after it came to light, it crawled about, climbed out of its basin, and then flew away. I tried my best to identify the species, but the closest I could get was that it resembled a small bat. It had a bat’s wings, but a body and tail like a lizard, which is quite confusing to a naturalist. This creature, they said, had been given to the man when it was "small small" (meaning extremely tiny) in some food or drink. If it had not been disturbed by that emetic, it would have grown up inside the man, killing him by feeding on his internal organs. There was no...

...It was not for a lack of information or verbal testimony in the case, but I would have felt more certain about the matter if I could have obtained that specimen in a bottle of pure alcohol. The only other instance of this "winged lizard" I heard of was at Batanga. There, a <term>witch-doctor</term> <note>a traditional healer or spiritual leader</note> had been dissected, and a winged, lizard-like creature was found inside him. The people of Batanga claimed this was the source of his power. I was reminded of this case the other day when I was in Cameroon. Two traders I know had been upriver and were forced to remain out all night in an open boat. One of them was quite ill after the experience, and I hear he has since died.

"No, Miss Kingsley," the other trader said to me, "it is not fever; we don’t quite know what it is, but we think Mr. —— must have swallowed a parasite."

Without intending any insult to the medical profession, after this discussion of their methods, I will move on to the subject of death.

Dying in West Africa, particularly in the Niger Delta, is made very unpleasant for the dying person by their friends and relatives.

When a person becomes unconscious, violent measures are taken to call the spirit back to the body. Pepper is forced up the nose and into the eyes. The mouth is propped open with a stick. The shredded fibers from the outside of an oil nut are set on fire and held under the nose. Meanwhile, a crowd of friends and relatives—tightly packed into the stiflingly hot hut—yell the dying man’s name at the top of their voices. They scream in a way that leaves them hoarse for days, just as if they were calling to someone lost in the wilderness, or to a person struggling while being dragged or lured away from them. "Hey, hey, don't you hear? Come back, come back! Look here. This is your place," and so on.

This custom is common among both Negro and Bantu peoples, but funeral ceremonies vary immensely—in fact, they differ with every tribe. These ceremonies form a subject whose details I will reserve for a separate work on <term>Fetish</term> <note>the term used by Kingsley and her contemporaries to refer to West African traditional religions and spiritual systems</note>.

Among the Okyon tribes, special care is taken when a woman dies and leaves behind a child older than six months. The underlying belief is that the mother’s spirit is certain to return to fetch the child. In order to pacify her spirit...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the rituals and beliefs surrounding death in West Africa. After describing the violent attempts to revive a dying person, the author now transitions to the specific customs regarding infants, twins, and the burial of mothers who die in childbirth.</meta>

# FETISH CHAPTER

To prevent the child from dying, it is brought in and held just in front of the mother's corpse. It is then gradually moved behind her where she cannot see it, and the person holding the child makes it cry out and says, "See, your child is here; you are going to have it with you." Then the child is quickly smuggled out of the hut, while a bunch of plantains is placed with the woman’s body and wrapped in the funeral shrouds.

They do not attempt to keep very young children, but instead abandon them alive in the bush. This is the fate of all children who are not born in what is considered a traditional or "orthodox" manner, or those who grow their teeth in an unusual way. Killing twins is practiced among all the Niger Delta tribes, and in districts beyond British control, the mother is killed as well—except in Omon, where there is a sanctuary.

In Omon, mothers of twins and their children are exiled to an island in the Cross River. They must remain on the island, and if any man goes across and marries one of them, he must remain on the island too. This twin-killing is a widespread custom among the West African tribes.

I doubt whether the Bantu peoples practice this as much, but I am skeptical of them regarding the subject of twins. They lulled me into an unsuspicious, restful state regarding twins and then deceived me, so I will not vouch for them. It happened this way: when I first arrived on the Coast, my friends told me every story they could think of until I frequently felt their souls were scorching with the effort. A brief experience with my friends’ conversation warned me that the phrase, "We have some very peculiar customs down here," was the <term>recurring theme</term> <note>original: "Leit Motif"</note> for the introduction of twins into the conversation. Regarding this subject as unfit for general discussion, I used to "smother" those twins by steering the conversation away as soon as I heard that warning note, and I became exceedingly skillful at this.

However, once I had passed the West African ports of Bonny, Calabar, and so on, and crossed the Bantu border line below Cameroon, I found that the subject did not arise. I was lulled into a sense of false security. All went well for some time, until one day I was walking with an Englishman across a stretch...

# XX TREATMENT OF TWINS

...of the country where there were several villages. At one of these, a major festival was clearly being held; a dance of women was taking place in the main street—the usual rhythmic shuffling and stomping to the "thump, thump, thump" of the native drums. In front of one house, a man and a woman stood on either side of the doorway. The most striking part of the scene was that their legs were painted white; since they weren't wearing clothes to cover them, the effect was quite startling. "Dear me, Mr. ——," I said, "that’s rather unusual." "We have some very peculiar customs down here regarding twins," he replied, before I—being caught off guard—had a chance to change the subject.

These customs (among the Akele <term>The Bakele people of Gabon</term>) meant that the mother of twins was confined to her hut for a year after the birth. Then, a great dance and specific ceremonies were held, during which the woman and the doctor—but not the husband—had their legs painted white. Once the rituals were over, the woman returned to her normal daily activities.

In West Africa, there is always a sense that twins are something supernatural or eerie. In those tribes where they are not killed, people believe they require great care to prevent them from dying of their own accord. I remember once, while among the Tschwi <term>Twi-speaking people of Ghana</term>, I tried to cheer up a sickly child with a wooden figure that was near it, which I thought was its doll. The child looked at me with its large, sad eyes pityingly, as if to say, "A pretty fool *you* are making of yourself." And so I was; I later discovered that the figure was not a doll at all, but an image of the child’s dead twin. It was being kept nearby as a home for the deceased twin’s soul so that it would not have to wander alone and, feeling lonely, call its surviving sibling to follow it into death.

The terror with which twins are regarded in the Niger Delta is incredibly strange and palpable. When I had the honor of staying with Miss Slessor <note>Mary Slessor (1848–1915), a Scottish missionary famous for her work in Nigeria, particularly for ending the practice of twin infanticide.</note> at Okÿon <note>Okoyong</note>, the first twins in that district were saved from ritual sacrifice, along with their mother, entirely due to Miss Slessor’s great influence with the local people and her own limitless courage and energy. In this case, the mother was an enslaved woman—an Eboe <note>Igbo</note>, the most expensive and valuable of slaves. She was the property of a

### FETISH CHAPTER

The mother of the twins belonged to a powerful woman who had always treated her—as most slaves are actually treated in Calabar—with great kindness and consideration. However, when these two children arrived, everything changed. She was immediately subjected to torrents of vicious abuse. Her belongings were snatched from her; her English china basins—possessions she valued most highly—were smashed, her clothes were torn, and she was driven out like an unclean object. If it had not been for the fear of provoking Miss Slessor's anger, the woman and her children would have been killed at that moment and their bodies thrown into the forest.

As it was, she was hounded out of the village. The rest of her possessions were jammed into an empty gin-case <term>A wooden crate used for transporting bottles of gin</term> and thrown to her. No one would touch her, as they were not permitted to touch her except to kill her. Miss Slessor had heard of the twins' arrival and set off barefoot and without a hat, moving at the rapid pace she usually takes down a forest path. After walking four miles, she met the procession: the woman was coming toward her while the rest of the village followed behind, yelling and howling. On her head, the woman carried the gin-case into which the children had been stuffed; on top of them was the woman's large brass skillet, and on top of that were her two market calabashes <term>Dried, hollowed-out gourds used as bowls or containers</term>. Naturally, upon arriving, Miss Slessor took charge of the situation. She relieved the unfortunate, weak, and staggering woman of her load and carried it herself, for no one else would touch it—or anything belonging to those "dreadful" twins. They set off together toward Miss Slessor’s house in the forest clearing, saved by the tact and courage that has given Miss Slessor an influence and power among the African people unmatched by any other white person.

She did not take the twins and their mother down the village path to her own house. Although the people of Okyön <note>A district in the Calabar region of Nigeria, also spelled Okoyong</note> would not have prevented her from doing so, the path would have become so "polluted" and dangerous to travel that the villagers would have been forced to cut a new one—no easy task in that part of the forest, I assure you. So Miss Slessor stood waiting in the scorching sun at the height of the hot season while a path was being cut just to enable her to reach her own grounds. The local people worked hard,

Her mother died a few days after her birth, so the child was taken and thrown into the bush by the side of the road that led to the market. This happened on a market day some distance from the town of Okoyong. This particular market is held every ninth day, and on the following market day, some women from the village near Miss Slessor’s house happened to pass along the path and heard the child crying feebly. They came into Miss Slessor’s yard in the evening and sat chatting about their day's shopping and other matters; during the conversation, they casually mentioned that they had heard the child crying and that it was quite remarkable she was still alive. 

Needless to say, Miss Slessor rushed off and brought that waif <term>A homeless, abandoned, or neglected child</term> home. She was truly in a terrible state, but just barely alive. Miraculously, she had been spared by the leopards and snakes that abound in this part of the forest, and even more miraculously, the driver ants <term>Aggressive, carnivorous ants that travel in massive columns and can overwhelm and consume small animals</term> had not caught her scent. Other ants, however, had bitten her severely; her nose, eyes, and other features were swarming with them and with flies. The cartilage of her nose and part of her upper lip had been deeply eaten away. Despite this, she is now one of the prettiest Black children I have ever seen—which is saying a great deal, for Negro children are very pretty with their round faces, their large mouths not yet coarsened by heavy lips, their beautifully shaped flat little ears, and their immense, melancholy, deer-like eyes.
