# FETISH <term>Practices or beliefs involving the worship of physical objects believed to have magical powers or to be inhabited by spirits</term> CHAPTER

The child was fairly quiet. This child is not an object of terror, like the twin children; it was just thrown away because no one wanted to be bothered to raise it. However, once Miss Slessor had taken on all the trouble of rearing it, the natives had no objection to petting and playing with it, calling it "the child of wonder" because of its survival.

With the twin baby, it was very different. They would not touch it and only approached it after some days had passed, and even then, only when Miss Slessor or I held it. If either of us wanted to do or get something and we handed the bundle to one of the house children to hold, there was a stampede of men and women off the veranda, out of the yard, and over the fence if necessary. It was a sight that was exceedingly comic, yet it was most convincing as to the reality of the terror and horror in which they held the infant. Even its own mother could not be trusted with the child; she would have killed it. She never showed the slightest desire to have it with her, and after a few days of nursing and recovering her strength, she was anxious to go back to her mistress. Her mistress, being an enlightened woman, was willing to take her back if she came without the child.

The main horror is undoubtedly directed at the child; the mother is killed more as a punishment for being so intimately involved in bringing the curse, danger, and horror into the village than for anything else.

The woman went back by the road that had been cut for her arrival, and she would have to live for the rest of her life as an outcast. For a long time, she would live in a state of isolation in a hut of her own which no one would enter. No one would eat or drink with her, nor would they partake of the food or water she had cooked or fetched. She would lead the life of a social leper, working in the plantation <term>A cultivated farm or garden plot</term> by day and going into her lonely hut at night, shunned and cursed. I tried to find out whether there was any set period for this quarantine, and all I could determine was that if—and it is a very significant "if"—a man were to marry her and she were subsequently to present to society an acceptable infant, she would be socially rehabilitated to a certain extent. However, she would always be "a woman with a past"—a thing the African, to his credit, has no taste for.

->“ THE CUSTOM OF OUR FATHERS ”<-

She would sit for hours singing, or rather mourning, a kind of funeral song over herself:

> “Yesterday I was a woman, now I am a horror—a thing everyone runs from. Yesterday they would eat with me; now they spit on me. Yesterday they would speak to me with kind words; now they greet me only with curses and denunciations. They have smashed my basin; they have torn my clothes,”

and so on, and so on. She did not complain against the people for doing these things; she only felt a bitter sense of injury against some supernatural power that had sent this withering curse of twins down upon her. She did not know why. She sang, “I have not done this, I have not done that”—and much of it was highly interesting information regarding her moral standpoint. 

I have tried to find out the reason for this widespread custom, which causes such a pitiful waste of life. In addition to the mother and children being killed, it often leads to other people—who are completely uninvolved in the matter—being killed by the relatives of the sufferer on the suspicion of having caused the calamity through witchcraft. Until one can grasp the underlying idea and destroy it, the custom will be hard to eliminate in a district like the great Niger Delta. But I have never been able to track it down, though I am certain a reason exists, and it is undoubtedly a very strange idea. The usual answer is, “It was the custom of our fathers,” but that always and only means, “We do not intend to tell you.” 

Another explanation is that the dislike is grounded in the idea that having multiple births is like the lower animals. I believe teeth-filing <term>The practice of sharpening or shaping teeth, often as a tribal mark or aesthetic preference</term> undoubtedly arises from this same logic. You often hear a native from a tribe that practices filing or knocking out teeth say contemptuously of those who do not follow the custom, “Those men have teeth exactly like a dog’s.” 

I admit that when you are a Niger Delta native, you have to be a little careful for fear of being mistaken for one of the lower animals—just as poorly-dressed young men in our society object to carrying paper parcels for fear of being mistaken for tailors’ assistants. Still, this idea does not explain the terror—the abject terror—with which twins are regarded. Nor does it explain the conviction that their existence and proximity bring down diseases, difficulties, and disaster upon everyone. I once overheard a rational reason given, but again, the reason was not strong...

<header>FETISH CHAPTER</header>

The source of information was intoxicated, which was reason enough for the lack of clarity.

Related to this custom of killing twins—and sharing, I suspect, the same underlying belief—is a common practice among West African tribes. This involves throwing away the body of a woman who has died in <term>confinement</term> <note>Death during pregnancy or childbirth before the infant is born.</note> without the child being born. Her belongings are burned, and her name and memory are entirely erased. The name of such a woman is never mentioned after the tragedy. Her body is thrown far away into the forest, away from the paths where the bodies of little children are typically placed. Those children are left near paths so that their souls might choose a new mother from the women passing by.

Funeral customs vary considerably between the Niger Delta peoples and the Bantu. I have never found the same unpleasant "death-charms" among the Bantu that are common in the Niger Delta. One of these customs involves the nearest relatives sitting around the body for an incredibly long time—especially considering the climate—before burial beneath the floor of the house. During this time, the assembled relatives frequently and deeply sniff the air around the body. Young children are even brought in and held over the deceased so they can sniff it as well.

I was once in a canoe with four men and women and three children when a corpse floated toward us on the current. My companions paddled toward it with enthusiasm. Once they had pulled it against the side of the canoe, they dipped their <term>calabashes</term> <note>Containers made from the dried, hollowed-out shells of gourds.</note> into the water surrounding the corpse. They drank bowl after bowl until they were completely full. Then, in their characteristic style of "swallow-or-choke and never mind the spilling," they poured bowls of water into the children until the poor infants were nearly overflowing.

"This is a good death-charm," they told me. 

"I wouldn't be surprised if it were," I replied. "Now, paddle away." 

I was terrified that these people—who, except for their customs, are kindly and affectionate—might bring the corpse on board to take it home to their families to make a brew for home consumption. It was a very unpleasant corpse, afflicted with <note>smallpox: A highly contagious and often fatal viral disease characterized by fever and skin pustules; Kingsley’s fear of infection was well-founded.</note> smallpox and other such things. I am told this custom occurs in the Niger estuaries and the Old Calabar regions. I was in Bantu territory at the time, but my companions were not of pure Bantu descent.

<header>BURIAL CUSTOMS</header>

The Calabar people bury their dead under the floors of their houses whenever the British consul is not watching them. In the case of a great chief, the head is removed and buried somewhere else in great secrecy for the reasons I have previously explained. While the body is buried a few days after death, the most significant part of the process is the "burial of the spirit." This ritual causes immense worry, trouble, and expense for all West Africans, whether they are of Negro or Bantu descent. Regardless of how the deceased behaved in life, their spirit is considered malevolent—as all spirits created by local tradition are believed to be. Because a family must accumulate a significant amount of wealth to afford this spiritual burial, a long time—sometimes a year or more—usually passes between the burial of the body and the burial of the spirit. 

The practice of delaying the final rites until a grand funeral can be afforded is also common in Cabinda and Loango. However, in those regions, the body is not buried in the meantime. Instead, it is placed on a wooden platform with slow fires burning underneath to dry it out. A mat roof is usually built over the platform to protect the body from the rain. Once it is sufficiently dried, it is wrapped in cloth and placed in a coffin until the family has enough money to complete the ceremony. The Dualla people have stricter requirements; I am informed that their death-dances must be held on the third, seventh, and ninth days after death. During these specific days, the spirit is believed to be particularly present in its old home. In all other cases, I should note, the spirit does not leave the house until its "devil is made" <note>A term for the final commemorative funeral ceremony that releases the spirit from the earthly realm.</note>. If this ceremony is delayed for too long, the spirit naturally becomes irritable and restless.

Among the tribes of the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>, there are many different types of burial, such as the cannibalistic practices of the Fan people. I should mention, however, that the Fan themselves told me they consider it decent to bury a relative first, even if they eventually dig the body up later to trade it to their neighbors. There is also the practice of earth-burial used by the Igalwas and M'pongwe. Furthermore, I am told by reliable local sources that several tribes of the Upper Ogowé, including the Adoomas, beat the body into an unrecognizable pulp as a method of disposal. I did not have the opportunity to conduct quiet research on burial customs while I was traveling past Njoli, because I was too busy trying to avoid needing a burial myself. Consequently, I am not entirely certain if this method is the general practice among these little-

<header>FETISH CHAP.</header>

...known tribes, as native traders have told me, who believe that it is—or perhaps it is reserved for the bodies of people believed to have been possessed by dangerous souls.

Destroying the body by beating it or cutting it up is a widespread custom in West Africa when dealing with dangerous souls. This practice is always followed with bodies that have contained "wanderer-souls"—those spirits that keep appearing in the successive infants of a family. One child dies, then another is born to the same father or mother and also dies, after causing the usual trouble and expense. A third arrives, and if that one dies too, the father finally reaches his breaking point. If he still wants more children, he simply breaks one of the corpse's legs before throwing it into the bush.

He believes this will serve as a warning to the wanderer-soul. It informs the spirit that if it persists in returning to his family, it must settle down and give up its restless ways. If a fourth child is born to the family, "it usually limps." If that child also dies, the understandably angry parent carefully cuts the body into very small pieces and scatters them, destroying the soul entirely.

The people of the Kama country on the lower Ogowé River are more superstitious and follow more rituals than the tribes further up the river.

The Ncomi, a Fernan Vaz tribe, are particularly steeped in <term>Fetish</term> <note>Traditional spiritual beliefs and practices involving charms or spirits.</note> practices. I once witnessed a funeral where they had been called in to lead the rites, and M. Jacot told me of a nearly identical event he encountered during one of his many missionary trips from Lembarene. I will share his version because of his much better understanding of the language.

He was staying in a Fan <note>The Fang people of Central Africa.</note> town where one of the chiefs had just died. The other chief (there are usually two in a Fan town) decided that his deceased <term>colleague</term> <note>original: "confrère"</note> should be properly honored and resolved to arrange a magnificent ceremony.

The Fan people openly admit they do not fully understand life, death, the immortality of the soul, or similar matters. Therefore, the chief called in the Ncomi, who are specialists in these subjects, to conduct the funeral rituals.

M. Jacot <note>Monsieur Jacot, a French missionary mentioned on the previous page.</note> said the chief made a speech explaining that the Fans did not know about these rituals. However, their neighbors, the Ncomi, were known to be well-versed in them and knew the proper things to do, so he had called them in to pay honor to the deceased chief. Then the Ncomi began and carried out their weird, complicated death-dance.

The Fans sat and stood around watching them in a ring for a long time. However, the Fans are a rational, common-sense, shrewd, and unimaginative people. To them, standing hour after hour gazing at a dance they did not understand—which consisted of a wriggle and a stamp, a wriggle and a stamp, in a solemn walk or prance, round and round—produced only a feeling of boredom. The dance was accompanied by a monotonous phrase thumped on a <term>tom-tom</term> <note>A traditional drum, typically played with the hands.</note> and a monotonous, melancholy chant sung in a minor key, interspersed every few minutes with an emphatic howl. Therefore, the Fans quietly slipped away and went to bed. This disgusted the Ncomi, and an argument broke out. 

In the dance I witnessed, the same thing happened. When the Ncomi saw the audience thinning out, they complained. They said they were performing this dance in honor of the Fans’ chief as a neighborly gesture, and the very least the Fans could do, since they could not dance themselves, was to sit still and admire the people who could. The Fan chief in my village saw the logic in this; he went and rounded up the Fans who had gone home early and made them come back to watch the performance some more. They did this for a time, but then they slipped off again or slept in their seats. The Ncomi were highly disgusted by those "brutes" of Fans, whom they regarded—as they put it—as <term>Philistines</term> <note>A person who is indifferent or hostile to culture and the arts, or who lacks refinement.</note> of an utterly dull-witted and degraded type.

The Ncomi themselves place the body into coffins. A barrel is the usual choice, but another frequent form of coffin they use consists of two gun-cases with the ends knocked out and the cases fitted together. These coffins are not buried in the ground but are placed in special areas within the forest.

Along the banks of the Ogowé <note>The Ogooué River in Gabon.</note> you will notice long stretches of uninhabited bush here and there. These are not all merely stretches of swamp forest. If you land on some of these and go in a little way, you will find the forest full of mounds—or

# CHAPTER XXI

## FETISH—(*continued*)

->In which the traveler discusses the legal systems of the local inhabitants, the beliefs governing burial practices, their ways of mourning the deceased, and the condition of the African soul in the underworld.<-

As great as the incidental miseries and dangers are for everyone in a village when a death occurs, those who undoubtedly suffer the most are the widows of a chief or a free man.

It is the standard custom among both the Negro and Bantu peoples <note>In the 19th century, these were the standard ethnographic terms used by explorers to categorize West and Central African populations.</note> that those who escape execution on the charge of having bewitched their husband to death must remain in a state of filth and humiliation. They are not even permitted to remove lice from their bodies until the "soul-burial" <term>A secondary funerary ritual intended to finalize the transition of the deceased's spirit to the afterlife.</term> is complete. This is because the dead man’s soul is believed to linger around them and is considered vulnerable to injury. Therefore, to prevent his soul from being damaged, the widows are confined to their huts. While this latter restriction is not always strictly enforced, it is theoretically held to be the proper conduct.

They maintain an attitude of grief and degradation, sitting on the ground and eating very little food, and only that of a coarse variety. In Calabar <note>A coastal city and port in modern-day Nigeria.</note>, their legal rights to property—such as slaves <term>Refers to the systems of domestic and internal slavery that existed in West African societies during this period.</term>—are meanwhile suspended, and they are forced to spend a great deal of money while the spirit awaits burial. When the body is buried, the widows must keep watch in the hut in pairs, keeping lamps burning constantly. They must also pay from their own personal estates to entertain all the friends of the deceased who come to pay him [respects...]

Consequently, it often happens that even a wealthy woman is bankrupted by the resulting expenses. I will not delve into the legal details of these cases here, for they are complex and primarily of interest to a student of African law <term>Kingsley uses "Negro law" to refer to the legal systems of West African ethnic groups.</term>.

Bantu women hold a much lower status regarding property rights compared to the rights held by Negro women.

The status of widows after the death of a husband among the M’pongwe and Igalwa <note>Ethnic groups primarily located in what is now Gabon.</note> is a subject of great interest; however, like most of their legal systems, it is very complicated. The brothers of the deceased are expected to take the widows as their own wives—though a younger brother is not permitted to marry his elder brother’s widows, an elder brother may marry the widows of his younger brother. Should any of the women object to this arrangement, they are permitted to "leave the family."

I must admit that the fundamental principle of African law in practice is often "the simple plan that those who have the power should take, and those who can should keep." <note>A reference to William Wordsworth’s poem "Rob Roy’s Grave."</note> This reality is particularly harsh for women and children who lack powerful, living relatives of their own. Unless a man's children are grown and influential enough in their own right, they have little hope of receiving a share during the distribution of his estate. Yet, despite this abuse of power, there is a definite and acknowledged law among both Negro and Bantu peoples to which anyone, regardless of class, can appeal—provided they have the resources to set the legal machinery in motion. 

The difficulty that children and widows face in sharing the distribution of a husband or father’s estate arises, I believe, from the principle that the husband’s brother is the true heir. This principle has become rigid and outdated near the European trading stations in the face of white culture. The reason for this tradition—where inheritance passes from a man to his brother born of the same mother—is undoubtedly rooted in the recognition that a brother by the same mother is certainly a close blood relation. In contrast, despite strict laws against adultery, the biological relationship to the children born of one's wives is considered less certain. Nevertheless

<header>XXI THE LAW OF INHERITANCE 485</header>

This is one of those obvious and easy explanations for things that one should be very careful about accepting. You must always remember that the African mind does not operate on the same logic as the European mind; what may be self-evident to you is not so to him, and vice versa <note>Latin: "the other way around."</note>. I have frequently heard African philosophers <note>Original: "metaphysicians."</note> complain that white men make great leaps in their reasoning and do not follow an idea step-by-step. You soon become aware of the meticulous way an African <note>Original: "Negro."</note> follows his own logic. With great patience, you can trace certain of his customs in a perfectly direct line back to their source in some natural phenomenon. Others, of course, you cannot, as the traces of the intermediate steps of the idea have been lost. This is due partly to the deep respect in which old customs are held—which causes them to regard the fact that their ancestors followed a practice as reason enough for them to do the same—and above all to the total absence of any records other than oral tradition. However, I have such great faith in the African's lack of original invention that I feel sure all their customs could be traced back—if only we had the records that have slipped away into the great swamp of time—either to some natural phenomenon, as I have mentioned, or to the practice being advisable for practical reasons.

The uncertainty of paternity <note>Original: "parentage of offspring."</note> may seem to be the underlying practical principle for these laws, but on the other hand, it does not sufficiently explain the varied forms of the law of inheritance. In some tribes, the eldest or most influential son does succeed to his father’s wealth; in other places, you find the peculiar custom of the head slave inheriting the estate. Based on these observations, I believe the underlying idea in the inheritance of property is the desire to keep the wealth of “the house” (that is, the estate) together. If the property were allowed to pass into the hands of those considered weak, such as women and young children, this preservation of the estate would not be achieved. Another strong argument against the theory that these laws arise from the doubtful relationship of the son to the father is that certain <term>ju-ju</term> <note>Religious objects, charms, or spiritual authority.</note> always pass to the son of the primary wife, provided he is old enough at the time of the father’s death, even in those tribes where the material wealth is inherited by someone else.

Certain tribes acknowledge the right of the women and children to share in the dead man’s wealth, provided that these...

An esteemed friend of mine, who helps manage affairs for Germany <note>Original: "the Fatherland."</note> there, was mediating a dispute <note>Original: "palaver."</note> recently with his characteristic patience. He applied a level of intelligent and elaborate care that I believe only a mind trained in the methods of German philosophy <note>Original: "metaphysicians."</note> could bring to such a tedious process. In these proceedings, everyone repeats the same thing at least fourteen times with the same tone and gestures; the only variations occur in the details and the facts of the case, which change depending on the individual speaking. This dispute was initiated by a son claiming to inherit part of his father's property. Finally, to the astonishment and natural horror of the learned judge, the defendant—the "wicked uncle"—argued through the interpreter, "This man cannot inherit his father's property because his parents married for love." There is no encouragement for such sentimentality in Cameroon, where legal marriage consists of a purchase.

In Bonny River and in Opobo, the inheritance of "the house" <note>A "house" in this context refers to a traditional West African trading organization and kinship group.</note> is settled primarily by a vote of the free men of the house. When the chief dies, their choice must be ratified by the chiefs of other houses. However, because white traders have had significant influence in Bonny and Opobo for a long time, one cannot determine how much of this custom is truly indigenous in origin.

Among the Fan people, the uncle is an important figure, as I have mentioned before, although the father has more rights than among the Igalwa. Here, I encountered a peculiar custom regarding widows. Mr. <note>Original: "M." (Monsieur)</note> Jacot mentioned one or two similar cases to me, one of which occurred in an Ajumba town. The widows were inside their deceased husband's hut, as is traditional. Fan huts are sturdily built from sheets of flattened bark, firmly tied together with bark rope and thatched. They never build them any other way except when they are in the bush collecting rubber or hunting elephants, at which times they make them from tree branches. Well, around the bark hut containing the widows, a second hut made of branches was erected. When this was nearly finished, the Fans began—

<header>XXI MODES OF MOURNING</header>

...[ure who com]menced pulling down the inner bark hut, and finally cleared it right out, thatch and all; the materials from which it had been made were then burned. I was struck by this performance because the Fans <note>The "Fans" refers to the Fang people of Central Africa.</note>, though surrounded by intensely superstitious tribes, are remarkably free from superstition¹ themselves. They take little or no interest in theoretical matters, except to obtain charms to make them invisible to elephants, to keep their feet on the path, or to enable them to see things in the forest. They focus on practical things of that sort, and they frequently gave me these charms to assist and guard me in my wanderings.

The M'pongwe and Igalwa have a peculiar funeral custom, but it is not limited only to widows; all the near relatives share in it. The mourning relatives are seated on the floor of the house, and a friend—Dr. Nassau told me he was often called in for this purpose—comes in and "lifts them up." He brings them a small present, which always includes a piece of soap. This custom is now becoming a symbolic vestige in Libreville and Glass. Nowadays, the relatives do not actually sit there unwashed and unkempt, desperately needing the soap. Among the Igalwa in the bush, however, I am told the soap is still very much needed.

It is not only the widows who remain—either in theory or in practice—unwashed; all the mourners do. The Ibibio people seem to me to wear the heaviest mourning in the form of accumulated dirt. Additionally, all the African tribes I have met have specific ways of cutting their hair—shaving the entire head, not shaving it at all, or shaving only half of it—when they are in mourning.

I believe that for all West Coast tribes, the duration of the mourning period is the time that elapses between the death and the "burial of the soul." I think a more thorough knowledge of the subject would show us that the Bantu also have a fixed time for the soul to linger on earth after death, but we do not have enough evidence on that point yet. The only thing we know for certain is that it is considered improper for a widow to remarry while her husband's soul is still nearby.

Among the Twi <note>Tschwi is an archaic spelling for the Twi-speaking peoples, such as the Ashanti and Fante of modern-day Ghana.</note>, she requires special ceremonies for her own sake. In Togoland, among the Ewe people, I know the mourning period lasts between five and six weeks. During this time, the widow remains in the hut, armed with a sturdy stick as a precaution against her husband’s ghost, so as to ward off attacks should he be ill-tempered. After these six weeks, the widow can leave the hut; however, because his ghost has not permanently departed and is likely to return to the neighborhood over the next six months, she must be looked after during this time. Then, after certain ceremonies, she is free to marry again. Thus, I conclude that the mourning period in all tribes is the duration during which the soul remains near its former possessions, whether or not these tribes practice a formal "soul-burial" or "devil-making" <note>A "devil-making" is a common West African English term for a commemorative funeral festival or celebration.</note>.

The ideas connected with the underworld to which the ghost travels are exceedingly interesting. West Africans <note>The author uses "Negroes" to refer specifically to the West African coastal peoples, as distinct from the Bantu-speaking peoples of Central and Southern Africa.</note> and Bantus agree on these subjects in only one particular: that no marriages take place there. The Twi people say that this underworld, Srahmandazi, is identical to this world in every other way, except that it is dimmer—a true shadow-land where men do not have the joys of life, but only the shadow of those joys. Therefore, according to the Twi proverb, "One day in this world is worth a year in Srahmandazi." The Twi, with their typical precision regarding such details, know everything about their Srahmandazi. Its entrance is located just east of the middle Volta River, and the path down is difficult to follow; when the sun sets on this world, it rises on Srahmandazi.

The Bantus are vague on this important and interesting point. The Benga, for example, although believing in the absence of marriage there, do not take steps to address the situation as the Twi do, who kill a supply of wives to take down with them. This reason for killing wives at a funeral is another instance showing that, however strange and cruel a custom in West Africa may be, and however much it may at first appear to be the product of a baseless superstition, you will find upon close investigation that it is rooted in a religious idea and an element of common sense. The common-sense element in the killing of wives and slaves among both the Twi and the Calabar <note>Calabar refers to the Efik and related peoples of the Cross River region in modern-day Nigeria.</note> tribes consists of the fact that it discourages poisoning. A chief explained to me in great detail that the government’s strict prohibition of ritual killings at funerals had serious consequences. Not only did it cause a man to enter the next world as a miserable pauper, but it also increased the risk of him dying prematurely. He explained that because his wives and slaves were no longer deterred by the prospect of being killed upon his death to accompany him, they would, at the slightest provocation, put "bush in his chop" <term>a West African English idiom meaning to poison someone's food using toxic forest plants</term>.

It is sad to think of this hardship being added to the few comforts of a West Coast chief’s life, as his life is already 99.9 percent filled with difficulties.

He argued that because people were no longer allowed to destroy them as they had in the past, these "vermin" were now destroying the "game" <note>The chief is using a hunting metaphor: the "vermin" are the witches, and the "game" refers to the law-abiding or "valuable" members of the community being targeted by witchcraft.</note>.

<header>FETISH CHAPTER</header>

"For," he said, "the witches here live almost entirely on the blood they suck from children at night. In the old days, they used to do this secretly, and they still do so where local customs remain unchecked. However, in districts where the Government claims that witchcraft is complete nonsense—and that killing those who practice it is outright murder that will be prosecuted accordingly—the witch flourishes exceedingly. They blackmail the fathers and mothers of families, threatening that if they are not paid off, they will take their child's blood. If they are not paid, the child slowly wastes away—most likely due to poison again."

I often think it must be the practical element in <term>fetish</term> customs that allows them to survive so remarkably in the minds of Africans who have long been under European influence and education. In witchcraft, for example, every intelligent local person knows that poison plays a large part in the matter, but the explanation they give you usually will not reveal this knowledge. It was not until I discovered how widespread the idea was of administering an emetic <note>A substance that induces vomiting.</note> to a "bewitched" person that I began to suspect my African friends possessed sound judgment.

A skilled <term>ju-juist</term> will tell you that all things act by means of their "life," which refers to their power or their spirit. Dr. Nassau <note>Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), an American missionary and ethnographer in West Africa.</note> tells me that the effectiveness of drugs is believed to depend on their benevolent spirits. When introduced into the body, these spirits drive away the malevolent, disease-causing spirits—I suppose it is a sort of "white blood cells versus pathogenic bacteria" influence. This same idea also underpins the custom of appealing to an <term>ordeal</term>, the outcome of which is supposed to be spiritual. Nevertheless, even while believing in this spiritual factor, the intelligent local person manages the practical side by bribing the witch doctor who prepares the <term>ordeal</term> drink.

The feeling regarding the importance of funeral rites is almost Greek in its intensity. If given a proper education, I am sure an African would understand the true inner meaning of the *Antigone* <note>A tragedy by Sophocles centered on the protagonist's struggle to provide a proper burial for her brother against state orders.</note> far better than any European alive today could. A moving story relating to this feeling was told to me some time ago by Miss Slessor <note>Mary Slessor (1848–1915), a Scottish missionary in Nigeria known for her work in the Calabar region.</note> when she was stationed at Creek Town. An old, blind enslaved woman was found in the bush and brought into the mission. She was in a

-># XXI KILLING AT FUNERALS<-

She was in a deplorable state, utterly neglected and starving, her feet torn by thorns and full of jiggers <note>A species of parasitic sand flea (*Tunga penetrans*) that burrows into the skin, often causing infection.</note>, and so on. Every care was taken of her, and she soon revived and began to crawl about. However, her whole mind was fixed on one thing with a passion that had made her indifferent to both her past sufferings and her present comforts. What she wanted was a piece—only a small piece—of white cloth. Now, I should mention that white cloth is strictly forbidden by the Missions, as it is used for <term>ju-ju</term> <note>A West African term for traditional religious objects, charms, or spiritual practices.</note> offerings. A rule must be made against giving it to those who have not converted; otherwise, the missionary becomes an accomplice to pagan practices. Consequently, the old woman was told she could not have any white cloth. She had been given plenty of garments for her own use, and that was deemed sufficient. 

The old woman, however, kept pleading, saying the spirit of her deceased mistress kept appearing to her, crying and asking for white cloth, and she felt she must obtain it for her. At last, finding it was not to be had at the Mission station, she stole away one day, unobserved, and wandered off into the bush. She was never seen again, and she undoubtedly fell victim to the many leopards that haunted the area.

Providing a proper burial for a deceased relative is the primary duty of an African’s life; its only rival in his mind is the desire to have a proper burial for himself. But in a devoted person, the passion for a relative's burial will outweigh his own interests, and he will risk his very life to fulfill it. He may know perfectly well that killing slaves and women at a deceased brother's grave means he will be hanged when the "Big Consul" <note>A reference to the high-ranking British colonial officials or judicial authorities in the region.</note> finds out, but in the Delta, he will do it anyway. On the Coast, both Leeward and Windward, he will spend every penny he possesses and, if necessary, even sell himself, his wives, or his children into debt-slavery to give a deceased relative a proper funeral.

I used to think this practice of killing at funerals would be more easily abolished in the Niger Delta than among the Twi tribes, but a deeper understanding of the Delta’s concept of the afterlife showed me I was wrong.

Among the Twi, the slaves and women killed are intended to form a retinue for the deceased and provide the riches needed to start life in <term>Srahmandazi</term> <note>The underworld or land of the dead in Twi (Akan) mythology.</note>, where there are markets, towns, and all things as they are on this earth. Therefore, the Twi would have little reason...

# FETISH CHAPTER

There is difficulty in replacing human sacrifice at funerals with gold dust, cloth, and other forms of wealth, though this is already being done in districts under European influence. However, in the Delta, there is no permanent underworld to live in. Shortly after reaching the underworld, souls are sent back to this world in the bodies of new babies. The wealth that is sent down with a man indicates the social class of the baby into which that soul will be "repackaged" and sent back up. 

Since wealth in the Delta consists of women and slaves, I do not believe the underworld gods of the Niger would recognize the status of a chief who arrived before them with, for example, ten <term>puncheons</term> <note>A large cask of varying capacity, used here for transporting palm oil.</note> of palm oil and four hundred yards of crimson-patterned velvet. They would say, "Oh, this is all very well as far as it goes, but where is your real property? The chances are you are only a trade-slave boy and have stolen these things." Consequently, the practice of killing at funerals will be a custom that is exceedingly difficult to eliminate in these regions. Imagine for yourself how horrifying it must be to send a dear and honored relative to the afterlife only for them to be at risk of returning to this world shortly as a slave. 

There is certainly a belief among the people that some souls may improve their status in their next incarnation. You often hear a woman saying she will be a man next time, or a slave saying he will be a freeman, and so on. However, I do not yet have sufficient evidence to show how or why some souls obtain this promotion. I believe a little more investigation will allow me to understand this important point. I once asked a Calabar man, "But surely it would be easy for a man's friends to cheat? Could they not send a chief's outfit down with a man, even if he was only an unimportant person in this life?"

> "No," he said, "the other souls would report him, and then he would be sent back as a dog or some other beast as a punishment."

My first understanding of how common this idea of reincarnation is was also gained from a Delta native. I asked, "Why on earth do you throw the bodies of your dead slaves away in the bush? In other places I have been, they tie a string to the leg of a dead slave. When they bury him, they bring the string to the surface and fix it to a peg with the owner's name on it. Then, when the owner dies, he has that slave again in the world below."

<header>XXI WHY NOT CONVERT THE GODS?</header>
<page-num>493</page-num>

"They are foolish men," he said, and he went on to explain that the ghost of that slave would be back on earth almost immediately, growing up ready to work for someone else. The soul would not wait for its last owner’s soul in the underworld. From the overflow of information that followed, I gathered that no man’s soul stays below for long, and also that a soul returning to a family—a process ensured by certain <term>ju-jus</term> <note>Spiritual objects, charms, or traditional religious systems in West Africa.</note>—was identified. When new babies arrive in the family, they are shown a selection of small items belonging to deceased members whose souls are still absent; the object the child grabs identifies him. "Why, he is Uncle John, see! He knows his own pipe;" or "That is cousin Emma, see! She knows her market calabash," and so on.

I remember discussing the difficulty of eradicating fetish customs with a very charming French official.

"Why not take an indirect approach, Mademoiselle," said he, "and convert the native gods?"

I explained that his clever plan was not feasible because you cannot convert gods. Even trying to educate gods is hopeless work. For countless ages, all races of men have been attempting to make their specific deities understand how they are expected to work and what they are wanted to do, and the result is anything but encouraging.

As I have dwelt on the repulsive aspects of Negro funeral customs, I must, in fairness to them, present their more positive side. There is a custom I missed very much after traveling south of Calabar, for it is a beautiful one. Outside the villages in the Calabar districts, along the sides of the most traveled roads, you will see structures made of branches. I do not think these are intended to be huts, but rather beds, as they are very similar to the Calabar style of bed, only made of wood instead of clay. A roof of mats is placed over them to provide protection against the rain.

These shelters—which Europeans wrongly call graves or fetish huts—are made by driving four rather long, sturdy poles into the ground. At a height of about three feet, four more poles are tied to create a skeleton platform, which is filled in with <term>withies</term> <note>Tough, flexible twigs or branches used for binding or weaving.</note> and leveled. Another set of five poles is tied above, and the roof is attached to these. On

<header>FETISH CHAPTER</header>

On the platform is placed the bedding belonging to the deceased, including the undercloth, counterpane, and so on. At the head are laid the pillows, which are bolster-shaped and stuffed with cotton-tree fluff or shredded palm leaves, and covered with some gaily colored cotton cloth. In every case I have seen—and they amount to hundreds, for you cannot walk even an hour away from Duke Town without coming across a dozen or so of these structures—the pillows are placed so that a person lying on the bed would face toward the village.

On the roof, on the bed, and on the ground beneath it are placed the household utensils that belonged to the deceased: <term>calabashes</term> <note>Gourds dried and used as containers or bowls.</note>, basins, wooden spoons, and manufactured iron ones ("boughten" ones, as they say in Devon). Other small possessions are hung on the stakes. I know of one made for the ghost of a poor girl who died, and hung upon its stakes are the dolls and little pincushions given to her by a kind missionary.

Food is set out at these places and liquor is poured over them from time to time; occasionally, though not often, pieces of new cloth are laid on them. Most of the items are deliberately damaged before they are placed on this "home for the spirit." I do not think this is done to prevent them from being stolen, because they are not all damaged enough to be rendered useless. There was a beautifully made spoon with a burnt-in pattern at one of these sites when I left Calabar to go south; when I returned some six months later, it was still there. At another site, there was a very handsome pair of market calabashes, also heavily decorated, which were only slightly chipped and in better condition than many used in the Calabar markets. I have no doubt that the spoon and the calabashes are still lying there, rotting among the <note>original: "débris"</note> debris of the pillows and other items. These places are only maintained while the spirit is awaiting burial, as they are regarded merely as a resting place for it while it waits for that ceremony. I should note that the body is not buried near them.

Despite the care taken to bury spirits, a significant percentage remain unburied for various reasons—such as the poverty of the relatives, the deceased being a stranger in the land, or an accidental death in some unknown part of the forest or the sea. These unburied spirits linger, posing a common danger to the village.

# XXI BANISHING THE SPIRITS

...which they may choose to haunt. Many methods are used to purify the villages of these spirits. One method, which was used in Creek Town, Calabar, until just a few years ago—and which I am told is still customary in some inland villages—was very ingenious and believed to be effective by those who used it.

Large, grotesque wooden images called <term>Nbakim</term> <note>Grotesque wooden figures used to attract and trap spirits.</note> were set up in the houses and decorated with strips of cloth and trinkets. Every November in Creek Town (though some sources told me it occurred every two years), a type of festival was held. Offerings of food and alcohol were placed before these images. A group of people, joined by the rest of the population, would make a thorough circuit of the town, traveling through every street and around every house while dancing, singing, screaming, and beating drums. In fact, they made as much noise as they possibly could—and the <term>Efik</term> <note>The dominant ethnic group of the Calabar region.</note> people of Calabar are very talented at making noise. After this had gone on for what was considered a sufficient amount of time, the images were removed from the houses while the crowd continued their terrific racket. The figures were then thrown into the river, and the town was considered cleared of spirits.

The reasoning behind the practice is this: Wandering spirits are attracted to the images and take shelter among the rags, much like earwigs or similar insects. The *charivari* <note>original: "charivari"; a loud, discordant mock-serenade or noisy parade designed to annoy or drive something away.</note> is intended to drive any spirits who might be away from their shelters back inside. The shouting of the crowd is to prevent the spirits from venturing out again while they are being carried to the river. Throwing the images and their rags into the water is meant to destroy the spirits or at least send them elsewhere. They did not pour boiling water on these "earwig traps" as Europeans might, but the intention was the same. Once this was finished, they created and set up new images for any new spirits that might enter the town; these were maintained and tended just as before until the next <term>N’dok</term> <note>A biennial purification ritual in Calabar meant to expel ghosts and bad luck.</note> ceremony occurred.

Because of the spiritual view that Africans take regarding existence in general, ceremonial observances form the largest part of even their common-law procedures. Among both the <term>Negro</term> and <term>Bantu</term> peoples, there is a recognized...

## FETISH CHAPTER

There is a code of law founded on principles of true but merciless justice. It is not often used because of the difficulty and danger for any individual who appeals to it, especially if that person is not backed by power; nevertheless, the code exists.

The African is particularly harsh regarding theft. He by no means "makes excuses for sins he is inclined toward by condemning those he has no interest in," <note>A reference to Samuel Butler's poem *Hudibras*: "Compound for sins they are inclined to, / By damning those they have no mind to." The author suggests that although Africans may enjoy stealing, they do not let that fondness lead to leniency in legal matters.</note> for theft is a thing he revels in.

Individuals are tried for theft based on circumstantial evidence, direct testimony, and ordeal <term>ordeal</term> <note>An ancient judicial practice by which the guilt or innocence of the accused was determined by subjecting them to a painful or dangerous experience.</note>. Laws relating to mortgages are practically the same among Negro, Bantu, and European peoples. Torts <term>torts</term> <note>A civil wrong that causes a claimant to suffer loss or harm, resulting in legal liability for the person who commits the act.</note> are not recognized, unless the following case from Cameroon points to a vague realization of them:

Person A lent his canoe to Person B in good condition so that B could go upriver and fetch some trade goods. B did not go himself, but instead let Person C—who was not B's slave, but another free man who also wanted to go upriver for trade—use the canoe. This was done on the understanding that as payment for the loan of the canoe, C should bring down B's trade goods as well.

A was not told about this arrangement at all. B claims A *was* told, but that A was so "blind drunk" at the time that he did not understand. Regardless, C goes upriver in the canoe and strikes a floating stump in the river, smashing a hole in the bow large enough to put your head through. C returns the canoe to B in this condition, and B returns it to A in the same state.

A sues B before a native chief, stating that he lent his canoe to B on the understanding—which is always implied in African loans—that it was to be returned in the same state as when it was lent, with only fair wear and tear expected. B first tries to get C to pay for the canoe, as well as the rent for the canoe, as compensation for the delay in bringing down B's trade goods. C calls B the illegitimate offspring of a green house-lizard and further pleads that the floating log was a "superior force" <note>original: "force majeure"; an unavoidable accident or "act of God" that prevents someone from fulfilling a contract.</note> and denies liability on all counts. B then uses this same "act of God" argument as his own defense in the case between A and B (citing authorities in support of this view). He also pleads that he is not liable because C is a free man and not his slave.

The case went on for a week; the judge was drunk for five days in an attempt to get his head clear. The decision...

## XXI THE PUNISHMENT FOR ADULTERY

In theory, the laws against adultery are extremely severe. The punishment is death, and this sentence is occasionally carried out. Recently, King Bell in Cameroon whipped one of his wives to death; consequently, the German Government deposed and deported him, because such acts cannot be committed with impunity so close to a government headquarters. However, as a general rule all along the coast, the death penalty for murder or adultery is usually reduced to a fine. Alternatively, if you are wealthy, you can send a substitute to be executed in your place. This is a frequent practice because it is less expensive—if you have a sickly slave—to offer him to be killed in your stead than to pay a fine, which is often exorbitant.

The act of "adultery" itself often consists of nothing more than placing a hand on a woman—even in self-defense against a violent woman <term>virago</term> <note>A woman of great stature or strength; often used disparagingly to mean a domineering or bad-tempered woman.</note>—or accidentally brushing against her on a path. Aside from witchcraft, these accusations of adultery are the greatest social danger to West Coast natives. Such claims are frequently made solely for the purpose of extortion or out of spite, without a shred of truth to them.

It is customary for a chief to frequently subject his wives to an ordeal regarding this matter. This almost always occurs after a major religious festival <term>devil-making</term> <note>A colonial-era term used by Europeans to describe West African masquerades or spiritual ceremonies.</note> or a dance that his family attended. The standard method for this trial by ordeal is through boiling palm oil. A pot is nearly filled with the oil and heated over a fire until it is boiling. Once it is seething, the woman to be tried is brought before it. She first dips her hands into water and is then administered the M’biam oath <term>M’biam oath</term> <note>A traditional judicial oath in West Africa, often involving a ritual substance believed to bring supernatural punishment to those who lie.</note>. She recites, or has recited for her, a long and elaborate ritual formula adapted to the specific circumstances. She then plunges her hand into the boiling oil for an instant and shakes the oil off as quickly as possible; the next woman then follows to perform the same act, and so on. The following day, the women's hands are examined. Those found to be blistered are judged guilty and punished. To avoid severe punishment, a woman may accuse some man of having bumped into her or sitting on a bench next to her, and so on, and the accused man

<page-num>498</page-num>
<header>FETISH CHAPTER</header>

He has to pay the fine. If he does not, in the Calabar district, <term>Egbo</term> <note>A powerful secret society among the Efik people of Old Calabar that enforced laws and collected debts.</note> will come and “consume the adultery fine,” and there will not be much of that man’s worldly goods left. Sometimes the accusation is volunteered by the woman, and frequently the husband and wife conspire together to fabricate a case against a man just for the sake of collecting damages. In West Africa, nothing ensures a man’s reputation remains untarnished except having enough power to make it dangerous for others to insult him.

The ownership of children is a major source of <term>legal dispute</term>. The law among <term>Black West Africans</term> and <term>Bantu peoples</term> is that the children of a free woman belong to her. In tribes that emphasize the importance of maternal uncles, significant authority is granted to that relative, while in other tribes, certain powers are held by the father.

The father has absolute power only over children born to enslaved wives if he is the legal owner of the enslaved woman. If, as is frequently the case, a free man marries an enslaved woman who belongs to another man, all her children are the absolute property of her owner, not her husband. The owner of the woman can take them and sell them, or do whatever he chooses with them, unless the free father redeems them (pays for their freedom), as he usually does. Even then, the woman may still remain the absolute property of the owner, who can reclaim her at any time.

This law causes the most complex <term>disputes</term> that are brought before the colonial authorities. There is naturally no statute of limitations in West Africa, because the people there do not concern themselves with the passage of time. A clever owner (A) might allow his enslaved woman to live with another man (B) without demanding the redemption fees as they become due—letting the debt grow, as it were, at compound interest. All the children of the first generation, both male and female, are the property of the owner (A), and all the female children of these children are his property even into the second and third generation and for all time. The owner (A) may die before he makes his claim, in which case the ownership passes into the hands of his heirs or assignees. They may demand payment immediately upon receiving their inheritance, or they may again let the debt accumulate for their own benefit.

<header>XXI OWNERSHIP OF CHILDREN</header>

...heirs. Anyhow, sooner or later the reckoning comes, and then there is trouble. Free men—let us call them X, Y, and Z—have married some of the descendants of the original owner A's enslaved woman. They have either purchased them outright or have conscientiously continued to redeem their children as they were born. Naturally, A or his heirs argue that X, Y, and Z have been wasting their time and money by doing so, because the people they paid had no legal title to the women. Conversely, X, Y, and Z contend that their particular wife, or her ancestor, was properly redeemed from the legal owner.

Remember that there is no documentary evidence available, and groups of "oldest inhabitants," all supposedly equally reliable, swear vehemently in favor of both sides. Just realize this, and consider that your Government mandates that native law must be supported whenever it is not "blood-stained." You may then begin to realize the dizzying complexity of a native <term>palaver</term> <note>A term used in West Africa for a talk, dispute, or legal case, often involving long negotiations.</note>. If you continuously attempt to follow such a case with the determination that justice shall be properly administered, it will certainly lay you low with an attack of fever.

The law of ownership is not entirely in favor of the owner; masters are responsible for any damage caused by their slaves, and this law is very burdensome and expensive for the owner of a "bad" slave. Indeed, when one lives here and observes the conditions of this state of culture, the conviction grows that, morally speaking, the African is far from being the brutal fiend he is often portrayed—a creature that supposedly loves cruelty and blood for its own sake. The African does not; and though his culture lacks our institutions, such as psychiatric hospitals, prisons, workhouses, and hospitals, he still has to deal with the same classes of people who require those services. Therefore, he deals with them through his own equivalent institutions: slavery, the whip, and death. You have just as much right, my logical friend, to criticize a West Coast Chief for his habit of using brass bars and bundles of tobacco as currency instead of sixpenny pieces, as you have to abuse him for clubbing a habitual thief. It is deplorably primitive, I admit, but I do not quite see by what alternative plan of government his could be replaced under existing conditions. In religious affairs—the affairs which lead him into the majority of his—

<header>FETISH CH. XXI</header>

...wrongdoings, his real sin consists in believing too much. Regarding his beliefs in witchcraft, the sin is the same. I believe that among all people, tolerance is often just another word for indifference. The African is certainly not indifferent to the subject of witchcraft, and I do not see how anyone could expect him to be. Put yourself in his place: imagine you have captured a man or woman who has supposedly placed a live crocodile or a <term>catawumpus</term> <note>A colloquial term for a fierce, imaginary animal or monster; in this context, it refers to a malevolent spirit or creature.</note> of some kind inside of you, or inside a dear relative or neighbor, so that it might eat your vital <term>viscera</term> <note>The internal organs of the body, especially those in the abdomen or thorax.</note> and cause you or your friend to suffer and die. How would you feel? You might feel a bit like lynching your captive, I imagine.

I must admit that the more I learn about the West Coast Africans, the more I like them. I grant that I think they are <term>fools of the first water</term> <note>A phrase meaning fools of the highest or most extreme degree.</note> because of their capacity to believe in such things; however, I suspect I have similar feelings even toward my own fellow-countrymen when they passionately believe in something that I find hard to accept.

## CHAPTER XXII

### FETISH—(*Continued*)

->In which the Traveler complains of the inconveniences arising from the<-
->method of African thought, and discourses on apparitions and<-
->Deities.<-

ALTHOUGH some of the African's mental qualities are underrated, I am certain there are others for which he receives more credit than he deserves. One of these is his imagination. It strikes the newcomer with awe, and frequently fills him with rage when he first encounters it; but as he matures and becomes accustomed to the African, he begins to see the "strings." For the African's imagination is not the "ethereal fancy flying free" mentioned by our poets, but merely the stage prop of a theater suspended by a wire or cord. The "wire" that supports the African's imagination may be a very small, thin fact indeed, or in some cases merely his inability to distinguish between animate and inanimate objects, which gives rise to his idea that everything possesses a soul. Everything has a soul to him, and to make matters even more confused, he usually believes in the existence of matter separate from its soul. But there is little he won't believe in, for that matter; and I feel thankful that Buddhism, Theosophy <term>Theosophy</term> <note>A religious philosophy that seeks direct knowledge of the divine or the mysteries of the universe through mystical insight, often incorporating elements of Eastern religions.</note>, and above all Atheism—which goes in circles and tries to prove that nothing can be proved—have not yet been introduced to the African's belief system. He would believe the whole lot if he had the chance, and his mind is in quite a muddle as it is. I suppose I speak with irritation, but I have suffered much from the African’s mental confusion.

The African’s lack of clarity in his language regarding whether he is referring to an animate or inanimate thing has landed me in many a dilemma. His failure to distinguish between male and female genders in his languages is a nuisance; it has nearly turned my hair gray and brought me to an early grave in one fell swoop. For example, I am a very lady-like person, and yet I am constantly called “Sir.” I hasten to assure you that I never even wear a masculine collar and tie, and as for covering the lower parts of my anatomy in—well, you know what I mean—I would rather die on a public scaffold. The other day, after circumstances went beyond my control during the afternoon, I arrived in the evening soaking wet at a white settlement. Wishing to find lodging for myself and my men, I made my way to the factory <term>factory</term> <note>original: "factory"; a merchant's trading post or warehouse common in West Africa.</note> of a firm whose representatives have always given me great and most courteous help. I fit for want place for my men."</note>. <header>VIVID DESCRIPTIONS</header>

scared him half to death, and he was intensely apologetic. I remarked that the shock had very nearly aged me thirty years, and he explained that the steward boy had merely informed him that “A white man has arrived from X” <note>original: "White man live for come from X"</note>, a place where he knew there was another factory <term>factory</term> <note>a merchant's trading post or warehouse common in West Africa.</note> belonging to his firm, and he naturally thought it was the agent from X who had come across. You rarely—indeed, I believe never—find an African with a gift for picturesque descriptions of scenery. The closest I ever encountered was from my cook when we were on Mungo mah Lobeh <note>Mount Cameroon.</note>. He proudly boasted he had been on a mountain up the Cameroon River with a German officer, and on that mountain, “If you fall down one side you die; if you fall down the other side, you die.”

You often hear graphic and vivid descriptions of events, but it is not Art. The effect is produced entirely by a blunt brutality of statement, as the African has no artistic restraint whatsoever. However, one fine touch that does not fall into this category was told to me by my late friend Mr. Harris of Calabar. Some years ago, he received a shipment of Dutch clocks with hanging weights, as is typical for a Dutch clock. They were immensely popular among the local chiefs and were all quickly sold except for one, which had been damaged during the voyage and had lost one of its weights. Mr. Harris, who was a man of great energy and resourcefulness, melted down some metal spoons to make a new weight and hung it on the clock. The day he finished this, a chief came in anxious to buy a Dutch clock, and Mr. Harris immediately sold him the repaired one. About a week passed, and then the chief returned to the factory with a sorrowful expression, followed by a boy carrying something wrapped in a cloth. It was the clock.

“You have treated me very badly, Mr. Harris,” <note>original: "You do me bad too much, Mr. Harris"</note> said the chief.

### FETISH CHAPTER

Mr. Harris immediately denied this with the forcefulness of injured innocence. The chief shook his head and spat heavily and sorrowfully.

“Don’t you know the clock you sold me?” <note>original: “You no sabe him clock you done sell me?”</note> said he. “When I look at the clock, it isn't today; it is tomorrow.” <note>original: “When I look him clock it no be to-day, it be to-morrow.”</note> Mr. Harris took the clock back to see what was causing this strange state of affairs. Of course, it turned out he had been too generous with the lead adjustment in the weight. Once this was corrected, the chief was no longer hurried toward his grave at such a breakneck pace; “but,” Mr. Harris remarked, “that clock was a fast runner to the very end.”

Phrases in the native languages often suggest a talent for imagery. For example, the <term>Efik</term> word for both stars and fireflies is <term>Ntan-ta fiong</term>. Some authorities translate this as “moon dust,” which is quite poetic; however, other experts say it means “made of the same material as the moon,” which reduces it to simple nonsense. The name for butterflies, which means “the cloth of the spirit,” has no critics; nor does the name for the pretty little gecko lizard that lives in houses and is now learning to walk on ceilings: “the spirit of the child,” and so on. 

I will not go deeply into the subject of African languages here, except to remark that although they are complex enough to allow their speakers to express nearly every variety of incorrect statement, they are not—with the possible exception of <term>Mpongwe</term>—sophisticated enough to enable a person to state their exact thoughts. Some of these languages depend heavily on gestures. When I was staying with the <term>Fang</term> <note>original: "Fans"</note> people, they frequently said, “Let’s go to the fire so we can see what they are saying,” whenever a decision had to be made after dark. The inhabitants of <term>Fernando Po</term> <note>Now the island of Bioko</note>, the <term>Bubi people</term>, are completely unable to converse with one another unless there is enough light to see the gestures that accompany the speech. In all these cases, I feel certain the African’s intelligence is far more advanced than his language.

The African is usually a frequent dreamer and dreams very loudly; however, he does not seem to attach great importance to them—certainly not as much as the <term>Native American</term> <note>original: "Red Indian"</note> does. I doubt there is much evidence to support the theory that man’s first concept of a spirit world originated from dreams.

<page-num>505</page-num>
<header>XXII ORIGIN OF RELIGION</header>

...and I believe the origin of human religious belief lies in human misfortune.

There is little doubt that the very earliest humans found, just as their descendants still do, that their plans were often frustrated, no matter how wisely or carefully they planned. They must have seen their companions overcome by death and disaster, resulting from both visible and invisible causes. The distinction between these two types of occurrences is not as clearly recognized by primitive peoples or animals as it is by more advanced societies. I doubt whether a primitive person relies solely on their five senses to understand the world any more than a member of the Royal Society <note>The Royal Society of London is the UK's national academy of sciences, representing the pinnacle of scientific rationalism in the author's era.</note> does. 

From this worldview, I am certain that a general idea arose—one found in all early cultures—that death was always the consequence of a malicious spirit's actions. In this view, there is no such thing as "accidental" or "natural" death, as we call it. After all, death is the most impactful aspect of life.

If a man is struck on the head with a club or shot with an arrow, the cause of death is clearly the malice of the person using those weapons. Therefore, it is easy for them to believe that a person killed by a falling tree, a capsizing canoe in the surf, or an eddy in a river is also the victim of some being using those objects as weapons.

Once a person has gained the belief that there are supernatural actors in the tragedy of life, the idea that disease is also a manifestation of an invisible being's wrath and power seems natural and simple. He knows that you can pay one person to harm or kill another. Therefore, he believes that for a fee, you can also persuade one of these superhuman beings—which we call gods or demons, but which the African views in a different light—to do the same.

A specific group of men and women then specialize in studying how these spirits can be managed, which leads to the creation of a priesthood. These priests—or "medicine men," as they are called in their earliest forms—gradually complicate and shroud their profession with rituals and mystery for their own benefit.

The primitive person is also aware of another major set of phenomena which, they soon learn, take no interest in human

This belief led to the development of a specialized priesthood that manages these spirits through ritual and mystery.</summary>

### FETISH CHAPTER

The sun that rises and sets, the moon that changes, the tides that ebb and flow—what do they care? Nothing. Furthermore, no matter what you sacrifice to them, you cannot make them care about you or your affairs. Consequently, the native turns his attention to those other spirits that take all too much interest, as is proven by those unexpected catastrophes. As their actions show, these spirits are entirely malicious, so he deals with them just as he would deal with a bad man whom he wished to manage. 

He flatters them and pays them fees; he deprives himself of riches to give to them as sacrifices, believing they will relish the gift all the more because it causes him some sort of pain to give it up. He holds the belief that the spirits will think it advisable to encourage him to continue giving by occasionally doing what he asks. Naturally, he never feels certain of them. He sees that one may sacrifice to a god for years; you may wrap him up—or more properly speaking, the object in which the spirit resides—in your only cloth on chilly nights while you shiver yourself. You, your children, your mother, your sister, and her children may go hungry so that food may rot upon his shrine; and yet, in some hour of dire necessity, the power will not come to save you—simply because he has been enticed away by gifts richer than yours.

You white men will say, “Why go on believing in him then?” But that is an idea that does not enter the African mind. I might just as well ask, “Why do you go on believing in the existence of hansom cabs <note>A hansom cab is a type of horse-drawn, two-wheeled carriage used as a taxi in the 19th century.</note>,” just because one hansom cab driver maliciously fails to take you where you want to go, or fails to arrive in time to catch a train you wished to catch.

The African fully knows the likelihood of his fetish <term>fetish: an object believed to have supernatural powers or to be inhabited by a spirit</term> failing, but he is equally aware of its power. I learned of one grandly tragic instance of this at Opobo <note>A coastal trade town and kingdom in the Niger Delta, modern-day Nigeria.</note>. There was a very great Fetish doctor there, universally admired and trusted, who lived out on the land at the mouth of the Great River. One day he himself fell sick, and he made ju-ju <term>ju-ju: a West African term for folk magic, charms, or the spiritual energy associated with a fetish</term> against the sickness; but it held on, and he grew worse. He made even more powerful ju-ju, but again in vain. Then he made the greatest ju-ju a man can make, and it achieved nothing, and he knew he was dying. And so, with his remaining strength, he...

<summary>The author explains the logic of West African fetishism as a pragmatic, if desperate, attempt to bribe malicious spirits. Faith persists despite failure because the spiritual system is viewed as a reality akin to a public service that sometimes fails rather than a false belief.</summary>

<page-num>XXII, 507</page-num>

# PARADISE LOST

...broke up, dishonored, and destroyed all the <term>fetishes</term> <note>Objects believed to be inhabited by spirits.</note> in which the spirits lived, cast them out into the surf, and died like a man.

Then horror fell upon the people when they realized what he had done. They burned his house and everything belonging to him, crying out to the spirits not to abandon them or hold this one man's deadly sin against the community. I rather doubt whether those spirits have come around yet, for Dr. Tompstone wrote to me last November—just when their annual festivals were in full swing—that to ensure fine weather, Opobo <note>A coastal city-state in what is now Nigeria.</note> "called in a noted consultant from upriver." The doctor adds, with a gracious sympathy for a fellow medical professional, "It has rained in torrents ever since. It is quite hard on him, as I believe he did his best and sacrificed a large number of chickens."

Regarding the gods of West Africa, I should mention that in almost all native traditions there, you will find accounts of a time when there was direct interaction between men and the gods or spirits who live in the sky. That interaction is always said to have been cut off by some human error. For example, the people of Fernando Po <note>An island now known as Bioko in Equatorial Guinea.</note> say that once there was no trouble or serious disturbance on earth because there was a ladder, made like the ones used to harvest palm nuts, "only long, long." This ladder reached from earth to heaven so the gods could go up and down to personally attend to earthly affairs. But one day a disabled boy started to climb the ladder, and he had reached a great height when his mother saw him and climbed up in pursuit. The gods, horrified at the prospect of women and children invading heaven, threw down the ladder and have since left humanity strictly alone. 

The Timneh <note>The Temne people of Sierra Leone.</note> people, northeast of Sierra Leone, say that in the old days, God was very friendly with men. When He thought a man had lived long enough on earth, He sent a messenger to tell him to come up into the sky to stay with Him. However, there was once a man who, when God’s messenger arrived, did not want to leave his wives, his slaves, and his riches. Consequently, the messenger had to return without him. God became very angry and sent another messenger for him called Disease, but the man would not go with him either—

<page-num>508</page-num>
<header>FETISH CHAPTER</header>

...and so Disease sent word back to God that he needed help to bring the man. Consequently, God sent another messenger named Death. Disease and Death together seized the man and took him to God, and God decreed that in the future, He would always send these messengers to fetch men.

The <term>Fernando Po</term> <note>An island in Equatorial Guinea, now known as Bioko.</note> legend may be taken as a fairly pure African myth, but I suspect the <term>Timneh</term> <note>The Temne people of Sierra Leone.</note> story is a transformed Arabic tale. Although I do not know of any specific Arabic story like it, they are infinite in number, and it has a certain recognizable tone. Additionally, these <term>Timnehs</term> are frequently in contact with <term>Muslim</term> <note>Original: "Mohammedan."</note> groups like the <term>Mandingoes</term> <note>The Mandinka people.</note> and others. 

In none of these African stories is as much importance given to dreams as is given to attempts to explain accidents and death. Surely it must have been more impressive and significant for a man to have his leg or arm snapped off by a crocodile in the river or by a shark in the surf—or to have been nearly killed, or seen a friend killed by a falling tree in the forest during the day—than to have experienced even the most extraordinary dreams. He sees that regardless of how terrifying his dream experiences might have been, he was not much the worse for them. This is not the case with physical injury; a lost limb or a lost life is more impressive and more necessary to explain.

I have never found any trace of sun-worship. The sky is, I believe, always associated with the great, indifferent, and neglected god: the <term>Nyan Kupon</term> of the <term>Twi</term> <note>Original: "Tschwi."</note> and the <term>Anzambe</term>, <term>Nzam</term>, and so on, of the <term>Bantu</term> races. The African believes this god has great power if he would only use it. When things go very badly for him—when the river rises higher than usual and sweeps away his home and plantations; when smallpox stalks through the land, and corpses float down the river past him day and night, jamming against his canoes tied to the beach and choking up his fish traps; and then, when finally the death-wail for the victims rises night and day from his own village—he will rise up and call upon this great god in a terror driven by despair, hoping that the god might hear and restrain the evil workings of these lesser devils. 

However, he evidently finds, as <term>Peer Gynt</term> <note>The protagonist of Henrik Ibsen's 1867 play.</note> says, "No, he does not hear. He is deaf as usual," <note>Original: "Nein, er hört nicht. Er ist taub wie gewöhnlich."</note> for there is no organized worship for <term>Anzam</term>.
