<page-num>509</page-num>

# SUNDRY APPARITIONS

Accounts of apparitions abound in all the West Coast districts. Although the African holds them all in great horror and terror, he does not see anything supernatural in his **“Duppy”** <note>A ghost or spirit in West African and Caribbean folklore.</note>. It is a horrid thing to encounter, but there is nothing strange about it, and he is ten thousand times more frightened than puzzled by the event. He does not want to “investigate” to see whether there is anything to it; he wants to get far away and immediately perform **ju-ju** <note>Spells, charms, or magical practices used for protection or influence.</note> against it.

These apparitions take a great variety of forms. First, there are all the true spirits, or nature spirits. Second, there are the spirits of human beings—these human spirits are believed to exist before, during, and after bodily life. Third, there are the spirits of objects. Probably the most horrid of the first class is the <term>Twi</term> <note>Original: "Tschwi." The Twi-speaking people of the Akan ethnic group in modern-day Ghana.</note> people's **Sasabonsum** <note>A legendary forest monster in Akan mythology.</note>. Whether Sasabonsum is an individual or a class of spirits is not quite clear, but I believe he represents a class of spirits where each individual shares the same characteristics, the same way of showing anger, the same appearance, and the same kind of home. I am a devoted student of his cult, and I am always coming across equivalent forms of him in other tribes besides the <term>Twi</term>. I think his legend is very ancient. I see no reason why gorillas should not believe in Sasabonsum; unfortunately, <term>Dr. Garner</term> <note>Richard Lynch Garner (1848–1920), an American researcher who traveled to West Africa to study primate communication.</note> has not provided us with a grammar and dictionary of "Gorillese," so I cannot question those interesting people on the point. As the <term>Twi</term> have their religious notions in a most tidy and definite state, we will take their version of Sasabonsum.

He lives in the forest, in or under those great <term>silk-cotton trees</term> <note>Massive tropical trees (Ceiba pentandra) often associated with spirits.</note> where the earth around the roots is red. This colored earth identifies a silk-cotton tree as the residence of a Sasabonsum. Its color is believed to come from the blood the spirit wipes off himself as he descends to his underworld home after a night’s carnage. All silk-cotton trees are suspected because they are held to be the roosts for **Duppies**. But the ones with red earth are feared with a great fear; no one makes a path by them or sets up a camp near them at night.

Sasabonsum is a friend of witches. He is of enormous size and red in color. He wears his hair straight, and he waylays unprotected travelers in the forest at night. In all districts except that of <term>Apollonia</term> <note>A historical region in what is now southwest Ghana and southeast Ivory Coast.</note>, he eats them. Round—

In Apollonia, he only sucks their blood. After encountering him, the natives of this district have crawled home, given an account of his appearance, and then died.

Colonel <note>Alfred Burdon Ellis (1852–1894), a British army officer and author who wrote extensively on West African peoples.</note> Ellis says he is believed to be relentless, and when angered, he can never be calmed or appeased. However, it is certain that human victims are constantly sacrificed to him in districts beyond European control; in districts under their control, the equivalent value of a human sacrifice in sheep and goats is offered to him instead. In Asante <note>Original: "Ashantee"</note>, he has priests and, naturally, human sacrifice. Farther away among the Dahomeyan <note>People of the Kingdom of Dahomey, in modern-day Benin.</note> tribes—where he has kept his habits but acquired another name, and seems to have evolved from a class of spirits into an individual (the usual way in which a god develops)—he has priests and priestesses, and they are truly fearsome. But among the Twi <note>Original: "Tschwi"</note>, <term>Sasabonsum</term> <note>A malevolent forest monster in Akan mythology.</note> is mainly dealt with by witches and people desiring the power to become witches. They derive their power from him in a remarkable way. I put myself to great personal inconvenience (risking fever, certain of mosquitoes, the high probability of encountering leopards and snakes, and feeling grave personal alarm and apprehension) to verify Colonel Ellis's account of the methods witches employ in this case. Finding his account correct, I quote it here because it is likely to be more concise than mine.

A <term>suhman</term> <note>A spirit-object or "fetish" used for protection or to harm others, common in Akan traditional religion.</note> prepared in one of the last three modes is frequently kept covered in <term>Shea butter</term>, but a wooden figure is never treated this way.

According to most natives, he then picks certain leaves and squeezes their juice upon the object, saying, ‘Eat this and speak.’ Then, if a spirit has entered the object—in other words, if the latter has become a <term>suhman</term>—a low hissing noise is heard. Being thus assured that the spirit is there, the man then asks a number of questions: Should the <term>suhman</term> be kept in a box or left out in the open? Should he be anointed with <term>Shea butter</term> or left dry? Those questions to which a low hissing sound is heard in reply are believed to be answered in the affirmative.”

In the two cases in which I saw a <term>suhman</term> procured, the methods employed were numbers 1 and 3. I have seen <term>ehsuhman</term> <note>The plural form of suhman.</note> in the possession of individuals that matched the appearance of the other kinds in every detail.

The chief use of a <term>suhman</term> is the power it gives its owner to cause the death of other people. These are not necessarily his own enemies, for he will sell charms made through the agency of his <term>suhman</term> to another person whose nerves were not strong enough to face <term>Sasabonsum</term> on their own. He can also provide other charms through its agency, such as those that protect houses from fire, or protect things and individuals from accidents on the road or in canoes. They can even protect the home circle from attractive but unprincipled young men, and so on.

The quantity of charms among the West Africans <note>Original: "Negroes."</note>, as among the <term>Bantu</term> <note>A major linguistic and ethnic group across central and southern Africa.</note>, is nearly infinite. Most of them are obtained from <term>suhman</term> holders, but not all. I suspect a <term>suhman</term> wears itself out making charms, for you will sometimes come across “dead” ones that you can buy. These dead ones are <term>ehsuhman</term> (plural) that have failed to work several times because the spirit has left them; whereas a live charm is treasured and treated as a sentient being. ...of feathers with a porcupine tail in the middle, and he used to always spray a little rum from his mouth over it whenever he was drinking.

As a rule, a person who possesses a <term>suhman</term> <note>A spirit-object or "fetish" used for protection or to harm others.</note> keeps that fact very quiet. The possession of such an item would cause half the catastrophes in the district—from the death of pigs, chickens, and babies, to fires and other accidents—to be blamed on him. This would lead to his neighbors bringing a "witchcraft accusation" <term>witch palaver</term> against him, and he would have to undergo a <term>poison-ordeal</term> <note>A practice where a suspect drinks a toxic substance; survival or vomiting is seen as proof of innocence.</note> and other unpleasant trials to clear his name. He does, however, always keep a special day in honor of his <term>suhman</term>; and if he is powerful, such as a king or a great chief, he will observe this day openly. King <term>Kwoffi Karri Kari</term> <note>Kofi Karaka, King of the Asante (1867–1874).</note>, whom we fought against in 1874, used to hold a major celebration for his <term>suhman</term>, which was kept in a box covered with gold plates. He sacrificed a human victim to it every Tuesday, accompanied by general festivities and dances in its honor.

I should mention that <term>Sasabonsum</term> <note>A malevolent forest spirit.</note> is married. His wife—or more accurately, his female form—is called <term>Shamantin</term>. She is far less malicious than the male form. Her name comes from <term>Srahman</term>—ghost or spirit; the suffix "tin" is an abbreviation of *tsintsin*—tall. She is of immense height and is white; perhaps this idea is derived from the white trunks of the silk-cotton trees where she always lives. Her method of dealing with the solitary traveler is certainly inconvenient for him, but it is kinder than her husband's ways. She does not kill and eat him as <term>Sasabonsum</term> does, but merely detains him for some months while she teaches him everything about the forest: which herbs are good to eat or to cure disease, where the game animals come to drink, what they say to each other, and so forth. I often wish I knew this lady, for the grim, grand African forests are like a great library in which, so far, I can do little more than look at the pictures. However, I am now busily learning the alphabet of their language so that I may one day read what these pictures mean.

I beg you, do not go away with the idea that goddesses are, as a general rule, better than gods. They are not. There are stories about them which I could—I mean I could not—tell you. There is one belonging also to the <term>Tschwi</term> <note>The Twi-speaking people of the Gold Coast (modern Ghana).</note> people. She lives—

<page-num>513</page-num>
<header>XXII THE ALBINO DEITY 513</header>

...at Moree, a village five miles from Cape Coast. She is, as is usual with deities, human in shape and colossal in size, and as is *not* usual with deities, she is covered with hair from head to foot—short white hair like a goat. Her dwelling is on the path to surf-cursed Anamabu near the sea-beach, and her name is Aynfwa. A worshipper only needs to mention the name of a person they wish dead while passing her home, and Aynfwa does the rest. She is the goddess of all albinos, who are said to occur more frequently around Moree than elsewhere. Ellis <note>Sir Alfred Burdon Ellis (1852–1894), a British army officer and author who wrote extensively on West African peoples.</note> says that in 1886, when he was there, they made up one percent of the entire population. These albinos are, <note>original: "ipso facto"; by that very fact</note> her priests and priestesses. In the old days, an albino only had to name a person anywhere whom Aynfwa "wished for," and that person was immediately killed.

I think I may safely say that every dangerous place in West Africa is regarded as the residence of a god—rocks and whirlpools in the rivers, swamps where <term>no man fit to pass</term> <note>A local idiom meaning "no man is able to cross" or "impassable."</note>, and naturally, the surf. Along the Gold Coast, at every place where you must land through the surf, the water fairly swarms with gods. A little experience with the mentioned surf inclines you to think, as those who dabble in spiritualism say, "that there is something in it." I would pit this West Coast surf—the <term>Calemma</term> <note>A Portuguese-derived term for the heavy Atlantic surf or "rollers" on the West African coast.</note> as we call it down South—against any other malevolent abomination, excluding only the English weather. 

Its ways of dealing with human beings are cunning and deceitful. In its most ferocious moods, it seizes a boat, immediately swamps it, and feeds its pet sharks with the boat’s occupants. If the surf is merely playing around, it lets your boat’s nose just "smell" the sand, and then says, "Thought you were all right this time, did you?" It then drags the boat back again under the incoming wave, or catches it under the stern and cheerfully throws it upside down over you and your belongings on the beach. 

They say variety is charming. Let those who say it, and those who believe it, just try a course of "surf-work," and I guarantee they will change their minds. Above all, let men who must deal with the demon-possessed surf of the West African coastline take care not to let their minds be entirely filled with the terror of drowning or being eaten by sharks; for in this business, those are actually minor dangers, even though they do occur.

The danger lies in your own boat. It is not given to every man to do what my giant friend, Captain Heldt, did: he swam ashore and crawled up the beach with three broken ribs and his legs temporarily paralyzed. This happened after a heavy surf-boat was hurled onto his back by a wave while he was attempting an independent venture to reach the shore following a wreck on the outer breakers. 

Let me add that when the Black boatswain <note>original: "bo’sn"</note> of the Windward Coast, or the equally Black <term>Padrone</term> <note>A headman or master of a boat crew, a term derived from the Portuguese word for "patron" or "master."</note> of the Southwest Coast, yells at you to jump into the surf, do it immediately <note>original: "one time"</note>. Never mind the sharks; instead, make sure to jump out on the windward side of the boat—the side the surf is crashing against, which looks like the worst side to choose. By doing this, you may stay clear of the boat itself. I do not recommend taking a white man’s advice about when to jump until you have researched his genealogy and confirmed beyond a doubt that he is a direct descendant of George Washington <note>An ironic reference to the legendary honesty of the first U.S. President.</note>. 

There was once a pleasant young doctor on a Southwest Coast boat who did not follow this plan. He did not realize that in this nineteenth century, it is every person's duty to save their capacity for belief for religious purposes. Instead, this doctor wasted his trust on "old coasters" <note>Experienced European residents or traders living on the West African coast.</note> and sea captains—most excellent people, but deeply human. I am one myself now, so I speak with authority; it is just that the information we shower upon newcomers is often too much for them to handle, and that was the case with this doctor. 

They had told him about the surf: how you had to jump and swim through the final breakers as soon as you heard the shout, and so on. So, when going ashore at Batanga, the brave boat-boys gave the rousing war-cry with which they customarily greet their enemy, feeling "that stern joy a warrior feels" <note>A quotation from Sir Walter Scott’s poem *The Lady of the Lake*.</note>. The doctor went over the side like a shot, much to the horror of the guilt-stricken sea captain who was in the boat. He made it through safely, however. 

Now and then, I admit, the newcomer wins. There was one man who came out on government business to Accra, where the surf is notorious. The boat capsized in the first line of breakers, and the surf that day was as violent as Accra has ever seen. When he finally got ashore, the "old coasters" thought he would be impressed and terrified; but no. He simply remarked that it was lucky he had such a...

And finally, as the preacher says, remember that it is highly advisable to have a clear conscience—at least regarding your past treatment of your <term>Kru</term> <note>An ethnic group from Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire renowned for their skills as sailors and navigators.</note> or <term>Accra</term> <note>People from the region of the modern capital of Ghana, often employed as skilled boatmen.</note> boat-boys—before you trust yourself to them to take you through the surf. There was once a wicked man on the Gold Coast who had mistreated his men. When they took him out through the surf to board the ship that was to take him home, there was the usual catastrophe. No one thought much of it, only saying, "It was hard on B., just as he was going home," until B.’s body washed ashore. Then, inside his clothes, they found three iron shark hooks with plenty of line attached. The men had used these to hold B. back from the shore, playing him like a fish until the surf beat the life out of him.

Please forgive this digression about the surf. However, a <term>coaster</term> <note>A European resident or trader living along the West African coast.</note> cannot help going on like this as soon as their favorite enemy is mentioned. I now humbly return to the subject of African apparitions. There is one thing about the surf that I do not understand: why do witches always walk stark naked along the beach beside it at night, eating sea crabs all the while? It is certain that this is a confirmed habit of theirs. I am told that while doing this, the witches emit a bright light. There is also a certain medicine—which, if you have it with you, you can throw over the witch—and then he or she will remain blazing until morning. They will run to and fro, crying out wildly in front of the white, crashing, thundering wall of surf. When dawn comes, the fire consumes the witch entirely, leaving only grey ash—and then the <term>palaver</term> <note>A West African term for a dispute, discussion, or legal case; here meaning the matter is concluded.</note> is settled in this world and the next for that witch.

A highly respected native minister told me during my last visit to Cape Coast that two weeks earlier, he had been away in the <term>Apollonia district</term> <note>A coastal region in the southwest of modern-day Ghana.</note> on mission work. One evening, he and a friend were walking along the beach. The night was so dark that you could only see the surf. It is never too dark to see the waves; they seem to possess a light of their own. They saw a flame coming toward them. After a moment of doubt, they knew it was a witch. Feeling frightened, they hid themselves among the bushes that edge the sandy shore. As they watched, it...

...came straight toward them and passed them, and they saw it disappear in the distance. My informant laughed at himself and very wisely said, “One doesn't have to believe those things here, but one does in Apollonia.” <note>Apollonia was a historical region on the coast of West Africa, located on the border of modern-day Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire.</note>

The Twi-speaking people <note>original: "Tschwis"</note> who live along the coast bring women who have recently given birth and widows to the surf and its spirits. This occurs after a period of eight days following either the birth of the child or the death of the husband.

A widow remains in the house until this period has passed, neglecting her appearance, eating very little food, and sitting on the bare floor in a posture of mourning. On the Gold Coast, burials happen very quickly—as people are always telling you—usually the day after death and rarely later than the third day, even among the local people. The spirit, or <term>Srah</term> <note>The ghost or spirit of a deceased person in local belief.</note>, of the dead man is supposed to linger around his wives and his house until the ceremony of purification is carried out. This is done, naturally, with a great deal of noise. The relatives of each wife go to her house with musical instruments—specifically tom-toms and that sort of thing—and they bring a large amount of mint, which grows wild in this country. They burn some of this mint in the house; the rest they place upon pans of glowing coals and carry around the widow as she walks among them down to the surf. Her relatives sing aloud to the <term>Srah</term> of the departed husband, telling him that now that he is dead and finished with the lady, he must leave her alone. This singing serves to warn all the women who are not relatives to get out of the way, which of course they always do carefully, because if they were to see the widow, their own husbands would die within the year.

When the party has arrived at the shore, they strip every rag off the widow and throw them into the surf. A thoughtful female relative, having brought a suit of dark blue <term>baft</term> <note>A type of coarse, often inexpensive cotton fabric.</note> with her for the occasion, then clothes the widow in it. She then returns home, where an appropriate festival is held, after which she may marry again. However, if she were to marry before this ceremony, the <term>Srah</term> of the deceased husband would cause trouble for husband number two or three, and so on, as the case might be.

<header>A WANDERING SOUL</header>

...a state of mourning for several months. A selection of people—including several slaves and one or two free men—are killed to escort the deceased to Srahmandazi <note>The Twi name for the underworld or land of the dead.</note>. In addition to these people, and in order to provide him with merchandise to maintain his household and status in the underworld, quantities of gold dust and rolls of rich velvet, silk, and satin are thrown into the grave.

Among the inhabitants of Cameroon, once you cross the Bantu border, velvets and other luxuries are buried with an important man or woman. However, I am told this is only done for the prestige of the living relatives, so that the world may say, "That person must be wealthy; look at how much merchandise he discarded at the funeral of his wife" (or father, or son, as the case may be). I doubt whether this is the true explanation. If it is, I would recommend that my German friends <note>A reference to the German colonial administration of Cameroon (Kamerun) at the time of writing.</note>, if they wish to intervene, introduce an income tax to Cameroon; that would certainly eliminate this custom.

The Twi people <note>original: "Tschwis"</note> believe that every human soul is allotted a specific amount of time for its earthly existence. For example, let us say a soul is destined for a thirty-year bodily life. If that person is killed at twenty-five, the soul must spend its remaining five years wandering around its old haunts, homes, and wives. In this state, it is called a <term>Sisa</term> <note>A wandering, often malevolent ghost of one who died prematurely.</note>, and it is a nuisance. It causes sickness, throws stones, pulls off roofs, and causes great trouble for the new husbands of its former wives. 

All of this happens because, having failed to reach its full term of life, the soul has not yet learned the way down the dark and difficult path to Srahmandazi, the entrance to which lies across the Volta River to the northeast. Knowledge of the path to Srahmandazi is something that grows gradually within a man's immortal soul (the other three souls are not immortal). Naturally, because the man was not allowed to complete his life, his soul's knowledge is imperfect. However, if necessary, a soul can be taught the way during the funeral "custom" <note>A traditional West African ceremony or ritual involving offerings and celebrations for the dead.</note> performed by relatives and priests. But in the case of a soul that has not finished its time on earth—or an "incomplete-life-earth-soul," as a German might call it—when it finally arrives in the land of the <term>Insrah</term> <note>The spirits of the dead (plural).</note>, it is in a weak and feeble state due to the difficulties of the journey. In contrast, a soul that has lived out its full, allotted span of life goes...

...immediately goes off to Srahmandazi as soon as its funeral rites are performed <note>original: "its 'custom' or 'devil' is made"</note> and gives its surviving relatives no further trouble. Still, there is a great difference of opinion on this point among all the Twi <note>original: "Tschwis"</note> and Ga men I have come across, and Ellis <note>Likely Alfred Burdon Ellis, an officer and ethnographer who wrote extensively on West African cultures.</note> likewise remarks on this difference of opinion. 

Some informants say that a soul that has been sent there before its time—although it is exhausted by the hardships it has suffered on its journey down—nonetheless recovers its health in a month or so. Meanwhile, a soul that has lived its full allotted span on earth is as feeble as a newborn baby upon arriving in Srahmandazi and takes years to recover. Other informants say they have no knowledge of these details. They state that the only difference they know between the souls of men who have been killed and men who have died naturally is that the former can always return. They believe that really the safest way of disposing of this class of soul is to use suitable spells and incantations to get it to enter the body of a newborn baby, where it can live out the remainder of its life. 

This method is not difficult to carry out because a <term>Sisa</term> <note>A wandering, often malevolent ghost of one who died prematurely.</note> is always looking for a body. It causes a great deal of harm by forcing itself into the bodies of sleeping persons whose own dream-soul <note>original: "dream-Srah"</note> is temporarily absent. But placing a Sisa into a new baby is a cruel thing to do because, as I have said before, it is held that some of these <term>Insisa</term> <note>The plural form of Sisa.</note> become wandering souls and are a trial to the baby's parents.

Before closing these observations on Srahmandazi, I will give the best account of that land that I am currently able to. Some day, perhaps, I may share the fate of the Oxford Professor in the book *In the Wrong Paradise* <note>A collection of stories by Andrew Lang (1886) depicting various afterlives.</note> and go there myself, but so far my information is second-hand. 

It is like this world. There are towns and villages, rivers, mountains, wilderness, plantations, and markets. When the sun rises here, it sets in Srahmandazi. It has its pleasures and its pains, which are not necessarily punishments or rewards, but are dim. All souls in it grow forward or backward into the prime of life and remain there, some informants say; others say that each inhabitant remains there at the same age as he was when he left the world above. This latter view is most like the Southwestern one. The former is possibly only an attempt to make Srahmandazi into a

<page-num>519</page-num>
# XXII THE TWI <note>original: "TSCHWI"</note> UNDERWORLD 519

It is not a heaven in conformity with Christian teaching, nor is it a hell.

I have much curious information regarding its flora and fauna. A great deal of both is seemingly indigenous. Additionally, there are the souls of great human beings—the <term>Asrahmanfo</term> <note>The spirits of deceased persons in the afterlife.</note>—and the souls of all the humans, animals, and objects sent down with them. I have had great and highly complex disputes with African <note>original: "Ethiopian"; in this historical context, the author likely refers to Black African theologians generally.</note> theologians on the question of what happens to the "soul of the soul of things" when an *Asrahmanfo* kills these objects for his support in <term>Srahmandazi</term> <note>The Twi name for the land of the dead.</note>. However, since nothing since the Middle Ages has matched these disputes in their confusion of ideas or the worthlessness of their conclusions, I will not subject you to them here. 

The ghosts do not seem to lose interest in earthly affairs. They not only hold local <term>palavers</term> <note>Formal legal or social discussions and disputes.</note>, but they also attempt to settle palavers left over from their earthly existence. When there is an outbreak of sickness in a Fante <note>original: "Fantee"</note> town or village and several inhabitants die, people often believe that a major palaver is occurring down in Srahmandazi. They think the spirits are summoning witnesses from earth, "under penalty" <note>original: "subpœnaing"</note>, as it were. 

Healers or priests are called in to discover which particular earthly grievance is the subject of the ghost palaver. Once they have determined this, they take evidence from everyone in the town regarding the matter—acting as if on a legal commission—and transmit the information to the court sitting in Srahmandazi. This prevents the living from being inconvenienced by having to take personal journeys to the underworld. Although the priests require a fee, it is cheaper in the end, because the funeral expenses for the witnesses would be even more costly.

Although it is far more elaborate and well-thought-out than any other African underworld I have ever encountered, the Twi Srahmandazi may be taken as a model for all African underworlds. The Bantu's idea of a future life is spent in a very similar place. As far as I can determine, there is no definite concept of eternity. I have even encountered cases where doubt was cast on the current existence of the Creator God, but I believe this has arisen from attempts to introduce rigid concepts into the African mind—concepts that are quite foreign to its true nature.

<summary>The author describes Srahmandazi as a mirrored version of the physical world where spirits continue their social and legal lives, even summoning the living as witnesses through illness. This Twi concept of the afterlife serves as a representative model for broader African beliefs, which emphasize continuity over abstract notions like eternity.</summary>

# CHAPTER XXIII

## FETISH—(*Concluded*)

->In which the discourse on apparitions continues, with some observations on<-
->secret societies—both tribal and murderous—and the related<-
->subject of leopards.<-

Apparitions do not always originate from human souls. For instance, all the gods of the Tshi <note>original: "Tschwis"</note> and Ewe peoples regularly appear to their priests and occasionally to the public, such as Sasabonsum <note>A powerful forest deity in West African folklore, often associated with malevolence and the color red</note>; however, these appearances are only harmless or beneficial to the priests. I have already cited the effect of Sasabonsum appearing to a layperson, and though I could provide many other examples of the harmful effects caused by the appearance of other gods, I will now only mention Tando, "the Hater," the chief god of the Northern Tshi, the Ashanti, and others. He is terribly malicious and human in shape; although he is not quite white, his complexion is significantly lighter than that of Bobowissi, the chief god of the Southern Tshi. His hair is straight, and he carries a local sword and wears a long robe. His well-chosen messengers are those dreaded driver ants (<term>Inkran</term>), which it is considered sacrilegious to disturb within Tando’s territory. He uses lightning, storms, and disease as his weapons, but disease is his favorite.

No trick is too cruel or spiteful for Tando. For example, he has a habit of appearing near a village against which he holds a grudge in the form of a male child. He wanders about crying bitterly until some kind-hearted, unsuspecting villager takes him in and feeds him. then, he develops a contagious disease that wipes out the entire village.

<header>CHAPTER ON FETISH</header>

This pattern of appearance and subsequent behavior is, unfortunately, not strictly limited to Tando; many spirits use it as a method for collecting overdue sacrifices, much like collecting back taxes. I have found traces of this belief among Bantu gods and spirits, and it causes a general reluctance in West Africa to care for waifs and strays of unknown origin.

Things other than gods and human spirits also have the habit of taking physical form. I once had to sit and wait for a long time at a bush path that appeared perfectly clear. This was because, at about that time in the afternoon, the ghost of a spear was known to fly across the path; if anyone was struck by it, they died. I also know of a certain spring haunted by the ghost of a pitcher. Many women, when they have gone alone to fill their pitchers at this forest spring in the evening, have noticed a very fine pitcher standing there already filled. Thinking that "exchange is no robbery"—or at least being willing to risk it—they have left their own pitcher and taken the better-looking one. However, as soon as they come within sight of the village huts, the new pitcher crumbles into dust and the water spills on the ground. The worst part is that when they return to fetch their own discarded pitcher, they find it shattered into pieces as well.

There is also another class of apparition, of which I have encountered two instances: one among the pure Negroes (Okÿon) and the other among the pure Bantu (Kangwe). I will provide the Bantu version of the event because the incident at Okÿon had happened a long time before the details were told to me, whereas in the Bantu case, it had happened just the previous evening. However, there was very little difference in the primary facts of the case, and it was significant because in both instances, the underlying concept was sacrificial.

The woman who told me the story was an exceedingly intelligent, shrewd, and reliable person. She had been to the trading post <term>factory</term> <note>A "factory" in this historical context refers to a merchant's trading station or warehouse</note> with some goods and had received a good price for them, so she was in a good mood upon her return home in the evening. She stepped out of her canoe and, leaving her slave boy to bring up her belongings, walked to her house. It was the typical home of a prosperous Igalwa native, having two distinct rooms and a separate kitchen <note>original: "cook-house"</note> nearby in a clean, sandy yard. She...

<header>XXIII BLOOD PALAVER</header>

She stepped on something disgusting in the yard, and upon entering the kitchen, found the slave girls gathered around a very small and weak fire, trying to cook the evening meal. She scolded them for not having a proper fire; they claimed the wood was wet and would not burn. She told them they were lying and that she would deal with them later. She then went into the room she used as a bedroom and stepped on something else on the floor in the dark. Those good-for-nothing young women had not lit her palm-oil lamp. Mentally concluding that they had been out flirting during her absence and resolving to teach them a lesson about the wickedness of such behavior, she sat down on her bed, only to land in a pile of messy, clammy, and damp material. 

This truly enraged her, for she was a strict housekeeper who kept her home and slaves in excellent order. Putting aside the business matters she had intended to dwell on when she entered her room, she called for Ingremina and the others in a tone that brought those young ladies to her immediately. She demanded to know how they dared to forget to light her lamp. They insisted they had not forgotten, but that the lamp in the room must have gone out just as the other lamps had, after burning dimly and sputtering. They further claimed they had not been out at all, but had been sitting around the fire trying to make it burn correctly. She proceeded to slap and pull the ears of everyone within reach. I say "within reach" because she was not very mobile, weighing, I am certain, over 250 pounds <note>original: "eighteen stone"</note>. 

Then she went back into her room and retrieved her beautiful English kerosene lamp <note>original: "paraffin lamp"</note>, which she kept in a box. Taking it into the kitchen, she picked up a piece of wood from the hissing, sputtering fire to light it. When she picked up the wood, she noticed that it was covered in the same sticky, disgusting substance she had encountered earlier that evening. It had the same faint smell she had noticed as soon as she had arrived home, and by now the entire air seemed thick and oppressive with it.

As soon as the lamp was lit, she saw what the substance was: blood. Blood was everywhere. The rest of the sticks in the fire were covered in it; it sizzled at the burning ends and ran off the other side in small streams. There were pools of it scattered across her clean, sandy yard. Her own room was reeking—the bed, the stools, the floor; it trickled down the doorpost; coagu-

The things she picked up off the table and shelf left rings of it behind them; there was more in the skillets, and the oil in the open palm-oil lamps had a film of it floating on the surface. Investigation showed that the entire rest of her house was in a similar mess. The good lady gave a complete catalogue of the household furniture and its condition, which I need not list here.

When the light came, the slave girls were terrified at what they saw. She called in the village aristocracy and asked their opinion on this <term>blood palaver</term> <note>palaver: a West African term for a long discussion, dispute, or serious affair</note>. They said they could make nothing of it at first, but subsequently formed the opinion that it meant something was going to happen. With the kind, helpful "cheerfulness" typical of relatives and friends, they suggested that they would not be surprised if it were a prophecy of her own death. This view irritated the already frustrated lady; she sent them about their business and started the slaves on house-cleaning. The blood cleaned up easily enough while you were working on it, but it kept reappearing in other places—and even in the spot you had just cleaned as soon as you left to go elsewhere. The morning arrived and found things in much the same state until "before sun-time"—say about 10 o'clock—when it faded away.

I cautiously tried to get my stately, touchy "dowager duchess" to explain why there was such a large amount of blood and how it got into the house. She simply said "it had to go somewhere," and refused to give rational explanations as *<note>original: "Chambers's Journal"</note>Chambers’s Journal* <note>A popular 19th-century weekly magazine known for its mix of science and ghost stories</note> does after telling a good ghost story. I found out later that it was officially decided to be a case of "<gloss>blood come before</gloss>" <note>A supernatural phenomenon where blood appears as an omen before a person dies</note>. At Okÿon, Miss Slessor <note>Mary Slessor (1848–1915), a famous Scottish missionary to Nigeria</note> told me regarding a similar case there that this was the common opinion regarding the phenomenon.

It is always considered uncanny in Africa if a person dies without shedding blood. You see, the blood is the life, and if you see it come out, you understand the "going" of the life, so to speak. If you do not see it, it is mysterious. # XXIII SUNDRY BLOOD NOTIONS

525

him and broke his neck without shedding a drop of blood. This supported the theory, for the blood that "had to go somewhere" had already appeared. In the Bantu case, I did not hear of a similar supporting incident happening.

Certain African ideas about blood puzzle me. I was told by a friend from Batanga, a resident white trader, that a short time previously a man was convicted of theft by the natives of a village near him. The hands and feet of the criminal were tied together, and he was flung into the river. He freed himself and swam to the other bank, escaping into the forest. He was recaptured, a stone was tied to his neck, and he was thrown in again. The second time he also got free and reached the shore. He was recaptured once more, and the chief then, with great regret, ordered that he be knocked on the head before being thrown in for a third time. 

This time the <term>palaver</term> <note>palaver: a West African term for a long discussion, dispute, or legal case</note> was settled, but the chief knew that he himself would die before the year was out by spitting blood from his own lungs because of the blood he had shed. I inquired about the chief when I passed this place more than eighteen months later, and I learned from a native that the chief was dead, and that he had died in exactly this way. The objection, therefore, was not to shedding blood in a general sense, but specifically to shedding it during a judicial execution. 

There may be some idea of this kind underlying the ingenious and horrific ways the Africans have of killing thieves—such as tying them to stakes in the rivers or pinning them down on paths for <term>driver ants</term> <note>aggressive, carnivorous ants known for traveling in massive columns and consuming any animal in their path</note> to kill and eat. However, this is only a conjecture; I have not had a chance yet to research this subject thoroughly. Obtaining reliable information about underlying beliefs is very difficult in Africa. The natives will say "Yes" to any imaginable thing if they think you want them to; furthermore, the variety of their languages is another great hindrance. 

Were it not for the prevalence of <term>Kru English</term> <note>a form of Pidgin English used by Kru mariners and traders along the West African coast</note> or trade English, investigation would be almost impossible. Fortunately, this quaint language is common, and the natives of different tribes communicate with each other using it. Thus, if you listen to the gossip around a fire in the evening, you can pick up all sorts of strange information. You can gain unusual, and often shocking, insights into the characters of your absent white friends and the religious beliefs of your current companions. For example, the other day I had a set of porters composed of four...

# FETISH CHAPTER

...Bassa boys, two Wei Weis, one Dualla, and two Yorubas. None of their languages matched, so they spoke "trade English," and some of it was quite lively talk, but I will speak more of that later.

I cannot conclude this brief notice of indigenous ideas without mentioning the secret societies; however, to cover this branch of the subject fully would require volumes, as every tribe has its own secret society. The Poorah of Sierra Leone, the Oru of Lagos, the Egbo of Calabar, the Yasi of the Igalwa, the Ukuku of the M’pongwe, the Ikun of the Bakele, and the Lukuku of the Bachilangi and Baluba are some of the most powerful secret societies on the West African Coast.

These secret societies are not essentially religious; their function is mainly judicial, and the spirit that particularly presides over them is not a "god" or "devil" in our sense of the word. The ritual for each differs in its details, but there are broad similarities between them. There are societies for both men and for women, but no mixed societies for both sexes. Those I mentioned above are all male, and women are strictly forbidden from participating in the rites or becoming acquainted with their secrets. This is because one of the primary duties of these societies is to keep women in order. Besides this reason, it is undoubtedly believed that women are detrimental to certain forms of <term>ju-ju</term> <note>ju-ju: a West African term for an object of spiritual power, a fetish, or the system of beliefs and charms associated with them</note>, even when those forms are not directly connected, as far as I can determine, with the secret society itself. 

For example, the other day a chief up the Mungo River deliberately destroyed his ju-ju by showing it to his women. It was a great ju-ju, but expensive to maintain, requiring sacrifices of slaves and goats. What with trade being poor, the fall in the price of oil and ivory, and so on, he felt he could no longer afford that ju-ju. He therefore destroyed its power to prevent it from harming him when he eventually neglected it. The destructive effect of women is likely not just based on the idea of their inferiority—for if inferiority were the only point, that chief would have neutralized his ju-ju with dogs or pigs—but rather arises from the perceived fact that women are notably deficient in true reverence for authority, as is demonstrated by the way they continually treat the authority of their husbands.

<header>DANGEROUS SKEPTICISM</header>
<sig>XXIII</sig>

...with boys entering the male society and girls entering the female society. Both societies are kept strictly separate. A man who attempts to uncover the female mysteries would be killed as surely as a woman who might try to investigate the male mysteries. Nevertheless, in 1893, I encountered an amusing case that demonstrates the unquenchable thirst for knowledge—as long as it is forbidden—which characterizes our sex. Alas! If only this passion for research <note>original: "Forschungsschwärmerei"</note> had filled us regarding other types of knowledge, we might have been the discoverers of the electric telegraph and a few other things of that nature.

This took place in the district just south of Big Batanga <note>Big Batanga: a coastal region in present-day Cameroon</note>. The male society had been very harsh toward the women for some time. One day, a brilliant mind among the women told her next-door neighbor, in strict confidence, that she did not believe Ikun <note>Ikun: a spirit or secret society associated with the Bakele people</note> was a spirit at all, but rather just a particular man dressed up in leaves. This blatant heresy spread rapidly—in strict confidence—among the women in general. They used to gather secretly in the house of the woman who started the theory to discuss the matter. Naturally, this was done in secret because husbands in that region are quick to use a machete or a <term>kassengo</term> <note>kassengo: a traditional West African weapon or club</note>.

Somehow, the men found out. Whether the women became too bold and winked when Ikun was mentioned, or pointedly asked how a certain man was doing the morning after an Ikun appearance, I do not know. Some people told me this was what happened. Others, however—who I fear were right, given the known slowness of men in connecting the dots and the betrayal of women toward one another—said that one woman told a man she had heard the other women were behaving in this heretical way. Regardless, the men found out and were deeply alarmed. Skepticism had spread so far by then that nothing short of burning or drowning all the women could eradicate it and restore the proper sense of awe to the female side of society. After much consideration, the men realized—since men are undoubtedly more gifted in foresight than women—that there was no particular use in restoring this awe if there was no female half of society left to be impressed by it. It was a mind-boggling problem for all the men, for it is clear that society cannot be held together...

Serious councils were held, and it was decided that the woman at whose house these treasonable meetings were held should be sent away early one morning on a trading mission to the nearest factory <term>factory: a merchant's trading post or warehouse</term>, a job she readily undertook. While the other women were away in the plantation or at the spring, certain men entered her house secretly and dug a large chamber out of the floor of the hut. One of them, dressed as Ikun and provided with refreshments for the day, got into this chamber, and the whole affair was covered over carefully and the floor re-sanded. 

That afternoon, there was a major manifestation of Ikun. He appeared in a most terrifying form; his howls were awful, and he finally went dancing away into the bush as night fell. The ladies had just taken the common-sense precaution of removing all goats, sheep, poultry, etc., into enclosed premises, for, like all his kind, he seizes and holds any property he may come across in the street. However, there was evidently no emotional thrill in the female mind regarding him. When the leading lady returned home in the evening, the other women strolled into their leader's hut to hear about what new cotton prints, beads, and things Mr. —— <note>original: "Mr.——" (name withheld by author)</note> had received at his factory by the last steamer from Europe, and other interesting subjects concerning Mr. ——. 

When they had thoroughly discussed these matters, the conversation turned to religion, and what fools those men had been making of themselves all afternoon with their Ikun. No sooner was his name uttered than a venomous howl, terminating in squeals of rage and impatience, came from the ground beneath them. They stared at each other for one second, and then, feeling that something was tearing its way up through the floor, they all fled for the interior of Africa with one accord. Ikun gave chase as soon as he got free, but because he was half-stifled, had cramped legs, and was much encumbered by his vegetable decorations, the ladies got clear away and no arrests were made—but society was saved. ## XXIII THE PRICE OF PROSPERITY

...regardless of the expense, to buy immunity from Ikun. They suspected that those ladies were probably in that hut on that particular evening, but they took no further action against them, except for making the rituals of Ikun particularly expensive. There ought to be a moral to an educational tale of this kind, I know, but the only one I can think of right now is that it takes a priest to outsmart a woman; and I always feel inclined to jump onto a table myself when I think of those poor, dear creatures sitting on the floor and feeling that awful thing clawing its way up right beneath them.

Ikun has the unusual habit of arriving from the sea in a canoe. The leaders of his society always see him first and go out to meet him in their canoes, bringing him ashore in his "Jack-in-the-Green" <note>A traditional English folk costume made of wicker and greenery; here used to describe the spirit's leafy or fiber-based ritual dress.</note> costume. Meanwhile, all the women rush about, herding ducks, chickens, children, sheep, and goats into enclosures, and then they hide themselves. He is the only member of his kind I have ever heard of who comes from the sea; they usually emerge from the bush like Egbo and Yasi, and his costume is made of forest materials anyway. There is another peculiarity of Ikun, which is his unique way of taking payment for a thing which all his fellow secret societies and spirits also supply—namely, the power to become wealthy.

For example, if a man desires this power, he goes to someone known to possess Ikun and asks him if he will share a certain amount of his power—say, enough to ensure he becomes a person earning a thousand pounds a year <term>thousand-pound-a-yearer: a very wealthy individual; a high-earner</term>. The man who possesses the power says that for this amount of power, the applicant must pay with the lives of fifty of his blood relatives. The man must take all these lives himself from time to time, secretly, as the opportunity arises. The spirits of the murdered then go to Ikun in the underworld and work for him as slaves; as they descend, every venture the murderer undertakes turns out profitably, and he gradually grows richer and richer.

It is a dangerous practice in this world because when your neighbors notice how your relatives are dying off and how you are prospering, they are likely to say you are "making Ikun." At that point, they descend on you, kill you, and seize your hard-earned wealth, and then have a dance in the evening; but I—

<header>XXIII FATTENING-HOUSES 531</header>

The most significant similarity among all these West African secret societies is their method of initiation.

If a boy belongs to a tribe that practices tattooing, he is tattooed and handed over to instructors who teach him the society's secrets and rituals <note>original: "formulæ"</note>. Along with other boys from his tribe undergoing initiation, he lives under the authority of several instructors for one year. He remains in the forest throughout this time, naked and covered in clay.

The boys undergo physical training to become accustomed to hardship. In some regions, they conduct raids to perfect this useful skill. They always adopt a new name and are believed, through the initiation process, to become entirely new beings within the magic wood. Upon returning to their village at the end of their training, they pretend to have completely forgotten their lives before they entered the forest; however, they only maintain this pretense during the homecoming festivities. They all learn a new, secret language to some degree, which is understood only by those who have been initiated.

Girls undergo a similar process of being removed from home and receiving instruction from initiated members. However, they are not always secluded in a forest grove; sometimes, they are kept in huts. Among the tribes of the Grain Coast <note>The coastal area of modern-day Liberia and Sierra Leone.</note>, girls remain in a magic wood until they are married. If they must leave the forest for any temporary reason, they must cover themselves in white clay. A similar custom exists in <term>Okÿon</term> <note>A region in the Calabar district of present-day Nigeria.</note> in the Calabar district. If a girl must leave the <term>fattening-house</term>, she must be covered in white clay. 

I believe this fattening-house custom in Calabar is not just about increasing a woman's weight to enhance her beauty, but is also an initiation rite. While the primary goal today is undoubtedly weight gain—as the girl is constantly fed calorie-rich foods like <term>fou-fou</term> <note>A staple food made from boiled and mashed starchy vegetables like yams or cassava.</note> soaked in palm oil—it remains part of their cultural transition. I have been told—though I suspect incorrectly—that the white clay covering the girl in the fattening-house (with an extra layer added if she goes outside) is meant to assist the weight-gain process by preventing perspiration.

The duration of the period of seclusion varies somewhat. In San Salvador, boys stay in the forest for six months. In Cameroon, the period is twelve months. In most districts, girls are betrothed in infancy, and they enter the forest or an initiation hut for a few months before marriage. In these cases, the time seems to vary according to the circumstances of the individual. This is not the case for boys; for them, each tribal society has a formally appointed course that ends at a set time. However, sometimes—as among some of the Yoruba tribes—a boy must remain under the rule of the society's presiding elders until he has killed a man. During this time, he is painted white and wears only a piece of grass cloth, if he wears anything at all. Once he has killed someone, he is considered to have reached manhood by demonstrating his courage and by securing the soul of the person he killed as a spirit slave.

The initiation of boys into a few of the basic beliefs <note>original: "dogmas"</note> of the secret society is by no means the only work the society performs. All of them serve a judicial function, and on the whole, they do an immense amount of good. Their methods are often somewhat unusual <note>original: "quaint"</note>. Running through the streets disguised in masks and robes, with an imitation tail swinging behind, while striking at everyone you meet with a whip or a machete <note>original: "cutlass"</note>, is not the European way of keeping the peace—or, perhaps I should say, maintaining the dignity of the law. But discipline must be maintained, and this is the West African way of doing it.

The Egbo of Calabar is a prime example of a secret society. Its details are exceedingly well-developed; it is not as vague <note>original: "sketchy"</note> as the Yasi, nor as violent <note>original: "red-handed"</note> as the Poorah. Unfortunately, however, I cannot speak with the same level of knowledge regarding the Egbo as I can regarding the Poorah.

The Egbo has the most levels of initiation, except perhaps for the Poorah, and it exercises authority over all types of crime except witchcraft. Any Efik <note>original: "Effik"</note> man who desires to become an influential person in the tribe must purchase his way into as high a rank of Egbo as he can afford. These ranks are expensive; I am informed that £1,000 or £1,500 in English currency is required for the higher levels. But it is worth the cost to a major trader—as an influential Efik necessarily is—for he can call upon his own rank...

<header>XXIII TRAPPING EGBO</header>

Because Egbo’s method of delivering an order to pay consists of placing an "Egbo" <term>a representative or symbol of the secret society’s authority</term> at a man’s doorway—and the man dare not venture outside his house until it is removed—this method is very successful.

Of course, the higher a man’s rank in Egbo, the greater his power and security, because members of lower grades cannot take legal action against those in higher ones. In fact, when a man encounters the symbols <note>original: "paraphernalia"</note> of a grade higher than his own, he must act as if he is lame, limping past it humbly as if the mere sight of it had drained all his strength. Naturally, high-ranking debtors dismiss <note>original: "flip their fingers at"</note> creditors from the lower grades.

After discussing these secret society spirits at such length, it might be helpful to explain what they are. They are all a kind of "something" that usually lives in the bush (with the exception of *Ikun* <term>a specific spirit or grade within the society</term>). Last February, I was traveling back toward Duke Town—late, as usual—and was near a town on the Qwa River. As I hurried along, I heard a terrific noise accompanied by drums in the thick bush where the path turned after a short stretch of open ground. Feeling cautious and alarmed, I hid in some dense undergrowth as the men making the noise approached. I saw it was some kind of *juju* <note>a West African term for spiritual systems, charms, or rituals</note> ceremony. They carried a sort of box on poles; their clothing was strange and unusually bulky over the upper parts of their bodies. They were dancing ecstatically around the box, which had one open end, while beating their drums and shouting. 

They were quite close to me, but fortunately, they turned their attention toward another part of the underbrush. If they hadn't, they might have captured something else entirely that evening! They surrounded the bushes they had chosen and clearly did their best to entice something to come out and enter their box. I was just as anxious as they were for them to succeed quickly; as you know, there are many unpleasant snakes and other creatures in the Calabar bush, not to mention driver ants <note>aggressive, swarming ants known for their painful bite</note>, which makes sitting in the brush quite disagreeable. However, they soon managed to get "something" into their box and celebrated joyfully, and

All that night, Duke Town howled, sang, and beat its <term>tom-toms</term> <note>drums</note> without stopping, for I was told <term>Egbo</term> <note>the powerful spirit and governing secret society of the Calabar region</note> had arrived in the town. <term>Egbo</term> is very elusive, even for a secret society spirit, and seems to hate publicity; however, when he is hidden inside this ark, he speaks authoritative observations on current politics, and his word is law. The voice coming out of the ark is very strange and does not sound like a human voice. I heard it shortly after <term>Egbo</term> had been captured. Based on what I saw, I suspect there was a person inside that ark the whole time, but I do not know for certain. It is hard enough for me to understand the details of these <term>ju-ju</term> <note>spiritual or magical systems and objects</note> rituals at present, let alone explain them rationally. I have heard that there is a tribe on the Slave Coast that has been proven to keep a small child inside the drum that serves as the home of their chief spirit. When the child grows too large to fit inside, they are killed, and another child—who has been trained by the priests in the meantime—takes the place of the deceased one until they, in turn, grow too large and are killed, and so on. I suspect this killing of the children is not for sacrifice, but stems entirely from the fact that just as former kings are dangerous to the state, former gods would be even more dangerous.

Very little is known by outsiders regarding <term>Egbo</term> compared to what there must be to learn. This is due to a lack of interest or a feeling of helplessness on the part of most white people, who cannot make sense of what seems to them a horrible pagan ritual or a jumble of nonsense.

It is still a great power, although its officials in Duke Town or Creek Town are no longer allowed to go around hacking and whipping people indiscriminately. This is because the <term>Consul-General</term> <note>the high-ranking British official representing government interests</note> dislikes that sort of thing, and the <term>Efik</term> <note>the ethnic group of the Calabar region; spelled Effik in original</note> people are learning that it is nearly as dangerous to oppose the Consul-General as it is to oppose their <term>ju-ju</term>. Therefore, I do not believe you will ever get the truth about it in Duke Town or Creek Town. If you want to understand the core concepts of these societies, you must visit remote areas where the local people are not yet afraid of being ridiculed or punished. I have included a fragment from my Duke Town diaries below to show that I did try my best for the sake of science.

<header>YASI DANCES AND POORAH</header>

> “They are at it down in Duke Town <note>one of the principal settlements of Old Calabar, Nigeria</note> tonight—not only beating the drum, but singing one of the ‘big tunes.’ I’ll just go down and see to it, even though it is pitch black and Calabar has not yet reached the sophisticated level of having oil street-lamps; still, there is plenty of sheet lightning. [Two and a half hours later]. It is an absolute scandal that they do not keep those Duke Town paths in a better state. They are nothing in this world but drainage ditches, and very poor ones at that. There really ought to be a fixed light at Mr. Fynn’s Ditch, or by the bridge; then you would know which was which before you were waist-deep in water.”

Of the secret societies on the South-West Coast, the <term>Ukuku</term> <note>a powerful regulatory secret society among the Mpongwe and related groups</note> seems to be the most powerful. The <term>Yasi</term>, belonging to those easygoing <term>Igalwas</term> and <term>M’pongwe</term> peoples, is now little more than a performance. You quite frequently come across <term>Yasi</term> dances just around Libreville. You will see a line stretched across the narrow street in a cluster of houses, from which branches are suspended to create a kind of screen. The women and children stay on one side of this screen, while the men dance on the other side to the peculiar, monotonous <term>Yasi</term> tune. 

The <term>Poorah</term> <note>also known as Poro, a significant male secret society in Sierra Leone and Liberia</note> I have spoken of elsewhere, but I may mention one thing regarding it which struck me as unusual. I was in the forest behind Victoria in the Cameroons. I recognized a peculiar look about a certain portion of the woods. The branches were bent and the vines were tied together in a way I had seen elsewhere, but which I had never noticed among the <term>Bantu</term> tribes. I was puzzled, and after passing this spot by a couple of hundred yards or so, I turned back to look at it again, telling my men to go on ahead. I examined the place closely for several minutes, then rejoined my men and said nothing.

Presently, one of my <term>Wei Weis</term> <note>likely Vai men from the Sierra Leone/Liberia region employed as laborers</note> said, “How do you know about those things, ma’am?”

“What things?” I asked, not wishing to lead him on.

“You looked at those things, ma’am; when you passed them, you went back to look at them again. Do you know about the <term>Poorah</term>, ma’am?” he asked in an accusing tone.

“Well,” I said, “what is it doing here?”

“Those Sierra Leone boys brought it here, ma’am,” <note>original: "Them Sa lone boys done bring him, ma"</note> was the answer.

<header>FETISH CHAPTER</header>

Until this point, I did not know that secret societies were exported from their own home districts.

I believe that these secret societies are always distinct from the "leopard societies" <note>infamous ritual murder cults in West Africa where members dressed in leopard skins and attacked victims with iron claws</note>. I have nearly enough evidence to prove that this is true in some districts, but not in all. So far, my evidence only goes to prove the distinction between the two among the West African peoples, not among the Bantu; and in all cases, you will find some men who belong to both. Some men, in fact, join all the societies in their district, but not every man does so. In all districts, if you look closely, you will find several societies that are separate from the regular youth-initiation ones.

These other societies are practically murder societies, and their practices usually include cannibalism, which is not an essential part of the rites of the great tribal societies like the <term>Yasi</term> or <term>Egbo</term> <note>a powerful secret society of the Efik people of Old Calabar</note>. In the Calabar district, I was informed by locals that there was a society where the newest member must provide the body of one of his own relatives for the entertainment of the other members. Sacrificial cannibalism is frequently occurring—or perhaps I should say being discovered—by the white authorities in the Niger Delta. There was a major outbreak of it at Brass early last year, and another recorded in the *Liverpool Mercury* on August 13th, 1895, occurring in Sierra Leone. This account is worth quoting. It describes the hanging of three murderers by the authorities and states the incidents which took place in the Imperi country behind Free Town.

One of the chief murderers was a man named Jowe, who had formerly been a Sunday school teacher in Sierra Leone. He pleaded in his defense that he had been compelled to join the society. The others said they committed the murders in order to obtain certain body parts for <term>ju-ju</term> <note>a West African term for spiritual objects, amulets, or the magical power associated with them</note> purposes—the leg, the hand, the heart, and so on. The *Mercury* continues with the statement of the Reverend Father Bomy of the Roman Catholic Mission: 

"He said he was at Bromtu, where the St. Joseph Mission has a station, when a man was brought down from the Imperi country in a boat. The poor fellow was in a dreadful state and was brought to the station for medical treatment. He said he was working on his farm when he was suddenly pounced upon—"

“Some twenty years ago, there was a war between the Taima tribe and the Paramas. The Paramas sent some of their warriors to lie in ambush in the intervening country, the Imperi, but the Imperi delivered these warriors to the enemy. Until that time, this fetish had been kept active and working by the sacrifice of goats. In doing so, they worked their vengeance on the Imperi by leading them to exterminate themselves in sacrifice to the fetish. 

For years, the country has been terrorized by this secret worship of **Boofima**. At one time, the Imperi started the **Tonga dances**, at which the medicine men pointed out the supposed worshippers of **Boofima**—the so-called **Human Leopards**. These were named so because, when seizing their victims for sacrifice, they covered themselves with leopard skins. Imitating the roars of the leopard, they sprang upon their victim, plunging two three-pronged forks into each side of the throat at the same time. 

The Government forbade the **Tonga dances** some years ago and is now striving to suppress the **Human Leopards**. In commenting on this account, which was evidently written by someone well-versed in the matter, I will only remark that sometimes, instead of three-pronged forks, sharp-pointed cutting knives are fixed into the paws of the leopard skin. The skin is fashioned into a type of glove that the hand of the "human leopard" fits into. In one skin I saw in the south, this was most ingeniously done. I am told the American Mendi Mission, which operates in the Sierra Leone districts, has a similar skin in its possession. 

In Calabar and Libreville, these murders used to be very common right near the white settlements. However, in Calabar, European jurisdiction is now too feared for them to be carried out nearby. In Libreville, the construction of the "Boulevard" between that town and Glass has cleared the practice out of its main haunt—the swamp path that was formerly there. Before the Boulevard existed, when the narrow track was broken by patches of swamp and ran through dense bush, it was notoriously unsafe even for a white man to travel along it after dark. 

In the districts I am familiar with where "human leopardism" occurs—from Bonny to the Belgian Congo <note>original: "Congo Belge"</note>—the victims are killed to provide human flesh for certain secret societies who eat it as part of their rituals. Sometimes it is used by a person acting alone to kill an enemy.

The "human alligator" mentioned is our old friend the "witch crocodile"—the spirit of a man residing within a crocodile. I have never personally encountered a case of a man in his physical body swimming around in a crocodile skin. I doubt any native would risk being inside a crocodile skin and swimming in the river among the genuine articles, for fear that the real crocodiles would see through his disguise both mentally and physically.

# XXIII A GIANT JU-JU

...could be sued for libel. Once, when I was in Calabar, a particularly energetic officer shot that crocodile, and the chief was immediately confined to bed with a wound in his leg. He claimed a dog had bitten him. Both the chief and the crocodile are perfectly healthy again now. I will say this in the chief’s favor: nothing on earth would convince me that he went foolishly wandering about the Calabar River in his physical body, whether in his own skin or a crocodile's.

The introduction of the <term>Fetish Boofima</term> <note>A potent ritual object or medicine often associated with secret societies and human sacrifice</note> into the country of the <term>Imperi</term> <note>A region in Sierra Leone</note> is an interesting point. It shows that these different tribes share the same powerful <term>ju-ju</term> <note>A West African term for a spirit, charm, fetish, or the religion associated with them</note>. Similarly, the Calabar <term>Egbo</term> <note>A powerful and prestigious secret society, also known as Ekpe</note> can enter <term>Okyon</term> and will be respected in some of the New Calabar districts. However, it is not respected at <term>Brass</term>, where the secret society is a distinct cult. 

Often, a neighboring district will send word to Calabar or Brass—where the powerful ju-ju resides—and ask to have one sent up to their district to maintain order. However, <term>Egbo</term> will occasionally be sent into a district without that district wanting it in the least; but, as in the <term>Imperi</term> case, once it is there, it is supreme. For example, if you were to send <term>Egbo</term> from Calabar to Cameroon, the people in Cameroon might be barely polite to it, but they would pay it no respect. This is because Cameroon has a formidable <term>ju-ju</term> of its own. It is said it can rise as high as the Peak, which stands at 13,760 feet. I never saw the Cameroon ju-ju do this, but I did see it suddenly grow from four feet to at least twelve feet in the blink of an eye. I was assured that it was only out of modest restraint that it left the other 13,748 feet out of the performance.

Cameroon also has its "murder societies," but I have not lived in the Cameroon River area long enough to speak about them with any authority. # CHAPTER ON FETISH

The girls went home with their water vessels, placing a fresh piece of palm leaf on top of the water to prevent it from splashing as they climbed the hillside of the bluff where the town stands. "Where is your brother?" their mother asked. They replied that they did not know, as they thought he was playing with the other children. As dusk fell and he had not returned, his mother went down to the riverbank and found that all the other children had already gone home. She made inquiries, but no one knew where he was, except that he had been playing on the beach. A thorough search began, but five long days passed before the boy was found. Then, his body—decorated with palm leaves—suddenly appeared lying on the beach. It had been slit lengthwise with long cuts all over the face, head, legs, and arms. The crime could not be solved by methods acceptable to Western law, but if the <term>witch doctors</term> <note>Traditional healers or spiritual leaders often responsible for identifying the causes of misfortune or crime</note> had handled the matter, a close relative of the dead boy would have been executed. Those locals who did not believe this relative was guilty claimed that the "people in the water" were responsible. These "people in the water" are a significant belief in <term>Cameroon</term>. As the saying goes, "They are just like people on land, except they live in the water."

Doctor Nassau <note>Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), an American missionary and ethnologist known for his work in West Africa</note> seems to believe that the tribal societies of the <term>Corisco</term> <note>An island off the coast of Equatorial Guinea and Gabon</note> regions are identical to the <term>leopard societies</term> <note>Secret societies whose members were believed to transform into or act like leopards, often associated with ritual killings</note>. He has had considerable experience with the workings of the <term>Ukuku</term> <note>A powerful secret society among the Benga people of the Corisco and Benito regions</note>, particularly during his early missions in the <term>Benito</term> <note>A river and region in what is now Equatorial Guinea</note> regions, where it nearly caused his death. I will not quote the excellent account he gave me of his adventures with the society, as I would prefer that everyone read his biography of his first wife, *Crowned in Palm Land*, for themselves. In it, they will find a series of vivid descriptions of what life is truly like in the Corisco region. It contains one of the most powerful and tragic pieces of writing in all of literature—the description of his wife’s death in an open boat at sea while he was trying to take her to <term>Gaboon</term> <note>Now Gabon</note> for medical assistance.

Regarding the Ukuku, he says the name signifies a departed spirit. "It is a secret society into which all males are initiated at puberty. Its rituals may not be seen by women, and its laws may not be disobeyed by anyone under penalty of death..."

# XXIII A TIMELY WARNING

...a penalty which is sometimes reduced to a fine—and a heavy fine at that. Its decisions are delivered like an oracle from a secluded spot by a man appointed for that purpose.

> “On minor occasions, any initiated man may impersonate Ukuku or issue commands for the family. On other occasions, such as in Shiku <note>Likely referring to a specific ritual, meeting, or market regulation ceremony</note>, to raise prices, the society imposes its commands on foreign traders.”

I have observed several cases where the Ukuku society took action against white traders. A friend of mine, a trader in the Batanga district <note>A coastal region in what is now southern Cameroon</note>, somehow provoked the hostility of the local branch of the society. As was common in the South-West Coast trade, he owned several small branch factories <term>sub-factories</term> <note>Small outlying trading posts located inland from the main coastal station</note> in the interior. He found himself placed under a <term>taboo</term> <note>In this context, a "social boycott" or "interdict" where the society forbids all interaction with an individual</note>; no local person came to his yard to buy or sell at the store, not even to provide food. He ignored the situation and waited to see what would happen. 

One evening, while sitting on his porch smoking and reading, he thought he heard someone singing softly beneath the house—which, like most European buildings in this area, was raised slightly above the ground. The song caught his interest, and he listened closely. It was clearly a local person singing, rather than one of his own <term>Kruboys</term> <note>West African laborers and sailors, primarily from the Kru ethnic group of Liberia, often hired by European traders</note>. Since he knew the language and had nothing else to do, he paid close attention to the matter.

The same line was sung softly over and over, so quietly that he could barely distinguish the words. Finally, hearing his local name mentioned among them, he listened even more intently through a knot-hole in the wooden floor. The song said, “They are going to attack your factory at... tomorrow. They are going to attack your factory at... tomorrow,” repeating until it stopped. He then thought he saw a figure, darker than the surrounding night, creep across the yard and vanish into the brush. 

Very early the next morning, he and his <term>Kruboys</term>, armed with guns, went to the threatened factory and occupied it in force. The Ukuku society arrived that evening to scout the situation; finding there was more resistance than they had anticipated, they withdrew.

Within the next twenty-four hours, he managed to successfully settle the dispute <term>palaver</term> <note>A term used in West Africa for a talk, negotiation, or legal dispute</note> with them. He never found out...

Indeed, there were and still are many locals who have reason to be grateful to him, for he is deservedly popular among the local tribes.
