Sometimes representatives of the Ukuku <term>Ukuku</term> <note>A powerful male secret society among the Mpongwe and related peoples of the Gaboon region, acting as a judicial and governing body</note> fraternity from several tribes meet together to discuss intertribal difficulties, thereby avoiding war.

Dr. Nassau <note>Robert Hamill Nassau (1835–1921), an American missionary and ethnologist known for his studies of West African customs and religions</note> distinctly states that the leopard society of the Bantu region is identical to the Ukuku. He says that although leopards are not very numerous there, they are very daring, made so by their immunity from human punishment. 

> “The superstition holds that any man who kills a leopard will be struck by a curse or an evil disease, curable only by a ruinously expensive three-week process under the direction of the Ukuku. Consequently, the natives permit the most terrible plundering and destruction until their sheep, goats, and dogs are wiped out; they are only roused to self-defense when a human being becomes a victim of the daring beast. Linked with this superstition is another similar to the German belief in werewolves: a belief in the power of human transformation <term>metamorphosis</term> into a leopard. A person so transformed is called an ‘Uvengwa.’ At one time in Benito <note>A region in what is now Equatorial Guinea</note>, intense panic prevailed in the community. Doors and shutters were rattled in the dead of night, and the marks of leopard claws were scratched onto doorposts. Tracks then appeared on every path. Women and children in isolated places saw their fleeting forms, were knocked down by their pouncing in the dusk, or heard their growls in the thickets. It is difficult to determine in many of these reports whether the predator is a real leopard or merely an Uvengwa—to the locals’ fears, they are practically the same. We were certain that this time the Uvengwa was a thief disguised in a leopard’s skin, as reports of theft always arise during such times.”

When I was in Gaboon in September 1895, there was great Ukuku excitement in a district just across the other side of the estuary, mainly at a village that enjoyed the grand and resounding name of Rumpochembo—named after a famous chief—and all these phenomena were widespread there. Again, when

# XXIII OF LEOPARDS

When I was in a village up the Calabar River, fourteen goats and five slaves were killed in eight days by leopards—the real animals, I am sure, in this instance. However, here, just as in the South, there was a strong objection to taking action against the leopard, and no measures were being taken except for making the goat-houses stronger. In Okyon, when a leopard is killed, its body is treated with great respect and brought into the hunter’s village. Messages are then sent to the neighboring villages, which send representatives to the village. The gall bladder is very carefully removed from the leopard and burned *publicly* <note>original: "coram publico"</note>, with each person whipping their hands down their arms to deny any guilt in the matter. 

This burning of the gall, however, is not "ju-ju" <term>ju-ju</term> <note>A West African term for a fetish, charm, or the supernatural power or ritual associated with it</note>; it is done merely to destroy it and to demonstrate to all men that it has been destroyed. This is because it is believed to be a deadly poison, and if any is found in a man’s possession, the punishment is death—unless he is a great chief, as a few of them are allowed to keep leopard gall in their possession. John Bailey <note>Kingsley's interpreter and guide</note> tells me that if a great chief commits a serious crime and is sentenced to death by a council of his fellow chiefs, it is not considered right that he should die in a common way, and so he is given leopard gall. A precisely similar idea regarding the poisonous quality of crocodile gall is held in the South.

The "ju-ju" parts of the leopard are the whiskers. You cannot obtain a skin from a local with the whiskers still attached; bold, reckless young hunters wear them stuck in their hair and brag immensely, while the elders shake their heads and keep a keen eye on their future conduct.

I must say the African leopard is a bold animal, although it is ungrateful of me to say a word against him after the way he has personally spared me. I will speak of his extreme beauty as compensation for my ingratitude. I truly think, taken as a whole, he is the most lovely animal I have ever seen. However, seeing him in the only way you can gain a full sense of his beauty—namely, in his native forest—is not a source of pure joy to a person of a nervous disposition like myself. I should remark that my nervousness regarding the big game of Africa is of a rather peculiar kind. I can confidently say I am not afraid of any wild animal—until I see one.

544 FETISH CHAP.

...it—and then—well, I will yield to no one in my capacity for terror. Fortunately, as I say, my terror is of a special variety; fortunately, because no one can truly manage their own terror. You can suppress alarm, excitement, fear, fright, and all those minor emotions, but real terror is as dependent on your inner constitution as the color of your eyes or the shape of your nose. When terror ascends its throne in my mind, I become preternaturally artful and intelligent to an extent utterly foreign to my true nature. Except in the case of close quarters with dangerous large animals—where I feel a surge of rage against some unknown person for allowing things like leopards, elephants, and crocodiles to roam loose in such a disgracefully dangerous way—I do not think much about it at the time. 

Whenever I have come across a fearsome animal in the forest and I know it has seen me, I follow Jerome’s <note>Likely a reference to author Jerome K. Jerome's humorous advice on facing danger in "Three Men in a Boat"</note> advice: instead of relying on the "power of the human eye," I rely upon the power of the human leg and execute a masterly retreat in the face of the enemy. If I know it has not seen me, I drop where I stand and keep an eye on it, hoping that it will go away soon. 

This is how I once came upon a leopard. I had been caught in a storm <term>tornado</term> <note>In West Africa, a "tornado" refers to a violent squall or thunderstorm rather than a funnel cloud</note> in a dense forest. The massive, mighty trees were waving like a wheat field in an autumn gale in England; I dare say a field mouse in a wheat field during a gale would have heard much the same uproar. The storm shrieked like ten thousand vengeful demons. The great trees creaked, groaned, and strained against it, and their "bush-rope" <term>bush-rope</term> <note>Strong, woody climbing vines or lianas common in tropical forests</note> cables groaned and snapped like whips. Every now and then, a thundering crash accompanied by snaps like pistol shots signaled that a mighty tree had strained and struggled in vain. The fierce rain fell with a roar, tearing leaves and blossoms to shreds and deluging everything. 

I was having a difficult time of it, climbing up over a pile of rocks out of a gully bottom where I had been nearly drowned in a stream. Upon getting my head to the level of a large rock, I observed right in front of my eyes—positioned broadside and perhaps a yard away, certainly no more—a large leopard. He was crouching on the ground with his magnificent head thrown back and his eyes shut. His forepaws were spread out in front of him and he lashed the ground with his tail. I am sorry to say that, in the face of that awful danger—and I mean the storm, not me—that...

# XXIII AN AWKWARD ENCOUNTER

The depraved creature swore, softly but repeatedly and profoundly. I did not take in all these facts at a single glance, because as soon as I saw him, I ducked under the rocks and thankfully remembered that leopards are said to have no sense of smell. However, I heard his observation on the weather and the "flip-flap" of his tail against the ground. Every now and then, I cautiously took a look at him with one eye around the edge of a rock, and he remained in the same position. My feelings tell me he stayed there for twelve months, but my calmer judgment puts the time at twenty minutes; at last, upon taking another cautious peep, I saw he was gone. At the time, I wished I knew exactly where he went, but I do not care about that detail now, for I saw no more of him. 

He had moved off during one of those weird lulls that you get during a storm <term>tornado</term> <note>In West Africa, a "tornado" refers to a violent squall or thunderstorm rather than a funnel cloud</note>, when for a few seconds the wild herd of hurrying winds seems to have lost its way and wanders around crying and wailing like lost souls, until their collective rage seizes them again and they rush back to their work of destruction. It was an immense pleasure to have seen the great creature like that. He was so evidently enraged and frustrated by the uproar and dazzled by the floods of lightning that swept down into the deepest recesses of the forest—showing every detail of twig, leaf, branch, and stone around you for one second, and then leaving you in a kind of swirling darkness until the next flash came. This, and the great, combined roar of the wind, rain, and thunder, was enough to bewilder any living thing.

I have never hurt a leopard intentionally; I am habitually kind to animals, and besides, I do not think it is ladylike to go around shooting things with a gun. Twice, however, I have been in a collision with them. On one occasion, a large leopard had attacked a dog who, with her family, was occupying a dilapidated hut next to mine. The dog was a half-bred boarhound and a savage brute in her own right. Being awakened by the noise, I rushed out into the dim moonlight, thinking she was having one of her usual fights with other dogs, and I saw a swirling mass of animal matter within a yard of me. I threw two mushroom-shaped local stools in rapid succession into the thick of it, and the meeting broke up into a leopard and a dog. The leopard crouched, I think to spring—

She recovered well after I applied plenty of ointment, for which she rewarded me with several bites. Do not mistake this for a hunting story; I no more thought it was a leopard than a harmless flower when I joined the fight. My other leopard encounter was also because of a dog. Leopards always hunt dogs because, once upon a time, the leopard and the dog were great friends. The leopard went out one day and left her cubs in the dog’s care, but the dog went out socializing, and a snake came and killed the cubs. There has been animosity between the two ever since. For the benefit of readers interested in hunting whose curiosity might have been piqued by the mention of <term>big game</term>, I should mention that the largest leopard skin I ever measured myself was 9 feet 7 inches, including the tail. It was a dried skin, and every man who saw it said, “It was the largest skin I’ve ever seen—except for one I saw somewhere else.”

The largest crocodile I ever measured was 22 feet 3 inches, and the largest gorilla was 5 feet 7 inches. I am assured by the missionaries in <term>Calabar</term> <note>A coastal city and port in modern-day Nigeria.</note> that a python was brought into <term>Creek Town</term> <note>A historic Efik settlement near Calabar.</note> during the <term>Rev. Mr. Goldie's</term> <note>Hugh Goldie (1815–1895), a Scottish missionary who lived in Old Calabar and wrote a dictionary of the Efik language.</note> time that was longer than the entire veranda of the Creek Town mission house. This python must have been over 40 feet long. I haven't a shadow of doubt that it was. People who stay at home will always doubt such large measurements, but experienced travelers in the wild do not. After all, if it amuses the homebodies to be skeptical, by all means, let them; they lead dull lives and it doesn't hurt you. You know how extremely difficult it is to preserve truly large specimens to bring home, and how, half the time, they fall into the hands of people who would not bother...

The largest python skin I ever measured was a damaged one that reached 26 feet. There is an enormous one hanging in front of a house in Luanda <note>Original: "San Paul de Loanda," the capital of modern-day Angola.</note> which you can go and measure yourself with relative safety any day; I believe it is over 20 feet long, though I never measured that particular one myself. The usual size for pythons is 10 to 15 feet—or rather, I should say that is the size you find with distressing frequency in your chicken coop.

I have no personal knowledge of the Lubuku secret society. I received a great deal of intriguing information about it from a Bakélé <note>A Bantu ethnic group from the rainforests of Gabon and neighboring regions.</note> woman who had heard it secondhand. However, her account confirms what Captain Latrobe Bateman says about it in his excellent book, *The First Ascent of the Kasai* (George Philip, 1889). I refer any ethnologist to his account in Note J of the Appendix. My information also suggested what he calls "a dark inference as to its true nature"—a nature that is by no means common to all African tribal secret societies.

In addition to the secret societies and the leopard society, there are certain <term>ju-jus</term> <note>A West African term for a fetish, charm, or religious object; it can also refer to the spiritual power or traditional religious system associated with such objects.</note> in the Niger Delta held only by a few powerful chiefs. The one in Bonny has its own complete language, and there is one in Duke Town <note>Located in Old Calabar, modern-day Nigeria.</note> so powerful that if you wish for someone's death, you only have to name them before it. "These ju-jus are very swift and sure." I would much rather drink with them than fight any of them—yes, by far.

# CHAPTER XXIV

## ASCENT OF THE GREAT PEAK OF THE CAMEROONS

->Setting forth how the traveler intends to climb the mountain called Mungo Mah Lobeh, or the Throne of Thunder, and in due course reaches Buea, which is located there.<-

After returning from Corisco, I stayed for a few weeks in Gabon <note>Original: "Gaboon."</note> and then regretfully departed on the *Niger*. My regrets, I should explain, arose from leaving the charms and interests of the French Congo <note>Original: "Congo Français."</note> and had nothing at all to do with sailing on one of the most comfortable ships of all those that stop along the West African Coast.

The *Niger* was heading back to Europe when I joined her, and in due course, we arrived at the Cameroon River, where I was once again under German rule. It would be very interesting to compare the various forms of European government in Africa—English, French, German, Portuguese, and Spanish—but to do so fairly would take up more space than I have available, for the subject is extremely complex. Each of these forms of government has its good and bad points. Each of them deals with regions of Africa that differ from one another—in the nature of their inhabitants, their geography, and so on—so I will not enter into any comparison of them here. I will merely remark that, on the whole, German colonial methods in Africa are more similar to English methods than to French ones, and that Germany has one of the main English faults in an exaggerated form—namely, a lack of proper appreciation for the work of the men who serve her in Africa. Time after time, I have come across cases of German officers in Cameroon who have served their country...

...good and noble service, yet who, upon their return to the Fatherland they loved so well, have found not only a lack of due reward, but worse. When the enthusiasm for colonial expansion dies out in Germany—as it may, given the lack of profit from her colonies caused by excessive spending—the sin of her ingratitude toward those men who have served her in Cameroon will catch up with her, and her best and bravest sons will no longer risk their honor in her service.

The worst case of German ingratitude toward Germans is the most recent: that of the late Vice-Governor of Cameroon, Herr von Lucke, whom I shall have reason to speak of later. This fine young officer, full of enthusiasm for his country and devoted to his Emperor, was driven to suicide by a malicious lie claiming that he had spoken disrespectfully of his Emperor. This lie was told by someone—I do not know who—but I suspect it was by some of those in Germany who seem to make it their special mission in life to disparage her greatest colony, Cameroon. No country and no ruler ever possessed a more devoted subject or a truer gentleman and soldier than Herr von Lucke.

I also see in German newspapers that Governor von Puttkamer has been accused of severity toward the natives in Cameroon. I, and those Englishmen who know him, have no hesitation in saying this accusation is also unfounded. I hope that Germany, sitting at home in "carpet slippers" <note>An idiom referring to armchair critics or those living in domestic comfort far from the reality of the field.</note> and in barracks, has realized by now that it is not qualified to judge Germans in Africa. I will say no more on this subject, however (as I am devoted to my "first-cousins," the Germans and the Danes, through both good and bad reports), but will return to my own minor experiences.

From the deck of the *Niger*, I found myself again confronted with my great temptation—the magnificent *Mungo Mah Lobeh*, or the "Throne of Thunder." Now, it is none of my business to climb mountains. There are almost no fish on them in West Africa, and very little good "fetish" <term>Kingsley uses this term to refer to indigenous religious practices, spiritual beliefs, or sacred objects.</term> to be found, as the population on them is sparse—the African people, like myself, loathe the cool air. Nevertheless, I feel quite sure that no white man has ever looked upon the great Peak of Cameroon without a desire arising in his mind to climb it and know in detail the highest point on the western side of the...

# THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROONS

...continent, and indeed one of the highest points in all Africa. However, do not imagine that the ascent is a common occurrence in a "coaster’s" <term>A person, usually a European trader or official, living and working along the West African coast</term> life; it is far from it. As a rule, the coaster firmly resists the temptation of Mungo <note>Mungo Mah Lobeh, the native name for Mount Cameroon, meaning "Throne of Thunder" or "Mountain of Thunder"</note>, being more strong-minded than I am; moreover, he is busy and only too often stricken with fever in the bargain. But I admit I am the exception, and I have given in to the temptation. I am the third English person to ascend the Peak and the first to have ascended it from the southeast face. The first man to reach the summit was Sir Richard Burton, accompanied by the great botanist Gustav Mann. He went up from Babundi—a place on the seashore to the west—as did the next twenty-five people (mostly Germans) who followed him. The first expedition to reach the summit from the same side I tackled was composed of the first lieutenant and the doctor from the German warship *Hyæna* <note>original: "Hyæna," German for Hyena</note>. These gentlemen had accomplished this feat just a few weeks before I landed at Victoria to make my attempt. I provide these details to excuse myself for later giving you a detailed account of the southeast face of Mungo Mah Lobeh.

The majesty and charm of this mountain are so great that its temptation is as strong for me today as it was the first day I saw it, when I was traveling down the West Coast of Africa on the *S.S. Lagos* in 1893. On that day, it happened to reveal itself from its surf-washed base to its sky-scraping summit. It is certainly most striking when you first see it—as I did—after sailing for weeks along the low shores and mangrove-fringed rivers of the Niger Delta. Suddenly, the great mountain rises 13,760 feet straight out of the sea, while nearby to the west, the lovely island mass of Fernando Po <note>Now known as the island of Bioko in Equatorial Guinea</note> towers to 10,190 feet. But every time you pass it, its beauty grows on you with increasing force, though it is never the same twice. Sometimes it is wreathed with indigo-black storm clouds; sometimes it is crested with snow; sometimes it is softly gorgeous with gold, green, and rose-colored mists tinted by the setting sun; and sometimes it is completely wrapped in dense clouds so that you cannot see it at all. But once you know it is there, it makes no difference, and you bow down and worship.

## XXIV THRONE OF THUNDER

There are only two distinct peaks to this magnificent formation that geologists bluntly call the "volcanic intrusive mass" <term>A body of igneous rock that formed from magma forced into older rock layers</term> of the Cameroon Mountains: namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, Big Cameroon and Little Cameroon. The latter, Mungo Mah Etindeh, has not yet been climbed, even though it is only 5,820 feet high. ...and Omon ranges. These are not related to Mungo, as they have a very different structure and composition. The geological specimens I brought back from them and from the Cameroons have been identified by geologists as schistose grit <term>A coarse-grained sandstone or metamorphic rock containing flakes of mica</term> and vesicular lava <term>Lava containing small holes or bubbles formed by gas</term>, respectively.

After spending a few pleasant days at the Cameroon River in the company of Frau Plehn—my poor friend Mrs. Duggan having already departed for England following the death of her husband—I traveled around to Victoria, Ambas Bay. Despite being solemnly advised by Captain Davies to "give it up, as it was no picnic," I began my attempt to climb the Peak of Cameroons as follows:

*September 20th, 1895.*—Left Victoria at 7:30 AM; the weather was fine. Herr von Lucke is still trying to be in three places at once. He has been conducting a series of experiments on this ever since I landed, and likely before, and is sadly convinced that it is impossible. Or, more accurately, in typical male fashion, he is attempting an experiment to be in *four* places at once, rather than falling ill as I would under the circumstances. He kindly accompanied me as far as the bridge across the lovely, cascading Lukole River. He then headed back at about seven miles per hour to look after Victoria and his sick subordinates in detail.

Accompanied by my crew, I continued up the magnificent new road the government is building. When finished, it will run from Ambas Bay to Buea, located 3,000 feet up the mountainside. Regarding its width and general design, this is the most magnificent road I have seen anywhere in West Africa, and it runs through a superbly beautiful countryside. It is, I would say, as wide as Oxford Street. On either side are deep drainage ditches to carry off surface water, lined with banks of various beautiful tropical shrubs and ferns. Behind these, walls of grand forest rise 100 to 200 feet high. The column-like tree trunks are either draped with flowering climbing plants and ferns or display soft red and grey shafts sixty to seventy feet high without a single interrupting branch. Behind this, the lovely foothills of Mungo rise high against the sky, colored a perfect, soft dark blue.

# XXIV AN UNFINISHED ROAD 553

The color of the landscape is magnificent. The soil itself is a velvety reddish-brown, and the butterflies—which are abundant—display themselves perfectly in the sunlight in their bright yellow, crimson, and peacock-blue patterns. After five minutes of experiencing the road, I find myself envying those butterflies. I do not believe there is a more lovely road in the world, and furthermore, it is a noble and enterprising thing for a Government to build it, considering the climate and the terrain. However, to get any genuine pleasure out of it, it would be necessary to hover like a bird or a butterfly; for of all the truly terrible things to walk on, that road, at the time I was on it, was the worst.

Of course, this was because it was unfinished; it did not yet have its top layer. On the section that was finished and paved, for about half a mile past the bridge, one could travel in a Bath chair <term>A light wheelchair with a folding hood, often used by invalids at spa towns</term>. The rest of it, however, would make you feel as though you needed such a chair for the rest of your life. It was one mass of broken lava rock, interspersed here and there with giant tree stumps that had been only partially cleared with gunpowder.

As we approach the end of the forest where the road terminates, it begins to rain heavily. I see a small house on the left-hand side and a European engineer supervising a group of very cheerful locals who are felling timber. He very kindly invites me to take shelter, saying it cannot rain this hard for long. my crew also express a desire for water, so I sit down and chat with the engineer under the shelter of his veranda while the men go to the water hole about twenty minutes away.

The engineer is an Alsatian <note>A native of Alsace, a region then under German control on the border of France and Germany</note> and had previously been employed on the Congo Free State Railway. He left that job because they stationed him at the terminal station on those dreaded Palaballa Mountains. Four men stationed there died of fever; when he contracted it himself, he applied for leave to go down to Matadi to see a doctor. His request was curtly refused, and he was told he must remain at his post until another engineer arrived to take over his duties. He stayed for several days waiting, but no one arrived or showed any sign of coming. He then discovered that the company had given orders to all their employees that he was not to be permitted on any train, so he walked down to Matadi on foot. How he managed it, knowing that...

I eventually see one of my men sitting right in the middle of the road on a rock, totally unsheltered, and a feeling of shame comes over me in the face of this man’s endurance in the rain. I conscientiously attempt to keep dry by holding up an umbrella, knowing that although it is hopeless, it is the proper thing to do.

My relatives—no, even Mrs. Roy, who is blind to a large percentage of my imperfections—say the most scathing things about my behavior regarding water. But really, my conduct is founded on sound principles. I know from a series of carefully conducted experiments, carried out on the Lynn River in Devonshire, that I cannot cross a river on slippery stepping-stones; therefore, knowing that attempts to keep my feet out of the water only end in my falling head-first and soaking the rest of my body, I take charge of Fate and wade.

This particular stream, too, requires careful wading, as the rocks over which it flows are arranged in a picturesque but perilous confusion. However, all goes well, and upon reaching the other side, I decide to "chuck it" <term>give up on the effort</term>, as Captain Davies would say, regarding keeping dry, for the rain comes down heavier than ever.

Now we are evidently dealing with a foothill, but the rain is too thick for one to see two yards in any direction. We seem to be in a ghostly forest, for the great palms and redwoods rise up in the mist before us and fade into the mist behind as we pass on. The rocks which edge and scatter the path at our feet are covered with exquisite ferns and mosses—all the most delicate shades of green imaginable, and here and there of absolute gold, looking as if some ray of sunshine had lingered too long playing on the earth and had been shut off from heaven by the mist, and so lay nestling among the rocks until it might rejoin the sun.

The path now becomes an absolute torrent of mud-thickened water, which cascades around one's ankles in a playful way, and around one's knees in the hollows of the path. Five seconds after abandoning the umbrella, I am wet through; however, it is not uncomfortable at this temperature—something like that of a cucumber frame <term>a small, glass-covered garden structure used for growing plants; a mini-greenhouse</term> with the glass panes on—if you can "clear your mind of all prejudice," as Dr. Johnson <note>Samuel Johnson (1709–1784), the famous English writer and lexicographer.</note> says, and forget the risk of fever which saturation entails.

As it is, a white sheet—or more accurately, considering its soft, stuffy woolliness, a white blanket—is stretched across the landscape to the southwest, where the sea would otherwise be visible.

We go downhill now, with water rushing into the backs of my shoes for a change. The path is fringed by high, sugar-cane-like grass that hangs across it in a lazy way, swiping you in the face and cutting like a knife whenever you catch its edge, all while pouring constant, sneaky streams of water down your neck. It does not matter. The entire Atlantic could not get more water onto me than I have already endured. Every now and then, I stop and wring some of it out from my skirts, for they are heavy. One would not imagine that anything could fall more thickly than this rain, but it can. When you are on the top of the hills, a cold breeze blows through the mist, chilling you to the bone. It bends the tops of the palm trees, sending down water by the bucketful with a slap, hitting or missing you as the case may be.

Both my men and I are by now getting anxious for our “chop” <term>West African Pidgin for food or a meal</term>, and they tell me, “We will see the big hut soon.” Soon we do see the big hut, but with faces of undisguised horror, for the big hut consists only of a few charred roof-mats and debris lying on the ground. A fire has destroyed that simple home. Our path here is crossed by another that goes east and west. After a consultation between my men and the Bakwiri <term>an ethnic group indigenous to the region around Mount Cameroon</term>, we take the path going east, down a steep slope between weedy plantations. Shortly, a steep little hillside appears on the left with a long, low hut on the top. We go up to it and I find it is the home of a Black Bible-reader from the Basel Mission <term>a Swiss Christian missionary society active in West Africa</term>. He comes out and speaks English well. I tell him I want a house for myself and my men, and he says we had better come and stay in this one. It is divided into two rooms: one in which the children who attend the mission school stay, and which contains a fire,

Soon my excellent little cook brings in my meal, and with him come two mission teachers—our first acquaintance in the white jacket, and another in a blue one. They lounge around and spit in all directions; then the chiefs begin to arrive with their entire families. They sidle into the room and obviously stare at the jug of rum <term>original: "demi-john," a large narrow-necked bottle typically encased in wicker</term>.

As usual, they are a nuisance, sitting on everything. No sooner have I moved an unwashed-looking chief off the wooden sofa than I notice another has silently seated himself in the middle of my open suitcase <term>original: "portmanteau"</term>. After removing him and closing it, I see another has settled on the men’s sack of beef and rice.

It is now about three o'clock, and I am still chilled to the bone despite drinking tea. The weather is as bad as ever. The men say that the rest of the road to Buea is far worse than what we have traveled so far, and that we would never get there before dark—and "for sure" we would not get there afterward, because by the time night falls, we would be in a "very bad place" <term>West African Pidgin "bad place too much," meaning a very dangerous or difficult location</term>. Therefore, much to their relief, I say I will stay here at Buana for the night and go up to Buea in the morning. For the moment, I think I will wrap myself in a blanket and try to get the chill out of my system. I give the chiefs a glass of rum each, plenty of tobacco <term>original: "head tobacco," which refers to bunches of tobacco leaves tied together at the stem</term>, and my best thanks for their "kind" visit, and then I turn them and the spitting mission teachers out. I drift off to sleep again for fifteen minutes but am soon woken by several enterprising sightseers pushing open the window shutters. Looking around, I see a crowd of black heads peering through the window opening. I politely inform them that the circus is closed for repairs and fasten the shutters. However, sleep is impossible, so I get up to see what my men are doing. They are comfortable enough around their fire, with their clothes hanging on strings in the smoke above them, and I envy them that fire. 

I then take a short walk to see if there is anything to be seen, but the scenery is much like what you would see if you were inside a blancmange <term>a thick, opaque, white gelatinous dessert</term>. As it is now growing dark, I return to my room, light candles, and read Dr. Günther’s book on fishes <note>Albert Günther’s "Catalogue of the Fishes in the British Museum" was a standard zoological reference of the time</note>. If this sort of weather continues, I expect I shall start developing fins and gills myself. 

The room soon fills with local people. Unless you watch the door constantly, you cannot see how they enter. You look at a corner one minute and it is empty; the next time you look that way, it is full of rows of white teeth and watching eyes. The two mission teachers come in and make a show of teaching a child to read the Bible. Having decided that the specific type of fins one wears doesn't matter much since they all work well, I write up my log. 

Around seven o'clock, I have the cook make me some more tea, and shortly after, I find myself facing the problem of where the two mission teachers will sleep for the night. This class of man has no resourcefulness in him. I find myself thinking worse of the effects of mission-teaching than usual as I prepare to try and get some sleep. It is not an elaborate affair, I assure you, for I only want to wrap myself in a blanket and lie on that plank. But the rain has soaked into the blankets and—horror of horrors—there is no pillow. The mission men have cleared their bedding out completely. 

Now, you can do without a good many things, but not without a pillow, so I hunt around to find something to make one with. I find a Bible in English, a Bible in German, two hymnbooks, and a candlestick. These seem to be all the small articles in the room—no, there is a parcel behind the books containing the mission teachers' Sunday trousers. I make a delightful arrangement of the books bound together by the trousers, with the whole affair wrapped in one of my towels. I never realized the advantage of Africans wearing trousers until now.

# XXIV HUSBANDS AND WIVES

Civilization has its advantages after all. But it is no use trying to get any sleep until those men are quieter. The partition separating my room from theirs is a structure of bamboo and mats; it is straight at the top, leaving a triangular space under the roof that is open to both rooms. The smoke from the fire and the conversation are also shared between both rooms. Kefalla is lecturing everyone in a dogmatic way, and some of the others are snoring. There is a new style of decoration along the shared wall. William Morris <note>William Morris (1834–1896) was a famous English textile designer and leader of the Arts and Crafts Movement</note> might have made something out of it for a dado <term>the lower part of an interior wall, often decorated differently from the upper part</term>. It consists of a row of undershirts stretched out in a line. I lubricate my revolver with Vaseline. I wish those men would stop their chattering. Kefalla seems to know the scandalous secrets of almost everyone, black and white, down in Ambas Bay <note>The bay where the settlement of Victoria (now Limbe, Cameroon) is located</note>, but I do not believe those last two stories. There are evidently great jokes in the next room now; Kefalla has thrown himself, still talking in the dark, onto the top of one of the mission teachers. Outside, the village women have been keeping up a most melancholy cooing sound for over an hour. Those foolish creatures are evidently worrying about their husbands who have gone down to the market in Ambas Bay and who, they think, are lost in the bush. I do not have a shadow of a doubt that the husbands who are not home by now are safely drunk in town, or resting on the grand new road the kindly Government has provided for them, either lying in one of the drainage ditches or tucked in among the lava rocks.

**September 21st.**—The cooing went on all night. I was woken around 9:30 p.m. by an uproar in the adjacent hut: one husband had returned in a belligerent condition and beaten his wives. Their squawks and screams, instead of acting as a warning to the other ladies, only encouraged the silly things to go on cooing louder and more pleadingly than ever—so that their husbands might come home and beat them too, I suppose. Whenever the absolute hardness of my wooden plank bed wakes me, I still hear them cooing.

No watchman is required to wake you by 5:30 a.m. on the top of a Cameroon foothill because, around 4:00 a.m., the damp chill that comes before the dawn does so most effectively. One old chief arrived early out of the mist and gave me a gift <term>the original text uses "dashed," a West African Pidgin English term for giving a gift or a tip</term> of a bottle of palm wine; he says he wants to...

It is pouring rain again now. We descend the steep hillock to the path we traveled yesterday, following it until we reach the point where the old path intersects it. Then, we turn up to the right, following the course of the old path, and leave Buana without a single pang of regret. Our route leads northeast. Oh, the mud! It is not like the relatively clear cascades of yesterday, but a sticky, slippery mess—intensely sticky and intensely slippery. The narrow path, which is filled with this sludge, is worn into a V-shape underneath, and I soon find that the safest way forward is to walk directly through the deepest mud in the middle.

The white mist blocks out all details more than ten yards away in any direction. All we can see as we first turn onto the path is a patch of enormous cocoyams <term>a tropical root vegetable with large leaves, also known as taro</term> on our right. After this comes an overgrown plantation and stretches of sharp sword grass hanging across the road. The terrain is not as level as—or rather, I should say, it is even more steeply uneven than—the land we crossed yesterday. On we go, patiently dragging ourselves through the mud in the valleys and toiling up hillsides among boulders and stretches of forest, for we have now moved beyond Buana’s plantations. We skirt the summit of one hill only to descend into another valley. It is evident that this is a succession of foothills leading to the great mountain, and we have not yet reached its actual slopes. As we continue, the hills become increasingly abrupt in shape, and the valleys become mere narrow ravines. # XXIV MUD-SLIDES

...a dry torrent bed, judging by the appearance of the chaotic, water-worn boulders. Currently, there are only isolated pools among the rocks, as the weather for the two weeks before I left Victoria <note>Now known as Limbe, a seaside city in Cameroon</note> had been fairly dry, and this rich, porous soil soaks up an immense amount of water. It strikes me as strange that while we are either ascending or descending the hills, the ground is less muddy than when we are skirting their summits. However, as my brother would say, "It is perfectly simple if you think about it," because on the inclines, the rush of water washes the soil away down to the bedrock. There is an outcrop of clay down by Buana, and though that was slippery, it is nothing compared to the slipperiness of this fine, soft, red-brown earth that makes up the soil higher up and also around Ambas Bay. This gets churned into a sort of batter when enough water sits on it; when there is less water, an ice slide is like child's play in comparison.

My men and I flounder about. Three times one of them, load and all, goes down with a squelch and a crash into the tall grass at the side, and says "damn!" with quite a European accent. As a rule, however, we proceed in single file, my shoes giving out a musical squelching sound and their naked feet making a "squish, squash" noise. The men take it very good-temperedledly and sing between accidents. I do not feel much like singing myself, particularly at one awful spot that was the exception to the rule that steep ground provides the best footing. This exception was a long, slippery slide down into a ravine with a perfectly glassy slope leading up out of it. I remember one of my tutors saying, "When on a long march, always assume the attitude you feel most inclined toward, as it is less tiring." There could not be the least shadow of a doubt about your inclinations regarding your posture here, nor about giving way to them, and so we arrived at the bottom of that ravine in a chaotic, tangled heap. 

As for climbing out of it, it was not mere inclination—it was a passion that possessed you. What you wanted to do was plant your nose against the hillside and wave your normally earthward extremities in the air, particularly when you were near the middle of the slope or close to the top. Two of the boys gave way to this impulse; I, of course, did not, but when I felt it coming on like a sort of fit, I flung myself sideways into the dense bush that edges the path.

Then we pass through an opening in the great "war-hedge" of Buea, a growing stockade some fifteen feet high, the lower part of which is wattled <note>woven with sticks and twigs</note>. At the sides of the path here grow banks of bergamot and balsam, returning good for evil and smelling sweetly as we crush them. Thank goodness we are in the forest now, and we seem to have finished with the sword-grass. The rocks are covered with moss and ferns, and the mist curling and wandering about among the tree stems is very lovely. I have to pause in life’s pleasures because I want to measure one of the large earthworms, which, along with smaller sealing-wax-red worms, are crawling about the path. He was eleven and three-quarter inches long. He detained me for some time while I gathered this information, because he was so nervous during the operation.

In our next ravine, there is a succession of pools, evidently part of a mountain torrent of greater magnitude than those we have passed, and in these pools, there are things swimming. I spend more time catching them with the assistance of Bum. I do not value Kefalla's advice, ample though it is, as being of any real value in the affair. I bag some water-spiders and two small fish. The heat is less oppressive than it was yesterday. All day yesterday, one was being alternately smothered in the valley and chilled on the hilltops. Today the temperature is more level—about 70° Fahrenheit, I believe.

The soil up here, about 2,500 feet above sea level, is exceedingly rich despite being laden with rocks. The higher we go, the more bergamot there is, as well as native indigo with the undersides of its leaves colored dark blue, and lovely coleuses with red markings on their upper leaves and crimson linings. As an <term>ichthyologist</term> <note>a scientist who studies fish</note>, I am in the wrong paradise. What a region this would be for a <term>botanist</term> <note>a scientist who studies plants</note>!

I have my gear brought into my room, where the loads steam and drip small rills of water onto the bare floor. Then, barricading the door with blankets and closing the window shutters, I rid myself of the "German territory" <note>Referring to the thick mud clinging to her clothes</note> I have acquired during the last twenty-four hours. My portmanteau having remained fairly watertight, I am able to emerge as a respectable person before society—that is, Herr Liebert, the German officer—and I hunt for my boys to get me some tea. This being done, I go out onto the veranda to talk.

"Society" has a dreadfully infected foot. Weeks ago, he injured it on the road; later, while cleaning a bad sore on one of his men, some of the pus got into his own wound. Consequently, he nearly lost his leg, or more accurately, his life. He lay in bed for thirteen days, and there was no doctor even down in <term>Victoria</term> <note>Now Limbe, Cameroon</note> to amputate the leg if it had turned to gangrene, as seemed likely. He makes light of it and hops about in a most energetic way, looking after seventy Black soldiers along with their wives and children. He gives them their rations, drills them, treats their illnesses, and manages everything else, while still longing to do more. 

Many of the soldiers are also suffering from bad feet because of the poor condition of the roads in this area. These soldiers are an assortment of <term>Wei-Weis</term> <note>Vai people</note> and <term>Su-Su</term> <note>Susu people</note> from Sierra Leone, as well as some <term>Yorubas</term>. They are smart men and well cared for. Their uniforms are far more practical and military than the absurd uniforms we give our <term>Haussas</term> in <term>Calabar</term>. However, the Fatherland ordains that they must wear braces <note>suspenders</note>, and these unnecessary items for an African are worn hanging loose, except by those men actually on duty.

The mist clears off in the evening around five o'clock, and the surrounding scenery is at last visible. <header>BUSH AMBUSCADES</header>

The mountain wall when viewed from Buea is very grand, although it lacks a snow-cap or glacier. The highest summits of Mungo <note>Mount Cameroon, or *Mungo Ma Ndemi* (Mountain of Thunder)</note> are not visible because we are too close beneath them, but its enormous bulk and isolation make it highly impressive. The forest runs up the mountain in a great band above Buea, then sends up long tongues of trees into the grass belt above. But I do not yet know what may be above this grass belt, for our view ends at the top of the wall of the great southeast crater. My men say there are devils and gold up beyond, but the German authorities do not support this view. Those Germans are so skeptical. 

This station is evidently on a ledge, for behind it the ground falls away steeply, and you get an uninterrupted panoramic view of the Cameroon estuary and the great stretches of low swamplands. You can see the Mungo and the Bimbia rivers with their many creeks and channels, and far away to the east, the strange, abrupt forms of the Rumpi Mountains. Herr Liebert says you can see the Cameroon Government buildings from here if only the day is clear, even though they are some forty miles away. Aside from a missionary of the Basel Mission, this distant view of those buildings is the only "white society" available at Buea. 

"Society" here says that the communication, though better than none, is slow. I suggested he should pay calls and indulge in conversation by means of a code of fireworks. 

"Ha!" says he, "you're like the Calabar major." 

"Which one?" I asked, for there are many types of majors. 

"The one who came here last dry season," he said, "who went up onto the mountain wall and set the grass on fire to show how he was getting along, and then had to run down for his life." 

I know that man, and a very excellent man he is, but he is not in Calabar, nor is he a major; however, "society" everywhere makes mistakes in technical details.

I hear more details about the death of poor <term>Freiherr</term> <note>Baron</note> von Gravenreuth, whose fine monument of a seated lion I saw in the Government House grounds in Cameroons the other day. Bush fighting in these West African forests is dreadfully dangerous work. Hemmed in by the bush along a narrow path where you must pass slowly in single file, you are a target for any and all natives invisibly hidden in the undergrowth. The "war-hedge" of Buea <note>A defensive barrier of thorny bushes and trees planted by the Bakweri people</note> must have created an additional danger and difficulty here for the attacking party.

<header>THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROONS CH. XXIV</header>

The lieutenant and his small band of Black soldiers had, after a difficult fight, succeeded in forcing the entrance to this area when their ammunition ran out and they were forced to retreat. The Buean people, regarding this as a victory, rallied their forces, and a lucky shot killed the lieutenant instantly. A follow-up expedition was quickly dispatched from Victoria <note>A coastal town in British Southern Cameroons, now Limbe</note>, and it corrected the Bueans' misunderstanding—along with several of the Bueans themselves. However, it was a necessary expedition. These locals were a constant threat to the more peaceful trading tribes, whom they would not permit to cross their territory. The Germans have treated the Bueans mercifully, as their large villages, such as Sapa, are still standing. A steady stream of locals now enters the barrack yard to sell produce or carry it down to the Victoria markets, appearing perfectly content and cheerful. This morning, I met a large, burly chief carrying his staff of office. I am told he is the chief of Sapa, whom Herr von Lucke has summoned to Victoria for a meeting <note>palaver: a West African term for a talk, discussion, or negotiation, often between locals and colonial officials</note>.

I finally left Herr Liebert because every time I spoke, he would hop up and rush off to show me something, which I am sure was bad for his injured foot. I went to check that my men were safely settled in their quarters. Kefalla was lecturing the soldiers in a very arrogant and moralizing manner. Herr Liebert has nicknamed him "the Professor," a name I have adopted, though I fear "Windbag" would be more accurate.

At 7:30 p.m., a massive tornado came rolling down toward us. Massive indigo clouds, with bright lightning flashing at the front, rolled out from over the wall of the great crater above. Then, with the spitefulness unique to tornadoes, it seemed to notice all the soldiers, their wives, and children sitting happily in the barrack yard—singing in a minor key and beating their beloved drums—so it dropped straight down on them with torrents of water. It sent lightning racing across the ground in lethal, glowing streams. Oh, tornadoes are such "lovely" things! I wonder what they will be like when we are up in their home territory, at the top of that formidable wall? I had no idea Mungo <note>Mount Cameroon</note> was so steep. If I had known—well, I am committed now!

## CHAPTER XXV

### ASCENT OF THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROONS—(*Continued*)

->Wherein is recounted how the traveler sets out from Buea and ascends through the forest belt to the top of the southeast crater of Mungo Mah Lobeh <note>The native name for Mount Cameroon, meaning "Throne of Thunder" or "Mountain of the Gods"</note>, with many dilemmas and disasters that occurred on the way.<-

September 22nd.—I woke at 5:00 a.m. It was a fine morning with a beautiful view toward the Cameroon River. The broad stretch of forest below, and the water-eroded mangrove swamps beneath that, were all a glorious indigo flushed with rose—the color of “the death of the night,” as Kiva used to call the dawn. No one was moving until six o’clock, when people emerged from their huts, stretched, and proceeded to begin the day in the typically casual, listless African manner. I am not stating this as a unique trait arising from their brain development; it is merely the natural result of the nights they enjoy so cheerfully. *Katzenjammer* <note>original: "Katzenjammer" — German for a hangover, literally "cats' misery"</note> is, I believe, the technical term for it.

My crew members are worse than the rest. I went to hunt for the cook. He propped one eye open with difficulty and let out a yawn so wide it nearly split his head in two. I shocked him awake by saying I intended to continue climbing today, that I wanted my food <term>chop: a West African term for food or a meal</term>, and that we needed to start immediately. He went off to announce my "horrible" intention to the others. Kefalla soon arrived on the scene, ready for an argument. 

“Don't you know <term>sabe: to know or understand, from the Portuguese 'saber'</term> that today is Sunday, Ma?” he asked, in a tone suggesting he thought this settled the matter. 

I “knew” quite unconcernedly. Kefalla scratched his head, searching for another argument, but he had already opened with his heaviest artillery; when that was repulsed, it threw his backup arguments into confusion. Bum, the headman, then turned up; he was still sound asleep internally but quite ready to come along. Bum, I have found, is always ready to do what he is told.

Herr Liebert now appears on the scene and says I can have some of his laborers. They are currently more or less idle because his bad foot prevents him from moving around much to direct them. After ensuring they each have a good day's rations of rice, beef, etc., I remove them from the party.

In addition to the laborers, I am to have Sasu as a guide; he is a Black sergeant who climbed the Peak with the officers of the *Hyena*. I eat my breakfast and then wait around, watching my men get ready to start very slowly. They spin some plausible stories about needing to cook food in case they cannot build a fire when we reach the top of the forest belt where we are to camp. I have never seen a forest in Africa where you could not start a fire, but knowing that my previous experiences have never exceeded 5,000 feet in elevation, I let them have their way. We set off around 8:00 a.m., departing with both good wishes and grim prophecies from Herr Liebert.

Led by Sasu and accompanied by "To-morrow"—a man who came to Buea from some unknown interior district, speaks no known language, and whose job it is to help cut a path through the bush—we go back down the path we came and cross the river again. This river seems to separate the main mass of the mountain from the foothills on this side. Immediately after crossing it, we turn up into the forest on the right-hand side. "To-morrow" clears an overgrown track for about half an hour and then leaves us.

Everything is soaking wet, and we swish through thick undergrowth before entering a darker forest where the rocky ground is richly decorated with ferns and moss. For the first time in my life, I see tree-ferns growing wild in luxuriant profusion. What glorious creations they are! Then we emerge into the middle of a koko <term>koko: taro or similar edible tubers</term> plantation. Next to sweet—

Potatoes are a nightmare to walk through, but give me <term>kokos</term> <note>coco-yams or taro</note> for a truly exhausting experience, particularly when they are wet, as they very much are now. These gigantic <term>arums</term> <note>plants of the Araceae family with large, broad leaves</note> balance little reservoirs of water on their leaves, which you tip over yourself as you pass through. Their big, round roots are perfect for falling over. They stick up above the ground, so you can jam your foot against them and pitch forward, or step on one and slip backward or sideways. The "entertainment" they provide a traveler is not repetitive, but it is infuriating. 

After struggling through these, we encounter the "war hedge" again. Following a determined struggle with various forms of vegetation in a muddled, tangled state, Sasu says, "No good, the path has been blocked up." There is much grave head-shaking between him and Sasu about whether any other route is practical, because no other path exists. 

I did not want to say "so much the better," because it would have sounded ungrateful, but I knew from my *Ogowé* <note>the Ogooué River in Gabon, where Kingsley had previously traveled</note> experiences that a forest which looks like a dense black mat from a distance is actually manageable underneath. There is a short path recently cut by Herr Liebert that goes straight up toward the forest above us. It had been made to reach a clearing where ambitious farming operations were being started before Herr Liebert hurt his foot. 

We go up this path; it is nearly vertical while it lasts, and it ends in a scrubby patch intended to be a plantation. It is more exquisite than words can describe, but it is not easy walking—particularly at one spot where a gigantic tree has fallen across a small, rocky ravine and must be crawled under.

As we climb higher, every few minutes we have to edge and squeeze through the aerial roots of some massive species of tree that is plentiful in this area. I am certain that if it were measured, one we passed through would have rivaled any Indian <term>banyan</term> <note>an Indian fig tree whose branches produce aerial roots that grow down into the ground to form additional trunks</note> in the extent of ground it covered. Imagine a vast, seemingly limitless cathedral with its countless columns covered—or rather, composed—of the most exquisite dark-green, large-fronded moss, with a delicate fern embedded here and there as an extra decoration. The white, gauze-like mist descends from the upper mountain toward us: creeping, twining around, and streaming through the moss-covered tree columns. Long bands of it stretch out sinuously and evenly for fifty or sixty feet or more, and then end in a puff like gun smoke. Soon, however, all the mist-streams merge and dominate the atmosphere, wrapping us in a clammy, cold embrace. It is not that smothering, wool-blanket-like fog that enveloped us down by <note>original: "Buana," likely referring to the lower settlement of Buea</note>, but something exquisitely delicate. The difference it makes to the beauty of the forest is the same difference you would find between placing a delicate veil over a beautiful woman's face and putting a sack over her head. In fact, the mist here was exceedingly becoming to the forest's beauty. Every now and then, growls of thunder roll out and vibrate in the earth beneath our feet. <term>Mungo</term> <note>short for *Mungo Mah Lobeh*, the native Bakweri name for Mount Cameroon, meaning "Throne of Thunder" or "Chariot of the Gods"</note> is making a big...

I have been feeling that the time for camping was long overdue for the past hour, and Kefalla openly said as much an hour and a half ago; however, he had such scathing things said to him about "civilians' legs" by the sergeant that I did not voice my own opinion.

Then I find the boys have not managed to start a fire despite all their fuss, and I have to demonstrate to them the lessons I learned among the <term>Fans</term> <note>The Fang people of West Central Africa, with whom Kingsley had traveled previously</note> regarding fire-making. We build a "fire-house" <note>a small, lean-to structure made of sticks and leaves to protect a fire from heavy rain</note> and then all goes well. I notice they do not make a fire in the Fan fashion, but build it in a circle.

It is clear that one of the laborers from Buea, named Xenia, is a good man. It is equally clear that some of my other men are only fit to carry advertising signs for Day and Martin’s shoe polish <note>Day and Martin was a famous 19th-century British manufacturer of "blacking" or boot polish</note>. I dine luxuriously on canned fat pork and hot tea, and then, still feeling hungry, I move on to canned herring. Canned herring is an excellent thing, but I have to hurry because I know I must climb through the edge of the forest onto the grassland to see how the landscape is formed during the brief period of clarity that almost always arrives just before nightfall. So, leaving my men comfortably seated around the fire eating their evening meal <note>original: "chop"; a West African English term for food or a meal</note>, I pass up through the fringe of the forest belt—heavily draped with lichen tassels—into deep jungle grass and up a steep, slippery mound.

In front of me, the mountain face rises like a wall from behind a series of hillocks similar to the one I am currently on. The face of the wall has two dark crevices on the right and left. The peak itself is not visible from where I am; it rises behind and beyond the wall. I stay to take compass bearings and look for an easy path upward for tomorrow. By now, my men have noticed their "Ma" <note>the nickname used by the guides for Mary Kingsley</note> is missing and are shouting for her miserably. Night falls very quickly because we are in the shadow of the great mountain mass, so I return to camp. Alas, how often our most energetic efforts to keep our fellow creatures from temptation are in vain! I knew spending Sunday among the soldiers would be bad for my men, which is why I came up here; but now, if you please, these men have been drinking the rum because Bum, the headman, has been too exhausted to do anything but lie in his blanket and eat. Kefalla is lecturing everyone with great detail and self-importance. The cook, who has been very depressed all day, is now strangely cheerful and sings incoherently. The other men, who want to sleep, threaten to "beat him up" if he "doesn't stop." It is no use—the cook continues to sing, and soon, succumbing to the irresistible charm of music, the other men join in the choruses. The performance continues for an hour, growing more slurred and muffled in tone before finally dying out as they fall asleep.

### XXV TIMBER LINES

A few yards away from the men's fire, a bird is whistling with a deep, rich note that I have never heard before.

*September 23rd.*—The morning is gloriously fine. I rouse the men, and we start at seven o'clock with Sasu (the headman), Xenia, Black Boy, Kefalla, and the Cook.

The great southeast wall of the mountain in front of us is completely clear of clouds, and there are thousands of bees in the forest. We notice that "tongues" of forest extend up the mountain in some places, reaching a hundred yards or more above the actual <term>timber line</term> <note>the edge of the habitat at which trees are capable of growing</note>. These tongues of forest become increasingly draped with lichen, and the trees become thinner and more stunted toward their ends. I believe these tongues always occur in areas where the wind does not have full force; all those near our campsite on this southeast face are situated this way. It is clearly not a matter of soil, as there is plenty of soil on this side above where the trees stop. Furthermore, on the western side of the mountain—the side facing the sea—the timber line is much higher than it is here. Nor is it the steepness of the slope that makes the timber line so low here, for the forests in the <term>Sierra del Cristal</term> <note>The Crystal Mountains in modern-day Gabon and Equatorial Guinea</note> grew luxuriantly on much steeper grades. There is evidently some specific local condition here, or else the forest would reach the base of the crater wall. I am not so unreasonable as to expect trees to grow on the wall itself, but their tendency to stop where they do requires an explanation.

We scramble up into the region of long jungle grass and continue our way across a series of steep-sided, rounded grass hillocks, each separated from the others by dry, rocky watercourses. The effect produced by the seed heads of the long grass around us is very beautiful; they look golden brown, and every seed head and leaf is jeweled with dewdrops. The grass on the sides of the hillocks a short distance away shows a soft, brownish-pink hue.

After half an hour of climbing, when we are close to the base of the wall, I notice the men ahead stopping. Catching up with them, I find Monrovia Boy down a hole—a small, deep <term>blow-hole</term> <note>a vent or opening through which air or water is forced</note> where I am told water is supposed to be found. But Monrovia Boy soon reports, "No live" <note>West African Pidgin English meaning "It is not there" or "There is none"</note>.

I now discover that we do not have a single drop of water, either with us or in

The men are sulky. Sasu, Peter, Kefalla, and the headman say they will wait and follow as soon as the cook brings the soda water. I press on, and soon I see Xenia and Black Boy following me. We reach the intervening hillocks and begin to climb the face of the wall.

The angle of this wall is steep. Its appearance from below is impressive because of its enormous breadth and its abrupt rise—climbing straight up for a good 2,000 feet without bend or dip. It is covered with short, yellowish grass, through which the charred, <term>scoriaceous</term> <note>resembling volcanic slag or cinders; porous and crusty</note> lava rock protrudes in rough masses.

I made my way up the wall. Once you are actually on it, it is not as vertical as it appears from below. My goal was to see what the terrain was like at the top, between the wall and the final peak. <header>NO WATER LIVE!</header>
<page-num>575</page-num>

On the way up, I came across holes similar to the one my men had gone down into looking for water. I suspect these holes were caused by gases from a hot underground layer of lava bursting through the cool upper layer. As I climb higher, the grass becomes shorter and sparser, and the rocks are more prominently displayed. Scattered among them are weather-beaten bushes bearing beautiful yellow flowers, like large yellow wild roses, though they are scentless. I should note that it is not a rose at all. 

In the rocky basins, a large <term>sedum</term><note>A succulent plant, likely of the Crassulaceae family</note> grows with a magnificent head of off-white and pink flowers. There is also a tall herb with soft, downy, silver-grey leaves and a very pleasant aromatic scent, and here and there are patches of good, honest parsley. Bright blue, fuzzy-looking flowers dot the grass in sheltered spots, and a very pretty, large green orchid is common. Above us is a bright blue sky with white clouds racing hurriedly toward the northeast and a fierce sun. When I am about halfway up, I think of the men, and, needing a rest, I sit down by an inviting rock grotto with a patch of the yellow-flowered shrub growing on its top. Inside, small ferns and mosses grow, all damp—but alas, there is no pool of water, and I am desperately thirsty by this time.

A belt of white cloud had now formed below me, so that I could see neither the foothills nor the forest. Soon, Xenia emerged from this mist, struggling upward while carrying my black bag. "Where are the men?"<note>Original: "Where them Black boy live?" In West African Pidgin of this era, "live" often meant "to be located" or "to stay."</note> I asked. 

"The men say their feet are too tired," said Xenia as he threw himself down in the little shade the rock provided. I took a cup of sour claret from the bottle in the bag and told Xenia to come up as soon as he was rested. In the meantime, I told him to shout to the others below and tell them to keep moving. Xenia did so, but observed sadly, "Even moving slowly still hurts the snail,"<note>A West African proverb meaning that even a cautious or slow pace is still a struggle for the weary.</note> and I left him to continue up the mountain.

When I reached the top of the rock where I had sheltered from the blazing sun, the mist cleared slightly, and I saw my men looking like tiny dolls. They were still sitting on the small hill where I had left them. Buea was clearly visible from this elevation. The ground where the Buea station stands appeared clearly as a ledge or terrace, extending for miles to the north-northeast and south-southwest. This ledge is a strange-looking landscape, covered with low brush from which rise great, isolated, white-stemmed silk-cotton trees. Below and beyond this lies a denser belt of high forest, and further down still stretches the vast mangrove swamp bordering the estuaries of the Cameroon, Mungo, and Bimbia rivers. It is a magnificent view, providing an example of the unique beauty often found in West African scenery—specifically, massive sweeps of color. Today, the mangrove swamps looked like a vast, plum-colored <term>damson</term><note>A small purple plum; Kingsley uses the color to describe the deep purple-blue of the distant swamps</note> carpet, threaded with silver where the waterways ran. It reminded me of a scene I once saw near Cabinda; upon climbing to the top of a hill, I suddenly found myself looking down at a sheet of violet-pink over a mile long and half a mile wide. This was caused by a climbing plant that had taken over a valley full of trees; it had reached their tops and then spread and interlaced across them, bursting into abundant, glorious, laburnum-shaped clusters of flowers.

After taking some careful compass bearings for future use regarding the Rumby and Omon mountain ranges—which were clearly visible and looked fascinatingly like my beloved Sierra del Cristal—I turned toward the wall of Mount Cameroon and continued the climb. The sun was blazing, its scorching rays reflecting off the rocks. However, it was more bearable now because the heat was tempered by a biting wind.

As the slope became steeper, I gradually moved toward the left until I came to a great gully, walled with rock as neatly as if it had been built by human hands. It runs down the face of the mountain, nearly vertical in some places and always at sharp angles. Yet, it was easier to climb this "lane" than the rough rock outside because the stones within it had been smoothed by mountain torrents over thousands of rainy seasons. Furthermore, the walls protected me from the biting wind—a wind that chilled me to the bone, as I had been sweltering for over nine months in tropical and equatorial swamps.

I climbed up this gully to the very top of the mountain wall,

I started along the ridge of my wall and went to its highest part toward the southwest, intending to see what I could of the view toward the sea and then to choose a place to camp for the night.

When I reached the southwest end and looked westward, I saw the South Atlantic far below, appearing like a plain of frosted silver. Out of it, barely twenty miles away, rose Fernando Po <note>The island now known as Bioko, part of Equatorial Guinea</note> to its 10,190 feet with that majestic grace unique to a volcanic island. Immediately below me, some 10,000 feet or so, lay Victoria <note>The coastal town now known as Limbe, Cameroon</note> with the forested foothills of Mungo Mah Lobeh <term>Mungo Mah Lobeh</term><note>The native Duala name for Mount Cameroon, often translated as "Throne of Thunder" or "Mountain of God"</note> encircling it like a crown, and Ambas Bay, dotted with rocky islands, lying before it. On my left, away to the southeast, was the glorious stretch of the Cameroon estuary, with a line of white clouds lying very neatly along the course of the Cameroon River.

In one of the chasms of the mountain wall that I had come up—the one furthest to the north—a thunderstorm was brewing. It seemed to be hanging onto or streaming out of the mountainside: a soft, billowing mass of dense, cream-colored cloud, with flashes of golden lightning playing about within it accompanied by soft growls of thunder. Surely Mungo Mah Lobeh himself, out of all the thousands of storms he produces annually, never made one more lovely than this. Soon the white mists rose from the mangrove swamps and turned rose-colored in the light of the setting sun as they swept upward over the now-purple high forests. In the heavens to the north, there was a vivid rainbow; one arch of it went behind the peak, while the other sank into the sea of mist below. This sea of mist rose and rose toward me, turning from pale rose to lavender, and where the shadow of the mountain lay across it, it turned to a dull leaden grey. It was soon at my feet, obscuring the world below, and it soon came flowing over the lowest parts of the wall top, stretching in great spreading rivers over the crater plain. The space around seemed boundless, and there was in it neither sound nor color, nor anything with form, except those two terrifying things. It was like a vision, and it held me spellbound as I stood shivering on the rocks with the white mist around my knees, until into my daydreaming mind came the memory of my men, who were anything but sublime. I turned and scuttled off along the rocks like an agitated ant left alone in a dead universe.

I soon found the place where I had climbed up into the crater plain and went down over the wall, descending twice as fast, but with ten times as many scratches and grazes as I had received during the ascent.

I found the spot where I had left Xenia, but Xenia was not there, nor did he answer my "bush call" to him. So I continued down toward the place where, hours ago, I had left the men. The mist was denser further down, but to my joy, it was warmer than on the summit of the wind-swept wall.

I had nearly reached the foot of this wall and had decided to settle in for the night under a rock when I heard a melancholy croak away in the mist to the left. I went toward it and found Xenia, lost on his own account and acting in a distinctly strange manner. Then I remembered I had been warned that Xenia was slightly crazy. This was a fine situation: a madman on a mountain in the mist. I found that Xenia no longer had my black bag; instead, he had a saucepan lid and an empty lantern. However, it was a new and weak moon, and although we were below the thickest part of the mist, it was dark.

Finding our own particular opening in the forest wall was about as easy as finding “our particular rabbit hole in an unknown hayfield in the dark,” and the attempt to do so provided us with a great deal of varied exercise. I am forced to be careful with my language, because my temper right now is only one degree below the boiling point. Thankfully, the rain now began to fall, and I drew the thick blades of grass through my parched lips as I stumbled along over the jagged rocks hidden under the now waist-high jungle grass.

Our camp entrance was quite easy to distinguish by daylight, for it was on the left-hand side of one of the forest "tongues"—the grassland ran down like a lane between two sections of forest here—and three conspicuously tall trees stood just over the entrance. But we could not see these landmarks in the darkness, so I had to keep having Xenia strike matches and hold them in his hat while I looked at the compass. Presently, we ran full tilt into a belt of trees which I knew from these compass observations was our section of the forest, and I fired a couple of revolver shots into it, near where I judged our camp to be.

This was instantly answered by a shout from several human voices in unison, and I went toward that shout in a slightly friendly—well, a very slightly friendly—state of mind.

I will draw a veil over that scene, particularly regarding my remarks to those men. They did not attempt to deny their desertion, but each one attempted to explain it.

...saying that it was not he but the other porter who "got too scared."

Since the Black sergeant was officially our guide, I asked him for his views on the situation. He said that when he returned to the camp the men were drunk. I suspect this was true, but it did not explain why he had gone back in the first place. I pointed this out, and Bum, the headman, jumped into the conversation with the claim that Black Boy had become "sick in his stomach; he had a very, very bad fever," and so he and the rest of the men had to escort Black Boy back to camp. This statement, while offering a possible reason for their return, was clearly a lie; Black Boy, who did not understand English, sat laughing and chatting by the fire during this moving recital of his supposed misery. These men should have rehearsed their excuses; then Black Boy could have put on a convincing show of agonizing pain to support poor Bum’s story.

I ended the discussion <term>palaver: a long and often tedious discussion or negotiation</term> immediately with a brief but vivid description of my opinion on the situation and ordered food. Having had nothing to eat except a cup of sour red wine <note>original: "claret"</note> since 6:30 A.M., and it now being 11 P.M., I was feeling faint. Then I was faced with another "wonderful" situation. It seems that when the Cook and Monrovia returned to camp this morning, the Cook was seized by a sudden urge to manage things—the kind of impulse that produces such disastrous results in African servants—and sent all the beef and rice down to Buea to be cooked, because there was no water here to cook it. Therefore, the men have nothing to eat. I had a few tins of my own food and gave them some, and within minutes they were as happy as kings, listening and cheering at the terrifying adventures of *Xenia*, who was posing as the Hero of Great Cameroon. I drank some soda water from the two remaining bottles and ate some canned herring, and then I wrote two notes to Mr. <note>original: "Herr"</note> Liebert asking him to send me three more large bottles <term>demijohns: large, narrow-necked glass bottles, often encased in wicker</term> of water, as well as some beef and rice from the store, promising faithfully to pay for them upon my return.

I certainly wouldn't prevent my men from climbing the peak above me after their "touching" conduct today. Oh, no; not for the world, the dear things.
