## CHAPTER XXVI

### THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROONS—(*Continued*)

->Recounting how the Traveler reaches the Southeast crater for a second time, with some description of the challenges of camping within the said crater.<-

*September 24th.*—It is a lovely morning. The grey-white mist in the forest makes it look like a dream of Fairyland, with every moss-grown tree trunk heavily jeweled with dewdrops. At 5:30 A.M., I wake the men, because Sasu the sergeant says he must return to his military duties. The men assume we are all returning with him since he is our only guide, but I send three of them down with orders to return to Victoria—two of whom were from the original group I started with. They are surprised and annoyed to be sent home, but they have "sore feet" <term>hot foot: likely referring to sore, blistered, or burning feet from the march</term> and issues with the usual source of African internal trouble—their "stomachs." I have no intention of opening a hospital for Africans with abdominal issues in that crater plain above. Black Boy is the other one being sent back; I do not want him to have another of his fits.

They depart, leaving me in the forest camp with Kefalla, Xenia, and the Cook. We wait for the water that the Monrovia boy was sent to fetch yesterday morning. There are a ridiculous number of bees around. They don't give me a moment’s peace; they crawl under the waterproof sheets over my bed and then act as if they are trapped, immediately losing their tempers. This is foolish, as all four sides of the shelter are wide open.

The ground, covered with leaves and dry wood, is swarming with large flies that look like our common housefly. However, both butterflies and beetles seem scarce. I must admit, I do not feel up to...

My face, and particularly my lips, are a misery to me, having been blistered all over by yesterday's sun. Last night, I inadvertently rubbed all the skin off one cheek with the blanket, and it keeps on bleeding. To add to the horror of horrors, there is no tea until that water arrives.

I wish I possessed the mountaineering spirit, for then I could say, "I’ll never come to this sort of place again, for you can get all you want in the Alps." I have been told this by my mountaineering friends—though I have never been there myself—and that you can go and do all sorts of stupendous things all day and return in the evening to a *table d'hôte* <note>original: "table d'hôte" — a communal meal served at a hotel at a set time and price.</note> at an hotel. But as I have not got the mountaineering spirit, I suppose I shall come fooling into some such place as this as soon as I get the next chance.

About 8:30, to our delight, the gallant Monrovia boy <term>Monrovia boy: a hired laborer or porter from Monrovia, Liberia.</term> comes through the bush with a demijohn <term>demijohn: a large, narrow-necked bottle, usually encased in wickerwork.</term> of water. I get my tea and give the men the only half-pound of rice I have and a tin of meat; they eat, become merry, and chat about their absent companions in a scornful, scandalous way. Who cares for hotels now? When one is in a delightful place like this, one must work, so off I go to the north into the forest. I leave the rest of the demijohn of water in the Monrovia boy's charge with strict orders that it is not to be opened until my return. I find quantities of beetles.

A little after two o'clock, I return to camp after having wandered about in the forest and found three very deep holes, down which I heaved rocks; in no case did I hear a splash. In one, I did not even hear the rocks strike, owing to the great depth. I hate holes, and especially do I hate these African ones, for I am frequently falling, more or less, into them, and they will be my end. So far, I have never fallen down a West Coast native gold mine, but I know people who have. However, I have tried all the other sorts, having pitched by day and night into those three to twelve feet deep made by the "industrious indigenous ones"—as Mrs. Gault calls them—digging out sand and earth to make the "swish" <term>swish: building material made of puddled clay or mud used for walls.</term> walls of their simple, savage homes. I have also fallen into those from twenty to thirty feet deep...

# XXVI A BAD FALL

...with pointed stakes at the bottom, skillfully arranged to impale elephants and leopards of the South-West Coast. But my worst fall was into an abandoned Portuguese well of unknown depth at Cabinda. I "still feel the place in cold weather," though I did not fall all the way down; my descent was stopped by a collection of brushwood and trash that had been thrown into it and had gotten stuck far down in the shaft. When I hit this underground wooden raft, I thought—I'm saved! The next minute, it occurred to me that the raft was sinking; and so it was, slowly and jerkily, but sinking nonetheless. I clawed around in the suffocating darkness for something on the side to hold onto, and I grabbed some tough vines <term>bush rope: thick, woody vines or lianas used as rope.</term> just as I became convinced that my fate was an inglorious and backwards version of Elijah <note>In the Bible, the prophet Elijah was taken up to heaven alive in a chariot of fire; Kingsley quips she was being taken downward instead.</note>, and I was being carried off, alive, to Sheol <term>Sheol: the Hebrew underworld or place of the dead.</term>.

The other demijohns <term>demijohn: a large, narrow-necked bottle, usually encased in wickerwork.</term> of water have not arrived yet, and we are getting anxious again because the men's food has not come up. They have been so exceedingly thirsty that they have drunk most of the water—though not since it has been under the Monrovia boy's care. But at 3:15 p.m., another boy comes through the bush with another demijohn of water. We receive him gladly and ask him about the food <term>chop: West African pidgin for food or a meal.</term>. He knows nothing about it. At 3:45 p.m., another boy comes through the bush with another demijohn of water; we receive him kindly, but *he does not know anything about the food.* At 4:10 p.m., another boy comes through the bush with another demijohn of water; since he knows nothing about the food, we are polite to him, and that's all.

A massive tornado, which had been lurking and growling nearby, suddenly settles over the forest and bursts, wrapping us in a dense fog along with its thunder, lightning, and rain. It was impossible to hear or make oneself heard even a few steps away because of the shrill whistling of the wind, the roar of the thunder, and the rushing of the rain against the surrounding trees. It did not feel at all like a storm was bursting over you; it felt as if you were in the middle of an engine room that had broken down spectacularly. After half an hour or so, the thunder seemed to lift off the ground, and the lightning began to come in sheets rather than in great forks that flew like volleys of spears through the forest trees. ### THE GREAT PEAK OF THE CAMEROONS

We settled things amicably with the mountain; it roared its rage at Mungo <note>Mungo ma Ndemi is a local name for Mount Cameroon.</note>, and Mungo answered back, quivering under our feet with an equally great rage. One feels here as if one were constantly dropping, unasked and unregarded, into painful and violent discussions between the elemental powers of the universe. Mungo growls and swears in thunder at the sky and sulks in white mist all morning; then the sky answers back, hurling down lightning and rivers of water with a total disregard for Mungo’s visitors. The way the water rushes down from the mountain wall through the watercourses in the jungle just above—then spreads out at the forest's edge into a sheet of water an inch deep that flies past us in miniature cascades, trying all the while to put out our fire—is quite interesting. (I exhausted my vocabulary on those boys yesterday.)

As soon as we saw what we were in for, we threw dry wood on the fire. It blazed just as the rain came down, so with our assistance, it fought a good fight against its fellow elements, spitting and hissing like a wild cat. It could have managed the water fairly well, but the wind came, very nearly putting an end to it by carrying away its protecting shelter of boughs. The shelter settled on “Professor” Kefalla, who burst into a lecture on the foolishness of mountaineering and the abundance of devils in this region. Just in the midst of these "joys," another boy came through the bush with another demijohn <term>demijohn: a large, narrow-necked bottle, usually encased in wickerwork.</term> of water. We did not receive him even civilly; I burst out laughing, and the boys went off in a roar. We shouted at him, “Where is the food?” <note>original: "Where them chop?"</note> “It is on its way,” <note>original: "He live for come"</note> said the boy. We then gave him a hearty welcome and a shot of rum. An hour later, two more boys appeared: one carrying a sack of rice and beef for the men, and the other a box for me from Herr Liebert, containing a luxurious supply of biscuits, candles, canned meats, a bottle of wine, and one of beer.

We are now all happy, though exceedingly damp. The boys sit around the fire with their big iron pot full of beef and rice, busy cooking while they talk. I hear Xenia giving wonderful accounts of our extraordinary feats of bravery, and the others giving terrible accounts of what they have lived through. ## XXVI WATERPROOF BEDS

At mealtime <term>chop: West African pidgin for food or a meal.</term>, they recount the latest news from Buea. James’s wife has run away again.

I have taken possession of two large jugs <term>demijohns: large, narrow-necked bottles, usually encased in wickerwork.</term> of water and the rum jug, arranging them around the head of my bed. The worst of it is those tiresome bees; as soon as the rain is over, they come in hundreds after the rum and frighten me constantly. The worthless wretches get intoxicated on what they can suck from around the cork, and then they stagger about on the ground, buzzing malevolently. When the men have had their food and a good smoke, we set to work and prepare the loads for tomorrow’s start up the mountain. Then, after more hot tea, I go to bed on my camp bed—listening to the soft, sweet murmur of the trees and the pleasant, laughing chatter of the men.

*September 25th.*—Rolled off the bed twice last night into the bushes. The rain has washed the ground away from under its outer legs so that it tilts; there were also quantities of large longicorn beetles <note>Longicorn beetles are characterized by their extremely long antennae, which are often longer than their bodies.</note> about during the night—the sort with spiny backs. They kept getting stuck to my blankets, and when I tried to remove them politely, they made a horrid fizzing noise and showed fight, raising their horns in a defiant way. I finally awake about 5:00 a.m., soaked through to the skin. The waterproof sheet has had a label sewn to it, so it is no longer waterproof, and it has been raining softly but steadily for hours. I wish the camp bed had had a ticket sewn on it too; nothing but my profound admiration for Kaiser Wilhelm, the Emperor of Germany <note>Kingsley was traveling through the German colony of Kamerun and often used equipment provided by or modeled after German military supplies.</note> (its owner), prevents me from poking holes in it. It sags in the middle and acts as an excellent rainwater tank. I have been saying things to it during the night about this habit, but the bed is so filled with the military spirit that it seems to say, “My orders are to be waterproof, and waterproof I’ll be.” Consequently, I decide to leave it behind, carefully drying it and protecting it as much as possible.

Around seven o'clock, we are off again with Xenia the foreman, the cook, the Monrovia boy, and a laborer from Buea—the water-carriers have gone home after having had their breakfast <gloss>morning chop</gloss>.

### THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROONS

About 600 feet above the small hills, a terrific rainstorm suddenly hits us, accompanied by a squealing, bitterly cold wind. We can hear the roar of the rain on the forest below. Hoping to get above it, we keep climbing, but that hope is in vain. The dense mist that accompanies the storm prevents us from seeing more than two yards ahead, and we drift too far to the left. I am behind the group today, strictly bringing up the rear. At about 1:00 p.m., I hear shouts from the vanguard, and when I catch up to them, I find them sitting on the edge of one of the clefts or scars on the mountain face.

I do not know how these quarry-like chasms were formed. They both look alike from below—the mountain wall drops vertically into them—and the bottom of this one slopes forward. If we had been unfortunate enough to go a little further to the left when we were lower down, we would have ended up at the bottom of it. We would have found ourselves walled in on three sides and been forced to retrace our steps. As it is, we have just reached its right-hand edge. 

Fortunately, as thick as the mist is, it was not thick enough to lead the men to walk over the edge. Had they done so, they would have been killed, as the cliff undercuts so deeply that we look straight down to the bottom of the scar, some 200 or 300 feet below, whenever there is a break in the mist. The sides and bottom are composed of and strewn with white, moss-covered masses of volcanic cinder rock. They are sparsely dotted with gnarled trees that have evidently been burned—one of my porters <term>boys: a colonial term for male servants or laborers, regardless of age.</term> tells me this was from the burning of this side of the mountain by "the Major from Calabar" <note>Likely referring to Major Claude Maxwell MacDonald, the British Commissioner in Calabar, who had previously explored the region.</note> during the previous dry season.

We continue up a steep grass-covered slope and finally reach the top of the wall. The immense old crater floor before us is the site of a seething storm today, and the peak itself is completely invisible. My men are quite demoralized by the cold. I find that most of them have sold the blankets I gave them at Buana; those who did not sell them left them behind at Buea. This was perhaps due to laziness, but more likely due to a confidence in their own power to prevent us from getting this far.

I believe if I had collapsed as well—and the cold tempted me to do so—

-># COLD TOO MUCH<-

...just as nothing else could—they would have lain down and died in the cold, sleety rain.

I spot a clump of gnarled, sparsely-leaved trees heavily draped with lichen, growing in a hollow among the rocks. I urge the men toward them for shelter, and they go like sheep bewildered by a storm. My bones are shaking within me and my teeth are chattering in my head, because after the intense heat I experienced here on Monday, I had not dared to dress heavily.

The men stand helpless under the trees. I hastily take the load of blankets that Herr Liebert lent us off a porter’s <term>boy: a colonial term for male servants or laborers; Kingsley uses it here for her porters.</term> back and undo it. I throw one blanket around each man and open my umbrella, spreading it over the remaining blankets. Then I give them each a shot of rum as they sit huddled in their blankets. I tear up a lot of brittle, rotten wood from the trees and shrubs, getting nasty thorns in my hands in the process, and set to work starting a fire with the wood and the driest moss I can find from beneath the rocks. With the help of the wood and Xenia—who soon recovered—along with a carefully scraped-up candle and a box of matches, the fire is soon blazing. Xenia holds up a blanket to shelter the flames while I use a cutlass to chop stakes to prop up the blankets, creating a "fire tent."

The other porters now recover, and I hustle them to build more fires. It is no easy task in the drenching rain, but it is work that must be done. We soon have three fires burning well. I grab a blanket—a wringing wet one, but still a comfort—and wrap myself in it. I order more wood to be gathered and stored around each fire to dry. Then, I stand over the cook while he heats up the men’s pre-cooked food <term>chop: a West African Pidgin term for food or a meal.</term> over our first fire. Once that is done, I have him make me tea—or what should more accurately be called soup, as it contains bits of rice and beef and tastes mostly of wood smoke.

By this time, Kefalla is back to his usual lecturing self, which relieves my mind, although he says, "Oh mother! It is cold, far too cold. Too much cold will kill us Black men, just as too much sun kills you white people. Oh mother!..." and so on. I tell him they only have themselves to blame; if they had come up with me on Monday—

# THE GREAT PEAK OF THE CAMEROONS

Once the men have had their <term>chop: food or a meal</term> and are curling themselves up comfortably around their now-blazing fires, Xenia insists on a theory that there is a better place to camp than this; he saw it when he was with an unsuccessful expedition that reached this point. Kefalla is foolish enough to go off with him to find this place, but they soon return, chilled through again and unsuccessful in their search. I understand they went to look for caves. I wish they had found caves, for I do not intend to claim our current campsite is anything special.

The bitter wind and lashing rain continue. We are sheltered to some extent from the former, but the latter is of that persistent sort that nothing but a granite wall would keep out.

Just at sundown, however—as is usual in this country—the rain stops for a while. I take this opportunity to get out my seaman’s jersey and go off over the rocks to have my struggle into it unobserved. It is a massive struggle to get that thing on or off at the best of times, but today it is worse than usual because I have to put it on over my soaked cotton blouse. Truly, at one point I fear I will have to shout for help or be suffocated, so firmly does it get stuck over my head. But I fight my way into it unaided and then turn to survey our position. I find I have been carrying on my battle on the edge of a deep hole whose opening is hidden among the rocks and scraggly shrubs just above our camp. I throw rocks down it—as we in <term>Fanland: the territory of the Fang people in modern-day Gabon and Cameroon</term> would offer rocks to an <term>Ombwiri: a spirit or deity in West African traditional religion</term>—and hear them go "*knickity-knock*, like a pebble in <note>The Carisbrooke Castle well on the Isle of Wight is famous for its 161-foot depth.</note> Carisbrooke well." I think I hear a distant splash, but it was a terrifying distance down. This mountain seems filled with these traps, and "one day some gentleman's porter" will be killed in one.

The mist has now cleared from the peak, but it covers the entire world below. I carefully take compass bearings of the three highest cones or peaks. Then I walk south over the rocky ground, and as I stand looking around, the mist

# CAMP FIRES

XXVI

The sea below is split in two for a few minutes by a fierce downdraft of wind from the peak, and I get a strange, clear, sudden view right down to Ambas Bay. It is just like looking down from one world into another. I think of how Odin hung and looked down into <term>Niflheim: the world of fog and mist in Norse mythology</term> <note>original: "Nifelheim"</note>, and then of how hot—how deliciously hot—it was way down there, and then the mist closes over it. I shiver and go back to camp, for night is coming on, and I know my men will require some "intellectual support" regarding the task of gathering firewood.

The men are now quite happy; over each fire they have made a tent with four sticks and a blanket—a blanket that is too wet to burn, though I have to make them brace the blankets against the windward side for fear of them scorching.

The wood from the shrubs here is of an aromatic and resinous nature, which sounds nice, but it isn't; the volumes of smoke it gives off when burning are suffocating. The men, who sit almost on top of the fire, are every few moments scrambling to their feet and moving away to cough out smoke, like so many novices in training for the profession of fire-eaters. However, they soon find that if they roll themselves in their blankets and lie on the ground on the windward side, they escape most of the smoke. They have divided up into three parties: Kefalla and Xenia, who have struck up a great friendship, take the lower, most exposed fire. The headman, the cook, and the Monrovia Boy have the upper fire, and the laborer has the middle one—he being an outcast for medical reasons. They are all steaming away and smoking comfortably.

I form the noble resolution to keep awake and rouse any gentleman who may catch on fire during the night—a catastrophe which is inevitable—and to see that wood is put on the fires. So, I elaborately settle myself on my wooden <term>chop-box: a crate used for carrying food and supplies</term>, in which I have placed all the <term>lucifers: early friction matches</term> that are not in the soap-box. The very address on that chop-box ought to keep its inside dry and functional, for it is addressed: <note>original: "An den Hochwohlgeboren Freiherrn von Stettin"</note> "To the High-born Baron of Stettin," etc. Because there is not a piece of ground even the size of a sixpence level in this place, the arrangement of my box camp takes time; but at last it is done to my complete satisfaction, close to a tree...

# THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROONS
## CHAP. XXVI

Against the tree trunk I lean, and I think—as I wrap myself up in my two wet blankets—what a good thing it is to know how to make oneself comfortable in a place like this. This tree stem is perfection; it is at just the right angle to be restful to my back. One can rely on Nature here not to let a person get thoroughly soft from too much luxury. So, I lazily watch and listen to Xenia and Kefalla at their fire nearby.

They begin talking to each other about their different tribal societies. Kefalla is a Vey, and Xenia is a Liberian. In the interests of science, I give them two bundles of tobacco to stimulate their conversation. They receive them with tragic grief because they have no pipes. So, in the interests of science, I unwrap my blankets and give them two pipes from my suitcase; then I bundle myself up again and pretend to be asleep. 

I am rewarded by hearing some interesting details. I form the opinion that both these worthy men, in the pursuit of their particular <term>traditional religious charms or fetishes</term> <note>original: "ju-jus"</note>, have come into conflict with white prejudices and are now fugitives from religious persecution. I also observe that they both have their own ideas of happiness. Kefalla believes it lies in a warm shirt, while Xenia believes it resides in warm trousers. Every half-hour, Kefalla takes his shirt off, holds it in the fire smoke, and then puts it hastily back on. Xenia, who is the one and only trouser-wearer in our band, spends fifty percent of the night on one leg, struggling to get the other in or out of these garments as they are either coming off to be warmed or going on after being heated. 

Those trousers of Xenia’s have something wrong about them. I don’t pretend to understand the garment, never having worn that sort of thing myself, but it is *my* belief he hitches them too high with those suspenders, which he wears in the **German style** <note>original: "Alemanni"</note>. 

Anyway, whether it is appropriate or not, they always seem to need taking off. Three whole times today, when we were on that wind- and rain-swept cliff, the entire group was brought to a standstill by Xenia having to stand on one leg and adjust his peculiar clothes. It’s a mercy he did not kill himself when he fell over while engaged in these operations among the rocks this afternoon. As it is, I see he has smashed the lantern glass again, so that I have to keep it under my blankets to

## XXVI: A DAMP BED

...prevent the candle from being blown out by this perpetual north-east wind.

There seem to be few insects here. I have only caught two moths tonight—one pretty one with white wings and small red spots, like an old-fashioned petticoat such as an early Victorian lady would have worn—the other a lovely thing in silver.

Then a horrid smell of burning flesh <note>original: "burning negro"</note> interrupts my writing, and I have to get up and investigate it. After some trouble, I find it is a spark in the cook's hair; he is sleeping sweetly all the while. I rouse him by nudging his shins and tell him to put himself out, and he is grateful.

My face is a misery to me; as soon as it dries, it sets into a mask, and when I move it, it cracks and bleeds.

(Later, *i.e.*, 2:15 A.M.). I have been asleep against that abominable vegetable of a tree. It had its trunk covered with a soft cushion of moss and pretended to be a comfort—a right angle to lean against and a softly padded protection for the spine from the wind, and all that sort of thing. In reality, the whole time it was nothing in this wretched world but a water pipe to conduct an extra supply of water down my back. The water has simply streamed down it and formed a nice little pool in a rocky hollow where I keep my feet. I am chilled to the very bone, so I have to scramble up and drag my box to the side of Kefalla and Xenia's fire, feeling sure I have contracted a fatal chill this time. I scrape the ashes out of the fire into a heap and put my sodden boots into them; they hiss merrily, and I resolve not to go to sleep again. 

5 A.M.—I have fallen asleep twice and have fallen off my box bodily into the fire in my wet blankets; I would surely have put it out like a bucket of cold water had not Xenia and Kefalla been roused by the cloud of smoke <term>smother</term> <note>original: "smother," meaning a thick, suffocating cloud of smoke or ash</note> I caused and rescued me—or the fire. It is not raining now, but it is bitterly cold, and the cook is preparing my tea. I give the men a lot of hot tea with a large handful of sugar, and they then get their own food hot.

### CHAPTER XXVII

#### THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROONS—(*Continued*)

*Describing how the traveler reaches the summit of Mungo Mah Lobeh <note>The native name for Mount Cameroon, meaning "Throne of Thunder" or "Mountain of the Gods."</note>, and descends from there to Victoria. To this is added some remarks on the natural history of the West African porter <term>West Coast porter: Native laborers hired to carry supplies and equipment on expeditions.</term> and the indigenous methods of making fire.*

*September 26th.*—The weather is uncertain, and so am I. I feel doubtful about continuing in these conditions, but I do not want to give up on the peak after enduring so much to reach it. The men, now dry and warm by the fires, have forgotten their troubles. However, I decide to keep going and ask for volunteers to accompany me. Bum, the headman, and Xenia announce they are willing. I pack two tins of meat and a bottle of Herr Liebert’s beer into the small wooden box. I insist that both men take a blanket each, much to their annoyance, and we set off across the crater plain before six o’clock. 

The landscape is rugged, with rocky mounds sparsely covered by tufts of grass. Here and there are patches of boggy land—not a true bog, but damp areas where small clumps of rushes grow. Scattered among the rocks are withered shrubs of broom, the yellow-flowered shrub I mentioned previously, and large amounts of very sticky heather. When you touch the heather, it feels as if it has been coated in syrup. One might imagine the entire species of these shrubs is dying out; for every one that appears partially alive, there are twenty skeletons that crumble to pieces as you brush past them.

The first part of the journey is downhill—or rather, the land slopes downward—but whether the path goes down or up, the details

The terrain is treacherous, though perhaps not quite as difficult as the lower hillocks of the great wall, where the rocks are hidden beneath long, slippery grass. We wind our way between the mounds, clamber over them, or scramble along their sides indifferently. The ground then levels out before rising toward the peak wall, so we steer North-North-East until we reach the face of the peak and begin a steep, difficult climb. We are all short of breath, though I do not think it is caused by the altitude; my own breathlessness comes from a cold I have caught, and I suspect the men's comes from eating too much breakfast.

We keep as straight a path as possible, but we are forced at an angle by strange ridges of rock that run straight down the mountainside. These are most exhausting to deal with, getting worse the higher we go. They are so decayed and weathered that they crumble into dust and fragments under our feet. The headman falls half a dozen times, and when we are about three-quarters of the way up, Xenia gives up. The cold and the exertion are too much for him, so I make him wrap himself in his blanket—which he is grateful for now—and take shelter in a hollow beneath one of the many rocky ridges. The headman and I continue. 

When we are about 600 feet higher, an iron-gray mist begins curling and waving around the rocks above us, like some savage monster guarding them from intruders. I wonder again if I was justified in risking the men; it is a real danger for them in these low temperatures, especially with the foul weather I know is approaching, though they do not. Still, we have enough food and blankets for them, and they can reach the camp in the plain below safely if the worst comes to the worst. As for myself—well, that is my own business, and no one will be a penny the worse <note>original: "ha'porth," a contraction of "halfpennyworth," meaning a trivial amount.</note> if I am dead within an hour. 

So, I pull myself onto the rocks and take my bearings, specifically noting Xenia's location. I should mention he has a tin of meat and a flask of rum with him. Then, I turn to face the threatening mist. It rises and falls, reaching out toward us like arms. Then Bum, the headman, decides to give up his third attempt to reach the peak. I leave him wrapped in his blanket with the bag of provisions and go on alone into the wild, gray, shifting, whirling mist.

I can see three distinct high cones before me. Then the mist, finding it cannot drive me back easily, resorts to desperate methods and lashes out with a burst of bitter wind and a sheet of blinding, stinging rain. I make my way up through it toward a peak which I soon see, through a tear in the mist, is not the highest. So, I angle off and go up the one to the left. After a desperate fight, I reach the cairn—only, alas, to find a hurricane raging and a fog in full possession, with not even a ten-yard view to be had in any direction. Near the cairn on the ground are several bottles, some of which the energetic German officers, I suppose, had emptied in honor of their achievement—an achievement I bow down before, for their pluck and strength had brought them here in a much shorter time than mine. I do not meddle with anything, except to take a few specimens and to put a few more rocks on the cairn, and to place my card among them, merely as a courtesy to Mungo <note>Mungo Mah Lobeh, the indigenous name for Mount Cameroon, often translated as "Throne of Thunder" or "Mountain of the Gods."</note>—a courtesy his Majesty will soon turn into pulp. Not that it matters; what is done is done.

The weather grows worse every minute, and no sign of clearing shows in the indigo sky or the wind-torn mist. The rain lashes so fiercely I cannot turn my face to it and breathe; the wind is all I can do to stand up against.

Truly, I am no mountaineer, for I feel no exultation, but only a deep disgust because the weather has robbed me of my main object in coming here: namely, to get a clear view and an idea of the way the unexplored mountain range behind Calabar trends.

No doubt, had the weather been clear, I would have been able to do this well, for the whole Omon range must be visible from this great summit of the Cameroons, which rises at right angles to it. For when I was in Okyon, close to this Rumby or Omon range, Mungo's great mass was perfectly visible looking seaward. My only consolation is that my failure to do this bit of work is not my own fault, except for my coming here at the wrong season, which was also beyond my control. # XXVII ON THE SUMMIT

QQ 2

This is the tornado season, rather than the true rainy season; otherwise, I might have had a clear day on the peak. I took my chances and failed, so there is no reason to complain.

Comforting myself with these thoughts, I start back down to find Bum. I manage to find him easily, and then we scramble down carefully together among the crumbling black rocks, determined to find Xenia. The scene is very grand. One minute we can see nothing except the black rocks and cinders under our feet; the next, the wind-torn mist parts in various directions, revealing the same wild landscape of massive black cliffs rising in jagged peaks and walls around and above us. I believe this walled cauldron we just left is actually the highest crater on Mungo <gloss>Mungo Mah Lobeh, or Mount Cameroon</gloss>.<gloss>1</gloss>

We soon become worried about Xenia, as this is a terrifyingly easy place to lose someone in such weather. But just as we pass below the densest part of the shroud of mist, I spot a tiny figure standing on one leg while putting on or taking off his trousers—our lost Xenia, without a shadow of a doubt. We head straight down to him.

When we reach him, we stop. I give the two men a tin of meat, take another and the bottle of beer for myself, and then make a quick sketch of the great crater plain below us. At the far edge of the plain, a massive white cloud

<gloss>1 Since returning to England, I have read Sir Richard Burton’s account of his first successful attempt to reach the summit of the Great Cameroons in 1862. His companions were Herr Mann, the botanist, and Señor Calvo. Herr Mann claimed to have reached the summit a few days before the other two joined him, but Burton seems to doubt this. > "Victoria mountain proved to be the shell of a massive double crater opening to the southeast. At that spot, a tremendous torrent of fire had broken through the weaker wall; the entire interior and its accessible breach now lay before me, plunging down into a vertical cliff. The depth of the bowl may be 360 feet. The total diameter of the two craters, which are separated by a rough partition of lava, is 1,000 feet... Not a blade of grass, not a thread of moss, breaks the gloom of this Plutonic <note>Plutonic: relating to the underworld; here referring to the volcanic, hellish nature of the pit</note> pit, which is as black as Erebus <note>Erebus: in Greek mythology, a region of the underworld representing darkness</note>, except where the fire has painted it red or yellow." 
This ascent was made from the west face. I entered the "Plutonic pit" through the southeastern break in its wall. I was the first English person to reach it from the southeast, the third of my nation overall to ascend the peak, and the twenty-eighth person to reach the summit, according to my well-informed German friends.</gloss>

# THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROON CHAPTER

[A massive white cloud] is rising from below, which bodes ill for our descent down the great wall to the forest camp. I am anxious to reach it before nightfall, especially after the poor accommodations we endured at our camp in the crater plain last night.

While I sit waiting for the men to finish their meal, I feel a chill at my back, as if something cold had settled there. Turning around, I see the mist from the summit rolling down toward us like a wall. In my experience, these high-altitude mists are always preceded by a strange breath of ice-cold air—though not necessarily a wind.

Bum then points out a strange funnel-shaped formation descending from the clouds to the north. I assume it is a large waterspout; it seems to be moving rapidly northeast. I sincerely hope it stays on that course, as we have more than enough to handle with the regular rain on this mountain without having to deal with waterspouts.

We head down the mountain as quickly as possible. Xenia is completely exhausted, and the Headman nearly breaks his neck with frequent falls among the rocks; my unfortunate boots have been shredded by the sharp stones. As we approach the large crater plain, it becomes a race between us and the pursuing mist to see who will reach the camp first. The mist wins, but we catch a glimpse of the camp's exact position just before it is swallowed up, so we reach it without much trouble. When we arrive around one o'clock, I find the men have kept the fires burning. Cook is asleep in front of one, with his hair smoldering from another small fire. I have him make me some tea while the others pack as quickly as they can. By two o’clock, we are all on our way down to the forest camp.

The men are nervous descending the mountain wall. Cook’s mishaps alone could fill books. The Monrovia boy <note>A Kru laborer, likely from Liberia</note> is by far the most skilled at this work. Just as we reach the tall jungle grass, the rain pours down and the mist rises. We endure the most difficult struggle of our entire trip as we try to find the opening in the forest that leads to our previous camp.

Unfortunately, I am forced to perform some unintended acrobatics...

### XXVII DESCENT

At the top of one of the highest, rockiest hillocks, I balance myself on one leg and take a rapid slide sideways. This ends in a very showy leap backward that lands me right on top of the lantern I am carrying today, among a pile of rocks. With fifteen feet or so of jungle grass towering above me, all the flair and beauty of my performance are completely wasted—much like I am—because my men are too busy with their own struggles in the mist to notice I am gone. 

After resting for a while where I fell, and debating the idea in my mind that I might be dead, I get up and laboriously clamber to the top of the next hillock. I shout for the men, and “Ma,” “ma,” <note>A respectful term of address used by the West African crew for Kingsley.</note> comes back from my flock from various points out of the fog. I find Bum and the Monrovia boy and learn that during my absence, Xenia—who always considers himself a pathfinder—has taken the lead and gone off somewhere with the rest. We shout and the others answer, and we rejoin them. It soon becomes evident to even the simplest mind that Xenia would have been better off attending to his own affairs instead of trying to act as a guide; we are now completely off the track we made through the grass on our journey up. We proceed to spend a cheerful hour or so in the wet jungle, plowing back and forth, trying to find our way.

At last, we find the top of a strip of forest that we all feel is ours, but Xenia and I disagree as to the path—the others simply follow like lambs to the slaughter wherever they are led. He wants to go down one side of the strip, and I want to go down the other. I get my way, and we wade along, skirting the bushes that fringe it, trying to find our opening. I admit I soon begin to feel uncertain about having been right, but soon Xenia, who is leading, shouts that he has found it. We limp in, our feet sore from the jagged rocks. Everything we are wearing, or have in our loads, is soaking wet—except for the matches, which fortunately I had placed in my soap-box.

I have never seen anything more dismal than the sight of that long-desired camp when we finally reach it. There are pools of water everywhere. The fire-shelter is a limp ruin, and the camp bed I have been thinking fondly of for the past hour is now a water cistern. I tip the water out of it and say a few choice words to the bed regarding its stubborn idiocy in obeying its military instructions to be waterproof.

Then, while the others are building the kitchen hut, the headman and I bring out the hidden demijohn <term>demijohn: a large-bodied bulbous narrow-necked bottle, often encased in wickerwork</term> of rum, along with the beef and rice. He soon manages this, and then I have my hot tea while the men eat their hot food; we have finally returned to the luxury of having two cooking pots.

Their wilderness education is evidently progressing, as they build themselves a large screen using branches and spare blankets to shield the space between the wind and the kitchen hut. I have Xenia cut some branches and place them on top of my waterproof sheet shelter, making us fairly comfortable again. The men are quite cheerful and very well satisfied with themselves.

Unfortunately, the topic of their nightly debating society is human conduct—a subject always filled with the dangerous possibility of differing opinions. With their mouths full of rice and beef, they are busy discussing the behavior of an absent friend, whom they generally regard as a spendthrift. "He earns plenty of money, but he never has any." "He throws it away on women and drink." "He doesn't buy clothes." This last point is clearly a very serious accusation, but Kefalla says, "What can a man buy with money that is better than the things he likes best?"

This philosophical outburst from Kefalla is followed by a verbal battle regarding the inherent worthlessness of women and alcohol; I will omit the specific details of this argument. However, a louder row soon breaks out, and the cook rushes toward me. Seizing his rum and water, he threw it at him; whatever did not land on the cook went into his supper in the pot. The cook shows an intense horror at the smell of rum in his rice, which is, coming from him, somewhat comical. There is a very peculiar look to the rotten wood on the ground around here; tonight it has patches and flecks of iridescence like one sees on herring or mackerel that have been kept too long. The appearance of this strange, eerie light among the bushes is very weird and charming. I have seen it before in dark forests at night, but never so much of it.

*September 27th.*—A fine morning. It is a blessing that my Pappenheimers <note>original: "Pappenheimers"; a reference to the loyal but somewhat undisciplined troops of Count Pappenheim during the Thirty Years' War, used here by Kingsley to describe her porters</note> have not recognized what this weather means for the afternoon. We are taking things very leisurely. I know there is no use in hurrying; we are certain to get a soaking before we reach Buea anyway, so we may as well enjoy ourselves while we can.

I ask my boys how they would "make fire if no matches were available." Not one of them thinks it is possible to do so: "It is beyond a man to do those things if he doesn't have a burning stick or matches." They are "coast boys" <term>coast boys: Africans from coastal regions more accustomed to European trade goods and lifestyles</term>, all of them, and therefore used to luxury; but it is really remarkable how widely matches have spread inland and how very dependent on them these natives are. When I have been away in districts where matches have not yet penetrated, it is exceedingly rare that the making of fire has to be resorted to. I think I may say that in most African villages, it has not had to be done for years and years. This is because when a woman's fire has gone out while she has been out at work all day, she just runs into some neighbor's hut where there is a fire burning, offers her greetings, and picks up a burning stick from the fire to run home with. From this practice comes a polite expression, equivalent to our "Oh! don't go away yet," which is "You have only come to fetch fire." This will be said to you all the way from Sierra Leone to Loanda, as far as I know, if you have been making yourself agreeable in an African home, even if your visit has actually lasted for a day or so. The hunters, like the <term>Fans</term> <note>Fan or Fang people: an ethnic group in Central Africa known to Kingsley as skilled hunters and warriors</note>, have to make fire and now do it with a flint and steel; but in districts where their "tutor" in this method—the flint-lock gun—is not available, they will do it with two sticks, though not always like the American...

Indigenous people's fire-sticks operate like this: one stick is placed horizontally on the ground while the other is twirled rapidly between the palms of the hands. Sometimes, however, two pieces of palm stick are worked in a hole in a larger piece of wood; the hole is packed with tree pith or silk cotton fluff, and the two sticks are rotated vigorously. On another occasion, I saw a Bakele woman make fire using a strip of raffia palm drawn very rapidly back and forth across a notch in another piece of raffia wood. Among most of the more settled <term>domesticated: Kingsley uses this term to refer to tribes more integrated into agricultural or colonial trade systems</term> tribes, such as the Efik or the Igalwa, if they are heading out to their plantation, they will enclose a glowing ember in a hollow piece of a specific type of wood that has its inner pith left inside. They carry this "fire box" with them. Or, if they are going on a long journey by canoe, there is always a fire kept in the bow of the boat, placed in a calabash <term>calabash: a dried gourd shell used as a container</term> full of sand—or, failing that, in a bed of clay with a rim of sand around it.

By 10:00, we are off, heading down to Buea. At 10:15, it starts to pour as only it can here; by 10:17, we are all in our usual state of bedraggled saturation, plodding down carefully and cheerfully among the rocks and roots of the forest, following the path we hacked and trampled for ourselves on our way up. It is dangerously slippery, particularly the section through the amomums <term>amomums: a genus of plants in the ginger family, common in the African undergrowth</term>. The stumps of the cut amomums are very likely to spike your legs badly—and, my friend, never, ever step on one of the amomum stems lying straight in front of you, especially when they are soaking wet. Ice slides are nothing compared to them, and when you fall—as you inevitably must, because everything you grab for support is either rotten or as brittle as Salviati glassware <note>original: "Salviati glass-ware"; refers to the famously delicate and ornate Murano glass produced by the Salviati firm in Venice</note>—you injure yourself in countless places on those previously mentioned cut amomum stumps. I speak from my own sad experiences, reinforced by my observations of the men's struggles.

By the time we descend back into the tree-fern region, the path is inches deep in mud and water. Several places where we have to drop five feet or so over rocky ledges are harder to navigate going down than they were going up, especially when we have to land on amomum stems. One wretched spot—a mud-lined, V-shaped hollow with an immense tree lying right across it, a tree that one of our storms <term>tornadoes: in this region, the term was often used for violent localized squalls or thunderstorms</term> has felled—

Honestly, the sheer amount of things left loose in Africa that really ought to be kept in zoos and greenhouses, rather than being allowed to run wild across the countryside, is enough to test the patience of a saint.

We then pass through a grove of those beautiful, massive tree-ferns. The way their young fronds emerge with a graceful curl, like the top of a bishop’s staff, is like a poem. However, as I am currently feeling irritable, I will point out that they are covered in horrible spines, just as most young plants are in Africa. 

Speaking of spines, I should mention that nothing—except perhaps that "precious" climbing palm (I never like to say what I truly feel about climbing palms, because one once saved my life)—can compare to the sturdy bush rope <term>bush rope: a general term for various species of woody climbing vines or lianas</term> that grows here in abundance. It is covered with short, strong, hooked thorns. It creeps along, hidden by more decorative plants, and your legs become entangled in it and, of course, injured. It drapes itself from tree to tree, and when your mind is occupied with other things, it catches you under the chin. This leaves you looking as though you have made a determined but failed attempt to slit your own throat with a saw. For years, that bush rope <term>bush rope: woody climbing vines or lianas</term> will wait for a man’s blood, and when he comes within reach, it will have its due.

We are well down now among the tree trunks, which are overgrown with rich, soft green moss and delicate, filmy ferns. I should think that for a botanist, these southeastern slopes of Mungo Mah Lobeh <term>Mungo Mah Lobeh: 'Throne of Thunder,' the Duala name for Mount Cameroon</term> would be the finest hunting grounds in all West Africa.

The vegetation here has reached its absolute peak of luxuriance, owing to the richness of the soil. The leaves of trees and plants that I recognize from elsewhere are far larger here, and the undergrowth in particular is significantly more lush and varied. Ferns seem to find a true paradise in this place. Everything, in fact, is growing at its very best. I suppose a friend of mine was exaggerating when he told me that near Victoria <term>Victoria: a coastal town in Cameroon, now known as Limbe</term> he had stuck his umbrella into the ground one evening and found leaves growing all up the handle by morning. Still, if such an incident could happen anywhere, it would be in this region.

We reach another fallen tree lying over another hole. We recognize this tree as an old acquaintance from near Buea, and I feel quite frustrated. I had put on a clean blouse and washed my hands in a teacup’s worth of water in a cooking pot before leaving the forest camp, just so I would look presentable upon reaching Buea. I did not want to give Herr Liebert <note>Herr Liebert was the German official in charge of the station at Buea.</note> the same trouble he had with the members of the first expedition to the peak; he said he found it difficult to distinguish the white members of the party from the black ones. After all my exertion, the only thing I have to show that is clean or even remotely dry is one cuff, which I have kept covered with a shawl.

We round a corner by the stockade of the station’s plantation and find ourselves at the top of the mud slide—or the new Government path, I should say—that leads down into the barrack-yard.

In the wild excitement that the sight of the barrack-yard and the official residence gives me, I feel a strong urge to toboggan down the path. ### XXVII MUNGO'S ERUPTIONS

It was only Society's laundry <note>Society was the name of one of Kingsley's porters.</note> drying from the wash that had alarmed me.

Our arrival brings Herr Liebert promptly to meet us, as kind, helpful, and energetic as ever, and once again anxious for me to take a bath. The men bring our soaking-wet gear into my room. After giving them their food and plenty of tobacco, I get my hot tea and change into the clothes I had left behind at Buea. Feeling fit for polite society once again, I go out and find the representative of his Imperial and Royal Majesty <note>Referring to the German colonial administration.</note> making a door, tightening the boards with wedges in a very clever and professional manner. We talk about things in general and the mountain in particular. The great southeast face is now clearly visible before us, with that clarity that usually occurs just before nightfall. It looks like a vast wall again, and I wish I were climbing it again tomorrow. When "the Calabar major" set the brush on fire during the dry season, it must have been a magnificent sight; it is no wonder those in Cameroon thought "the great colony" <note>original: "die grosse Kolonie"</note> was going to be destroyed like Pompeii by a terrible eruption from "the great colony's largest fire-breathing mountain" <note>original: "der grossen Kolonie am grössten feuerspeienden Berg"</note>.

The northeastern edge of the mountain's slope seems unbroken all the way to the peak. The large crater where we camped must be a very old one in the mountain's history, and the current summit seems to have been thrust up out of it. On the western side facing the sea, I am told the slope is generally continuous, though there are several craters on that side; seventy craters in total have been identified so far on Mungo <term>Mungo: short for Mungo Mah Lobeh, or Mount Cameroon</term>.

The last reported eruption occurred in 1852, when signs of volcanic activity were spotted by a ship captain passing by at sea. The lava from this eruption must have flowed down the western side, as I have encountered no fresh lava beds during my travels on the other side. Herr Liebert has no trust in the mountain at all and announces his intention to leave Buea with his troops at the first sign of renewed volcanic activity. # THE GREAT PEAK OF CAMEROONS

If practical skill is a virtue, why not follow the example of Pliny the Elder? <note>Pliny the Elder was a Roman author and naval commander who died while investigating the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.</note> Herr Liebert continues to plane the wood for his door and says it is not part of his orders to make scientific observations on volcanoes during an eruption. When it is, he will do so—but until then, he most decidedly will not. He adds that Pliny was an admiral, and sailors are always as curious as cats.

Buea seems to be an intense place for weather even without volcanic eruptions. During the entire tornado season (of which there are two each year), over-charged tornadoes burst in the barrack yard. From the 14th of June until the 27th of August, you never see the sun because of the terrifying and continuous downpours of the wet season. At the beginning and end of this "cheerful" period, a month-long tornado season occurs, and the rest of the year is dry—hot during the day and cold at night.

They are talking about turning Buea into a sanatorium <term>sanatorium: A medical facility for long-term illness or recovery, often located in climates thought to be therapeutic.</term> for those stricken with fever. I somehow do not imagine that it is a suitable place for a man whose nerves have been stripped raw by fever and quinine <note>Quinine was the primary treatment for malaria; in high doses, it caused severe side effects including irritability, tremors, and temporary deafness.</note>, and who is very susceptible to chills. However, all the colonial governments on the Coast—English, German, or French—are completely obsessed with the idea of building sanatoriums in high-altitude places. This is despite the fact that their experience has clearly shown that these locations are worthless in West Africa. A man’s only real chance is to get out to sea on a ship that will take him beyond the three-mile-deep fever-belt of the coast. 

I hear grand accounts of other people who have climbed the peak, or tried to; I gather most of the failures were due to the porters. Herr Leist went up once from Babundi and once from this side. On this side, he failed because the three men he had with him nearly died from the cold. They would have died completely if he and Herr Yost, who was with him, had not taken a great deal of trouble to wrap them in blankets and rub them, and then, for the sake of the men, return down the mountain. My headman, Bum, was with Herr Leist when he attempted the sea-facing side from Babundi, and he says they turned back then because it was too steep. I am certain the porters collapsed on that side too, if the truth were known. The only point I congratulate myself on is getting my men up so high and back again without injury; but, as they said, I was a "father and a mother" to them—and I have been a very stern, though kind, set of parents.

I cannot help thinking how perfectly Rudyard Kipling’s observations on the camel <note>Kingsley is referencing Kipling’s poem "The 'Oonts," where "'oont" is Anglo-Indian slang for a camel.</note> fit the African carrier; for, like the supply camel:

> He’s a devil, an ostrich, and an orphan child all in one.

Also:

> He’ll gall and chafe and lame and fight,
> He smells most awful vile,
> He’ll lose himself forever, if you let him stray a mile.
> He’s game to graze the whole day long
> And howl the whole night through;
> And when he comes to greasy ground
> He splits himself in two.

Volumes upon volumes, all illustrated with snapshots and stuffed with statistics, could not give you a more accurate account of him. For instance, there are those two who wandered down that other path this afternoon; they are just now coming down the slope in front of us, thank goodness! I was beginning to decide it was my parental duty to go out and find them.

Herr Liebert gives me some interesting details about the founding of the station here and the trouble he had with the plantations. Only a short time ago, the soldiers brought him some black wood spikes which they had discovered with their feet, set into the path leading to the station’s <term>koko</term> <note>Also known as taro or cocoyam, a starchy root vegetable that is a staple food in West Africa.</note> plantations for the purpose of laming the men. Upon further investigation, they also found pits, carefully concealed with sticks and leaves, with the bottoms lined with nasty thorns—also placed there with malicious intent. 

The local <term>Bakwiri</term> <note>An ethnic group indigenous to the slopes of Mount Cameroon.</note> chiefs were called in and asked to explain these occurrences in a region where a peace treaty had recently been signed. The chiefs claimed it was all a misunderstanding; those traps had not been placed there to kill soldiers, but only to "attract their attention"—intended to kill or injure their own fellow tribesmen who had recently been stealing from the plantations. 

That is the West African way entirely all along the Coast; the "child-like" native will go out and shoot you with a gun just to draw your attention to the fact that a tribe you have never heard of has stolen one of his wives, whom you have never seen. It is the sweet infant’s way of "stirring up public opinion," but I do not admire or approve of it. If I—

...if I am to be shot for a crime, for goodness’ sake let me commit the crime first.

*September 28th.*—I traveled down to Victoria in one day, having no desire to renew or expand my acquaintance with the mission station at Buana. It rained torrentially all day long. I wonder what it is like here in the rainy season; something rather like the climate of the Atlantic seabed, I imagine.

My boots are a terrible nuisance today. I managed to get them dried last night for the first time since I left Victoria, and now they are as stiff as boards. Xenia brought them to me this morning, and I congratulated him on being able to do without boots; however, he proudly pointed to his deformed toe joints and informed me that he once wore boots regularly—better boots than mine, and boots that were "all shiny." I am certain Xenia has had a checkered past; he is from the <term>Republic of Liberia</term> <note>A West African nation founded in 1822 as a colony for free people of color from the United States.</note>. I wonder whether he is a fugitive president or a defaulting bank manager? I am told they have copies of all the high points of American culture there.

The old chief at Buana was very kind today when we were passing through his territory. He came out to meet us with some of his wives. Both men and women among these <term>Bakwiri</term> <note>A Bantu ethnic group indigenous to the Mount Cameroon region.</note> are tattooed, or rather painted, on the body, face, and arms, but as far as I have seen, not on the legs. The patterns are handsome and more elaborate than any others I have seen. One man who came with the party had two figures of men tattooed on the area where his waistcoat would have been. I gave the chief some tobacco, although he never asked for anything. He accepted it thankfully and, handing it to his wives, guided us on our path for about a mile and a half. Having reached the end of his district, we shook hands and parted.

After all the rain we have had, the road was, of course, worse than ever. As we were going through the forest toward the war hedge <note>A defensive barrier or fortification, typically made of thorny plants or wooden stakes, surrounding a village.</note>, I noticed a strange sound—a dull roar that made the light, crumbly earth shake under our feet. I remembered with alarm the accounts Herr Liebert gave me of the strange behavior of rivers on this mountain: how near <term>Buea</term> <note>A town on the eastern slopes of Mount Cameroon which served as the capital of German Cameroon from 1901 to 1919.</note>, about 200 meters below where you cross it, the river plunges entirely down a hole. ...the mountain that falls right into another hole and is never seen again, just like the <term>Buea River</term> <note>A river near the town of Buea on the slopes of Mount Cameroon.</note>. He told me how there are underground rivers in certain places which, though never seen, can be heard roaring and felt in the quivering earth underfoot during the wet season, and so on. I judged that our current roar arose from some such phenomenon and, with a touch of "feminine nervousness," I began to fear that the rotten, waterlogged earth we were standing on might give way and engulf us all, and we would never be seen again. 

But when we reached the next ravine—the one where I found the fish and water spiders on our way up—things explained themselves. The bed of this ravine was filled with a raging torrent of great beauty, though it looked quite alarming to anyone wanting to cross to the other side. On our right was a waterfall about thirty feet high, carrying tons of water. The brown water, streaked with foam, dashed down into the swirling pool before us. At the other edge of the pool, hitting a ridge of higher rock, the water sprayed up in a lovely arc <note>Original: "flange"</note> about twelve feet high before taking another and deeper plunge to form a second waterfall. My men shouted to me over the roar that it was "a bad place." They never give me half the credit I deserve for recognizing danger, and they said, "The water all goes into a hole down there; we might go too if we fall." 

"Don’t fall!" I yelled, which was the only good advice I could think of to give them just then.

Each small load had to be carried across by two men along a submerged ridge in the pool where the water was only chest-high. I had a difficult time getting through it, even with the help of my invaluable <term>Bakwiri</term> staff. But no harm occurred. In fact, we were all the better for it—or at least cleaner. We encountered five torrents that had to be waded through during the day; none were as dangerous as the first, but all were superbly beautiful.

When we turned west just above the woods we had to pass through before reaching the main road, the view of <term>Victoria</term> <note>Now the city of Limbe, Cameroon.</note> nestled among its hills and facing the bay was divinely lovely and glorious with color. I stepped out onto the road, where I found my friend, the Alsatian engineer <note>Alsace was a region then under German control, reflecting the German colonial administration of Cameroon at the time.</note>, still thriving and busy with his cheerful gang of woodcutters. I made a brief halt here and had some soda water. I was not anxious to reach Victoria before nightfall, but I did want to arrive before dinner. While I was chatting, my porters came through the wood, and the engineer most kindly gave them a shot of brandy each; I owe their final arrival in Victoria to that drink. I left them resting again, fearing I had timed my arrival just after nightfall poorly, and continued down that road. It was more terrible than ever now to my bruised, weary feet, but it was even more lovely than ever in the dying light of the crimson sunset. All the dark shadows among the trees were glittering with countless fireflies—and so I made it safely into Victoria, sneaking up the Government House hill by the private path through the Botanical Gardens.

Idabea, the steward, appeared, and I asked him to let me have some tea and bread and butter, for I was dreadfully hungry. He rushed off, and I heard tremendous activity going on in the room above. In a few seconds, water poured freely down through the dining room ceiling. It was the **bath palaver** <term>palaver</term> <note>A West African Pidgin term for a fuss, trouble, or a lengthy business; here, the "bath situation."</note> all over again. The excellent Idabea evidently thought a bath was severely needed—more so than such trifles as tea. Fortunately, Herr von Lucke <note>The German Resident or official in charge of the district.</note> was away in town, looking after his duties as usual, so I was cleaned up before he returned for dinner. When he did return, he had the satisfaction a prophet should feel. I had gotten half-drowned, and I had caught an awful cold—the most awful cold in the head of modern times, I believe—but he did not openly gloat over my afflictions.

Now that my men had all reported themselves safe, I went to my comfortable rooms. However, I could not go to bed, because the warmth and beauty down here were so fascinating. As I sat on the veranda overlooking Victoria and the sea, in the dim, soft light of the stars with the fireflies around me and the lights of Victoria below, I heard the soft rush of the Lukola River and the sound of the sea-surf on the rocks. The drumming and singing of the natives all matched and blended together. “Why did I come to Africa?” I thought. Why! Who would not come to its twin brother, hell itself, for all the beauty and the charm of it! <note>Kingsley often used dark humor to contrast the extreme physical hardships of West Africa with its immense natural beauty.</note>

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### THE ISLANDS IN AMBAS BAY <note>original: "Bay of Amboises"</note>

It was my intention when I landed at Victoria to either obtain a canoe and travel to the Rio del Rey—a river bordered by black mud and mangrove swamps—or to ask the Ambas Bay Trading Company to take me to their trading station on that river in their small steamer. Once I reached the Rio del Rey, I knew I could hire a canoe to take me through the creek into the Akwayafe River, which is a fourteen-hour trip by paddle. From there, I expected to be able to travel by canoe to meet a remarkable gentleman, Mr. Holmes. I was confident that he would find a way to get me to Calabar, provided I could only manage to let him know that I wanted to go there.

If the desire to get myself killed—an accusation often made against me—had been my only motive for visiting West Africa, I would have strictly followed this elaborate plan. This is especially true because Herr von Lucke said it was extremely dangerous during the tornado season to travel by canoe on the open, deep sea from Victoria to Rio del Rey. He pointed out the violent storms that suddenly sweep down from the mountain and the difficulty of handling the native boats. With his usual precision regarding statistics and details, he noted that two out of every six native canoes making that journey were lost with everyone on board. He added that it would be much better for me to go to Calabar...

...in the *Nachtigal*, a powerful little guard-ship that serves as the yacht for the Governor of the Cameroons. "True, O King!" I replied, "but I am not the Governor of the Cameroons." He bowed and said he knew that, but the *Nachtigal* would be coming to Victoria in a few days. She was on her way to Calabar with Herr von Besser, who was the German representative on the Calabar-Cameroon Delimitation Commission <note>A commission established to define the border between the British Niger Coast Protectorate and the German colony of Kamerun.</note>. He was certain that Governor von Puttkamer would allow me to travel with her. Based on my previous experience of Governor von Puttkamer’s kindness and courtesy, I felt Herr von Lucke was right. I gladly accepted this generous offer and settled in to wait for the *Nachtigal*—a very pleasant wait indeed.

The first day after my return from the mountain, Herr von Lucke suggested what he called a "walk." I knew this meant a journey of fourteen miles or so, conducted at a steady pace of five miles an hour. Being as stiff as a table leg, I declined. He then suggested a boat trip to see the islands in the bay. I did not decline that, and off we went.

The Bay of Amboises, commonly called Ambas Bay, is undoubtedly the most lovely and fertile spot on the entire western side of the African continent. Experienced mariners who have traveled widely say it has few rivals in either beauty or fertility in any other part of the world. Since my own experience of the world is strictly limited to England and West Africa, I find it impossible to imagine any place more perfect in its loveliness, majesty, color, and charm. It is surrounded on the landward side by mountains that rise out of the dark, clear waters to heights ranging from 3,000 to 13,760 feet <note>The height of the Great Cameroon peak, or Fako.</note>. At their feet lies a narrow strip of flat shore where the pretty, long, ribbon-like town of Victoria nests among mango trees. It is a soft brown native town, speckled here and there with a few white European buildings. In the bay itself are three islands—Ambas, Mondoleh, and Bobia—along with several pinnacle rocks where trees grow like energetic acrobats out of the clefts and crevices.

Ambas and Bobia Islands are perfect gems of beauty. I cannot say I admire Mondoleh as much. To me, it always looks exactly like one of those flower stands packed with ferns and plants...

<page-num>XXVIII 611</page-num>
<header>MONDOLEH ISLAND</header>

—the sort that you come across in drawing rooms back home, with wire legs. I do not mean that Mondoleh has wire legs under the water, but it looks as though it might. It is a dense cluster of vegetation, half a mile long and 200 feet high, with rocky but fertile soil formed from a combination of decomposed rock and plant matter. 

On Mondoleh, there is a very nice house, built, I believe, by that tireless consul Sir H. H. Johnston <note>Sir Harry Johnston (1858–1927), a British explorer and colonial administrator</note>, formerly of Calabar and now of East Africa. For as long as we have held Calabar, it has been regarded as an unhealthy place to live—so unhealthy, in fact, that it was taken for granted that anywhere else must necessarily be better. At first, when consuls were established there, they and the missionaries thought it advisable to leave during the rainy season and go to Fernando Po <note>An island in the Gulf of Guinea, now known as Bioko</note>. We held that island until 1858 as a naval depot for the suppression of the slave trade. Then, by way of several yellow fever epidemics, Fernando Po demonstrated that it could not be considered a health resort, and Mondoleh was selected as a more suitable site for a consular residence. 

This house was then built near the island's summit on the seaward side and was used until the Niger Coast Protectorate was formed under the governorship of Sir Claude MacDonald. This energetic officer soon recognized that, regardless of how healthy Mondoleh might be, it was an inconvenient spot for a consul to use as his primary residence. For one thing, it was a difficult place to get onto, and for another, it was a difficult place to get off of. The only way to do either was to wait for a passing warship <term>man-of-war: a large, armed sailing ship</term> or to go tossing about in this very windy stretch of the rocky Atlantic in an open rowboat <term>gig: a light, fast boat carried aboard a ship</term>. 

Additionally, there was not enough room on the island for the expanded staff and the Hausa troops. Consequently, Sir Claude built the current, fine Government headquarters in Old Calabar. Since he was not a man who would leave his staff to live or die in a place where he would not live himself, he sold the house at Mondoleh to the German Governor. The Governor was very anxious to possess it, for it was the only piece of British territory left in Cameroon, and its acquisition effectively rounded off the German Empire's holdings there. It is not currently used as a residence for anyone except a black caretaker and his family.

# THE ISLANDS IN THE BAY OF AMBOISES

Governor von Puttkamer <note>Jesco von Puttkamer (1855–1918), a German colonial governor of Cameroon</note> believes in the health benefits of living in residences open to sea breezes—a belief I do not share. Nor, evidently, did the builder of the residence on Mondoleh, for the breezes are carefully blocked out by a thick plantation of giant bamboos and deep, heavily-latticed porches, which make the interior of the house very dark. Landing at Mondoleh is also difficult; the surrounding water is deep, and the island’s sides are steep and rocky. From the small landing area, there is a terrible sort of staircase, carefully constructed with logs and stone, leading up the steep hillside to the residence. I shall never forget either climbing up or coming down those stairs. On one side, there is every opportunity to take a headlong dive into the deep Atlantic, and on the other is dense brush; furthermore, no two steps are the same height or the same distance apart. A friend of mine who had once tried them assured me it was "exactly like climbing the Tower of London when you were drunk." He may have been right, for the steps certainly gave me a feeling of bewilderment after the first dozen or so in the blazing heat. When I was last there, the heavy storm rains <note>The author uses "tornado rains," referring to the seasonal West African squalls</note> had caused a landslide from the top of the island to the bottom. It now appears as a yellow scar and nearly swept the staircase away entirely.

Ambas Island is the outermost island in the bay. It is smaller and lower than Mondoleh and has very few trees. Indeed, most of it is covered only with brush and grass, as there is not much soil among its rocks. It now belongs to an officer of the ship *Hyæna*, who won it in a raffle for 500 marks <term>German currency used in the colony</term>. But although Ambas Island is very beautiful and so forth, I do not think the return on the investment will be high for some years to come. It has no human habitations or inhabitants yet, and its population consists of goats and pigs. The most noticeable thing about Ambas Island is the fact that both the English and the Germans have recorded it incorrectly on their nautical charts. Bobia is the most interesting of all three islands. It is in line with the Pirate rocks. Indeed, it is actually one of them, only slightly larger than its neighbors, and it is sometimes called Pirate Island. Its sides are perfectly vertical, and you can reach the top by a projecting rock ridge that runs up the cliff on the northern—

# XXVIII BOBIA PIGS

...side. I did not go up because, on the day I was taken around it, the weather was too rough for us to reach the rocky ledge where one lands. Strangely enough, this rocky and least fertile of all the islands in Ambas Bay is densely populated by many fisherfolk and their wives, families, pigs, and goats. They all live together in a village on the summit, facing out to sea. Facing toward the mainland, they have built a long bench at the top of a sheer cliff. There, the fishermen sit in a row for most of the day watching Victoria <note>The coastal town of Victoria, now Limbe, Cameroon</note>, while their wives look after the rest of the residents and perform various odd jobs. I imagine these good women must lead anxious lives, constantly fearing that either the children or the livestock might fall from the village into the sea. 

At night, Ambas Bay is dotted with the torches of these fishermen, as they seem to do most of their fishing by spearing. They must be very industrious in their trade because, among other inconveniences, Bobia has no fresh water. All water must be purchased and transported from the mainland, and there is no room for a plantation. Furthermore, the pig population is too large to allow for agriculture. I deeply regret that I was unable to bring home a Bobia pig. One of them would have caused quite a sensation at the Royal Agricultural Show. 

These interesting animals are black, as is common for African pigs. Their heads make up two-thirds of their size; after a very small and flat section of body, they end in an extraordinarily long tail. Their temperaments are lively, playful, and extremely nomadic and predatory. In a burst of affection, the Chief of Bobia gave one to Herr von Lucke <note>A German official in the colonial administration</note> just before I arrived in Victoria. While waiting to start my ascent of Mungo <note>Mount Cameroon</note>, I spent a good deal of my time assisting Idabea and the steward boys in chasing this pig. 

Herr von Lucke had given strict orders that it was to be kept tied up, and he solemnly warned his staff that they were responsible for its safekeeping. However, it was always somehow slipping its leash and escaping. I used to encounter it in the Botanical Gardens and in so many unexpected places that I would not have been surprised to see it anywhere.
