When I returned to Victoria <note>Modern-day Limbe, Cameroon</note>, one of my first inquiries was about that Bobia pig. I immediately saw that I had stirred up sad memories and learned that the cook—who had been its primary caretaker—was under arrest, though out on bail, because of it. It seems the pig got loose as usual, and when the hunt began, no pig could be found. The cook, fearing the anger of the German authorities, rushed off into town and seized the first pig he could lay his hands on. 

Now, this pig belonged to a lady—a woman of spirit—and she struck the cook, and she swore the cook struck her back. Regardless, the cook carried off his prize and tied it up in place of the Bobia pig, trusting that his busy master would not notice the difference between the two animals and would never hear of his raid. His hopes were in vain. Herr von Lucke saw that this succulent little porker was not the original gift from Bobia. With a truly Roman sense of duty <note>A reference to strict, impartial adherence to the law</note>, he handed his own cook over to be tried by the native court, which was presided over by the Baptist minister and two local chiefs. The case lasted nearly all day, and the entire Government House staff had to be absent from their work to give evidence regarding the character of the cook, the pig, and so on. In the end, the case went against the cook; he had to pay damages to the injured lady and return the captured pig. As for what became of the original Bobia pig, I do not know, as it had not been found by the time I left Victoria.

The mystery of why so many people choose to live on this isolated rock is just as great as the mystery of that pig's whereabouts. Their own explanation is that the people on the mainland were too wicked for respectable people to live among; in short, as Mr. Micawber <note>A character from Charles Dickens' *David Copperfield*</note> would say, they were driven onto the island. However, you can very rarely believe what people in West Africa say about themselves. On the other hand, the people on the mainland claim that they are the injured innocents, and that the men of Bobia live on that island specifically to carry out piracy more effectively. This is the reason for the name "Pirate Island" that Bobia carries, and that—but then again...

<header>BAPTIST MISSIONS</header>
<sig>XXVIII</sig>

You can hardly ever believe what people say about each other in West Africa, so the problem remains unsolved.

The Pirate Rocks extend southwest from Bobia Island and are completely uninhabited. It is possible, at certain stages of the tide in calm weather, to get from Bobia to the nearest rock, on which there are a few trees. The next rock has a remarkable hole in it through which the water erupts in a great jet; as the weather was rough the day we circled it, this was a magnificent sight. The other rocks above water are merely rocky pinnacles.

These are by no means all the rocks in Ambas Bay, which—like Corisco Bay, though to a much lesser extent—is not nearly as good a harbor as it appears on a map.

In 1858, the Spanish Government decided definitively to retake possession of Fernando Po <note>Modern-day Bioko, Equatorial Guinea</note>, which had been lent to the English for the purpose of forming a naval depot for suppressing the slave trade. In May of that year, the Spanish <term>man-of-war</term> <note>A heavily armed sailing ship</note> *Vasco Nuñez de Balboa* arrived at Clarence <note>Modern-day Malabo</note> and issued a lengthy proclamation, one article of which stated:

> “The religion of this colony is that of the Roman Catholic Church, as the only religion of the Kingdom of Spain, to the exclusion of any other; no other religious profession is tolerated or allowed except that practiced by the missionaries of the aforementioned Catholic religion, and no schools are permitted.”

This proclamation, says Mr. Hutchinson—who was then the British consul for the Bights <note>The Bights of Benin and Biafra</note>—fell like a bombshell among the inhabitants of Clarence. They had been under the religious supervision of the Baptist missionaries since 1843 and, since their first settlement there under Captain Owen in 1827, had considered themselves safely under the protection of the British Government and therefore entitled to perfect liberty of religious worship. A formal protest was immediately made by the Baptists against this proclamation, arguing that it was contrary 

> “to that liberty of worship decreed and allowed by Don J. O. de Lorena, captain of the Spanish Navy and commander of the <term>brig</term> *Nervion*, in the year 1844, and confirmed by the Spanish Consul-General (the Chevalier Guillemard) in the year 1846.”

The Baptists requested that the enforcement of the previous decree be delayed until a final appeal could be made to the Queen of Spain. The commander of the *Balboa*, Don Carlos Chacon, courteously expressed his willingness to forward this petition to his Queen, and this was done. However, because the situation remained highly unsatisfactory for the Baptists, they decided to leave Clarence <note>Modern-day Malabo</note> and establish a settlement at the foot of Cameroon Mountain in Ambas Bay. At that time, this area was considered British property, and they named the settlement Victoria <note>Now Limbe, Cameroon</note>. 

The Baptist missionary at Clarence in those days was a Mr. Saker, to whom we owe a great deal of valuable scientific information about this region; his name is still held in great reverence among the native Baptists on the West Coast. This gentleman, along with his family and two or three families of the native members of his church, went to Victoria and acquired a large stretch of land there—a possession that has been officially recognized by the current German Government. They built their new church and schools, and to this day, they remain the leading group in Victoria under the leadership of Mr. Wilson, who arrived there as a boy with Mr. Saker. Mr. Wilson has been appointed as a magistrate and presides over a court whose other members are two local chiefs; this court handles all the minor offenses of the native population. 

The Baptists of Victoria have no white minister among them but appear to be a very well-organized and prosperous group. They harbor a sense of grievance against the English for the way they were first abandoned to the Spaniards and then handed over to the Germans, yet they still maintain a sentimental attachment to the English. However, from what I could observe, they have little to complain about regarding how the German Government has treated them—which is a very different approach from that of the Spanish Government. The Spaniards essentially confiscated the extensive property that the Baptists had received from the West African Company at Clarence. The Spanish version of this event is that the West African Company were the true wrongdoers, as they had no right whatsoever to transfer the land to the Baptists since the land was not theirs to give.

<header>XXVIII AMBAS BAY</header>

He held a high opinion of its value as a harbor and of the highlands above it as a site for a sanatorium. In 1856, Mr. MacGregor Laird sent a lengthy statement to Earl Grey based on Mr. Saker’s information. Looking back years later, this memorandum is highly interesting, even though almost all the assertions in it have now been proven false. For example, Ambas Bay is described as "being capable of being made a most complete naval station." Further on, it is called "a good open harbor, accessible at all times to ships of the largest class and easily navigated."

In June 1858, Mr. Saker sent a communication to Consul Hutchinson in which the advantages of Ambas Bay as a harbor were listed in detail. However, a survey of the bay made in 1859 by Commodore Wise of the Royal Navy, aboard the H.M.S. *Vesuvius*, did not prove the bay to match the description given by the enthusiastic missionaries. One important point in the bay, described in the Reverend Mr. Saker’s chart as having four to six <term>fathoms</term> <note>A fathom is a unit of length equal to six feet, used primarily to measure the depth of water.</note> of water, was found by Mr. Brown—a Master in the Royal Navy who was in charge of the soundings—to have only six to nine feet. From that day to this, people have continued to discover hidden pinnacles and rocky shoals in the bay.

I have now been to Ambas Bay five times on those very sturdy vessels, the *British and African* and the *Royal African* steamers, and I have never seen one of them anchor deep inside Morton Cove, as the inner part is called. As for warships, although their official guide, the *West Coast Pilot*, says "the anchorage is excellent in all parts of Ambas Bay with good holding ground, and a depth of six to seven fathoms," I have never seen a warship foolish enough to act on this statement and come well inside. The *West Coast Pilot* certainly does go on to say, "It forms a <term>lee shore</term> <note>A shore toward which the wind blows, making it dangerous for vessels as they could be driven onto the land.</note>, and there is an incessant swell," and then "that the prevalent wind is Southwest, to which the bay is quite open." These later observations may be what discourage warships from coming well inside. As for the merchant ships, although they have a sort of friendly regard for the *Pilot*, they do not trust it unless its statements agree with their own personal knowledge.

"...due to its unique location and local environment, it is likely that Ambas Bay will be found to be one of the healthiest places on the West Coast of Africa." In reality, this statement is completely unsupported by facts. There are no truly healthy locations on the West Coast of Africa at all; therefore, it cannot be "more healthy" than others. At best, it might be "less unhealthy," but it is not even that. Ambas Bay, the Cameroon River, and the Gaboon are the three deadliest spots between Calabar and the Congo.

The notion that Ambas Bay and the slopes of Mount Mungo <note>Now known as Mount Cameroon.</note> could provide a reliable <term>sanatorium</term> <note>A medical facility for long-term illness, typically associated with recovery in a favorable climate.</note> for the fever-stricken West Coast likely originated from Mr. Saker's reports. It is a theory that persists, floating in the air long after experience has removed its foundations—much like the false belief that there are no sharks south of the Congo. It is a hopeless task to try to debunk such an idea. No matter how many sharks ostentatiously show themselves south of the Congo, or how much fever occurs in Ambas Bay, these claims survive.

I have never visited Ambas Bay without encountering severe cases of fever. During my last stay there, the wife of the Basel missionary died of fever. Everyone except Mr. von Lucke—the head agent of the Ambas Bay Company—and myself suffered from fever to some degree. This is quite understandable when you look at the situation through the lens of personal experience. The area is extremely hot and humid. The cold winds from the mountains and the morning sea breezes contribute to the primary cause of a fever attack: a sudden chill.

The idea that a sanatorium might be built high on the mountain, above the so-called "fever line"—an imaginary boundary that shifts depending on local conditions—at first seemed reasonable. However, a closer understanding of the mountain's unique weather patterns has proven this idea to be wrong as well.

<header>THE FEVER LINE</header>

I say other Roman Catholics deliberately, because these missionaries generally live in a healthier manner than members of other West African missions. There are many reasons why the upper slopes of Mungo <note>Now known as Mount Cameroon.</note> do not provide the healthy environment expected of them. The primary reason is the extremely heavy rainfall. At Babundi, I am told, there was recently a panic among the natives because it had not rained for an entire week. This extraordinary event led them to believe that something was seriously wrong with nature and that a disaster was imminent. However, a pragmatic businessman told me this story must be baseless, because it has never been dry for a week at Babundi.

The reason for the heavy rainfall and soaking mists that fall on the mountain is that it is surrounded by vast, steaming swamps: to the north lie those of the <term>Rio del Rey</term> <note>Spanish for "River of the King."</note> and Calabar; to the south are the swamps of the Cameroon, Mungo, and Bimbia Rivers. Meanwhile, its great height traps the heavy, moisture-laden clouds drifting in from the Atlantic. In addition, cold air rushes down the mountainsides in drafts, condensing the moisture in the hot, saturated lower layers of the atmosphere.

In West Africa, one often hears that the 3,000-foot elevation mark is the limit for <term>malarial fever</term> <note>Malaria.</note>, but I do not believe this is anything more than a theoretical idea. In fact, there are few places in West Africa besides Mungo where this theory could even be tested. Buea and De Buncha, the site of Mr. Thomson's sanatorium, are located at roughly this altitude. There has not yet been enough experience with Buea as a health resort to make a final judgment, but the high prevalence there of <term>phagedænic ulcers</term> <note>original: "phagedænic"; rapidly spreading and destructive skin ulcers, from the Greek for "devouring."</note> does not inspire confidence in the air...

Buea, however, has an advantage over De Buncha: it possesses a fine water supply. In fact, as far as is currently known, it is the only significant water source above 2,000 feet on the mountain. When you are in Victoria, especially on the evening of a hot, dry day, you can see a thick band of white mist encircling the mountain. This occurs where the moisture-laden hot air rising from the forests and swamps meets the cold air of the upper mountain. As it condenses, it deposits not only water but also "exhalations" <note>The author refers to the miasma theory of disease, prevalent at the time, which suggested that illnesses like malaria were caused by "bad air" or vapors from decaying organic matter in swamps.</note> from the swamplands. Every morning and evening, you can see great plumes of mist rising from the forests on the foothills around Victoria, making the entire district look like a massive, smoldering fire. 

Currently, transporting a sick person up to either Buea or De Buncha would be very difficult. Even if these difficulties were resolved—as they will be once the road to Buea is finished—I do not believe a fever patient would find much benefit above the 3,000-foot level. In fact, they would face a high risk of chill and dysentery. 

I consider the idea of finding a high-altitude location in West Africa suitable for a <term>sanatorium</term> to be one of the most dangerous beliefs held by government authorities. It leads them to build houses in remote areas and send fever-stricken men there to die. This robs the sick of their best chance for recovery: getting out to sea. 

The ideal sanatorium for the West African Coast would be a hospital ship assigned to each district. Since this is practically impossible, the next best solution would be for the tireless Mr. A. L. Jones <note>Sir Alfred Lewis Jones (1845–1909), a prominent British shipowner and partner in Elder Dempster and Company.</note> and the Elder Dempster shipping line to provide a dedicated hospital cabin on every one of their vessels. 

The downside to this plan is that transporting a sick man through the heavy Gold Coast surf to reach a ship would be dangerous. Furthermore, in the river regions, mail steamers must travel from one mangrove-swamp river to another. They often enter places like *Forcados*, where, due to the "iniquities" <note>Referring to the treacherous sandbars and poor navigation conditions at the mouth of the Lagos lagoon.</note> of the *Lagos Bar*, vessels are delayed for days. There they lie idle in the sweltering heat while waiting for cargo. South of the river regions, along the southwest coast, these objections would be less significant. However, that region is not nearly as much in need of sanatoriums, and the...

The white men living there are fewer and more scattered than on the West Coast or in the Oil Rivers <note>The Oil Rivers Protectorate was a British protectorate in the Niger Delta region, named for the palm oil produced there.</note>. The next excitement after cruising in the bay was the arrival of the *Nachtigal* early in the morning. She had brought the Governor from Cameroons; I am sorry to say he was nearly dead with fever. The Doctor, who had been anxiously expected here for some time, hurried everywhere and rapidly improved the health of Victoria <note>Victoria, now known as Limbe, was a coastal town in the German colony of Kamerun.</note>.

Herr von Puttkamer kindly invited me to breakfast on board the *Nachtigal* and confirmed Herr von Lucke’s statement that I was welcome to travel on her to Calabar. He said as soon as he returned to Cameroons, he would be sending the ship back with the Commissioner.

I had a very pleasant afternoon and gathered a good deal of material for a work on the *Natural History of Governors*, which I do not intend to publish. I consider the Governor of Cameroons to be the best; he is the most experienced, for one thing. He was Governor in Togo before he came to Cameroons and was also in Lagos and on the Niger for some time. It is like this: after being in West Africa for a short time, particularly if you have been traveling in the bush, your wardrobe is always in a sparse and threadbare state. For example, when I was in the Cameroons, I had only one dress—and one only—that I considered fit to maintain the dignity of a representative of England. So, of course, when I went to call on the representative of another power, I had to wear that dress. Then, naturally, I had to go out in open boats to visit warships or take bush walks in it; and just as naturally, the squalls and rain came down by the ton. I did not mind the thunder, lightning, or wind. What worried me was the certainty that that precious rain would wash the color out of my outfit.

Governor von Puttkamer has a personality trait not shared by any other Governor on the Coast. He enjoys the sea, so during breakfast, the *Nachtigal* <note>German for "Nightingale"; the Governor’s official steamship.</note> was ordered to steam around the bay, which she did energetically. Fortunately, I like the sea too, or else—well! As it was, the only inconvenience we suffered was a heavy jolt in the middle of the meal. We thought we had discovered a new rock, but found we had only struck a sleeping whale. I do not know what the whale thought, but it made a considerable commotion and left the bay without a word of apology to the Governor.

The *Nachtigal* left Victoria the next day, as it was considered too unhealthy a place for the Governor to stay after his severe illness, and went around to Man-o'-War Bay. The day after, Herr von Lucke took me to the plantation in Man-o'-War Bay, where the Governor was staying for a few days.

Man-o'-War Bay is a very unusual and charming bay to the south of Ambas <note>Ambas Bay, the site of the British settlement of Victoria (Limbe).</note>. It has a narrower inlet and is not quite as deep as the latter, from which it is separated by a high, rocky promontory of hills. I do not think it has been carefully <term>sounded</term> <note>Measuring the depth of water using a weighted line.</note>, but there is deep water close alongside its shores, which rise very steeply into densely wooded mountains. The main peculiarity of it is that through a rock wall at its eastern end, there is a natural tunnel in the rock. You can row through this in a boat and find yourself on another body of water that has no other inlet or outlet; it is, if possible, even more beautiful than Man-o'-War Bay itself.

<header>XXVIII          VERANDAS</header>

though much smaller. It would be an exquisite place for smuggling.

On the southern shore of Man-o’-War Bay is a beautiful little quay and landing place for the grand plantation colloquially known as Frederickshafen, after its energetic custodian. This plantation is the property of a syndicate, with the main shareholders being the firm of Woermann; its magnificent condition and grand output ought to do much to soothe that firm’s feelings regarding their great losses over their Gaboon plantation. The house belonging to it is the finest house I know in West Africa. It is built of brick and wood and has the customary deep veranda surrounding it, but with this important difference: this veranda is enclosed with glass windows. These prevent the inner rooms from being too dark to work in and also stop the veranda from being drafty. 

On the West Coast, these are two dreadful faults in European-built houses. You cannot imagine what intolerable gloom and discomfort arise from the usual English-style house here. These abominable structures are made of corrugated iron—roof and all—with only the frame and floors made of wood. Sometimes the lower part of the house is enclosed and used for stores and offices; sometimes it is left open, but the living rooms are always on the first floor <note>In British English, the "first floor" refers to the level above the ground floor.</note> and open out onto a veranda. 

The sides of this veranda are usually closed in by Venetian shutters with windows at intervals. During the tornado <note>In West Africa, a "tornado" refers to a violent thunderstorm or squall rather than a localized funnel cloud.</note> seasons, these shutters and windows must be closed on average twice a day. During the wet season, they are kept closed for most of the six-month period. Consequently, you have to live on the veranda, for the inner rooms are then “as dark as ignorance,” and the shutters only keep out a portion of the rain. They also divide the fierce storm winds into strips of draft that cut into you, causing fatal fevers and sending all your papers flying, while the storm or the wet-season rain plays like fifty thousand demons drumming on your corrugated iron roof. 

Now, these problems were avoided in the house at Frederickshafen. When the windows around the veranda were shut, the glass kept out the wind while letting in the light, and the roof was made of tiles rather than being a horrid, noisy tin affair.

Herr Fredericksky most kindly showed me all over his plantation. When it was first established, the cautious planter then in charge planted both coffee and oil palms so as to have a backup should the coffee fail; and indeed, coffee has failed to a large extent throughout the Victoria district. It becomes afflicted with a type of blight similar to honeydew <note>A sticky substance excreted by aphids and other insects that often leads to fungal growth.</note>, and on this honeydew grows a large black mildew which mats the coffee berries together and ruins them, although it does not seem to harm the health of the tree very much.

However, cacao <note>The tree and seeds from which chocolate and cocoa are made.</note> thrives exceptionally well in the Victoria district and has remained free of disease so far. Consequently, the coffee on this plantation and in the native-owned farms around Ambas Bay is being replaced by cacao. This plan has been followed so effectively that the profit on cacao exported by small-scale native growers last year amounted to £1,000, and this large plantation alone ships an average of 400 bags a month. During the two "flushes" <note>Peak periods of growth or harvest.</note> that occur each year, as many as 600 to 650 bags a month are shipped; during the off-seasons, the volume is between 200 and 300 bags.

The ambition with which capital has been invested here, and the wisdom with which it has been employed, is very remarkable for a West Coast undertaking. In such ventures, as a general rule, there is usually one without the other, or a notable absence of both.

Near the main residence, there are large, well-built houses equipped with the proper machinery for drying the cocoa. This follows the fermentation and washing process, which takes place in another building located at the far end of the plantation to be near a suitable small river. Remarkably, these two sets of buildings are connected by an excellent tramway, which is very carefully and solidly constructed. It is ten times more pleasant and safer to travel on than the Congo Free State Railway. The small cars, upon which either you or bags of cocoa sit, are pushed by energetic laborers—a distinct improvement over West African steam engines. After conscientiously inspecting the drying and fermentation sheds, and enjoying the faint but pleasant smell of the mauve-colored cocoa sitting in heaps on the floors in various states of fermentation, we proceeded to seriously study cacao cultivation; and I was led by the two

<header>HINTS ON FORESTRY</header>

Giant German gentlemen walked me over acre after acre of plants in various stages of growth, from those just showing leaves above the ground to those whose beautiful golden fruit was being gathered by gangs of laborers brought in from the Batanga region, the Kru Coast, Sierra Leone, and other places. If it had not been for driver ants <term>aggressive, migratory ants known for their painful bites and tendency to swarm</term>, I feel sure I would have acquired enough information that afternoon to enable me to set up a plantation on my own and make it profitable. 

As it was, I simply made a mental note that it is best to cut down the forest to start a clearing in the middle of the dry season, let the trees and brushwood dry for a while, and then set them on fire. Then, just before the rains, I was to plant three cacao beans <term>the seeds from which cocoa and chocolate are made</term> in a single hole. I learned with pleasure that I did not need to bother removing the massive, charred tree trunks that lay about in glorious confusion. In fact, it was advisable to leave them, as they provided shelter for the young plants from excessive sun. Furthermore, I did not need to worry about planting my groups of three beans in tidy lines, but could just stick them in generally wherever I felt inclined. This was a comfort, for I do not know how anyone could do otherwise when the ground is covered with a tangled network of fallen trees, ranging from sixty to one hundred feet long and three to thirty feet in circumference. 

Once these seedlings reached a certain size, they were to be carefully transplanted into a cleared piece of ground—a nursery—where they would be planted in proper rows. Just as we reached the nursery, and my education was flowing along like a peaceful, pleasant stream, forty-eight searing hot pincers were driven into me. I knew then that "joy's short life was overpast" <note>original: "joy's short life was overpast" — a poetic reference to the sudden end of happiness.</note> for that afternoon; in other words, I had stepped into a column of driver ants. 

Resolving to endure the pain stoically, I said nothing. Seeing that there were no more of the enemy on the ground immediately around me, I bit my lip and did my best to maintain an appearance of interest in cacao. However, the only thing that actually interested me just then was whether either of my companions also had ants on them.

They never mentioned the ants. They had a slight difference of opinion over coffee disease, and a lengthy discussion on—

<header>XXVIII HOMEWARD BOUND</header>

I owe a debt in these matters to Cameroon—a debt I will never forget, even though I can never repay it.

The third announcement regarding the *Nachtigal* finally proved true. With my worn-out baggage, I traveled on her under the supervision of Herr von Besser to Old Calabar. There, I received every hospitality from Mr. Moore and Mr. Wall. My good friends Sir Claude and Lady MacDonald had left for England several months earlier—for the last time, as it turned out, because shortly after arriving in England, Sir Claude was appointed British Minister to Beijing <note>original: "Pekin"</note>.

When I arrived at Calabar, I found that the *Bakana*—commanded by Captain Porter with Mr. Peter Campbell as chief engineer—was expected to arrive any day. Since she was a sister ship to the *Batanga* and thus one of the finest vessels in the service, I decided to wait for her. During the few days I had available, I went up to say goodbye to Miss Slessor <note>Mary Slessor (1848–1915), a celebrated Scottish missionary in Nigeria who lived among the Efik people</note> at Okyon.

We had a comfortable voyage to Sierra Leone, where a gloom fell over the entire ship following the death of the purser, Mr. Crompton. It was one of those terribly sudden, hopeless cases of "Coast fever" <term>a historical term for various tropical fevers, most often malaria or yellow fever</term>, which are so common on the West Coast. In that region, no one knows from day to day whether they or those around them will be gripped by malarial fever and sent to their grave within a matter of hours.

<header>XXVIII HOMEWARD BOUND</header>

I owe a debt in these matters to Cameroon—a debt I will never forget, even though I can never repay it.

The third announcement regarding the *Nachtigal* <note>German: "Nightingale"</note> finally proved true. With my worn-out baggage, I traveled on her under the supervision of Herr von Besser to Old Calabar. There, I received every hospitality from Mr. Moore and Mr. Wall. My good friends Sir Claude and Lady MacDonald had left for England several months earlier—for the last time, as it turned out, because shortly after arriving in England, Sir Claude was appointed British Minister to Beijing <note>original: "Pekin"</note>.

When I arrived at Calabar, I found that the *Bakana*—commanded by Captain Porter with Mr. Peter Campbell as chief engineer—was expected to arrive any day. Since she was a sister ship to the *Batanga* and thus one of the finest vessels in the service, I decided to wait for her. During the few days I had available, I went up to say goodbye to Miss Slessor <note>Mary Slessor (1848–1915) was a celebrated Scottish missionary in Nigeria who lived among the Efik people and worked to end practices like the killing of twins</note> at Okyon.

We had a comfortable voyage to Sierra Leone, where a gloom fell over the entire ship following the death of the purser, Mr. Crompton. It was one of those terribly sudden, hopeless cases of "Coast fever" <term>a historical term for various tropical fevers, most often malaria or yellow fever</term>, which are so common on the West Coast. In that region, no one knows from day to day whether they or those around them will be gripped by malarial fever and sent to their grave within a matter of hours.

# APPENDIX I

## TRADE AND LABOUR IN WEST AFRICA

Since I believe that the trade of the West African Coast is its most important feature, I hope I may be forgiven for discussing this subject. My primary reason for doing so is the fact that independent travelers are rare in the Bights <note>A "bight" refers to a curve or recess in a coastline; here referring to the Bight of Benin and the Bight of Biafra</note>. The last one I recall hearing about was that unfortunate gentleman who went to the Coast for pleasure and lost a leg on the Lagos Bar <note>A hazardous sandbar at the entrance to Lagos Harbor that was notorious for shipwrecks and accidents</note>. Now, I have not lost any part of my body anywhere on the Coast, and therefore I have no personal prejudice against the place. I do not represent any particular party, and I ask the more experienced "old coasters" <term>veteran European residents or traders on the West African coast</term> to remember that "an observer often sees the game most clearly."

First of all, it should be remembered that Africa does not possess ready-made riches to the extent that many people believe. It is not like India, filled with the accumulated wealth of ages, waiting for an adventurer to arrive and "shake the pagoda tree" <term>a 19th-century slang term for making a quick fortune in the East, named after a gold coin called a pagoda</term>. In Africa, the pagoda tree only grows over hoards of buried ivory; even then, it is a stunted specimen compared to those that grew over the treasure houses of Delhi, Seringapatam <note>A historic city in India, known for its siege in 1799 where the British seized vast treasures from Tipu Sultan</note>, and hundreds of other places equally rich in gems and gold. Africa contains a great deal of wealth—physically more than any other continent in the world—but this wealth is deeply embedded in its physical makeup. It requires hard work to extract it, especially in one of its wealthiest regions, the West Coast. There, gold, silver, copper, lead, and petroleum are protected from miners by the deadliest forms of "African fever" <term>a historical term for various tropical fevers, most often malaria or yellow fever</term>. Likewise, the goods prepared by the local people for trade are equally guarded by disease. It requires men of a specific character to work and export these goods successfully—men blessed with great luck, courage, patience, and diplomacy.

Regarding the first sub-division, one can say the most positive things about the West Coast trade; the means of transport are actually ahead of the trade in all districts except the Gold Coast. I know this is an unpopular opinion, so I will attempt to explain. First, as for sea communication to Europe, the West Coast is extremely well-served. The two English steamer lines managed by Messrs. Elder Dempster—the British African and the Royal African—are conducted with great enterprise, and their devotion to trade is almost pathetic. Even if there is only the slightest rumor (and sometimes I think they don’t even wait for the rumor, but "go in" as an experiment) of a puncheon <term>a large cask, typically holding about 80 gallons</term> of palm oil or a log of timber waiting for shipment at a remote port consisting of only a single house, one of these vessels will head for that port to collect the cargo. In addition to the English lines, there is the German Woermann line, which is equally devoted to cargo—I might almost say even more so, for it is frequently reported that Woermann liners will wait offshore for the crops to actually grow. I cannot personally vouch for that, but I know that the time allowed to a Woermann captain by his owners to travel between Cameroon and Big Batanga—just around the corner—is eight days.

These English and German lines, having reached a friendly agreement regarding freight costs, operate in the Bights of Benin, Biafra, and Panavia without any rivals, except for the occasional vessels chartered by the African Association to bring out a large cargo, and the four sailing vessels belonging to the Association. These sailing ships give an eighteenth-century appearance to the rivers and have great adventures navigating the sandbars of Opobo and Bonny.¹ The Bristol ships on the Half Jack Coast <note>The coastal area around the modern town of Jacqueville in Ivory Coast</note> are not rivals, but rather a type of floating factory; they ship their goods home and receive supplies through the regular steamer lines. The English and German liners, therefore, carry the bulk of the trade from the entire coast. Their services are complex and frequent, but they are easy to understand once you realize that the English lines are divided into two categories—Liverpool boats and Hamburg boats—either of which may call at Havre <note>Le Havre, France</note> when necessary. The Liverpool line serves as the mail line to the more important ports, while the Hamburg line...

# TRADE AND LABOUR IN WEST AFRICA

The line is almost entirely composed of cargo vessels calling at the smaller ports as well as the larger ones.

There is another classification of these routes that must be understood. The English boats are divided into: 
1. A line ending at Sierra Leone and calling at the Îles de Los; 
2. A line ending at Akassa; 
3. A line ending at Old Calabar; 
4. A line ending at São Paulo de Loanda <note>now Luanda, Angola</note>. 

In addition, there is a direct line from Antwerp to the Congo, chartered by the Congo Free State government. Division 4, the "South-westers," are the fastest vessels as far as Lagos, for they only stop at the Canaries, Sierra Leone, off the Kru Coast, at Accra, and off Lagos. They then run straight from Lagos into Cameroon without stopping at the Rivers <note>the Oil Rivers of the Niger Delta</note>, reaching Cameroon in twenty-seven days from Liverpool. After Cameroon, they cross to Fernando Po and stop at Victoria, then work their way steadily down the coast to their destination. From there, they head back up, doing everything they can to secure cargo. However, they never succeed as much as they would wish. Consequently, being "hungry in the hold" <note>having empty cargo space</note> by the time they return to the Bight of Benin, they are liable to "smell" cargo and stop to collect it. Therefore, they are not necessarily the fastest ships returning home.

Two French companies run to the French possessions, subsidized by their government (just as the German line is, while our English lines are not): the *Chargeurs Réunis* <note>original: "United Shippers"</note> and the *Fraissinet*. The South-west Coast liners of these companies run to Gabon and then to Cotonou, near Lagos, then back to Gabon and down as far as Loango, calling on their way home at the other ports in the French Congo. They are mainly carriers of imported goods because they run on a strict schedule. On the South-west Coast, unless a schedule has a flexible, "eternal" quality to it, it is impossible to successfully collect export goods.

Below the Congo, the rivals of the English and German lines are the vessels of the Portuguese line, *Empreza Nacional* <note>original: "National Company"</note>. These run from Lisbon to the Cape Verde Islands, then to São Tomé and Príncipe, and then to the ports of Angola (Luanda, Benguela, Moçâmedes, Ambrizete, etc.). They currently carry the bulk of the Angola trade because of the preferential customs duties on goods shipped in Portuguese vessels.

The service of English vessels to the West Coast is weekly, to the Rivers fortnightly, and to the South-west Coast monthly. This shipping enterprise is the primary achievement that England should be proud of regarding West Coast trade.

Any of these English boats will go anywhere that a ship can possibly go, and their captains' local knowledge is a thing...

# APPENDIX I

England as a whole should be proud of these achievements, and the rest of the civilized world should regard them with awe-struck admiration. The fact that they leave no room for further development in maritime shipping has been demonstrated several times by the collapse of shipping lines that attempted to rival them—such as the Prince Line and, more recently, the General Steam Navigation Company.

But although the West Coast trader has these vessels at his disposal, he by no means has an easy time or inexpensive methods for loading his goods on board, except at Sierra Leone and in the Oil Rivers <note>the Niger Delta region</note>. I have already mentioned the Gold Coast surf and the Lagos bar; the *Calemma* <note>a heavy, rhythmic swell or surf</note>, as we call the South-west Coast surf, is nearly, if not quite, as dangerous as the surf on the Gold Coast. Indeed, I believe it is worse, though I have had more experience with it. It often has to be navigated in native dugout canoes rather than the well-made surf-boats used on the Gold Coast. However, while these surf-boats are safer, they are also more expensive than canoes. A high-quality surf-boat costing £40 or £60 has an average lifespan of only two years in the Gold Coast surf, so from a commercial standpoint, there is little to choose between the two types of surf conditions when all is considered.

Regarding inland transport, the difficulty is even greater. However, in the majority of the West Coast possessions held by European powers, there are great facilities for transport provided by the network of waterways near the coast and the great rivers running far into the interior.

These waterways are used by the local people as virtual roads; in many districts, they are practically the only roads that exist for transporting goods in bulk, or that are required to exist given the current state of trade. But there is room for more European enterprise regarding river navigation. My own opinion is that if British capital were invested in small, suitably-built river steamers, it would be found to be more profitable than building railway lines. Waterways that could be developed in this manner include the Cross River, the Volta, and the Ancobra. I am not saying there would be any immediate profit from these river steamboat lines, but I do not believe there will be any profit, immediate or remote, from railways in West Africa. This question of transport is currently regarded as a pressing issue throughout the continent. For the well-being of certain parts of the West Coast, such as Lagos and the Gold Coast, railways are considered essential. I do not pretend to speak for Lagos, as I have never been ashore there. I have seen a little of the Gold Coast and heard a great deal more, and I think I may—

# TRADE AND LABOUR IN WEST AFRICA

I can safely say that building a railway would not be difficult on this terrain, for it is solid, firm land rather than stretches of treacherous swamp. The main difficulty in constructing railroads here will be landing the materials through the surf. This challenge cannot be overcome except at enormous expense by building piers, but it might be bypassed by sending the equipment ashore on small bar-boats that could navigate up the Volta or Ankobra rivers. 

One might argue that if the equipment were taken up the Volta, “it would be nowhere near where anyone wanted it.” However, the rigid belief that goods must be landed at places where there are government headquarters—such as Accra and Cape Coast, locations where the surf is at its absolute worst—seems to me to be a mistake. The landing place at Cape Coast could be made safe and easy by spending a few thousand pounds to “develop” the rock that currently provides shelter *once* you manage to get to its leeward side, but this would only improve safety for surf-boats. No other type of vessel could work this stretch of beach.

On the other hand, there is plenty of room for developing the Volta, as it is a waterway that a vessel with a six-foot draft can ascend for fifty miles from July until November, and for thirty miles during the rest of the year. The worst feature of the Volta is its treacherous sandbar—a vast semicircular sweep with heavy breaking waves—which is too dangerous for most boats to cross. However, a steamer designed like the Lagos bar-boats might manage it; the *Bull Frog* reported depths of nineteen to twenty-one feet on the bar in 1884, one hour before high tide. 

Because there is no such bar-boat available, and because it is impossible to send goods out in surf-boats across the bar, cargo from Ada <note>original spelling: Adda</note> (Riverside)—the principal town on the Volta, located about six miles upriver from its mouth—must be carried across the spit of land to Beach Town. From there, it is brought out through the shore surf, which is the most dangerous stretch of surf on the entire Gold Coast. 

The Ankobra <note>original spelling: Ancobra</note> is a river that penetrates the interior through a district very rich in gold and timber, and it is strongly suspected of containing petroleum. It is between eighty and one hundred yards wide as far up as Akanko. During the rainy season, it maintains a depth of three and a half to four and a half fathoms <note>approximately 21 to 27 feet</note>, and boats are taken up to Tomento, about forty miles from its mouth, carrying goods to the Wassa <note>original spelling: Wassaw</note> gold mines. However, the sandbar of the Ankobra is shallow, offering only six feet of depth, although it is firm and stable, unlike the shifting bars of the Volta and Lagos. In the sixteenth century, the Portuguese used to travel up this river and operate in the country with better profits than we do today.

The other major river of the Gold Coast, the Pra <note>original spelling: Bosum Prah</note>, which enters the sea at Shama <note>original spelling: Chama</note>, is of no use for navigation from the sea. It is obstructed by rocks and rapids, and its sandbar is only—

If any district ever required them, the Gold Coast does. There has been much talk for some time about the government constructing a line, and a survey for it has been made, but I believe this survey was unsatisfactory, and a new one is being considered. It is hoped that it will soon enter the construction phase, for the local government owes a heavy debt to the commercial trade—from which it draws its entire revenue—to provide this infrastructure. If our new acquisition of Ashanti <note>original: "Ashantee"</note> is to be developed, it must have a railway connecting it with coastal trade. This line does not necessarily need to run directly into Kumasi <note>original: "Coomassie"</note>, but it must be near enough to Kumasi to allow goods to be sold there at only a small increase over coastal prices.

It is an easy mistake to imagine that the natives in the interior are willing to pay much higher prices for goods than the coastal natives. It is true that they are currently forced to pay an average of seventy-five percent more to the coastal natives, who presently act as middlemen between them and the white traders. However, if a white trader goes into the interior, he must face two major hurdles: first, the difficulty of getting his goods there safely; and second, the opposition of native traders who can and will drive him out of the market unless he is supported by easy and cheap means of transport. 

Take the current case of Kumasi. Suppose a merchant wants to transport £3,000 worth of trade goods from the coast to Kumasi. To transport this, he must employ 1,300 porters <term>carriers</term> at one shilling and three pence <note>1s. 3d.</note> per person per day. The journey takes eight days to get there and eight days to return—sixteen days total—which amounts to a cost of £1,300, without even accounting for loss or damage. In order to buy local produce with these goods and cover these transport costs, as well as shipping expenses and other overheads, he would have to sell his goods in Kumasi at a far higher price than on the coast. Consequently, the native traders would easily undercut him and drive him out. 

Furthermore, as long as a district remains in the hands of native traders, no progress or development occurs. It would be a grave error to allow this to happen in Kumasi, now that we have finally done what should have been done in 1874 <note>The year of the Sir Garnet Wolseley’s expedition during the Third Anglo-Ashanti War.</note> and taken actual possession. Kumasi is a magnificent location that, if managed properly for a few years, will become a major interior market, attracting trade routes from throughout the interior. It is not currently a great center because of the oppression and exploitation <term>usury</term> that the Kings of Ashanti have inflicted on everyone within their power, and...

These factors have caused Kumasi <note>original: "Coomassie"</note> to primarily attract one type of trade: slaves. These individuals were used in their frequent human sacrifices, and a higher price could be obtained for them here than from the Muslim <note>original: "Mohammedan"</note> tribes to the north under French control. Regarding other trade goods, they have naturally flowed into the markets of the French Sudan for years, instead of passing through territories like Ashanti <note>original: "Ashantee"</note> into the markets of the British Gold Coast. Unless we build a railroad to encourage European traders to move inland and create a market that draws these trade routes toward Kumasi, we will find ourselves in a few years complaining, "What is the use of Ashanti?" and so forth. This is our foolish habit; we never realize that the West Coast is only valuable if it is made so through European effort.

The new administration <note>original: "*régime*"</note> on the Gold Coast is certainly more active than the previous one—more aware of the importance of expanding inland—and a twenty-five-foot-wide road is planned all the way to Kumasi and beyond, which is an excellent development in its own right. However, it will not do much for trade. While the pacification of the country and the increased security for personal property provided by our rule will help the local people bring their goods to the coast, it will not significantly help us take our goods inland. Carriers will charge just as much for transporting goods along a road as they do along a bush path. This is fair, as it is just as much work for them—and often more—as I know from my experience with the government road in Cameroon. 

In a country like West Africa, there is no doubt that a soft bush path—covered in a thick layer of moss and leaves and shaded from the sun by interlocking branches—is much better for traveling than a hard, wide, sun-drenched road. This road might be valuable for military expeditions, but such expeditions are not common occurrences on the Gold Coast. Furthermore, the road cannot be used by pack animals <note>original: "draught animals"</note> because of horse-sickness and the tsetse fly, which appear as soon as one enters the forest beyond the coastal <note>original: "littoral"</note> region. Therefore, this road should not be considered an equivalent to steam transport; it will only serve to bring down a small trickle of local trade and likely won't increase that amount significantly.

The issue of transport is, of course, not limited to the Gold Coast. South of Lagos, there is a massive river system through which trade slowly flows via local hands to the European trading posts <note>original: "factories"</note> on the riverbanks. However, because this trade is controlled by local merchants, it is only a fraction of what it could become if managed by Europeans; and any mineral...

<header>APPENDIX I</header>

The wealth that may exist in the heavily forested regions of the country remains unexploited and unknown. The difficulty of transportation here significantly hinders the extraction of timber wealth; it is completely useless for the local people <note>original: "natives"</note> to fell even a magnificent tree unless it is close enough to a waterway to be floated down to the trading post <note>original: "factory"</note>. This is why they cut ebony, barwood, and camwood into small logs <note>original: "billets"</note> that a man can carry. The French and Germans are both now following a strategy of penetrating as far as possible into the interior via waterways and then constructing railways. Building these railways is relatively easy in terms of inclines <note>original: "gradients"</note> and the lack of dense forest once the waterway leads to the vast, park-like plateaus that generally lie behind the forest belt and the inevitable mountain range. The most significant of these railways will be the one built by Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza <note>original: "M. de Brazza"</note> up the Sangha <note>original: "Sanga"</note> Valley toward Lake Chad. Once this railway is built, it will destroy the trade in Cameroon and the Oil Rivers <note>The "Oil Rivers" refers to the coastal region of the Niger Delta</note>, especially the latter. In Cameroon, the Germans have dismantled the monopoly held by the coastal tribes—something we have failed to do in our territories under the Niger Coast Protectorate. The Royal Niger Company, however, has broken through and taken full control of a large interior region. Every Englishman should feel proud of this achievement, as it is the only instance in West Africa where we have matched the French and Germans in the courage and initiative required to penetrate the interior. Fortunately, the regions the Company has taken over are wealthy, unlike Senegal, which is described as being "made of sand and savage savages." Where else in West Africa, outside of the Company, can you find men who deserve to be named as explorers in the same breath as de Brazza, Captain Binger, and Zintgraff?

I fear that one day, when it is too late, we will realize how foolish we were to remain stationed on the seacoast, merely organizing our settlements and establishing schools and drainage systems. We will find our possessions in the Rivers and along the Gold Coast to be worthless—particularly in the Rivers—because trade will inevitably flow toward the markets along the French railroads behind them. The middleman tribes that we support charge a commission <note>original: "toll"</note> of seventy-five percent on all trade passing through their hands. Furthermore, the British Government is showing a strong tendency to impose such high taxes <note>original: "duties"</note> on the only commodity the local people truly care for—alcohol—that they will take their goods to markets where alcohol is more accessible, even if they must pay a fifty percent commission at those markets.

<margin>¹ *A Naturalist in Mid Africa*, 1896.</margin>

I will speak more on this later, but for now, let us return to the issue of transport. Mr. Scott Elliot,¹ writing about East African regions, has provided a very interesting contribution based on his personal experience and official statistics. Because many of his observations and figures apply equally to the West Coast, I hope I may be forgiven for quoting him. He argues in favor of utilizing every available mile of waterway. Regarding Lake Victoria <note>original: "Victoria Nyanza"</note>, he states that "it is possible to place a steamer on it for £12,677. Estimating the cost of maintenance, fuel, and operating expenses at £1,200 a year (a generous estimate), a capital expenditure of £53,000—consisting of £13,000 for the steamer and £40,000 to generate three percent interest—would allow this steamer to transport about thirty tons at a speed of five to ten miles an hour for £1,600 a year. This makes it possible to transport a ton for a halfpenny per mile, whereas it would require about £53,000 to build a railway only eighteen miles long."

I am informed that the railway in the Congo Free State has cost approximately eight times that amount per mile. Further on, Mr. Elliot says: "In America, the surplus population from Europe and the markets in the Eastern States have made railway development profitable overall. However, in Africa—until pioneer work is completed and the prospects for colonization and plantations are stable enough to attract a significant number of settlers—it will be financially ruinous to build a long railway line."

I am not quoting these figures to discourage those on the West Coast from building railways, but only to persuade them to have their government build them in the right direction: specifically, into the interior, where further trade expansion is possible. Judging by other trends in English colonies, I suspect that if left to the typical spirit of English West Coast enterprise, the tracks would be built along a route that allows engine drivers to keep the Atlantic Ocean in sight, rather than heading in the direction where we should truly be looking. I must admit, I am not an enthusiast for "civilizing" the African people. I believe the French method of dealing with Africa is currently the best: claim as much of the continent as possible on the map, and ensure your flag is treated as a sacred object by the locals <note>original: "natives"</note>—something they would not dare attack. Once this is accomplished, you can move away from the French plan and gradually develop trade in an English manner—but not in the style <note>original: "à la"</note> of Sierra Leone <note>The text ends abruptly here, likely referring to the administrative style of the Sierra Leone colony.</note>

<header>APPENDIX I</header>

Sierra Leone. But carry out your pioneer work first. There is an excellent foundation for British pioneer work on our coasts within the trading community; trade is the primary way to win the trust of Africans, and English traders and their goods are highly regarded throughout West Africa. This pioneer work must be undertaken or subsidized by the government—as has been done in the French territories—because the West Coast does not offer the same attractions to the average traveler as, for example, East Africa with its magnificent herds of big game, or the northern frontier of India with its mountains and fascinating cultural relics and monuments. Traveling in West Africa is exhausting and very hazardous to one's health. Many men would not hesitate for a moment to go there if the primary danger were local hostility; however, they pause at the prospect of a journey that likely involves months of trekking through wet, gloomy forests punctuated by the occasional swamp,¹ and which will almost certainly end in an ignoble death from fever in some miserable, squalid village.

Reckless spending to open up the country should be avoided, as it severely burdens the future—even if partially successful—because the debt becomes too heavy for the territory to bear, as seen in the finances of the Congo Free State. If such spending leads to failure, it discourages further efforts. What we currently need in West Africa are three or four explorers like Binger <note>Louis-Gustave Binger (1856–1936), a French officer and explorer who mapped the Niger River bend</note> and Zintgraff <note>Eugen Zintgraff (1858–1897), a German explorer of the Cameroon interior</note> to expand our territories northward, eastward, and southeastward until they control the inland trade routes. There is no reason for these men to enter from the West Coast and risk death or debilitating illness from fever before they even begin their work. If only half of what is said about Uganda is true, it would be a suitable base for them to start from; they could then travel west to reach the current borders of our West Coast possessions. This corridor of territory across the continent would give us control over, and connect us with, all inland trade. Due to our own passivity and foolishness, we can now never establish a north-to-south corridor in Africa.

<header>TRADE AND LABOR IN WEST AFRICA</header>
<sig>T T</sig>

West Africa is extremely wealthy in some areas, but certainly not in all; vast tracts of the region consist of mangrove swamps, and other large expanses are composed of miserably poor, acidic, sandy clay. It is impossible within the space I have available to provide a full description of the locations where these unproductive districts occur, but you will find them here and there all along the coast after leaving Sierra Leone. The acidic clay seems to be new soil recently formed on the mainland from dried-up mangrove swamps. A good, rough rule of thumb is: do not start a plantation on soil that does not already support a hardwood forest. Large areas on the Gold Coast <note>modern-day Ghana</note>, even where the soil is good, are now useless for cultivation because they have been deforested by the local inhabitants' wasteful farming methods, combined with the Harmattan <note>a dry, dusty West African trade wind</note> and the long dry season.

The regions with the wealthiest soil are not in British possession, but are held by Germany, France, Spain, and Portugal—namely, Cameroon and its series of volcanic islands: Fernando Po, Príncipe, and São Tomé.

The rich volcanic soil of these locations will allow them to compete in plantation agriculture with any part of the known world. Cameroon is undoubtedly the best of these because of its superior water supply from rivers. Although it is not strictly within the region of the "double seasons" <note>areas with two rainy and two dry seasons per year</note>, it is located right on their northern limit. Furthermore, the height of Mount Cameroon—13,760 feet—condenses the moisture-laden air from its surrounding swamps and the Atlantic, so that rain is quite frequent throughout the year. When you are within the region of the double seasons just south of Cameroon, the rainfall is no heavier than that of the Oil Rivers <note>the Niger Delta region</note>, yet it is better distributed. This is a crucial factor for the success of plantations such as tea and tobacco, which require showers at least once a month. To the north of Cameroon, there is no prospect of either of these profitable commodities being produced in a quantity or quality that could compete with South America, India, or the Malayan regions; therefore, these northern areas will have to rely on coffee and cacao plantations. South of Cameroon, the French Congo possesses the wealthiest soil and an excellently balanced climate. The soil of the lower Congo is bad and unproductive near the river. Cabinda <note>original: "Kacongo"</note>, the small piece of Portuguese territory north of the Congo's banks, and that part of Angola as far as the Bengo River, are composed of much the same landscape as the French Congo, though less densely forested. All of Angola is an immensely wealthy region, except for the area around Luanda, where the land is saturated with sand for about fifty square miles, and those regions in the extreme south and southeast, which lie within the Kalahari Desert.

# APPENDIX I

Coffee grows wild throughout Angola in those districts distant from the dry coast-lands—particularly in the districts of Golongo Alto and Cassengo, where it grows in great profusion. One can travel through entirely uncultivated stretches of it, covering thirty miles at a time. Now that merchants have taught them its value, the local inhabitants are collecting these wild berries and bringing them in in large quantities. In addition, the English firm of Newton and Carnegie has started plantations in Cassengo. The greater part of these plantations consists of clearing and tending to the wild coffee, but they are also regularly planting and cultivating young trees, as it has been found that the yield per tree is immensely increased by cultivation.

Six hundred to eight hundred bags a month were shipped from Ambrizette alone when I was there in 1893, and the amount has since increased. It will increase even further when that slow but very respectable little railroad line, which proudly calls itself the Royal Trans-African <note>The Luanda Railway, intended to link the coast to the interior</note>, has completed its sections into the coffee district. It was about thirty miles away at Ambaca when I was in Angola, but by now it may have progressed further. However, I do not think it is very likely to have gone far, and I am convinced that the railroad will not become "trans-African" in my lifetime. Still, it has an "immediate future" compared to what any other West Coast railway can expect; for besides coffee, Angola is rich in malachite and high-quality gum, and its superior administration will attract the rubber trade from the Kasai region of the Congo Free State.

In our own possessions, the establishment of plantations is being carried out with much energy by Messrs. Miller Brothers on the Gold Coast <note>modern-day Ghana</note>¹; by several private capitalists, including Mr. A. L. Jones of Liverpool, at Lagos; by the Royal Niger Company in their territory; and by several head agents in the Niger Coast Protectorate. Sir Claude MacDonald provided every incentive for this trade development and gave great material help by founding a botanical station at Old Calabar <note>a coastal city in modern-day Nigeria</note>, where plants could be obtained. He did his utmost to try and encourage the local population to embark on plantation-making, ably supported by Mr. Billington, the botanist in charge of the botanical station.

¹ The export of coffee from the Gold Coast in 1894, given in the Colonial Report for that year (published in 1896), was valued at £1,265, 3 shillings, and 4 pence; cocoa was valued at £546, 17 shillings, and 4 pence. The greater part of this coffee goes to Germany.
The export of coffee from Lagos, given in the Colonial Report for 1892 (published in 1893), was valued at £12. No figures on this subject are given in the 1894 report, published in 1896; I cite these figures to show the delay by the Colonial Office in publishing these reports and the difficulty of obtaining reliable statistics on West African trade.

A few chiefs, as a favor, took coffee plants, but they are not enthusiastic; the slaves that would be required to tend the coffee and keep it clear of weeds in this lush forest region are currently more profitably employed in preparing palm oil.

I have already mentioned the coffee plantation at Man o' War Bay, as well as those in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note> which, although they are not shipping as much as the German plantations at present, will soon be doing so. In addition to coffee and cacao, attempts are being made in the French Congo to introduce the Para rubber tree. I frequently visited a large plantation of these near Libreville and found them to be doing well. This would be an excellent tree to plant among coffee, as it is very clean and orderly and seems to take to West Africa very naturally. However, it does not produce a crop quickly; I am informed that it must be left for at least three or four years before it can be tapped at all, so, as gardening books would say, it should be planted early.

It is very possible that many other trees producing tropical products valuable in commerce might be successfully introduced into West Africa. The cultivation of cloves and nutmegs would be very profitable here, as related species of trees and shrubs are indigenous. However, the first of these trees takes a long time before bearing fruit, and the cultivation of the second is a risky venture. I have found allspice growing wild in several districts, though not in large quantities. Cotton with a fine, long fiber <term>staple: the length and quality of individual fibers in a crop like cotton or wool</term> grows wild in abundance wherever there is open ground, but the natives do not cultivate it. When attempts have been made to encourage them to collect it, they do so, but they bring it in very dirty. Since the traders have no machinery to compress it like the equipment used in America, it does not pay to ship. 

Indigo is common everywhere along the Coast and is used by the natives for dyeing, as is a teazle plant which produces a very fine, permanent maroon color. Besides these, there are many other dyes and drugs used by them—colocynth <note>a bitter plant used as a purgative</note>, datura, soap bark, cardamom, ginger, peppers, strophanthus <note>a plant used both as a heart stimulant and an arrow poison</note>, nux vomica <note>the source of strychnine</note>, etc. However, the difficulty of getting these things brought to the traders in sufficient quantities prevents them from being exported to any significant extent. Tea has not been tried and is hardly worth trying, though there is little doubt it would grow in the Cameroons and the French Congo, where it would find an excellent climate and almost any elevation required. But I believe it has been discovered in recent years that tea, like coffee, is not as dependent on high altitudes as was once thought...

Vanilla grows with great luxuriance in Cameroon <note>original: "Cameroons"</note>. In Victoria <note>modern-day Limbe, Cameroon</note>, a grove of gigantic cacao trees is heavily overgrown with this lovely orchid in a most perfect way. It does not seem to injure the cacao trees in the least, and there are other kinds of trees it will take to equally well. I saw it growing happily and luxuriantly under the direction of the Roman Catholic Mission at Landana; but it requires a continuously damp climate. Once started, vanilla gives little or no trouble, and its pods do not require any very careful processing before being sent to Europe. This is a very important point, for a great hindrance—the main hindrance to plantation enterprise on the Coast—is the difficulty of finding careful and skilled laborers.

I once had the pleasure of meeting a Dutch gentleman—a plantation expert—who had been sent down the West Coast by a firm trading there, as well as in the Malay Archipelago. He was prospecting, for a heavy fee, to see whether it would pay the firm to open plantations there rather than in Malaysia. I believe his final judgment was against the West African plan because of the difficulty of finding skilled natives to tend young plants and prepare the products. He regarded tea as quite hopeless because of this difficulty, and he said he did not think one would ever get Africans at as cheap a rate, or who were as nimble-fingered at rolling tea, as one can get Asiatics. 

No one knows until they have tried it how much trouble it is to get an African to do things carefully; but it is a trouble, not an impossibility. If you don’t die of fever from sheer worry and vexation, the task can be done, but in the meantime, it is maddening. I have spent many a day’s work on plantations instructing cheerful, willing, and apparently intelligent <term>Africans</term> <note>original: "Ethiopians," used here as a general term for Black Africans</note> of various sexes and sizes on the mortal crime of hoeing up young coffee plants. They completely understand. “Oh, Lord! Master, I am not able to do such a thing.” But they are! You go along tomorrow morning, and you’ll find your most promising pupils swinging their hoes around, talking about the disgraceful way their dearest friends behave, while destroying young coffee plants right and left. 

They are just as bad, if not slightly worse—particularly the women—when it comes to picking coffee. As soon as your eye is off them, the branch is off the tree. I know one planter who lives like the Surprise Captain in W. S. Gilbert’s ballad <note>A reference to the *Bab Ballads* by W. S. Gilbert, likely referring to a character who appears unexpectedly to catch others in the act of wrongdoing</note>, lurking among his groves and suddenly appearing among his pickers. This, he says, has given them a feeling of uncertainty as to when and...

# TRADE AND LABOR IN WEST AFRICA

That book had an illustration depicting a planter sitting on his porch, with a glass of something cool at his right hand and a pipe in his mouth, watching a large plantation full of hard-working locals picking berries into baskets on all sides.

**LABOR.** — The labor problem is one that must be studied and solved before West Africa can progress much further than its current state of development. The climate is such that the country cannot be worked by white laborers; everyone familiar with the region believes this state of affairs will remain until an effective cure for malaria is discovered, something significant happens to the angle of the earth’s axis, or some radical change takes place in the nature of the sun. The West African climate shows no signs of improving whatsoever. If it shows any sign of change, it is for the worse; in recent years, two extremely deadly forms of fever have been identified here: malarial typhoid and blackwater fever. Malarial typhoid seems confined to districts where Europeans have focused heavily on drainage systems, which is discouraging in itself.

The labor problem was imported along with European civilization. Civilization has not progressed to any significant extent, but the labor problem has; being a persistent nuisance, it has taken to West Africa like a duck to water and is now thriving. However, it has not yet reached its peak; it is just waiting for the abolition of domestic slavery—and then! Meanwhile, the problem grows with the demand for hands to carry out plantation and public works. On the West Coast—that is to say, from Sierra Leone to Cameroon—it is worse than on the South West Coast from Cameroon to Benguela.

The Krumen <note>The Kru people of Liberia, traditionally employed as sailors and deckhands</note>, the Accra <note>People from the Gold Coast, modern-day Ghana</note>, and the Sierra Leoneans are currently the only available solutions on the West Coast. The first group are as fine as deckhands and shore-workers as you could reasonably wish for, but they are no good for plantation work. The second, thanks to the practical training they have received from the Basel Mission <note>A Swiss missionary society known for providing vocational training</note>, are very good artisans, cooks, or clerks, but are also unsuitable for plantation work except as overseers. The third group are poor artisans, but excellent clerks or subordinate officials; however, they are so untrustworthy that one can almost rely on them to swindle any employer. Lagos produces a large number of educated natives, but owing to the growing prosperity of the colony, these are nearly all employed within Lagos itself.

# APPENDIX I

An important but somewhat neglected factor in the problem is the nature of the West African native. Because I believe a calm and unbiased study of this factor would provide a satisfactory solution to the problem, I venture to offer my own observations on it.

The Kruboys—as the white men call the natives of the Grain Coast, regardless of an individual's age—or the *Menekussi*, as the Efik people call them, are the most important people in West Africa. Without their help, working the Coast would cost even more lives than it already does; in fact, it would be practically impossible. Ever since vessels began regularly visiting the Bights <note>The Bight of Benin and the Bight of Biafra</note>, the Kru man has had the helpful habit of joining ships and doing all the heavy work. 

Their first teachers were the slave traders, who initiated them into this habit and instructed them in ship’s work so they could benefit from their services while navigating vessels along the Slave Coast. To prevent any Kruboy from being mistakenly taken as a slave—which would have offended these useful allies—the slave traders persuaded them to always tattoo a basket-work pattern down their foreheads and out to the tip of their broad noses. This is the most extensive piece of genuine tattooing I know of in West Africa, and the Kruboys still maintain this fashion. 

Their next teachers were the merchants, who have taught and still teach them "beach work": how to handle cargo, process oil <term>Refining or testing palm oil for trade</term>, and make themselves generally useful in a factory <term>In this context, a merchant's trading station or warehouse</term>—or, as the Kruboy puts it, to "learn sense." 

To religious teaching, the Kruboy seems remarkably resistant for an African. However, the two lessons he has learned—ship and shore work—are the best that white men have taught Black men so far, because they have not resulted in the negative consequences that followed other lessons. Unfortunately, the Kru man of the Grain Coast and the Cabinda of the Southwest Coast are the only two tribes that have benefited from this kind of education. There are many other tribes who would have done their teachers just as much credit, had circumstances led the traders and slavers to turn their attention toward them. 

But circumstances did not allow for that. So today, just as a century ago, you must hire the Kruboy to help you if you intend to do any work, whether missionary or mercantile, from Sierra Leone to Cameroon. Below Cameroon, the Kruboy does not like to go, except to work at the shore of an English trading house. He has suffered much from the Congo Free State <note>A private colony in Central Africa owned by King Leopold II of Belgium, notorious for the brutal exploitation of laborers</note>, as well as from the Spaniards and Portuguese, who have not respected his feelings regarding his desire to return...

Every year, or every two years at the most, he returns to his own country because of his deep-seated dislike for agricultural work and for carrying heavy loads through the wilderness.

The pay for a Kruboy averages about £1 per month. There are different ways this total is reached. For example, some missionaries pay each man £20 a year, but the worker must provide his own food <term>chop</term>. Some traders on the South West Coast pay £8 a year, but they provide their workers with full rations and give them a piece of cloth every week. British warships on the West African Station, like other vessels, must hire them to spare the white crew from heavy labor. They pay the Kruboys the same wages as white sailors—£4 10s. a month plus rations. Needless to say, service on warships is popular, even though it prevents our friend from almost every opportunity for stealing chickens "and other things of which I may not speak," as the Greek historian Herodotus would say. I do not know how the navy pays the Kruboys, but I believe it is in cash. In the social circles I frequent most on the Coast—the merchant navy and the trading community—he is always paid in goods, such as cloth, gin, guns, tobacco, and gunpowder. These are adjusted slightly to fit his individual preferences. Each of these articles has a recognized value, and just as our coins can be exchanged, one can get "change" for a gun or any other trade item here.

The Kruboy much prefers being paid in goods. I well remember a vivid scene between a Captain and King Koffee of the Kru Coast while they were shouting over the terms for hiring workers during one voyage out. At the time, the Captain thought I was a member of a temperance society <note>W.W.T.A.A.: Likely the World’s Woman’s Christian Temperance Union or a similar organization</note> and pointedly asked Koffee to let him pay the workers in money instead of gin and gunpowder. King Koffee’s face was a sight to behold. If the Captain, whom he had known for a long time, had stood on his head and turned bright blue with yellow spots right before his eyes, it would not have been as much of a shock to His Majesty. "What good is that thing, Captain?" he asked, his voice ringing with disbelief and astonishment. <note>Original: "What for good him ting, Cappy? What for good him ting for we country, Cappy? I suppose you gib gin, tobacco, gun he be fit for trade, but money——"</note> "What good is money in our country, Captain? I suppose if you give gin, tobacco, or a gun, they are useful for trade, but money—" Here His Majesty’s feelings surpassed even his great command of language, and he spat with profound emotion and expression. The Captain’s expressive face was a battlefield of despair and grief at being forced to participate in a trade so unpopular in missionary circles. However, he controlled his feelings enough to carefully arrange...

### APPENDIX I
