The somewhat cumbersome wages the Kru worker <term>Kruboy: a member of the Kru ethnic group from the coast of Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, traditionally employed as sailors or laborers on European ships.</term> receives at the end of his term of service—after subtracting items taken on credit and adding what he has "found"—are certainly a source of great worry to him. He obtains a wooden box from the factory carpenter or buys a tin one, and puts his tobacco and small items inside. He then buys a padlock and locks up his treasure, hanging the key with his other charms <term>jujus: amulets or objects believed to have protective or magical powers.</term> around his neck. At this point, he has some peace regarding this portion of his belongings. However, it is only a temporary peace, for the day must eventually come when a clever genius arises among his fellow countrymen who will try to see if one key can open two locks. When that possibility becomes known, I can foresee nothing for the Kru worker but a nervous breakdown. Even now, with his mind at rest concerning the items in his box, he lives in a state of constant anxiety about those outside of it, which must lie on the deck during the return voyage to his home. He has to keep a watchful eye on them by day and sleep spread out over them by night for fear of his companions stealing them.

I cannot understand why he takes all this trouble regarding his possessions on the voyage home if current reports are true: that all wages earned by working men become the property of the tribal elders when they return. I personally doubt this is the case; rather, I suspect there is a very heavy tax levied on them. After all, the Kru worker is very much a married man, and the tribal elders must support and protect his wives and families while he is away at work. I would not be surprised if the law mandated that these wives and families "revert to the State" if the man fails to return within his appointed time. There must be something besides homesickness to account for the intense worry and apprehension shown by a detained Kru worker. I am certain the tax is heavily collected in cloth, for the men told me that if it were made into garments for themselves, they did not have to part with it upon their return. Needless to say, this causes our friend to turn his attention to needlework during his return voyage. I have often seen the main deck looking as if it had been taken over by a frenzied Dorcas working party <note>A church-sponsored group of women who sewed clothing for the poor, named after the biblical figure Dorcas (Tabitha).</note>.

Surprisingly little is known about the laws and language of these Kru people, considering how closely they associate with white people. I believe this stems not from the difficulty of learning their language, but from the ease and fluency [with which they speak ours...]

# TRADE AND LABOUR IN WEST AFRICA

The Kru speak their own version of our language—<term>Kru-English</term> <note>Also known as West African Pidgin English or "Trade English."</note>, or "trade English," as it is called. Therefore, it is unnecessary for a hot and tired white man to learn the <term>Kru mouth</term> <note>The Kru language or dialect.</note>. What particularly makes me think this is the case is that I have picked up a little of it myself. I found that I could make a <term>Kruman</term> understand what I was aiming for using this, along with my small vocabulary of <term>Bassa mouth</term> <note>The Bassa language.</note> and <term>Timneh</term> <note>The Temne language.</note>, on occasions when I wanted to say something to him that I did not want generally understood by others. 

The main points regarding the <term>Krumen</term> are well known by "old coasters" <note>Experienced European traders or residents on the West African coast.</note>: their willingness to work if they are well-fed, and their habit of signing up for twelve-month work terms before returning to "our country" (their home). A trader who is satisfied with a worker gives him a "book" <note>A letter of recommendation or a written contract.</note> when he leaves. This note tells the captain of any vessel that the trader will pay the man's passage back to his factory whenever he is ready to return to work. The period a man remains in his beloved "our country" seems to last until his savings are spent. 

One can imagine some sad partings in that far-away land. "My loves," says the Kru worker to his family, his voice heavy with tears, "I must go. There is no more cloth; I have nothing to cover myself before an easily-shocked world but this worn-out scrap of cotton." Then his family weeps with him—or, what is more likely, though less poetic, they spit with emotion. He tears himself away from them and comes aboard a passing steamer in the "uniform of Gunga Din" <note>A reference to Rudyard Kipling’s poem; it means he is wearing next to nothing.</note>—very little in front and even less behind. He travels down the coast on the strength of the little slip of paper from his white employer, which he has carefully treasured. He then works incredibly hard <note>original: "works like a nigger in the good sense of the term"</note> for another term to earn more goods for his folk back home.

Those men who are traveling to work for the first time, and those without "books," have no difficulty getting passage on the steamers. A captain is glad to take as many on board as he can, since he is certain to receive their passage money and a premium for them, because the demand for Kru labor is so high. 

However, even this system of working the West Coast has been greatly hindered in recent years by the actions of the French Government, which has imposed a tax on every laborer leaving their ports on the Ivory Coast. I believe this tax has now been removed or much reduced. As for the Liberian Republic, it simply collects its revenue in a completely unjustifiable way by taxing the <term>Krumen</term> who ship out as laborers. The <term>Krumen</term> are not their property, and the Liberian government does not dare to interfere with them on shore; however, due to a certain deal involving the famous Rubber <note>Likely referring to the Monrovian Rubber Company or similar concessions in Liberia during the late 19th century.</note>...

# APPENDIX I

Through their monopoly, the Liberians obtained some ready cash, which, with great foresight, they invested in two small gunboats. These allowed them to enforce their taxes on the <term>Krumen</term> <note>Members of the Kru ethnic group, known for their skill as sailors and laborers.</note> in their small canoes. I do not feel as much sympathy for the <term>Krumen</term> or their employers in this matter as I perhaps should, because the <term>Krumen</term> are fools <note>original: "silly hens"</note> for not going ashore and wiping out Liberia, and the white men are fools for not—but I had better leave that opinion unexpressed.

The ability to manage <term>Kruboys</term> is a great accomplishment for anyone working on the West Coast. One man will get 20 percent more work out of his staff and always keep them cheerful, fit, and ready; meanwhile, another will get very little out of the same group of men except frustration for himself and damage to his goods. However, this essential and important factor in trade cannot be taught with ink. Some men fall into the proper way of managing the "boys" very quickly; others may have years of experience and yet fail to learn it. The rule is: make them respect you, and make them like you, and then the job is done. 

But first dealing with a <term>Kruboy</term>, despite all his good points, is very trying work. They give a newcomer a terrible time while they are experimenting on him to see how far they can take advantage of him. They do this very cleverly, but shortsightedly, *in the African fashion* <note>original: "more Africano"</note>, for they spoil the tempers of half the white men they have to deal with. It is not necessary to treat them brutally—in fact, it does not pay to do so—but it is necessary to treat them strictly and to keep a steady hand over them. Never let them become overly familiar, and never let them see that you have made a mistake. 

When you make a mistake in giving an order, let it be understood that your way of doing things is a particularly clever trick of your own; if it fails, let it be their fault. They will fully realize this if it is managed correctly. I speak from experience. For example, once, because the "superior sex" <note>A humorous, ironic reference to men.</note> was bedridden with fever and making his temperature rise by worrying about getting some ebony logs out to an annoying river steamer—which insisted on signaling loudly for cargo just then—I said, "Leave it to me; I'll get it shipped all right." 

I then proceeded, with the help of three <term>Kruboys</term>, to raft that ebony out. The situation was difficult, and the way the ship's captain kept pacing frantically around his deck while shouting in a foreign language—which was nevertheless quite easy to understand—was distracting. However, I did not bother providing the information he requested regarding exactly what kind of idiot I was; he was neither a psychiatrist nor an anthropologist, and he had no right to that information. 

Instead, I placed a raft made of a very light wood (of which we had a large supply) onto the tow line. This raft held up the ebony, and the current carried it down to the steamer successfully. Then we hauled the line back and sent him more using this improvised plan. Just to hurry things up—since delaying a ship is a deadly crime—some of that ebony was also sent out in a canoe, and everything ended happily. The <term>Kruboys</term> <note>Men of the Kru ethnic group, widely employed as sailors and laborers on the West African coast.</note> considered themselves to have been spectators of yet another manifestation of "white intelligence." 

In defense of the captain's remarks, I must admit he could not see me because I was positioned behind a stack of wood. Nevertheless, I do not mean to suggest that this method of shipping ebony is a good one. I will not be trying it again anytime soon; the situation cannot be managed unless you have, as God provided me, a very swift current. Furthermore, although I did shout a few things back to the captain from behind the woodstack once things were going well, I did not feel right accepting his apologetic invitation to come on board for a drink.

If written in full, my experiences with <term>Kruboys</term> would make an excellent manual for a newcomer, but they are too lengthy for this appendix. My first experience with them on a short journey into the bush aged me considerably. Ever since then, I have avoided escorting <term>Kruboys</term> through the West African wilderness among irritable local gentlemen and their bold, impudent wives.

I have always admired men for their strength, their courage, their enterprise, and their unceasing struggle for "the beyond"—for something more. But I did not realize how immense this latter characteristic could be until I had to deal with <term>Krumen</term>. One might have been excused for thinking that a man without property taxes, without pockets, and without the diverse, desire-creating culture of modern European civilization and education would necessarily be limited in his desires. 

But one would be wrong—profoundly wrong—to think so. For the <term>Kruman</term> longs for and demands as many things for his body as the late <term>Faustus</term> <note>A legendary scholar who traded his soul to the devil for infinite knowledge and worldly pleasures.</note> did for his soul. This interesting creature would have to be categorized among the apes at once if wanting very little were the crucial test for determining—

Later, when I got to know the Krumen well, I learned that they not only desired the vast majority of articles they saw, but did more—they obtained them. At least, they obtained some of them without asking me; commodities such as chickens, palm wine, old tins and bottles, and even other men’s wives were never safe. One member of that first gang of boys demonstrated "self-help" to such a remarkable degree that I named him Smiles <note>A reference to Samuel Smiles, the author of the 1859 book *Self-Help*, which championed the virtues of industry and perseverance.</note>. His original name—"You-be-damned"—was both long and improper, necessitating a change of some sort. However, even this name change brought no comfort to someone like me, who was still burdened by conventional ideas regarding property. I found frequent roll calls necessary so that the crimes of my friend Smiles and his companions would not accumulate to an unmanageable degree.

The routine used to go something like this: "Where is Nettlerash?" "He is drunk, Master." "Where is Smiles?" "He is in town, stealing, Master." "Where is Black Man’s Misery?" But I will draw a veil over these confessions, for there is simply no artistic restraint in a Kruman when he is telling the truth—or otherwise—about a fellow human being.

After gaining enough experience with this gang to fill a hat (always remembering that "one of the worst things you can do in West Africa is to worry yourself"), I recalled the advice I had received from my cousin, Rose Kingsley. She had successfully ridden through Mexico during a period when it was undergoing a particularly violent revolution, and her advice was "to always maintain a firm manner." I thought I would try this on those <term>Kruboys</term> <note>Men of the Kru ethnic group, often employed as laborers.</note> and said "NO" instead of "I wish you would not do that, please." I cannot say it was an immediate success.

"NO," I said in my sternest tone, and after buying other items, we moved on. The wet season in West Africa arrived, and those red parasols bled. To this day, my scientific soul has never been able to account for the vast amount of crimson dye those miserable cotton things poured out, plentifully drenching myself, their owners—the Kru boys <note>The Kru (or Krumen) are an ethnic group from Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire renowned for their skills as sailors and laborers on European ships.</note>—and everything we were associated with that day. I am quite prepared to hear that some subsequent traveler has found a "red trail" in Africa itself, like the ones one often sees marked upon maps. When they do, I hereby claim that real red trail as mine.

I confess I like the African on the whole, a thing I never expected to do when I went to the Coast with the idea that he was a degraded, savage, cruel brute; but that is a trifling error you soon get rid of when you know him. The Kru boy is decidedly the most likeable of all Africans that I know. Wherein his charm lies is difficult to describe, and you certainly need the patience of Job and a conscience made of stretching leather to deal with the Kru boy in the African climate and survive. In his better moments, he reminds me of that charming personality, the Irish peasant; for though he lacks the sparkle, he is full of humor and is the laziest and the most industrious of mankind. He lies and tells the truth in such a hopelessly uncertain manner that you cannot rely on him for either. He is ungrateful and faithful to the death, honest and thievish, all in one and the same specimen.

Ingratitude is a crime very frequently laid to the account of all Africans, but I think this is unfair; certainly, I have never had to complain of it, and the Krumen often show gratitude for good treatment in a grand way. The way those Kru boys of the gallant Captain Lane helped him work the Lagos Bar <note>A notoriously dangerous sandbar at the entrance to the Lagos lagoon in Nigeria.</note> and save lives by the dozen from the stranded ships upon it—and hauled their "Master" <note>original: "Massa"</note> out from among the shark-filled foam every time he went into it when the lifeboat capsized—would have done credit to the lifeboat men of Deal or Norfolk. However, the secret of their devotion is their personal attachment. They do not save people out of the surf based on abstract moral principles. The African at large is not an enthusiast for moral principles, and one and all, they will let nature take its course if they don’t feel particularly keen on a man surviving.

Half of the African’s ingratitude, although it may look very bad on paper, is really not so very bad; for half the time, you have been asking him to be grateful to you for doing things for him, or giving him things, that he does not care a bit about. I quite share his feelings; for example, I feel the same toward half the things in civilized countries that I am expected to be glad to get. “Oh,

"How nice it must be to be able to get about in cars, omnibuses, and railway trains again!" Is it? Well, I do not think so, and I do not feel glad about it. Similarly, we will take an African case of ingratitude. A white friend of mine put himself to an enormous amount of trouble to save the life of one of his sub-traders who had been in an accident, and he succeeded. It had been the custom of the man's wife to bring the trader small presents of chickens and other items from time to time. She grunted, and the next morning she brought him a present of the most miserable, skinny, one-and-a-half-feathered chicken you ever laid eyes on. They match" <note>original: "Massa, fo sure them der chicken no be 'ticularly good chicken, but fo sure dem der man no be 'ticularly good man. They go"</note>.

I have referred at great length to the Krumen <note>The Kru people of Liberia and Ivory Coast, often employed as sailors and laborers.</note> because of their importance, and also because they are the natives whom white men deal with as servants more than any others. In Cameroon, the Germans are now largely using the Batanga natives on the plantations. The Duallas, the great trading tribe in the Cameroon River, are too lazy <term>lazy: The author is reflecting common colonial-era prejudices regarding the work habits of established trading tribes.</term> to do any heavy work. They also tried to import laborers from Togoland, but this attempt was not a success, ending in the revolt of 1894, which cost several white lives. Public works are carried out, as they are in our own colonies, by criminals in the chain-gang. 

The Germans have had many accusations hurled against them by people of their own nationality, but on the whole, these "atrocities" have been much exaggerated and only half understood. They certainly have not amounted to anything like the things that have gone on in the "philanthropic" Congo Free State <note>A reference to the Belgian Congo under King Leopold II, which was notoriously brutal despite its official humanitarian pretenses.</note>. The food distributed by the German Government is the best government ration given on the entire West Coast. When they allowed me to have some of their native employees—as when I was up Cameroon Mountain, for example—I bought rations from the government stores for them. I was much struck by the soundness and good quality of both the rice and the beef. Furthermore, the rations they gave out to those Dahomeyans or Togolanders who revolted were so much more than they could, or cared to, eat, that they used to sell much of it to the Duallas in Bell Town. The main issue that has brought the Germans into disrepute with the natives they employ is their military spirit. This leads to a desire to regulate everything, along with another attribute of that military mindset: nagging. You should never nag an African; it only makes him confused and then sulky. When he is sulky, he will simply lie down and die just to spite you. But despite the Germans' tendency toward this unpleasant habit of military regularity and so on, the natives from the Kru Coast, Bassa, and the French Ivory Coast return to them time and again for stints of work. Therefore, there must be a great deal of exaggeration regarding their bad treatment, for these natives are perfectly free to choose whether or not to work for them.

The French employ Loango "boys" <note>In this period, "boy" was a common colonial term for a male servant or laborer regardless of age.</note> as factory hands. These people are very bright and intelligent, but as a M'pongwe man who knew them well said: "They are much too likely to be devils to be treated too kindly." They are also undoubtedly prone to poisoning people, which is an unpleasant habit in a house servant. Their military forces are composed of Senegalese <term>Laptot</term> <note>Senegalese sailors or soldiers in the French colonial service.</note>. These are very fine, fierce men; I believe they are superior as fighters to our Hausas, and they are very devoted to—and well-treated by—their French officers.

The trade returns—with the balance all on the wrong side—clearly show that the Frenchman does not know how to expand trade in his territories. Nevertheless, he does know how to take possession of Africa better than we do, and this means he knows how to deal with the natives. The building up of the French Congo <note>Congo Français</note>, for example, has not cost a third of the human lives (black or white) that an equivalent portion of the Belgian Congo <note>Congo Belge</note> has, nor has it cost a third of the expense of Uganda or Sierra Leone. 

In England, it is customary to focus on their commercial failure and draw the mistaken conclusion that France will soon abandon the effort when she finds it does not pay. This is an error because commercial success—making the venture profitable—is not the French ideal in this matter. It is our own ideal, and I am the last person to say our ideal is wrong; but it is not the French ideal, and I am the last person to say France is wrong either. In England, you will often hear people say regarding French annexation in Africa, "Oh, let her have that death trap, and much good may it do her!" France knows very well what good it will do her. She will cheerfully take everything she is allowed to obtain quietly as a concession <note>original: "sop"</note> for her silence regarding Egypt, and she will cheerfully fight you for the rest—and no one can blame her. She knows Africa is a superb training ground for her officers. Sham fights and autumn maneuvers have a certain value in forming a fighting army, but ten years' worth of these parlor games combined cannot compare to one month of real warfare for preparing an army for its actual duties. 

France knows well that the real work will come some day—and not far off—for her army. She cares little how soon it comes, for she has no ideal of peace before her; she never has had, and never will. The next time she tests her strength against one of us Germanic <note>original: "Teutonic"</note> nations, she will be armed with men who have learned their trade well on the burning sands of Senegal, and they will be very difficult to defeat. 

We do not need Africa as a training ground for our army; India is as magnificent a military academy as any nation requires. However, we do need all the territory we can get in West, East, and South Africa as a market, and it is here that we clash with France. Not only does France fail to develop the trade of her colonies for her own profit, but she also stifles general trade through her preferential tariffs and other measures. Consequently, we cannot enter her colonies and trade freely, even though she and Germany *can* come into ours. We can go into her colonies and do business with French goods, and this is done; however, French goods are not as suitable in their manufacture, nor can they be sold at a high enough profit to build a large trade. Yet France places few obstacles, if any, regarding plantation ventures. Still, these ventures are not highly profitable in Africa at present because they are so hindered by the scarcity <note>original: "dearth"</note> of good labor.

The United Presbyterian Mission, which works in Old Calabar <note>Now part of modern-day Nigeria</note>, was founded with the intention of starting a mission that—once white men had established it—would be run by educated Christian black people from Jamaica, where this mission had long been established and had prospered. However, it was discovered that these individuals, although primarily of African descent, had lost the natural resistance to the deadly malarial climate that their ancestors possessed. This loss occurred because of their forced removal from Africa, in some cases over the course of only one generation. Consequently, the mission is now run by white people. This is not because these good people have a greater resistance to the fever than the Jamaican Christians, but because they are more devoted to the evangelization of the African people; the black assistance they do receive comes from a few educated Efik people <term>Effiks: An ethnic group from the Cross River region of Nigeria</term> of Calabar, with the exception of Mrs. Fuller.

The Congo Free State has imported laborers from both the West Indies—principally Barbadians—and China. In both cases, the mortality rate has been horrific—even higher than the white mortality rate, which experts estimate at 77 percent for the Congo. Therefore, the experiment has failed. It might be argued that much of this mortality resulted from how these laborers were treated in the Free State; however, the case of the Annamese <note>Vietnamese people from the former French protectorate of Annam</note> in the French Congo <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>, who are well treated, proves this is not entirely the cause. These Annamese are political prisoners resulting from the French occupation of Tonkin <note>original: "Tong-kin"; the northern region of modern-day Vietnam</note>. The mortality rate among one group of 100 men employed to clear a path through swampy ground from Glass to Libreville—a distance of two and a half miles—was seventy percent. This occurred even though the swamp was not particularly bad by swamp standards and was swept by sea air the entire way.

Even if the experiment of imported labor had been successful for the time being, I believe it would be a serious mistake to import labor into Africa. My reason is that Africa itself possesses the most magnificent supply of labor in the whole world. Surely, if her children could build up the prosperity and trade of the Americas, as they have, she should be able to build up her own under proper guidance and good management. However, good guidance and proper management are exactly what is needed—and what is currently lacking. It is impossible to cover this complex issue fully here, and I will merely ask unbiased people who disagree with me to consider whether they do not think that since so much has been achieved with one African...

The future of Africa cannot be separated from the future of its native people by importing "yellow races" <note>original: "yellow races"; likely referring to East Asian laborers</note> or Indians. Similarly, the missionary question cannot be separated from the future of the African natives. Therefore, this subject must be addressed. 

I begin my remarks by stating that I have a deep personal respect for several missionaries. Naturally, it is impossible to know individuals such as Mr. and Mrs. Dennis Kemp of the Gold Coast, Mr. and Mrs. Jacot, Mr. and Mrs. Forget, Mr. Gacon, and Dr. Nassau of Gaboon—along with many others—without immediately recognizing their beautiful characters and noble intentions. Indeed, taken as a whole, missionaries must be regarded as incredibly brave, noble-minded men. They risk their own lives, and often those of their wives and children, definitely sacrificing their personal comfort and safety to do what they believe is their simple duty. 

However, it is their methods of working that have produced the results in West Africa which everyone truly interested in the region must regret. One is forced to make an admission that goes against our British <term>insular: narrow-minded or isolated; here, referring to British cultural pride</term> prejudice: that the Protestant English missionaries have had the most to do with making the African "useless" <note>The author implies the education makes them unfit for both traditional life and colonial labor</note>.

The negative effects of their teaching have arisen primarily from the missionary's failure to recognize that the difference between the African and themselves is a difference of kind, not just of degree. I am aware that several prominent ethnologists <term>ethnologist: a person who studies the characteristics of different peoples and the relationships between them</term> support the missionaries' view. However, many anatomical facts suggest otherwise, and an even larger number of facts relating to mental traits point the other way. I am certain that a Black man is no more an "undeveloped white man" than a rabbit is an undeveloped hare. The mental difference between the two races is very similar to the difference between men and women in our own society. An exceptional woman, whether mentally or physically, will surpass an average man, but no woman ever equals a truly great man. 

The missionary to Africa has done exactly what my father found them doing to the Polynesians:

> "regarding the native minds as so many jugs only requiring to be emptied of the stuff which is in them and refilled with the particular form of dogma he is engaged in teaching, in order to make them the equals of the white races."

This method of procedure works in many different ways. It eliminates the parts of the native "fetish" <term>fetish: a term used by the author to describe traditional West African religious beliefs and social laws</term> that acted as a healthy restraint on the African. Admittedly, the children in the mission school are better than the children—

They are outside of it in some ways; they show a great talent for learning anything that comes their way—but there is a significant difference between white and black children. The African child is a very serious creature. It comes into the world in large numbers and looks upon it with its large, sad eyes, as if it were carefully weighing the question of whether or not this is a suitable place for a respectable soul to live. Four times out of ten, it decides that it is not, and dies. If, however, it decides to stay, it spends between two and three years in a grim and deep study—occasionally letting out howls which end suddenly in a sob—but it never whines. At the end of this period, it begins to eat with a spoon, walks about, and makes itself useful to its mother or enters the mission school. If it remains in its native state, it has no frivolous toys; a little hoe or a small <term>calabash: a dried gourd used as a container or utensil</term> are considered better training. If it goes to the school, it picks up the lessons taught there with astonishing speed—raising hopes for its future which are only too frequently disappointed in a few years’ time.

The African does not become joyful until he reaches the age of indiscretion; but when he reaches this age, he always cheers up considerably. Then, whatever his previous training may have been, he takes to what Mr. <note>Rudyard Kipling, the famous British author and poet</note> Kipling calls "boot" <note>This likely refers to imported trade alcohol, a common subject of Kingsley’s critiques</note> with great enthusiasm—and he consumes an enormous quantity of it. For the next sixteen years, barring accidents, he "lives wildly"; he lives wildly and carefully, terrified by his many <term>fetish: traditional West African spiritual beliefs and ritual prohibitions</term> restrictions if he is a pagan. But if he is in that partially converted state where you usually find him after someone has labored for his soul—then he lives wildly without any restraint.

It is most unfair to describe Africans in this state as "converted," whether in missionary reports or in attacks against them. They are not converted in the least. A truly converted African is a very beautiful example of a Christian; but those Africans who are the main subject of missionary reports—and who provide such material for those who mock them—have merely had the restraint of fear removed from their minds in the mission schools without the greater restraint of love being put in its place.

The missionary-made man is the curse of the Coast, and you find him in European clothes and without them, all the way from Sierra Leone to <term>Loanda: Luanda, the capital of Angola</term>. The pagans despise him, the whites hate him, yet he thinks enough of himself to remain comfortable. His conceit is marvelous; nothing equals it except perhaps that of the type of person common among us which the *Saturday Review* <note>A prominent British weekly magazine of the era</note> once aptly described as "the suburban agnostic"; and the missionary man is very much like...

...the suburban agnostic in his religious method. After a period of mission-school life, he returns to his <term>country-fashion: traditional African customs and native way of life</term> and deals with the <term>fetish: an object believed to have supernatural powers, or the religion associated with it</term> connected with it very much in the same way that a suburban agnostic deals with his religion; that is, he removes all the inconvenient parts. "I wouldn't be surprised if there might be something to the idea of the immortality of the soul and a future Heaven, you know—but as for Hell, my dear sir, that is rank superstition; no one believes in it now! And as for keeping the Sabbath and food restrictions—what utter rubbish for enlightened people!" 

This is how the backsliding African deals with his "country-fashion" ideas: he eliminates the idea of immediate spiritual retribution and so on, but keeps polygamy, the dances, and all the lazy, hazy-minded native ways. The education he received at the mission school in reading and writing fits him for a commercial career, and since every African is a born trader, he embarks on it—and there are quite disgraceful things that happen! On the West Coast, he frequently sets up a business for himself; on the Southwest Coast, he usually becomes a sub-trader for one of the great English, French, or German firms. On both coasts, he makes himself disliked and brings down harsh criticism on all black traders, expressed in language more powerful than polite. This wholesale denunciation of black traders is unfair because there are many perfectly honest native traders; still, the majority are recruited from the failures of missionary schools and are utterly bad.

"After this, therefore because of this" <note>original: "*Post hoc non propter hoc*"—a logical fallacy suggesting that because one thing follows another, the first must have caused the second</note> is an excellent maxim, but it is one that never seems to enter the missionary’s head down here. Highly disgusted and pained by his pupils' behavior, but absolutely convinced of the excellence of his own teaching methods and the spiritual equality of all Christians regardless of color, the missionary stands up and says things about the bad influence of white traders that one can easily understand him saying. He states that they lure the pupils away from the <term>fold: the church community</term> to their destruction. Nevertheless, these claims are not true. 

Then the white trader hears these accusations, gets defensive, and says things about the effect of missionary training on the African. His words are true but harsh, because it is not the missionaries' intention to turn out skillful forgers and total liars, even though that is practically what they do. My role, when I stumble into this state of mutual blame, is to get myself into trouble with both parties. The missionary thinks I am misguided for regarding the African’s behavior as part of his natural character, and the trader considers me a soft-headed idiot when I state that it is not the missionary’s individual fault that a lamb recently acquired from the church has gone down the <term>primrose path: a path of ease and pleasure that leads to ruin</term> with

The two things to which the missionary blames for his lack of success are polygamy and the liquor trade. Now, polygamy is—like most other subjects—a difficult thing to form a fair opinion on, especially if you make a careful study of the facts before forming that opinion. Therefore, if you wish to produce an opinion that is generally acceptable in "civilized" circles, it is advisable to follow the usual recipe for forming opinions: just take one of your own prejudices and pair it with the so-called opinions of the class of people who share that same prejudice. I have become so entangled with facts that I cannot follow this plan. Consequently, I am compelled to think that polygamy is not an entirely unmixed evil for the African, and that at the African's current level of culture, it cannot be eradicated. 

This conclusion arises from two reasons. The first is that it is perfectly impossible for one African woman to do all the housework, prepare the food, fetch water, cultivate the plantations, and look after all the children belonging to one man. She might be able to do it if she had the work ethic of an English or Irish cleaning woman <term>charwoman: a woman employed to clean a house or office</term>, but she does not. An entire village of African women does not do as much work in a week as one of those cleaning women will do in a day. Furthermore, the African woman is quite indifferent to the extent her husband may flirt with other women, as long as he does not give them more cloth and beads than he gives her. 

The second reason for polygamy lies in a custom well-known to ethnologists. This custom is so widely practiced that one might say it is constant throughout all African tribes, though there are many tribes whose domestic relationships have not yet been carefully observed.

Regarding the liquor trade—no one seems inclined to speak the truth about it in West Africa. What I say must be understood to apply only to West Africa, because I do not like to form opinions without having had opportunities for personal observation. The only part of Africa where I have had these opportunities is the region from Sierra Leone to Angola. Reports from South Africa show that an entirely different and most unhealthy state of affairs exists there, resulting from its invasion by a mix of European nationalities and low-quality individuals who are greedy for wealth. West African conditions are no more like South African conditions than they are like those in India. On the whole, the missionary party has gravely exaggerated both the evil and the extent of the liquor trade in West Africa. I make...

I make an exception in favor of the former superintendent of the Wesleyan mission on the Gold Coast, the Rev. Dennis Kemp. He had enough courage and integrity to stand up at a public meeting in Liverpool on July 2nd, 1896, and state his opinion that "the natives of the Gold Coast were remarkably moderate in their drinking; but he believed that spirits were of no benefit to the natives, and they would be better off without them." I have quoted his entire remark, as it is never fair to quote only half of what a person says on any subject. However, I do not agree with the second half of it; furthermore, the Gold Coast natives are no more moderate—perhaps even less so—than other tribes on the Coast. 

I have attempted elsewhere <gloss>1</gloss> to show that the liquor trade is by no means the most significant factor in the failure of missions on the West Coast. Instead, the missionary party has used this issue in an unjustifiable way because they know the campaign against alcohol is currently popular in England. It also has the advantage of making donors at home view the African as an innocent creature who is led astray by wicked white men. This makes the African appear even more interesting, more worthy, and in greater need of donations than ever. I would quite like to see the African lady or gentleman who could actually be "led astray"—in my experience on the Coast, all the influencing has worked the other way around.

I am not saying that every missionary on the West Coast who makes false statements on this subject is an original liar. Usually, he is merely following his leaders and repeating their observations without investigating the evidence around him. The missionary-supporting public in England and Scotland is also largely to blame. They have a perpetual thirst for thrilling details about the number of baptisms and "spiritual experiences" among the people they pay others to risk their lives to convert. They also crave dramatic accounts of the difficulties these emissaries must face. 

As for the general public who believe these statements, I think they are prone to accept them as true—without bothering to investigate calmly—because of the social problems they see around them directly caused by drink. They assume similar statements regarding other people must also be true. I have no hesitation in saying that in the whole of West Africa, during an entire week, there is not even a quarter of the drunkenness you can see on any Saturday night during just a couple of hours in Vauxhall Road <note>A road in South London that, in the late 19th century, was associated with poverty and heavy drinking.</note>. Furthermore, you will not find in a whole year of investigation on the Coast even a seventieth part of the evil, degradation, and premature health decline that you would see there.

In a later letter, Mr. Robertson noted that he had been "assisted in performing the analysis by an expert in alcohol chemistry, who stated that this sample did not differ in any significant way from, and was neither more nor less harmful to health than, gin bought in various parts of London and submitted for analysis."

In addition to this analysis, I also have one of Messrs. Peters' gin, which is equally satisfactory. Since Van Huytemers and Peters are the two primary suppliers of the gin sent to West Africa, I believe this refutes the "poison" claims. It should provide sufficient evidence for anyone who is not a strict teetotaler. Strict teetotalers are principled people, and I respect them more than those who do not practice teetotalism themselves but think it is a good thing to impose on others. Furthermore, there is no use arguing with them because they believe all alcohol is poison and will not accept any evidence to the contrary, so "the matter is settled" <note>The author uses the phrase "palaver done set," a West African Pidgin English expression meaning the discussion is over or the dispute is resolved.</note>. However, a large majority of those who attack the African liquor trade—or believe the attacks are justified—are not teetotalers themselves, and therefore should be capable of forming a fair opinion.

My personal knowledge of the district where most of the liquor is imported—the Oil Rivers <term>Oil Rivers</term> <note>The delta of the Niger River in modern-day Nigeria, named for the palm oil produced there.</note>—was gained in Duke Town, Old Calabar. I have been there four separate times, and last year I stayed there continuously for several months. During that period, if Duke Town had been inclined to go on a drinking binge, it certainly could have done so; the police and most of the government officials were away at Brass due to the Akassa conflict <note>A reference to the 1895 raid by the Nembe people on the Royal Niger Company's headquarters at Akassa.</note>, and the few officials and white traders who remained were bedridden with an epidemic of malarial typhoid. 

But Duke Town did nothing of the sort. Night after night, I used to be alone in the heart of the town at Eyamba’s market by Prince Archibong's house, watching the "devil-making" <term>devil-makings</term> <note>A common term used by Europeans at the time to describe West African religious ceremonies or masquerades.</note> ceremonies taking place there, and the amount of drunkenness I saw was exceedingly small. I did the same at the neighboring town of Qwa. My knowledge of Bonny, Bell, and Akkwa towns, Libreville, Lambaréné, Cabinda, Boma, Banana, Nkoi, Luanda, and others is extensive and detailed. I have spent hours in them when all the missionaries and government officials were safe in their distant houses. If the evils of the liquor trade were even half as bad as they are claimed to be, I certainly would have encountered them in terrible forms—but I did not.

I will not quote the statistics of the case here, as they are easily accessible to anyone through government reports.

...interested in the matter. I consider their value to be small unless combined with a knowledge of the West Coast trade. The liquor enters through a few ports on the West Coast and passes into the hands of those tribes who act as middlemen between the white traders and the interior tribes who produce trade goods. It is thereby spread over an enormous extent of thickly inhabited country.

We English have no direct contact with the interior trade—except within the territory of the Royal Niger Company. The Delta tribes with whom we deal in the Oil Rivers <term>Oil Rivers</term> <note>The delta of the Niger River in modern-day Nigeria, named for the palm oil produced there.</note> survive on this trade between the interior and the coast. They prefer to use spirits as a medium of exchange because they earn the highest percentage of profit from them and suffer the lowest percentage of loss from damage while handling them. 

Alcohol does not get spoiled by dampness, as tobacco and cloth do. Indeed, in addition to the moisture supplied by their humid climate, the middlemen add a large quantity of river water to the spirits before the product leaves their hands. Meanwhile, with other trade goods, it is a constant struggle to keep them free from moisture and mildew. In their coastal towns, there are immense stores of gin in cases; they would no more think of drinking this themselves than we, if we were butchers, would think of eating all the stock in our shop. 

A certain percentage of spirits is consumed in the Delta, and if spirits are needed anywhere, they are needed in the Niger Delta region. About one-eighth of what is used here is for fetish-worship <term>fetish-worship</term> <note>A historical term for West African traditional religious practices involving spiritual objects or "charms."</note>. It is poured out on the ground or mixed with other items to hang in bottles over fish-traps, and so on, to create residences for guardian spirits who are expected to come and take up their abode in them. 

The principle of "spirits for the spirits"—similar to the phrase "sweets to the sweet"—is universal in West Africa. Those photographs you are often shown of dead chiefs’ graves with bottles on them merely demonstrate that the deceased was taking a little liquor with him for his own use in the underworld. He believes the underworld has a chilly and damp climate, and he takes a little extra to give a propitiatory drink <term>propitiatory peg</term> <note>An offering intended to appease or gain favor; a "peg" is a term for a measure of spirits.</note> to one of the ruling authorities there—or to any old friend he may come across in the Elysian Fields <note>A reference to the Greek concept of the afterlife; here used to describe the West African spirit world.</note>. 

This is possibly a misguided pagan practice for him to follow, and it is generally held in European circles that the underworld such an individual will go to is neither damp nor chilly. But even granting this, no one can deny that the world he spends his life in here is damp, and that the natives of the Niger Delta live in a saturated forest swamp region that reeks with malaria. Their damp, mud-walled houses are frequently flooded, and they themselves spend the greater part of their time wading through the...

...foul-smelling mangrove swamps. Then, for five months of the year, they are enveloped in the almost continuous torrential downpours of the West African rainy season. This is followed in the Delta by the so-called "dry" season, with its thick morning and evening mists and air that is rarely above the dew point. Furthermore, their food is of poor quality and insufficient quantity; in districts near the coast, it is noticeably deficient in meat of any kind. Given these conditions, I think the desire for spirits and tobacco is quite reasonable. When they are taken in moderation, as they usually are, they are anything but harmful. 

The African has not a shadow of a doubt on this point, and he will have some form of alcohol. When he cannot get the "white man’s spirit"—*min makara* <note>original: "min makara"; a term used in Calabar for imported European liquor.</note>, as he calls it in Calabar—he takes the "black man’s spirit," *min effik*. This is palm wine. Although it has escaped the abuse heaped on rum and gin, it is actually worse for the native than either of these. He has to drink a disgusting quantity of it because he does not get the stimulating effect as quickly from palm wine as he does from gin or rum, and the enormous quantity consumed at one sitting will distribute its effects over an entire week. 

You can always tell whether a native has had one glass too many of rum, or half a gallon or so too much palm wine. He soon recovers from the first, while the palm wine makes him a disgusting nuisance for days. The constitutional effects of palm wine are also worse, for it produces a specific type of kidney disease which—if it does not end the life of the sufferer in a sudden seizure—kills him gradually with dropsy <term>dropsy</term> <note>An archaic term for edema, the swelling of soft tissues due to the accumulation of excess water.</note>.

There is another native drink which causes great misery for the African in the form of intoxication combined with a severe bilious attack <term>bilious attack</term> <note>A historical term for a digestive upset or headache attributed to excess bile or liver issues.</note>. It is made from honey flavored with the bark of a certain tree, and since it is very popular, I had better not spread it further by giving the recipe. Imported gin keeps the African away from these abominations, with which he must disrupt his internal organs before he can get the stimulus that enables him to resist this vile climate. In particular, it will keep him from his worst intoxicant, *lhiamba* (*Cannabis sativa*), a plant which grows wild on the Southwest Coast and on the West Coast for all I know, as well as the African or bowstring hemp (*Sanseviera guiniensis*). 

The plant that produces *lhiamba* is a nettle-like plant growing six to ten feet high. The natives collect the tops of the stems, with the seeds still on them, in little bundles and dry them. It is evidently the seeds which they regard as the important part, although they do not collect these separately. However, you hear great arguments among them when they are buying and selling a little bundle over the quality of the...

<header>APPENDIX I</header>

As the seeds are shaken out, "A" says, "*Chi! Chi! Chi!*" <note>original: "Chi! Chi! Chi!"; an exclamation of disappointment or dismissal.</note> "This is worthless; there are no seeds." "Aï, Aï," <note>original: "Ai, Ai"; an exclamation of disagreement or emphasis.</note> says "B," "there were never so many seeds in a bundle of *lhiamba* <term>lhiamba: a local name for cannabis or hemp</term>," and so on. It is smoked, similar to the *ganja* of India, rather than consumed as a preparation like *bhang*. The method the Africans in the Congo used to smoke it was very unusual. 

They would hollow out a small hole in the ground and build a little dome over it. They would place a few hemp tops inside, followed by several stones heated red-hot in a fire. Then the dome was sealed up and a reed was stuck through it. One man after another would go to the reed and draw as much smoke as possible into his lungs with one prolonged, deep breath. Each would then step aside and cough in a hard, hacking, and distressing way for ten minutes at a time, before returning to the reed for another pull. 

In addition to the unpleasantness of hearing their coughing, *lhiamba* causes trouble with the men because it spoils their tempers. it makes them moody, irritable, and prone to quarreling with each other. When they take an excessive dose, their company is more terrifying than tolerable. I once encountered three men who had reached this state and a fourth man who had not, but was part of the group. They fought with him and broke his head <note>likely meaning they caused a scalp wound or concussion</note>. We then proceeded on our way. One man took flying leaps at certain spots, occasionally climbing trees and throwing himself into the bushes alongside the path because he saw "pools of moving blood" on it. (He remarked as he sat where he fell, "If the blood had not kept moving, I could have managed it.") The others were preoccupied with various creatures that—judging from their descriptions—I was truly thankful were not actually there. 

The men’s state of mind, however, soon cleared. I must say this was the only time I encountered *lhiamba* producing such strong effects. Usually, the men just have that racking cough that lets you know what they have been up to and quarrel for a short time. However, when they take a whiff of *lhiamba* in the morning before starting a march, the effect seems beneficial, enabling them to cover ground easily and endure a long journey without exhaustion. Still, a small shot of rum is far better for them. Many other intoxicants made from forest plants are known to and used by the "witch doctors" <term>witch doctors: a historical term for traditional healers and spiritual practitioners</term>.

You may ask: "Well! If it is not polygamy and not drink that makes the West African as useless as he currently is for developing the country, what is it?" In my opinion, it is the type of instruction he has received. I do not mean that this instruction is necessarily bad in itself, but rather bad—

...from being unsuited to the type of man to whom it has been given. It tends to develop his emotionalism, his laziness, and his vanity, but it does nothing to develop those parts of his character which are underdeveloped and in great need of it; thereby throwing the man's entire character out of balance.

The greatest inferiority of the African compared to the European lies in the matter of mechanical understanding. I admit that I regard not only the African, but all people of color, as inferior—inferior in nature, not just in degree—to the white races. I say this although I know it is unscientific to lump all Africans together and then generalize about them, because the differences between various tribes are very great. Nevertheless, there are certain constant traits in their character, regardless of the tribe, that allow us to generalize for practical purposes by making a simple distinction between Negroes and Bantu. On the subject of this division, I may remark that the Negro is superior to the Bantu. He is both physically and intellectually the more powerful man, and although he does not adopt Christianity easily, he does often adapt well to civilization. 

The native officials mentioned by Mr. Hodgson <note>Sir Frederic Hodgson (1851–1925), a British colonial administrator.</note> in his letter to the *Times* on January 4, 1895, who satisfactorily managed the postal and government printing work of the Gold Coast Colony, as well as all the subordinate customs officials in the Niger Coast Protectorate—indeed, I might say all of them across the British possessions on the West Coast—are educated Negroes. I am aware that all sea captains consider this latter group to be "poisonous nuisances," but then, every typical sea captain regards customs officials as poisonous nuisances anywhere, regardless of their color. In addition to these, you will find, especially in Lagos, excellent full-blooded Negroes wearing European clothes and possessing European culture. The most successful among them are lawyers, doctors, and merchants, and I have known many African women who have achieved the same level of culture as their husbands. 

On the West African coast, you do not find the Bantu people as advanced, except for the M'pongwe; I am convinced that this tribe is not pure Bantu but originates from Negro stock. You will find that the educated Black people on the Bantu coast (from Cameroon to Benguela) who are not M'pongwe are Negroes who have traveled there to earn money. However, this class of African belongs to the clerk class, and we are currently concerned with the laborer. The African’s own way of performing any mechanical task is the simplest way, though not the easiest and certainly not the quickest. He has all the foolishness <term>chuckle-headedness: stupidity or foolishness</term> of that overrated creature, the ant, for his head never saves his heels <note>"His head never saves his heels" is a proverb meaning someone does extra physical labor because they failed to use their intelligence to plan more efficiently.</note>.

# APPENDIX I

Watch a gang of boat-men getting a surf-boat down a sandy beach. They turn it sideways to the direction in which they want it to go, and then roll it over and over bodily. This causes structure-straining thumps to the boat, accompanied by a great deal of advice and accusatory shouting at one another. Unless under white supervision, they will not use a slipway, nor will they put rollers under the hull. Watch a gang of natives again trying to get a log of timber down into the river from the bank, and you will see the same sort of thing—they have no concept of using a lever or anything of that nature. 

Remember that, unless under white direction, the African has never produced even a low-quality piece of cloth or pottery, nor a machine, tool, picture, or sculpture. He has never even reached the level of picture-writing. I am aware of their clever methods for transmitting messages, such as the cowrie shells strung in various ways used by the Yoruba <note>An ethnic group inhabiting western Africa, mainly Nigeria, Benin, and Togo.</note>, but even these do not equal the picture-writing of the South American Indians, nor the drawings a Native American makes on a raw elk hide. They are far inferior to the graphic sketches of mammoth hunts left to us by prehistoric cave dwellers.

This absence of mechanical aptitude is very interesting, though it likely has a very simple underlying reason: the conditions under which the African has lived have not required a higher mechanical culture. In his native state, he does not need to get heavy surf-boats into the sea; his own light dugout canoe is easily slid down. He does not need to cut down heavy timber trees and move them to the river, and so on. 

However, this state of affairs is now being disturbed and even destroyed by the influx of white enterprise. Consequently, he must alter his ways or there will be grave trouble. It is encouraging to note, however, that the African is almost as teachable and as willing to learn handicrafts as he is to adopt other things, provided his mind has not been poisoned by misleading ideas. The results already obtained from the Krumen and the Accras <note>The Krumen (Kru) and Accras (Ga people) were West African ethnic groups frequently employed as sailors, laborers, and artisans in colonial trade.</note> are good. The Accras are not as skilled as they might be because they are, to a certain extent, spoiled. Due to the labor shortage, they receive higher wages and more tolerance for mediocre work than they deserve or their work is worth. However, they have not yet fallen under that deadly spell cast by so many white men on so many black men—the idea that it is the "correct and proper" thing to avoid manual labor and instead get some subordinate to do all that work for you, while you

She notes that while modern industry requires new skills, Africans are capable of learning handicrafts if they avoid the elitist stigma against manual labor.</summary>

...to read and write. This false ideal, formed by the native from his observations of some of the white men around him, has been the cause of great mischief. He sees that the white man is his ruler—rich, powerful, and honored—and so he imitates him. He attends mission-school classes to learn to read and write, and as soon as an African learns these skills, he turns into a clerk. Now, there is no immediate use for clerks in Africa; there is certainly no room for further development in this line of work. What Africa wants at present, and will want for at least the next 200 years, are workers: planters, plantation hands, miners, and seamen. Yet, there are no schools in Africa to teach these things or the doctrine of the <term>nobility of labor</term> <note>The Victorian-era moral concept that hard physical work is inherently virtuous and dignified.</note> except for the technical mission schools.

Almost every mission on the Coast has now either just started a technical school or is collecting funds at home to start one. However, in the majority of these, crafts such as bookbinding, printing, and tailoring are being taught, which are not currently in demand. Still, any technical school is better than none. Aside from practical considerations, these schools are indirectly of great religious value to the mission. There are many instances in missionary records of a missionary receiving great encouragement from the natives when he first begins in a district. At first, the converts flock in, get baptized in batches, go to church, attend school, and adopt European clothes with an eagerness and enthusiasm that frequently goes to their devoted pastor's head. But after a few months, their behavior is enough to break his heart. 

Dressing up in European clothes amuses the women and some of the young men for a long time—in some cases permanently—but the older men and the bolder youths soon get bored. When an African is bored—and he is easily bored—he tends to decline morally. It is in these situations that an industrial mission would be so valuable to the spiritual cause. By employing and occupying the more dominant lower faculties of the African's mind, it would give the higher faculties time to develop. I have frequently been told, when advocating for technical instruction, that there are spiritual objections against it. Since my own views do not allow me to understand these objections, I will not discuss them. Also, several authorities—not just mission authorities—state, along with <term>ethnologists</term> <note>Scientists who study the characteristics of different peoples and the differences and relationships between them; in this context, often associated with 19th-century racial theories.</note>, that the African is incapable of learning except during childhood.

Prof. A. H. Keane <note>Augustus Henry Keane (1833–1912), an Irish ethnologist known for his theories on racial hierarchy.</note> says:
> “their inherent mental inferiority, almost more marked than their physical characters, depends on physiological causes by which the intellectual faculties seem to be arrested before attaining their normal development”;

...and further on, “We must necessarily infer that the development of the African and the white person proceeds along different lines. While with the latter, the volume of the brain grows with the expansion of the <term>cranium</term><note>Originally "brain-pan."</note>; in the former, the growth of the brain is instead halted by the premature closing of the <term>cranial sutures</term><note>The fibrous joints connecting the bones of the skull.</note> and the lateral pressure of the frontal bone.” <sup>1</sup> You will frequently encounter the claim that the African child is as intelligent as—or even more so than—the white child, but as soon as they pass beyond childhood, they make no further mental progress. Burton <note>Sir Richard Francis Burton (1821–1890), a famous English explorer and geographer.</note> says: “His mental development is arrested, and from then on he grows backwards instead of forwards.”

Now, it is daunting work to contradict these statements, but with all due respect to those who made them, I must do so. I find comfort in knowing that many men with more personal experience with Africans than these authorities agree with me—although, at the same time, we utterly disclaim the opinion that the African is "a man and a brother." <note>A reference to the famous abolitionist slogan "Am I Not a Man and a Brother?"</note> He is a man, certainly, but not of the same species; and I agree that his cranial sutures do close early. Indeed, I have seen them almost disappear in the skulls of men who died quite young. However, I think most anthropologists today are beginning to realize that the immense value they placed on skull measurements and cranial capacity a few years ago was excessive and does not have as great a bearing on intelligence as they once thought. 

An enormous amount of material on <term>craniology</term><note>The scientific study of the shape and size of the skulls of different human races.</note> has been carefully collected, mainly by the French. It is exceedingly interesting but full of difficulties and yields very diverse results. Take, for example, the brain weights provided by Topinard:

...if the African does choose to have the top of his head close up early, the entire attempt to prove that he is a "child-form," or represents "arrested development," is—well, not supported by the facts. The very comparison between the intelligence of white and black children to the disadvantage of the former is completely wrong. The white child is not his inferior; he may not be as quick at picking up "parlor tricks," but then, how would either child compare in that regard to a French poodle?

Based on my observations, what happens to the African is exactly what happens to the European: when he passes out of childhood, he enters a period of <term>hobbledehoyhood</term><note>An awkward, clumsy adolescence between boyhood and manhood.</note>. During this period, his skull might as well be filled with wool on the inside as it is covered with it on the outside. But after a time—during which he has succeeded in frustrating and discouraging the white men who had such high hopes for him when he was a child—his mind clears up again and functions perfectly well.

It is utter rubbish to say, "You cannot teach an adult African," or that "he grows backwards." Even without white interference, he becomes increasingly cunning as time goes on. Does anyone who actually knows them feel inclined to tell me that those old <term>palm-oil chiefs</term><note>Powerful West African leaders and merchants who grew wealthy through the palm oil trade in the 19th century.</note> have not learned a thing or two during their lives? Or that a well-seasoned inland trader has not? Go down to West Africa yourself, if you doubt this, and carry out a series of experiments with them in subjects they understand—trade subjects. Try to get the better of a group of mature adults, male or female, and I can promise you that you will return a wiser and a poorer man, but with a joyful heart regarding the African’s capacity to grow up.

Whether he achieves this by adding complexity to his brain or by increasing his gray matter, we will leave aside for now. All I wish to emphasize regarding the African people at large is that they have been mismanaged in recent years by the white races. The study of this question is very interesting, but I have no space to enter into it here in detail. In my opinion—and I emphasize it is my own only when I am expressing "heresy"—this mismanagement has been a byproduct of the wave of hysterical emotionalism that has swept through white culture, and for which I have an instinctive hatred.

I have elsewhere briefly pointed out the harm caused to the native mind by misguided missionary efforts,¹ but it is not the missionary alone who is doing harm. The government is nearly as responsible. It does this either out of fear of <term>Exeter Hall</term><note>A London meeting hall that was the center of evangelical and humanitarian lobbying groups, often criticized by colonialists for interfering in colonial administration.</note> as a powerful voting interest, or simply from the tendency to consolidate everything into the hands of a...

Whether it is a council or a government office that is constantly nagging, legislating, and inspecting, it makes little difference; the result is bad. It fills me with the greatest admiration for my country to see how she maintains her lead despite this. I believe she will always keep it, because I think it is impossible that this phase of emotionalism—and no, my French friends, it is not hypocrisy, it is only a temporary fit—will last. We shall soon regain our clear senses and say to the world, “We do this because we think it is right; because we think it is best for those we govern and for ourselves—not because of the 'wickedness of war,' the 'brotherhood of man,' or any other notion born of fear.”

There are many ways in which current ideas, acting through the government, cause harm in Africa. British government officials receive very little and very poor encouragement if they push inland to expand our sphere of influence—even when their knowledge of local conditions shows that expansion is necessary—because the authorities at home fear other nations will say we are rapacious land-grabbers. Well, we always have been, and they will say it anyway; where, after all, is the harm in it? We have acted in unison with nations who, for sound reasons of their own, have reduced Portuguese possessions in Africa because we were afraid of being thought to support a nation that practiced slavery. I always admire a good move in a game or a brilliant bit of strategy, and that was a masterpiece. Now, the responsibility for the affairs of the Congo Free State <note>The Congo Free State was a large state in Central Africa from 1885 to 1908, privately owned by King Leopold II of Belgium and notorious for atrocities committed during rubber extraction.</note> rests on our heads, while France and Germany smile sweetly. They know that these affairs will soon reach a state where they can step in and divide that territory between themselves without a stain on their character—all "in the interests of humanity." That entire rich region should now be ours by right of the efforts of explorers like Livingstone, Speke, Grant, Burton, and Cameron <note>A group of prominent 19th-century British explorers who mapped the African interior and the sources of the Nile.</note>.

Furthermore, our attitude toward commercial competition seems to me to lack dignity. We are only just beginning to realize that it is a fight, even though this commercial war has been going on since 1880—ever since, in fact, France and Germany recovered from their war of 1870 <note>The Franco-Prussian War.</note>.

If we are to carry on this commercial war with any hope of success, we must abandon our “Oh! that’s not fair; I won't play” attitude. Above all, we must have no more government restrictions on our foreign trade. In West Africa, government restriction settles like autumn dew upon the liquor traffic. It is a case of giving a dog a bad name and—

...hang him. Moreover, raising the import duties on liquor may bring a good revenue to the government, but it is a short-sighted policy—for liquor is the commodity for which there is the best market in West Africa. The natives have no enthusiasm for cotton goods, as they reportedly do in East Central Africa, and the supply they currently receive—which is cheap and of good quality—is as much as they require.

If the question of the abstract morality of introducing clothes, versus introducing liquor, to indigenous races were fairly examined, the results would be interesting—for dressing native populations in European clothes has a negative impact on them and leads to higher mortality. Indeed, this entire question of trade with less developed races is full of curious and unexpected points. Generally speaking, the introduction of European culture—whether administrative, religious, or commercial—has a destructive effect on all such races. The administrative and religious sectors have completely eradicated many of them; however, trade has never wiped out a race when separated from the other two factors, and it certainly has had no bad effect in tropical Africa.

With regard to the liquor trade, try to put yourself in the West African’s place. Imagine, for example, that you want a pair of boots. You go into a shop, prepared to pay for them, but the shopkeeper says, “My good friend, you must not have boots; they are immoral. You can have a tin of sardines or a pocket handkerchief; they are much better for you.” Would you take the sardines or the pocket handkerchiefs? More importantly, would you feel inclined to take them instead of your desired boots if you knew there was a shop in a neighboring street where boots were to be had? There is a "neighboring shop-street" for all our West Coast possessions, held by either France or Germany.

I do not for a moment deny that the liquor trade requires regulation, but it requires more regulation in Europe than it does in Africa, because Europe is more prone to intoxication. In Africa, all that is needed is that the spirits sent in should be pure and not sold at a strength exceeding 45° below proof. <note>45° below proof is approximately 31.5% alcohol by volume (ABV).</note> These requirements are already fairly well fulfilled on the West Coast, and I can see no reason for any further restrictions or additional taxes <term>imposts</term>. If further restrictions in the sale of liquor are desired, they are not needed for the interior trade where the natives are not prone to excess, but in the larger coastal towns. In those towns, there is a population of natives who are the remnants <note>original: "*débris*"</note> of the disintegrating process of European culture. But even in towns like Sierra Leone and Lagos, these men are...

English manufacturers, I may remark, have succeeded in producing the cloth goods best suited for the African markets, but in recent years there has been an increase in the quantity of other foreign-made goods used in the West Coast trade. The imports from France, Germany, and the United States to the Gold Coast for 1894 (published 1896) were £217,388 0s. 1d., and the exports were £212,320 1s. 3d. The Consular Report (158) for the Gold Coast says that while the trade with the United Kingdom has increased from £1,054,336 17s. 6d. in 1893 to £1,190,532 1s. 3d. in 1894—roughly a 13 percent increase—the trade with foreign countries has increased by more than 22 percent, specifically from £350,387 3s. 5d. to £429,708 1s. 4d. 

In the Lagos Consular Report (No. 150), similar comparative statistics are not provided, but the increase in that location is probably greater than on the Gold Coast, as a heavy percentage of the Lagos trade passes through the hands of two German firms. This increase in foreign trade within our colonies seems to be even more significant in other parts of Africa; a Foreign Office Report from Mozambique states regarding Cape Colony that “while British imports show an otherwise satisfactory increase, German trade has more than trebled.”²

There is a certain school of philanthropists in Europe who say that it is not advisable to spread European trade in Africa. They argue that the native is provided by the bountiful Earth with all that he really requires, and therefore he should be allowed to live his simple life and not be compelled or urged to work for the white man’s gain. ...people, because I like the African in his traditional state <note>original: "bush state"</note> best. One can understand any truly compassionate human being being horrified at the extinction of native races in the Polynesian, Melanesian, and American regions. However, their view is full of error regarding Africa. For one thing, I am glad to say that the African does not die off under European control as those weaker races do; instead, the population increases. 

This fact makes it impossible to accept their plan <note>referring to preservationist or isolationist arguments mentioned previously</note> as practical politics, especially in districts under European control. The "bountiful earth" does not provide much in Africa when using native agricultural methods. These methods were sufficient when a percentage of the population was shipped to America as slaves. Now, however, they only suffice to keep the natives in a low state of development—a state that is maintained at its current level only through trade. 

The condition of the African native will be dreadful if this trade is not maintained. Indeed, I would say it must be increased in proportion to the expansion of European government control. This governmental control does many things that are good in themselves and look glorious on paper: it prevents the export slave trade, suppresses human sacrifice, and stops internal warfare among the natives. In short, it does everything except suppress the terrible rate of infant mortality (the reasons for which I need not discuss here). By doing these things, it increases the native population without doing anything to increase the means of supporting that population. In fact, the government even threatens to decrease these means by importing Asian laborers <note>original: "Asiatics"</note> to perform work such as road building, and so on.

It may be argued that there is no fear of the trade that supports the native disappearing from the West Coast. However, it is important to remember that the goods this trade depends upon—the materials brought to the traders' factories by the natives—are mainly (except for the coffee and cacao of the Southwest Coast) wild products <note>original: "bush stuff"</note>. These are uncultivated, merely collected and roughly prepared. The natives collect these resources so wastefully that they cannot last indefinitely. 

Take rubber, for example, which is one of the main exports. Due to the wasteful methods used in its collection, it is being wiped out of entire districts. The trade in rubber begins on a section of the coast where, for some years, the supply is so rich that it can be collected almost at the native’s back door. However, because he cuts down the vine to harvest it, he eventually clears it all out. Every year, he must travel further and further inland for a load. His ability to go beyond a certain point is eventually blocked by hostile interior tribes who are not under European control. Furthermore, it must remain profitable for him to make these long journeys. The market prices at home take little notice of his difficulties because of the more carefully collected supply of rubber sent into the home markets by...
