South America and India; therefore, the native loses out. When he has cleared the districts accessible to him, trade there comes to an end, and he no longer has the means to purchase the things he grew to enjoy during his time of prosperity. The Oil Rivers <note>The Niger Delta region, so named for its high export of palm oil</note>, which produce the largest volume of trade among the West Coast possessions, depend entirely on palm oil for their commerce. If anything were to happen to the oil palms, such as a blight, or if a cheap substitute for palm oil were found in Europe <note>original: "at home"</note>, the population of the Oil Rivers would starve, even at its current density. 

The development of trade is essential for the survival of the natives. Discovering forest products that can be sold in Europe and establishing plantations—whose products will replace those he is currently destroying so recklessly—will provide a more secure future than any number of acts abolishing domestic slavery or the establishment of trial by jury and similar institutions. If European <note>original: "white"</note> control progresses without the creation of plantations or the expansion of trade into the interior, the condition of West Africans will be miserable—far worse than it was before the overseas slave trade was suppressed. 

In the healthier districts, the population will grow to the point of overcrowding and will face starvation. The malaria of the coastal region will always keep both the Black and European <note>original: "white"</note> populations low. However, if the trader leaves and the region is left only to government officials and missionaries, the native will lose the incentive to work or the comforts that help him survive the climate—comforts which trade currently allows him to obtain. Consequently, the coastal native will sink, by way of <note>original: "via"</note> vice and degradation, to extinction. This process will likely be made even faster and more painful by raids from wild tribes coming from the overcrowded interior.

I do not claim this will happen immediately to the West African, but "a little more and how much it is, a little less and how far away" <note>A reference to Robert Browning’s poem "By the Fire-side"</note>. Remember that human beings are subject to the same biological laws as other creatures: if you remove the things that prey on them, they are likely to outgrow the food-producing capacity of their environment. 

It may be said this is not the case; look at the Polynesians, the South American Indians, and others. You may observe them as much as you like, but what you see there will not help you judge the African. The African does not wither away like a flower in the presence of Europeans—not in the least. Consider the population growth of the natives in the Cape Colony <note>original: "Cape territory"</note> and what they have endured on the West Coast. American Indians, whaling captains, and sailors of every kind and nationality have visited him "frequently and freely." He has taken in all kinds of religious doctrines; cotton fabrics, patent medicines, imported alcohol, and—as the author of the Lagos Annual Colonial Report poetically notes—twine, whiskey, wine, and woolen goods. Yet the West African is still here among us by the millions—playing his drum <note>original: "tom-tom"</note>, paddling his dugout canoe, and living in his palm-leaf or mud hut, ready and able to endure more "Western influence" <note>original: "white man stuff"</note>. 

Except for an occasional tendency to suffer from mania or depression when educated for the clergy, or dying when he—and especially she—is confined in a sweltering, corrugated-iron schoolroom with excessive clothing and too much mental labor, he survives in a way that I believe you will admit is interesting. It is a survival that commands my admiration and respect. 

But today, there is a new factor in his relationship with the European <note>original: "white"</note> races: the factor of domestic governance. I do not believe the African will survive and thrive under this control if it continues to take the form that current European <note>original: "white"</note> ideas intend. On the other hand, I do not think he will be forced to try, because under current conditions, European control will not become very thorough. In the event of a European war, government attention will be diverted from West Africa. The African will then do what he has done several times before when European oversight <note>original: "the white eye"</note> has lapsed for a decade or so: he will return to his former ways, just as he did in Kacongo after the Jesuits organized <note>original: "tidied him up"</note> him, and as he must have done after his interactions with the Phoenicians and Egyptians. 

I believe travelers in the remote future will still find him with his drum in his dugout canoe, just as willing to sell the wreckage <note>original: "débris"</note> of our exports to his ancestors as "great curiosities" at a high price. I cannot imagine exactly how much he will charge for a Devos patent kerosene <note>original: "paraffin oil"</note> tin or a Morton’s tin, but it will be a steep price—similar to what he currently asks for Phoenician "Aggry" beads <note>ancient glass beads found in West Africa, often of uncertain origin</note>. 

There will be then, as there is now and as there was in the past, individual Africans who rise to a high level of culture, but that will be the extent of it for a very long time. To claim that the African race will never advance beyond its current level of development is an overstatement, despite the significant evidence supporting that view; however, I am certain he will never advance beyond it by following the path of European culture. The environment he lives in is unsuited for it, and his own nature is entirely against it. The truth is that the West African mind contains far too much superstition and too...

...little of anything else. Our own methods of instruction have not been of any real help to the African, because what he needs to be taught is how to work. Bishop Ingram would have been able to write a more cheerful and hopeful book than his *Sierra Leone after 100 Years* if the people of Sierra Leone had received a thorough grounding in technical skills <note>original: "technical culture"</note> suited to the requirements of their country. Instead, they have been given a ruinous education at the cost of millions of pounds and hundreds of lives of good, though misguided, white men. It is possible for a West African native to be shaped by European culture into a very respectable man—not the same kind of man as a white man, but a man a white man can shake hands with and associate with without any loss of self-respect. However, it is by no means necessary for the African to adopt any European <note>original: "white"</note> culture at all to become a decent member of society. In fact, the opposite is true; the percentage of honorable and reliable men among those living in the bush <note>original: "bushmen"</note> is higher than among the educated men.

I do not believe that the white race will ever pull the black race up to its own particular peak in the mountain range of civilization. For various reasons, both polygamy and slavery are essential to the well-being of Africa—at least for those vast regions that are agricultural—and these two institutions will require the African to have a civilization peak of his own. Unfortunately for the energetic reformer, the African is not keen on "mountaineering" in the range of civilization. He prefers to remain down below and be comfortable. He is not arrogant about this; he admires high culture very much, and respects the people who inconvenience themselves by pursuing it—but would he do it himself? No. And if he is dragged up into the higher reaches of a self-sacrificing <term>self-abnegatory: the act of renouncing or rejecting one's own interests or desires</term> religion, sixty percent of the time <note>original: "six times in ten"</note> he falls back damaged—a morally crippled man—into his old traditional ways <note>original: "swampy country fashion valley"</note>.

# APPENDIX II

## DISEASE IN WEST AFRICA

As great as the delays and difficulties are in developing the vast natural resources of West Africa due to labor problems, there is another cause for delay that is far greater and more terrible—namely, the deadliness of the climate. “Nothing hinders a man, Miss Kingsley, half as much as dying,” a friend said to me recently, after nearly putting his opinion to a practical test. Other parts of the world have more sensational outbreaks of death from epidemics of yellow fever and cholera, but no other region in the world can match West Africa for the steady, relentless killing that malaria inflicts on the white men who come under its influence.

You will hear malaria talked about glibly; but you will find few men ready to explain what malaria actually is or what it consists of, and those few do not agree on the story <note>original: "by no means of a tale"</note>. It is very strange that this terrible disease has not attracted more scientific researchers, considering the enormous death rate it causes throughout the tropics and subtropics. A few years ago, when the specific microbes for everything from measles to miracles were being “isolated,” several bacteriologists isolated the malarial microbe. Unfortunately, they did not all isolate the same one. 

A summary <note>original: "*résumé*"</note> of the various claims regarding these microbes is impossible here. Whether one of them was the true cause, or whether they all have an equal claim to that title, is not yet clear; for malaria, as far as I have seen or read of it, seems to be not so much a single distinct form of fever as a group of fevers—a genus, not a species. Many things suggest this is the case, particularly the different forms that so-called malarial poisoning takes in different locations. This subject may be further divided and complicated by the controversy over whether yellow fever is native <note>original: "endemic"</note> to the West Coast or not. That it has occurred there from time to time...

<summary>The author identifies the deadly climate and malaria as the primary obstacles to West African development, noting that the disease is a complex group of fevers rather than a single ailment. She highlights the lack of scientific consensus regarding the specific microbes responsible for the high mortality rate among Europeans.</summary>
<keywords>West Africa, malaria, public health, colonial development, microbes, bacteriology, yellow fever, climate, Mary Kingsley</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of malarial and yellow fevers in West Africa, moving from general classifications to specific recorded outbreaks and the debate over treatments such as quinine.</meta>

from time to time, there can be no question: at Fernando Po in 1862 and 1866, in Senegal quite frequently, and at least one epidemic at Bonny was definitely yellow fever. However, in the case of each of these outbreaks, the disease is said to have been imported from South America—brought to Fernando Po by ships from Havana, and to Bonny by a ship that had previously visited South American ports with a cargo of mules. The bedding used for these mules was not cleared out of the ship until she arrived in Bonny, where it was thrown overboard into the river; the yellow fever broke out immediately afterward. 

On the other hand, South America accuses West Africa—specifically the Guinea Coast—of originally exporting yellow fever through slave ships. This is certainly a strange claim, because native Africans rarely suffer from severe malarial fever. While they do catch it, and you are often told that someone has "yellow fever," they rarely die from it. Usually, the individual feels truly miserable and sick for a day or so and then recovers.

Regarding hematuria <note>likely referring to blackwater fever, a severe complication of malaria</note>, there is also controversy. One very experienced and excellent authority doubts whether this is entirely a malarial fever, or whether it is, in some cases at least, brought on by overdoses of quinine. Dr. Plehn asserts—and his claims are strongly supported by his great success in treating this fever—that quinine has a very harmful influence once the characteristic symptoms have appeared, and that it should not be administered. 

I hesitate to advise this myself, as I fear encouraging anyone to abandon quinine, which remains our primary weapon against malaria. This hesitation does not stem from a lack of faith in Dr. Plehn; he has studied malarial fevers in Cameroon with the greatest energy and devotion, applying a logical German intellect trained in the rigorous German tradition—and for such subjects, no better training exists. His brother, also a doctor, was stationed in Cameroon before him and is now working just as hard in the German East African possessions. When these two eventually publish the results of their joint investigations, it will be the most important contribution to our knowledge of malaria ever produced. It is impossible to overstate the importance of such work to West Africa. The person who will make West Africa profitable will be the scientist who provides us with something more effective against malaria than quinine. 

It is too much to hope for such breakthroughs from the medical men currently working on the Coast. They are busy doctoring day and night, and are often forced not only to treat but also to personally nurse their white patients. The rest of their time is consumed by issuing health certificates to steamers and struggling with the various and terrible sanitary problems presented by the native towns.

...and so on, few can have sufficient time or strength left in them to carry out a series of experiments and cultures. However, they can and do supply researchers in laboratories back home with excellent material to carry the work through. Meanwhile, we wait for those researchers and do the best we can.

The net results of laboratory investigation, according to French doctors, show that the protozoan malarial bacillus—the microbe of <term>paludism</term> <note>an archaic term for malaria</note>—is amoeba-like in its movements. It acts on the red blood cells, leaving nothing of them but the dark pigment found in the skin and organs of malaria patients.^1 German doctors make a practice of performing microscopic examinations of a patient's blood. They say that the microbes appear at the start of a fever attack, increase in quantity as the fever intensifies, and decrease as it fades. From these investigations, they are able to judge fairly accurately how many <term>remissions</term> <note>periods when the fever abates</note> may be expected. In fact, they can judge the severity of the case which, combined with the knowledge that quinine only affects malarial microbes at a certain stage of their development, is very helpful in treatment.

I should also mention a very peculiar point regarding hematuric disease <note>likely blackwater fever, a severe complication of malaria characterized by blood in the urine</note>, which is the most deadly form of West Coast fever. As far as we know, this disease has always been present on the South-West Coast—at Loando, the Lower Congo, and Gaboon. However, it is said not to have appeared in "the Rivers" <note>the Oil Rivers, or the Niger Delta region</note> until 1881, and to have spread along the West Coast from there. My learned friend, Dr. Plehn, doubts this; he says people were less observant in those days. However, the symptoms of this fever are so distinct that I believe it would have been completely impossible for the old West Coasters not to have distinguished it from the usual remittent or intermittent fevers, had it occurred there in the past with anything like its current frequency. But we will leave these theoretical and technical considerations and turn to the practical side of the question.

You will always find many people ready to give advice on—

# APPENDIX II

fever, particularly how to avoid getting it, and you will find the most dogmatic of these are people who have been singularly unlucky in the matter, or people who know nothing of local conditions. These latter individuals are the most trying of all to deal with. They tell you, truly enough no doubt, that malaria is in the air—in the vapors from the ground, which are strongest about sunrise and sunset—and in the drinking water. They insist that you must avoid chills, excessive mental and bodily exertion, and that you must never get anxious, or excited, or lose your temper. 

Now, there is only one item on this list—the drinking water—that you can actually avoid. Because of the great variety and rapid growth of bacteria encouraged by the tropical temperature, the high humidity from the heavy rainfall, and the vast extent of the swamps, it is practically impossible to destroy them in the air to any satisfactory degree. When I first went to the West Coast, I was presented by scientific friends with two devices supposed to do this. One was a lamp in which you burned some chemical; it certainly produced a smell that nothing could live with—but then, I am not "nothing," and there are enough smells on the Coast already. I gave it up after the first half-hour. 

The other device was a muzzle—or a respirator, I should say. Well! All I have to say about that is that you would need to be a better-looking person than I am to wear a thing like that without causing a panic in the district. Furthermore, orders to avoid the night air are even more difficult to obey. May I ask how you are supposed to do without air from 6:30 P.M. to 6:30 A.M.? Or what other air is available then except night air, heavy with malarial vapors?

You have a better chance with the drinking water, as I will explain shortly, but you cannot avoid the chill. When you are at work on the Coast, even with the greatest care, the sudden drop in temperature that occurs after a <term>tornado</term> <note>a violent squall or thunderstorm common in West Africa</note> coming at the end of a sweltering day is sure to affect anyone. As for the orders regarding your temper, neither the natives, nor the country, nor the trade help you in the least to remain calm. Still, you must remember that although it is impossible to fully carry out these orders, you can do a great deal toward doing so. Preventive measures are the most important thing, for it is better to escape fever altogether, or to get off with a light case, than to make a sensational recovery from <term>Yellow Jack</term> <note>a common historical nickname for yellow fever</note> himself.

There is little doubt that a certain type of person has the best chance of surviving the Coast climate—an energetic, lean, high-strung but light-hearted creature, capable of enjoying what—

...whatever there may be to enjoy, and are incapable of dwelling on discomforts or worries. It is quite possible for a person of this type to live and work hard on the Coast for a considerable period, possibly with better health than they would have in England. However, the robust, stout, and energetic should avoid West Africa like the plague. One after another, I have seen men and women who looked—as the saying goes—as if they had a long lease on life, arrive only to die. It gives one a sense of horror when they arrive at your West Coast station; you feel like an accomplice to murder. But what can you do, except have yourself mocked as a doomsayer and eventually attend the funeral?

The best ways to avoid the danger of the night air are as follows: eat your evening meal around 6:30 or 7:00 PM (8:00 is too late); sleep under a mosquito net whether there are mosquitoes in your district or not; and have a meal before heading out in the morning. This should be a good hot cup of tea or coffee with bread and butter if you can get it; if not, eat something left over from last night’s supper or even *aguma* <note>A local West African food, likely a starchy paste or porridge</note>. Regarding meals, we inevitably come to the controversial question of stimulants. All the evidence suggests that alcohol—of the right sort, taken at the right times and in the right quantities—is extremely valuable. Consider the case of the missionaries, who are almost all teetotalers. They are young men and women who must pass a medical examination before coming out, and their lives on the Coast are far easier than those of other classes of white men. Yet, the death rate among them is far higher than in any other group.

Mr. Stanley <note>likely the explorer Henry Morton Stanley</note> says that wine is the best form of stimulant, but that it should not be taken before the evening meal. Certainly, on the South-West Coast, where a heavy but high-quality red wine imported from Portugal is the common drink, the death rate is lower than on the West Coast. Beer has been given a thorough trial in Cameroon since the German occupation. Authorities believe it is partly responsible for the fact that cases of <term>hematuric fever</term> <note>Now known as blackwater fever, a severe and often fatal complication of malaria</note> are more common in that region than in others. However, this subject requires scientific, comparative observation across various parts of the Coast. Cameroon is at the start of the South-West Coast, where the percentage of hematuric cases compared to <term>intermittent</term> and <term>remittent</term> <note>Types of malarial fevers characterized by periodic or fluctuating fevers</note> fevers is much higher than on the West Coast.

# APPENDIX II

The task is enormous, and in addition to the history of <term>hematuric fever</term> <note>Also known as blackwater fever, a severe complication of malaria involving the breakdown of red blood cells</note>, he would be confronted with the problem of a type of fever that seems to be a recent addition to West African afflictions: the so-called <term>typhoid malaria</term>, which in recent years has entered the Rivers <note>The Oil Rivers region of the Niger Delta</note> and apparently intends to stay. This fever is, I should mention, practically unknown at present in the South-West Coast regions where the "leave the garbage to the sun" method of sanitation is followed. At present, the treatment of all diseases affecting white people on the Coast basically consists of treating <term>malaria</term>, because whatever disease a person catches takes on a malarial quality that masks its true nature. Why, I knew a man who had as severe an attack of <term>smallpox</term> as anyone would wish to avoid; for days he behaved as if he had <term>remittent fever</term>, and then he broke out in the characteristic rash. He only ended up having all his earthly possessions burned and receiving endless carbolic acid dressings for his trouble.

I do not suppose this does much harm, as the malaria is the main thing that needs curing—unless <term>Dr. Plehn</term> <note>Friedrich Plehn (1862–1904), a German physician who studied tropical diseases</note> is right and <term>quinine</term> is harmful in cases of <term>hematuria</term>. His success in dealing with this fever seems to support his opinion; and the French doctors on the Coast, who dose it heavily with quinine, certainly have a very high death rate among their patients with the hematuric form, although they very rarely lose a patient to other types of malarial fever.

But to return to those preventive measures: having done what we can with the air, we will turn our attention to the drinking water. In addition to malarial microbes, the drinking and washing water of West Africa is liable to contain <term>skin-dwelling</term> <note>original: "dermazoic"</note> and <term>internal</term> <note>original: "entozoic"</note> organisms. If you do not take care, you will contract <note>original: "get from it into your anatomy"</note> *fungal skin infections* <note>original: "Tinea versicolor"</note>, *scalp ringworm* <note>original: "Tinea decalvans"</note>, *body ringworm* <note>original: "Tinea circinata"</note>, *barber's itch* <note>original: "Tinea sycosis"</note>, *crusted ringworm* <note>original: "Tinea favosa"</note>, or some other member of that wretched family. Not to mention being nearly certain to host *whipworms* <note>original: "Trichocephalus dispar"</note>, *large roundworms* <note>original: "Ascaris lumbricoides"</note>, *pinworms* <note>original: "Oxyuris vermicularis"</note>, and eight varieties of <term>nematodes</term> <note>parasitic roundworms</note>, each with an awful name of its own and unpleasant consequences for you. Finally, there is a peculiar horror, a <term>filaria</term> <note>Likely *Loa loa*, the African eye worm</note>. This is not a fern, as its pleasant-sounding name might lead you to believe, but a worm that gets into the white of the eye and lives there quite actively. It causes distressing itching, throbbing, and pricking sensations, though it does not affect the sight until it happens to cause inflammation. I have seen the eyes of natives simply swarming with these <term>filariae</term>. A curious thing about the disease is that it usually begins in one eye, and when that becomes overpopulated, an "emigration society" sets...

...out for the other eye, traveling there under the skin of the bridge of the nose; during its transit, it looks like the bridge of a pair of spectacles. A similar, but not identical, worm is fairly common on the *Ogowé* River and is likely to get under the <term>epidermis</term> <note>The outer layer of the skin</note> of any part of the body. Like the one affecting the eye, it moves very actively, passing rapidly under the skin and causing terrible pricking and itching, though I have seen very little inflammation in those cases. 

The treatment involves removing the thing, and one must be careful to get it out whole; for if any part of it is left inside, <term>suppuration</term> <note>The formation or discharge of pus; festering</note> sets in. Therefore, even if you are personally convinced you have removed it successfully, it is just as well to wash out the wound with carbolic acid or <term>Condy’s fluid</term> <note>A historical disinfectant made of sodium or potassium permanganate</note>. The most frequent sufferers from these <term>filariæ</term> <note>Small, parasitic thread-like worms</note> are the local people, but Europeans do catch them. I hear there is an account in the *Lancet* <note>A famous British medical journal</note>, October 17th, 1894, of one that was extracted from the eye of a European. This case came from Calabar, but the disease is more frequent on the South-West Coast.

Do not confuse this filaria with the <term>Guinea worm</term> (*Filaria medinensis*), which can grow up to ten or twelve feet in length and has different habits. It is more stationary, and it lives in drinking water inside small crustaceans (<term>cyclops</term>). It commonly appears in the human host’s leg and grows rapidly, coiled round and round like a watch-spring, appearing as a raised area under the skin. 

The local treatment for this pest is to very cautiously open the skin over the head of the worm, secure it in a small split piece of bamboo, and then gradually wind the rest of the creature out. Only a small portion can be wound out at a time, as the site is very prone to inflammation. If the worm should break, it is certain to become severely inflamed, and a terrible wound will result. You cannot wind it out by the tail because you would then be, so to speak, turning its fur the wrong way, and it would catch in the wound.

I should remark that I strongly advise anyone who wishes to start a canoe journey early to ensure that no local member of the party is currently dealing with a Guinea worm. Winding the worm is always reserved as a morning task, and since many other tasks are similarly postponed until morning, it leads to significant delays.

I know, my friends, that each and every one of you claims that the drinking water at your particular location is of singular beauty and purity, and that you always tell the houseboys to filter it. However, I am convinced that the water is no more to be trusted than the boys themselves, and I am utterly amazed that people of your intelligence trust this trio of water, boys, and filter in the way you do. One favorite haunt of mine gets its drinking water from a

...cemented hole in the backyard into which drains a very foul-smelling, black little swamp. This is surrounded by a ridge of sandy ground where several groups of local houses are situated; their inhabitants improve their finances and their drainage by taking in laundry.

The other day at <term>Fernando Po</term> <note>Now Bioko, an island in Equatorial Guinea</note>, I was assured as usual that the water was perfect—a "beautiful spring coming down from the mountain," and so on. During the afternoon, business took me up the mountain to Basile; for the first part of the way, I followed the course of that very stream. The first "objects of interest" I noticed in the drinking-water supply were four locals washing themselves and their clothes. The next was the bloated carcass of a dead goat resting in a crystal-clear pool. The path then left the stream, but upon reaching its source, I found an interesting little colony of Spanish families that the government had imported in their entirety, including children. They had a nice, neat little cemetery attached, which the doctor—His Excellency—told me was "mostly filled with children, who were always dying from worms." So much for the drinking water! As for what that beautiful stream was absorbing when it was out of sight—I did not see it, so I do not know—but I am certain it was some filth or another.

But there is no use arguing; it is the same everywhere: Sierra Leone, the Grain Coast, the Ivory Coast, the Gold Coast, Lagos, the Rivers, Cameroon, the <term>French Congo</term> <note>original: "Congo Français"</note>, <term>Kakongo</term> <note>A historical kingdom and region in modern-day Cabinda and DRC</note>, the <term>Belgian Congo</term> <note>original: "Congo Belge"</note>, and Angola. When you ask your white friends how they can be so reckless about the water—which they know is a concentrated brew of the malarious earth, exposed day and night to the malarious air—they all stand up and say theirs is fine. They claim they have "an incredibly good filter" and that "they tell the <term>boys</term> <note>A colonial term for male domestic servants</note>" what to do, and that they themselves often add wine or spirits to the water to "kill the microbes." Vanity, vanity! In every single place I know, men have died and worms have eaten them.

The safest way of treating water I know is to boil it vigorously for at least ten minutes, then immediately pour it into a jar with a narrow neck and plug it with a wad of fresh cotton-wool—not a cork. If you dislike the flat taste of boiled water, plunge a piece of red-hot iron into it, which will make the flavor more pleasant. *You can carefully filter the water before boiling it if you like.* A good filter is an excellent thing for clearing drinking water of hippopotamuses, crocodiles, water snakes, catfish, and the like; I dare say it will even strain out sixty percent of the living or dead Africans that might be in it. But if you think it is going to stop the microbe of <term>marsh fever</term> <note>A historical name for malaria</note>—my good sir, you are mistaken. And remember that you must give up cold...

...water, whether boiled or unboiled, altogether. For if you take boiled or filtered water, put it into one of those water-coolers, and leave it hanging on the porch exposed to the day or night air, you might as well save yourself the trouble of boiling it at all.

The remedies for these diseases are nearly as dangerous as the diseases themselves. Let the newcomer remember, when dealing with quinine, <term>calomel</term> <note>Mercury(I) chloride, historically used as a purgative</note>, arsenic, and spirits, that these substances are not sugar and he is not a glass bottle. He should use them all—the first two fairly frequently—but should not wait for an attack of fever and then pour them into himself by the spoonful. 

The third remedy, arsenic—a drug highly regarded by the French, who believe that if you establish an arsenic <term>cachexia</term> <note>A state of physical wasting and ill health</note> you will not develop a malarial one—should not be taken except under a doctor’s orders. 

Alcohol is undoubtedly extremely valuable when, for reasons beyond your control, you have caught a chill. Remember always that your life depends on quinine and that it is vital to keep your system sensitive to it. You will not do this if you keep taking heavy doses for no reason; you will also make yourself deaf in the process. I have known people to take sixty grains of quinine in a day for a <term>bilious attack</term> <note>A digestive or liver-related illness</note> and turn it into a disease they only survived by the skin of their teeth. 

However, the <term>prophylactic</term> <note>preventative</note> action of quinine is its greatest benefit, as it only has power over malarial microbes at a certain stage of their development. It does not affect the fully matured microbe to any great degree. Therefore, by taking it when in a malaria-infested district—say, in a dose of five grains a day—you suppress the malaria that you are bound to get into your system, even with every care. 

When you have become very chilled or overtired, take an extra five grains with a little wine or spirits at any time. When you know you are coming down with a fever—indicated by a headache, aching limbs, the sensation of cold water running down your back, and a terrible temper—send for a doctor if you can. If, as generally happens, there is no doctor nearby, take a compound calomel and <term>colocynth</term> <note>A desert plant used as a powerful laxative</note> pill, fifteen grains of quinine, and a grain of opium, and go to bed wrapped in the best blanket available. 

When safely there, drink plenty of hot tea or, better yet, a hot drink made from fresh lime juice, strong and without sugar (fresh limes are almost always available; if not, bottled lime juice works well). Then, during the "hot stage" of the fever, do not go fanning yourself, and do the same during the "perspiring stage." If you catch a chill then, you may turn a mild fever into a fatal one. If, however, you stay conscientiously rolled in your blanket until the perspiring stage is well over, and stay in...

# APPENDIX II

Stay in bed until the next morning; chances are you will be all right, though a little shaky in the legs. You should continue taking quinine in five-grain doses—up to fifteen to twenty grains a day—for a week after any attack of fever, but you must stop taking the opium pill. The most important thing in West Africa is to maintain a high level of health; this will enable you to resist fever. However, it is exceedingly difficult for most people to do this because of the difficulty of getting exercise and good food. 

But regardless of what you do, it is almost certain you will contract fever if you reside on the Coast for more than six months, and on the Gold Coast, the chances are two to one that you will die from it. Without precautions, you will probably catch it within a <term>fortnight</term> <note>two weeks</note> of first landing, and your chances of surviving are almost zero <note>original: "nil"</note>. With precautions, in the <term>Rivers</term> <note>The Oil Rivers Protectorate, a region in the Niger Delta</note> and on the Southwest Coast, your bout of fever may be less dangerous and uncomfortable than a bad cold in England.

Yet remember, before you choose to join the ranks of the <term>West Coasters</term> <note>European residents or traders on the West African coast</note>, that 85 percent of them die of fever or return home with their health permanently ruined. Also remember that there is no such thing as becoming acclimated to the Coast. It is true that there are a few men there who, although they have lived in West Africa for years, have never had fever, but you can count them on the fingers of one hand. There is another group who have been out for twelve months at a time without a touch of fever; you would need the fingers of both hands to count them, but no more. By far the largest group is the third: those who suffer a mild bout of fever every two weeks and then one day, for no apparent reason, get a severe case and die from it. A very large fourth group consists of those who die within two weeks to a month of going ashore.

A person's fate depends solely on their ability to resist so-called malaria, not on their system becoming used to it. The first group of men I mentioned have some unknown element in their constitutions that makes them immune. In the second group, the power of resistance is strong and can be renewed periodically by a trip home to a European climate. The third group experiences a state of cumulative poisoning; the fourth suffers from acute poisoning.

Let the newcomer who goes to the Coast take the most optimistic view of these statements and let him consider himself destined to be in one of the two most favored groups. Let him take every precaution short of becoming frightened—which is as deadly as taking no care at all—and he may—I sincerely

...hope he will survive; for a man who has the courage and determination to go and fight in West Africa for things worth fighting for—duty, honor, and gold—is a man whose death is a profound loss to his country.

The trade coming from West Africa truly brings to mind the phrase that cargoes are bought with the "lives of men," leaving "wives and mothers most despairing." <note>A reference to the song "Caller Herrin'," originally describing the dangers faced by North Sea fishermen: "Wives and mithers, maist despairin', ca' them lives o' men."</note> Yet, as heavy as the price is that England pays for her West African possessions, to those of us who know the men who risk and lose their lives for them, England receives a fair value in return. She is the greatest manufacturing nation in the world and, as such, requires markets. Today, she needs markets more than she needs new colonies. A colony annually drains thousands of a nation's most enterprising and energetic citizens, leaving behind their elderly and dependent relatives. Furthermore, a colony eventually becomes a competing manufacturing center to the mother country. In contrast, West Africa will remain for hundreds of years a region that supplies the manufacturer with raw materials and accepts manufactured goods in exchange, providing a healthy profit margin. Maintaining our West African markets costs the lives of only a few dozen men each year—though far too often they are lost forever. However, the trade they carry on and develop there—a trade worth nine million pounds sterling annually, according to Sir George Baden-Powell <note>Sir George Baden-Powell (1847–1898) was a British politician and colonial official who wrote extensively on the economics of the Empire.</note>—allows thousands of men, women, and children to remain safely and comfortably in England, supported by the wages and profits arising from the manufacture and export of goods used in that trade.

So, I trust that those at home in England will give full honor to the men still working in West Africa, or those rotting in the overgrown, snake-infested cemeteries and forest swamps. These are men whose battles have been fought on lonely beaches, far away from home and friends, and often without the help of any other white man. Sometimes they fight against <term>savages</term> <note>The author's contemporary term for indigenous West Africans.</note>, but more often they face a far deadlier enemy. They lack the <term>anodyne</term> <note>a medicine or source of comfort that numbs pain</note> against death and danger that comes from the companionship of hundreds of fellow soldiers in a fight against a visible foe. Instead, they face an enemy that can only be seen in the hallucinations of delirium, which flows like poison through burning veins and aching brains—the dreaded West Coast fever. May England never again dream of abandoning or gambling with the conquests won for her by those heroes of commerce, the West Coast traders; for of them, as well as of men such as Sir Gerald Portal <note>Sir Gerald Portal (1858–1894) was a British diplomat whose mission to Uganda helped establish British control in East Africa.</note>, it truly may be said: of such is the Kingdom of England.

# APPENDIX III

## DR. A. GÜNTHER ON REPTILES AND FISHES¹

*Report on a Collection of Reptiles and Fishes made by Miss M. H. Kingsley during her travels on the Ogowé River and in Old Calabar. By Dr. A. GÜNTHER, F.R.S.* <note>F.R.S.: Fellow of the Royal Society, a prestigious award granted to individuals who have made a substantial contribution to the improvement of natural knowledge.</note>

->[Plates I.—II.]<-

Miss Mary H. Kingsley, after returning from her first visit to the West Coast of Africa in 1894, brought back a diverse collection of zoological specimens. This collection was large enough to demonstrate her deep interest in the wildlife of the countries she visited. Last year, she set out from England again with the goal of extending her travels into the interior of the Gaboon region. Since she intended to follow the course of the Ogowé River for part of this expedition, she readily agreed with my suggestion that she should not miss the opportunity to collect the fish of this great river.

Her means of preserving and transporting the specimens were naturally limited, as Miss Kingsley traveled alone with a native crew. Furthermore, while crossing the region of the rapids—which stretches for several hundred miles—her canoe frequently overturned. Nevertheless, she succeeded in bringing home, in excellent condition, a collection of eighteen species of reptiles and about sixty-five species of fish. These will be listed or described in this paper, along with several other specimens, particularly <term>entomological</term> <note>entomological: relating to the scientific study of insects.</note> samples.

During a brief stay at Old Calabar and a visit to the island of Corisco, some freshwater fish were added to the main collection from the Ogowé River. These will also be included in this paper; however, the marine species are omitted because they are already well known.

---

¹ Reprinted by permission from the *Annals and Magazine of Natural History*, 6th series, No. 100. April, 1896.

<meta>This page continues Dr. A. Günther’s introduction to his report on the biological specimens collected by Mary Kingsley, focusing on the history of exploration and scientific study of the Ogowé River region.</meta>

<header>DR. A. GÜNTHER ON REPTILES AND FISHES</header>

Thirty years ago, little more than the name of the Ogowé River was known. However, between 1860 and 1870, French officials and traders began to map its course inland. They discovered a long stretch of rapids in its middle section that makes navigation dangerous and, in some places, impossible for any vessel larger than a small boat. Among those early explorers, an Englishman named Mr. R. B. N. Walker played a leading role,¹ leading two expeditions in 1866 and 1873 and reaching Lopé in the Okanda country. The survey of the river's upper reaches was later completed by Messrs. de Brazza and Balay.

Everything known before 1860 regarding the reptiles and fishes of the Gaboon region was compiled by Auguste Duméril in his treatise, *Reptiles and Fish of Western Africa* <note>original: "Reptiles et Poissons de l’Afrique Occidentale"</note>, published in *Archives du Muséum*, volume 10. In the list at the end of his work, I find that he mentions eight freshwater fishes from the Gaboon, all of which were from the coastal region of the country. In 1867,² I described the collection made by Walker on the Ogowé, adding seventeen species to the known wildlife of the area, ten of which were previously unknown. This list was expanded by six other species found by Buchholz and identified by Peters (*Reports of the Berlin Academy*, 1876, p. 244). Two years later, M. Sauvage began to publish the results of his examination of the specimens that had accumulated in the Paris Museum (*Bulletin of the Philomathic Society*, 1878, pp. 90-103), providing a complete account of the scientific knowledge of this fish population in his treatise, *Study of the Fish Fauna of the Ogowé* <note>original: "Étude sur la Faune ichthyologique de l’Ogôoué"</note>, in *New Archives of the Museum*, volume 3, 1880. In this work, he lists thirty-seven species, though he knew some of them only through the writings of his predecessors. He increased this number to forty-six in a final supplementary list (*Bulletin of the Zoological Society of France*, volume 9, 1884).

In this paper, I have added sixteen species from Miss Kingsley’s collection to the records of Gaboon wildlife:

*Gobius æneofuscus*, Günther.
*Eleotris senegalensis*, Steindachner.
*Ophiocephalus obscurus*, Günther.
*Ctenopoma gabonense*, <term>new species</term> (likely the same as *Ct. multispine* described by Sauvage, but <note>original: "nec Ptrs."; Latin meaning "not the species described by Peters."</note>).
—— *nanum*, <term>new species</term>.
—— *Kingsleyæ*, <term>new species</term> (likely the same as *Ct. Petherici* described by Sauvage, but <note>original: "nec Gthr."; Latin meaning "not the species described by Günther."</note>).

### *POROMERA*.

*Poromera*, [described by] Boulenger, *Catalogue of Lizards*, volume iii, page 6.

The nostril is located between two <term>nasal scales</term> and the <term>suture</term><gloss>seam or joint</gloss> between the <term>rostral scale</term><gloss>the scale at the tip of the snout</gloss> and the first <term>labial scale</term><gloss>lip scale</gloss>. The lower eyelid is covered in scales. A <term>collar</term><gloss>a fold of skin or row of scales on the throat</gloss> is present. The back is covered with scales that are larger than those on the tail and are strongly <term>keeled</term><gloss>having a raised ridge down the center</gloss>; these keels form continuous longitudinal ridges. The sides are covered with much smaller scales. The <term>ventral</term><gloss>belly</gloss> scales are rather large, <term>imbricate</term><gloss>overlapping like roof tiles</gloss>, and keeled, with the keels again forming continuous series. The fingers and toes are slender, with a double row of smooth, very small <term>scutes</term><gloss>enlarged scales</gloss> on the underside. There are <term>femoral pores</term><gloss>small openings on the underside of the thighs</gloss>, but no <term>inguinal pores</term><gloss>pores near the groin</gloss>. The tail is long and cylindrical.

#### *Poromera Fordii.*

<note>original: "Tachydromus Fordii"</note> *Tachydromus fordii*, [described by] Hallowell in the *Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia*, 1857, page 48.
<note>original: "Poromera Fordii"</note> *Poromera fordii*, [described by] Boulenger, <note>original: "l. c."</note> in the work previously cited.

This species has the general appearance of a lizard in the genus <note>original: "Tachydromus"</note> *Tachydromus*. 
The scutes on the upper side of the head show longitudinal ridges, located either along the middle or following the curve of their margins. The front nasal scale meets its counterpart at the center line behind the rostral scale. The front <term>frontal scale</term> is longer than it is wide; there is a single small, unpaired scale between the rear frontal scales. The <term>vertical scale</term><gloss>a large shield on the top of the head</gloss> is bell-shaped and twice as long as it is wide. There is a pair of front <term>occipital scales</term><gloss>scales at the back of the head</gloss>,

[The scale is] half the size of the posterior one, with a central <term>occipital</term><gloss>a scale at the back of the head</gloss> between them. The ear opening is very clear and vertically long. The collar is more distinct in front of the shoulder joint and almost disappears across the chest. The <term>dorsal</term><gloss>back</gloss> scales are arranged in eight longitudinal rows, and the <term>ventral</term><gloss>belly</gloss> scales in ten rows. The <term>preanal region</term><gloss>the area in front of the vent</gloss> is covered by ridged scales that hardly differ in size or shape from the scales preceding them. There are about twelve <term>femoral pores</term><gloss>small openings on the underside of the thighs</gloss>. All the tail scales are strongly ridged.

When the front leg is pressed backward, it does not reach the groin; when the hind leg is extended forward, it reaches the ear. The back of the thigh has a fine, grainy texture.

The upper parts of the body are brown, though they appear iridescent green after the outer layer of skin (<term>epidermis</term>) is removed. On the front of the back, there is a black lengthwise stripe on each side of the center line; these two stripes merge together further down the body. There is a faint greenish stripe along each side of the neck. The underparts are whitish.

I have provided a full description of this lizard because the specimen found by Miss Mary Kingsley at <note>Lambarene: A town in Gabon on the Ogooué River.</note> seems to be only the second one known to exist in scientific collections. Its specific identity as <note>original: "Tachydromus Fordii"</note> Ford's swift-running lizard—as named by Hallowell—might be questioned. This is because Hallowell described the specimen in the museum of the <note>Philadelphia Academy: The Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia.</note> as having only six rows of belly scales; he also described the scales of the preanal region differently. However, since there is a great deal of agreement in other respects between the two specimens, and the location (<note>Gaboon: Gabon, West Africa.</note>) given by Hallowell also suggests they are the same species, I am using the name provided by that author.

### *Dipsadoboa assimilis*

*Dipsadoboa assimilis*, Matschie, *Report of the Society of Friends of Natural Science in Berlin* <note>original: "SB. Ges. naturf. Fr. Berl."</note> 1893, p. 173 (Togoland); Bocage, *Journal of Sciences, Lisbon* <note>original: "Jorn. Sc. Lisb."</note> iv. 1895, p. 17.

The specimen obtained at Lambarene matches *D. assimilis* more closely than *D. unicolor* regarding the number and arrangement of the <term>labial shields</term><gloss>the scales bordering the mouth opening</gloss>. 

Professor Bocage also identifies his specimens from Fernando Po as *D. assimilis*. Interestingly, I now have evidence that the <term>type</term><gloss>the original specimen used to name the species</gloss> of *D. unicolor* came from that same island; a few years ago, I received a specimen from Fernando Po that is identical to *D. unicolor*. Therefore, based on our current findings, both *D. unicolor* and *D. assimilis* (if they are indeed distinct species) appear to exist on Fernando Po, while *D. unicolor* does not seem to extend to the mainland.

### *Atheris anisolepis*

*Atheris anisolepis*, Mocquard, *Bulletin of the Philomathic Society* <note>original: "Bull. Soc. Philom."</note> 1887, p. 90.
*Atheris læviceps*, Boettger, *Zoological Gazette* <note>original: "Zool. Anz."</note> x. p. 651; *Report of the Senckenberg Society* <note>original: "Ber. Senckenb, Ges."</note> 1888, p. 92, plate <note>original: "tab."</note> ii. fig. 7 (head).

This is an adult specimen from Lambarene. The specimens that Boettger used for his description came from Banana in the Congo delta. In my opinion, the main identifying features of this species are the number and size of the scales and the two rows of <term>suboculars</term><gloss>scales located directly below the eye</gloss>. These are more reliable markers than the degree of <term>carination</term><gloss>the presence of ridges or keels</gloss> on some of the scales on the top of the head, as that feature changes with age.

Thanks to the kindness of Professor L. Vaillant and Dr. Jentink, I have been able to re-examine the original specimens described by Schlegel and Mocquard. This has allowed me to form a clear opinion on which species of *Atheris* should be recognized. They are the following:

1.  ***A. squamigera*** (Hallowell), which is the same as *A. subocularis* (Fisch.), and probably the same as *A. Burtonii* (Gthr.). This species has 17 rows of scales (though *A. Burtonii* has 19). It has only one row of tiny subocular scales; occasionally, these are partly <term>confluent</term><gloss>fused or merged</gloss> with the upper lip scales.
2.  ***A. anisolepis*** (Mocquard 1887), which is the same as *A. læviceps* (Boettger 1887), and includes part of *A. chloroechis* (Boettger). This species has 22–25 rows of scales. It has two rows of tiny suboculars; while the lower row is sometimes incomplete, it is always marked by several scales.

A Goby which seems to be very common in the freshwaters of Liberia and the Cameroon River, and is abundant in the Ogowé River, where numerous examples were obtained by Miss Kingsley at Kondo-Kondo, is identical with the species discovered by Peters in the Zambezi. However, it is not—as Dr. Steindachner thinks—identical with the West-Indian *G. banana*, which has considerably smaller scales on the tail. *G. æneofuscus*, therefore, belongs to the freshwater fauna of Tropical Africa, extending right across the continent. 
*Gobius lateristriga*, A. Duméril, *Archives of the Museum* <note>original: "Arch. Mus."</note> x. p. 247, plate <note>original: "pl."</note> xxi. fig 1, if not identical with this species, is, at any rate, closely allied to it; unfortunately, the author has omitted to describe the scales, dentition, and other important characters.

## CTENOPOMA, Peters.

After examining a much larger number of specimens than I had available some years ago, I have concluded that the variation in species characteristics is limited. Consequently, there are more distinct species than I was previously willing to recognize. Furthermore, the distinction between this genus and *Spirobranchus* is not as sharp as once thought; the <term>armature of the opercles</term><gloss>bony spines on the gill covers</gloss> is not equally developed in all species, and very young Ctenopomas apparently lack it entirely. At present, I categorize the specimens before me under the following specific names:

The body is almost as elongated as in *Ctenopoma multispine*, to which this species is closely allied. The mouth is moderately wide, and the maxillary bone does not extend beyond a vertical line drawn from the center of the eye. The entire margin of the suboperculum is armed with prominent spines; part of the interopercular margin <note>the edge of the bone between the gill cover and the throat</note> is also spiny. The space between the anal and caudal fins is equal to, or even longer than, the diameter of the eye. The ventral fin does not reach the vent <note>the anus</note>. The pores on the head are rather small and inconspicuous. The coloration is uniform.

->*Ctenopoma nanum*, <term>species nova</term> <note>original: "sp. n."</note>. (Plate I, figure B.)<-

->Dorsal fin 15–16 spines/9 rays. Anal fin 8 spines/9–10 rays. <term>linea lateralis</term> <note>lateral line scales</note> 27. <term>linea transversalis</term> <note>transverse scale rows</note> 2½/9.<-

The body is stouter than in *Ctenopoma multispine* or *Ctenopoma gabonense*; its greatest depth is contained two and three-quarters times in the total length (excluding the tail fin) and is nearly equal to the length of the head. The snout is as long as the diameter of the eye, which is contained four and three-quarters times in the length of the head. The space between the eyes is somewhat convex and no wider than the eye socket itself. The mouth is quite narrow, with the upper jaw bone <note>maxillary</note> not reaching back as far as the vertical line from the center of the eye. 

The armor on the gill cover is weak; there are only a few spiny teeth above and below the notch in the operculum, and none at all on the lower gill cover bones <note>the suboperculum and interoperculum</note>. The distance between the anal fin and the tail fin is equal to the diameter of the eye. The sensory pores on the head are completely covered by scales. There are five rows of scales on the cheek, with the lowest row covering the edge of the preoperculum. The pelvic fins reach past the start of the anal fin, with the two outer rays extending into long filaments. The body is marked with darker vertical bands; there is a faint, slanted, irregular dark band running from the eye toward the base of the pectoral fin.

Two specimens from the Gaboon region, measuring 67 millimeters long, are in the British Museum; they were collected alongside specimens of *Ctenopoma Petherici*.

This species lacks teeth on the palatine bones, and I cannot see any teeth on the vomer, though the front of that bone is visible and not covered by the mucous membrane. Naturally, I considered the possibility that these specimens might be the young of one of the other species. However, besides being consistent with each other and differing from the other species in the number of fin spines, the relative size of the eye and the width of the space between the eyes clearly indicate that they are either mature or nearly so.

The fish is blackish in color, with a large, blurry black spot at the end of the tail, just before the base of the tail fin.

Teeth on the front of the roof of the mouth <note>vomerine teeth</note> are developed, but there are only traces of teeth on the side of the roof of the mouth <note>palatine teeth</note> at the front of the bone. The coloration is the same as in the adult.

All three specimens are from Kondo-Kondo.

### *Chromis latus*, Günther

Warri.
The typical specimen was most likely from the same locality, as the late Mr. Fraser was known to have collected in, or to have received collections from, the Niger delta.

### *Chromis ogowensis*, <term>new species</term> <note>original Latin: "sp. n."</note>

? *Chromis microcephalus*, Sauvage, *Bulletin of the Zoological Society of France*, volume ix, 1884, page 196 (<note>original Latin: "nec," meaning "not of"</note> Bleeker).

->Dorsal fin: 15 spines/11 rays. Anal fin: 3 spines/8 rays. Pectoral fin: 13 rays. Lateral line scales: 27. Transverse scale rows: 3/11.<-

The scales on the cheek are arranged in three series. There are twenty-eight notched teeth on each side of the upper jaw. The upper jaw bone <note>maxillary</note> ends some distance before reaching the vertical line aligned with the front of the eye. The depth of the body is a little less than one-half of the total length (excluding the tail fin), and the length of the head is a little less than one-third. The eye is two-ninths of the length of the head, which is much less than the length of the snout and the width of the space between the eyes <note>interorbital space</note>. The pectoral fin has the third and fourth rays elongated, extending to the first spine of the anal fin. The tail fin <note>caudal fin</note> is squared off <note>truncated</note> and covered in scales. The body has indistinct cross-bands. The fins along the midline <note>vertical fins</note> are blackish; the dorsal fin has black longitudinal stripes, which run horizontally on the spiny portion and diagonally on the soft portion; there is a large, oval black spot behind the last dorsal spine. The pelvic fins <note>ventrals</note> are black. There is a black spot on the gill cover <note>opercular spot</note>.

### *Hemichromis bimaculatus*

*Hemichromis bimaculatus*, Gill. *Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia*, 1862, page 137; Steindachner, *Notes from the Leyden Museum*, volume xvi, page 49.
*Hemichromis auritus*, Gill, <note>original: "l. c." (loco citato), meaning "in the place cited"</note> page 135.

This species is related to *H. guttatus* and *H. subocellatus*, but has a deeper body and a taller spiny dorsal fin.

->Dorsal fin: 14 spines / 10 rays.  Anal fin: 3 spines / 8 rays.  Lateral line: 24 scales.  Transverse scale rows: 3 / 10.<-

The depth of the body is contained 2½ times in the total length (excluding the tail fin <note>caudal fin</note>), and the length of the head is contained 2¾ times. The length of the snout is equal to the diameter of the eye, which is one-fourth of the length of the head and equal to the width of the space between the eyes <note>interorbital space</note>. The teeth are cone-shaped <note>conical</note>, brown, and uniform in size. There are four rows of scales on the cheek. The opening of the mouth is quite narrow and slightly slanted <note>oblique</note>, with the lower jaw protruding slightly; the upper jaw bone <note>maxillary</note> does not quite reach the vertical line aligned with the front edge of the eye socket <note>orbit</note>. The length of the eighth dorsal spine is two-fifths the length of the head. In adults, the soft-rayed parts of the dorsal and anal fins, as well as the pelvic <note>ventral</note> fins, extend into points. The upper body is brownish, with a deep black spot on the edge of the gill cover <note>operculum</note> and another in the middle of the body. There are three or four rows of round bluish spots on the cheek and gill cover. The fins have no spots.

### *Clarias gabonensis.*

->*Clarias gabonensis*, Günther, Annals & Magazine of Natural History 1867, volume 20, page 110.<-

->Dorsal 76-78. &nbsp;&nbsp; Anal 56-60. &nbsp;&nbsp; Pectoral 1/10.<-

The vomerine teeth <note>teeth on the roof of the mouth</note> are hair-like <note>villiform</note>, forming a band that is a little broader than the band on the upper jaw <note>intermaxillary band</note>, without any backward projection. Each half of the intermaxillary band is twice as wide as it is broad, and at the sides, it barely extends as far as the vomerine band. The top of the head is bare, finely grainy, and marked with lines <note>striated</note>. The bone at the back of the head <note>occipital process</note> is triangular with a rounded end, and its base is a little longer than its sides. The fontanelle <note>skull opening</note> is oval-shaped and does not extend into the base of the triangular process. 

The length of the head is one-fourth of the total length (excluding the tail fin <note>caudal fin</note>); the snout is narrow, with the width of the space between the eyes <note>interorbital space</note> being less than half the length of the head. The barbels are moderately long; the one by the nostril reaches the root of the pectoral fin, and the maxillary barbel reaches the start of the dorsal fin, which is nearly opposite the end of the pectoral fin. The anal fin is not low. The vertical fins are separated from each other by a small gap. The coloring is a uniform blackish-brown.

### *Clarias buthupogon.*

? *Clarias læviceps*, Gill, Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia, 1862, p. 139.
*Clarias buthupogon*, Sauvage, Bulletin of the Philomatic Society <note>original: "Bull. Soc. Philom."</note> 1878, p. 96.
*Clarias gabonensis* (*Clarias megapogon*), Sauvage, New Archives of the Museum <note>original: "N. Arch. Mus."</note> iii. 1880, p. 39, plate i. figure 2 (not Günther).

->Dorsal 84-87. &nbsp;&nbsp; Anal 65-67. &nbsp;&nbsp; Pectoral 1/8.<-

The vomerine teeth <note>teeth on the roof of the mouth</note> are hair-like <note>villiform</note>, forming a fairly broad band without any backward projection. This band is as broad as the upper jaw band <note>intermaxillary band</note>. Each half of the upper jaw band is twice as wide as it is broad, and both the upper jaw and vomerine bands extend the same distance across the mouth. The top of the head is covered with a very thin skin and has fine, somewhat scattered granules. The bone at the back of the head <note>occipital process</note> sticks out in the shape of an isosceles triangle, and the back edge of the head is deeply notched on each side of this process. The soft spot in the skull <note>fontanelle</note> is oval-shaped, with most of it located in front of the base of the process. 

The length of the head (measured to the end of the process) is between two-sevenths and one-fourth of the total length (excluding the tail fin <note>caudal fin</note>). The width of the space between the eyes <note>interorbital space</note> is slightly less than half the length of the head. All the whisker-like barbels <note>barbels</note> are very long; the nasal barbel <note>near the nostril</note> reaches beyond the head, and the maxillary barbel <note>on the upper jaw</note> reaches past the start of the anal fin. The pectoral fin <note>side fin</note> reaches as far back as the first ray of the dorsal fin. The anal fin is low; both the dorsal and anal fins extend all the way to the base of the tail fin. The sides of the head and neck are marked with small white spots.

The specimens were collected at Kondo-Kondo and on Corisco Island. The original description of *C. læviceps* is as follows:

> "The height at the anus is one-tenth of the length; the head (viewed from the side) is one-sixth, and its breadth is one-eighth; the surface is smooth; the maxillary barbels are twice as long as the head. Dorsal 86, Anal 61,"—

This description is quite insufficient for an exact identification of specimens. The type specimen <note>the original specimen used for the description</note> probably came from Liberia.

*Chrysichthys Büttikoferi*, Steindachner, Notes from the Leyden Museum <note>original: "Notes Leyd. Mus."</note> xvi. p. 60.

This is a species clearly distinct from *Ch. macrops*, as it has an adipose fin <term>a small, fleshy, rayless fin behind the dorsal fin</term> that is much shorter and further away from the dorsal fin. In this respect, it agrees with *Ch. nigrodigitatus*, which generally has a more narrow snout and a narrower mouth. However, I have examined large specimens which are difficult to assign to either of these two species with certainty. The difficulty is increased because I find that there are specimens with eleven and with thirteen anal rays <note>fin rays on the underside of the fish</note> in both the narrow-snouted form (*Ch. nigrodigitatus*) and the broad-snouted form (*Ch. Büttikoferi*). Possibly more than just these two species should be distinguished. Miss Kingsley found *Ch. Büttikoferi* at Kondo-Kondo and on Corisco Island.

### *Barilius bibie*. (Plate II. Figure C.)

Possibly *Leuciscus bibie*, De Joannis, Guérin, Magazine of Zoology <note>original: "Mag. Zool."</note> 1835, Fishes <note>original: "Pisc."</note> plate 4;
Günther, Fishes <note>original: "Fish."</note> volume 7, page 293.

Dorsal rays 10. Anal rays 18. Ventral rays 9. Lateral line scales 54. Transverse scales 8/4 <term>8 scales above the lateral line and 4 below</term>.

The body is compressed; its depth is two-ninths and the length of the head is one-fourth of the total length (without the caudal fin <term>the tail fin</term>). The head is oblong with a pointed snout, which is equal to the diameter of the eye or two-sevenths of the length of the head. The width of the interorbital space <term>the area between the eyes</term> is equal to the diameter of the eye. The mouth is wide and oblique; the narrow maxillary <term>upper jaw bone</term> extends to below the middle of the eye, and its end is hidden below the suborbital bone when the mouth is shut. The preorbital bone <note>original: "Præorbital"</note> is about half the area of the orbit <term>the eye socket</term>. The first suborbital bone is narrow, much narrower than the second and third, which almost entirely cover the cheek, leaving only an uncovered space about equal to the size of the first suborbital. The origin of the dorsal fin is somewhat nearer to the tail than to the back of the head <note>original: "occiput"</note>; the origin of the anal fin is below the middle of the dorsal fin. The caudal fin is deeply forked. The pectoral fin is shorter than the head and does not reach the much shorter ventral fin. The scales are thin, with very distinct radiating ridges <note>original: "striæ"</note>; the lateral line sweeps down in a curve toward the abdomen and, following the lower profile, ends below the center of the caudal fin. The fish is silvery, with twelve bluish vertical bars along the middle of the side and a large blackish spot at the base <note>original: "root"</note> of the caudal fin.

the end of the snout than to the root of the caudal <term>tail</term> fin. Except for a small specimen from the Nile, *L. bibie* has remained undiscovered in that river until the present time. De Joannis does not mention the bluish cross-bars, which are, however, very faint. It is highly desirable that specimens from the Nile be compared directly with West African ones.

I cannot reach a definite conclusion as to whether *Barilius senegalensis*, described by Steindachner (Reports of the Vienna Academy of Sciences <note>original: "SB. Wien. Akad."</note> 1870, volume 61, page 564, Plate <note>original: "Taf."</note> 5, figure 2) from the Senegal River, should be categorized as this species. It has 59–63 scales along the lateral line <term>a visible line of sense organs along the side of a fish</term>, and the maxillary <term>upper jaw bone</term> extends past the center of the eye.

I am equally uncertain regarding *Opsaridium Buchholzi*, described by Peters (Monthly Reports of the Berlin Academy of Sciences <note>original: "MB. Berl. Akad."</note> 1876, page 251, figure 4). It also comes from the Ogowé River; but, judging from the description and illustration, Peters's fish has fewer scales in the lateral line (46), a smaller eye, and a longer snout (though the specimens are about the same size). It also has a longer maxillary, which reaches past the middle of the eye. Peters depicts his fish without any color markings.

Assuming that there are two distinct species of *Barilius* in West Africa, from a geographical perspective, *B. senegalensis* would probably prove to be identical to the Nile fish, while the Ogowé specimens described by Peters and myself might prove to be the second species. However, this assumption is not confirmed by the descriptions provided by various authors. Thus, as none of the existing descriptions fully agree with our specimen, I am currently applying the oldest known name to it.

### *Mormyrus lepturus.*

*Mormyrus lepturus*, Günther. *Proceedings of the Zoological Society* <note>original: "P.Z.S."</note> 1871, page 670, plate 69, figure B.
? *Mormyrus granaïsquamis*, Peters. *Monthly Reports of the Royal Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin* <note>original: "MB. Berl. Akad."</note> 1876, page 250.

I originally described this species from two young specimens three inches long. Miss Kingsley has rediscovered it at Talagouga and collected specimens that appear to be adults, measuring up to 190 millimeters in length. Thus, I am able to correct several points in my original diagnosis.

->Dorsal fin: 20–24. Anal fin: 25–29. Lateral line: 42–44.<-

The snout is blunt <term>obtuse</term> with the mouth at the tip <term>terminal</term>; with age, the lower lip thickens into a short fatty <term>adipose</term> bump. The upper profile is somewhat more curved than the lower. The eye is small, shorter than the snout (in adult specimens, it is only half as long as the snout), and located in the front half of the head. The teeth are of moderate size, notched, and few in number. The height of the body is two-sevenths of the total length (excluding the tail <term>caudal</term> fin), and the length of the head is two-ninths. The tail base <term>caudal peduncle</term> is slender and about as long as the head, with its depth being one-third of its length. 

The dorsal fin starts a little behind the start of the anal fin, midway between the base of the tail and the head. The pectoral fin is a little shorter than the head, extending to the middle of the pelvic <term>ventral</term> fin, which is only half as long and ends a long way from the vent. The scales on the front part of the body <term>trunk</term> are of moderate size; they gradually increase in size toward the rear and are largest on the back part of the tail and on the tail base <term>caudal peduncle</term>, where they are arranged in three rows on the side. The fish is brownish or silvery, and darker on the head. Two black vertical bands descend from the front and rear dorsal rays to the anal fin, spreading more or less over that fin.

### *Mormyrus sphecodes.*

*Mormyrops sphekodes*, Sauvage. *Bulletin of the Philomathic Society of Paris* <note>original: "Bull. Soc. Philom."</note> 1878, page 101; *New Archives of the Museum* <note>original: "N. Arch. Mus."</note> volume iii, 1880, page 55, plate ii, figure 4.

->Dorsal fin: 22. Anal fin: 26. Lateral line: 65.<-

The teeth on the palate and tongue are well developed. Sauvage’s description is fairly applicable to a specimen from Talagouga that is 138 millimeters long, but I count only 65 transverse rows of scales, whereas Sauvage states there are 82. The diameter of the eye is only one-eighth of the length of the head in our [specimen]...

### *Mormyrus Kingsleyæ*, new species <note>original: "sp. n."</note> (Plate II. figure A.)

->Dorsal 17. Anal 22. Lateral line 56.<-

The snout is short, rounded, and parabolic, with the small mouth located on the lower front side <term>antero-inferior</term>. There are five notched teeth above and six below. The eye is small, half the length of the snout and barely one-seventh the length of the head. The body is somewhat elongated; its greatest depth is contained 4⅓ times in the total length (excluding the tail <term>caudal</term> fin), and the length of the head is also contained 4⅓ times. The tail base <term>caudal peduncle</term> is compressed and moderately long, though shorter than the head; its depth is half of its length. The dorsal fin begins behind the start of the anal fin and is twice as far from the end of the snout as it is from the base of the tail <term>caudal</term>. The length of the base of the anal fin is equal to the length of the head. The pectoral fin is shorter than the head and nearly reaches the pelvic <term>ventral</term> fin. The pelvic <term>ventral</term> fin is more than half as long as the pectoral fin, and half as long as the distance from its base to the vent. The scales are quite small; there are eight in a diagonal <term>oblique</term> series running from the first anal fin ray to the lateral line, and five horizontal <term>longitudinal</term> series on the side of the tail base <term>caudal peduncle</term>. The fish is a uniform brown color.

### *Mormyrus Marchei*

? *Petrocephalus Marchei*, Sauvage, Bulletin of the Philomathic Society <note>original: "Bull. Soc. Philom."</note> 1878, p. 100.

# APPENDIX IV

## ORTHOPTERA, HYMENOPTERA, AND HEMIPTERA

*A List of the Orthoptera, Hymenoptera, and Hemiptera collected by Miss Kingsley on the River Ogowé, with Descriptions of some new Genera and Species.* By W. F. KIRBY, F.L.S., F.E.S. <note>Fellow of the Linnean Society and Fellow of the Entomological Society</note>, etc., Assistant in the Zoological Department, British Museum (Natural History).

The collection formed by Miss Kingsley, though small,¹ contained several species of considerable interest in addition to the new discoveries. For this reason, I have thought it worthwhile to prepare a complete list. Eight species in all are described here as new, and it has been necessary to establish two new genera for two of them. It is, however, regrettable that in most cases only single specimens were received, and several of them were immature; otherwise, the number of new species might have been larger.

### Order <term>ORTHOPTERA</term> <note>The order of insects including grasshoppers, crickets, and cockroaches</note>.

### Family <term>Blattidæ</term> <note>The cockroach family</note>.

### Subfamily <term>PANCHLORINÆ</term> <note>A subfamily of cockroaches, often green or wood-colored, found in tropical regions</note>.

### <term>TRICHOMERA</term>, new genus <note>original: "gen. nov."</note>.

*Female.*—*Wingless* <note>original: "Apterous"</note>: the front of the head is rounded and projects beyond the prothorax <note>the first segment of the thorax</note>; the face is hardly slanted; the antennae are thickened at the base and taper toward the tips; the prothorax is moderately arched with the back angles rounded off; the angles of the mesothorax <note>middle segment of the thorax</note> and metathorax <note>hind segment of the thorax</note> are less rounded and more extended toward the back; the tibiae <note>the fourth segment of an insect's leg</note>

---

¹ This collection is entirely from Lambaréné <note>Modern spelling of Lembarene, a town in Gabon</note> (River Ogowé). I have no lists of the collection of insects from Calabar.—M. H. K. <note>Mary Henrietta Kingsley</note>
