...strongly spined above, but the <term>femora</term> <note>the third segment of an insect's leg, similar to a thigh</note> have no spines and are only covered with fine hair. The abdomen is very broad, and the <term>supra-anal plate</term> <note>the plate covering the anus from above</note> has a triangular notch at the end that reaches nearly half its length. The <term>cerci</term> <note>paired appendages at the end of the abdomen</note> are very broad and pointed at the tips, being slightly shorter than the supra-anal plate.

The spineless femora place this genus in the <term>Panchlorinae</term> <note>a subfamily of cockroaches</note>, though in shape it resembles the females of some <term>Blattinae</term> <note>the subfamily of cockroaches containing many common species</note>. The male is likely winged.

### *Trichomera insignata*, new species <note>original: "sp. n."</note>

Body length: 20–21 mm; width: 13 mm. <note>original: "Long. corp. 20-21 millim., lat. 13 millim."</note>

*Female.*—Blackish with <term>testaceous</term> <note>dull brownish-yellow or brick-red</note> markings. The face is nearly smooth and shiny black below the <term>vertex</term> <note>the top of the head</note>; the sides, mouth, and a band between the eyes and antennae are brownish-yellow. The vertex is brownish-yellow in front, with blackish streaks extending into it from behind. The head and thorax are covered with fine down. The <term>prothorax</term> <note>the first segment of the thorax</note> and the sides of the <term>mesothorax</term> and <term>metathorax</term> <note>the middle and rear segments of the thorax</note> are finely punctured, while the middle of the meso- and metathorax and the abdomen are rather coarsely granulated. 

The mesothorax is brownish-yellow and somewhat speckled with reddish-brown. Its center is filled with a large blackish blotch that has two projecting angles on each side in front and behind. The two innermost rear projections extend to the back edge of the prothorax, and the second of the front projections connects to a large, oblong black patch bordering part of the sides of the prothorax. The meso- and metathorax are bordered on the sides with reddish-brown and several irregular brownish-yellow markings. On the abdomen, these markings continue more regularly, forming a central series that is nearly parallel, along with two outer series. The first of these is nearly straight, and the second connects with the brownish-yellow border below the side angles of the segments. The supra-anal plate is black with a broad brownish-yellow band on each side. The cerci are black, and the antennae are reddish, shading into brown. The <term>pectus</term> <note>the chest or underside of the thorax</note> is brownish-yellow, and the underside of the abdomen is brown.

Two specimens were obtained.

### Family Mantidæ <note>Praying Mantises</note>.
#### Subfamily *Mantinæ*.
##### Hierodula, Burm.

A single immature specimen of this genus. It is notable for the very heavy black band on the front femora and <term>tibiae</term> <note>the segment of the leg between the femur and the foot</note>, and for the black spines on the tibiae.

# Family **Phasmidae** <note>stick and leaf insects</note>.

## Subfamily **PALOPHINAE**.

### *Palophus centaurus*.

*Palophus centaurus*, Westw. Cat. Phasm. p. 91, n. 233, pl. xxxi. fig. 1 (1859); Brogn. Nouv. Arch. Mus. Paris, (3) iii. p. 195, pl. viii., pl. ix. figs. 1-4 (1892).

This is one of the largest winged African stick insects. A single female specimen was included in the collection.

## Subfamily **PHASMINAE**.

### **BATHYCHARAX**, new genus <note>original: "gen. nov."</note>

*Female.*—Wingless <term>apterous</term>, rather stout, and covered in small bumps <term>granulated</term>. The antennae are somewhat shorter than the front <term>femora</term> <note>the third segment of an insect's leg, similar to a thigh</note> and consist of 23 segments, most of which are long and cylindrical. The <term>scape</term> <note>the first or basal segment of the antenna</note> is flattened and about twice as long as it is wide; the second segment is also longer than it is wide and considerably longer than the following segments. The front legs are much longer, and the front femora are much thicker than those of the last two pairs of legs.

This genus is easily distinguished from *Phasma* (*Bacillus* according to other authors <note>original: "auct."</note>) by its granulated body and the cylindrical segments of the antennae.

### *Bathycharax granulatus*, new species <note>original: "sp. n."</note>

The insect is a uniform brown, except for the face, which is marked with black on the upper part and yellow on the lower part. The head has a row of four raised bumps <term>tubercles</term> at the back. The <term>pronotum</term> <note>the top plate of the first segment of the thorax</note> has three incomplete grooves and a crosswise groove that divides it nearly in half; there is also a distinct ridge <term>carina</term> on each side. The <term>mesonotum</term> <note>the top plate of the middle segment of the thorax</note> is thickly granulated and has three central ridges; the side ridges do not extend to its end, but the central ridge continues along the <term>metanotum</term> <note>the top plate of the rear segment of the thorax</note> and the abdomen. In the abdomen, segments 2 through 8 (counting the <term>median segment</term> <note>the first abdominal segment, often fused to the thorax</note> as 1) gradually decrease in length. The ninth segment is short and wider than it is long <term>transverse</term>. The tenth segment is three times as long as it is wide, gradually narrowing, and extending for half its length beyond the <term>operculum</term> <note>the plate covering the reproductive organs</note>. The <term>cerci</term> <note>paired appendages at the end of the abdomen</note> are very short, rather broad and rounded, and stick out slightly on each side at the base of the tenth segment. The underside of the body has a central ridge along its entire length behind the <term>propectus</term> <note>the underside of the first thoracic segment</note>, which itself has ridges on the sides. Most of the rear part of the body is ridged on the sides, both above and below the middle. The legs are ridged <term>carinated</term> and grooved <term>sulcated</term>. The first segment of the front <term>tarsi</term> <note>the foot segments</note> is about as long...

The antennae are reddish on the half near the base, shading into a blackish color, and consist of at least 40 segments. The scape <note>the first segment of the antenna</note> and the second segment are thickened; the scape is one and a half times as long as it is wide, the second segment is barely longer than it is wide, and the third segment is twice as long as the fourth. The remaining segments taper and gradually decrease in length until just past the middle, where they become longer and more cylindrical. The top of the head <term>vertex</term> and the thorax are densely marked with small pits <term>punctured</term>, with the thorax being more coarsely pitted. The thorax features two strong spines at the front corners, a strong spine on each side with a raised ridge running between them, and a row of eight large spines at the back. There is one additional large spine on each side slightly in front of the others. On the yellow lower ridge of the thorax, most of the spines are red with black tips. The spines on the legs are described in the section defining the genus. The dividing ridge of the thorax is brownish; in front of it are two pairs of shallow brownish depressions, and behind it is a row of five on each side that curve outward, along with two or three more pairs in the middle. The abdomen is smooth and somewhat coppery in color <term>cupreous</term>, with some scattered pits toward the ends of the segments.

This species closely resembles *C. erinaceus* (Fairmaire) from Gabon, but it is only half the size. This description is based on two males and one female, which show very little structural difference. This suggests that the insect mentioned by Dr. Karsch as the female of *Cosmoderus erinaceus* (in the *Berlin Entomological Journal* <note>original: "Berl. ent. Zeitschr."</note> vol. 31, p. 59) likely belongs to a different genus, and quite possibly to *Aprophantia*, which is described below.

The curious wingless insects belonging to the family Hetrodidae <note>armored ground crickets or katydids</note> must be very numerous in the warmer regions of Africa. Almost every collection from these regions, no matter how small, contains one or more new species if it includes any Orthoptera <note>the order of insects comprising grasshoppers and crickets</note>. I will take this opportunity to add the description of a new genus and species in a footnote, as it appears to have been confused with *Cosmoderus erinaceus*.<sup>1</sup>

### *Aprophantia maculata*, new species.

Body length 38–48 millimeters.
Brownish-yellow <term>testaceous</term> (likely green when alive); the tips of the spines, a double row of more or less complete spots on both sides of the femora <term>thigh segments</term>, and a patch over the openings <term>foramina</term> on the front tibiae <term>lower leg segments</term> are black. The antennae are brownish-yellow with five long black bands that increase in length, the last one being at the tip. The male has some faint brown markings on the face, with two running up from above the frontal horn and one on each side beyond it, angled outwards. The male also has some faint, sunken brown marks on the top and sides of the thorax, nearly identical to the species in the true genus *Cosmoderus*. In the female, these markings are absent and the color is darker, especially at the sides of the thorax, the front and back of the abdomen, toward the ends of the tibiae, and along their ridges <term>carinae</term>. The male has three pairs of spines on the underside of the femora and two additional spines on the outer ridge of the hind femora; it also has six pairs of spines on the four front tibiae and eight or nine rows of spines (not all in pairs) on the hind tibiae. The female differs by having five pairs of spines on the hind femora, but the legs are otherwise spined nearly the same as the male.
Described from a single pair (male and female) from the Cameroons.

### Order HYMENOPTERA <note>Bees, wasps, and ants</note>.
#### Section TEREBRANTIA <note>Boring or piercing insects</note>.
#### Subsection ENTOMOPHAGA <note>Insect-eating parasites</note>.
#### Family **Braconidæ** <note>Braconid wasps</note>.

->*Bracon plumosus*, new species <note>original: "sp. n."</note><-

->Body length 11 millimeters; ovipositor length 10 millimeters <note>original: "Long. corp. 11 millim. ; long. ovip. 10 millim."</note><-

*Female.*—The head, antennae, and abdomen (including the petiole <term>the narrow waist-like segment</term>) are black on the upper side; the underside of the head and the mouthparts are brownish-yellow <term>fulvous</term>; the jaws <term>mandibles</term> have two teeth and are tipped with black; the thorax is entirely reddish-brown <term>rufous</term>. Front legs: the hip-like segments <term>coxae</term> and the base of the thighs <term>femora</term> are reddish-brown, but the rest of the leg is missing; the middle legs are reddish-brown, though the feet <term>tarsi</term> and the top of the lower leg segments <term>tibiae</term> are black; the hind legs are black, with a white spot at the end of the hip-like segments on the top, and the second joint of the legs <term>trochanters</term> is reddish-brown. The underside of the abdomen is white, with a row of five long black dashes on each side, the first of which is split in two <term>bifid</term> at the front. The ovipositor <term>the egg-laying organ</term> is reddish-brown and becomes partly black toward the end; above it are two long and rather thick black bristles <term>setae</term>, which are densely feathery <term>plumose</term> past the middle; the final third of the fine hairs <term>cilia</term> are white; the very tip of the bristles is spoon-shaped <term>spatulate</term> and whitish underneath. The wings are smoky, and the cross-veins <term>transverse nervures</term> are bordered with nearly transparent <term>subhyaline</term> areas.

This species is probably related to *Bracon semiflavus*, as described by Brullé.

### Subfamily OPHIONINÆ <note>A group of slender, orange-colored parasitic wasps</note>.

### *Ophion latipenne*, new species <note>original: "sp. n."</note>

->Body length 26 millimeters; wingspan 53 millimeters; width of the forewings 9 millimeters <note>original: "Long. corp. 26 millim. ; exp. al. 53 millim. ; lat. al. ant. 9 millim."</note><-

*Female.*—The body is reddish-brown <term>rufo-testaceous</term> and slightly fuzzy <term>pubescent</term>. The back of the head <term>occiput</term>, the antennae, the legs, and particularly the sides of the face are slightly more yellowish. The eyes have a slight notch <term>emarginate</term> in front, just above the antennae; below the antennae, the inner edges of the eyes are nearly parallel or very slightly curved inward. The antennae are fuzzy and have about 50 segments <term>joints</term>. The third and fourth segments are ring-shaped <term>annular</term>, and the fifth segment is the longest. The remaining segments are cylindrical and are barely longer than they are wide in the middle; they gradually taper and grow longer toward the tip, with the last segment being cone-shaped <term>conical</term>. The tips of the jaws <term>mandibles</term> are black. The simple eyes <term>ocelli</term> are very large and fill the space between the compound eyes at the top of the head <term>vertex</term>. They are black, except for the very front of the bottom part of the middle ocellus and the outer sides of the two rear ocelli.

The thorax and abdomen are covered in very fine and dense pits <term>punctured</term>. The middle section of the thorax <term>mesothorax</term> has two converging lines that are slightly yellower than the rest of the body, but these are only ridged <term>carinated</term> at the side edges. The rear section of the thorax <term>metathorax</term> also has a central ridge <term>carina</term>. The abdomen is very large, raised, and somewhat flattened on the sides <term>compressed laterally</term>. The hind legs are longer than the others. All of the lower leg segments <term>tibiae</term> are equipped with a pair of spines at the ends. 

The wings are fairly broad and translucent yellow <term>yellowish hyaline</term>. They are more strongly tinted yellow at the base and along the front edge <term>costal area</term> of the hind wings. Toward the tips, the wings are a bit smoky-colored, especially the hind wings. The wing veins <term>nervures</term> are reddish-brown along the front edge <term>costa</term> and toward the inner margin, but they are otherwise blackish. The front wings have three clear spots <term>bullae</term>—one on the lower curve of the cell near its end, one on the returning vein <term>recurrent nervule</term>, and a third on the cross-vein running upward from the end of the internal vein.

The Ophionid wasps <term>Ophionidae</term> of Africa are quite numerous, but very few have been described so far.

### Subsection DIPLOPTERA <note>The group of wasps that fold their wings longitudinally at rest</note>.

## Family **Eumenidae** <note>Potter wasps and mason wasps</note>.

### *Eumenes decipiens*, new species <note>original: "sp. n."</note>.

*Eumenes melanosoma*, Smith, MS., not Saussure <note>original: "nec. Sauss."</note>.

Body length: 15–17 mm; wingspan: 25–27 mm. <note>original: "Long. corp. 15-17 millim. ; exp. al. 25-27 millim."</note>

The head is black on top, and the inner corners of the eye sockets are yellowish. The antennae are rusty-red <term>ferruginous</term> but black on the upper surface. The face is rusty-red, very long, and beak-like; it is sometimes yellow, with only the mandibles and a space at the base of the clypeus <term>the shield-like plate on the face</term> remaining rusty-red. 

The prothorax <term>the first segment of the thorax</term> is red, featuring a large triangular black spot that nearly fills the rear angles on each side. The mesothorax <term>the middle segment of the thorax</term> is black. The tegulae <term>the small scales protecting the wing bases</term> are large and black, bordered on the outside with reddish coloring. The scutellum <term>a small plate on the thorax</term> is black, with a short yellow dash running from its tip between the bases of the wings. The postscutellum is black with a yellow dot on each side. The metathorax <term>the final segment of the thorax</term> is black and deeply grooved <term>sulcated</term> in the middle, forming two long triangles with reddish tips into which an oblique yellow line runs from the side. 

The breast <term>pectus</term> is black, turning red toward the seams <term>sutures</term>. The stalk <term>petiole</term> and abdomen are black, shiny, and much more finely punctured than the thorax. The petiole is reddish-brown <term>rufous</term> underneath and bordered at the back on the upper side with a pale yellow line. The first segment of the abdomen is bordered at the back on the upper side with a yellow line that is widely broken in the middle. 

The legs are reddish-brown; the front (and sometimes middle) shins <term>tibiæ</term> are lined with yellowish marks. The feet <term>tarsi</term> are covered with grayish down <term>pubescence</term>, and the four rear legs are more or less blackish on their upper side. The wings are iridescent purplish and somewhat transparent <term>subhyaline</term>.

This species agrees very closely with the description and illustration of the Javanese *E. melanosoma* described by Saussure, but it appears to be distinct. Specimens in the British Museum from Sierra Leone were labeled *E. melanosoma* by the late Frederick Smith. This species belongs to the group of *E. aethiopica* described by Saussure.

### *Synagris dentata.*

*Synagris dentata*, Saussure, *Studies of the Vespidae Family* <note>original: "Études Fam. Vesp."</note> volume 1, page 80, plate 13, figure 3 (1852).

A common African species.

## Subsection ANTHOPHILA <note>The group containing bees</note>.
### Family Apidae <note>Honey bees, bumblebees, and their relatives</note>.
#### Subfamily *MEGACHILINAE* <note>Leaf-cutter and mason bees</note>.
##### *Euaspis abdominalis.*

One specimen.

#### *Aspongopus*, Laporte, species.

An immature specimen, apparently related to *Aspongopus femoralis*, described by Stål; it is black, with the tegmina <term>the thickened forewings of a bug</term>, the borders of the abdomen, and the femora <term>the "thigh" section of the insect's leg</term> being a greenish copper color. The last joint of the antennae is reddish-brown <note>original: "rufo-testaceous"</note>, except at the base.

#### Subfamily *TESSARATOMINAE*.

#### *Piezosternum mucronatum.*

*Pentatoma mucronata*, Palisot de Beauvois, *Insects Collected in Africa and America* <note>original: "Ins. Afr. Amér."</note> page 46, Hemiptera plate 6, figure 5 (1805?).

One specimen, which is considerably smaller than *Piezosternum calidum*, described by Fabricius. It matches reasonably well with Palisot de Beauvois’s illustration cited above; I have no doubt that illustration was based on an African specimen, although it has recently been identified as the American species *Piezosternum subulatum*. Whether or not this small form is a distinct species from *P. calidum* remains to be seen, as a full series of specimens would be required to compare their characteristics. Therefore, I am temporarily keeping Palisot’s name for it.

#### Subfamily *PHYLLOCEPHALINAE*.

->Genus — ?<-

An immature specimen, apparently belonging to a new genus similar to *Macrina*, described by Amyot.

### Family **Pyrrhocoridae** <note>Red bugs and cotton stainers</note>.

#### Subfamily PYRRHOCORINAE.

##### *Antilochus submaculatus*, new species <note>original: "sp. n."</note>.

Body length 16 millimeters <note>original: "Long. corp. 16 millim."</note>.
The head is red; the occiput <term>the back of the head</term> and vertex <term>the top of the head</term> are black nearly as far as the base of the antennae, though the upper orbits <term>the area around the eyes</term> are red. The lower part of the head under the proboscis is blackish, except at the back. The head features a central groove and is wrinkled and pitted <note>original: "rugose-punctate"</note>. Close to the back is a wavy line, behind which the narrow area is finely punctured. The antennae are black, with the terminal joint being brownish-yellow <note>original: "testaceous"</note> and turning brown toward the tip. The scape <term>the first segment of the antenna</term> is curved, thicker than the remaining joints, and slightly shorter than the second and fourth joints, which are equal in length; the third joint is somewhat shorter than the scape. The rostrum <term>the beak-like mouthpart</term> extends as far as the hind coxae <term>the basal segment of the insect's leg</term>; the basal joint is grooved. 

The thorax is black, bordered all around with brownish-yellow; the inner edge of this border and the posterior <note>original: "hinder"</note> lobe are marked with large punctures. The front lobe has a central groove and is not punctured, except on a narrow triangular space in front. The scutellum <term>the small triangular plate on the insect's back</term> and the clavus <term>the inner part of the forewing</term> are sparingly punctured, while the corium <term>the thickened outer part of the forewing</term> is more thickly punctured. The scutellum and tegmina <term>the modified leathery forewings</term> are black; the clavus is bordered with a narrow red line at the base and on the inside. The corium is rather broadly bordered with reddish-brown <note>original: "rufo-testaceous"</note> on the outside; this stripe then crosses to the end of the clavus and curves outwards again, leaving most of the center and the apex black, as is the membrane <term>the thin, translucent part of the wing</term>. 

The legs are black; the coxae, trochanters <term>the second segment of the leg</term>, and the base and under surface of the femora <term>the "thigh" section of the leg</term> are coral-red. The tarsi <term>the feet</term>, except for the basal joint, are yellowish-grey underneath. The pleura <term>the side plates of the thorax</term> are black, bordered with brownish-yellow above and in the sutures, and with red below. The abdomen is coral-

# APPENDIX V

## THE INVENTION OF THE CLOTH LOOM

->This story was recorded from an Igbo <note>original: "Eboe"</note> person, but practically the same story<-
->can be found among all the cloth-making tribes in West Africa.<-

In ancient times, there was a man who was a great hunter, but he had a wicked wife. When he prepared charms <term>The original "medicine" refers to spiritual or magical preparations common in West African hunting traditions.</term> to put on his spear, she performed counter-magic against his spear. He knew nothing of this and went out to hunt bush cows <term>The West African forest buffalo (*Syncerus caffer nanus*).</term>.

Eventually, he found a large bush cow and threw his spear at it, but the animal charged and drove its horns through his thigh. The man crawled home and lay in his house, very sick. A traditional healer <note>original: "witch doctor"</note> discovered which of his wives had cursed the spear, and she was killed. For many days, the man could not go out hunting. However, because he was a great hunter, his heart yearned for the forest, so he dragged himself to the bush and lay there every day. 

One day, as he lay there, he saw a large spider spinning a web on a bush, and he watched it closely. After a while, he saw how the spider caught its prey and realized that the spider was a great hunter. The man said, “If I had hunted as this spider hunts—if I had made a trap like that and placed it in the bush, then stood aside and let the game get into it and exhaust itself to death quickly (quicker and more safely than they do in pit-traps)—that bush cow would not have gored me.” 

So, after some time, he tried to make a net like the spider’s out of vines <note>original: "bush rope"</note>. He succeeded and placed his net in the forest, where he caught gazelles, pangolins <note>original: "earth-pig"</note>, and porcupines. He made more nets, and each one he made was better than the last. He eventually recovered and became an even greater hunter than before. 

One day, he made a very fine net, and his wife said, “This is cloth; it is better than our bark cloth because it does not shrivel when the rain touches it. Make me a cloth like this, and then I will beat it with the mallet and wear it.” And the man tried to

<summary>This page recounts an Igbo folk tale explaining how a hunter, inspired by observing a spider's web, invented hunting nets and eventually the concept of woven cloth.</summary>
<keywords>Igbo folklore, West Africa, weaving history, cloth loom, hunting myths, spider web, cultural technology, Mary Kingsley</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Igbo origin myth from Appendix V regarding the invention of the loom. The hunter, inspired by a spider's web, seeks to improve the shape of his hunting nets before eventually transitioning to weaving cloth.</meta>

He attempted to do this, but he could not give it a proper shape. He said, “Yet the spider achieves a shape in his cloth. I will go and ask him about this matter again.” He went to the spider, brought him an offering, and said: “Oh, my lord, teach me more things.” Then he sat and watched him for many days.

<image-desc>A black and white photograph showing a vertical loom made of rough wooden sticks. A rectangular section of cloth is being woven, featuring horizontal stripes of light and dark colors. Several vertical and horizontal poles make up the frame, with weaving tools and extra thread visible. In the bottom right corner of the photo, there are small characters "W & S LD".</image-desc>

->LOOM AT EQUETTA.<-

Eventually, he saw more—his eyes were opened—and he observed that the spider made his net on sticks. So, he went home and gathered the fine bush rope <term>Likely fibers from the Raphia palm or similar lianas used for cordage in West Africa.</term> that he had collected and brought there to make his hunting nets. He took them to the bush near the spider and, by fixing the strings onto the branches, he made a new net. This time, he achieved the correct shape, and he went on to make many more nets.

<summary>This page describes the hunter's continued observation of a spider to learn the secrets of weaving, specifically how to use sticks as a frame to provide shape to his nets. This developmental step represents the mythical transition from simple cordage to the structure of a loom.</summary>

--- Page 792 ---
<meta>This page continues the Igbo origin myth from Appendix V regarding the development of the loom. The hunter, having learned to use a frame of sticks from the spider, begins to experiment with finer materials like grass to transition from net-making to cloth-weaving.</meta>

<page-num>736</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX V</header>

...this way, and every net he made was better. His wife was pleased and bore him sons, and in time the man realized that he did not need all the branches of a bush to weave his net upon, but only some of them. So, he took these home and set them up in his house, and wove his nets there. After a time, his wife asked, “Why do you make this material for me with that coarse vine <term>bush rope: a general term for various climbing plants and lianas used as cordage in West Africa.</term>? Why do you not make it with something finer?” 

He went back into the bush, brought offerings to the spider, and said, “Oh, my lord, teach me more things!” He sat and watched the spider, but the spider only continued producing silk from its belly. The man said, “Oh, my lord, you surpass me. I cannot do this thing.” 

As he went home, he reflected and noticed that there are trees and there are vines—both thick and thin—and then there is grass, which is thinner still. He took the grass and tried to weave a net with it; he succeeded in this task and made many more nets, and every net he made was better than the last. His wife was pleased and said, “This is good cloth.” 

The man lived to be very old and was a great chief and a great hunter. For it is good for a man to be a great hunter, and it is good for a man to please women. This is the origin of the cloth loom.

This occurred in ancient times. Nowadays, men have thread on spools from the white man, for the white man is like a great spider; but this is how the black man learned to make cloth.

<vocab>origin of the loom, spider, bush rope, cloth-making, folklore</vocab>

It frames the invention of weaving as a means to please women and achieve status, while noting modern transitions to imported thread.</summary>

# The Cambridge Natural History.

->Edited by S. F. HARMER, M.A., Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge, Superintendent of the University Museum of Zoology; and A. E. SHIPLEY, M.A., Fellow of Christ’s College, Cambridge, University Lecturer on the Morphology of Invertebrates.<-

->To be completed in ten volumes. Octavo <note>original: "8vo"</note>, price 17 shillings net each.<-

Intended in all respects to be a standard natural history, accurate enough to be of use to the student and at the same time popular enough for the general reader who desires trustworthy information regarding the structure and habits of all members of the Animal Kingdom, from the Protozoa to the Mammals. The volumes are fully illustrated by original figures, drawn from nature wherever possible. When complete, the series will be one that should be indispensable in all libraries, whether public or private.

->NOW READY.<-

**FLATWORMS.** By F. W. GAMBLE, M.Sc., Victoria University, Owens College.
**NEMERTINES.** By Miss L. SHELDON, Newnham College, Cambridge.

**EARTHWORMS AND LEECHES.** By F. E. BEDDARD, M.A. Oxford, F.R.S., Prosector <note>An official who dissects corpses or animals for anatomical demonstration</note> to the Zoological Society, London.
**GEPHYREA, etc.** By A. E. SHIPLEY, M.A., Fellow of Christ’s College, Cambridge.

## SHELLS. Volume III.

**MOLLUSCS AND BRACHIOPODS.** By the Rev. A. H. COOKE, M.A., A. E. SHIPLEY, M.A., and F. R. C. REED, M.A.

> *FIELD.*—"We know of no book available to the general reader which provides such a vast fund of information on the structure and habits of molluscs."

**PERIPATUS.** By ADAM SEDGWICK, M.A., F.R.S. **MYRIAPODS.** By F. G. SINCLAIR, M.A. **INSECTS.** Part I. By DAVID SHARP, M.A. Cambridge, M.B. Edinburgh, F.R.S.

# JOURNAL OF THE RIGHT HONORABLE
# SIR JOSEPH BANKS, Baronet <note>original: "Bart."</note>, Knight of the Bath <note>original: "K.B."</note>, President of the Royal Society <note>original: "P.R.S."</note>.

## During Captain Cook’s First Voyage in H.M.S. Endeavour, in 1768–71, to Tierra del Fuego <note>original: "Terra del Fuego"</note>, Tahiti <note>original: "Otahite"</note>, New Zealand, Australia, the Dutch East Indies, etc.

## Edited by Sir JOSEPH D. HOOKER, Fellow of the Royal Society <note>original: "F.R.S."</note>.

->With Portraits and Charts. Octavo <note>original: "8vo"</note>, 17 shillings <note>original: "s."</note> net.<-

*NATURE.*—“This journal, which now sees the light after varying changes in fortune <note>original: "vicissitudes"</note>, will take its rightful place on our bookshelves by the side of Darwin’s ‘Voyage of the Beagle’ and Moseley’s ‘Challenger Notes’ as one of the classics of scientific travel. Sir Joseph Hooker, in realizing a hope he has held, as he tells us, since he was a boy, adds another to the many services he has rendered to science by presenting to us this journal in the delightful form it has assumed under his editing. . . . As a narrative, the journal is full of charm. It comes before us, old as it is, with all the freshness of a first impression.”

*DAILY CHRONICLE.*—“This journal—and we only wish we had more space to quote from it—belongs to that class of literature which never grows old or out of fashion, but will retain a human as well as a scientific interest to the end of time.”

*STANDARD.*—“The diary will have a permanent interest because of the vivid picture it draws of regions which previously civilized races either had not visited, or, at any rate, had not stayed long enough to influence.”

*TIMES.*—“Probably many will be grateful to Sir Joseph Hooker for giving them an excuse to re-read the story in the rich and interesting pages of Sir Joseph Banks’ journal.”

*MORNING POST.*—“The editor of this volume has performed his work in a way that deserves high praise <note>original: "calls for high commendation"</note>. By careful <note>original: "judicious"</note> selection, he has produced a work that will be widely appreciated as an absorbing book of travels, and will also have a peculiar attraction for all who concern themselves with the progress of scientific investigation."

*LEEDS MERCURY.*—“This book is as interesting as any recent work of travel which we have encountered, and it throws light, often of an unexpected kind, on the incidents and progress of early exploration in the Pacific.”

*ATHENÆUM.*—“Naturalists and literary men have now to thank Sir Joseph Hooker, the grandson of Mr. Dawson Turner, for saving <note>original: "rescuing"</note> this most interesting record from being forgotten <note>original: "oblivion"</note>, and for enabling us to place it side by side with Cook’s own journal.”

->MACMILLAN AND CO., LTD., LONDON.<-

### FOURTH EDITION, with a Supplementary Chapter on the ARMENIAN QUESTION.

# TRANSCAUCASIA AND ARARAT:

->Being Notes of a Holiday Tour in the Autumn of 1876.<-

## By JAMES BRYCE,

->Author of "The Holy Roman Empire," "The American Commonwealth," etc.<-

->With an Engraving and a Colored Map.<-

->Extra crown octavo <note>A book size approximately 5.25 by 8 inches.</note>, 8 shillings and 6 pence net <note>Approximately 42.5 pence in decimal currency; a significant sum in the late 19th century.</note>.<-

*DAILY NEWS.* — "To that delightful travel book, the author has now added a supplementary chapter giving the history of the last 'Twenty Years of the Armenian Question.' It is a chapter of modern history which Mr. Bryce has special, and perhaps unique, qualifications for writing. . . . He is a historian who possesses both brilliant talents <note>original: "parts"</note> and an impartial temperament."

*WESTMINSTER GAZETTE.* — "We trust, however, that this chapter will be widely read and studied. Mr. Bryce, with the experienced hand of a historian, identifies the key <note>original: "salient"</note> points of the situation during the past two decades and groups them in a manner that reveals at a glance the incriminating <note>original: "damning"</note> facts as far as the Great Powers and the Sultan are concerned."

*SPEAKER.* — "Has long since earned its right to be considered one of the most delightful books in the delightful genre to which it belongs. . . . It is because Mr. Bryce, in this supplementary chapter, gives us what is—so far as we know—the most precise, connected, and complete sketch of the origin and history of the Armenian question in its modern aspect that we give a double welcome to this new edition of an old friend."

*GUARDIAN.* — "To the new edition of his delightful tour in Transcaucasia in the autumn of 1876, Mr. Bryce has added a chapter on 'The Recent History of the Armenian Question.' As a statement of facts it is excellent, and, although we do not entirely agree with Mr. Bryce in his conclusions, they are suggested <note>original: "indicated"</note> rather than stated; they have not been allowed to bias <note>original: "colour"</note> the narrative of the events that have made the last two years memorable even in the history <note>original: "annals"</note> of Turkish oppression."

*SCOTSMAN.* — "Mr. Bryce's 'Transcaucasia and Ararat' is deservedly one of the classics of modern travel. But the book has an interest beyond that which it possesses as a narrative of journeys and mountain climbs in an interesting region of the world. It deals with races, places, and political questions which have recently been brought <note>original: "thrust"</note> prominently to the world's attention by terrible events."

->MACMILLAN AND CO., LTD., LONDON.<-

# New Books on Ethnology.

## THE BUDDHIST PRAYING WHEEL:

A collection of material concerning the symbols of the wheel and circular movements in custom and religious ritual. By WILLIAM SIMPSON, R.I., M.R.A.S., F.R.G.S., Honorary Associate of the R.I.B.A. <note>Royal Institute of British Architects</note>. With numerous illustrations by the author. Demy octavo <note>A book size approximately 5.5 by 8.75 inches</note>, 10 shillings net.

> *DAILY NEWS.*—"This is a most curious subject, treated by Mr. Simpson with a depth and variety of learning far beyond what one would find in nine hundred and ninety-nine out of a thousand critics."
> *TIMES.*—"A very interesting account, based on personal observation, of the well-known instrument of worship and ritual used chiefly among the Buddhists of Tibet."
> *PALL MALL GAZETTE.*—"Mr. William Simpson's scholarly and interesting work. . . . His theories are most striking and educational."

## THE SACRED TREE,

->Or the Tree in Religion and Myth. By MRS. J. HENRY PHILPOT. Illustrated. Octavo, 8 shillings and 6 pence net.<-

## THE GOLDEN BOUGH.

A Study in Comparative Religion. By J. G. FRAZER, M.A., Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. Two Volumes, octavo, 28 shillings.

> The *SATURDAY REVIEW* says:—"There is no doubt that the clarity and logic of his work give it a most convincing quality. Mr. Frazer belongs to the new school of religious researchers who begin at the opposite end from the old starting point. Until quite recently, mythologists began with the 'high gods' of established official, priestly, and literary religions. These they explained as well as they could, chiefly by studying the origins <note>original: "etymologies"</note> of their names. The new plan is to begin with the remains of ancient rituals which survive in peasant practices and tribal <note>original: "savage"</note> customs. The theory <note>original: "hypothesis"</note> is that the peasant has changed very little in his traditional practices from rites that were old even before Homer and Hesiod established the standard beliefs <note>original: "orthodoxy"</note> for the Greeks. His book is clear and entertaining, logical and learned. It is probably the best work on a specific aspect of early religion to appear since Mr. Tylor's *Primitive Culture*."
>
> The *ACADEMY* says:—"His reading is exceptionally broad, covering not only the standard authorities, ancient and modern, but also including numerous obscure specialized studies <note>original: "monographs"</note> on the local folklore of all countries. He is not merely learned <note>original: "erudite"</note>, but capable and clever; so that his book, presented as a first installment of a much larger work on primitive religion, will certainly place its author in the front rank of living mythologists. . . . It must be frankly acknowledged that we are indebted to him for an important work, which calls attention to an aspect of primitive religion that has been previously neglected."
>
> The *PALL MALL GAZETTE* says:—"We may as well begin by saying outright that Mr. Frazer has written a great book—a book worthy to rank alongside Tylor's *Primitive Culture* and Herbert Spencer's *Principles of Sociology* as one of the main foundations of the new science of human belief and social systems <note>original: "institutions"</note>. What is even better, not only has he given us many ideas untouched by either of them, but he has also performed the valuable service of compelling us to reconsider and reverse some of our most cherished convictions. His work is an admirable intellectual stimulant <note>original: "mental rouser"</note>. . . . It is learned, clever, sharp, logical, and almost always convincing."

### MACMILLAN AND CO., LTD., LONDON.

# ROUND THE YEAR

## A SERIES OF SHORT NATURE STUDIES

### By Professor L. C. Miall, F.R.S. <note>Fellow of the Royal Society</note>

->With illustrations, primarily by A. R. Hammond, F.L.S. <note>Fellow of the Linnean Society</note><-
->Crown octavo <note>a standard book size</note>, 5 shillings<-

*GUARDIAN*—
> "I wish that all books on subjects classified as scientific were written in this pleasant style—a style conveying human sympathy and the strong desire to awaken in other minds a spirit of healthy investigation into the wonders and mysteries of the things around us."

*SPEAKER*—
> "It is a charming book, written with the greatest simplicity by a man of the highest scientific achievements; it therefore possesses undeniable merits."

*SATURDAY REVIEW*—
> "Although there is not a single dull passage in the book, the insight and research shown are remarkable, and none of the many subjects can be described as being treated superficially."

*PALL MALL GAZETTE*—
> "We have rarely encountered a more fascinating book for curious young minds; it is one in a thousand."

*RURAL WORLD*—
> "A delightful companion, and we doubt if a more suitable gift book will be published this season."

*MANCHESTER GUARDIAN*—
> "Though intended especially for young observers, the adult reader will find much that is both useful and interesting if they are, as the author says, someone who cares for 'live natural history.'"

*DAILY NEWS*—
